An AD&D adventure set in the Forgotten Realms. The Grandaddy of all isometric (top down) open world RPGs. The Gold Standard from 1998 by which all others of its type continue to be weighed, measured and found wanting. And while it's nice to see a resurgence of newer titles embracing this classic genre, Baldur's Gate is still yet to be dethroned as far as I'm concerned by anything that has come along since in terms of gameplay, story and immersion.
Although the graphics were revolutionary for its time, they're obviously well dated by today's standards. But once you get drawn into its story, colorful NPCs and atmosphere its technical limitations just fade away and it still holds up just fine.
Kudos to Beamdog for bringing this classic into the modern era of PC gaming.

I was so hyped for this game. I love exploration and I don't like horror games so I thought this was a good choice for me, given that the game is not incredibly scary (it is still a bit scary for me, but in a good way). Sadly, it didn't meet any of my expectations.
TECHNICAL:
The game looks nice enough. I was so looking forward to a game built and developed on UE4. We have UE4 since years and nobody using it. Unfortunately it is unbelievably poorly optimized. With a 970, it stutters like hell even at 1920x1080 on medium details. Framerate goes from 35-37 fps to 60+ fps for no reason. Shadows glitch all the time.
GAMEPLAY:
Lot of exploration that turns into an extremely boring and long and slow walk. You can fast travel but only to camps you already visited. You can sprint, but only briefly because it's cold and you get tired. If you exaggerate, you have to wait even more because your sight is so blurred you can't see anything so it is even worse. The scenery is all the same, the map system is quite weird because the map does not actually (in my opinion) reproduce exactly every little cranny and path that you can take, making you disoriented. I was expecting a wonderful mix between snowy and icy spots, lost woods, abandoned buildings in small villages.....but no, the whole point in the game is to run (walk) around like crazy and finding some 'hot' spots that will be shown on the map.
Miasmata did that well, with the whole triangulation system. In this game exploration is just hit and miss and breaks immersion.
I hate badly optimized games....there is no reason why the game should run this bad on my system and the developers were just too lazy to even investigate and release some performance improving patch.
So, the game is nothing particularly good, plus it is for sure not well enough optimized, so I don't recommend it.

Overall, this game is good. It's not great, but it's not awful either. I'm only giving it a thumbs up because there is no middle rating.
The setting of this game is decent. It's kind of a victorian steampunk-meets magic sort of setting. It's been done before, but Dishonored kind of handles it in a different way than say, Arcanum or something like that does it. There's also a rat plague going on and a mysterious figure named the Outsider who appears to be the source of all the world's magic. So there's definitely alot of interesting nuggets of lore in the game. The problem is that that's all there is, just nuggets. The game focuses mostly on the gameplay insread of the story and setting. I would have liked to see the world and lore be more developed, since the game does have a good foundation upon which to build. The developers claim it's completely immersive which feels like an exxageraton because the world is so poorly developed. I would say it's just, "meh".
Which brings me to the plot. Just like the setting, there's a GREAT foundation for a legendary story. Like I said, there's this crazy rat plague going on, a mysterious and mystical "outsider", etc. But what's such a buzzkill is that these things are SUPER important to the story, but we never really find out much about them. By the end of the game, we don't learn where the rat plague comes from or what's up with the outsider. There's just so many really cool plot threads that get totally shoved to the side and ignored, in favor of a generic assassination/betrayal plot. I really don't understand developers who focus on really mundane plots instead of the real interesting (and more important to the world) stuff. The ending feels like a wasted opportunity to do something really memorable and cool, but I'll probably just forget this one. The ending is really vague and generic, it doesn't feel as if what I have done had any importance. And as far as I can tell, it really doesn't matter what choices you made throughout the game like the developers claim. There's also a really cliche twist in the game which tries to copy Bioshock, but fails to have the same impact because they didn't make you care about the characters.
Which brings me to my next analysis, character progression. This is also heavily inspired by Bioshock as well. It's basically sword in your right hand and magic spell, ranged weapon, or special item in your left hand. Only, this system has even less complexity and customization than Bioshock. For one thing, there are very few spells in the game (about 4 I believe) and each only upgrades once. There are 4 passive improvements as well, each only upgrading once. This system is really shallow and a tad boring. Most of the time you can cruise through this game without much difficulty simply by spamming the teleport spell (which is utterly broken and OP). In fact, I'd say it's the most important ability in this game. Secondly, this game heavily favors combat over stealth. The vast majority of the abilities, upgrades, and items are clearly designed for combat. Grenades, pistols, lethal crossbow bolts, spike traps, spells that kill, sword upgrades, etc. The only two things useful to stealth oriented characters are sleep darts which are very limited, and the teleport spell. The possession spell is designed for stealth but is a bit clumsy to use for various reasons. So pretty much if you're playing a stealth character, upgrading is really boring because there's nothing that can help you.
The next point is gameplay. The gameplay is only mediocre. Stealth is rather boring because as I already mentioned, most of the upgrades and items in the game favor combat. Stealth gameplay basically consists of spamming teleport to move from cover to cover and using sleep darts if you get caught. It's super hard as well because you have a lot less options than in combat. The other flaw is that there is no non-lethal abilities for combat. A shock stick to replace your sword so you can merely knock guys out in combat would be nice. Gas grenades, spells that incapicate but don't kill, etc. The gameplay is divided into two binaries, stealth non-violent, and combat violent. You can use some stealth with a lethal playthrough but it is limited in effectiveness. But like I said, this game clearly favors the combat approach. Which is a shame because it sets up killing as evil and gives you a worse ending, and non-lethal which is good and gives you a happier ending. This is obviously a boring and kindergarten view of morality as well as choice and consequence.
So overall, this game doesn't live up to the claims the devs make. It does everything absolutely mediocre and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ With the game being so short, you would think they could put more effort into it. I can't recomend it for the full price, but it's not an awful way to spend a night if you've got five bucks.

I was starving. I did not have enough food. I was getting tired, I didn't bring my bedroll. I had too much equipment, yet it was too precious to drop. I had a rifle and 6 rounds. I saw a deer in the distance. I shot one time, missed. Cursing to myself, I missed again. Everyone says the third time is the charm and it is. I shot the deer and took all its meat, leaving the guts and fur behind, for at the moment, it was dark. There were wolves in the area, and I knew the smell of fresh meat attracted them. I couldn't sprint, I just walked very slowly. I prayed to the gods, hoping that I would survive, somehow. There was a blizzard and fog surrounded me. I just had a sliver of hope. I don't know where this came from, I just hoped. It was a weird feeling, one of determitation or maybe, survival?
It was dark and I finally get to the  farmstead. I go in and sleep a bit. Then I cook the venison. I eat the fatty venison, filling my stomach. I then go to sleep and wake up. I see a light filtering in through the window, thinking that it was morning. I go outside and what  I am met with is the prettiest thing I have ever seen. I stare in astonishment at the Northern Lights. I gaze at it, like a child hoping for something. I look around and the landscape is covered with a bright purple and green. After a day of suffering, I was met with a beautiful gift.

UPDATED:  I changed my review to recommended since the sandbox mode is fantastic and well worth the price if you enjoy this kind of game.
I've been playing this game for a couple years now through its development in sandbox mode and have really enjoyed it.  Yes, some of the mechanics are a bit crude and yes, it can be quite tedious at times - but I like the simplicity.  I also like that it doesn't fetishize guns like a lot of other survival games.  I'm also from, and live on, the island where the game is developed (and takes place... kind of...), and I just really wanted it to turn into something great.  It has a fantastic foundation.
Throughout the past couple years, I've always been impressed that it has had constant updates that have made huge improvements to gameplay, ui, and content.  However, within the past year I guess resources have been shifted to story mode and some of the frustrating issues of the game have just... remained.  In sandbox mode, as you progress from surviving a couple of days to multiple weeks, these issues really start to stand out.
The meat issue.  A deer will yeild 10kg (22lbs) of meat.  Okay - that's reasonable.  But buddy will gobble that away in just two days.  I mean, come on.  Thats like 15,000 calories - it should last at least a week.  If you could store things outside in the cold...
You can't store food in the cold (maybe they've fixed this now?).  That's a pretty fundamental aspect of wilderness survival, especially long-term.  There should be a robust system for caching food - hangs, boxes, etc.  If you can't stockpile, then what's even the point?
Wolves.  I get it - geomagnetic blah, blah, blah.  They're all hopped up on goofballs and want to kill everything.  But if they're going to be such a central part of the game, then maybe don't make them so one-dimensional.  Vary their behaviour or something... That's one of the most terrifying and dangerous things about animals in the wild - they're unpredictable. These things are just robots.  They get boring really quick, and the keyboard-mashing defence mechanic is super lame.
First-Aid.  Bad mechanic. Unintuitive. It was much more user-friendly before.
I could really get into it and nitpick, but those are the most frustrating issues with the survival aspect.  "Oh, that's not so bad!" you say?  Well it isn't.  I think those things could be fixed.  And may even be fixed in the future.  And even despite these issues, I really enjoy sandbox mode.  I like that I can sink a bunch of hours into a character, become really invested in them over the course of weeks, only to make some stupid, miniscule mistake and unceremoniously die.  That feels super real to me. So why the thumbs down? Two words:
STORY MODE.
Holy mother of god the story mode of this game is ♥♥♥♥ing horrible.  This is the videogame equivalent of The Room.  The most amateur writing I have ever experienced.  At least with The Room it's funny.  This is not.  It's cringey.  I've never rolled my eyes so much.  I want to give contructive feedback, but god ♥♥♥♥in DAMN.  Seriously, get an editor. Please. Get. An. Editor.
I think maybe an alien wrote this - something that doesn't understand human logic and emotion, because the dialogue totally illogical, melodramatic, lacking motivation... Characters feel completely undeveloped and say things that don't make any sense in the context of the conversation.  Everytime a dialogue sequence occurs I have to take my headphones off and go do something else until it's over.   Every character is some goofy trope, which totally goes against the atmosphere of the rest of the game.  Why is Gimli the dwarf in this♥♥♥♥♥♥?  Why does the old woman have a cloth over her eyes??  Have you ever met a blind person??  Have you ever met a person??
The whole 'doing missions for people in order to progress' mechanic.  After the first person you encounter, (the old crone - ooo someone read Joseph Campbell...), the whole bit of running errands for people gets super stale.  The part about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ old bear who APPEARS IN FRONT OF THE DOOR as soon as the mission starts and then, since Gimli gives you all this bad advice on how to kill it, you have to just get mauled a million ♥♥♥♥ing times until you can unload enough rounds into it... And that's the way you're supposed to do it.  The whole thing is just so poorly and hastily hashed together - it really feels like a pre-release version (which is what I thought it was when I first started into it - I actually thought it was placeholder dialogue and animations).
Additionally, there are absolutely no segues into story sequences.  When Gimli gets attacked by the bear, it's just suddenly happening.  I thought the game was playing the wrong sequence or something since there was no transition from gameplay into cutscene.  Likewise when you're in the dam and the convict(?) appears.  I walked into a room and suddenly I was hurt.  But there was no cue.  No audio, no animation...  No context to tell you what was going on.  Which might actually work to the story's advantage if the game was more polished.  And then you're in another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue scene.  (Seriously - to the writer of this stuff: you REALLY needed to workshop this script before it got locked down).
One last thing - to the developers.  Ya'll, if you're going to make something regional, you've got to respect the region.  You've taken a lot of inspiration from the Island for sure, but you fail to express it in any sort of nuanced way.  In sandbox, it felt pretty good - rooted enough to be interesting, but abstracted enough not to feel forced.  Now that I've experienced story mode though... damn...  I'm not even going to get into that...
In conclusion: The sandbox mode is great.  It's meditative.  You'll play for hours planning out your next moves, stashing gear, exploring, contemplating, wandering from town to town looting.  And then suddenly you'll make a mistake, get stuck in a storm, attacked by a wolf, or whatever and you'll have to think fast or die.  I love that.  So play the sandbox and the challenges and enjoy them.  But do not go near the story mode.  It will ruin the entire experience.

I enjoyed it but I enjoy immersive horror like this game was designed to provide.
A bit of advice for interested players:
- The order you collect notes doesn't matter, they will unlock the journal/article entries sequentially regardless of which order you find the note items in the world. I started over once because I thought maybe I was getting the notes in a 'bad/confusing' order, but it turns out it makes no difference.
- The map you have lies in a few cases. There are a number of places where the map shows a viable path that are actually blocked. This is somewhat realistic, since the blocks were usually things like rockslides and such that would not be reflected on the map if they happened recently, but it did mean a lot of trudging along routes that were ultimately dead ends.
- While there are mechanics that influence whether you die, I had a few occasions where I felt like I died randomly without any clear reason. This didn't detract me much, since I just loaded back in at the last note node, but I can imagine it irritating some players.
- Performance is rough. My PC is moderately high end and I was regularly getting 15fps or even lower in places.
The cautious above aside, it was a very immersive environment, visually striking with very well done, chilling audio.

Kholat is an horror-adventure/exploration game based on the Dyatlov Pass Incident. The tragic and mysterious event involved nine Russian hikers who ventured out to the Kholat Syakhl mountains in high hopes to climb its daunting size but, unfortunately, met an untimely end. The reasoning behind their deaths is still unsolved to this day.
What I Enjoyed:
Walk in the park - Despite the dreadful and mournful wintery setting, the game visuals are at its highest peak, creating a lot of realism and utilizing it to present a haunting experience that will surely leave players’ skins crawling. Every sway of the frosted pine trees to the brisk, snowy winds are so evident in detail that it only furthers the fear players will endure when embarking on the Dyatlov Pass trail. The title fully optimizes the immersiveness in the game by adding stunning imagery as well as sounds that results in an unpleasant yet necessary experience to grasp the terror that had befallen the nine mountaineers.
Storytelling - The game dwells deep into laying the foundation of the Dyatlov Pass incident by relishing players who have no prior knowledge to the horrific events that took place; it provides basic information while foretelling theorized depictions of what resulted on that eventful night. The story paints grotesque imagery at the beginning which hooks the player off the bat and opts for an interesting playthrough.
Simple is best - The gameplay mechanics is not meant to detract from the story or the exploration by keeping the game style simplistic, which allows it to not be the focal point of the game. While possessing the generic run, zoom, and flashlight commands, the game also introduces players to a map and compass that are unlike other games’ versions as this maps does not record your current location. Instead, this special map reveals conspiring events and potential savepoints in disguise as campfires.
What I Disliked:
Square one - The difficulty appears when players are not utilizing the map and compass effectively, which results in endless walking/running around the same dead tree stump or the same creepy, grinning totem poll. To prevent this, you must understand how to get to the desired location by locating the set of coordinates written on your map. This, unfortunately, requires some map navigational skills and proper compass usage as well as memorizing key landscape structure. Overtime, those who are prone to stubbornness (like myself) who are using these available tools prove more as an annoyance and tedious.
Turtle’s pace -  The threats in this game seems to be minimal at times. As the game implements a running command that ends so sporadically, it offers a nerve-wrecking sensation when pursued by predators but will frustrate you when simply try to find an unexplored area. This results in a whole playthrough the almost appears to go at a turtle’s pace. Players must use the running command spaciously and in spurts or risk exerting the character’s stamina. Sadly, the recovering time is longer than the running duration so plan your actions accordingly.
Conclusion:
The story of Kholat brought me through an unnerving adventure, successfully making me question every sudden sound I heard. The game did a wonderful job with the atmosphere but the endless roaming sometimes made the game feel like a walking simulation instead of a horrific adventure. Despite that, I really enjoyed the time I’ve had playing this game and found myself lost in its storytelling.

I have no idea why the game was so inticing when watching videos on YouTube, perhaps it's the "cooperative" nature of watching someone play. This game, as others have pointed out, is truly open world. Don't get me wrong - open world is fine for some games where you discover new equipment, quests, and characters. Kholat does none of these. You simply walk around and look at things. Again - don't think this can't be done well (look at the excellent Dear Ester), but Khloat simply mysteriously lacks atmosphere. Real life mystery? Check. Snowstorm? Check. Nighttime? Check. Monsters? Check. Yet...this game makes you feel no dread. You don't have to hide and you don't have to get your character to safety. You simply walk.
On the bright side, as I said earlier the intro video is a good summation of the real life mystery and the visuals of the game are pretty great. I would recommend Kholat only as a novelty, or to someone who truly, truly wants to play this type of game.

This is one of the most complex games of Solitaire ever invented.
Play involves "drawing a card"- you "open a room", which may have a number of special properties, including suitability for installing resource generators, getting resources for free, etc.
This, in turn, involves drawing further "cards"- whether any monsters spawn from "cards" you have chosen not to "put into your deck" (using Dust to "power them up").
So managing your "deck" is essentially how you play this game; the "heroes", their levels and gear are mere mitigation used to hedge risk.
This sounds OK in theory, but in practice, this game is very poorly balanced, and due to severely penalizing modding (it's literally not allowed to set the difficulty upwards if you mod the game), it's never going to be properly balanced by modders and is therefore chock-full of newbie traps, poorly-designed difficulty curves and bad design decisions, like weapons that don't scale well with monsters, random item drops that don't scale, heroes that are basically just statistical trash, shops that frequently don't sell anything you actually want, regardless of cost, a "wit" system that's supposed to boost production but barely gives enough to be worthwhile with practically all of the heroes with the Operate skill (and items that can give it are worthless, since practically none of the non-Operator heroes have enough "wit" to matter), etc., etc., etc.
Worst feature?  You literally cannot get rid of party members if you want to trade up, short of suiciding them, with potentially disasterous consequences.  You meet a half-dozen other folks, but you cannot have them join you in any way.  It's a game design decision that makes me shake my head; the choice of whether to stretch one's Food to cover more people, but possibly get stretched too thin and die due to having a weak party, would have enriched the game.  But I suspect that the "4 is the limit" aspect was hard-coded into the UI long before "you'll recruit heroes you find randomly"- it feels like it, anyhow.
Basically, this is a messy experimental project where I think the developers lost track of the statistical meaning of their design decisions quite early in the process and, due to their absurd penalty on modding, it's unlikely to ever get polished and fixed by the player community, which is a real shame, because the central idea ("make the world's most complicated Solitaire and make it look like a RTS / Tower Defense game to get gamers to buy it") was very interesting indeed, and in theory, this should be a very good game.
But as it stands, this won't stay on my hard-drive for very long; once I figured out that certain combos of heroes work all right, and realized that runs are essentially pure RNG and involve very little actual skill, beyond managing the "cards" and doing statistical guesswork, and that more than half of the "upgrades" and "defenses" were basically worthless... well, I feel like this was a clever Idea that arrived half-baked, wasn't ever really addressed at a deep level by the developers and can't get fixed by modders, not that it would matter a lot at this late date.
It's too bad, really; this is a game where most of the problems are clearly fixable, but won't ever get fixed.

The player will follow the story of twin Assassins Jacob and Evie Frye. Basically, their plan throughout the entire game is to bring down the Templars, led by Crawford Starrick, in London. Alongside this road, you will meet a number of historical characters you'll recognise, such as Karl Marx, Charles Dickens, Frederick Abberline, Queen Victoria and more.
Jacob's Story:
The story is build up in such a way that in every sequence you will hunt one of the Templars controlling London and at the end of the sequence kill them, with the ultimate goal to kill baddie-in-charge Crawford Starrick. The good thing about that is that you will be busy at all times. The bad part, however, is that it's quite bland, there's not much to it. It feels like a checklist of Templars, and you'll just eliminate everyone on that list one by one, without much thought to it. You also don't really get to see much of the bad things these so-called Templars are said to do. Of course there's an exception, but since all the Templars only appear one sequence, the awesomeness this particular Templar (going by the name of Maxwell Roth) has, is only brief.
Evie's story:
Being concerned about the Templars getting hold of a First-Civilisation artifact called the Shroud™ of Eden™, she tries to get the Shroud from the Templars, killing everyone in her way.
Ending:
The gameplay in this game is great.
Riding carriages:
It looks great, it feels great, it IS great.
With plenty of different carriages to ride, in different colours as well, this piece of gameplay is perfect. You can hijack any carriage, drive any carriage, be on top of carriages, be in some carriages to hide, shoot the horses of enemie carriages to see the carriage flip. Also I like being able to step out of the carriage at the side I want to step out of it. Driving the carriage sometimes feels a little clumsy, which is perfect considering that carriageriding at high-speed IS clumsy.
New "Gadgets":
Combat:
You can select 3 different main weapons for in combat, being a cane-sword, a kukri knife and brass knuckles. They all essentially work the same, but have different animations and visuals.
The combat itself is the known attack/counter/stun principle, with the addition of a Multi-Kill sequence. The Multi-Kill sequence is a short animation that you can activate once two or more enemies are very low health. Activating it, however, is clumsy. Often have I been frustrated by it not activating when two enemies are low health, or activating only for two enemies when four enemies are low health. When it activates, though, it is quite nice. Aside from that, the combat flows like a river.
Stealth:
Not much changed. Standing in a group of people that totally don't look like you belong with them will still hide you from your foes, and enemies still can't look through walls, so that's great. However, there is the addition of the so-called stealth mode, which makes your Assassin put on the Assasin hood and makes him/her crouch, sometimes looking really dumb... but it works, so that's nice.
Assassinating one works the same way it always has, so I'm not elaborating on that. An assassination mission however, has gotten the addition of optional objectives that either make assassinating your target easier, or unlock a special assassination opportunity. It works great, enhances the replayabilty and it's good that you don't need to do them.
Loading Screen:
You are able to run around in the loading screen again, which is better than to stare at a black screen, so there's a plus.
For anyone expecting this game's customisation to be anything like Unity: it's not. There's not a whole lot of customisation.
There are 3 main weapons, as mentioned afore, with each of them having different variant that look differently and have other stats in terms of damage and so. Same goes for the pistol and the assassin gauntlet.
You cannot see your weapons unless in combat, which is kind of a bummer. No cane-walking in London guys...
There are some outfits to choose from, but in my opinion, a lot of them look like they originate from a crappy steampunk convention and I think they don't at all look realistically, so I never changed my outfit much.
There are some buyable (with in-game currency) and unlockable colours to your outfits, making some parts of your outfit have that colour. Only one colour can be selected at a time.
Besides the main outfit, Jacob has a belt, and Evie has a cloak, which functions like a cape like Ezio's (although Evie doesn't put the cloak around her like Ezio does when being idle). There are plenty of variant for the belts and capes, but once again, most of them don't really fit in.
Walking around with a hood on, without crouching like you escaped from the asylum in the game, is sadly not possible (there's a glitch on the Thames that does enable this, though). Instead, in normal stance, Evie walks around without anything on her head, whereas Jacob has headwear: a cap for the first outfit, and a top-hat for every other outfit. Jacob's top-hat has one huge problem though, it has a red band around it which doesn't change colour when you change the colour of your outfit. So unless you dye your outfit red, it doesn't look good.
London looks amazing and is very detailled.
I myself didn't like the colours used in the game, so I resorted to making a SweetFX preset for the game to give London more of a IMO Londonish atmosphere I like. Aside from colour, the graphics are very good.
Clothing physics are at a new best, but they are on PC locked on 30FPS. Setting it to 60FPS is however easy to do, just google a tutorial for that. (Note that I normally don't really look at FPS, but seeing one 30FPS element in a 60FPS environment is just cringy).

It's a Zachtronics game. If you've played other Zachtronics games (Ironclad Tactics doesn't count) then you know what you're getting into and therefore don't need to read any of these reviews.
If you're new to Zachtronics puzzle games and are interested, START HERE! Opus Magnum is the most accessible one by far as it doesn't punish players with cost, cycle, or area restrictions. You can create whatever wacky thrown-together solution you want and as long as it works you're good. After that's done, there's the kicker: making it a
solution. Optimizing a solution is the true meat of all Zachtronics puzzlers and is what provides the games with so much replayability. When you complete a puzzle you can see how well you compare against all others who have completed it, informing you of how far you have to go.
Game length: Maybe ~20-30 hrs if you're rushing, but who would do that?
Puzzle difficulty: Easy to Excruciating (varies on puzzle
solution type)
Replayability: Just... one.. less... cycle...
Actual game length: 100s of hours, there's a bonus chapter, journal puzzles, and the Steam Workshop for more puzzles than your poor cerebrum could ever handle
Final rating: A lump of dead brain matter / 10

This is an excellent game. What I like most is that I don't have to be a computer programmer or engineer to be able to play it. You do need a decent sense of spatial awareness, but at least it's only in 2 dimensions. I've played a few other Zachtronics games like Spacechem and Infinifactory and I inevitably had to give up relatively early (20% progress or so) because they got impossibly hard. It was like juggling Rubik's cubes and solving them while calculating the trajectory of a space flight to Mars. The possibility space just kept expanding until it was an order of magnitude beyond my abilities. Opus Magnum leaves it up to the player, not the game, to decide when they're done. If you just want to unlock the next set of puzzles, there's usually an obvious but terribly inefficient method of solving the current one.
Elegant solutions are their own reward. It's a great feeling to go back to an older puzzle with new insight and improve all 3 metrics that you're graded on: cost, area, and cycles. There are just enough tools to give you the creative freedom to try different approaches, but not so many that you become overwhelmed and unable to get started.
I don't know what else to say other than this is a clever game that makes me feel smart, but doesn't just give me that satisfaction with no effort. I haven't looked at other people's creations yet, but I bet that would make me feel dumb again.

If you liked Spacechem, you should most certainly like this game.  In some ways its "easier" than Spacechem in that you have a much larger puzzle area, but trying to optimize your solutions down to be fast, or efficient, or small can still be quite challening.

UPDATED:  I changed my review to recommended since the sandbox mode is fantastic and well worth the price if you enjoy this kind of game.
I've been playing this game for a couple years now through its development in sandbox mode and have really enjoyed it.  Yes, some of the mechanics are a bit crude and yes, it can be quite tedious at times - but I like the simplicity.  I also like that it doesn't fetishize guns like a lot of other survival games.  I'm also from, and live on, the island where the game is developed (and takes place... kind of...), and I just really wanted it to turn into something great.  It has a fantastic foundation.
Throughout the past couple years, I've always been impressed that it has had constant updates that have made huge improvements to gameplay, ui, and content.  However, within the past year I guess resources have been shifted to story mode and some of the frustrating issues of the game have just... remained.  In sandbox mode, as you progress from surviving a couple of days to multiple weeks, these issues really start to stand out.
The meat issue.  A deer will yeild 10kg (22lbs) of meat.  Okay - that's reasonable.  But buddy will gobble that away in just two days.  I mean, come on.  Thats like 15,000 calories - it should last at least a week.  If you could store things outside in the cold...
You can't store food in the cold (maybe they've fixed this now?).  That's a pretty fundamental aspect of wilderness survival, especially long-term.  There should be a robust system for caching food - hangs, boxes, etc.  If you can't stockpile, then what's even the point?
Wolves.  I get it - geomagnetic blah, blah, blah.  They're all hopped up on goofballs and want to kill everything.  But if they're going to be such a central part of the game, then maybe don't make them so one-dimensional.  Vary their behaviour or something... That's one of the most terrifying and dangerous things about animals in the wild - they're unpredictable. These things are just robots.  They get boring really quick, and the keyboard-mashing defence mechanic is super lame.
First-Aid.  Bad mechanic. Unintuitive. It was much more user-friendly before.
I could really get into it and nitpick, but those are the most frustrating issues with the survival aspect.  "Oh, that's not so bad!" you say?  Well it isn't.  I think those things could be fixed.  And may even be fixed in the future.  And even despite these issues, I really enjoy sandbox mode.  I like that I can sink a bunch of hours into a character, become really invested in them over the course of weeks, only to make some stupid, miniscule mistake and unceremoniously die.  That feels super real to me. So why the thumbs down? Two words:
STORY MODE.
Holy mother of god the story mode of this game is ♥♥♥♥ing horrible.  This is the videogame equivalent of The Room.  The most amateur writing I have ever experienced.  At least with The Room it's funny.  This is not.  It's cringey.  I've never rolled my eyes so much.  I want to give contructive feedback, but god ♥♥♥♥in DAMN.  Seriously, get an editor. Please. Get. An. Editor.
I think maybe an alien wrote this - something that doesn't understand human logic and emotion, because the dialogue totally illogical, melodramatic, lacking motivation... Characters feel completely undeveloped and say things that don't make any sense in the context of the conversation.  Everytime a dialogue sequence occurs I have to take my headphones off and go do something else until it's over.   Every character is some goofy trope, which totally goes against the atmosphere of the rest of the game.  Why is Gimli the dwarf in this♥♥♥♥♥♥?  Why does the old woman have a cloth over her eyes??  Have you ever met a blind person??  Have you ever met a person??
The whole 'doing missions for people in order to progress' mechanic.  After the first person you encounter, (the old crone - ooo someone read Joseph Campbell...), the whole bit of running errands for people gets super stale.  The part about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ old bear who APPEARS IN FRONT OF THE DOOR as soon as the mission starts and then, since Gimli gives you all this bad advice on how to kill it, you have to just get mauled a million ♥♥♥♥ing times until you can unload enough rounds into it... And that's the way you're supposed to do it.  The whole thing is just so poorly and hastily hashed together - it really feels like a pre-release version (which is what I thought it was when I first started into it - I actually thought it was placeholder dialogue and animations).
Additionally, there are absolutely no segues into story sequences.  When Gimli gets attacked by the bear, it's just suddenly happening.  I thought the game was playing the wrong sequence or something since there was no transition from gameplay into cutscene.  Likewise when you're in the dam and the convict(?) appears.  I walked into a room and suddenly I was hurt.  But there was no cue.  No audio, no animation...  No context to tell you what was going on.  Which might actually work to the story's advantage if the game was more polished.  And then you're in another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue scene.  (Seriously - to the writer of this stuff: you REALLY needed to workshop this script before it got locked down).
One last thing - to the developers.  Ya'll, if you're going to make something regional, you've got to respect the region.  You've taken a lot of inspiration from the Island for sure, but you fail to express it in any sort of nuanced way.  In sandbox, it felt pretty good - rooted enough to be interesting, but abstracted enough not to feel forced.  Now that I've experienced story mode though... damn...  I'm not even going to get into that...
In conclusion: The sandbox mode is great.  It's meditative.  You'll play for hours planning out your next moves, stashing gear, exploring, contemplating, wandering from town to town looting.  And then suddenly you'll make a mistake, get stuck in a storm, attacked by a wolf, or whatever and you'll have to think fast or die.  I love that.  So play the sandbox and the challenges and enjoy them.  But do not go near the story mode.  It will ruin the entire experience.

Dragon Age: Origins is a very personal, high fantasy RPG set in the world of Thedas in the beginning stages of the Fifth Blight. The world feels genuine and raw, steeped in culture and lore-rich history. The first half hour had me completely involved in the storyline (Human Noble) and, compared to the first half hour of this game's successor, Dragon Age: Inquisition, I was left feeling emotional and - most importantly - invested.
The cast of characters (I'm with Alistair, Leliana, Morrigan, Sten, and my beloved Mabari Warhound as of this point) are colourful, extremely diverse, and 100% unique. There is not a single similarity between them, meaning interacting with one to the next isn't as simple as a click of the button on the same dialogue option; they all react differently and regard you as to how YOU react to them. In short, these characters are fully mapped out and as close to realism in terms of natural biological responses as one can get in a video game. I find this system unique and engaging, and I have to consider the characters I'm adventuring with, rather than treat them as the systematic pack mule/tank of other RPGs.
I will honestly admit I generally judge a game for everything from the graphics and soundtrack to the story and the characters. I like good-looking games. I like fluidity, updated graphics, all the bells and whistles. I do also like a game capable of causing me to laugh, cry, fling the controller/keyboard aside in a fit of frustration (with the story, not game mechanics). I like a story I can discuss and think about, and I adore characters who I enjoy exploring alongside and having intricate discussions with. I like a video game to leave an impression on me.
But returning to graphics... I played DA:I first and it is a lovely looking game. I was concerned, prior to playing Origins, I'd be less interested in its lackluster appearance. I was wrong by a long shot. BioWare poured their heart and soul into DA:O and it shows. I'm thoroughly impressed and I'm looking forward to finishing the game.
*Bonus praise for the multiple beginnings!
(Any nitpicking or instances in the game I didn't like I will address when I've finished the game. I am so far enjoying the experience and want to fully round out my thoughts and feelings about it. I might seem a little biased, but I have only my experience with Inquisition to base Origins against.)

I'll be writing this review mainly directed to people who don't really know much about Dungeons & Dragons or old-school cRPG's.
One of the first games to have branching story paths that actually worked and meant something. Lots of consequence, lots of choices, lots of endings.
The story of the game is very well written and also interesting. If you're willing to read up on the background information a little to get a grasp of what the D&D world is like, particuarly this one, then you'll understand the games story better. Even if you don't read any background information you'll still pick up on it as you play, and you'll still be able to enjoy it.
The first few hours of the game are a little slow and sort of random. During these few hours (about 2-3 hours or so), lots of random things will be thrown at you just to let you practice on how the game works. You'll meet random companions, random attacks, and have some pretty pointless but rewarding side quests. Like I said, these are just to warm you up on the rest of the game.
One of the main points of the game is maintaining a party. You'll meet many companions along your adventure which you can either allow into your party or not. You must watch each players health, weapons, stats, and so on. It sounds complicated when you first read about it, but it's pretty easy once you get used to it. Your companions will get tired, get wounded or their weapons will break. You have to watch out for all of these things and help them out as much as you can. Fortunately for people who have a hard time making characters, you will only have to make your own character (which is the leader of the party) as all other companions will have their own stats and abilities. With that being said, you must know how to use and level up their stats and abilities.
The combat can be a bit tricky at first, especially once your party gets pretty large. You are able to pause the game, point out each individual party member who to attack, then unpause. Having your whole party attack the same enemy at once works on lower level enemies, but as you start to face larger groups of monster and/or more challenging enemies, you have to use strategy to determine how not to get your party instantly killed.
The character creation is quite big for this game. You can chose between a few races, pick between many classes which have their own sub-classes (Such has Cleric/Ranger or Cleric/Thief, etc.) and have quite a bit of stats to level up. You won't be leveling up as easily or quickly as many of todays RPGs. I didn't upgrade my main character until about 2 hours into the game while doing a bunch of side-quests and killing lots of enemies. Leveling up is meant to feel rewarding and having an actual impact when adding points to stats and gaining new abilites.
The world is nicely drawn in this game too. The graphics on the Enhanced Version doesn't look much better than when I played this game years ago, but at least it's in widescreen.
Exploring the world is also a huge point in this game. The world isn't all one seamless level, but instead it's broken up into large sections which usually have other sections within them, such as caves and castles. Most of the places you're allowed to freely enter, but others are restricted.

One of the most epic fantasy role-playing computer games ever created. Based on the ruleset of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons. It can be played like a Diablo style hack'n'slash, but it is more beneficial to use pausing to give orders to your party. Although it can be hard and frusterating at times, once you get used to it, it becomes easier to prepare for major battles so you don't end up having to restart from too far behind. I really cannot recommend this game enough for any fan of a traditional RPG, especially since this one is keeping so true to the original pen and paper.

I have put some time into Project Zomboid, and I saw it through NerdCubed. I was hesitant at first to get the game, because the game is in early access, but the constant updates and quick posts on what they are doing easied me into buying it in the early access state. Project Zomboid is the zombie apocolypse you have been begging for, and I have been begging for. You could go for 7 Days to Die, but there are just different aspects to them that seperate them as a whole. Project Zomboid is akin to gameplay of Cataclysm Dark Days Ahead, where you pick your situation that you are, e.i. the famous Really Bad Day, where you are sick defenseless in the shower and the house is burning down.
At first, Project Zomboid was very bare with what you could do, but it has grown with systems such as the skill system and more crafting. You could download workshop mods, but I never really done that since there will be more and more updates introducing new systems and objects to the game. The game is growing as I type this, and I know they are working on cars right now in the game, and soon they will be working on more stuff like npc's. They really want this game to work, and it shows they want this game to be successful, so I assure you that the wait is worth it.
Now, there are somethings that I have to say about the game that rub me the wrong way. That is the combat, and the way the game kind of ends up being a boring chase scene. This is a huge note, do not engage in combat unless you think you can A) Easily get away, B) Take down a boat load of zombies, C) You are going to die because you have already been hurt by a zombie already. What I mean by this, is the system of you become infected is an instant kill that won't kill you right away. When the video showcase for this game says," You aren't the Rambo of the apocolypse." You are not the Rambo, and don't try to be. I have lost a countless amount of characters to being scratched or bitten by just fighting two zombies. So combat boils down, by either pulling one zombie away and beating it to death or running away and ducking into a house and awaiting your death or for the walkers to get bored and wonder off. This right on the spot for a zombie apocolypse for combat reasons, but this gets stale after hours into the game and you haven't found a gun to just mow down zombies, but even that isn't a good idea for the trope that zombies can hear that loud boom stick.
Another problem I have is the health system, I really love these health systems, and I have a guilt pleasure for them. The body injury system, that is what I am calling it for now, is a system that is something that makes healing feel like you aren't just standing there waiting for health to regenarate. Though, for a game that doesn't have that many different injuries to obtain as you explore and fight it feels bare and just serves as an annoyance. There are minor and deep cuts, bites, broken bones, and the chance the wounds are bleeding badly or slightly, or open wounds can become infected. There isn't much in the way, and the flair of it dies out quick.
Both these problems could be cured, by either adding more serious injuries, like having to cut off a limb to survive the bite of a zombie or pushing dislocated arm back into place. Combat cane be fixed with finishers or styles of combat that can take zombies out quicker but using it to much can exhaust your character. There can be different types of zombies, I know they probably won't do that, but running zombies just doesn't really cut it as a change in gameplay, just really forces you to run away quicker. Those are just my biggest issues with the game, there are some other issues but going over them would seem nit picky.
Overall, I really like Project Zomboid for it aspiring to be, and that is the harsh zombie apocolypse survive game that a lot of people have been asking for and not a triple A title that focus more on action then the living in a zombie infested world, I compared it to Cataclysm slighty, but I find Cataclysm has higher diffucultly spike when it comes to exploring and how to survive. Project Zomboid takes the survival in a different direction, and I would certainly recommend this game for what it is now since I am sure the game will expand more and more as the update the game which will keep the game fresh and alive.

This is not a game that you want to pay into.
Shady development tactics, gestapo moderation, and features promised in August of 2016 still not delivered - in November of 2017...  There are plenty of reasons to tell you "Don't buy this garbage."  The best one is this; this game has been on Steam since November 8, 2013.  In that time, they have seriously proven the skepticism about Early Access games to have a valid point, and their model has given indie development a bad name.  It's because people like this shirk their duty as developers, to screw around, make up excuses, and treat their community like sub-humans, that Early Access has the stigma that it does.
To really get to the point, there are a lot of reasons by personal principle to rally against a game, but I'm going to start by saying that I bought this one when the early "Kate and Baldspot" story was actually featured.  I have far more hours tracked than what Steam displays, because I played this when I was still a senior in High School. That's been quite some time, now, and it's only now that I finally gave up on it.
It's funny, giving up on this game is different than you might think.  A lot of people walk away from it and check in on the updates once in a while; I did this for the sake of humor, I kind of liked coming back, say, two to three months to see absolutely nothing had changed, yet they had something behind the scenes *almost* ready that they somehow deemed "progress."  Then they throw in a gimmick, like Vehicles, almost a year after promising a new animation set.  In this case though, there's only just enough progress to say the game's not dead, but not enough progress to show the game's actually going somewhere.  This is endless development, it isn't going anywhere, and gimmicks like vehicles are only put in to sell more copies of the game.
Then it hit me.  That's the business model.  This game still sells, even after all this time.  It's popular, it's still marketed, and the police force is still in action. It's quite clear they put plenty bread on the table, and as a customer, you're not going to have anything to show for it.
People keep buying this because there's something they expect to get out of it, and honestly, this is the big problem.  The Indie Stone's people don't care about the game, itself, even their moderators are disillusioned with the entire thing.  There isn't any passion there.  In my experience, games without passion have never been worth buying. Instead, this failed project is treated as a daily income maker, and if a game sells, that's a meal for the day.  They constantly insult and look down on the community they've managed to alienate over all these years, blaming them for their development team being emotionally weak and incapable of withstanding any amount of criticism, and it has its own enforcement arm in the forum that will try to bully dissenters, then permanently ban anyone who decides to take the same tone as the moderation does (sarcasm and belittlement are great when the moderator does it.  Try to spar with the same humor, and you're punished for it and they make something up).  Let's put it this way:
It's great to see these harassment tactics employed in a modern forum.  I'd honestly thought we'd moved past that stage of 'development,' (if you can call it such, with this game) but censorship is definitely a "Plus" going for this moderation.
They have a community rule, called "Be lovely."  In my experience and the experience of others who have seen the mess that can happen with commentary regarding this game, this means, as an outside critic, don't get too attached to "discussing" the negatives of this game with anybody who's too obsessed with it. You will be hated for your conflicting opinion. If you really want to open up truth and reality of who a lot of these people are, open up a thread about "NPCs."  Maybe title it "Where are the NPCs."  You will be ringing a dinner bell where you will be attacked by a horde of blind sycophants that go beyond making excuses, but try to find ways of insulting you on a personal level instead of even trying to acknowledge the topic. This game has a fairly toxic leftover-community, because if you choose to criticize the slow development progress, failure to include promised features, or the outright lies promoted - and then buried - by the people running the joint, these angry trolls will stack up their comments, which seem inherently sanctioned by the moderation at this point.  When a community behaves this way, you either have a damned good game, or people so devoted so something they don't want to let go that it affects their behavior. I've put well over 300 hours into PZ, and I'll tell you, this game isn't anything special.  Want to fight back? The thread'll get locked, or they'll shut you down and ban you from discussions. That makes it pretty hard to respond ;)  At this point in development, that's now a permanent ban rather than a temporary one; first offense. They're well on their way to becoming the next Derek Smart collective.
It's funny how they make you not want to mention the biggest missing element of the game. Hey fanboys, I don't mean to trigger you (and I know damn well that it does), but yes, we're on the topic of NPCs. Just because I know it triggers you. Indie Stone had them in the game at one point, took them out, made a few false promises (like they'd come in after the new animation sets,) then they failed those promises (such as never delivering new animation sets).  It doesnt stop there; this development team was so utterly incompetent with their promises, that the mods make it a point to emphasize that they intend NOT to be transparent, at this point. I mean, how many hoops do you have to jump through to get information about upcoming developments as a paying customer?  They make it a point to LIE about not wanting to be transparent with the community, because poor Lemmy or whomever had to talk to a troll!  Which, really, was a paying customer who probably saw through their sharade early on. When you have a community member that will follow you from a thread to a different situation altogether to harass you for criticising the game, the jokes about "rabid fanboyism" just aren't going to do them justice. You know the community's toxic when you have to worry about Norman Bates tracking you down for your review.
When active, legitimate topics are being shut down by the team, it's time to start being suspicious.  When critics are silenced, you draw a line. This isn't a game that you want to invest in, you're better than this scam.

- Detailed sprite work
- Tutorials for a newbie

- Modes such as Single elimation tournaments, G1 Climax style round Robin leagues, mission mode etc

Cons:

Is this the studio's first game? It feels like a small studio's first game. In that case it's not bad for a first try. But as a game for the consumer - I can't recommend it. Maize has no notion of pacing, gameplay, or variety of any description, on top of being poor value for money. The 4.4 hours it took me to finish it, a third was spent reading post-it notes of which there are hundreds, and another third running around hunting objects. At optimal efficiency you can easily finish it in a couple of hours, which, for 20€, is a hard sell.
Entire game is spent hunting down items in diabolically restricted levels, in ordert to stick those items in their designated slots to progress further. The only sligtly different interaction I had to do was a dancing minigame at the end, that's it. Needless to say you get sick of it pretty fast. It feels like a point and click adventure from a first person perspective.
Normally those games, such as Sam and Max series, or my facourite - Runaway series, have a fantastic story and writing to compensate for your having to slog through the dumb object hunting. This game doesn't.
The story exposition for this game essentially consists of the same 4 jokes being repeated over and over again. I will list them here, so you can understand how true that statement is:
- "Stop pressing Q"
- "We are corn and we are stupid, let's go take a nap."
- "Everything is stupid, you (the player) are an idiot, and I am a grumpy Russian bear!" (and if I say this enough times, it will be funny, yes?)
- "You collected another random item so we can write how dumb you are for collecting it. Haha."
That's it. While it was funny the first couple of times I heard/read it, it, as any dumb joke, quickly grew old. All the dialogue, written or narrated, is trying to be humours via repeating over and over the exact same jokes and lines. It's getting old very fast, and naturally doesn't make those jokes any better because they are being repeated over and over. I can give you a hint: repeating the same thing over and over doesn't make it better, like this game repeating the same lines over and over. Because it constantly repeats the same jokes and flows the dialogue in exactly the same way all the time, which quickly grows old, because repeating something so many times is pointless and only builds frustration. And Maize repeats. Over and...
You get the idea.
Also, as a personal complaint - it was very frustrating for me, as a Russian, to hear the nonesense that this bear was occasionally spewing. There are 180 millions of us. And more who speak our language. If you are gonna put so much emphasis on the leading character being Russian, you can at least make the effort to get someone who knows the language to record the lines. Even CoD does it better - they speak with horrible accents, but at least what they say has actual meaning, and makes sense within the context. I am not normally sensitive to this, but this game was so ploughing in-the-face with the whole "HEY LOOK AT ME I AM RUSSIAN AND GRUMPY" idea, that it really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off sometimes.
I think the studio has potential, but this game, sadly, does not.

**As a forewarning, there are minor spoilers. There really isn't much of a storyline, but I go in depth as far as gameplay goes.**
So I spent a good few hours on the game, getting a feel and really seeing what it has to offer. The fact that it is in alpha was a little worrysome, given how many games are labeled with early access and seem to die without much improvement or support. This game, so it seems, is different.
It's a refreshing change, it's truly quite unique in multiple aspects ranging from gameplay to art and design. This game is most certainly sandbox in nature, but it actually carries a very strong similarity to Dwarf Fortress, and almost seems like a branched-off, reskinned version of it. I can only imagine the vast amount of direction and improvement this game has in store if only the developers remain diligent and active.
To start.. As of the current build -524, you have the option of choosing a biome, starting location, and race. I haven't experimented heavily with these options; I've only had the pleasure of one play in which I haven't come all that far. That being said, once you choose your world, you then choose where in said world you will build your camp. Naturally, you'll want to choose an area with plenty of trees, wildlife, and minerals. Upon choosing, you're dumped off without much of a tutorial, which usually seems like an overwhelming experience, however.. This game is fairly straight foreward. After a few minutes, I quickly learned my way around the UI, the different tools, navigation, and issueing commands to my Hearthlings. Before long, the first raid on my settlement had taken progress. I immediately knew the general idea of what to do, click the large, red sword icon, right? It was as simple as that; my Hearthlings ran to a safe position as my assigned soldiers made short work of the beast. As of right now, the game doesn't seem to be too unforgiving. I am expecting that to change as I come further along and mine deeper into the ground.
Graphically speaking, this game is very crisp and clean. There are a few annoyances which are more gameplay issues than graphics, but I'll get to those in a bit. The game has a bit of a minecraft appearance, but one with customer shaders and higher quality picture. Textures are almost non existant, but I can do without those, it simply works for this game. All in all, there isn't a whole lot of clutter, which can really turn into a big problem for games like this.
In terms of bugs, this game definitely has its share, but it's to be expected. I feel confident that more and more bugs will be fixed as time continues, the support website seems very much alive with devs attempting to help those who experience issues. A few bugs I've personally come across include goblins exploding into sunlight instead of fighting my soldiers, a Hearthling that never wakes up from his sleep, and not being to change to a specific class despite having met all requirements. Obviously two of these can be considered game breaking, however I'm not letting it kill my opinion of this game. Save often is the best fix for most problems.
As for one final in-depth review, this game is, as I mentioned, like a replica of Dward Fortress, though with FAR less features. I suspect this game is very heavily influenced by Dwarf Fortress. You have the ability to custom-build structures, or choose from a preset list. You can place said structures where ever they fit. You can alter the environment by taking down trees, creating mines, etc. As you create mines, it really opens up many different possibilities for construction ideas. Perhaps an underground fortress? All in all, in the short amount of time that I've played this game, I'm enjoying it a lot. If they can implement some more features or similarities from DF such as complex contraptions, many more monsters and biomes, etc, I'll be thrilled. Perhaps even a mode to take complete control of a single, hero-like individual to explore the lands, loot, plunder dungeons, and seek bounties, much like DF. I might be going a little far comparing the two, but regardless, the game can (hopefully) only improve from here.

Meh.  It's cute; like you might think you are going to get something like minecraft but it's really not.  You can dig blocks out of the dirt but that's just to harvest randomly placed ores.  And, you have to be really attentive to how you give your dig instructions or they will dig a hole they can't get out of... and starve without warning.  Beyond that it's kind of like any other crafting game; you have to have your tradespeople level up before they can build certain things, or unlock more types of trades/specialties. What you cannot do is control any of the villagers.  The only controls you have are your build queue, you can designate areas for mining, loot collection, you can set up zones for farming plants, animals, trapping, (much like Sim City)  and you can order an 'alert' where all the villagers run to your designated safe-zone, marked by a flag.  You can relocate the flag as your village changes.  The only villagers you can slightly control are the footmen, which have 3 or 4 basic instructions that really all amount to the same thing... "move here and fight any threats".  The threats are nothing too severe... the occasional zombie, golem etc that wants to steal your stuff or kill your villagers.  Oh, and don't forget to cancel your footmen's orders when the fighting is done or they will stick to their new post, and starve without comment.
The pace is ponderous... it has 2 speeds, neither of which is fast enough to make the time go by, but the accelerated speed is too fast to be able to react well to some of the hostiles that show up.  It'd be nice if it had instad of 1x/2x, it had 5x/10x and option to drop to normal speed when a zombie alert shows up.
So... it looks like a good game for younger kids but I think the crafting system and build-requirements are just a touch too complex for them.  Anyone else may enjoy it until they come to the realization... this is really all there is.

Kholat is a survival horror game based on true events that took place in Russia decades ago, when hikers were found dead for unknown reasons. The game begins without further introductions to its lead character, whose identity or motivation are never revealed during the game. Then, Kholat turns into a mountain hiking game as we take such mysterious character to find some notes spread on the mountain are - that's the best part of the game. The scenarios look stunning and the sound effects, plus the great musical score creates one hell of an atmosphere. It's possible to walk for a long time and get completely lost amidst all the snow and rocks; the game is truly disorienting, which increases the immersion. Also, considering the player has to get through everything using only a map and a compass (which I never figured out how to use), it makes for a very challenging experience, but very fun nonetheless.
Each note found, reveals a little (very little) more about what has been happening in the region during the last century, including the real life event. The supernatural elements are heavily based on Lovecraft - people dreaming about a powerful, nightmarish being from another dimension and going insane - however, the in game supernatural elements are completely random and off tone with the rest of the game. The shadows, who are the main 'enemies' on the game, have no pattern at all. Sometimes you can just sprint next to them and poof, he's gone. Besides of the lack of coherence when it comes about the supernatural elements, the invisible barriers were the most annoying bits of Kholat. There are lots of moments when you are forced to walk a lot to find a new way, when the character could have easily jumped a rock, a feat which clearly any average human being would have been to pull off. Except the protagonist of Kholat.
The game lenght is very short - it took me around 6 hours to finish it getting almost every note (missed a few). But the truth is, if you don't feel like mountain hiking and being scared by wolves (wolves were the scariest part of the game, even though they only howl and never show up), this game might be really boring. I recommend it but with some reservations.

How this game garnered so much acclaim I'll never know.
Do you want to perpetually:
-Get lost in a very confusingly samey (albeit very pretty) environment even though you have a map and a compass?
-Get killed by the same apparition over and over again, almost always nowhere near a save point so you have to traipse through (hopefully, if you remembered) the same trail until you find a way around the said apparition?
-Piece together a threadbare story in the form of notes that makes you realise, "I walked around for several hours for around five minutes of actual importance and a predictable ending"?
If you answered "yes" to any of the above, then this game is for you!
To be fair, I bought this game because Sean Bean and It's Pretty To Look At, and I'm a soundtrack nut.
Maybe others will like this sort of game, maybe I'm just getting older and lack the patience these days, but I couldn't help  but feel bored while wandering around and looking for something of import. The substance of the narrative was just far too sparse. If Sean Bean is narrating, I want to hear a lot of him! Not a couple of minutes of dialogue in total. If I'm meant to explore a beautiful world and discover things, I want to discover a lot of things, or at least different things, not just a handful of pedestrian notes. Leave me a book to find, not a pamphlet!
On the flipside:
-Stunning environment, even on medium settings (I played on highest settings for a bit and stood still...breathtaking)
-Chilling minimalist soundtrack
-Makes you aware of the Dyatlov Pass Incident
-Sean Bean
Probably just about worth buying on sale.

Wolves.  The bane of my existence.
My first three characters died at their teeth without lasting a week.  My fourth character was starving in the cold when he was attached by a wolf and managed to fend it off.  Seeing that the beast was wounded, and being out of food myself, I followed him across the wastes for what seemed like hours.  Starvation set in, and it was a war of attrition to see who would die first.
The wolf finally succumbed to his wounds.  As I plunged into the carcass to harvest the fres wolf meat, my vision blurred, and my fourth character starved to death and slipped into darkness.
Finally, my fifth character got the trick of dealing with wolves.  With careful application of fire, flares and bait,  I avoided them with relative ease. Without a rifle melee fights were common, but with the help of a trusty hatchet I was able to fend for myself.  The threat was real, but slowly my character collected materials and managed to live for over a month.

After weeks of trudging across four maps and scavenging like a wild animal (and without seeing a single rifle for miles around), I finally managed to get together enough materials for a bow and arrows.  Finally, I would bring the fight to the wolves.  I stalked across the ice to find one of their number heading straight towards me.  With careful aim and a heart of vengeance, I felled the beast with a single shot.  Joy at last.
I harvested what I could from the animal, certain my luck had changed.  Back at my camp I built a roaring fire and began to cook a meal fit for a king as the sun slowly set, a song of joy on my lips.
In the middle of roasting my third wolf steak I heard a growling coming to my side.  I looked up, and was greeted by a huge bear who appeared in my camp out of nowhere, braving my fire to avenge his fallen wolf brethren. He did not give a damn about my puny bow and arrow and mauled me without mercy, leaving my broken body bleeding in the snow.
Bears.  The other bane of my existence.  10/10.

I am absolutely addicted to this game! Even before the story mode was released I'd play the sandbox mode and then challenge modes to no end. I love survival games and no other game comes close. I admit the story is a bit...odd... but it is still very early and really has potential to become fantastic. The first two episodes are made up of "go fetch" missions, which can get a bit annoying. But I have total faith in this game and I love this game. The controls are simple, the atmosphere, weather, artistry, and sheer survival skill are above and beyond anything I expected. One minute you're in perfect health under a clear sky and in an instant it can all fog over and you're face to face with a bear and no weapon. Absolutely thrilling game, you never know what to expect next.

This is one of the only survival games on the market that I would recommend. Although it isn't finished yet (like most survival games right now), it's in an incredibly playable state. It's unique and not only because it's single player with no zombies and ISN'T a buggy mess. It's a real survival experience with a huge focus on immersion, exploration and the constant struggle between life and death in the Canadian wilderness.
The art style is gorgeous, the sound design is phenomenal and it's given me some of the most intense, compelling experiences I've ever had playing a video game. Freezing to death in a snowstorm, desperately trying to find your way back to shelter while wolves howl all around you is not something you soon forget.
The developers have done early access (or games in development) right with frequent updates, significant improvements and good community interaction. I really can't recommend the game enough, I've played it for 57 hours and the game isn't even finished yet. That's in sandbox mode which is in a super polished state with multiple large maps, tons of places to explore and many, many, many ways to die.

Liking this game is like trying to enjoy Kix cereal. It's sort of good ... but it just doesn't do it for you.

In one case, despite being an RPG, it lacked variety - in a lot of aspects. One being that there was limited customization in the gear you received, which is fine considering that's how most of the other games are, but it still would have been a nice touch. Second, the gameplay in general was fairly repetetive. The miniquests were the exact same quest but in different locations, which became stale after one or two go-throughs.
On a separate issue, the switch between characters was an interesting application that made the game a bit more dynamic. The only problem with that is it took away from the game and made it less immersive. It also made the characters seem less personal and isn't exactly what the game needed.
All things considered, the atmosphere was very nice. There were also a lot of new elements that played surprisingly smooth into the game.

I think I am beginning to get sick of Assassin's Creed. Yearly release after yearly release really starts to drain on a man, and while I have only started since AC4, playing all major releases and Rogue since then, the fatigue is starting to kick in for me. Don't get me wrong, it is not as bad as Call of Duty, it is hard as hell to get as bad as Call of Duty, and they are taking a break in 2016 to develop things more, but the basic gameplay mechanics carrying over and over again with not much change is very CoD like. Regardless of that, though, I still played through the latest game, Assassin's Creed Syndicate, and finished it through. So what did I think of it? Let's take a look.
STORY: There are two stories in here, so first we're going to look at the story we actually care about. You play as both Evie and Jacob Frie, two assassin's and siblings who, after getting fed up with their assassin bretherin, go to London to liberate it from the Templar's and their local leader, Crawford Starrick. The story is the usual AC type deal: you have historical figures you come across and you take part in some historical events int he game. It's fine enough, and while for the first two or three chapters I did not care too much, I do have to admit that later on I got back into it. The other story is the same modern day ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and I do have to admit, it is just horribly boring and it takes you out of the good atmosphere the game puts you into. At least back in AC4 and Rogue you're only taken out every 4 or 5 sequences and you got some fun things to do, here you're taken out at least every other sequence, sometimes sooner, and there aren't even any of the cool hacking mini-games. I hope that next time you can just get the option to disable the other story so I can just play the main story.
GAMEPLAY: Just like every previous AC game in the past, namely Unity. If you don't know Assassin's Creed gameplay by now, I guess I'll sum it up; parkour, assassinations, kind of stealth. They did take out the lockpicking minigame from Unity, which I kind of miss. Instead they added a new grappling hook, which is kind of neat to mess around with. There still is no ship gameplay back in the game and combat still doesn't feel as fluent as it did back in AC4, though it feels a bit better than Unity did, though I don't mind too much I suppose.
GRAPHICS, SETTING, AND PERFORMANCE: London looks lovely, I have to say. I remember Unity's Paris looking a bit better, but London still looks very nice. Performance was also pretty stable as well, stayed around 50-60, mostly to the higher end of that, and there weren't too many glitches in game. The setting of Victorian London is cool as well, you can go to monuments like Buckingham Palace and Big Ben, which is always neat, and it looks and feels like London would've felt like.
CHARACTERS AND VOICE ACTING: Evie and Jacob are alright enough. Jacob first came off as an idiot and Evie came off as a♥♥♥♥♥♥ but after a while I started to like the both of them. The puzzles are great, and you aren't locked into one solution. Aside from a few unique parts, there are no constraints to how much you can build, and you have infinite space - which means that there are practically infinite solutions to any one puzzle. Once you finish a puzzle, you get to see how your stats - cost, cycles, and area - stack up to other players, so there's an incentive to optimize your designs. You can also record GIFs of your solutions and share them, I thought that was a neat feature. There's also an optional little Solitaire-like minigame you can play, but I haven't really bothered with that, as the main appeal of the game lies in the actual puzzles for me.
They're stunning. The parts all move individually, and they're all designed and animated beautifully. Once you put an intricate machine together, it's so satisfying to just watch all the parts move in harmony like a well-oiled machine. There are also some really well-drawn backgrounds for each story area.
The story is... surprisingly decent. Obviously, though, it's not the main focus of the game. I've only played up to the third chapter out of five, so I can't really make a complete judgment here. But it's enough to keep you occupied and provide a 'reason' behind each of the puzzles, if that makes any sense. Overall, it's nothing special, but it's certainly not bad. If you're buying this game for the story, though, then you might want to look elsewhere.
Practically infinite. As I said before, there's an unlimited number of solutions to each puzzle - you can build a gigantic, clunky machine, a tiny efficient one, or anything between. I'm sure you could spend hours on every puzzle trying to optimize it in all 3 categories.
The execution is flawless, with beautiful graphics and a surprisingly decent story to go along with the (already great) puzzles, if you're into that. There's almost nothing to critique about this game.
