I had a brief introduction to the Fire Pro universe with Fire Pro Returns on PS3 (brief because my secondhand PS3 broke 2 weeks after I managed to get the game!). I read about the enthusiasm the fans have for this game and as an ex-wrestling nut (I'm slowly getting back into it now via NJPW and the independent circuit) I had to give it a go.
I give the game a thumbs up because I am an 'old school' wrestling fan and can appreciate the mechanics and uniqueness of the game. People who find aesthetics to be important may be turned off by this game; graphically this game is not based on realism but on some sort of nostalgic, squared circle, fantasy escapism; graphically it hasn't really changed in years. Also, the timing based system gives each match an element of unpredictability which I like ( the last WWE 2K game I played, 2K13,  was too easy and I won whenever I wanted. Perhaps WWE 2K games are more difficult now but winning got boring (even though I would complain if I lost!)).
Personally, I find FPW to be Pro Evolution Soccer to WWE's FIFA. The fact you can edit the wrestler's tendencies means they can act like their real world counterpart would do, and this makes each wrestler feel like an individual. This is evident as it is very common for players to create 'edits' (or 'CAWs' in WWE2K speak), and watch the PC sim the matches rather than play the matches yourself. When I played WWE 2K, the moves each wrestler had was different but the mindset/ tendencies/ mentality was the same. Much like Pro Evo's Player ID (where every player plays like he would in real life) versus FIFA's dominance with licenses where every team would 'look' like they do in real life, but actually when you play FIFA, every AI controlled team 'plays' exactly the same. Tough to say style over substance as the WWE 2K games can offer things (real WWE roster, Universe mode etc) that FPW doesn't. As a result, FPW suits a person who can get lost in their own imagination and create story lines in their heads, as well as enjoy the community element as you will rely on strangers to create your desired roster for you (or you can create edits yourself).
Please note, FPW is in early access and I can safely say that the monthly updates are great as Spike actually listen to what's being said on the threads/ forums and make adjustments accordingly. They understand that the people who are playing FPW now are, by and large, the same people who were playing FP before, and this makes loyal fans even more loyal. Also, as it is a PC game, mods and all sorts are making their way into the game to make the experience even more immersive.
If pure aesthetic glitz and glamour is your thing (FIFA's licenses and presentation, for example) is your thing then you may not be convinced by FPW, but if you want a fighting game mechanic that is truly unique, and you consider yourself a long time wrestling fan (I say 'long time' as I assume younger players won't get their heads around the graphics/ mechanics/ easy DIY roster building) and have never played this game before, then I suggest you by it now before the price goes up. Personally, I think the game will get better as time goes on (at the time of writing they have just released another patch with new arenas) and FPW should be considered a rite of passage for any gaming wrestling fan.

I went into this not expecting a whole lot.  It was part of a recent Humble Bundle, and wasn't the "main" title, so I set the bar really low.  But this game was so worth playing.
The visuals are gorgeous.  The style of the artwork is just amazing.  Everything looks spectacular.  The animations are all very well done and all of the characters and scenery just oozes personality.
Music is equally grand.  All of the tunes fit the locale really well.  Sound effects are minimal, but effective.  Voice acting is great and all of the characters feel very alive and real.
The actual game play itself is... minimal.  It serves as a means to deliver the content, and not really the drawing point itself.  There's no way to "fail", and there's no time limits so you aren't really under any pressure.
Story is good, and has at least two unexpected twists that I didn't see coming.  Humor is everywhere, the notes you find, descriptions of items, interaction between characters, etc.
If I had to give a negative, it is that there's probably not a whole lot of replay value.  There isn't anything you can really do differently to experience the story in an alternate way, so when you're done, you're done.
Overall I'd say 8.5/10.  Really worth playing through.

Evolve is a game that had potential, but dropped the ball before its release and has been fumbling ever since.
The concept of Evolve is a great, but difficult to balance around; you're either on a team as one of four hunters, each set in their own class, or a monster with the ability to evolve (depending on the game mode). Most of the hunters are pretty solid, though there are some lackluster ones (again, depending on game mode), while the monsters are just pretty powerful overall. Don't get me wrong, the monsters aren't perfect, but besides Behemoth the rest can be seen as either strong, or nearly overpowered, when it comes to the usual matchmaking you'll see these days.
The player base is very low right now as well and I doubt it'll be growing anytime soon, which is a problem as this is a PVP game at heart. You could gamble and play with some CPU's, which you most likely will if you actually find a match, and but they're really not the best at decision making and you don't even get to pick who they will be or what perk they can take, though you can take them over which is sort of nice.
There are also some game mechanics that don't really make much sense, such as the monsters sneak pounce and fuel being used while climbing terrain. The sneak pounce is actually pretty nice and makes sense, but I really wish you could break out of it on your own, or not be able to use it if there's only one hunter left.
The balancing when it comes to Evolve also seems off, though it's difficult to truly say that with what you are given; low player base, usually uncoordinated teams and an environment that usually favors the monster. Hunters and monsters alike are both hit with nerfs and buffs, but it just seems these changes hurt hunters more than they do monsters. Again, it is difficult to balance around the concept of four vs one, but there are just too often times where the monster feels too strong and is given a lot more leeway to make mistakes. You also need to play for a very long time to level up your hunter and your monster level, which increase your buffs the higher rank they are, though you cannot choose which perk you would like to level up and it does it in a set order for you.
Then there's the problem that started it all, the DLC. Don't get me wrong, DLC can be a good thing when done well, but when it comes to Evolve it's done pretty poorly. When Evolve released it was set at a full price of sixty US dollars and already had several DLC planned before release. The game was designed to revolve around the DLC, which is not that odd these days, but with all the problems the game currently has it is not what the game needs. Some of the strongest monsters and hunters you must buy so if you choose not to spend extra money on the game you're left with the original three hunters per class and two monsters.
Evolve was an enjoyable game on release and I've enjoyed it for a good amount of time, but there are sadly too many problems with it in its current state and it's doubtful they'll be fixed anytime soon if at all. I do hear the player base is active on consoles, though always do your research before making your purchase.
Thanks for reading.

Gameplay:
Ah, the real meat of the review, the gameplay is good. but it has so many stages of good. now, starting off, the game can be quite difficult, but once you get the hang of it, it is good. every once in a while there are noises like dogs, gunshots, helicopters etc which can attract zombies, causing you to have to escape and build a new fort. one of my favorite things about this game is the permadeath. when you die you die for good, which adds a fair bit of challenge. there are traits that you can select before starting. traits have to be evenly balanced. advanced guide:
.
Character Creation
The character creation menu.
As soon as you start a new game, you will be greeted by the character creation screen. To get a guide to the character creator, visit the player page. It will guide through and break down all the screens that you will find, as well as explaining traits and perks for different occupations. If you're new, you may want to take the Thick Skinned trait, which will allow you to survive injuries which would be fatal to other characters.
However, do realize the following: death is inevitable. It tells you as much when you start up the game and the first few times you play, you'll likely find yourself in an unfortunate situation from which there's no escape. It just happens. It's not because you're bad or anything, it's just that you're new. As long as you learn from the experience you'll be in much better stead to play new games with future characters.
Some sample builds follow below, but first, a brief discussion about traits and the tradeoffs of certain traits. Currently the game is unfinished and some traits require balancing, whereas others deal with features which have yet to be implemented properly yet.
Easy manageable negative trait examples would be Coward/Pacifist, Slow Reader, Hearty Appetite, and High Thirst. Coward/Pacifist doesn't have much of a negative impact, as you should run from zombies instead of attempting to fight them early on until you acquire a Baseball Bat, Axe, or fire (Campfire Kit). Slow Reader doesn't have any "negative" effects, per se, as it doesn't actually lower any skills. It's just a timesink, as reading takes more time than normal, but it isn't an issue as long as you make sure you're safe before you start reading. Hearty Appetite and High Thirst are also not difficult to balance, as you'll be needing to eat/drink only somewhat more, so it's manageable if you keep a steady supply of food/water available.
Sleepyhead and Overweight are less manageable to an extent but are still worth taking. Sleepyhead applies in the same sense of Slow Reader, as you'll need more sleep, so you just need to make sure you're safe before sleeping. While Overweight does reduce your starting Fitness skill by two points initially, it can be balanced if you make a habit of running, and Fitness could rise above normal if you survive long enough.
Early Game
The start of your adventure can be the toughest part of the game. If you're a new player, you'll want to read the tutorial thoroughly in order to accustom yourself to the game's basics such as moving around, opening containers, and defending yourself. Note that as of build 29, one section of the tutorial is incorrect, Holding left click does not charge an attack as indicated, instead holding ctrl or right click charges an attack. Doing so also enters stealth mode, which can be used for sneaking around.
You'll spawn in a house or trailer when you begin in Project Zomboid. One early priority aside from securing a bag/weapon/etc, should be making sure ground floor windows have Sheets on them. If not, look in dressers and bedrooms for some spare Sheets.
If you are unable to find enough Sheets and you spot a medium to large horde outside of more than one of your windows, do not be frightened but be cautious. They should not notice you as long as you stay away from the offending window and keep quiet, as in no running, shouting, or swinging a weapon against something.
You may likely have to get out of dodge, unless you like hordes of hungry zeds possibly smashing through your windows. Instructions are below as to what you should do, should it possibly end up this way.
You'll want to run away and lose a horde's line of sight until you can find a better safehouse or if you can, catch the attention of nearby zeds and lead them away from your area before a horde's breaking line of sight, just to make things a little safer. Otherwise, you are fine to stay a night or two if you have enough ground floor Sheets, as long as you're quiet and don't make too much noise. However, keep in mind there may be a risk of zeds breaking in from helicopter noise or ambient gunshot noises, and the helicopter noise will occur only a total of two times for the first month.
Gathering food (eat perishables first, save non-perishables for later unless you're absolutely starving, which is unlikely in the beginning) is also a priority, and so is gathering and filling containers such as Empty Mugs and Cooking Pots with water, stashing them away for when the power eventually goes out. The power will shut off anywhere from one to two days from the first day (if you're really unlucky) or 1-2 months normally.
overall, a 9/10.

I'd give Kholat a flat 9/10 and here's why.
It ultimately comes down to a lot of personal preference. The game makes heavy usage of the typical, slow, and unsuspecting explorer, and bases its gameplay on it. It's not a game where you're constantly running away from jump scares like in games such as outlast. If you're looking for jumpscares, this isnt the game for you. It's a more psychological approach to horror. The horror and fear aspect comes from the immersive world Kholat puts you in. The sound of the wind howling, the sound of an old mountain creaking, and the wolf howls in the distance all work together to create a very atmospheric and eerie/dark environment for you to explore. It's very slow paced for the most part, although there are a few faster segments towards the end of the game. The game also explicitly tells you to pay attention to your surroundings, and I didn't truly understand what they meant until I saw massive skulls formed from the rocks, staring right at me as I slowly made my way through a pass.
Pros:
-Incredible detail to the environment
-Eerie sounds make the game even more immersive
-Level of helplesness not as high as say outlast
-Psychological and introspective
-No campaign order (you can travel to any point of interest in any order) Noce for the free roam aspect.
-Relatively smooth (Running an i7-4790k, GTX970) Max graphics (looks incredible) @ 1080p
->Average 55-60 fps w/ v-sync on. Occasional frame-rate drop to 40 (not sure why? Rendering environments-shifting from cave to snowstorm maybe? idk)
-VOICED BY SEAN BEAN! How badass is that?
Cons:
-Nothing to do after you finish the game
-Lacks replay value (wouldn't play this game multiple times as it's essentially the same exact story)
-relatively short game. about 10 hours tops. Sure you can make it last as long as you want if you just wander the paths over and over again.
-Feels like the story is unfinished. The game mentions a lot of really interesting conspiracy theory-esque conversations that don't really give closure to the story (that may just be because of the actual story/inciedent game is based off of.)
TL;DR: Buy this game if you like immersive horror, don't buy it if you want an outlast-esque game.
I definitely reccomend this game if your rig can handle it, and if you're looking for a slower paced immersive game to lose yourself in.

A superbly polished 'factory game',
Every puzzle feels like constructing an elaborate wind-up toy, then watching it go.
Like 'Beseige', there's no fixed solution to your construction - so this game absolutely shines in letting you discover your own way - separating it from otherwise humdrum sequencer-only puzzles, and this is the title's real gem, I feel.
The game records solution metrics for cost, cycle count and grid area used, so there's some lasting incentive to go back and 'hone' your constructions afterwards.
Opus Magnum additionally includes a delightfully mellow element-garden solitaire game, which (like playing-card solitaire) can brickwall you at times, but it makes the wins that much more satisfying.
Well done Zachtronics: I feel there's a lot of scope to expand here, so I'm looking forward to more like this!

I hesitated to get this because some reviews suggested this game was maybe a bit "dumbed down". I regret hesitating.
It is easier and progress through the levels is quite a lot faster than previous games. But there is lots of content and if you want to seek the challenge : it is absolutely there. Nothing thrills me quite like trying to tip my score (especially in cycles!) "off the chart". When I managed to solve probably the simplest puzzle in the game (not counting tutorials) in 28 cycles, I felt the utter satisfaction brought by a plan coming through.
If you enjoyed previous games in the series, definitely get this. The hexagonal mechanics make it all "fresh" again but some of the old tricks will still help you nail an awesome solution.
If you're new to this "genre" of machine-building-puzzle-games, this might be the best starting point yet. There's nothing "hidden", it's just like building a real physical machine that moves marbles around and sticks them together. And if you don't like optimising, the play space is big enough to accept thousands of totally different workable solutions.
My only criticism at this point is that the "reach" of the grabber arms could be visualised a little better (e.g. show ghost arms when you hover over one, with a little rotatey arrow to match the instructions, and show the "sweep" of the arms). Thinking in hexagons is surprisingly difficult, and I've felt trial and error when preventing atoms colliding as they sweep past each other that isn't "fun" problem solving, and can be a bit tedious at first.
Anyway, if you want to play a puzzle game : get it. Don't hesitate.

With its fantastic mechanics and grim but dull setting, Dishonored remains a favorite of mine, and a great accomplishment for the genre.
who after being betrayed and blamed for the murder of his beloved Empress to whom he served as an agent and personal bodyguard, meets a being shrouded with incredible mystery.. A higher entity referred to as the Outsider.
With the assistance of the Outsider, who chooses neither evil nor bad, only whatever is of interest to him, Corvo gains 'magical' powers.
Dishonored does a great job in balancing your set of physical tools and magical abilities. Neither are enforced. These only give to the already vast variety of playstyles and add through the magical aspect of this game a great deal of depth to the gameplay and mechanics.
As a silent protagonist, Corvo is an empty shell the player is supposed to fill.
Little to big differences in the world are made as a result of your actions in it. Your actions have impact. The way you affect the world is not common.
It's not just what you say to this person or that character, it's your playstyle.
You dared not to hurt a soul? From that you gain as part of your reward cleaner sewers. Meaning less weepers (a certain type of enemy) to avoid or kill or render them unconscious.
You've been a good boy? Good job, little sweet Emily's drawings is that of a happy, sunlit place. You've been bad? Well, you can see that reflected upon the new dark, sinister characters in the paintings.
This succeeds in making you feel regret for acting as you did, playing as you did as Dishonored manages to get you emotionally invested in Emily's character, and when you see her drawing of you, smiling bright, you smile in real life. But when you don't get to see that happy creation, cheerfully titled 'Daddy' you see the masked murderer you are.
Whether you choose to see her turn you into her savior or her fear, a tower with flowers and a rainbow or murderer with a bloody knife and a pile of bodies is for you to decide through your playstyle alone. It's important to mention that these specific details are not forced, as you might not even notice them while playing through the game. They are worth glimpsing at though.
This all sounds awesome, right? What a wonderful mechanic.
Well, not necessarily. The only reason to purchase any game at all and play through it, is for the sake of your personal entertainment. It's your game, you should choose to play it however you wish to. Now, although I am all for the specific player-action-affected events I stated above, Dishonored has one heavy punishment for the player should he choose to be a bad boy.
Paintings are one small thing. Game ending is another. And that is broken. Unknowingly, you will be punished by the game's ending if you carelessly killed all who stood in your way.
This is wrong. This is not a 'your choices matter' game. This is a game you play for the fun in its gameplay and mechanics, for its openness in level design, letting you move on from this place to the next however you'd like to.
Giving you a bad ending is a needlessly unforgiving and punishing mechanic.
Your way of enjoying this game shouldn't be a negetive deciding factor for the ending which you receive.
For stealth-action fans, I'd consider this game a must have in your game library.
Of course, not that you can't have incredible fun with it if what you're into is decapitating enemies or watch them being eaten and devoured alive by swarms of rats controller by you. Honestly, it can be just as satisfying as bypassing every guard without being noticed.
Dishonored is a fantastic game. Its setting is an incredible fit. Its mechanics in gameplay are a joy to use and the animations do a magnificent job in delivering the satisfaction of a kill. And while the story may not be the most interesting, I did find myself invested in some of the characters and I did find myself immersed to extreme measures with the world of Dishonored to the point where I found myself reading the different notes and excerpts scattered throughout the game to enrich my knowledge of the interesting lore behind it all.
I'd also like to mention the DLC expansions in which you get to play as one of the antagonist and see through his eyes and reason. The extra story enables you to experience and understand the mindset of the very person who set you upon this path for the sake of money and greed. A path which brought nothing but horrors bestowed not only upon you, but the entire city as well. If you liked Dishonored, these are a must-buy.
Overall, it was one hell of a ride and I enjoyed it immensely.

I am terrible at writing reviews but I wanted to write down some thoughts about this game.
TL;DR A very good game with an interesting (unique) concept and maps with amazing details, you really get the feeling you are in a tropic place/toxic industry/snowy-north-place and so on. Small community and some character most be bought :( The game is good balanced so you can have success with any character, Turtlerrock studios are releasing free content also (monster, characters, maps, skins etc). The lore is told to you naturally and its interesting to hear the hunters conversation and then by yourself put the small pieces of information (you get before everygame) to a big picture. It's fun to play the game, and after all, isn't that the important thing?
First of all, I find the gaming experience very unique (in a good way), this 4 hunters tracking down 1 big awesome monster is something I have not played before and I found the concept and the idea to be very good.
There is some negatives though and that is mostly the small comunity that is only getting smaller. What I would say is the most annoying thing is that sometimes you find a game very quickly, and sometimes it takes forever. When you actually play the game though, it is really fun.
Here is the thing: The GAME is really good, fun, and unique, but the reason people put "No" in recommendation is mostly because of 2 things:
1. DLC and/or characters are unavailable and must be bought, this is something I found sad, I myself dont have all the characters for example (but I am highly enjoying myself when I play). This don't affect your success/winrate in anyway for the simple reason all character are good balanced and equally strong.
2. Small community/take long time to find game. This is not something that is going to get better for the simple reason that everyone are putting "NO" on recommendation.
Some things about the gameplay and the game in general (which IMO I think they did great):
The game is balanced, Turtlerock studios have really tried to make it balanced for each character and team so nothing is "OP". In competitive the hunters have a little higher winrate (~54%) but when you are going solo I guess the monster have a little higher winrate for the reason the communication may not be great.
Anyway, all the different characters that are unique in their own way, and that every map have high details, good graphics and just overall looks amazing if you stop for a second and just watch. The maps are all on the planet Sheer and it goes from snowy places to hot tropical forest to toxic industry. The different species are allso very well done and some are extremely dangerous (Tyrants!).
The intro scene when you are in the plan and jump down to the map is also very well done, and usually there is a small conversation between 2 characters that often gives us hints about what they did before they got recruted by Cabot and before helping the planer Sheer. The way they conversate and build their story overtime is very enjoyable and feels natural and realistic (I like that!).
Turtlerock have done improvments after they hear feedbacks, thet announced the Hunt 2.0 when people found they didnt play with player of the same skills. They have fixed a lot of bugges and I rarely find any nowadays. They have giving out some free characters for the people have haven´t bought any DLC so they also get some new stuff. Meteor Goliath, abilities are same but the cooldown are different, dmg is change and now got an fire that have some damage over time, also he looks different. Rouge val that are now played completely different and Blitz Markov that builds up more dmg as long he keep his lighting in contact with the monster. So we can say that they have released 3 new characters free, or they are nearly new atleast. And I think they will release more free stuff (also all maps are available and they will probably release more maps in the future). They have lowered the price on the game and on all DLC so I would say its priceworthy, and even right now when im writing its on sale, though it might not be when you are reading this.
Everything I have said is my opinion, you are free to disagree. Have a great life stranger.

There are a ton of reviews about the stalled development and lackluster updates. I bought the game anyway because the concept sounded good and I love these types of games. It's really easy for me to enjoy survival base building games.
This game is just boring. There's not much to do. There's one enemy: the zombie. It's trivial to kill with your bare hands and even easier with a weapon. Yes you can die from a single attack and getting surrounded is sure death, but killing the same stupid enemy by the thousands gets old real fast.
You would think the survival mechanics would make up for it. That's what I thought but they don't. The survival aspect of the game is slow, cumbersome and sinfully boring. In short, it is a series of right-click context menus and progress bars. Need a tree branch? Find some trees, right click on the ground, click forage and watch your character stand still as a progress bar slowly fills above their head. You might find one. Maybe. Want to water your plants? Oh boy. Well, you'll want to fill your inventory with various water jugs until you can barely move. Then right click a water source and select fill. Do this for each of jug. Then walk over to each plant and right click to select water -> select jug -> select amount. Several times for each plant. Not sure if your plants need water? Don't bother looking at the soil or the plant, you'll need to open another context menu.
Want to cook some food? Get ready for a series of context menus and progress bars. Want to build a cool base? Context menus and progress bars. Does your character need a rest? Context menus and progress bars. Want to read a book to get better at something? Context menus and progress bars. There are hardly animations to accompany any of this (apparently these have been in limbo for two years).
This kind of stuff can be forgiven if there is depth to the gameplay, or a cool story, or really anything but there is just nothing here. This isn't dwarf fortress where you imagination is running wild with possibilities. There are no possibilities.
Most everything breaks after a few uses. Stand in a forest all day to find 2 chipped rocks and tree branches. Use them to craft a few axes. Watch those axes break after 2 uses each. And now you need to sleep because standing in the forest looking for sticks and stones is exhausting.
Was that a woman screaming? A dog barking? A gun shot? A helicopter? Nope. Don't bother looking. It's just a dumb noise meant to attract some more boring zombies in a boring empty world.
I didn't care that this game had been in development for forever and I still don't. It's just not worth your time or money and I wouldn't bet on that changing anytime soon.

I've always liked the ideas behind Zachtronics games, and I own all of them besides Infinifactory, but this is the first one to really get me hooked. I can't really put my finger on what does it for me, but this is easily my Zachtronics game of choice now.

Expectation:
Finally a Zachtronics puzzler I can play.
Reality:
Stuck for over an hour in a puzzle in chapter 1 and there 5 more chapters to go.

Best Zachtronics game yet.
So I'm a fan of the Zachtronics formula: simple yet engaging narrative over an extremely well-polished puzzle mechanic. I've played (and enjoyed) Space Chem, Ironclad Tactics, and Shenzhen I/O, but Opus Magnum is, well, an accurate title.
The story is not deep, but I honestly found myself eager to open every new puzzle just to read the missives and conversations. The characters have a surprising amount of personality for ones you never actually meet or interact with, and I felt connected to them.
The mechanic is *extremely* satisfying. As usual, it has been tested an tweaked and feels like there aren't really any rough edges. Moreover, I feel like they did a very good job with the scoring system. Yes, it still uses the classic "here's a histogram of what all the other players did", but I felt very much more in control of how I wanted to optimize my crazy alchemy machine. Some puzzles I'd make as fast as possible, area and cost be damned; some I'd try to be frugal; some I'd strike a balance. (For those of you who love compact solutions, there's all of the production alchemy puzzles in the epilog---it's a nice bump in difficultly after you've finished the main story, definitely recommended.)
As for drawbacks, there are a few: it's not an especially long game. I mean, there will *always* be more puzzles, but you can completely explore every corner of the game in not too short order, so you will eventually lose that "oh, well *that's* a neat trick I hadn't thought of before" feeling. Also, at least in the version I played, I felt the controls weren't explained completely. I mean, you can totally get by with what they tell you, but there's a whole other set of options that make it much smoother and quicker to create machines (for instance, they didn't need to wait until the epilog to tell you that you can rotate pieces while you have them picked up with the mouse). If you poke around in the steam discussions, you can pick these up without too much trouble (holding alt and clicking on an instruction is my personal favorite---fast-forward-and-pause). I definitely recommend getting used to the keyboard shortcuts; it's much faster and smoother to create machines.
Anyways, long story short, Zachtronics basically remade Space Chem, except better in basically evey dimension. If you like that, get this. It's totally worth it.
It is so satisfying when after watching your machine fail you finally figure out what you did wrong and fix it.

SpaceChem is a masterpiece.
The challenge here is to create specific chemical compounds by rearranging the atomic structure of the given compound(s) and delivering them to the destination through a pipes. You accomplish this using a series of reactors which can add, remove or re-arrange the atoms of a compound: each of these is a puzzle in and of itself. Deciding how many and which type of reactor to use in each level provides a sort of macro puzzle. Many levels limit the type and/or number or reactors available, providing variety in addition to aesthetic and compound differences. You can save and load reactor layouts, allowing you to use them in different levels.
Each level is so brilliantly complex in that you are not only trying to construct the most efficient way to modify the compounds within each reactor, you must also consider the overall purpose of each reactor in sequence: given that most compounds require several different reactors to change them into the desired result.
Additionally (yes, there is more: bear with me, it will be worth it!), each level must be completed within a certain time frame or 'cycles'. Transporting each compound from the start to the destination takes time, as does modifying them through each reactor. If not designed efficiently, you may end up with bottlenecks in your chain of reactors, leading to the overall level time being too slow. This is usually fixed through some minor tweaking and provides another level of strategic planning to the each levels.
I found the muisic to be quite enjoyable and the astheic both functional and pleasing to look at. There is an overacrching story, which is told between levels. It is very well written, and quite interesting. I fear however, that I will never see the end of the story, due to my own incompetence and to the sheer complexity and intricacy of the puzzles.

Look, I know it's hard. I understand that individual atoms are awkward to manipulate and bond and warp, but don't give me that. I don't care if the foods not great, or the machines are broken, or if there's a giant cyclops pyramid shooting lasers at you; get it done.
Oh, and nice work on that quarterly.

I got this game in the Humble Bundle and decided to try it out. The concept interested me, "sentient corn?!" For some reason, I thought this was a horror game... It's not, just so you know.
PROS:
+ Story kept me playing through to the end. It was the only thing that kept me playing, and I honestly don't know why I felt I had to finish the story, but still.
+ Music is well-done. Not stellar, but quite well-done.
+ Tom and Bob are hilarious. I actually wish there had been more of their memos lying around.
+ Visuals are nice. Not exceptional, but I liked them.
CONS:
- Extemely easy. The game feeds you everything you need. It's simply a matter of wandering around until you find the right object.
- There is literally only one place in the game where you can die, as far as I can tell. And I died there, because it's a real shock when the section starts. But whatever, it's not hard at all, you just have to move fast.
- The folio is useless. I believe it's supposed to help you understand things a little better? Instead, you pick up rocks. And garbage. And get insulted by the descriptions.
- Vladdy is annoying. He's funny for the first two minutes, then tiresome. The best part about him is that he walks so slowly you usually don't have to listen to his teddy-bear-feet squeaking.
- Saw the ending coming from about halfway through the game. Rather disappointing.
- So short. As you can see, I finished the whole game in under 5 hours. And there's no replay value, because there's only one way to do everything, and only one story.
- Occasional movement glitches. I'd run into an invisible *something* in the middle of a field.
CONCLUSION:
I'm glad I got this game as part of a Humble Bundle. If I'd bought it on its own, I'd be disappointed.
That said, if you have 5 hours to spend and you don't want to test your anything, this fits the bill nicely. But don't pay full price.
FINAL RATING: 2/7

8/10
+
- You can always count on Bioware to create interesting, lovable characters (for the most part). I particularly liked the 'banter dialougue' between them during gameplay which seemed less structured and linear than Mass Effect. Alistair and Morrigan were my favourites. Their banter was hilarious.
+
- For me, the music in this game was right up there with The Last of Us. The second I booted up and heard the title screen track I knew it was getting added to my spotify playlist.
+
- I liked that you had the option of real-time combat or (my preferred) paused, tactical combat. The ability to roll back the viewing angle into a birds-eye view was apprecated too. Regardless of which style you choose, you still have to choose each move and watch it get played out for you. Some find this tedious, but I enjoyed the more strategic vibe.
+
- As with all Bioware games I've played so far, the VA was insanely good. There's nothing worse then getting pulled out of the moment by rubbish acting
.
+
- I like fantasy worlds and this was exactly that. Right down to the Elves, Orcs, and Dragons. I've read large parts of the codex and had a look online at the expanded lore (books etc) and I can see there's tons of it. The more thought and effort put into expansive world, the better.
+
- The choices I made felt like they mattered in this game. I spent way too long agonising over possible outcomes before making a major decision and to my delight (and sometimes horror) I saw a lot of it come true.
+

- I was surprised to find an active modding community around this game considering its age. There was a plethora of (Nexus) mods to choose from and I spent too much time digging through them all. I personally went for
and
as well as some others.
-
- I had read about the fade level online and was anticipating it. I didn't hate it as much as I thought I would, but I definitley wasn't having a blast playing through it. The Orzammar section, on the other hand, was torure. I don't know if it's because i'm just not a fan of traditional high-fantasy Dwarves (I hated all Dwarven ruins in Skyrim too), or because it was genuinly unlikable, but holy Christ I was bored. I had such a hard time motivating myself to push through this level that I stopped playing for over a month. I can't see myself replaying this game purely because of this chunk.
-
- After a couple hours I was too engrossed to care, but there is no denying the graphics and textures in this game are outdated. I'm sure there are mods to help with this, but if you want to play vanilla and care way too much about the visuals then it's hard to recommend this game.
In conclusion, I had a mostly great time playing this game. I can't see myself replaying anytime soon, but I will 100% be playing the sequels and Bioware's other old games.

Project Zomboid is easily one of the most played games in my Library, standing at, at the time of this post, 1,214.2 hours. I've owned this game for years now, and have seen both the good, and the bad.
The Pros:
+++ This game does what so few others actually do. Realistic survival in the apocalypse, forfilling a nich in the gerne while still applying to the whole zombie apocalypse. You have your standard inventory, but if you want have a backpack? Sure, that backpack has it's own inventory space- But fill up that backpack too heavily, and it can still weigh you down. You want some of that river water? Sure, make sure to clean it first. Weapons, including guns, will break with over use. Eat bad food for months on end, and you'll find yourself a tad bit unhealthy. Want power after the power cuts? Gotta find a generator- But your character needs to know how to connect properly before he can use it.
And most of all, Beware the all powerful bite. You're not immune. If you are bitten, prepare to join the ranks of the undead.
+++ Play the game how you want to. You want to loot the entire map and amass a horde of goods? Be my guest. You want to craft your own improvised tools? Be my guest. Do you want to turn the mall into a fortress of (un)death? Be my guest. Or maybe, you want to build your own Anti-Zombie fortress. Scavange for food, or farm/hunt/fish your food.
+++ In addition to realism above, contend with not just the dead, but your own personal feelings. If you find yourself trapped in a building, you have to find a way to entertain your character, lest his own bordem, and eventually depression, cripple him before the undead leave. You can carry more weight than your main limit- Bare in mind however the heavier it gets after that, the slower, and more tired you become. Beware weather slowing and sickening you. Don't leave corpses around, unless you want to fall ill. Be ready to deal with different kinds of wounds, not all can simply be bandaged and left alone.
+++ Pure single player customability. The game offers a very wide variety of options for your game, down to integers. You want zombies to hear you chop a tree from blocks away? You can make it so. You want them to run you down like an olympic sprinter? That can be arranged. You want to find boxes of construction supplies everywhere? That can be arranged? You want to find /none/ at all? That can be arranged.
You want it to rain every five seconds? Fine. You want it to be dry as hell? Cool. Maybe you want farming to go fast, slow, produce more, produce less, maybe you want generators everywhere, maybe you want the map power to stick around for almost forever.
You can either make it the easiest apocalypse ever, or get down and dirty in worst case scenario class three outbreak hell.
+++Active Dev Community
While some may blast the development community for not adding in NPC's as of yet, don't let that disuade you from believing the Dev's are lazy. They make a constant log of their activites every monday, and often showcase their latest work. They are constantly putting out new beta versions of their game for anyone to help test, and once they fix enough bugs, they slam it all toghther, and work on the next set. For an early access game, such communication from the development team is a good sight, when compared to games such as *Cough* Starmade *Cough*
+Game Atmosphere
Take a walk around the town in game, even with zombies off. Seems like it's abandoned, yes? Even pristine?
As time goes on, that'll change. At first, you'll notice corpses in houses killed by no one, but tons of empty bleach bottles, or half taken medicne tablets. You'll see little signs, such as West Points "They will not take me" written in between buildings.
Fast forward a few months. Vines crawl up the sides of buildings, grass make their way into a growing system of cracks on the road. Trees begin to close into civilization. Enough time, and what were once plains in some areas, will be newborn forests, and what was once a thriving town in life, is a slowly decaying hunk of concrete and metal. And that's without the zombies.
Even worse, while NPC's aren't around, you'll hear 'Meta game events', or the Game's version of a left for dead AI director. Listen as dogs bark in the distance- And zombies near you go away to investigation. Helicopters from the outside world will roam, spot you, fly over- And draw the dead to you on accident. Gunshots sound in the distance, but when you go to investigate, you only find a few corpses of the dead. While the game has yet to introduce NPC's since it's very first few builds, it makes it clear that you're not the only one surviving, and that you could be on the road, unspotted by the hordes, only for some fool META GAME npc to fire off a shot blocks away, and the hungry eyes turn to you in their search.
+++Modability
Hydrocraft in of itself is something you'd want to check out. While the base game provides a lot in of itself, Hydrocraft is simply a /must have/ for those wishing to fill out the game world, and gives you many, many options on how to play the game. But it is by no means the only one- There's even a mod that adds in a tempoarily version of NPCs, if you're willing to do a little file work!
Cons:
-While the graphic design doesn't truely bother me, and infact pleases me, some people around me find that the isometric style of the game is a tad off putting, some prefering a first person experince, which they won't find here. While the game uses a sigh system to determine what your character can actually see or hear at any given point or time, this fact alone may bother you.
---Development time.
The DEV's /are/ active, and they /do/ develope a lot- However, while I personally find nothing wrong with their work time, others would like to poke at how they have yet to do NPC's for /years/. While this can be attirubted to the fact that they have to work everything else out, so that they can code in an NPC's ability to use it, it is something to note that some features wildly praised, are something you won't see for a while yet- They have their priorites.
-S/MP
Single player can become quickly, and utterly boring, if you're the type to play with others. There is simply so much to do with no set goal save 'survive', that playing alone seems... A waste of time almost. Thankfully, multiplayer exists, but beware a certain amount of server induced bugs that cause 'lag bites' or wonky combat.
It is, all in all, a game I thoroghly enjoy, perhapes too much given my record of it, and is something that for it's price, is incrediably worth it in my opinion. And if you get a few friends toghther to start playing a single map on it? All the power to you, my friend.

Alright, I'm going to give you the full rundown of everything I know about this game:
Technical aspect: The game isn't particularly fantastic looking, but it's easy enough on the eyes. Performance-wise, you may need to lower some of the settings to get good performance.
Community aspect: There is no community. If you're going to play this game, play it with four other people and get in a Discord or something. Matchmaking is a desolate wasteland.
Pricing aspect: Unless this game is on a good sale (50% off or more), it's not worth it. I don't want Turtle Rock/2K to be rewarded for their frankly-♥♥♥♥♥♥ practice of creating a game as a platform to sell an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of DLC. Granted, the hunters ARE unique, as are the monsters, but 5 bucks per hunter, 10 per monster is just crazy.
So why is my recommendation a yes?
Because of the sheer potential the game has. 4v1, each character has a VERY unique, VERY important role. Getting your teamwork down pat is absolutely crucial, and when you do it right, it feels SO BLOODY GOOD. It's amazing. In addition, while they're charging for most of it, the new hunters DO seem fairly cool, unique, and nuanced.
Any time I think or hear of this game, I'm overcome with sadness. It's a fantastic core gameplay loop that got drowned out in bad PR---deserved, of course---due to its terrible business model. If you can find a bunch of other people to play it with in a private room, this can be an absolutely worthwhile purchase, but only if those very-specific conditions are met.
Dammit, 2K.

I'm not one for horror games, and actually liking them, but this game is just great.  From the start you're just thrust into a world of the unexplained, finding various bits of information and piecing together your own version of what is going on.  There isn't some giant guy following you around and getting you to run faster into the unknown.
There isn't a limited battery life.
There isn't mundane "quests" that are just busy work to prolong the life of the game.
There is just an explorer, looking for answers as to what this place is about. Strange phenomena lurk nearby, catch you off guard, and give you a sense of "something is out there, I don't know what it is, I don't know where it is, but it is out there" is always tugging at your mind.  That, in my eyes, is more frightening than anything I've played in other horror games.
Try it, it's worth the price of admission.

Baldur's Gate is a very popular classic RPG, much beloved by many fans of RPGs of the era. As someone who did not play the game on the original release, it is all very fresh for me in spite of the rather dated visuals and gameplay. While the enhanced edition does improve on the visuals tremendously, the game still feels very dated. It is excellent for nostalgia, and I am sure fans of the original will rejoice in the release. Those of us who never played the original may find it a bit more difficult to enjoy, with a somewhat high bar for entry and a necessity for at least a basic understanding of AD&D rules. It is an excellent game for its time, and if you enjoy classic RPGs you will love it. However if you have not played the original and do not have the patience to learn a complex game system, you may not like it.

Under the veneer of "sci-fi dungeon crawler/roguelike tower deference," this game is fundamentally a resource management game with an unhealthy dose of random. There is, presumably, some element of skill involved, although I can't see how it's possible to adequately plan when resources are tied to your progression through a dungeon of unpredictable shape and length. Similarly, whether you survive or not when transporting the crystal to the level exit appears to be purely at the whim of the game itself; so far as I can tell, the only strategy is to run and hope you don't die.
A good rogue-lite gives you the sense from the beginning that your deaths are your own fault and you will get better. Dungeon of the Endless leaves no such impression. If anything, a few runs convinced me most or all of my deaths will be out of my control, and any successes I have will likewise be unearned and arbitrary.
Oh, and it's not even remotely fun.

Alright. This review is from someone who never played the original Baldur's Gates.
For me, this game was really hard to get into. I kept starting it, spending an hour trying to get the highest roll on my character, and then when I got to the game, the graphics just completely turned me off. I felt like maybe I was just too late and my palate had been tainted by newer games. So about a week ago I decided to force myself to spend a couple hours to give the game a fair shot. I am very pleased with myself that I made that decision.
The characters, atmosphere, dialogue trees, and challenging fights really make this game quite enjoyable. Character customization feels limited compared to newer titles like Neverwinter Nights 2 and Dragon Age Origins, but you can see very clearly how this game is the early ancestor of those titles. Despite the limitations of being an older title, Baldur's Gate feels incredibly deep. It's also a lot darker in some ways than most newer rpgs are.
I suppose if I'm being objective, I can name a couple criticisms.
It seems like your party members sometimes have a hard time going to a spot that you tell them to, especially if you have your whole party selected. For example, one of the party members will randomly decide to take the long way ALL the way around a mountain instead of just going a much shorter distance to his destination. So it kind of forces you to be on your toes and really micromanage your party's individual movements, and not in the "good" "hardcore rpg micromanagement" kind of way.
Actually, that's the only criticism I can think of. I like this game so much I decided to make my avatar Xzar. "Montaron! I... I never loved you!"
Easy 8/10 if taking its age into consideration. Newer or more casual gamers may not be able to get into this game very easily, but you should really give it your best effort!
Edit: Seems like a lot of people are complaining about crazy bugs and other problems. Just for the record, I never had a single problem. But just keep those in mind.

Only five hours in but I'm having a TON of fun, and it's only in alpha.
THE QUICK VERSION: Do you like Gnomoria (or Dwarf Fortress)? Do you like Minecraft? If you answered "yes" to either of these, you'll most likely enjoy this game. If you answered "yes" to both, you'll DEFINITELY enjoy this game.
THINGS TO LIKE:
+ The building system is the most robust of any citybuilder I've seen to date. You not only get to lay out buildings for your Hearthlings to construct (very intuitively, in my experience!) but you get to place furniture within and without at your whim. There's already a great deal of different types of furniture and decor your Hearthings can craft.
+ The music is excellent. It's rich and well composed, and it gives the game a very quaint feel.
+ Game generation is simple but fun and really makes you feel like you're having an impact on your game before it even starts. You roll a set of Hearthlings, each with their own stats, and can even name them. You also get an amount of gold to spend on a selection of items to start yourself off with. You select your options in storybook form when the game asks you to pick between two types of Hearthlings (one medieval-ish group and one nomadic, desert-like group), two types of biomes (temperate or desert), and two types of game (either you can be raided by enemies or you can't). Then your map is generated and you select where on that map you want to settle. Each region has access to different resources.
+ Trade events. Just about every day, a trader will come by offering different deals. You can buy or sell certain goods from some, some will ask you to make them x number of items then come back after a set amount of time to trade you something agreed upon for them... It keeps things fresh and gives you new ways to get resources you maybe don't have access to based on where you settled.
+ Hearthling jobs. There are several different jobs in the game and they all feel useful. Every Hearthling starts off as a basic laborer, who can only gather resources, haul them, or build. With items (most of which are constructed by the various crafting jobs), you can promote a hearthling to any number of other jobs such as Farmer, Carpenter, Tailor or Trapper. Every job has levels that increase as your Hearthling performs that job and gains experience. At each tier, a new ability is unlocked. These range from increased speed to the ability to randomly create high-quality furniture that takes on a finer appearance than the base item being crafted. Many jobs are also laid out in a tree wherein you must have a Hearthling of level x in one job to promote to another. For example, Cook requires Farmer at level 3.
+ The ability to save your building designs for easy placement later.
THINGS THAT NEED WORK:
- Currently it's very difficult (possible though!) to build a second floor that functions. I'm sure this will be ironed out as the game plods along in development, though.
- A few of the job abilities aren't implemented yet, but this will definitely be remedied later just on nature of the status being "not implemented".
- You get occasional errors when trying to do things, pretty much always in regards to building. They haven't crashed the game for me, it's basically just the game telling me the engine didn't understand what I was trying to do.
- Sometimes the building bugs a bit, but all that generally means is that you have to cancel building and start designing from the start again. Bit of a pain, but with trial and error, you'll get where you're going, and this is sure to be ironed out in the long term.
FINAL VERDICT:
It's already an incredibly addictive game for me. In its current state, I'd rate the game a solid 7.5/10. It has the potential to be at LEAST a 9. If for whatever reason you trust my opinion, I'd tell you this game is worth the buy right now. It's one of the sharpest alpha states I've ever seen for a game and there's already so much to enjoy and lose hours in. Five hours in, I've only scratched the surface of jobs and the like and I'm still going strong. I can see myself easily logging over 100 hours in this thing.

As one who has played this game on and off for close to 20 years,  this is THE classic WW2 online flight sim.  If you want realistic flight models, an opportunity to fly in historical events run by the community and supported by the publisher, and a mature community, then this is for you.
Most of the negative reviews will be for the graphics and to an extent the difficulty of the flight models.  It takes a little time to learn how to fly effectively, but the payoff is that you are getting as close as it gets to what it might feel like to have flown one of these planes into action in WWII.  Great community of people, good trainers, and most of the all, the weekly S3 series is immersive and REAL.  Want to experience what it was like to escort B17's deep into Germany against the Luftwaffe, where you are constantly looking over your shoulder wonder if those dots on your high 6 are 190's?  This is it!  The rush of making a clean kill in these series is as good as it gets!
I think the game needs a graphics update, and some work on gameplay, but if realism, immersion, and a great mature community are important, then this has it in spades.

Last but not least, the music is great, which is good because you'll be listening to it a lot.

Highly recommended game if you're into indies, and a mix of tower defence with rogue-like elements. The game offers you a "Too easy" difficulty which I skipped and went directly into easy thinking "Meh, how hard can it be?" Only to be devoured by waves of diverse monsters on the 2nd floor. The characters are diverse, each with their pros and cons that fill multiple roles into a team of 4, there are also 4 characters from TF2 which I absolutely love being a veteran of that game. Multiple "modules" to build from which offer resource income, support, defensive and offensive towers. Think tower defence, resource management and beautiful atmospheric monster hunting in a space ship with odd characters and lovely backgrounds.

The game has two difficulties, "very easy" and "easy" which are actually "normal" and "hard." This is the only thing that bugs me about the game. Make sure if you play the game to play on "very easy" for your first playthrough. There are also different game modes that you can unlock for more replayability once you've beaten the game that make it even harder.
The game is a fun roguelike defense. Two different genres combined. Think FTL, Binding of Isaac, or Darkest Dungeon combined with a typical wave defense game like Plants vs Zombies, Bloons, or Kingdom Rush. You explore each floor room by room and power these rooms while gathering resources and setting up your defenses until you find the exit and escape to the next floor. Your characters can level up and get equipment as well. It even has multiplayer capability.
I definitely recommend this game if you enjoy roguelike games as well as tower defenses.
I am terrible at this game, but I'm sure someone who could get the hang of it would have a blast.

A recommended classic.
If you pick this one up, consider that it's nearly 17 years (I think) old.
While this game won't win any awards for graphics these days, the gameplay is still the only one available to my knowledge that centers around the WW2 B-17 bomber. Consider this being a game about 17 years old though. Graphics for that time was stunning as I remember it, and while it somewhat struggles today, it still holds up enough to be playable.
In the game you can control all different crewmembers, as much or as little as you like, so if all you want to do is tag along and when time comes for the bomb run, you'll do that, that works fine. On the other end is taking care of navigation, fighting off bogeys, piloting the aircraft and so forth. So do all you want, or as little as you want, it up to you. If you really want to dig into it, there's also the option to sign up as squadron commander, wich will mean that you'll plot targets and the approach to said targets, pick bombs to use etc.
Considering the age, the options available, and the amount of different difficulty settings available, this game really shows what kind of work could be put into a game back then. You can either go with a simpler approach of gameplay, you can do the full simulation, or anything in-between, and enemy/friendly experience can also be adjusted depending on the experience you want. What you'll find out though is that this is a very good game of doing bomber missions over Germany 1943-1945.
Of course, a remake would be very nice, but it doesn't look like that will  happend, and no one has even bothered to re-work or mod the current game, other than some nose art and olive drab skins, but bottom line is that this is the only real B-17 game around. So if that's what you want to experience, this is the way you do it.

This game gives you the feeling as no other does. Many people play IL-2 Sturmovik to get the feeling of true dogfights and bombing. While this game is old, it still offers immaculate physics as well as the opportunity to control every aspect of the daily bombers life. Positions go from various gunner positions, the navigator, radio operator, bombardier, and even pilot. It doesn't quite stop there, as one can even take it a step further and control friendly/enemy fighter aircraft operating in the airspace with the B-17. You can step foot down on the runway as a bomber commander, or take it a step higher and take control of the entire bombing squadron. As the squadron leader, you can plan the missions (including loadout, select what bombers, and what point you wish to bomb on the map) and also be part of the mission inside of the leading bomber. This game gives me a feeling of excitement as I wait for my 1000 lb. General purpose bombs spill their way into Brest harbor, ruining enemy trading routes. I'm proud to have this in my library, and can honestly say I've put many hours well spent into this game.

As some others may have mentioned - Warbirds is, at it's heart, an on-line, massive multiplayer, very realistic WWII flight simulation. It has  extensive offline options that can be enjoyed for itself - well worth the price - these are used by members of the on-line community to hone their skills and as a learning center for new players to develope their flying skills. They can be enjoyed for themselves but the real action is head-to-head play online.
It certainly does NOT require continual in-game purchases to upgrade and/or grinding to get into an aircraft that is competitive. From day one - in off-line and on-line play (depending on historical arena timeframes & subscription) all aircraft and loadouts are available. The selection is entirely up to you.
The flight models are as realistic as the WB development team can make them and they are based on actual performance data. Some aircraft are more forgiving than others - just as they were in real life. There is a learning curve as in all flight sims. A joystick will be the preferred controller - you don't need a super pricey model.
And the community is very welcoming and helpful, esp. for new players.  Well worth the investment!

(3 years of prior experience before Steam version)
Right first things first this isn't War Thunder so if you are looking for flashy graphics this isn't the combat sim for you. Where this sim compromises on graphics it makes up for it in its large open area online combat in arenas spaning 100s of square miles full of targets, such as airbases, towns, docks, supply depots and carrier battle groups. The aim is in closing the enemies bases/towns etc. to allow friendy troop transports to paratroop and capture them for your side, with victory being achieved when you control all of the map (though don't expect it in a single day cause as mentioned they are LARGE maps).
Flying is not to difficult as long you don't stall ('Realistic' flight mode), I recommend using a joystick not a gamepad, and flying the training and offline combat in easy flight mode first in order to get a feel of the 100+ aircraft (all of which are available to fly, none of this unlocking and paying for special types), though I do stress that all online flight is with the 'realistic' flight mode so get the hang of flying with it on before venturing into the online arenas.
The aircraft models are are mixture of realism and the need to allow ease of playability, and I will say straight away to head off the 'they don't fly realisticly' crowd, of course they won't this is a COMPUTER SIMULATION (this is why I put qoutes unquotes Realistic above), as with all sims compromises had to be made in order to have a large number of combat flyable types within a 4gig package ALL READY TO FLY FROM THE GET GO!!
That being said each aircraft has its own quirks, and you need to know whether the type you are flying is a 'Turn and Burner' Like say the Spitfire and A6M Zero or a 'Boom and Zoomer' like the Bf109 and F4U Corsair, because this will dictate how you use them in combat. Also bombers, you need to know whether you will need a full fuel load or not cause this will dictate whether you would be able to take off or not with that heavy bomb load of yours.
The online community is for the majority freindly and approachabl with great comradeship within the arenas and the different sqauds available to join once you have been flying online a while. Though the number of online players will Vary from day to day and within in the different timezones due to us all spread out over different countries.
I also recommend getting the free downloadable TeamSpeak com system since this is where all squad voice coms are controlled.
As a note basic online membership is around $13 a month or there abouts (don't qoute me on that) and that gets you unlimited access to the main arena.
I am sure to have forgotten to mention a large number of things but these are what I could remember off the top of my head for the time being.

This is a great game and a must have for any fan of the Fire Pro Series.  Is the next level to Fire Pro Wrestling Returns.

If you weren’t ready to rumble, now would be the perfect time. Fire Pro Wrestling World is the latest installment of the beloved Japanese pro wrestling series which also marks its first appearance on the PC. Old school fans will remember fumbling through complicated menus and memorizing a handful of Hiragana letters in order to play. Not anymore! This groundbreaking grappler has never been more accessible and the addition of the Steam Workshop means it’s never been easier to fight your wildest dreams to the death.
The formula hasn’t changed much, but it didn’t have to. Take your surprisingly-detailed 2D combatant into the 3D squared circle and wreak havoc. A new tutorial mode exists to make things easier on rookies, but everything is as straight-forward as ever. Only a jabroni would even consider button mashing. Fire Pro has always been about perfectly timing your moves and balancing your stamina en route to a flawless victory. Tag teams, steel cages, barbed wire, battles royal, landmines, kickboxing, MMA rules, or just plain old fashioned pro wrestling are just a few of the options available to you. Outside of the fighting, Fire Pro has always been about customization. Design your own refs, rings, belts, movesets, and, of course, wrestlers, with an easy-to-use editor featuring an impossible number of combinations. It’s the only wrestling game you’ll ever need and arguably the only one that ever needed to be made. Fight!

THE DEFINITIVE pro-wrestling game. Fire Pro Wrestling World iterates on past titles, adding a slew of new match types, moves, customization options, easy modding, and online multiplayer for the first time ever.
Unlike other wrestling games which operate on stamina and special move gauges, Fire Pro allows its players complete freedom in how a wrestling match is played out. On the one hand, it boasts solid striking and a deep pacing system where early on small moves soften the opponent up for big moves. This makes matches feel tight and competitive, while still feeling like a pro-wrestling match (as opposed to a fighting game). On the other, players are also free to allow their wrestler to take big moves early, to heighten the drama or create a squash match. Also available are MMA (both ring and octagon), boxing, K1, and deathmatches (both barbed wire and explosive), tournaments, and league play.
Thanks to Steam Workshop integration, you don't have to dive into the somewhat-tedious character creator, and your active rosters can be as varied as you wish. At the time of writing, my personal subsribtion count sits at almost 750 wrestlers-- spanning many eras and promotions of actual pro-wrestling, to TV, anime, games, books, and movies. If you've ever wanted to see Trump get a fork jammed in his forehead by an angry Homer Simpson, for example, you can absolutely get that done in this game. Factions, stables, promotions, and the like are easy to set up and transfer wrestlers into. You can even set whether a particular group is loved or jeered by the crowds.
Also exciting is the devs' embrace of the modding community. Many mod-packs exist (some even stickied on the steam discussion board by the developers), allowing for basic things like ring textures all the way to rule changes or completely new match types (inferno deathmatch! explosive balloon deathmatch! K1 rules!). Mods are exceedingly simple to apply, as well.
I've yet to play any online matches, so I'll not comment on the netcode other than to say I haven't seen many complaints about it. I will mention that the game supports at least four local players for all your tag-team and fatal four-way needs, and also allows for a mix of player-controlled and AI wrestlers to participate together.
All in all, Fire Pro Wrestling World understands what pro-wrestling is about: freedom of expression. From the minutae of holding a button to sell a slam long enough for your opponent to climb a turnbuckle and make themselves famous, to the much broader strokes of deciding who you want in your game, in what promotion, in what ring, in what match type, for what belt, FPWW has it all.

Getting an headache has never been so much fun. SpaceChem is a puzzle game where you lay down a path for two "Waldo"s (cursors) to make modifications to atoms and molecules. These two Waldos can activate commands like grab/drop, add/remove bond, rotate, input/output ect. The game starts simple, but gets more challenging over time, but never overwhelms you.
The power of this game is the complexity while it only uses these simple commands, testing your creativity and making solving puzzles oh so rewarding. And with the provided level-editor and active community, you have access for a near-infinite amount challenging puzzles. Buy SpaceChem if you like puzzles and the rewarding feeling of solving them.

If you're a science geek, a logic nerd, or just anyone that enjoys stretching their think-sponge, play this game. It's got a fun story, and makes you solve crazy puzzles to advance.
8/10 - Think-sponge likey.

Fiendish puzzler involving manufacturing chemicals by linking together atoms to create one molecule at a time.  This game is essentially an excercise in programming process flow with logical functions.  At its best it makes you feel smart, at its worst you're stuck for hours with no progress feeling very dumb, certainly a game you have to work at for your rewards.

Hands down, this is one of the best puzzle games I've ever had the pleasure of playing. It may seem intimidating, but you don't need to know anything about chemistry to play. It almost reminds me of those exercises where your partner is blind-folded in an obstacle course and relies on your instructions to manoeuvre through it and manipulate objects, only instead, your telling a teeny-tiny machine what to do with atoms. It really is worth checking out if you really like puzzle games that allow creativity with multiple solutions and make you think.

The puzzles require a great amount of thinking. Solving them and watching your algorithmic solutions execute is very rewarding. The learning curve is perfect, each new level is challenging just enough. It never gets boringly easy, nor does it get desperately difficult, though close enough to keep the brain busy.

My Overall rating for KHOLAT:  80/100
Kholat is a survival atmospheric horror game, where you should do two things. Both finding the clues and enjoying the atmosphere of rough Russian mountain country. Produced by Polish developers, game was supposed to rely more on visuals and this should intense the story, mysterious and creepy in its very nature. Lets see in details on the aspects of the game.
GAMEPLAY
+ Open world
+ Impressive atmosphere
+ Useful devices - a map and a flashlight
+ Accesible notes
+ Main anomalies
+ Nice story about speculative incident
o Map orientation
- Inability to jump
Gameplay is decent, and it reminded me another game designed in this way (The Vanishing of Ethan Carter). What I evaluate as the most positive, is open world and atmosphere. You are able to explore the world as you wish and the night at Russian mountain accompanied by perfect soundtrack. Yes, you have to seek for notes and clues behind the Dyatlov Pass Incident, but you can give yourself a beautiful time just walking around and enjoying the sceneries.
Also, the story is perfectly designed, it does not show the only right possibilities, but it lets you have your own theory by giving another point of view, which you can live through the notes and environment.
It is a great idea to use only map and compass for orientation, furthermore, you have to rely on your memory, because there is no "GPS" to show, what your current position is. But, there is one confusion, though the North is on the lower side of the map, when you are going north, you are approaching the upper side. After realising this, the orientation is a piece of cake. And there needs to be mentioned, that compass and flashlight are going nuts, when anomalies approach, so you know you have to walk away swiftly.
The most negative was the inability to jump. Seriously, one rock and your progress is delayed, until you find a route around, what may disguise players from playing this game.
CHARACTERS
+ Beautiful voice acting
+ Sean Bean narration
+ Believable settings
+ Mixing with other event even beyond Soviet Union
o Mystery behind our hero
I like Sean Bean's reading of some notes and telling the crucial points. Even the voice of the female student is perfect, you can see, as the events went from paradise to complete horror. Settings were believable, everything is messed with another events, which are transcending even the existence of Soviet Union.
What confused me is our role, but the end was really creepy and shocking, I recommend to collect all notes to reveal it, you will be shocked. I did not know until the last moment, what might discourage people from playing the game.
VISUALS
+ Perfect sceneries
- Tree glitches and resolution
Sceneries are awesome, it can be called "Scenery Porn", they are really enjoyable, each screenshot can serve as wallpaper. But the resolution is not very well adapted for 1920x1080 screen, it is well compensated while playing, but after recording, you can see, that it is a bit lower, and I can not help myself, that nowadays, 1080p is a standard in gaming industry. I have encountered few glitches, when snow was "dancing" on the trees. Just details.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Well set according to the situation
+ Beautiful vocals
Soundtrack has no mistake, if you like the game music, it has a reasonable prize, for buying. It enhances the atmosphere and serves as a well designed addition to the game. Brilliant.
CONCLUSION
Kholat is a specific genre of game, very often named also as "walking simulator". I have to admit, that not everyone should like the game, but if you seek something, that will give you a decent story, stunning environment and some amount of creepiness, you will be pleasured. I also think, that even players outside this genre might be pleased.
So in the end, even despite some scars on the game, as inability to jump or confusing orientation in the beginning, I can recommend the game and soundtrack as well.
Go to the Russian wilderness and seek out the truth! Strongly recommended.

I played and completed Kholat live on stream last night
, me and my viewers were really enjoying the experience.
The things I liked: the atmosphere, the tension, the fact we had to use a compass and map; never have I ever had to be ofay in orienteering to play a game before, genius! The music was phenomenal, and I will be purchasing the soundtrack.
I didn't like the masses of uninterupted space I had to traverse, the long and boring journal entires. There is such a thing as too much text. I found it odd how some of these were voice acted and others were not. I didn't like how the game doesn't actually tell a story, the narrative was convulted and didn't really explain anything. I have pieced together parts of the puzzle and I may have come to 2+2=5, because this game is confusing, long winded and not very easy to understand.
As an experience I loved it, but as a horror game it was kinda meh! I found myself going from being cautious and being in awe at the bewildement I found myself, to just trudging along from place to place only getting shocked when I got startled by a cheap jump scare from a monster that just pops up out of nowhere with no visual or audio clues to warn of any impending danger.
The game has some big flaws, but on the flip side of that I did thoroughly enjoy my playthrough of it.
One thing that has left a sour taste in my mouth, was that god awful ending, that instead of the 'a ha' moment you're expecting, a moment that explains everything or stitches things together, you get..... nothing. It's open to interpretation, but because of how convulted the narrative is, how too many things are over explained, it is very diffuclt to comprehend exactly what they were going for, and it kinda makes the whole experience feel pointless!
Pros:
- Atmosphere
- Soundtrack
- Design
- Visuals
- Orienteering
Cons:
- Ending
- Narrative
- Not enough horror
- Too much uninterrupted traversal
- Sporadic jump scares without any warning of impending dangers
- Convulted
- Way too much text
As a game I would give this a 5 out of 10, but as an experience, because believe me, it was a great experience reagardless of it's gaming flaws, i'd give it a 7 out of 10.

Would I recommend this title? Yes, yes I would. I'm not going to gush on a game when it has so many flaws, I have to be neutral when writing these reviews, but I really enjoyed myself playing Kholat, and I didn't allow the flaws to ruin my time with this game.

Kholat is an okay horror game.  It's not bad but compared to the other horror games I've played this one is a bit slow.  Boring actually. I like realism but that's a bit extream.  This game is very non-linear and open world.  That's good in one aspect but since the navigation is very basic it's easy to get lost and the game doesn't nudge you in the right direction.  The only hints the game gives you is map coordinates written on a wall or you'll hear paper blowing in the wind to let you know you're near a note.  The good things about this game is the enviromental sounds, ambient sounds and graphics.  It really makes you feel like you're there.  For an open world horror game it's good but not as high-paced as other horror games.
