Very different to most zombie games, this is an isometric game with a heavy emphasis on 2D art assets and survival tactics. You have to manage your hunger, sleep, equipment, skills and most importantly, you have to avoid the walking dead horde outside. You can barricade windows, craft equipment and cook food. First things first - it is still far from finished. That hasn't stopped me playing just over 500 hours though. For a tenner that is possibly the best value game ever (besides Sensible Soccer).
Be aware that progress is slow because they're a small team with ideas that sometimes stretch the boundaries of what is realistically possible. That being said, it's the best zombie survival/strategy game going. Updates are only released when 99% finished - loads of betas to play about with as well.
Sure we'd all love the elusive NPCs introduced - arguably ahead of cars which in my opinion have taken up way too much time - especially when there's a perectly good public mod already out there. IMO NPCs should have been priority to add extra depth (again there's community mods but they're not perfect).
Overall it's an absolute bargain - you will care for your character until dying from a huge variety of reasons. It may take an hour of game-time, it could take years. This is why NPCs could offer a long term 'endgame' - but for now PZ aint't about that!
Final note - use the recent and well updated mods. Hydrocraft adds plenty of depth for example, and is kept relatively up to date to work with the latest versions. Cars mod is - in my opinion - better than the official beta version.

If you know Zachtronics games, you should have some idea what to expect here. Unlike previous games though, there are far fewer constraints placed on the player during each puzzle. With the exception of the final chapter (Which takes place after the main story and is an optional set of bonus challenges) there's no restriction on space, so you're free to let your machines sprawl as far as needed to get the job done. That's not to say the game is 'easy' per sei; it just means you can brute-force a solution that isn't very efficient if you just can't figure out how to get past a specific puzzle. There's plenty of room to optimise each solution, and when your machines work perfectly there's a sense of hypnotic beauty to them.
In summary, this is both a worthy choice to a veteran of these games, and an excellent place to try them out for the first time.

Short version: AWESOME!  If you like sandbox puzzle games, then this is a must-have.
Long version: In typical Zachtronics style, Opus Magnum has a very small set of "rules" you need to learn to play the game, which is basically assembling elements of a factory to produce end-products from basic ingredients. But these rules work for solving an unlimited number of puzzles. And use of the Steam Workshop means that you will be able to play new and interesting puzzles designed by other players for a really, really long time.
In Opus Magnum, you aren't constrained by floor space, or how efficiently you build your machine to solve the puzzle.  Where the real challenge comes in is that you can optimize your machine for area, cost, or time -- or a combination of the three. If you don't want to optimize, you can just solve the puzzle however you want -- which means if you want an "elegant" solution rather than a more optimal one, no problem.  This is the hallmark of Zachtronics games -- come up with a solution *your way*. Play how you want -- the game only stipulates what tools you can use and what the end result for each puzzle needs to be -- how you get there is entirely up to you. And this means you can also play the same puzzles over and over again and enjoy yourself every time.

Like Spacechem (more like The Codex of Alchemical Engineering if you remember that Flash game), only much more freeform in allowed solutions. Really fun if you like this kind of thing. A bit easier than usual Zachtonics fare due to the flexibility, but many wouldn't see that as a bad thing as his previous titles have been very difficult. The challenge here isn't so much beating the game, though that's not a cakewalk. The real challenge lies in optimizing solutions.
This is one of very few games I've immediately restarted upon beating it. The community made puzzles do a lot to extend the game as well, and are presented very nicely. Presentation and polish in general are very good, you can really see how Zach's games and team continue to evolve over time. I was a little disappointed that the story ended where it did but that's often the mark of an engaging storyline. The story doesn't add much to the game directly but it adds an enjoyable and interesting ambience and gives some context for the puzzles you're solving.
Here's hoping for some more official levels and a continuation of the intrigue!

I expect most people will find this game because they used to own it many years ago and wanted to revisit it. Good news - it still works on modern kit. Mostly.
If you're just uncovering this game, it's a bit of a gem but it's a sim, not an arcade game. Don't expect to pick this up in 5 minutes, and for the first few goes have the manual open on your phone or something. You'll need it! There's good tutorials in it but note the tutorials in the game don't tell you what to do. They're supposed to be played alongside the manual.
The game itself is big enough to support hundreds of hours of play (note the steam counter only tracks time spent in the launcher dialog). Each mission can consume an hour or so of time, making it quite frustrating when you've fought your way to the target and your bombs miss anyway. It's a sim and that happened in real life too!
You can do as much or as little as you like during the missions. Natural instincts are to take over the pilot role (being a flight sim and all), but this is probably one of the harder jobs as you need to manage the engines and the such as well as fly the plane. The co-pilot will assist, but perhaps best left alone until some of the keyboard shortcuts are mastered. I started by just taking over the bomb aiming (go through the tutorials), and a spot of navigation after each time jump. The navigator usually has the plane in slightly the wrong place, so you just have to drag it back once you've worked out where you are.
What is currently stopping me from exploring other bits of the game is I'm struggling to get the joystick working. This effectively prevents me from taking up the gunner and pilot positions. Other reviews suggest it could be some conflict with the mouse, so once I've had my fill of navigating and bombing I may investigate this a bit further.
In summary, if you like getting involved and want the full sim experience, there's a lot to be had from this game. If you just want to fly around and bomb some stuff for 5 minutes at a time, this isn't the game for you I'm afraid.

I tried Stonehearth on a whim after I had sworn to myself that I would never play an Early Access game ever again. This game has simply reaffirmed my convictions in this matter.
This is not to say that this game is terrible - it's not. It has potential, and there are a lot of good things about it. It has cute animations, enchanting music, and a nice crisp graphic style (although I must admit that the minecraft-esque aesthetic is getting a little old at this point).
As for how it plays, it is a minecraft derivative (not necessarily a bad thing), though instead of building and defending your settlement by yourself, you must order AI-controlled peons to do it for you. This is an excellent premise on paper, and sometimes it works beautifully. Watching your peons work, collect, harvest, eat, sleep and fulfill their tasks is sometimes very rewarding.
However, in many other ways, this game leaves something to be desired. The UI is confusing, tutorials are nonexistent, the camera controls are clunky, the building tools are even clunkier, and the minion AI is so glitchy that they will fail to build even the simplest of structures. Even the basic building designs that are shipped with the game will be left incomplete by your peons once they start building despite having all of the materials available. This forces you to scrap those structures in an attempt to build them again, and of course, there's no guarantee that your peons will actually finish them the second time they try.
Other crippling bugs include peons who will simply freeze in place and refuse to move. Even when they become exhausted and start to starve, they won't move even to help themselves. The only way I've found to fix this is to reassign them to another job, but in doing so, they lose all of their accumulated levels. Not fun!
Issues like these are a bit concerning, considering that the game is over halfway through Early Access by now. But even with the bugs aside, Stonehearth seems to be sorely lacking in content. The plain, empty expanses of the landscape really aren't very stimulating and there's very little to do out there. Once you get your settlement up and running (and it's not hard to do, despite the fact that most of your houses will be missing the odd door, wall or roof), you will simply repel invader attacks over and over again, collect whatever loot they drop, and continue to farm your crops.
This might actually be fun if the inventory management was enjoyable, but it's not. You can't really manipulate the objects in-game directly, so you have to rely on your peons to manage the plethora of items that you will craft and collect. Usually this means that they will throw them into an unsorted jumble within your stockpile; other times, they will squirrel it away in crates and boxes. If you have more than one, it will be anyone's guess as to which one they've put it in. If one of your items is missing and you can't seem to track it down, good luck finding it!
Stonehearth gave me a few moments of fun within the hours that I played it, but mostly I just felt bored and frustrated. It's a shame, because I really like the idea behind it. I may revisit it once it leaves Early Access, but if what I've seen is indicative of the final product, I could probably take it or leave it.
The good news is that the developers are providing regular updates and are obviously very dedicated to this project. It should improve over time. I really hope it does.

Great game. I recommend this game to anyone who likes creative sandbox games and even the casual RTS gamer.

Its great for releasing your inner creativity. Think of building something in Minecraft or Terraria, except not having to place each individual piece yourself. You design the building in a design mode and when you are finished editing you hit the build button and then your people do all the work. This makes building larger more complex structures much less time consuming. There is a building template saving feature so that your creations can be saved for other games. If you make a massive structure simply save it and you can copy paste it to another world, all you need is the materials.
The combat is fun as well, but can be turned off if you wish to play in the sandbox mode. Being able to assign units to gaurd (footmen) roles and creating/finding better gear for them to use. The game gets progressively harder to a point then seems to level out and nothing can defeat your footmen. But again its alpha and the combat was only just released so its basically there to be tested and tuned.
Multiplayer has not been implemented yet but it is planned in the future and I believe that this game has some great potential at some fun multiplayer gameplay.

I want to love this game.  There are a lot of good things going for it.  It has an interesting and original graphical style, the gameplay can be a lot of fun and can be really intense at times.  After playing a bit of the campaign since its recent release out of early access, I can't say I consider this a great game.  Good, yes but not great.  My reasoning on this is pretty much that they make the game unrealistically harder than it should be.
My main complaints here are:
1.  When it gets dark, you can't see at all.  Outside, I could see an argument for you not being able to see anything at night, since there is no light pollution presumably.  I don't know about you, but if the sun is shining brightly through a window in a house, I usually don't have to light a match to see what is in the room.  Kind of ridiculous unless they just expect you to crank up the gamma.
2.  You can't defend yourself unless you have a ranged weapon.  Seriously, if I have a hatchet in my inventory and a wolf is running towards me, I should be able to smack that wolf in the head instead of having to wait for it to knock me over, tear holes in me while a frantically press a button to stop it.
3.  It takes too long to do some tasks.  Breaking a branch into 3 sticks doesn't take 10 minutes.  Even if they are in-game minutes, it doesn't take that long.
4.  The game needs a little more love thrown into the details.  It just feels like all the broad strokes have been finished but since it is a full release, I expect a bit more refinement.  There's a lot of clipping as far as geometry in the models, the clothing you wear doesn't change how see yourself--equipping gloves, for example, will still show you doing all actions with bare hands.  The voice acting is pretty good, but for some reason they couldn't voice act all the dialog, just like 30% of it and the rest is just text.  There are some problems with sound--when wolves growl, they always sound like they are right next to you, even if they are 100 feet away.  Some words are randomly capitalized for seemingly no reason...idk if this is a Canadian thing or what.  But that's just me being a grammar purist.
I'm not sure if some of these issues will be fixed in days to come or if this 1.0 release is going to be more or less the final product.  I get this is a smallish indie studio, maybe they are just lacking the manpower or the monetary means to get all these things done.  I find my immersion and enjoyment of a game increases when the game is very well polished, but to me The Long Dark just isn't there yet.

I only recommend this game for the sandbox mode, and even then, it's fairly repetitive. Otherwise, just give this game a pass.

Yet another excellent offering from Zachtronics.  Puzzle games reimagined with a nearly-infinite number of viable solutions, limited solely by your intuition and creativity.  Fantastic, with superior replayability.

If you've played previous Zachtronics games this is just as good as the rest.
If you haven't, Zachtronics makes a unique type of puzzle game that rely on you coming up with your own solutions rather than trying to figure out what the designer wanted you to do. All you're given is an input and an output, and it's completely up to you to figure out how you want to solve the problem. After completing a puzzle, you're going to want to go back and look at your machine to see how it can be improved. Finding an efficient solution to a problem you were struggling to even solve is an amazing feeling that you can really only find in a game like Opus Magnum.

Dungeon of the endless is a rogue-like game crossed with elements of tower defense. It mixes exploration of random levels with several interesting mechanics, in regards to the skill tree's that develop your characters and your available resources.
Your basic quest is to make it through a base by finding the exit in each level - once you do you must carry a crystal through to the exit. But there is a catch...as soon as you pick the crystal up an infinite number of enemy swarms the level, and you must hold them off while one of your squad carries the crystal to the exit.
To aid you in doing this you can build various devices - turrets to attack enemies, or ones that increase your defense or heal you. However, each turret takes resources to build and energy to power them. Resources are gathered by opening doors in the environment / killing enemies - but the more doors you open the more enemies can pour out when you finally make the dash to the exit.......
Every resource in the game is tied to this aspect - food (which heals you, or can be used to level up), science (the more you have the higher you can upgrade devices) and parts (x amount are needed to build each device) are all gained by advancing through the level. It's a balancing act - the more you explore, the more you can do, but by extension you will face more hazards.
The rogue-like element is this......die and you go back to level one.......Yes, it erases any saved game and sends you right back to the start. I'm sure by now you have an idea of why this game is getting a thumbs down, despite me finding it moderately entertaining - at least for a while.
It quickly becomes very boring. The random levels can either be: overly easy, or tediously complex, and the game doesn't develop at all. The furthest I have got so far is level three, and that's after about thirty attempts - doing the same limited thing over, and over, and over, and over again.
For all the complexities of the systems in the game they sadly don't add much variety. And while it can be quite thrilling for your first few games it doesn't take long for the thrill to wear off. Repetitively slogging through samey environments, fighting enemies that, although different in looks and attacks, you just end up doing the same thing all the time. You don't control characters in combat, and levelling them up (which takes food, so you can't heal them) makes them tougher, but it doesn't do any more than that to liven up the gameplay.
If you really, really get your kicks from strategic gameplay then this might keep you engaged, but for me personally I felt like I'd seen everything it had to offer within half an hour of playing it. Now it's become this mindnumbing excercise that I don't think I'll pursue anymore.
Sadly it reminds me of Darkest Dungeon in that regard - an interesting concept, but one that ultimately makes for a dull experience. And Dungeons of the Endless doesn't have the insanity hook that livened up DD when it got stale, or the gleefully wicked narrator, or the appealing graphics, or the great sound effects. Whereas I played that game for about forty hours before getting bored with it, I find Dungeons of the endless is already proving tedious.

Don't be put off just because "ew it looks like a super nintendo game". If that's your thinking, then the game is too advanced for you. This is a game in which you can not only create Hulk Hogan, but you can fine tune his AI logic to make him act exactly like Hulk Hogan would. Try doing that on that "other" series.
Since everything is sprite based, your created characters will all look like they belong in the same ring together.
The gameplay is simple, but so complex at the same time. You walk around until you knock into each other, at which point the wrestlers will grapple. As soon as the animation finishes, that's when you want to hit your attack buttons. First person to register an attack wins the grapple and gets the move. You have to start with your small grapple moves first! If you try going for your chokeslams and powerbombs right away, you will be reversed out of your boots. You need to start small and build up, like an actual wrestling match.
Strikes are going to be difficult at first if you have not played this series before. You need to get the distance just right. Too close and you will miss the attack. It can be very hard at first: For the PS2 entry in this series, I took it out of the box, played it for an hour getting frustrated at it, powered it off and shoved it in my game storage for a month. Saw it again after that, tried it again, and once I got the striking down and it all clicked, then I started having a lot of fun with it. Don't let the strikes put you off this game like it did me. You can and will learn, and once you do you will be glad you didn't give up.
"Do you recommend this game?" If you are a wrestling fan, I cannot possibly recommend it enough. Give it a try, you might find a whole new world out there that is very different from the WWE universe, and it might be a little scary at first, but we'll all love to help you out on your way to becoming the world champion.

There's a lot I can say about this game. Admittedly, a lot can also be interpreted as me being a fanboy because this has become one of my alltime favourite games. In terms of variety, story options,  and stuff to do, Inquisition probably beats it out. In terms of quality, heart, fun and uniqueness, Origins still stands the test of time.
To address the combat firstt. It's probably one of the weaker aspects of the game (whether that breaks the appeal to the game I feel is completely up to the individual player). When I say weak, I do not mean it is bad, or attrocius. Rather one can see that it probably needed more polishing, or a slight redesign on how it worked. So the combat system is your standard click to attack, click on an ability on the bottom of your screen (or a number key it is bound to) to use that ability. Standard classic rpg stuff. You can move around. and where you position yourself relative to the enemy has some effect on the damage you do. It should be mentioned, if you move away from an enemy when they started to attack they will probably still hit you, regardless of how far away you have moved. Annoying but manageable. It works. Whether or not it works well, once again, general consensus seems to be that it is passable.
Now on to the good bits. The story of this game is your typical doomsday tale. Evil lurking, odds stacked against you, form team of heroes to fight the evil, make story choices that could impact the game, sacrifices along the way. When you take a broad look at it, looks solid but nothing too impressive. This game though earns my respect for taking something classic and still making it fun and exciting in the modern age. The characters you meet feel real, they make jokes, they get annoyed, mad, sad. They express their interest in cheese or shoes to you for some reason. It's really the little nuances. If you act like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ they'll tell you to your face that you're an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even your character (who isn't voiced save for some combat lines) still feels real (al beit, most of that is due to individual player investmenet in pc). They have character development that doesn't just amount to some fluff text, but can actually affect the structure of your party and some story elements.
The story still feels grand and exciting. It's calm when it needs to be, and can get hectic when you least expect it. There's a lot of lore that exists and it (fortunately for some) isn't usually forced down your throat when you asked your elf companion how his day was. For those interested in the world, there is a lot of text and codex pages to read that help build that sense of "I'm just living inside a part of the world that has existed already, not just created conveniently for me to save the day." You can within a few hours discover every location in the game (for the most part), but there is still a lot you can/have to do in said location to progress the story. And for your typical save the world stories, expect twists and turns that you may not have expected (wow, am I abusing the English language today). It's slightly darker than your average fantasy tale (rip children), and it does it's best to avoid the most annoying fantasy cliches ("People are not simple. They cannot be summarized for easy reference in the manner of: 'The elves are a lithe, pointy eared people who excel at poverty.'")
If anything, this game is probably the final testement to the rpgs of old. One final tribute that blends classic elements with newer takes on it and a more modern taste. Graphics aren't amazing, but they aren't ugly. In all honestly, the gothic and darker aethetics/style is more noticeable than graphical quality. This game may not be for everyone (takes a while to truly get going), but I'd recommend it to anyone who either adores rpgs to death, or for those who on their way  to buy First Person Shooter Slasher 7: The Tales of Jum[ Man and Quick Time boy, encounter the D&D group and wonder why they love the genre (tis but a friendly jab).

TL:DR The combat system works, though it is flawed and shows in the period where it is long sessions of combat. This type of story has been told before, but it has taken every effort to make it feel like a new journey. The characters are genuine and fun to interact with. Before BioWare made Dragon Age, Jade Empire, Knights of the Old Republic, and Mass Effect, they created a true work of art in Baldur's Gate. It uses 2nd edition Advanced Dungeons & Dragons as the ruleset, and is to my mind, the closest thing that you can find to a true D&D experience in video game form to date. This isn't a hack and slash, folks; it takes planning, party management, and depending on the characters, an inventive use of your available spells. But if you're smart enough to be up to the challenge, Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate II are enthralling experiences worthy of your time.

You know you're in for a rough time when you're playing a game that's tagged as a rogue-like and it starts with only two difficulties, "easy" and "too easy," and you get wrecked on the second level, despite doing perfectly the rest of that level, and having picked up an extra party member and having lots of defensive lasers and teslas.
The game's premise is that you open doors to rooms. You open a door, and either something good or something bad is in it. You generate resources each time you open a room, and you spend those resources to upgrade characters, buy new resource-generating devices, research new such devices, build defensive structures, etc. If you send power to a room, it is lit so you can see what's going on inside it, and enemies cannot spawn inside it. Any rooms that aren't powered but have an open door will typically have enemies pop out of them. You can take and remove power as you please, but must power any rooms in between your power source (the crystal you defend the whole level), and the room you want powered. The rooms' contents are random. Find the room that is the exit, and when you're ready to leave, you have to slowly carry the crystal from its starting point to the exit. The assault that comes is simply awful. It's an unending stream, which means if the exit is in a room that isn't powered, and that's the only direction that all enemies are spawning from, it becomes impossible to beat the level.
Was this my fault? Technically, yes. I had no idea it was going to happen, but if I'd known better, I would have deliberately turned the power off in certain rooms to distribute enemies and make sure I could exit, now that I look back on it. However, this being a rogue like, my honest mistake doesn't mean I get to reload, fiddle around with my defense, and keep trying it until I progress in the game. Oh no, instead, being a rogue like, I have to start the whole damn thing over. While I'm sure there are people who brag about how good they are or make comments about how terrible they are while making backhanded compliments about their skill, the problem here is that the game appears to have enough levels that it would take several hours to complete, and every single error could mean having to do it all over again.
This game is disrespectful of players' time, whereas a rogue like such as FTL seems to go so much faster with a shorter length so that losing doesn't feel as detrimental, and has so many fun little things to do, even on runs where you may fail, such as killing enemies by sucking the air out of a room, or taking over an enemy ship by teleporting on-board and killing its crew. Maybe FTL is longer but it doesn't feel as long? I've never beaten FTL, but I still think fondly of it and don't regret my time playing it. This game will mostly please the masochists and difficult-game braggarts. Masochists get abused by the game and feel like they deserve it, which pleases them, and difficult-game braggarts take pleasure in knowing they have the exclusionary pleasure of completing a game most players won't be able to complete, so they can brag about it on forums and talk about how "easy" it was to people who can't win and are frustrated. That last type of player is kind of a jerk, but the masochists aren't "hurting" anyone but themselves, so I'm totally cool with that.
In summary, the game will make you start over from the very beginning if you make a big enough mistake, and I saw no relevant unlocks that I got to assist in playing again. The game's levels take too long except probably for people who are really good at the game anyway, meaning starting over is just an incredible disappointment. I would be a bit iffy on whether I'd keep trying if the game saved between levels, but with a total restart every time, no freaking way am I going to spend my time trying to progress in a game deliberately designed to take away ALL of my progress if I even make one mistake.

I only have one more location to explore in Kholat, but I think I've played enough and got enough out of the game that I'm a position to do a review.  It's not going to be around much longer (victory is near!).  I've gotten alot of notes, reports and journals but might finish the game with a few missed, although I think I've gotten enough out of the story.  Also have all but one tent location it seems.  Anyways, time for a review!
This is a pretty solid survival/adventure game.  Kholat is somewhat creepy, tense and grinding because of the atmosphere, constant snow and chase sequences.  It does have a couple of good jumps and a few areas are downright intense because you're racing against time to keep out of the clutches of an instant death mist that's chasing you.  So the gist of the gameplay is that you're running around on a snow-covered mountain where things aren't as they seem and a bunch of supernatural goings on are occuring trying to piece the a story together by collecting as much written information as you can.  The last folks that traversed this mountainous impasse didn't make it back alive to tell their story.
The game isn't flawless that's for sure, but I enjoyed alot of it.  It's like a point and click adventure with light elements of Amnesia and Outlast, because you can die and you will die as you trial n' error your way to each key location.  The game is immersive enough that you really feel like you're lost in the mountains, freezing to death and all around completely ******.  After some frustration I was able to successfully use the map to figure out where I was at and where I needed to go.  You basically gather your bearings at different base camps before setting out on the next hunt for reports, diaries and journals.  Along the way you will traverse mountains, valleys, forests, stumble on a few signs of where life once was and encounter numerous one hit obstacles that will render you dead,
The graphics and atmosphere are great.  This game grinds in much of the way that the highly underrated Cursed Mountain did and feels a bit like John Carpenter's The Thing.  The landscapes are beautiful to behold and even though the map is not quite as huge and daunting as you initially think, there's a good sense of vastness and scope that really puts you into the heart of adventure.  The story unfolds in semi-confusing bits of prose narrated by Sean Bean, a female actor and yourself.  Due to the difficulty of travel, there is a sense of accomplishment when you successfully reach new locations and landmarks, and even though the pace is a ruthless slow burn, it's dangerous and fun.  The map/compass system is challenging.  As a dogged old school gamer I figured it out with no videos, walkthroughs or otherwise and it took me time.  This game makes you feel lost, isolated and generally f*cked but the more you play and discover things, the more the map fills in and becomes easier to navigate.
Sound design deserves a special mention here because it's probably creepier than the actual evil spirits you're up against.  You will hear different cues providing clues to what situations, discoveries and key locations are nearby.  As I first played the game I found myself running everytime I heard one of these sounds thinking I was about to be attacked.  Eventually, I figured out that these were things I was supposed to stop and take notice of, so keep your ears open while playing this one (not just for monsters!).  Never before in a game did I get friggen excited over the sound of a rustling piece of paper, but Kholat makes you yearn for minute pleasures.  These cues also provide the location of game saving tents and I had no crashes or problems in terms of saving (knock on wood) 5 hours into the game thus far.  Though glitches do occur.
Unfortunately, Kholat is not without its negatives.  While the save system wasn't a problem for me and was just spaced out enough for my liking, prepare for some cheap deaths.  As an adventurer, I think it was a little bit silly that you couldn't jump.  I do understand that not being able to jump made travel more difficult, but it was somewhat nagging when you couldn't hurdle a two foot ledge.  I died a decent amount during Kholat.  Sometimes warranted and sometimes very cheaply.  I stepped on a ghosts head that was stuck in the ground because of a glitch, died descending ledges that the game didn't want you to go down and ended up dead because the game would be playing smoothly one minute with alot going on and lagging like hellfire the next.  Though I never lost large amounts of progress, there are certainly some ludicrous things that will kill you, so prepare to do things over a few times even if the cause of your demise was completely out of your control.
Though some runs for key story pages are tense and exciting (the forest), the enemies are kinda stupid.  There is no stealth system whatsoever to avoid them.  They killed me far away and out of sight, chased me to the ends of areas and other irritating stuff.  You can stun them with your flashlight, but it's never worth it.  The spirits don't provide too many problems and can be easily avoided the majority of the time, yet other times you will die at their hands while cursing the very mountain you're climbing.  They weren't a particularly interesting opponent either and sometimes were so stupid they wouldn't bother you if you walked by them right in their field of view.  The whole system was somewhat poorly implemented in my opinion and definitely a major buzzkill on the tension.  A few other cheap one hit kills will take you down.  For example, I got hit by the same falling rock 3 times a row, and whether I'd wait, rush or run, the game would lag up and I'd get killed.  I passed that part by luck and luck alone.  Thankfully, none of this stuff puts you so far backwards that it's game-breaking, just rather cheap, laggy and poorly conceived.
The story is solidly narrated but is mostly confusing.  Those hammy diatribes and goofy bits of poetry don't make much sense even if Bean did a good job with the narration.  It just doesn't make alot of sense and I found myself less involved with what was going on with each passing journal page instead of becoming more intensely engrossed.  Despite the story being rather overblown and not so well-written, the desire to push on and see what location is ahead more than made up for the yarn not pulling the gamer in as much as it should.
Overall, Kholat has been an enjoyable experience and I'm looking forward to wrapping it up either later tonight or tomorrow.  I don't think the couple of things left to do would change my score drastically, because I know endings are not usually all they're cracked up to be and it's the gameplay itself that concerns me.  Did I have fun playing Kholat?  Yes.  Was it a perfect game?  No.  Will I pick it up a second time fro the beginning?  No.  But do I regret spending the money?  No, not at all!  A good horror themed game for players that would rather the scares come from the atmosphere than a bunch of silly jump-gimmicks.  Pure adventure fans might find it worth a look as well.
Here's the breakdown:
Pros:
-Excellent graphics
-Sound design is not only top-notch but important for gameplay
-Solid voice acting
-Overbearing sense of dread and isolation like a good horror flick
-Exploration is mostly fun
-Cool compass/map system (You really do feel like you're lost and trying to find your way)
-Some solid set-pieces and chase sequences
Cons
-Laggy gameplay can lead to cheap deaths
-Boring enemies with awful AI will either stupidly ignore you or murder you ruthlessly
-Muddled story
-Could use more actions (jump, climb)
-Limited tasks/objectives leads to some tedium late game
-No stealth system when stealth is part of your mission
Overal rating:  7.5/10

Project Zomboid is one of those games where first impressions matter. When you start a playthrough, the ominous music and "This is how you died" displayed against a black screen give off an almost nihilistic atmosphere. Once your character spawns, you have a little house that (hopefully) will have some food, water, a backpack and a weapon. You can choose to try and board up your home, or go out and brave the zombie hordes. It's your choice. As long as you have your wits about you, you will survive, but if you make one mistake it can cost you your character's life.
Features (to name a few):
- Cooking
- Fortification of any house
- Full character creation suite
- Mod support
- Multiplayer
- Custom game modes (Last Stand, You have one day etc.)
- Customisable survival settings (i.e. you can have WWZ-esque hordes of sprinter zombies)
- Vehicles (currently in beta)
- Zombies that pose a threat
- Thousands strong zombie hordes
- Drinkable bleach :)
In conclusion, if you want a true zombie survival simulation where common sense, rather than weird game mechanics, is what determines how long you last, then Project Zomboid deserves your money.

Kholat is an aquired taste. The extended bouts of exploration and note collecting will be tedious for some, but the environment and soundtrack are beautiful and atmospheric. The game is heavily reliant on narrative, developing the story little by little with each note that you find scattered across the desolate, snowy landscape. The voice acting is excellent and delivered with convincing emotion. You aren't completely safe on your journey, in that you'll occassionally come across enemies that will pursue you, but are not an especially difficult threat.
The game is by no means without its (rather frustrating) flaws. Progress will be slow as you cannot run for any significant amount of time before being winded. The compass/map system is confusing and will get you lost on the twisting, large map. The enemies are minor irritations and while the first couple of encounters may startle, the effect soon wears thin. There are occassional glitches that will result in your character becoming stuck in the environment or falling right through it into voids unknown.
Ultimately though, you'll want to keep searching to know what happens next, with an ending open to various interpretations. If you're patient and you like a haunting story with good atmosphere, you'll enjoy Kholat.

My biggest caveat though is the core gameplay. It just doesn't feel all there(Of what little there is to begin with). Admittedly most games of this type don't offer much for gameplay, but in Kholat it just felt glaringly obvious there needed to be more going on here than just collecting paper. For instance, the map is fairly decently sized and you spend a great deal of time traversing it, but so little ever happens in it with the exception of a few easily distinguishable areas. Adding to that as well, if you're trying to be through and think you missed a path to explore and want to backtrack... Think again. This game likes to have one-way paths forcing you take the long way back around if you know you happened to miss something. Manual, player saves would fix both these issues.
Developers, stop doing only automated checkpoint saves. STOP IT.

Kholat is a visually gorgeous game and provides an interesting story but it isn't without it's flaws and missed potential.
Kholat is a game that sets it's story around the Dyaltov Pass Incident, based on a true event you take control of the main protagonist to collect and discover clues about what happened leading up to the incident. The main objective is to venture throughout the very large mountainscape in search of logbooks in order to piece together the events of this incident and what really happened.
The game opens with you heading off a train to the mountain with a lovely piece of music setting a very sombre and dark mood. After exploring the first main area you will eventually find yourself on the mountain after a series of strange events. From here you are given a compass, map and a flashlight to freely explore the surrounding area.
While the main gameplay can boil down to what is known as a "Slender clone" this game takes that formula and ups the production value really well. Visually the game is gorgeous, huge snow storms, large caves and the surrounding areas all feel very dark and it sets a tone of dread that helps build the games overall atmosphere.
The game allows you to have complete freedom on how you tackle the story, a narrator will speak to you throughout the game  giving you an idea of where to go and written on your map are several coordinates that act as a story checklist. Upon visiting each one you will be given a piece of the story. To accompany those are logbooks and notes scattered throughout the area that give additional story.
While venturing through the large mountain scape you'll find ghastly spirits wandering the hills looking to get you. The spirits can be seen moving around and sometimes can appear when hit by light from your flashlight. The flashlight helps you find your way through the darker areas but also serves as an indicator for when the spirits are around making use of the flashlight at proper times is a big part of the game because while it can be handy it can also be deadly if it hits a spirit.
The audio is very well done, good voice acting from actor Sean Bean, an eerie yet beautiful score and some great environmental effects like creaking doors, crashing rocks, haunting spirit cries and pounding snow storms really set you in these environments. Making use of the audio is also important when finding additional story elements, listening for notes blowing in the wind is important in finding the nessecary clues to piece together the entire story.
With the above said however the game is not without it's flaws and missed oppourtunites. The first major flaw is the mapping and navigation system. Opening up your map displays coordinates of where you will need to go next but there is no way to tell exactly where you are on the map because there is no indicator. There are a few major landscapes in this game like a radio tower, a wooden cabin, an altar and various camps around the environment. While I believe the main idea the developers  were going for was to have these as point you can use to tell exactly where you are it makes traversal at time tedious.
The game feature very large open areas and it's very easy to get lost forcing you to find anything you can to figure out an idea of of where you are. While this can lead to a feeling of being lost after awhile it loses it's effect and can result in long periods of just wandering. The compass which comes with the map is almost useless and really doesn't help much. The camps allow you fast travel between them which helps very much but finding them first can be time consuming.
The map also feels very out of scale, the map is not a 1:1 map but even establishing where you are and heading in a direction shown on the map it sometimes doesn't work and you can easily end up lost making one wrong turn forcing you to backtrack often. I feel like having some sort of indication would help move the game along at a quicker pace which would really help with the aimless wandering, a few times i found myself losing a bit of interest because I was lost wandering around in circles because I fell down somewhere.
Going into this game after watching the trailer I was expecting a game filled with an eerie atmosphere which it delivers on however I feel like this game really could have pushed for some more scary elements. This part feels like a huge missed potential and while there are one or two of these which are great (stepping into the wooden cabin and having the windows an ddoors slamming was great) there just wasn't enough here and after awhile you begin to see the main spirits as less of a threat and more of just something in the way because there is nothing to make you fear them.
Overall the game length comes in at around 4 hours from my experience (dependant on how well you figure out travel) and while the game is fairly basic it's presentation makes up for it very well. It's a fairly enjoyable games if you can look past the flawed navigation system.

I wouldn't call this game a horror game. For those of you looking for an experience like the FNAF series, Amnesia, or even Slenderman, don't buy this game.
From my impression, Kholat is a suspensefully atmospheric completionist adventure game where you experience gorgeous scenery, intense music, a haunting environment, and Sean Bean. Kholat is suspenseful, but hardly scary: jumpscares are rare and predictable, and there isn't an overabundance of horror imagery. It could be called a gateway into the horror genre for gamers who aren't comfortable with the bigger horror titles. For what Kholat gives, it does it fairy well.
Now I should give my critique of what Kholat could have done better.
-Sean Bean honestly isn't the best voice actor, neither is any of their other voice actors for the game. Not terrible, but sub-par for the atmosphere the game is trying to create.
-There's not nearly enough enemies. Overall, the Ural Mountains seem quite empty with the exception of the primary points of interest.
-A little too paranormal right off the bat. The plot flow could have been stuctured much better
Kholat is structured like a dungeon crawler, where you set off towards a  coordinate, the environment getting more and more spooky as you go, encountering some spooky creatures that try to kill you, then you reach the point of interest, find a spooky (not really) clue, and return to home base, where it's safe, then repeat until you unlock everything. Fun for some, not for everyone. The plot isn't scary, and neither is the gameplay after a few hours of exploration.
Story: 5/10

Scariness: 6/10
Replayability: 4/10
Final Verdict: Not bad at all, but could've been a lot better. I bought it on sale, so i felt like $12 was worth it, but don't buy it for the full price. The game is beautiful, but it doesn't get any deeper as you play, and at the end you feel like you didn't really accomplish much. That said, it's still pretty fun if you take it for its face value.

I have played Stonehearth for 341 hours and have enjoyed playing through the developing stages. The game is becoming more polished and seems to be headed in a positive direction. I would recommend this to someone who enjoys a sandbox building and crafting games where they can design towns and villages with a little bit of hostile goblins thrown in to the mix.
I do not recommend this yet for someone that is expecting a finished polished product or get upset when an error message pops up.
The Good
- I find the game extremely fun to play with the ability to design your own houses and structures.
- The pace of the game is relaxing and the music is very soothing.
- The Heathing are amusing as they try to carry out your commands
- There are more creatures to worry about now as Giant Zombie, Stone Golems, Eants, and what looks like a mutant alligator roam the land. Undead Villages complete with crazed necromancers pop up and flood the night with undead critters.
- The ability to create Mods will mean continued content. I hope that this also continues to develop end game content.
- Weekly twitch feed keep you updated on developments and lets you give feed back to the developers.
The Bad
- There are still errors when trying to build structures, and it takes a while to learn what works and what does not. It seems the building logic really wants you to lay down your design in a certain way. I watched a twitch feed were the designer was working on this to allow the engine to be more flexible.
- The Hearthling become idler as your town, village, Kingdom expands. I am unsure if this is caused by distance, memory issues or pathing (although sometime it’s because I ran out of wood). The developers have work hard and these issues have improved greatly since I started playing it. (I still have to chop my own wood of course)
- The end game is not there yet.  There is a basic scenario evolving Blood thirsty goblins which ends after 4 or 5 encounters.  Following that you only have to fend off random creatures once or twice a day.
I will continue to play and follow this game as it develops.
I've been enjoying this game imensily.  Looking forward to the full release (few bugs annoy me... but its E.Access so all good).

A very engaging city building title, Stonehearth offers many hours of fun. Being an early access title does mean that there will be issues, don't buy the game if this is a problem for you. If your are interested, but unsure just follow its development. That said the game is very fun. From my very first play through I played for 15 hours because I was so captivated by this game, bugs and all. The development team has done a very good job of weeding out said bugs. After my initial play, I too set the game aside with the intentions of returning once more progress was made with performance and gameplay. Well the devs came through! Many of the frustrating bugs I was dealing with have been fixed and on top of this many optimizations and features added. I am playing the current unstable branch (Alpah 14) at the time of writing this review. Irregardless, I was very happy to see that the team behind the game is very active unlike other titles I have bought.
The game is very simple: manage and provide for your hearthlings and watch them and the villiage grow. This simplicity is nice, but there is more depth to be found if you just look. Town building is very fun and very customizable. There is a set pallete of default building schematics at the start, but with a little imagination and creativity there is much you can do with the tool to design your own buildings. Also modding is being actively encouraged for the game by the devs.
Many of the negatives in some of the reviews have been addressed, atleast in the "unstable branch," though that is not to stay new ones won't pop up. Again this is early access and with that in mind buyer beware. If you choose to buy this product look into it before doing so. In my short time so far with the game I have been impressed with the pace of development and the game itself. The forums for the game are active and the devs stream weekly on twitch, just check out their site.
Overall, I am very happy with my purchase and look forward to he future of the game because it does look very bright. If you're on the fence, do your research, watch lets plays and see if this is really something for you. If you enjoy city building this game is very fun and relaxing, just give yourself time to get acquainted.

Oooooookay!!! Here is my review, I'm very torn over this game and its for this reason. BUGS. The game isn't "broken", even in pre-alpha. It is a very playable and fun game IF you can make it long enough without a UI or engine crash, Bear with me as this is kind of long, but very worth the read if you want an HONEST review of the product youre buying
Pros:
*SUPER FUN- Ive played many RPG's, RTS's, etc. but this game is one of the most mind numbingly addicting games I have ever played.
*Complete Sandbox- Like Minecraft, but better.
*Ranking Systems- Hearthlings rank up in their profession, giving them cool perks.
*Versatility- Plotting out farmland, building houses around designated land, etc. You build YOUR town how YOU want. To a point at this stage in the game.
*GEAR- I love love love the armor and weapon progression for your soldiers
*Custom building- You arent stuck to templates, although they are provided.
Cons:
*BUGGY AF- Remember, it's still in alpha. However, nothing is more frustrating than getting so far into a game then recieving a pop-up "UI Crash" report. Seems to happen every hour. Villagers glitch into walls, they wander off miles just to collect random sh*t on the ground, usually dying in the process. They sit and DIE when being attacked. Guards don't wake up from sleep to respond to threats.... this is a big deal when invaders come at NIGHT only and all of your guards are sleeping. Needless to say, the bugs make the game frustrating as hell at times. Once, my entire village got stuck in defense mode, starving to death looking out for enemies that weren't there.
*LACK OF EDITING- after or during building process. This is probably the single handedly most frustrating aspect of this game. If you design a massive, beautiful building, spend the time and resources to build it, then realize you fuzzed up, youre SOL. You have to tear down adn rebuild the entire thing, which can take the better half of an hour.
*Villagers forget/refuse to do assignments. Sometimes it is simply because they have a long checklist before they get to that particular assignment. However, many times, they will just stop building walls, digging caves, or collecting resources. And no matter how many times you remind them, they will sit there and do nothing instead.
*Mining is sloppy. There is no realistic ability to build UP inside caverns, you have to always dig down.... which is annoying to say the least.
*Lack of defensive features...This broke my heart. Sure you can build a mkaeshift stone wall. Sure you can build a really tall building and call it a guard tower, but in a game where you are attacked by zombies and skeletons every night, this game NEEDS operational wartime structures. Maybe a tower your guards actually post themselves in, or a palisade where an archer <--also much needed--> can be stationed. Especially when you go to war with the goblin chieftans, they attack, steal, and raid you every chance they get. It would be nice to see more organized troop and defense structures, as well as a more convienent way to get up to different floors of buildings.
Overall, I still think this game is amazing. Please don't be turned off from my review. I refuse to sugar coat it for you. The price tag is too high to lie to you. HOWEVER, I stand by my opinion that this game is beautiful, the soundtrack is wonderful and overall this piece has some fantastic potential. I will continue to play this game, and I STRONGLY urge you to support the development of this game and buy it. The devs care, releasing updates and bug fixes periodically, Buggy? yes. Lacking? Barely, but yes. But its still in alpha!  My rating comes to an 8/10 in its current state! I think this can and will quickly be a game to watch though, as long as the community continues to support it.

I don't normally write reviews but this game has a special place in my heart.
I picked up Dragon Age: Origins in 2009 for the Xbox 360. I popped in the disc and started up a new character.  Very simple character creation. You choose your gender, race, class, and origin story: a feature I had never seen. Six different starts, each with different characters, equipment, and interactions that influence the story throughout the game. So, I being a young teenager at the time, I started up a Male Human Warrior, who I wanted to put in the biggest armor I could find. After the opening cutscene and following conversation, I wandered around an amazing castle with so many things going on. After a while of talking and learning the controls, I finally made it to the first combat sequence: Giant rats. Very overused, but effective at introducing fighting. As a warrior, I just sat there, swinging my sword and taking hits from tiny rodents. No real chance to use my abilities, but I knew I would fight again. Oh boy, was I right. After more walking and talking and a brief cutscene, the castle and my character are attacked. So I fight my way through with some companions and finish up the origin story within 30 minutes.
I repeated this process with a wide variation of genders, races, and classes until I had gone through all of the origin stories. I did not feel any repetition or unnecessary dialouge and combat. Even now, many years later, I love going through the story from the beginning and experiencing the rich story that is only one part of a massive world full of lore.
I know this game came out years ago, but it still has a place in my top 5 games of all time. People who enjoy a good story and a fun, but more tactical combat system should definitly look into this game.

The combat allows you pause and give commands to allied NPCs, just like in KOTOR. A nice touch and since AI is dumb in just about every game it is a welcomed function. However, the combat itself is just point and click and it takes 3 seconds just to swing a damn sword. If you've played kotor and WoW, the combat is the aborted ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of those two games. One of the worst combat systems/mechanics I have ever seen in a game though its not as bad as Risen's combat.
I would have already had well over a hundred hours or more with this game but I just, I just can't stand the combat. It is a chore to fight. Fighting should be fun, interesting, fast, and hands on. Not ♥♥♥♥ing left clicking or pressing the number keys. With this combat system, you can't even block. Something that is vital to survival when swords, spells, and arrows are being flung around.
Story is important yes, but gameplay is just as important, especially the combat.
Tip: Do research on a game's combat system before purchasing. Thankfully I got this while it was on sale. I haven't touched this game in ages though I may come back to it just for the sake of completing it.

I know we call games "classics" a lot for such a young medium, but ...
Dragon Age: Origins - Ultimate Edition is not one game. Choose one of six unique origin stories - each of these is a coherent story in itself. Then embark on the epic main story, made of six adventure-packed chapters, (seven, with Warden's Keep), that can be strung together and approached in any order you choose. Then, missing the eight or nine companions (one of them is a secret potential companion until late in the game) you just spent the better part of sixty hours with, embark on another chapter with two new ones to catch up with an old friend! And after /that/, go face down another epic threat with five new companions (and one old one). Then go back in time to explore through gameplay the backstory of one of your original companions. And if you're still not done, you can play as an undead monster and kill all of the heroes.
Origins is just - big.
And somehow it never feels empty. Every map has NPCs with minor tasks they need your help with, and codexes that adapt to your chosen origin story. It even keeps a journal-format record of every conversation you have with every NPC. While the world-spanning plot might get most gamers invested, the petty politics of your traveling companions, with their personal questlines and constant bantering and bickering, not to mention their lengthy potentional romance subplots, is sure to provide most with a personal favorite and a more personal stake in the game.
It's not my favorite game or story. The dialogue can sometimes try too hard to be witty and come out wooden or childish, and for all its brilliant execution and clever worldbuilding the overall plot is cliche high fantasy with nothing much to say. But it really does deserve its title as a classic, as a tabletop gamer this is one of the closest experiences to a really good campaign money can buy, and I'm in awe at the sheer amount of effort that went into this thing - something no amount of next gen graphics (that this game obviously doesn't have) can replicate.
It's more than worth its list price, not even mentioning that it frequently goes on sale for about //$5//.

Assassin's Creed Syndicate follows the AC formula but in a much more refined way than ever before.
I think I can best explain what I mean by giving an example: a mission tasks me with assassinating the foreman of a sweat shop. I enter through a window on the top story and hide up in the rafters to examine the situation. I see the foreman on one side of the floor below me and two enemies on the other side. There are some barrels hanging from the rafters that I'm on top of that I can drop on an unsuspecting enemy (or foreman in particular). Now as a long time AC fan I expect the foreman's patrol route to take him right under those barrels (very convenient). So I wait there for him to walk under me, but he never does. His patrol route takes him very close to assassination range, but not quite close enough. So for the first time in an AC game I have to use my brain. I shoot his henchmen on the other side of the room with a hallucination dart that sends him into a rage against the other enemies and the foreman comes to check him out. Before he can get all the way across the room, I cut the ropes on the barrels and complete the mission. This assassination "puzzle" isn't a huge difference but it makes the game so much more enjoyable. In the other games each mission was like a connect-the-dots picture where they already connected most of the dots and let you put in the last one or two. I'm not saying the system in Syndicate is perfect: it's not too hard to figure out how to get the foreman under the barrels, but at least it's not like I'm waiting in some bush for the target to walk into that specific bush right when no one is looking. The system can be improved upon but it does make every assassination feel more like a puzzle and if Ubisoft continues with that pattern I think we can expect some much better games in the future.
It would've been nice to get something new and exciting in Syndicate like sailing in Black Flag, hunting in AC3, or the brotherhood from Brotherhood. The grappling hook makes getting collectibles feel more like a puzzle but other than that it's really only useful for getting up tall buildings or crossing alleys faster. Driving feels good but with fast travel and the grappling hook you're really only going to be driving if a mission tells you to do so.
Combat feels fantastic, but it seems like combos and multikills decide when they do or don't want to work (that could be my own fault if I missed a tutorial somewhere). The outfits and weapons have different stats to suit your playstyle, but I found that the bonuses they provide weren't really big enough to notice, even with the late game items.
Having two playable assassin's sounds like a really cool idea on paper. In practice it works but it's not as game-changing as the designers probably hoped it would be. Evie has bonuses to stealth and Jacob has bonuses to combat. They also have their own unique active and passive skills. I might be alone on this opinion but I found that the combat is way too easy to ever need a bonus and ended up only playing Evie unless a mission required me to be Jacob. What I think was a HUGE missed oppurtunity was that while playing as one character, the other character is completely absent. What would have been awesome is if you could use the twin that you aren't playing as some sort of super brotherhood member that you could call in to take out or distract a guard. Maybe you could both be in combat and you could set up crazy cooperative moves with each other. Now, they're mostly separated because of narrative but you really shouldn't let the story get in the way of good gameplay.
The world design isn't the best or the worst of the series. The different areas of the city have their own general character and charm to them but when it comes down to the smaller details of the world everything starts to blend together. The artistic direction is nice, especially in the more colorful areas. and the graphics are pretty nice.
The story is slow and boring in the middle but the beggining is alright and the end is great. There's nothing super special about any of the characters, most of them feel like ripoffs of other AC characters but they're still mostly enjoyable and the main villain is great. The modern day portion hasn't been good since Black Flag and that hasn't changed with Syndicate. Unless they bring back a larger story arc like Desmond's they should really just get rid of the modern story entirely: it doesn't add to the game and it's confusing. The 1800's story is okay.
I've pre-ordered every AC game since Brotherhood. Revelations was a low point. Unity was a lower point. After playing Unity and hearing that Syndicate would have similar mechanics I decided for the first time not to pre-order. I waited for a sale and bought it at half price. It would've been worth it at 3/4 price. Syndicate hasn't brought the series all the way back to it's glory but it's a step in the right derection. I hear a lot of people say that AC games are rushed. I can see how that's true, but I can also see that Ubisoft is getting better at rushing them. Practice makes perfect I guess. Also I hear that they're working on a new AC game and instead of rushing it, they'll be working on it for a lot longer than usual and giving it the attention it deserves. I'm sticking to what I said before, Syndicate is essentially a much better version of the exact same game that Ubisoft makes every year. If you're new to the franchise, Black Flag is still a better place to start but if you want more after that, Syndicate is worth your money.

A classic that put Bioware on the map. It is in depth, challenging, rewarding, charming, and most of all it's DND. Modern players most likely won't like the learning curve or the slow pace unless they already have some tabletop experience. The best way to think of this game is a "simulated DND session where the PC is your DM." (Dungeon Master for those unfamiliar with the term.)
Play IF:
You like rich story
You like table top games (DND, Pathfinder, Shadowrun, etc.)
You seek a challenge
Love the DND Campaign setting "Forgotten Realms" (This is where the more recently release "Neverwinter" MMO and the famous RA Salvatore Drow novels takes place....in this game you can run into the Drow himself by the way.)
You want a steep learning curve that once understood makes for an indescribable feeling of accomplishment.
You like traditional high fantasy settings
You like controlling more than your own character (Success depends on orders given to up to six party memebers.)
You like various flavored NPCs to recruit (There is a large amount of potential party members to pick up or kick out of your party and they react to how you choose to play the game.)
You want replayability (Play it as the ultimate good guy then go back and slaughter everyone no matter who they are.)

You may just fall in love with a genre of game that is nearly  forgotten today.
That being said...here's to the current crpg renaissance.

Get ready for some serious RPGing. It's intimidating at first but the game will eventually grow on you. Beware action heroes this is a real-time point and click RPG, not a sword swinging, spell slinging killing game. Take this review from the perspective of a non DND player.
General information-

Strong association to character, class and story (Alignments, Class restrictive to alignments, Characters take note of story events and alignments)
Combat takes place with unseen dice rolls for hitting and damaging targets. Magic once used has charges (depending on the type of mage/wizard)
Every class seems to be resourceful and well thought out with a serious amount of balance for the first time player. (Thieves are extremely useful, as are mages/wizards. Detecting traps and uncovering magical items are what these classes can be used for)
5 NPCs can be used in a party. (It's recommeded to actually have a party, this game isn't a cake walk without one. Alternatively 5 players can also be used if you can ever get a game going)
Items and spells are locked to class restrictions so planning is a character is a useful way to succeed in your adventures!
Careful planning before encounters are advised when going into unknown territory (Unlike some games where running through the front door would be the norm)
Sleeping in game is a option for recovery of spells and healing.
Banter between player character/other characters is a welcome breeze for character delevopment and story telling. (I know it's a bioware game, shut up lol. This is normal I get it.)
IMMERSION. Try to become the character if you will :3.
Auto-saving frequently will save your keyboard from a Dark Souls/Skyrim wrath-like reaction.
When characters in your party die they can be resurrected but will drop all items on the floor where they died.
Positives and Negatives-
+Some voiced lines but mostly text.
+Played with the pause feature actually being a critical part of play.
+The class system is what you would expect from a DND experience, maybe lack luster (Unmodded/hasn't played DND)
+A strong focus on story telling. Although the second is where it get's beefy.
+Extremely strong character roster, much better in the sequel but still worth a buy.
+Not too flashy. Most games have extremely flashy fights and what not to make the game appear more dramatic than it is. This game just hits it right in the dot for me. It's more of a + than a negative really.
-Poor multiplayer, what else needs to be said? I had a bad time connecting to people and keeping it stable. Probably just me but who knows.
-While it has strong story telling the story is lacking in this edition, buy the second one and with mods you can play this version on the second BG2.
-Old style graphics. Think like Rune Scape/Helbreath/Diablo 2/ Etc
-Ran on my PC but might not for others, friends have told me concerns of the game being unable to run correctly, their spec's vary.
TL:DR - DND simulator with a top down perspective and real time combat (With pause feature). Interesting story and characters. 7/10 a good buy if its your first game in the series, wait for a sale don't buy the game for $20, see GIF

To start this off, I need to say that I’ve played Project Zomboid for most of its development history, going all the way back to when it was a tiny map back before the developers had to start all over from scratch. I’ve been keeping an eye on its development ever since, as I believed that it had some great potential. I even supported its Greenlight on Steam. However, in my honest opinion, today’s Project Zomboid is a game that I really wish had taken a different approach. The elements are there: it’s a challenging game that rewards you with immense satisfaction once you get established and don’t have to worry about everything that goes bump in the night. Sure, it can be a little rough to learn at first, but when you break it down it’s a good example of a survival game done right (for the most part).
As much as I could praise the game (as I’ll be honest, I greatly enjoyed it) I just can’t recommend it in its current state. I won't be going into the good things about the game in this review, as I think they would overshadow something more important. I feel like the developers have lost sight of what their original plan was, and that they’ve also become unaware or unwilling to acknowledge the community’s more pressing concerns. Quite simply, this is a game that has effectively stalled out – and it did so years ago. Focusing on new features is fine, but putting an unnecessary amount of detail into them is taking it too far and only leads to long waits and lots of disappointment.
As for the latest example of what went wrong: cars. Cars have been in development for the better part of almost a year and a half now as of writing this. So much time has been spent on things that we just don’t need in a game like this. We’ve been wanting cars for quite a while, but not like this…
- Detailed vehicle conditions? Just give the entire thing a health value, and give some visual cues that it’s been damaged… we don’t need a part-by-part breakdown of what needs fixing. If it hits zero, just let it stall out and be unusable unless it gets fixed.
- Varied gas usage? Just give vehicle types different sized tanks and have them use fuel by percentage points, so larger vehicles use more gas in comparison to smaller ones.
- Gear shifting? I’ll just drop a quote from one of the “news” updates regarding this, “…Firstly while playing around with sound implementation we realized that the noise of gear shifts was fairly vital…”
- Rollover physics? While I can see it being a fun addition, I don’t see this being something that needed its own focus point for who-knows-how-long.
- Suspension? Is this really necessary? Really?
I’m sure there’s more that I could pick at, but I neither want to look any further or believe I need to say more to make my point clear. Give us functional, relatively simplistic vehicles, not this over-thought-out mess.
Of course, there are other things that I feel should have been left out entirely or should have waited until after all the major features were in the game and it could finally be called a “full release” (nutrition, clothing degradation, detailed first-aid)… while not bad, it should have waited. Some features that have been the subject of their attention for quite some time, such as new animations and models, still have yet to make it into the game in favor of their recent vehicle obsession.
Where are cellars? Fort Knox? Increased building height? Creative mode? NPCs? I’m sure I’m missing some, but you tend to lose track after several years go by with no news other than “vehicles, vehicles, vehicles, animations, vehicles, vehicles”. This game could have released years ago if they just addressed the things people wanted most, then they could have spent the time afterwards working on new extensions of existing features or new additions altogether. Instead, we are left with a game that is left looking more and more abandoned part way through development, and with the current pacing of content it is likely to have a full release sometime after 2020.

If you enjoy Zombie Survival games and isometric perspectives, I'd highly recommend checking Zomboid out.  The demo is pretty limited but between that and if you watch some videos on youtube you can probably figure out if it's up your alley.
The crafting and construction systems are pretty robust and there's a lot of things you can do with fortifications and basebuilding.  You can modify existing structures, adding new floors, perimeter walls, traps and the like.  It's also possible to build from scratch.
Combat is rather basic but functional.  It does what it needs to but never really rises much above being adequate.  This is mostly fine as a part of the game is weighing each encounter with zombies and deciding if it's worth the time/calories/risk to clear them out or if you just want to move on.
The profession system is pretty neat and helps to encourage differing playstyles based on your starting choices.  They tend to give a starting bonus to certain skills as well as a multiplier to increasing those skills during play along with potentially some unique perks.  As a cat burglar for instance you have a boost to sneaking so you'll probably end up favoring a stealthy playstyle which feels rather different than a more combat-oriented or generalist character.
One of my only gripes with the game is the ways it handles difficulty.  Normal and below the zombie populations are sparse, unaware (quite easy to sneak up on a zombie with level 0 out of 10 sneaking skill) and their respawn is very slow and limited.  You will also eventually be swimming in more loot than you could possibly waste unless you are burning down every building you come across.
On hardcore zombies are hyper-vigilant (even at level 6-7 sneaking you will frequently pull multiple zombies from a great distance away).  They're also very robust and the worst kind of stupid.  They will randomly start attacking doors, windows and walls simply because they are there (no sound or vision of movement from you or other zombies to set them off).  They respawn incredibly fast, in places that make no sense and they tend to mob together in huge hordes completely disproportionate to the population of the area they're in.
I'd recommend making a custom sandbox and tuning the experience to what you find enjoyable as the presets are rather all-or-nothing when it comes to difficulty.
Overall, this game is pretty enjoyable, and especially for the asking price I'd find it hard not to recommend it.  It's got all the things you'd expect from a Zombie Survival game, with a neat little twist in that it's from an isometric perspective.

I'd definitely recommend Kholat for any fan of survival horror - the environment is beautifully haunting, the creaks and moans of the forest will make your heart pound (play with headphones!), and there is an intriguingly dark story that will keep you hunting for more answers.
That said, this immersive experience could have been vastly improved by tending to some missed opportunities - first and foremost being environmental puzzles. This game is purely a horrific adventure of discovery, which I did enjoy, but felt some simple yet brain twisting environmental puzzles would have made the beautiful and chilling environment even more intimate, and would have slowed down the pace of the gameplay while also making it more dynamic.
Enemies (or I should say enemy) could have also used some dynamism. Once the enemy is aware of you, there's really no getting away or hiding unless you just keep sprinting as much as you can until you get even more lost. I did like that you couldn't fight the enemy and that getting away was difficult, but encountering them would have been much more interesting if I had more opportunities to hide.
Lastly, there were some missed opportunities in the environment itself. There are a few wonderful scripted moments when you walk up to an abandoned radio tower, a burnt forest, a rotting church, but when you get to these awesomely dark scenes you just grab the note and get the hell out of there - I wanted to spend more time in these places (*cough* environmental puzzles *cough*).
People complain about the compass and map in this game, but I think this is one of its most immersive qualities and an impressive way to bring a subtle level of strategy and skill into the game - I wanted more elements like this!
Overall I felt this was a great survival horror experience and was well worth the price, but could have been a legendary survival horror experience if more elements of the game were developed, like the absence of environmental puzzles and more ways of dealing with the game's enemy.
