Back in Late 90's/Early 2000's, wrestling games were everywhere, with great titles such as  the Smackdown, the early Smackdown vs Raw, and of course the old Aki wrestling games for the Nintendo 64. We got great wrestling experiences unlike the ones we get today from 2K studios. The wrestling games that 2k makes every year improve few things, and are lacking in features compared to the games from when we were kids. But if there was one game from that old period that stood out from the rest, it was Fire Pro Wrestling Returns (the sequel to the game “Fire Pro Wrestling”). It wasn't like any other game, it had old school 2D graphics, customization for nearly everything, and it had a fantastic grapple system, in short, the game was a masterpiece. The series began in Japan during the late 80’s, and none of the games from the series were sold outside of Japan until 2005. Sadly, this was the last Fire Pro game to be developed for another 10 years. But after waiting for so long, fans of the Fire Pro series are getting the sequel they’ve always wanted.
Well, here it is, Fire Pro Wrestling Word, let’s talk about the customizability. The game is just as customizable as its previous installments, if not better. With the ability to create and edit wrestlers as well as referees, players are sure to love this game, though It is lacking in the amount of clothes you can put on a wrestler. you can create as many wrestlers as you want, as long as you have the space for it. You can also change the settings of matches with things like background music, DQ, count out, etc. The devs have also revealed on Twitter that they are going to allow you to upload custom music to use as wrestler entrance themes, as well as background music. One issue I had with the game was how complicated creating a custom wrestler was. You have to download them from the workshop, and then you have to go to create new wrestler/model wrestler to set them up to a promotion and team. This confused me as I spent multiple hours downloading wrestlers off the workshop only to not no where they were, I had to use google to figure it out.
The grappling in this game is alot different than most wrestling games. The wrestlers grapple by walking into each other, then an animation plays of them locking up, where you need to go through a sort of quick time event in order to do a move. It takes a few hours to get used to it but when you do, It works great. Another Flaw I have is that in order to hit your opponent you have to be a precise distance away from them or it won’t connect.
I must say for an early access game, it’s pretty clean, I have only discovered one real bug. Sometimes when a computer opponent has a weapon, their player model will start to turn in different directions really fast, which always make me dizzy whenever I see it. Overall this is a very high recommend for fans of the wrestling genre. I can’t wait for them to finish it, this could end up being the greatest wrestling game of all time, only time will tell. Finally, I give this game a 7/5 in true Dave Meltzer fashion due to its great customization, unique gameplay, and an affordable price.

The Long Dark may have given a new meaning to the Early Access stage. It was initially released as “early” as September 2014 (same age as my Steam account) and until August 2017 it remained in Early Access, thus a really long wait for the dev team to finally implement a storyline along that lovely survival mode. The game I’m writing about is special for a couple of reasons. First, its 2013 successful Kickstarter campaign was a following to the already secured funding from the Canada Media Fund. The public sector joined forces along with public funding, in order to finance one of the best video games focusing on the Canadian wilderness. The second and most important feature, is that Long Dark is a very thorough survival simulation. It leaves next to no details or variables out of the equation. No easy feat considering that Hinterland Studio Inc. is a developer with no previously released projects.
I received a review copy several months ago but delayed my review for The Long Dark on purpose since I always like judging a video game for the merits and potential strength of its narrative as well, not just gameplay diversity and fun factor. As always, I’ll be completely honest and I do have to confess that I expected a subpar story, filled with plot holes and clichés. What I witnessed instead, is an emotional tale featuring metaphors to both life and death. They aren’t even disguised by subtlety and I couldn't fathom just how deep this “rabbit hole” would go.
Before leaving Early Access and playing in that notoriously unforgiving survival “sandbox mode”, I imagined at the very least that it would have to be a story about a stranded person, having to fight nature and overcome/tame it somehow. I knew that a journey would have to feature locations far more diversified than the intial six maps and an ending to this simulated ordeal. I didn’t expect this struggle for survival to feature two main characters, each connected to the other in an emotional way. Players shall get to experience The Long Dark from the perspective of utility pilot Will Mackenzie (at least in the two out of five episodes released so far) and his former wife, Dr. Astrid Greenwood.
Just by having that as a feature instead of an option, speaks volume about the future plans for this game’s storyline. At the time of this writing, I definitely can’t tell you how it will end (nor was I ever inclided to spoil it, anyways) even in broad terms. Three more episodes shall be released in the future and The Long Dark shall reward both its veteran player base and the new wave, by offering all the future story content, absolutely free. Who can argue with that? I will try to summarize at least a few crucial details about the main characters and their motivations.
Will is regarded as a “bush pilot” (person used with flying over/landing on rough terrain and equally difficult weather conditions) and he reluctantly agrees to transport his ex-wife to a remote location in the vast northern wilderness from Canada for a cryptic reason which he doesn’t question a lot. Astrid is carrying a tightly locked briefcase and insists on departing at once, despite the impending snow storm which shall ultimately force Mackenzie to crash land. They are separated and wounded, hungry, thirsty, freezing and in mortal danger from the inexplicably aggressive wildlife. But they must endure and survive to meet once again. The Story Mode is named “Wintermute”. That is a hint by itself.
Just like its “Canadian wilderness rival” Kona, Unity Engine is powering The Long Dark as well. Apart from the different visual style separating these two, the gameplay experience went on smoothly. I could run them both, maxed out and at 4K resolution without ever worrying that the frame rate will drop below 60. It goes without saying that both titles feature plenty opportunities for epic screenshots, thanks to their minimal User Interface and a HUD which fades away, when not in use.
Do I still have to emphasize how dark the nights in The Long Dark, really are? It’s right there in the game’s title afterall. I didn’t expect this either but I wasn’t as shocked as going from Vice City’s neon-lit ‘80s streets to the gritty realism in Grand Thef Auto IV and its depressing depiction of night life. No, I was aware that survival in the dark, in the middle of freezing nowhere basically, should force players to seek shelter at once. I am glad that The Long Dark didn’t feature the unmodded skyline from Skyrim. Epic, yet far from reality and the Aurora Borealis (northern lights) musn’t distract you from the approaching pack of starving wolves since you’re just a regular Joe, not Dragonborn.
Overall, the visuals stood out in a nice way, the HUD allowed me to take as many screenshots as I pleased (& on my terms) while the textures had some minor flaws from time to time. Nothing game breaking and at least from afar, it wasn’t much of an issue. Eye candy doesn’t mean everything and The Long Dark is anything but plain. Looks or otherwise. The visual style is a mix between comic book and cel shading, but without visible outlines.
If the soundtrack will certainly satisfy your ears, wait until I tell you about the voice acting. It’s a Mass Effect reunion, without you know, the actual Mass Effect gameplay and feel. Ladies and gentlemen, Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer! Jane and John Shepard, if you never bothered changing their in-game names. These two voice actors made the ME trilogy a lot better and they have now used their talent in The Long Dark with the same kind of convincing enthusiasm. Sure, there isn’t nearly as much dialogue in the game but even monologues require skill. Otherwise you get a “stellar” performance such as Destiny’s “Dinklebot”. I prefer silence than phoning in your lines for a quick paycheck.

Why can't I add clothes to a fire?

Why can't I find a simple compass or at least put custom markings on the map that let me know where I am?
Why can't I use the Canadian flags for fire or to create a patriotic winter outfit? (Survival is surely more important than nationalism.)
Why can't I use a fresh deer/bear corpse for a few hours of sleep and warmth? (Bear Grylls did.)

If the graphics was the only thing that mattered, then Kholat would be a tremendous success. Seriously the game looks beautiful (especially for an indie open world game). But the most important thing is the gameplay and this game is sadly severely lacking in content. The world is absolutely barren, there is nothing but you and the ocasional shadowy figure which kills you instantly if you come too close. You are no fighter, you even lack the ability to jump, which prevents you from entering areas, which any normal human being should be able to access. The only thing you are allowed to do is collecting diary pages and notes, which gradually unveils the story. Collecting notes is also one of two ways to save the game (the other is fast travel), so it is entirely possible to scout out a large portion of the map without saving only to die and have to do it all over again. Combine this with an absolutely dreadful map system and you have a very irritating game. Yes, you have a map, but it's inefficient at best. It doesn't show your position and you cannot put any notes on it (missed opportunity). Sometimes you find coordinates, which tells you your position. But all this effort just isn't worth it, I ditched the map very quickly and managed relatively fine, I mean the world isn't that big. Way to make a big portion of the game irrelevant.
Running is as you might have already figured out your main activity in this game. But your stamina is very very low, run for too long and your wision becomes blurry, which forces you to stop. So learning how to sprint in short bursts becomes essential. Let's return to the shadows/ghosts or whatever they are. They are very easy to see, because they leave behind bright orange footsteps. But sneaking around them can be tricky because there is no stealth system, one time I've been hidden in a bush and was detected, other time I stood in plain sight an wasn't detected. So the only thing that triggers their AI is proximity. Keep your distance and they will never be a threat to you. But if you trigger them, you can run away from them, if you react quickly. Hovewer, this usually involves running away from the direction you were going, and you might end up in a completely different area then you wanted to. This is probably the only time, where the coordinates scatered throughout the world will actually come in handy.
So, we've established that this game doesn't offer too much in the gameplay area, the main focus must be the story. The story, which is told throughout the notes, it ranges from diary pages of the Dyatlov expedition, to insane ramblings which make everything more confusing. Instead of bringing answers, everything you read/witness raises more questions. It does hovewer a decent job describing the Dyatlov incident at the beginning.
Let's sum this up- this game lacks in gameplay, lacks in storytelling, the map system is tedious, the world looks nice but is completely empty. You have to ask yourself, is that worth the asking price?

Man, it's right about now that I kinda wish I'd learned how to use a COMPASS properly, back when I was in the Boy Scouts.  But alas...always eluded me.  There's some trick about it I just don't seem able to fathom.  Oh well.  Chalk it up to yet another failure in a life chock-full of 'em...

With a little luck, you don't share this same problem, and even if you do...this will still be one of the most flat-out, full-on atmospheric journeys you'll ever undertake.  Unless you actually holiday in places like the Dyatlov Pass in REAL LIFE, in which case you are a SCARY ♥♥♥♥ING PSYCHO.  Or at least a much, much bigger Man than me.  But for the rest of us cowards, this game will immerse you in a world of snap-frozen freakiness, and as an added bonus, if your sense of direction/ability with compasses is as bad as mine, you can add the frustration of getting frequently lost into an already nerve-fraying foray into the unknown.  Not since Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs have I experienced such an enjoyably "oppressive" game...but instead of the constant clanking of epic machinery and scary pig-men, we get relentless snow-storms and...well, you'll just have to see for yourself (apologies for the spoiler about the pig-men in Machine For Pigs, but you probably guessed that one already for yourself).

More plot than Slender!  More gameplay than Dear Esther!  So if you fancy a (rough) combination of those two, Kholat may well be one of the best purchases you will ever make in the magical land of Steam.  Put on some headphones, turn off the lights, leave a window open if it's Winter (to simulate the freezing conditions; c'mon, you know the pneumonia's worth it)...and prepare for one of the most chilling (pun intended) games you'll ever play.  All this, and voice acting by Sean Bean!  What the ♥♥♥♥ are you waiting for?  Hell to freeze over?!  Be a MAN, dammit!!  Speaking of which, if they ever make this game compatible with the upcoming Oculus Rift, I'll end up with more hair on my testacles than I'll know what to do with.  (Actually, come to think of it...I'm not really sure what purpose the hair on them presently serves, but...that's a philosophical discussion for another time, perhaps.)  C'MON, BUY THE ♥♥♥♥ING GAME ALREADY!!!

This game is beautiful and haunting. Between the music, the scenery, feeling truly lost, and constantly feeling watched wherever you go, this game is immersive and atmospheric in the absolute best way. This game is horror done right. While there was only one time that nearly gave me a heart attack, every moment of gameplay was tense and uneasy.
Throughout the first hour or so, I honestly had no idea how to navigate. I had no idea where to start or what to look for. But slowly, the game allowed me to learn naturally instead of forcing a tutorial down my throat. Needless to say, by the end of my time on Kholat Syakhl I was an expert navigator. The sense of accomplishment from that alone was extremely satisfying.
In terms of graphical fidelity, this game is very impressive. The textures especially were simply gorgeous. They all look like you could reach out and just feel the bumpiness of the rocks or the grit of the dirt. The mountains give you beautiful snowy forest vistas, while the caves are cold and damp, literally dripping with ambiance.
The soundtrack is quite good, although it's not necessarily one I'd listen to outside of actual gameplay. A couple tracks are sweeping and nice to listen to, but by and large the soundtrack is full of gripping drums and blaring low horns. It does a great job of keeping you always looking over your shoulder. There are some vocal tracks, and they are used appropriately. One at the beginning, one towards the end that fits well with a note you find just before you get a story beat, and one in the credits that, in my opinion, was maybe the weakest of the vocal tracks.
Pros:
Beautiful graphics
Simple controls that do only what you need
Rewarding navigation difficulty curve (maybe a negative for you - YMMV)
Interesting story that ends in such a way to keep you guessing and speculating
Pretty good soundtrack
Top notch voice acting
A lot of content and scenery to discover
Cons:
I might've liked a few more graphical options
Stamina mechanic (though this is just a personal dislike in games, and a minor gripe at worst)
If you're a seasoned horror vet as I am, you won't be scared out of your mind constantly. Look elsewhere if you want that
No manual saving
All in all, this game is an 8/10 from me. Or a must buy. Whatever scoring appeals to you, it's worth a buy, even at full price. This is by far one of the best horror games to hit steam in recent memory, and from an indie studio no less. Thank you, IMGN.PRO, for such an engrossing experience!

Even in 2015, Baldur's Gate plays surprisingly well. I've never tried the original version to compare it to, but the enhanced edition has no issues whatsoever, and doesn't feel too dated in any way other than the 2nd edition dnd system in place.
Arguably the best part about the game is the new character additions. Neera, the Wild Mage, in particular makes the game a lot more enjoyable to play, especially for those who are hooked on the excellent Dragon Age but want to revisit the past. If she weren't written so well she might have seemed like a superfluous add-on, yet she is a delightful character and until I was made aware that she was a new addition to the enhanced version I simply thought she was one of the original cast and was just more developed than the others. Therein lies the enhanced edition's one potential problem. If you've been toying with the idea of playing Baldur's Gate for years, as I have, then now is the time to play it, and the enhanced edition is absolutely the way to go.

What can one say in front of such magnificence? These two RPGs are simply the pillar of western production of this genre, and when the two are combined in a single game they definitively are among the top 10 of the must-play for every PC gamer out there, no matter the age.
BG:EE and BG2:EE are simply THE definitive Dungeons & Dragons experience, including almost all the possible 2.5 Edition Core and several optional rulebooks of the Forgotten Realms setting and translating them into a marvellous duo of 3rd person games.
Although both games are very old (they were developed and published between 1998 and 2001 by Bioware / Black Isle Studios), they have been “enhanced” and made available on modern systems (including Windows 7/8/10 PCs, OSx, Android and IOS) by the guys at Overhaul Games / Beamdog, who not only re-tooled the original Infinity Engine to make it run on modern platforms, but also added several other goodies that were not present in the original release, in addition to bug fixes and standard “curator” jobs.
I could go on for pages and pages describing in detail the marvels of the Baldur’s Gate Series, but I’ll try to cut it short and stick to a much shorter format.
- Ever dreamed of taking your typical AD&D session with your friends out of the pen & paper setting to a PC screen? This game is for you!
- Charismatic characters and companions: Minsc the Ranger (and Boo!), Jaheira, Viconia, Xzar, Sarevok… what else can I say?
- Longevity: both games combined are well over 100 hours of gameplay
- Replayability: seriously, there are hundreds of possible combinations of classes / races / kits / alignments / companions / choices to completely change your experience at every playthrough
- Every action you make affects the game world, like it is expected from a proper Western RPG. Apart from some scripted events to progress with the main story, the rest is up to you
- Multiplayer: join with 5 friends to create a fully custom party!
- The (new) developers are supporting the game with patches and fixes, and they actually listen to the community
- Compatible with most of the original BG / BG2 community mods
- Runs on every system, even your mobile phone / tablet (NOTE: the Android / IOs versions are separate purchases). HW requirements are very low
- After more than 16 years from my first BG playthrough I still cannot find a single flaw in any of these games. They are simply a masterpiece.
In a nutshell, these games set THE standard all the following RPGs on the market were measured against, and none of them was able to surpass Baldur’s Gate until now.
Buy them, play them, enjoy them. 12/10, would pickpocket Drizzt again

I've been wanting to play Maize since it released on December 1st, 2016; needless to say I was ecstatic when it came packaged in my Monthly Humble Bundle for June. You see, Maize is a game about sentient corn... yes, you read that right. Cornstalks have come to life thanks to a top secret experiment. They're able to eat, breathe, and do what they love most... nap. Though it's nowhere near a horror game in the traditional sense, this title has a unique quirky sci-fi attitude to it that's garnished by a derogatory sense of humor.
For the sake of not spoiling the fantastic story, I'll only continue on to say that you also make an interesting friend along the way; one who follows you around while insulting you, yet helping you perform tasks to achieve the next puzzle solution. Maize is a game that centers around problem solving, and while in theory that might sound boring, in practice it's a lot of fun. The enigmas are generally easy to solve once you've found the right item, but they're creative and surrounded by publisher/developer Finish Line Games' own brand of sarcastic wit. Whether it's finding funny bantering notes left by two of the title's main characters, picking up one of 75 collectible items with humorous descriptions, or reading the text that pops up center-screen once you've completed a puzzle.
Finding your way around in the semi-linear world of Maize is made easy thanks to the bright orange boxes that the developers use to close off certain areas when they're not in use. The world is large enough, thanks to the extra corridors and paths that each section contains. It never feels like you spend too long in the same spot, though you'll need to revisit areas from time to time to solve older puzzles. The 3-4 hours that you'll spend in-game will feel like a cinematic adventure, thanks to the high quality nature of the graphics, and the style leaves Maize somewhere in limbo between a dream-like adventure, and a darker, more adult Pixar film. It should also be noted that the optimization of this title is completely on point.
If you're down for a new kind of excursion that involves a sci-fi experiment gone awry, complete with puzzle solving and talking corn, then Maize is the game for you. You also need an appreciation for somewhat dry, sarcastic, and degrading humor; for instance, if you're sensitive to being called "idiot" a lot, do not apply here. It's amazing how the developers gave such a detailed life to characters that are never even seen in the game, through the use of post-it notes alone, and the ending of the game is sure to leave you at least a little shocked. For it's quality and length of time, Maize is definitely worth the $21.99 CAD, and the developers are Canadian to boot. So what do you have to lose, eh?

Next and what I found a much bigger problem was that the game felt so hand-holdy that it felt like a walking simulator instead of an adventure-puzzle game. Overall, unless at least one of these is fixed, I wouldn't recommend the game at its current price.

Opus Magnum is a great puzzle game. In it you have to build Transmutation Machines transforming and bonding elements into others, This is achieved by placing simple parts, like an arm that can rotate left or right and giving them simple instructions. Unlike other Zachtronics games the mechanics can be learned quickly and aren't very technical.
Unlike most puzzle games often times it isn't very hard to find a solution. But after finding one it is compared to the solutions of all other players in the categories of "cost", "cyles" (time) and "area". This is were the game gets really interesting. You can optimize your solution to be very good in one of those categories and only ok in the other two. Or kind of good in everything. It's left up to the player.
In this sense you need some ambition to truly enjoy this game. But the game does a good job in instilling the desire of wanting to be just a bit better in the player.
Big bonus points for having the option to create a gif of your creations in order to brag about them on twitter.

Opus Magnum is much more accessible than Zachtronics previous games, and possibly their best.  It's the free and open form of gameplay mean you are looking for a solution, rather than the solution.
It is still a fiendish puzzle game, casting you as an alchemist making machines to transmute and create molecules. But it is much more user friendly and accessible this time, with no restrictions at all. The aim is first to create what-ever based on a given input.   When you have built a machine, you are compared with what everyone else have done, and you can see how effective you have been, based on histograms of average costs  (gold, #cycles and area size), and it is up to you if you want o go back and try  to optimise it for a greater score in either category. It is a great incentive to just try to tweak it just a little bit more to cut down the cost or the cycles it uses, and creep a little bit higher up on statistics.
The game give you all the tools from the get go, and there are no penalties, which means you do exactly what you want to complete a level. Whether you then want to spend time optimizing your creation, or just see what kind of silliness you can do. The game has a very gentle learning curve and a very good tutorial which teaches you everything you need to make the machines work. As it gives you all the tools you need from the start, complexity is introduced by the nature of the inputs and outputs, not by giving you new things to learn as you progress.  It already have a lot of levels, and access to user created levels (through Steam Workshop at the moment).  It also looks very good, and the ability to create shareable gifs of your working machines is a stroke of genius.

Bottom line, very fun and accessible puzzle game, highly recommended

Zachtronics returns to his roots with this brilliant little puzzler.
When I was a student, rather than studying I used to waste my time playing a little flash game; "Codex of Alchemical Engineering". This game is an amazing reboot of the same core concept, with a gorgeous aesthetic. It's amazingly satisfying to just sit back and watch your machine do it's thing.
The UI has benifited from a number of simple tweaks that makes it easy to chain stages in your production process. Earlier stages will automatically restart their cycle before the later stages have completed. It takes away all the hassle of time offsets and starting that was one of the only downsides of some of the other Zachtronics puzzlers.
As with all Zachtronics puzzlers, getting a solution to each puzzle is only the first step. The real fun begins when you try and optimise your solution. Each solution is scored on three key metrics. Cost, Time to Run, and Area. It's impossible to simultaneously optimise all three of these, leading to the ability to re-play and re-play puzzles, trying to derive solutions that optimise different aspects. Some of my friends are a tad competitive, so of course I have to beat them...........
If you loved Space Chem and Infinifactory, then you WILL love this game.

What can I say about Baldur's Gate that hasn't already been said? Even though I'm mostly a hardcore adventure game player, this game beats most others hands down. The storyline becomes increasingly interesting as it progresses, and as the territory opens up more and more. Combat is won by intelligent strategy, and the game can be played a multitude of ways. It follows the old classic Dungeons and Dragons rules, where low armour class, for example AC0 or AC -2 is better than Armour Class 6. Somehow this adds to the authenticity of it all. The inventory screen is great: very satisfying, with great sound effects, and clearly one of the models for the World of Warcraft inventory screen. Personally I preferred the inventory screen on the original classic release, but it's not much of a gripe really.
Where this beats WoW hands down is in story. "Quests" all fit together in a coherent whole, so that they are not mere fetch quests or kill-20-mana-monster affairs, but are intriguing sub-plots, which help you piece together the story. And if you don't do a quest fast enough - for example saving a loved one - one of your party members can get upset and attack you. Yes, your party members can attack each other, and this can be a nightmare when facing opponents who can Charm you, etc.
The number of curios in this game, from hamsters to pantaloons, is brilliant, all of which make it seem like a detailed world you progress in. You can steal or kill good characters if you wish, but this has ramifications. You also have to keep party members happy if they are of different alignments, and they occasionally have conversations with each other, which come out in the audio voice acting - which is terrific. The soundtrack is truly incredible. Michael Hoenig did an awesome job.
This really is a fantasy roleplay game, as opposed to a slash'n'bash affair. Fans will probably dive straight to the plough fields to see if the ankheg armour is there. It seems impossible that this game is so old now - released in 1998 - but was and still is light years ahead of its time in terms of sheer playability. The modding community was also very active after its sequel Baldur's Gate II and Icewind Dale, creating mods such as The Darkest Day, and all sorts of weird and wonderful exploits, all of which could make the game even more interesting, given a sensible level of tweaking. Someone even produced a huge all-encompassing Big World package a few years back which brought as many mods together into one package.
You can multi-class and be a mage/druid and fighter as your main character - you can have six in total at any one time, but you can always sack someone and re-hire later. You can die! Quite easily if you are not sensible, so progress saving is a must. You can walk around like a travelling halberd salesman with a bag full of weapons, or travel light, as you wish. The level of detail in this game indicates that the creators were big fans of D&D, and did I mention that it all ties in to Ed Greenwood's Forgotten Realms campaigns, popularised by R.A. Salvatore's books? No, I didn't did I. Also big props to Beamdog for simply providing me with a Steam key after I gave them my purchased serial. A company doing things right. Bioware is now a household name, but even after the publishing of Baldur's Gate they were not so well-known - but Bioware were not the publishers - they were the
. One of the designers, James Ohlen, was also a lead designer for Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, which also has a truly great story. Another, Ray Muzyka, was bizarrely a practising physician, along with his co-founder Greg Zeschuk. Proving once and for all, that D&D is for everyone.

Better than Dragon Age Inquisition, but tedious at times. Your character is actually YOUR OWN, and you should understand what I'm saying if you played Dragon Age Origins, Dragon age 2 and Dragon age inquisition. Dragon age was better off without the dialogue wheel or the character voice acting, as each time you made a different character in Dragon age Origins, it felt completely new, unlike its sequels, where you felt like you were playing the exact same character but with a different class or race.
You could be a complete psychopath, nuetral, angelic, or just plain mean depending on your dialogue choices and they were actually sentences which showed you exactly what you were going to say, not just coloured icons --- in dragon age origins. In its sequels, you could be a bully, or a sarcastic bully, or 'diplomatic', which means nice guy. In DAO People actually react to you being a different class or race, there are more dialogue options, the side quests are actually side quests and not mmo fetch quests (I'm looking at you DAI), you have to actually plan a strategy to win fights with enemies and not just slam the keyboard, and the main story makes more sense. The side quests actually have different endings to them. Yeah! It's not just -go there and -go here, you actually take part in them and have to decide which road you have to take. I realized after playing DAI, how much more superior this game is.

This game feels intense, strategic, smart, and immersive. It conveys the feeling of desperation that a crash survivor would feel when having to fight through hordes of hostiles against seemingly impossible odds. It is hugely satisfying when you pull through a particularly intense horde and make it to the next floor. I have failed a three dozen times for every victory, but the characters feel more like survivors when you actually survive that one time out of three dozen. This feeling is enhanced when you play this game in coop mode. 10/10 would recommend.

tl;dr: Great concept but gameplay is spent watching progress bars complete for hours while your character stands still. All the while, the devs waste years in development on a game that will never be complete, nor fun. 3/10.
Alright, I'm done. I've played as much as I could of this game and I've completely snapped and I can't stand this game anymore. I do want to commend the devs on a great idea for a game, but I just can't say I recommend it. I could bring up the years that this has been in early access (like I am now) or I could just focus on what gameplay there is and try and explain to others how this game is the antithesis of fun (like I will next).
Basically it's the zombie apocalypse................... How original, right? Well, when this game first came out years and years ago it might have been a little more fresh. Unfortunately for Project Z, neither this game nor genre stand the test of time. But that's only half the problem with this game. Every single action is as follows:
* right click,
* then move mouse,
* then hover over option,
* then new menu appears,
* then move mouse to new option,
* then click the new option,
* And then you wait for a progress bar to complete.
While you wait there is no animation of the character doing anything. No change in your surroudings while progress is being made. Nothing. You just sit there and watch a progress bar fill up while your character just stands there.
At first you don't mind. It's a game of action and planning. It's a game of survival.. but as you'll soon realize, none of that matters because you only experience that for about 10 minutes out of the hours and hours of play each instance brings. Most of your time is literally spent watching a progress bar slowly complete while your character just stands there. A progress bar to read. A progress bar to cook. A progress bar to construct. A progress bar to fill a water bottle. A progress bar to water a plant. A progress bar to repair. A progress bar to jerk off. Ok maybe not that last one, but you get the point.
The real problem is that the game is literally one loading screen after the next. NOTHING HAPPENS AT ALL. Sure a zombie could walk up on you and you get to hear that screeching sound when your character is surprised (oh yeah, that wears off after the 3rd to 400th time you hear it). But the reality is you are watching a character standing with a loading bar over its head 99% of the time. And that's the game. Eventually you'll die, or live forever because there is no end game, but no matter what, you'll spend countless hours watching a mother ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥ucking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥fart licking horse vomiting boring as♥♥♥♥♥♥loading bar go by as you slowly age in real life.
And if that wasn't bad enough, the game has the audacity to mock you while you're playing. You need to cook something? Here's 10 drop down menus to make a stir fry dish. Then the game has the BALLS to send you a status update on your character that says, "Getting Bored, Occupy yourself, or seek entertainment." ARE YOU ♥♥♥♥ING SERIOUS!? No KIDDING I'm ♥♥♥♥ING BORED. This crappy game is telling me that my character is bored? I'M BORED IN REAL LIFE TOO!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
I think the joke is on us for giving the devs our money. They have proven to deliver too little too late and to mock us while we play it. I found this game to be a solid concept that is completely lost and muddled with features that are overly tedious and in desperate need of streamlining. I keep hearing Steve Jobs yelling, "WHY ARE THERE SO MANY BUTTONS?" Worse yet is this game is a progress bar simulator where nothing ever happens. I'm sorry, but this game is just the exact opposite of fun, and I'm usually the kind of idiot that like this kind of micromanagement garbage. 3/10.

If you want this game, you want it for the sandbox. The story mode is just an odd... decision that to me feels like Hinterlands hired a completely outside team to develop.  Its a linear story shoved into a distinctively non-linear game.  From what I understand any further developments on the game will be focused on the story. Maybe it'll get better? But when you botch the intial roll out, it doesn't provide much faith.
As to the sandbox or challenges, you will probably enjoy it for a few runs.  But with each attempt, you might notice the glaring issues that really have not changed since the game first went EA.  The two things that stop me playing is the time you spend watching a little spinning wheel and then surprise wolves.
Time is very important resource in TLD, you will need to carefully manage it to last more than a week. Almost every action your character makes will take a chunk of time, leaving you to stare at an hourglass.  The reliance on this is probably the most significant issue I have with the game and what spurred this review.  Most tasks use time dilation to lesson the amount of time you are out of the game but where it feels jarring though is when you start searching through buildings.
Some loot will be strewn about on tables or tucked away in a corner. But most of it will be in a drawer that you click on and wait to search.  You have a rather interesting system of random placement that requires actually looking under a table or lighting a lamp for those hard to reach spots.  Then you have a few dozen containers or cabinets that you click and wait on.  I suppose its a tradeoff between types of effort, a tedious system of having to check under every sofa for a candybar against repetitive clicking and waiting.
In summary, they missed so many opportunities to add depth to core gameplay mechanics through smaller challenges that left me feeling quickly bored. Rather than learning some sort of minigame in harvesting a deer or sewing patches on my jacket, you watch that spinning wheel to level up the skill.
The wolves (and I guess to a smaller extent the bears) are the most direct threat to your playthrough.  You will be attacked by them at some point, there's really no getting around it.  Which means you'll be mashing your LMB in the hopes of not taking too much damage.  This mechanic is terrible and has hardly changed since it entered EA. Rather than a more nuanced quicktime event where you guide your stabs or something with a bit of skill, you suddenly perform an action that I don't seem how anyone could enjoy.
When you couple this combat with the wonky AI design, bugs, and spontaneous spawning of wolves, it can rapidly wear on your patience. My last playthrough on stalker difficulty ended when I turned a corner and a pack of wolves spawned behind me. One was glitched into a tree, another went right into attack mode and the other waited patiently for its turn to kill me. Mind you they spawned in a previously empty field that wolves hadn't spawned in before. I bought this game about a year and a half ago, when it was in Early Access. At the time, I read the reviews, and decided to buy it for the sandbox feature, which was working and had many positive comments. And I have no regrets about that decision.
Sandbox is awesome, with preset settings, but randomly generated loot and 4 difficulty modes : Pilgrim, Voyager, Stalker, and Interloper (Easy, Normal, Hard, Nightmare). You die a lot, but there's a certain joy in challenging your own best record and laughing at your pitiful deaths. And there's a sense of serenity in the game created by the images and sound effects. It comes across as a well-deserved love letter to Canada.
It's a bit disappointing that the biggest threat is the unrealistic wolves that attack you, but nothing is perfect, and playing on Pilgrim mode, without wolf attacks, is pretty boring since there's no challenge in the weather or scarcity of supplies if you have the least capability with video games. So I spend most of my time playing on Voyager mode and would recommend the sandbox mode of this game.
Now the Story Mode, which the game was originally designed for, has been completed and released, and I find myself frustrated. Aside from multiple basic bugs (cut scenes not playing, for example), the difficulty, rather than being set at Voyager (the average mode), has been set at Stalker (hard mode), with no ability for the player to adjust modes in order to enjoy the story. The game also decides where to save, rather than giving the control to the player, and gives you only the one save slot. This tactic worked fine for sandbox, where the point was the challenge (or if that wasn't the point for you, you could play Pilgrim). It doesn't work for a story, where you may have to replay the same bits over and over again, or can even get stuck in a no-win situation where death is inevitable because of your situation and condition when the game chooses to save for you.
This left my feelings about the game split about 50/50 over the positives and negatives. What pushed me over the edge to a negative vote was the feedback from the community over issues. You comment on the game being broken, the wolves being too aggressive, the inability to save, etc... and you get lectures from people about killing wolves with tools you don't have in story (and which never worked all that well in sandbox), that you should play sandbox for 50 hours (I've played it for more than that, and it doesn't make a difference, and if I hadn't and were a new player being told I had to play sandbox before I could experience the story, I'd be royally brassed off since if I buy a game for the story, I want to be able to play the damn story), and praising the devs for their commitment to their vision when they provide no difficulty control, set the difficulty at hard level (which used to be the most difficult level except that fans who mastered it asked for an even harder difficulty, and while I don't begrudge them wanting a nightmare mode, I do begrudge them then looking down on people who don't play in nightmare mode regularly, and may have given the developers the wrong idea about where to set the story skill level in the first place) and refuse to provide the ability to save. While I can respect artistic vision, the current vision is leading to an awful experience playing the story. And the overall experience in the forums has increased my negative view of the game as a purchase at this point.
So, are you buying this game for a potentially unplayable story, or for the sandbox mode survival challenge? That's really the question you should ask yourself before you put your money down. If you're up for the challenge, then I wish you the best of luck (ie not starting your first game randomly dropped in the middle of nowhere during a snowstorm in the middle of the night with barely any clothes on -- And no, that's not a criticism, it's just an amusing possibility of something you may have to overcome in a start point).

is 2015’s entry to the popular Assassin’s Creed franchise. With claims that the franchise is growing stale and 2014’s Assassin’s Creed Unity, the franchise needs to win its fans back. Does it, though? As a huge fan of the series who detested ACIII and Unity, I think it did.
Set in 19th century industrial London, the story follows the twins Jacob and Evie Frye on their quest to take a mega baddie Templar whose name I totally forgot. Does that say enough about the story? Not really. The story of Assassin’s vs. Templars is getting a bit stale by the 9th entry in the series and the game does not offer anything new in that regard. What it does though is throw us right into the action of that conflict without dragging out the first part of the game by giving us how the twins joined the creed or any backstory. I personally found that a bit refreshing.
Jacob and Evie’s personalities and methods are different. He likes to use brute force and go out with style while she likes to plan ahead and do things discreetly and stealthily. Their banter is one of the highlights of the game’s narrative, I just loved watching the two of them go at it on screen. Their journey to take down the Templars in London makes them cross paths with historical figures such as queen Victoria, Charles Dickens, and Charles Darwin. The two also form a street gang called the Rooks in hopes of battling the Templars’ gang which controls the city.
The game does nothing to progress the modern day story just like Assassin’s Creed titles since Black Flag.
Overall, the story was nothing groundbreaking yet fun to experience with a slightly disappointing ending.
For the first time in the series, you control two characters that you can be switchable at almost any time. Their differences are stark since Jacob is more of a brute that can sustain a great deal of damage while Evie is better suited for stealth missions. The Assassination missions are a highlight in the game. They are grand in scale with a number of ways to achieve the end goal. I think that they can be compared to Hitman Blood Money’s missions though a bit smaller.
Out of all the missions that I played, only one of them was a boring tailing mission! Outside the game’s main missions, there are a plethora of side missions including the 7 districts to liberate from Templar influence. Each district has 4 different kinds of side missions you need to complete in order to liberate said district with a finale consisting of an epic gang war.
As for the movement, the parkour mechanics improve upon those of Unity and they do a great job at it. Free running has two dedicated buttons now; one takes you up while the other one takes you in the opposite direction. This new system is great, but only when it works. I found myself having to climb all the way down a building and climbing back up just get over a small gap thanks to the lack of a jump feature. Yes, you cannot jump since there isn’t a dedicated command to do so. The new rope launcher is a welcome addition to the series and is actually one of my favorite gadgets. It makes traversing the streets of London faster and more fun. Think of yourself as a 19th century Spiderman. Drivable carriages were also a welcome addition since the city is so large (30% larger than Unity’s Paris). I did find one odd thing about climbing, though, it feels as if the player can only move in a grid because sometimes I would try to climb certain objects that were normally climbable in previous AC games but couldn’t as Jacob (or Evie) would just skip them and go over them.
Combat is finally fun to play and not only to watch! Much needed improvements were made to the combat which makes it fast, fluid, and most importantly, fun. The brutal combat animations make Jacob and Evie look as badass as they dress.
It is important to note that the game is the first Assassin’s Creed title not to feature any form of multiplayer since Assassin’s Creed Brotherhood. To be honest, I don’t really miss it.
The game is beautiful to gawk at. The busy streets of London feel alive with carriages, workers, children, merchants and all sorts of people roaming around. Gang wars also come to life with two dozens of NPCs battling it out while you mow them down with great combat animations and executions. Facial animations were also great except the weird and quirky facial animations of gang members. Location wise, London itself is a good location for an Assassin’s Creed title, but I feel that the European locations are growing a bit stale since I feel that they are mostly the same.
Voice acting is superb that, especially Jacob and Evie’s which makes their banter even more enjoyable. Music is atmospheric and fits the game. Other than that it isn’t as memorable as ACII’s or Revelations’.
TL;DR:
Pros:
Cons:
Overall, Assassin’s Creed Syndicate is a solid new entry in the franchise that is better treated as an individual game since it does nothing to advance the overall Assassin’s Creed story arc. The game features improved combat and parkour and a fun, self-contained story.

The combat is excellent. Most of the powers you get are pretty cool in their own right, but combining them in various ways with both your own weapons and the enemies' weapons (as in, using their own weapons against them) really makes them awesome. That said, I felt held back by sly comments from my comrades in the story, who kept reminding me I was an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for killing so many of their enemies. Sure, there are plenty of non-lethal options, but if you give me this amazing set of kick♥♥♥♥♥powers to chop my enemies into tiny little bits in a great variety of ways, I want to use them to their full potential without being called out on it all the time. Some people might like this interaction between story and combat, but I'm not one of them.
I got bored about 2/3 of the way through. The story didn't really interest me anymore at that point, and the level design (while overall pretty good) was getting monotonous. I quickly settled on a combination of powers and weapons that seemed to work for every situation and never felt like the level design encouraged me to try anything new. I actually stopped playing and didn't finish the last bit until today, 3 years after release. It took that long for it to feel fresh again, and I still have no interest in playing the DLC.

Before Origins, I played Inquisition as I had a PS4 and turned up on recommended on Amazon. I got so invested into the game and became interested in the earlier installments so I bought Origins on sale. I played as a Dalish elf first and initially hated the gameplay; it seemed slow and it felt like I did not need to do anything apart from right click on an enemy and wait for it to die. However, the story really gripped me along with the banter (more like insult throwing competition) between Alistair and Morrigan (and other characters like Oghren and Zevran later on) and I just HAD to know what happened next. There are so many moments that got to me emotionally whether it was happiness or anger.
As I progressed, the gameplay grew on me and I realised right clicking on an enemy and pressing the occassional button for a special attack was not going to cut it for a few of the battles and I had to formulate strategies with the other characters and decide who to attack first. Maize is an interesting concept.  It revolves around sentient corn, a topic that doesn't garner much attention in any media. Unfortunately, the game is let down by muddled intentions, monotonous gameplay and an over-reliance on lazy humour. If you got this for free or can pick it up for less than £3, go for it. Just don't expect anything close to a-maize-ing.
Walk somewhere, pick up item. Walk somewhere else, pick up item. Walk somewhere else, use all items on new environmental item until something happens. It's not the most gripping gameplay loop, and leads to a fair amount of unnecessary backtracking and frustration, some of which seems to only exist to artificially extend the lifetime of the game's story. This wouldn't be an issue if environments were exciting and interesting to traverse, but they aren't. The game really starts to feel like a slog towards the end stages, where some item combinations become nonsensical and trial-and-error based. Even for a semi-walking-simulator, Maize's gameplay is bottom of the barrel stuff. Also, why can't we rebind keys? Holding shift to sprint the entire game is such a chore.
I mean, the story is pretty unique. It's not as deep as you might think, and it doesn't really go anywhere until the end, but it's not too bad. That said, given that Maize is pretty much a walking simulator, the story certainly won't blow you away. Some aspects of it are fairly amusing - a few of the optional pickups are pretty funny and some of the more subtle jokes might produce a few giggles. However, the majority of the game's humour is lazy, clichéd and tiresome. Characters aren't fleshed out whatsoever, and the game seems to really, REALLY want to be Portal. It's so frustrating (you might notice how much this word crops up), because a longer, more well-crafted story could have been excellent. The concept is great! The foundations are laid! It's such a shame they didn't do more with this.
They're alright. Nothing cutting-edge. Bloom is slightly overdone and there's a weird blurry filter over everything (which becomes even more annoying on lower settings), but the game itself doesn't look too awful. The maize fields are initially a fairly creepy area to explore, but the other areas are more cookie-cutter and less interesting. Animations are actually not too bad, though character models are mediocre.
Surprisingly decent - the music is suitably creepy and helps create an unnerving atmosphere. However, there's just not enough of it. A couple more tracks and I'd be praising this game's audio. Voice acting is hit-and-miss - the actual voices aren't so bad, but some of the dialogue is just incredibly poor (a particular example being that of a certain fluffy character, who was so painfully unfunny and trope-ridden that I muted a couple of his cutscenes).
Without a walkthrough, it took me 2 hours, 30 minutes to complete this. £15 for a sub-3-hour experience with zero replayability is a massive rip-off. If this game was fantastic I'd still be criticising the price tag. It's not even a GOOD game, so its price is absolutely ridiculous. Never buy this game for anything more than £3.
I didn't experience any bugs, but it seems other reviewers have, so YMMV. The main thing to criticise here is the obscene initial load time, upwards of a minute. Why? The game isn't particularly well optimised either - I drop more frames here than I do on PLAYERUNKNOWN's Battlegrounds, strangely enough.

Kholat is a game that opens in a small Russian town covered in snow. This first area is new and unfamiliar and the game certainly doesn't lead you by the hand at all, it leaves you alone to discover the harshness of the landscape. You come to the opening of a forest and this is where the horror truly begins.
Kholat  leaves you on edge most times with the eerie noises and a sense of loneliness. The monsters you encounter resemble mere shadows that turn orange the more aggresive they become, once they are fully aware of you they will kill you causing you to start at the last save point. The story of the game will leave you wanting more as you pickup each of the notes, journal entries, or case files.
Kholat is an amazing looking game, mostly due to its rendering of the Russian wilderness. From the snow on the ground to the ghosts of pasts incidents everything is detailed and distinct. The environments are all very intricate, every single part is made to be different with markers to help you on your way. The music and sounds are possibly the best part of the game with most tracks being a haunting piano score or the sounds of the wind and storms. The attention to the sound is part of what makes the game atmospheric with little knocks and sounds of wolves making you feel like you may not be as alone as previous thought.
Kholat's weakest point is its gameplay, as certain bits of it tend to infuriate more than scare. The game's concept is a simple collect pages and avoid the monster gameplay, the problem being is your character is not really fit to navigate the landscape or run from the monsters. your character is able to look far distances, run, as well as use  one of the items you are given to navigate.
Your character cannot jump, and when he runs he can jolt for about 3 seconds before getting tired out and requiring a significant amount of time to recover. Kholat is an expansive free roam game where low stamina is a very bad thing to have and the compass you are given becomes another issue as well. The compass, initially, is a very hard item to use entirely because you end up spending half of your time figuring it out hoping something doesn't kill you while you do. A large saving grace for the game is the ability to fast travel from campsite to campsite.
I won't discuss the ending as it is something you just have to experience for yourself. DO I hate this game? No, I actually highly recommend playing it as the horror feel is always present, it's a very nerve shattering experience and it's easy to get caught up in the information the game gives you. If you enjoy games like Dear Esther and Slender: The Arrival, I recommend trying the game out, be warned though, the game can be oddly frustrating at times, and is not recommended for just one sitting.

3) The new NPCs are mostly great. I especially adore Neera, who is so very different from the rest, maybe with the exception of Tiax. I also like Dorn, because both BGs generally lacked evil party NPCs that weren't overacting or plain insane.

Project Zomboid é um jogo de Survival Horror, semi-realista numa visão isométrica de um mapa. Neste jogo, você cria um personagem com vários atributos que pode ser melhorados, mas apenas um vacilo e seu progresso já era.
O game é muito dificil e demora algum tempo antes de se acostumar, e é importante ser tático e ter paciência. Sair dando tiros nunca vai dar certo nesse jogo. O importante é evitar confrontos contra zumbis, melhorar seu personagem e sua casa, além de manter seu personagem bem, alimentando-o, dando água a ele e o divertindo, de uma maneira parecida como The Sims.
Aliás, essa é uma ótima maneira de descrever o jogo: The Sims com zumbis, ou The Sims com DayZ.
Mas o jogo não é perfeito. Estranhamente, ele tem erros de otimização, que mesmo não sendo graves pode estranhar quem tem ótimos PCs e tão rodando um jogo com gráficos pixelados isométrico. O jogo em si também sofre de uma certa falta de diversão, em ocasião: Muitas vezes não terá nada acontecendo no jogo e você ficará na frente do computador, sem fazer nada.
Em repetidos jogos falhos com alguns amigos, notei que a gente sempre faz a mesma coisa antes de inevitavelmente morrer. Isso pode ser um problema para iniciantes: Ficar começando e fazer a mesma coisa o tempo todo, e se frustrar ainda mais depois.
O jogo tem potencial, e estou interessado na nova atualização com veículos. Recomendo, mas tenha em mente que o jogo pode ser monótono, e se está procurando um jogo de ação com zumbis, nem pense em comprar.

(Disclaimer: Hours listed at time of review says 13ish, but that does not reflect actual time played. I've put in at least 25-30 hours over the course of the Early Access development cycle, for some reason, Steam didn't register play time on ANY of my games about a yearish ago)
"Adventures in Babysitting: Prepare to Die Edition" (Or, "How I Learned to Ignore The Story Mode and Give Survival A Chance")
The Long Dark suffers from a lot of problems related to reasonable design decisions that ultimately fail to meet my personal expectations regarding the game, as I've come to realize over the last few years. Now that the story mode is out, I've decided to jump in, which resulted in quickly breaking my ankles on a metaphorical level, and dissapointing me on actual level.
Wintermute begins with an identity disorder: is it a tutorial for a survival game, or is it a puzzle game? You literally only get through the first hour through trial and error, and somewhat time sensitive decisions. You find a jacket! But it has to be unfrozen and then dried out so you can use it. You found meat! But it will likley poison you even after cooked, and then there's a chance your antibiotics won't work. You must now try and climb out of the ravine! But you're also told the injuries you've sustained in the plane crash prevent you from climbing... so you try climbing ANYWAY, you fail, and the game then puts you in a state of full health and all your meters are filled. How do you climb? Why, just look for the identical rockfaces that allow you to climb, finally putting you in a position to explore.
Then the babysitting comes in. Your meters seem like they won't take a lot to maintain, except for your heat meter. Unless you find better clothing, you're stuck making fires regularly. Good luck with that, as you don't have a lot of mechanics in Story mode to worth with. Unlike Survival Mode, you don't have:
-A Skill system that improves your skills as you do them
-Crafting recipes to help guide which materials are more important than others
-Feats: a small amount of persistant "goals" that once reached affect every playthrough afterwards, which you can customize
You're stuck with a linear path where exploration is simultaniously needed, yet discouraged. The story is told with a high quality of voice acting, but the diologue leaves much to be desired. By the end of the first cut scene, I never wanted to hear the phrase "It's been years" uttered in a game ever again.
Survival mode is another story, but at the price of $34.99 I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone. It's a game that expects you to die a lot, because unless you find shelter, and spent the majority of your time INSIDE, you likely won't survive. And if you DO survive, you're not likley to enjoy the exploration this game has to offer. The maps are very expansive, and they connect to each other, ensuring you can find everything... but the game doesn't feel like it wants you to "play" much. Also? You don't really improve by "learning" if you're placed in a different location every time you start a new one. Your most important lesson: if you don't find shelter soon, you will die, and venturing into unknown territory means your survival could be low.
Fires are the major issue I have with the game. It seems like you have plenty at your dispossal, but without a hatchet you're limited. Sticks burn very quickly, and firelogs are scarce. Since you need coal to map the area, you're bound to find yourself deciding to go one way or the other: do I map things out or do i use it to keep warm, never figuring out where I'm at? But no worries: the map doesn't tell you where you're at unless you already know where you're at... does that make sense? A lot about this game doesn't make sense. Why would my meat spoil when I'm surrounded by sub-zero temperatures? You want me to cure animal hides and intestines for several days to make weapons? Why would I need these weapons if I'm able to survive for months at a time?
I will definitely be giving Survival a harder try, because I WANT to think I could get used to it... but at the same time, I don't expect I will.

When I first saw this game on Youtube, I thought: "What a waste of a spot. This guy could be playing something interesting instead. This is sooooo boring". Then he finished whatever he was working on and it worked and it looked so satisfying, I couldn't stop looking at it. I kept thinking to myself - how can something so boring be so satisfying?
Needless to say - puzzle games are generally not my thing. But I just had to try it for myself after that. The game isn't expensive, so I figured - why not?
And I bought it. Tried it. And it worked. And I felt a little bit smart, because I went for the "area" and made the smallest thing possible. And then I went for the next one. And the next one. And... you know, that's just it. It's very satisfying to see something work as intended. And then you start thinking - ok, it works... but... how can I optimize it?
And there's another aspect of satisfaction - seeing someone else do it and compare to your solution. Just to see how different brains approach the same problem.
Basically, it's not a game for everyone. But if you are like me and think "What is this? Who could even enjoy something like this?" - give it a try. You may be surprised that YOU could enjoy this.

The dev team for this game are very good - the best ive seen for this genre of game. Development is promising, and the game itself is continually growing. I love this kind of game, however, in its current state, stonehearth is probably worth between $5 and $10.
The game is very easy - I've so far been able to repel every attack, destroy every enemy base etc with two soldiers (I might have been overdoing it adding the second soldier, too!).
Building is very bugged - I've had to cancel innumerable buildings as my villagers couldnt construct certain things or have gotten themselves stuck whilst trying. Being able to watch individual pieces on your building be placed by your citizens is cool but has lead to so many issues when actually performing this key functionality.
Progression is basic and unfulfilling - you are a fully self-sustaining within 1-3 days of in-game time. Sure, this might not be a problem, as the game may intend to focus on thriving rather than surviving. However, thriving is impossible as the game cannot seem to handle having >12 citizens (at such numbers, you will see a lot of idling, and citizens with professions flat refusing to do their allocated job whilst there are other things to do - and no, the citizen management screen does not resolve these issues).
Keep it on your watchlist, but unless you are looking for a very surface-level experience, steer clear until further down the development cycle.

This. Game. Is. Amazing. However, it has pros and cons.
Pros
-Very promising game. This game is amazing, especially for such an early build of it.
-Great concept with great features. The building is buggy, but how it works is great. The class system is nearly perfected in terms of mechanics, just needs more classes.
-Extremely entertaining and very fun to play, very calm and peaceful. This game is relaxing to play, and enjoyable overall.
Cons
-Needs more content, this game is great as is, but I feel as though I've accomplished everything there is in the game, which didn't take long. However, this is an extremely early version of the game, so that is expected of a game in this stage.
-Combat needs some working on, I've had a lot of trouble with using the party system within the game and I feel it needs some improvements.
-Optimization is a major issue. Yes I know its not a priority this early in development. But it is very difficult to make villages with 20ish or more people because it gets very laggy. Optimizing the game will allow for people to make bigger and better villages which would be absolutely amazing for this game.
Overall
This game is amazing, the pros may or may not outweigh the cons, thats a matter of opinion. However, I am glad i purchased this game because it is very promising, and I feel as the developers are dedicated to making this game the best it can be. You may want to wait until the game is more developed before buying, but pick it up at some point, either now, or after its more developed.

Game-play is an engaging cross between Role Playing Game (with hero level ups and hero to hero interactions and back story) and Tower Defense. The album element is akin to both "in game achievement" and further immersion in the game's universe and back story. Tower defence elements and, in particular, dust/energy management make for significant floor layout strategies. Humour runs rampant through character dialogues and item names and descriptions. Somehow this game manages to blend not taking itself seriously and yet being a serious game to play.
One part Original Rogue, one part Deadspace/Doom (re. creature vibes), one part nostalgia (Other endless references, graphics, game style et al.). I have found this to be highly entertaining and it will easily be a "go back to" game even when finished/fully unlocked.

Dungeon of the Endless is a randomly generated pixel dungeon crawler, featuring awesome playable characters, the highest level of replayability, and a unique leveling system. You can place traps to fend off the monsters that exist for the sole purpose of demolishing your fun times. As you go deeper, the amount of monsters increases, and the amount of dust used to fuel the light that keeps monsters at bay decreases. This game is so completely awesome, and I totally suggest you check it out.

I wanted to like this game. It has many elements that I love, but there were a few sticking points which proved to be too much. First I'll go for what was good:
- A puzzle game in the general genre of Myst
- Intuitive controls
- Decent graphics
- Funny (somewhat original) storyline, with funnier optional backstory elements scattered throughout
Now, what I disliked:
- I have a GTX 1070. I had to turn the settings down to Medium to keep my computer from overheating. Weird.
- The voice acting was very racist. Cockney British = stupid characters. Hillybilly American = stupid. High British = Intelligent/condescending. Russian = angry/insulting/bad grammar. WHY.
- It felt like the developers didn't trust the player to understand the very simple plot, and after each VERY STRAIGHTFORWARD cutscene, would put hovertext explaining the cutscene to you.
- Several areas were named inconsistently from the rest of the scheme, making them difficult to remember when referenced by other things.
- You have an inventory, and literally the first item you pick up is the last item you use, so it's sitting there clogging up your inventory the entire game, which adds up to a lot of extra button presses to switch past it.
- On similar lines, you don't gather inventory items in the order that you need them, and the item descriptions are not contextual. For example, right at the very beginning of the game, I came across a broken handle of a shovel or something before I entered any buildings. In the item description, it said something along the lines of "You want to use it to knock over the wardrobe on the second story of the farmhouse, because you don't like it," or something like that. What farmhouse? What second floor? What wardrobe? This made that entire puzzle ruined, and it was like the first puzzle. This pattern continued throughout the whole game.
- On the subject of puzzle difficulty, there are no items that you come across that you don't use, and puzzles generally don't let you do anything to them outside of solve them. This makes the whole process pretty linear.
- What makes the story even more linear are these giant walls of orange boxes. I don't think they're a DJT reference, but they're just as annoying. You're in a field of corn, which you could easily just walk through, but because there's a pile of orange boxes on the grass path, I have to rule out that path. It seems very much like lazy writing.
- There are a few twists in the game which are meant to be funny, as underscored by the hovering text which follows them with cheeky (read: ♥♥♥♥♥♥) one-liners, but the jokes come off as trying to hard, and the twists raise boatloads of more questions than they answer.
I could go on, but I leave with the main reason I do not recommend the game. The rest of the above reasons I could legitimately deal with, given how short the game is, but this following one is an absolute deal breaker for me (this involves some minor spoilers):
- Pretty early on in the game you casually create a sentient AI robot who calls himself Vladdy by slappying a teddy bear, a keyboard, some ram, and a backpack together. This character is meant to be your comic relief, but completely ruined the game for a great number of reasons.
1. You can't advance the game without him. He's essential. Yet he's an NPC. In a solo puzzle game. It's baffling.
2. Your character is the ONLY one which does not speak, which makes a sidekick turn into a commentator. See #3.
3. All Vladdy does is insult you, calling you stupid probably in the ballpark of 50 times. Why would I pay to have my childhood recreated like that?
4. Vladdy's functional usage is to enter vents after you get him. Some of the time. But they're the same size vents as the main character has used many times up to that point, except these grates hang down an inch lower over the vent. Ooh~ And Vladdy's character model is easily short enough to just stroll through the vents, but for absolutely no stinking reason, he lays on his face and epileptic fits himself SLOWLY into the vent, where all sorts of extremely interesting-sounding action happens off screen while I'm sitting there staring at a black hole in the wall. The whole time, Vladdy is swearing and insulting and screaming out in pain, but eventually fixes the issue and slowly convulses back out of the vent, where the white hovertext has the gall to inform me that Vladdy did not like the torture I just had to listen to him endure for the last three minutes. No♥♥♥♥♥♥ Sherlock.
5. Vladdy insults the other characters in the story, and at one point, goes on a killing spree and murders like 20-30 of them. To fix this, you press play on a boombox and they switch from trying to murder him to midstride doing a conga line with him. Again, I think another failed attempt at comedy.
6. The single worst feature of the entire game is Vladdy's walking. I get it. He's a sentient teddy bear. But did you have to make him walk so mindnumbingly slow? Vladdy walks at about 1/10 your speed, 1/20 your running/normal speed. So he's left in the dust as soon as you move. Then, at complete random, he'll teleport to your feet while screaming some insult at you in an incredibly weird racist Russian accent. Even that, I could deal with, I think. But his walking. Good god his walking. It involves a very high-pitched squeak that will haunt your nightmares. It will keep you awake at night. Especially since vertical distance doesn't seem to have an effect on his teleportation, so if you have something to do at the bottom or top of a flight of stairs (happens more than once) you have to listen for the five minutes of squeaky toy footsteps as this motherclucker slowly humps his way down the steps.
So, I did what any sane person would do. I turned off sound effects. Ahhh. No more Vladdy feet. Oh but wait. All characters but Vladdy have their voice lines slotted NOT in the VOICE SOUND as would be rational, but no. They're slotted in SOUND EFFECTS. At its best, Maize feels every bit as lived-in and real as something out of Portal. It's loaded with personality and tons of little story fluff tidbits that add to the experience of poking around in first-person, smashing objects together in a classic point-and-click adventure style. Where some puzzles might be too much of an illogical reach, the game helpfully highlights where various items might go to speed you along.
And if that were the start and finish of Maize, it'd be a delightful, short little game with few, if any, flaws.
But it feels weirdly dissonant when you run into speaking characters whose one-note sense of humor is out of place in a game that otherwise clearly takes great pride in its cleverness. The animatronic bear, Vladdy, feels like he was added for marketing purposes. There's no reason the player would need him to crawl into vents and fix things when the player does both of these tasks once in a while. When such a task is for Vladdy alone, it's an excuse to go to a cut scene and have a one-dimensional rude cartoon grumble at you while you wait for him to do the things that you, the hero of the story, have already proven yourself capable of. We get it. The bear is gruff and calls everything "stupid." The sentient corn stalks are idiots who like to take naps. The scientist is put-upon and calls everyone "stupid." They're flat personalities. Can we spend less time on them and get back to what works?
And that's sort of the overall function of any of the speaking roles: functionally unnecessary, and not nearly as funny as the game's environmental storytelling. It doesn't ruin the game, but one can't help but think about how good Maize could have been if the writing time and company resources had been put into accentuating what Maize got right.

I am writing this review after putting about 50+ hours into the game and basically getting to the point where I can withstand any enemy attack the game throws at me.  It took a lot of trial and error, restarting multiple times, and reloading saves to get there.  The game is early access and there are quite a few bugs.  Once you get past that you have a wonderful game that in some ways reminds me of FTL, only I get to build my ship how I want.  You have crew members who level up stats as they perform tasks, you have various weapons and defenses for your ship.  You can choose to fight, bribe, or warp jump away in combat situations.  You have ships that wish to buy/sell resources and crew members.

The game is very difficult at first, until you get in the mindset of building stuff that you need and then removing it only after you have resources to start expanding your ship.  You constantly need to balance your research between weapons, defenses, and upgrades for ship components.  As you build the size of your ship, you encounter bigger and bigger enemy ships.  This type of game may not be for everyone, but I have had a very enjoyable (sometimes frustrating) time learning and playing this game and am eagerly looking forward to what this game will become in the future.  Don't give up on it after dying for the 5th+ time early on.  It takes some patience and luck with mining asteroids to get the resources you need to build.  In the end, I am very happy I took a chance on this game and see myself coming back to it again and again.
