I personally thought it was a decent game, though not the best. When I first heard that Syndicate was going to a thing, I was a bit sceptical because of the trainwreck that Unity was, but I wasn't disappointed when I tried the game myself.
Pros:
- One of the main gimics of Syndicate was liberating zones in London, similar to liberating Borgia territories in Brotherhood.
- Visually impressive; nice attention to detail to the player's surroundings.
- The new gadgets, such as the grapple hook, were really cool to use throughout the game.
- The game wasn't excruciatingly hard like Unity was.
Cons
- Not the greatest story, especially the ending. I even thought Unity's ending was better.
- The fight against the headmaster of the templars got repetitive.
- The Queen Victoria missions were boring and sometimes even harder than they had any right to be.
- While I thought it was really neat to play as Evie Frye's grandaughter during World War 1, I see quite a few plot holes even after reading about her in the archives.
- I was fine with having to level up to get better materials, weapons, armor, and et cetera, but it should require much less XP to level up.
If you're a fan of the series, then you might like this game. However, I understand why many people don't like this game.

[disclaimer] I have played all AC games on a powerhouse of a pc, with mouse and keyboard. I have not played unity, since the PC port was a broken mess, so that's my perspective.
Let's start with a TL;DR: This game is the most assassin's creedy game of all time. It does all the things the others did really well, but not much else. Excluding black flag, that one spiced things up. As a fan of the series you get what you expect and as someone who has never liked them you will not like this one either. However for someone (whoever that might be) who has never heard of them, but is really interested in playing as an assassin in times gone by, this is the best one in the series.
Combat system:
Fighting is mostly the same as always as far as your inputs are concerned. You can hit things, shoot things, break their defense, we have seen all of it in the previous titles, only this time we got a level system so fights can actually get tough if you are in the wrong part of town early on. the Introduction of a near-death-state allows you to set up multikills in a real fun way. Animationquality is superb as usual and due to the addition of the second main charackter you get twice as many special animations. Great job ubisoft, killing thugs has never looked better in an AC game. I will however say that I still think that their fighting system is shallow and doesn't hold up to the likes of Prince of Persia (the good ones), Dark souls, Devil May Cry and all the other relevant fighting systems out there. At least it is more fun than unmodded skyrim is, but I won't give credit for that, Skyrim's combat is dated, clunky and uninspiring.
Skill Tree:
This one is the only real innovation to the series. (maybe it was in unity, but I'll continue to ignore unity because I don't play broken games) At first I thought: "Big whoop so they wen't pseudo rpg on us. It's propably gonna be as much of a sorry excuse for linear progression as the introduction of currency was in AC2.", but they actually put some effort into this system. The upgrades you can get here are really fun for the most part, while of course balanced for casual players, so some of these are pretty op. We do have the occasional "get more flat HP or deal more flat DMG, but some of the others include auto loot on takedowns, heal on multikills or various upgrades to the eagle vision, however most, if not all (can't quite remember sorry) of those were standart for "Revelations" Ezio. I guess not everyone is a Florentine Master, so they have to work for it. Also due to the 2 charackter model you don't have to decide wich playstyle you wanna go for. Evie naturally builds as a sneaky Sam-Fisher archetype, whereas Jacob is more of a Brawler. They do have a few unique upgrades each, so this setup is recommendet, but you can totally go Sneaky Jacob and Brawler Evie if you so desire. I went with the standart though, because of charackter flavour.
Enemies:
Much like in Revelations, we have different kinds of guards. This time is the Blighters, a templar-sponsored group of thugs, the coppers, who are... well, coppers and of course the actual templars who are kind of on the side of the blighters but tougher and rarer.
For the first time ever, some of them are actually challenging (No, I didn't think the templars in AC1 were a challenge, hidden blade counter was 1hit). At least early on if you are underleveled. Unfortunately the very welcomed spike in difficulty gets eliminated more and more, the further you go down that skilltree of yours, until you eventually become the superhuman angel of wrath we know and "love" in the series. Yeah, opinions devide on this matter.
Setting:
Got to say, I got a softspot for victorian London. The place is oozing flavour, of course rebuilt authentically, as we are kind of getting used to with AC games. Britishness all over the place, Jacob even gets a Tophat in one outfit, there are sword canes as weapons and so many more things. Great Job, I love it.
Soundtrack:
Superb, my favorite in the series, however I'll shut up about it, since people apparently have differen't opinions on this one too. Almost like there are different taste of music than mine. Strange.
Main Charackters (Jacob and Evie):
Jacob is your stereotype wisecracking, gunslinger. Starlord esque. A bit clishee, but likeable. He also is a dummie sometimes, but in a fitting way.
Evie is more serious, sneaky and traditionally Assassin-like. An Altair (towards the ending of part one) kind of woman. The two of them clash in cutscenes and have a littlesibbling rivalry every time they meet.
Not my favorite Assassin's but better than Connor for sure.
Their outfits and moves however are absolutely gorgous.
The two work well together and it's so much fun to see them be a team. Unfortunately for some reason the story decides to pit them against each other for the majority of the time. Wasted potential
Sidecharackters:
I found the sidecharackters to be some of the worst ever in the series. I don't remember a thing henry green did, nothing any of the historical charackters said or done sticked to my mind and even though, they were again brilliantly researched and pseudo accurately represented with some of their quirks and charackter traits, I just don't remember any of them as strikingly interesting, even though I played every single of their side missions. No Idea why, maybe it is because I got bored by all the busy work some of them asked me to do. They just felt like nicely coloured vessels for sideplots, that had no real reason to be in the story other than AC games got to have historical charackters. None of them come close to how great Leonardo was in AC II.
I just remembered one exception: Maxwell Roth. He is a joker type charackter, an anarchist and criminal. He was the most fun antagonist and also the only fun one. Actually I liked him quite a bit and I ave no Idea why I forgot about him earlier. Guess I was just thinking about the good guys.
Story:
Well, I was so engaged by the dynamic between Evie and Jacob. They are superfun together and work really well as a team. Sadly, the story spends like 99% of the time, keeping them apart. It wasn't fun for me to see the rift grow and eventually close between them, because we all knew from the start, that there would be a happy ending. As a result we don't have tension and we don't have the amazingly fun interactions between the charackters that do shine trhough every now and then. Sadness. Could have been great but is sort of ok in the end. I will not spoil more of it, but there isn't much to spoil, it's rather standart for an AC game and please don't get me started on the real world stuff. I think the fact that the real world part of Black Flag, where they made fun of themselves, the gaming industry and "Abstergo", their big bad being their best ever sais it all. In my opinion it is useless shovelware to the max again.
Main Missions:
The main missions have an interesting spin on them too. Most of them offer loads of ways to complete them, but a few, storyrelated ones with extra spice and specialties. Great job, they are less handholding and more intersting than ever. I don't want to spoil too much, just enjoy them.
Sidemissions aka Busywork:
Wow. I don't even know where to start with the open world missions. in my opinion, they are beyond bad. Mind numbingly repetetive, busywork without any redeeming qualities. Brotherhood and Revelationsesque you got to free London, district by disrict, only this time it is way more work and none the better.
Pros
Great Setting,great soundtrack, fun new tools, Skilltree, Levelgate for enemies, the siblings are fun together.
Cons
More of the same, mindless busywork, no pirateships , the siblings are constantly seperated.

So, Syndicate.
Twins try to wrestle control of London from the Templars. We learn that in the first 5mins and nothing changes till the very end.
If you like the Gameplay or like poking around old London and meating real historical characters, great.
If you like a good story ala Black Flag this is woeful and abysmal. No story telling because there is no story.

I recently acquired this game on a friend's account in order to test it to see if it was fit for human consumption yet or not. So many Early Access titles are just not ready for public use. This is not one of them. It took me 20 mins to establish that not only was this a stable and efficient engine, but the depth they have included was staggering.
I play a GREAT many survival games, some "a little like real life" and some are so close that you dream about them as though you were there (See The Long Dark). While the graphic engine is simplistic in nature, it is more than complex enough to suck you into the world. After 10 mins of learning to "move things around" from your bags to containers and such, getting your feet under you, then...all your "The Walking Dead" and "Dawn of the Dead" training starts coming out.
Once you've worked the interface out and are comfortable with it enough to function, you then slip easily into your "survival boots". Your senses go high, you mind starts running in the background on its own, plotting out what-ifs for anything that might happen, all the while you are actively looting your first house (likely your own house).
As you gather things you quickly come to understand that you can't (and shouldn't) take everything. You are now alone in the dark. You have no help coming...and as long as you stay quiet and inconspicuous, you have a lot of time to think on your plan of survival and start to pool resources together and get your feet under you.
The crafting engine can seem overwhelming at first, but it is actually quite forgiving as long as you have the curiosity to read the possible designs and think to yourself "how can I make this help me". And to have a hoarding nature will help...gather ALL the stuff you find and put it into a workshop style environment. Then you sit down and quietly tinker all night long from one thing to another.
The physiological and psychological aspects to the game are amazing, even to this old survival sim veteran. As I sat there with a screwdriver, disassembling a remote control for its I.R. sensor, I looked over and realized that I have become well-adapted to being (in this case) 5 things at once...I am a little hungry...I am a bit tired...I am getting bored...I am having some pain in my left forearm (due to glass from breaking a window last night)...and I am being soothed by the sound of the rain outside. The depth of ailments, conditions, and afflictions are really amazing. If you were to be stabbed, you wouldn't just "Lose 25 hp and get 'bleeding' condition". No no...you would take the hit...stab...I've been hurt...then blood spurt 3 seconds later...I am bleeding and it's severe...then 10 seconds after, I am getting scared (seeing so much of your own blood) and in some pain...then 20 seconds after as you stuble towards your camp, I am in tremendous pain and am wailing out and cannot help it...30 seconds...I am cold and trembling and sliding into shock.
Apply sterile bandages (you made yesterday from whiskey and ripped bed sheets)...and the conditions slowly subside over time. This makes for an IMMENSELY more engrossing event than "I got stabbed and lost 25 hp".
I am just scratching the surface of the jewel...and already I have declared "You have SOO earned my money on this game". I bought my own copy and am likely to purchase a 4-pack for the rest of my gaming unit. Multiplayer HAS to be just righteous.
So for TLDR: Well worth the money, take 10 mins and learn the interface, then go live your life in this REALISTIC survival simulation. Make your own server, tweak your "in my end of the world zombie apocalypse things would be like this..." settings. Then immerse yourself into a sim that will carry you for 100s of hours as you push your boundries and your imagination.

Project Zomboid
my pride and joy of a game. I loved the survival in this game. I loved the freedom to build a fort, I loved to scavange, I loved the fear of a hoard attacking me in the middle of the night.
For the wise ones, you'll notice I used "what I don't want", "was" and "loved". Why in the past? Because Early Access.
The game has a really slow, slow, slow, slow and painful development time. Updates are rare and far apart. I don't mean "IWBUMS beta branch". Those are updated. But stable, official updates are rare. For ages we have been teased for cars. Build 38, the latest one at Sept 22nd 2017, is the pre-car build, even though cars have been in "IWBUMS beta branch" since almost the start of this year. The lacks of updates made me put the game off and stop playing for large periods of time, and when I do come back, there is little change for me to want to keep playing for more than 1-5 hours.
But nevertheless. It is still a good game. The devs do need to get a grip of themselves and work. I'm not saying they aren't working, but they need to work better. AI survivors and enemies have been teased for years. There is no excuse to keep delaying it and keeping this game in EA until Half-Life 3 is released (which is never). The game could be a lot more if a bit more of elbow-greese is added to it. But... I do like the game. I still enjoy the concept. I wish I had someone I could trust, and was a close friend that liked the game too, to play coop. Maybe then, I could like the game a bit more.

This is bear grylls dialled to 11. A survival against the elements game that really squeezed what little fun the game has, as it showed off  how extreme its environment is.  Your character can get - Dehydrated to dangerous levels in seconds. Suffer from Hypothermia in seconds despite wearing warm dry, clothing. Hydrated and well fed? Not to worry the game will soon have you acting like a parched man in a desert and starving to death in seconds. You've got meters to fill young man, so get scavenging.
The story mode - Wintermute. Involves our protaginist taking his ex wife out in a plane during a severe storm.  An incident occurs and you guessed it, the plane crashes. The hero wakes up some miles from the plane and after learning basic survival skills, you the player are  finally allowed to go in search of the crashed aircraft and the characters ex wife.
While on the trail of the protaginists ex wife, who despite being in the same accident, clearly isn't having the problems the player is having, (also  betraying a considerable lack of concern for her pilot/ex-huband)  I encountered a wolf feeding on a dead deer. The game advised that one should avoid wolves. Which is odd as this game was clearly  blocking any further progress with a bloody wolf, which you then have to try and fight/chase off. Duly after some savage beatings the poor old hero suffered wounds which you the player simply don't have the resources to treat.
As my character slipped into the long dark after suffering these fatal wounds compounded by severe dehydration, hunger and hypothermia, which occured within seconds of the wolf attack, I finally ran out of patience with the game.
In short this a extreme weather walking simulator with extreme weather conditions, so extreme I kept wondering when product placement for Discovery Extreme weather was going to show up.
When it isn't trying to taunt you with how extreme its gaming environment is,  it constantly hassles you with various meters which must be satisfied min by min. Sleeping, heating, eating and drinking. All of which require resources or shelter which are difficult to find.  Making the game part resource management in addition to the walking, which you must do to progress the story.
The sand box version appears to have no real end goal apart from how much of this you can endure before switching off. The story mode, I had hoped, would keep me more engaged. It didn't. I was to engaged with the constant nagging of the heat, sleep, drink and eat meters demanding my attention during the 4 days of game time that elapsed. Two hours real time.
In the end this game was making me work far too  hard for any nuggets of fun that could be found in the wastes. This game wasn't hard as much as it was simply annoying.
The main characters are voiced by the same persons who voiced Shepard from Mass Effect. 'nuff said

I can say without a doubt this is the nicest, most soothing and quite charmingly original variant of "solitaire" I have ever played. For a start, it's actually fun. There are four different main colours of marbles each with a corresponding symbol for them, making it much easier for us colourblind folks to tell them apart (very appreciated there), and each matches to another of its exact kind There are also these grey coloured marbles which can match with each of the four basic coloured marbles, or themselves. You get a set number of each (8 of each main coloured one, and four of the grey ones). There are also a set of five paler grey marbles with a different symbol on, and six different coloured unique marbles with metallic colourations. These six marbles are unmatchable except in a specific order, and each metallic marble only matches with one of the paler grey marbles, with the sixth metal marble being able to be cleared without matching it with anything.
The idea is to clear the board entirely, and as you reach certain milestones, you unlock a nice little story between two friends talking about the game and its past, and learning a little about each other. There's a hundred levels in all, so the price is a little steep, but there's a lot of love gone into this game clearly, so I don't mind too much, and the written story is quite nice and the characters are interesting.
There is this weird unrelated tutorial thing you have to do first before you can play this game though, but the tutorial is pretty quickly over with and is actually fun where you combine the same marbles together like atoms or something, and to be honest I wish the game had been more about that? But this nice calming, soothing solitaire-esque game is really just too nice to be upset about this.

One of my favourite games of all time. A dark fantasy RPG with strategy. This isn't some utopian land with elves and magic. It's a wartorn land with racism, slavery and oppression.
You play as a Grey Warden, the only ones that can stop a Blight, essentially the end of the world. You will lead a group of followers in a war against the Darkspawn, the ones responsible for the Blights.
This game uses a combat system similar to Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, which is not surprising since bioware also made the first of the two games. Using real time combat with a pause feature to plan and look at the battlefield, auto-attacks and activated abilities. This can be incredibly boring for some, but at the harder difficulty settings it can get really tense if you haven't built your party well.
The story is great, with a varied cast of characters lining it with exposition, fleshing out encounters and giving great sidequests that sometimes make an impact on other missions. Your party members are great as well (though that's a given considering this is BioWare), You have everything from a witty, if childish, templar turned warden, to a perpetually drunk berserker that's constantly making advances on every woman he sees(and male elves). These characters are properly fleshed out through conversing with them in camp, them giving their opinion in certain conversations, banter between the party when exploring and their own personal sidequests. The acting also helps.
The dialogue in this game is fantastic. Without having a voiced protagonist they freed up alot of space to have more options, more spoken dialogue from other characters, and let the player choose a voice type for combat as well as actions taken outside of dialogue.
The game also lets you customise your characters with a lot of options, and something many of these types of games lack: hair styles. It's one of the most defining visual traits, and there are a ton of styles to choose from. It also allows for a lot of other options, but the most important thing is your origin, These are determined by your race and class. Humans can choose from the noble origin, elves choose from City or Dalish, Dwarves choose from noble or commoner, and mage choose from circle mage. Having these origins, playing through them and having several dialouge options based on these are a great way of adding character to your Warden.
The visuals do hold up today, at least according to me. If you think the textures of certain objects are low res, there are a few mods to fix that. The colour palette is on the darker side of the spectrum, while still being varied and still have colour.
That being said It's not flawless. There are still many bugs and glitches in this game, particularly the Awakening expansion. Still, there are also som mods that fixes these issues. This is where the Dragon Age wikia was extremely helpful. Even if you are not using the guides on the wiki, i would still recommend checking the bugs section of many of the quests in Awakening, and even the base game, simply because they generally have links to fixes made by fans.
I've mentioned mods a couple of times, and that is because it's very easy to install mods. You only need one third party program, and that's not necessary for about 90% of the mods I've seen on nexus mods. I do however suggest that you read through the mod description and some comments on the mod, to check if they work, issues present within the mods, if it works well with other mods you have installed or conflicts that can be fixed.
tl;dr.     Solid game, satisfying, if slow, combat. Story and characters are well written and executed. Character creation is good. Great visuals. Many bugs, but can be fixed.
All in all, a solid 9/10

In Dragon Age: Origins you play in the fantasy kingdom of Ferelden, choosing to be either a Human Noble, an Elf living in the city or in the forest with Dealish clans, Drawven Noble or outlaw or a Mage. While having different origins, your character will end being forced to join the Grey Wardens - an ancient order of warriors fighting local Orcs equivalent, the Darkspawn. However, during a massive battle alongside the king, Grey Wardens were betrayed and wiped out. With the king dead, the usurper on the trone, Grey Wardens blamed for kings' murder and Darkspawn horde coming, it's up to you to save the day.
The game often feels trapped between the service of the genre and trying to be its own thing. It is apparent in both the story and the mechanics. On the one hand, it wants to simplify the character creation and management, ditching too many classes for the old standard of Warrior, Mage, Thief. But then it just lets those classes turn into all classes so familiar from D&D like Bards, Assassins, Rangers etc. with sometimes changed names (Barbarian being in this version a Berserker and Paladin being a Templar), as if it felt obliged to compromise with nostalgic Baldur's Gate fans.
Similarly, the plot is a very standard fantasy where you go and help Elves, Dwarves, Mages and humans and in exchange, they will aid your armies against the Darkspawn. The two main villains consider of a non-entity that is so blatantly just a thing to slain it takes a form of a dragon and a guy with his head so deep into his♥♥♥♥♥there are actual theories he has been brainwashed or something. Enforced even further when you notice how much his portrayal in expanded Universe outright clashes with things he's doing in the game. By the time I was offered to spare him and learn more about him I was so sick of him acting like a dumb man-child I just cut him down. Similarly many characters that will join your party seem to be forced into recognizable character archetypes like wise old mentor, proud warrior race guy, heroic Paladin or Korgan Bloodaxe and you will need some serious patience to see through these masks to discover them in their full nature.
However, there are good moments in the world and the plot. Not really built on the final dilemma of every main quest, where you have to purposely be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to not see the glowing message which is the right option. But on dilemmas, you will constantly face through the game in side quests, companion quests or even character interactions. Those are allowed to provide real world building and complexity both in regards to morality as well as personalities of your companions, that make this game such an amazing and entertaining experience - you honestly want to discover this world once you can forget how bad the main plot is. The DLCs allow to explore it even further with characters like Morrigan or Leliana getting their own epilogue and prologue, respectively and new character, Shale, being extremely charming. Dragon Age: Awakening fairly improves on those points, actually adding some of that complexity to the main quests as well, at least concerning the Architect. While also adding more interesting characters.
What the Ultiamte Edition could use s clearing some bugs, like it crashing sometimes or forcing me into having to listen to Leliana's rant about cheating on her with Moriggan literally a conversation after my Warden rejected her feelings because he was already dating Moriggan. If this is the Ultimate edition then why these problems still exist?

!! Disclaimer! Review Copy Provided By Developer !!
(Video review linked at the bottom)
The horror genre is slowly becoming a mess, games that focus on cheap jump scares are flooding Steam and other services while very few games that are actually “scary” hit the market. Kholat steps away from the “jump scare” subgenre and shows us that there is still some hope for the horror game genre.
Kholat, based on the actual event of the Dyatlov Pass Incident, is a fantastic horror game that shows the industry how a horror game is done right. To give a little bit of backstory, the Dyatlov Pass Incident is an event that happened in January to late February in 1959 when 10 Russian students went on a hike in the Ural Mountains on the eastern side of Kholat Syakhl. After one of the students went back due to illness the others pushed forward and were never heard from again. So a group went to explore in hopes to find their whereabouts. The remaining 9 students were all found dead from various, and still unexplained reasons.
Based off these real-life events the story of Kholat is one of the best stories I’ve heard told in the horror game genre. Narrated by the famous Sean Bean, the games writing, narration, and story are all fantastic. The narration I will say is good, but not the best, solely for immersion purposes. Most of the voice actors seem to have british accents, which works well for Sean Bean but not the others. The diary entries are narrated by a british actor, playing a Russian student. I would have liked to see these entries narrated by a Russian voice actor, but this is just me being nitpicky. I wouldn’t consider this a con, just thought I’d mention it. The sound in this game is excellent, the sound effects and music fit the game perfectly and create very tense feeling situations. One thing I loved was oddly the sound effects of walking in the snow. As a Canadian I can say the developers nailed those sound effects right on the head. The atmosphere in this game is amazing, wandering in harsh mountains has never been so enjoyable. The mountains and caves are all beautifully designed, the various places of interest all feel distinct and unique in their own way. (Mild spoilers here) From burnt and hell-like looking forests to sacrificial altars and abandoned bunkers, these places all hold story significance while providing the tense atmosphere that makes this game true horror.
The gameplay is simple and only requires your inner explorer. You start off in an abandoned Russian town with no markers, no arrows, no nothing. Just your willingness to explore. You will eventually find your way around where the real game begins. You go to a whole new area, deep in the Ural Mountains where you must just simply explore with your handy map, compass, and flashlight. Keep in mind, this area is completely non-linear and open. The map has coordinates of all the places of interest but I found all of these places without any real navigation involved. The flashlight I found to be extremely useless as most areas are lit by the full moon in the sky. I guess if you were playing the game at a low brightness to add to the experience the flashlight would be a very nice touch. The game itself is around 4-6 hours in length and is filled with many little notes and diary entries to collect if you feel like getting more backstory.
Lastly, the performance of this game is quite good, I will say though having to play through the entire game in 30fps was quite annoying. I feel as though my processor was bottlenecking my graphics card in this game, I could play the game on medium-high and maintain a solid 30fps. This game does require a decent rig. The game is powered on Unreal Engine 4 and it looks amazing. I could easily see this game being used for benchmarking purposes.
In most horror games the “horror” is caused by cheap jump scares that startle, not scare. Kholat on the other hand uses it’s interesting backstory, immersion, beautiful yet creepy atmosphere, and fantastic sound to be possibly this years best horror title.

Puts the indie horror genre to shame really.
Graphics: They're pretty, and it has a great atmosphere, right at the start, but it gets extremely repetitive after a short time. Every area is just the same. White snow, more white snow, and a snowy cave here and there. The exception is a forest with burnt tree stumps.
Your equipment:
-You have a torch but there is absolutely no motivation to use it because your stuck in a wintry white wonderland, and it doesn't help during the blizzards.
-A compass which is side-on and doesn't prove useful because:
-The map isn't accurate to the trails and doesn't show the proper direction and shape of the paths always. It becomes a guessing game of trust the map, or your gut instinct for direction. The gut is usually more reliable.
-Your an obese individual who can jog for no more than 10m before going into shock and losing vision for a short time. If anything it just stretches out a game which would otherwise be completed in less than an hour.
The horror: Encounters are predictable. It is extremely easy to avoid any confrontation throughout the game, except at a few scripted events which you *almost* can't avoid. There is only one type of enemy. A semi-transparent orange ghost who has the eyesight of a mole. You pretty much have to run towards him within 5m and shine your torch in his face to get his attention...at which point you get an achievement for doing so.
You see him coming (walking with the speed of a tortoise) from far away, giving you plenty of opportunity to open up a can of sardines, make a sandwich, eat the sandwich, then come back to your computer and hit the w key to slowly walk away from the impending doom...
Gameplay/Story progression: The game consists of picking a direction, making your way to a landmark, picking up notes along the way, then repeat. There are only a handful of unique areas scattered across the map and there is nothing else to see or do there except pick up the next piece of paper to complete your diary of...notes.
There are alot of notes to collect around the place, but they all pretty much say the same thing:
"Today the weather was cold. We set up camp and I heard a creepy voice calling out to me, but if I tell the others they'll think i'm crazy. I think I heard something walking around outside but the others think i'm crazy. I must be crazy. The locals talk about a ghost",
or the even more cliche "Human subject 226 was a failure. Bring me more test subjects so we can create a supernatural psychic being which will probably turn around and kill us when we're done. I'll write about it while it's happening too. Where's my cup of coffee?"
The ending (Spoiler...sort of): There is no ending. It's abrupt, unsatisfying, absolutely nothing scary chases you and nothing really happens. No shocking revelation, no real conclusion. You just find the tent from the incident. Screen fades to black. It leaves a disappointing taste in your mouth. It's not the good 'I want to play more' disappointment. It's wondering why I just wasted 3 hours roaming a map for...that...
I wouldn't buy this game for more than $3.

If you thought Doom was a game imbued with hatred- if you thought HATRED was a game imbued with hatred- on playing this you will assuredly realize that comparatively those games are love-letters to Humanity.
Never before and likely never after shall I play a game more thoroughly filled with contempt. Contempt for itself, contempt for it's creators and contempt for you, the Player. Contempt for everyone and everything masked by irony with the joke being that they are joking.
That, is the primary takeaway from the game. It along with everyone and everything in it is unlikeable, twee, condescending and loathing of self and pretty much everything else. But hey, that's just, like, my opinion... right?
Well then let's look at the brass tacks.
Gameplay : None. You go get thing to get other thing to put in thing to advance thing, The advancement of said thing often has no real connection to anything you did.
Story : Minimal. You do all these things for reasons you don't even know but are retroactively sortof explained. Also the game would like you to know you are an idiot and/or insane. (In this feature you are utterly united with every other character in the game) The story, such as it might be called, is more satisfactorily resolved with everything going up in Nuclear Fire in the perhaps singular instance in which it is even possible to fail. Worse, said end is more or less FUNCTIONALLY IDENTICAL TO THE ACTUAL ENDING.
Humor : Ah, the thing that really could have saved it! Humorous violation of expectation! Charming wit! All missing from the game! For it's 'wacky absurdity' it's nigh entirely predictable and pretty much all of the jokes revolve around how stupid you and the other characters are. It's not nearly enough to carry even the alarmingly short amount of time one plays the game.
Graphics : Marginally better facial animations than Mass Effect : Andromeda.
I got this game as a gift and I want a refund of the time I gave it in goodwill and optimism. I bear the giver no ill-will of course, it may even prove useful as an insight into particularly twisted psyches.
Meanwhile if I seem uncivil in this I suspect if I had bought it myself this review would be entirely unpublishable. Consider spending your money on a less bitterly insecure and loathing-filled game.

Said to be the best strategy game of all time. Not an understatement exactly. It's not as needlessly complex as most turn based strategy games. It's not as hectic as realtime strategy and it's not as shallow as most indie strategy out today. This is a really well balanced strategy game with destructable environments, funding, research, base maintenence and manufacturing. Very entertaining game and well worth the price.
Story - What's it all about?
X-COM starts on January, 1999. You are in charge of X-COM, an extraterrestrial defense force, funded by almost all of the major countries from back in the 90ies. Russia, Brazil, China, USA, India, South Africa, Libya, Egypt and all of the major european countries like France, Germany, UK and not some others like any Nordic ones or Netherlands, Austria. Probably because these countries wouldn't or couldn't fund a project such as an extraterrestrial defense force. Regardless, you are now supposed to cover the 'entire globe'. Well not entire, you will only have to cover the ones that do fund you and since many countries actually doesn't fund you, you can safely let aliens land in their areas. But if you're like me, you will probably want to go ahead and cover as much territory as possible anyway.
Gameplay - How does it play?
You are in charge of everything. You put up your base, you intercept and shoot down all of the UFOs, you lead your tactical squads on mission, conduct research and manufacture weapons. This game is amazing in all you can do and research is vitally important to you as it leads your progress throughout the game (like research bloody should!). At the start of the game you know nothing about these aliens and even as a player that kinda frightens you because these aliens, already from the absolute start of the game, they utilize far more superior weapons than your own. As the game progresses, the aliens don't really, but if you're able to stay in the game for long enough and have spent some fair amount of money in scientists you will realize that you can reverse engineer the alien technology and even construct even more superior weapons than them: GENIUS!
Criticism - But what isn't that great?
Well for instance, the aliens start out vastly superior to your people in every respect. This is not bad in of itself but it makes some of the future things you can construct somewhat redundant. For instance; you can construct armor for your soldiers eventually, but it doesn't protect well as the aliens fire incredibly damaging salvos of plasma matter at them which basically melts the armor instantly. Without the armor your soldiers only have 1 hit point as far as you're concerned but even with the armor they barely raise that to 2 hit points. Also, when one of your people dies; you cannot recover their armor. Which means that you must make a 20000 dollar armor for every individual you want to protect.
My other criticism with the game is that many of the expenses doesn't make much sense. For instance; you never buy interception planes. No you RENT them! What the earth? And when they get shot down (not if), you don't even have to pay anything. I think they could just as well have sold the interceptors instead, but seeing as it is the very first plane for a very long time I can see why they decides to make the planes that way. The funny thing is that the rent of bloody 600'000 dollars and you have to pay every month! I know it's state of the art but holy cow man. USA's funding is barely 700'000 - 800'000 and they expect you to have a base there plus at least one interceptor to keep all of the aliens at bay!?
Of course I am nitpicking a little but that's what great with the game: It doesn't really have any flaws other than that. Sure the aliens are hard as balls to fight but that's the point of the game!
Conclusion - So what rating do you propose?
I propose a rating of 6 out of 6. This game is bloody amazing strategy game. It's almost as if it was made for me. The amount of content in it is huge for a DOS game of barely 6 MB and even by today's standards it's incredibly fun to play.
My personal BEST game of the 90s and it's even better with Seb76's UFO Extender mod!

Utterly impressive--X-COM represents a classic history lesson in PC strategy games. I was not expecting to see the depth this game provides. Strategy games are not really my preferred genre, but I have to admire the early contributions this game gave to the strategy genre and give props where they are due. Twenty year ago, this was cutting edge stuff.
Gamers that haven't played something this aged will have to look beyond the low resolution graphics and clunky user interface to understand that developers used to focus primarily on game play--an aspect this game provides an abundance of. Regardless, other than for nostalgia, history, or research, I would suggest something a little more modern. But if you do decide to give it a shot, this predates in-game tutorials so you'll want to read the manual if you really want to know what is going on...all 134 pages of it.

Starship Theory is a great game. In theory.
After spending 3 hours into a single playthrough, I had a good grasp on the mechanics and the game was actually a quite pleasant experience after the initial rush. Then I got another fire on my ship, I had plenty in the past but the crew just put them out. This time, they ignored it. Eventually, the fire burnt through my entire ship and they would only put out the fire where it was spreading, and not the largest flame.
Another run, going well, and I built another room to my ship, it was seperated by an airlock but apparently you can only exit an airlock in one direction, so when another fire started on the other side there was no way to put it out.
This is a game where you don't learn the mechanics and function within those parameters, you learn game breaking glitches and ways to get around them (IE Next run I will be commanding crew to put out fires, as I looked this up and is possible) and I will not be using airlocks as doors even though that's the best way to set up your ship.
Aside from these issues, the game is very entertaining and enjoyable. Should you decide to purchase this game, you should know your in for a bit of an initial learning curve and a lot of frustration should you encounter a situation like I did.
I cannot recommend this game until it is more polished and a tutorial is added.

Not to worry the game will soon have you acting like a parched man in a desert and starving to death in seconds. You've got meters to fill young man, so get scavenging.
The story mode - Wintermute. Involves our protaginist taking his ex wife out in a plane during a severe storm.  An incident occurs and you guessed it, the plane crashes. The hero wakes up some miles from the plane and after learning basic survival skills, you the player are  finally allowed to go in search of the crashed aircraft and the characters ex wife.
While on the trail of the protaginists ex wife, who despite being in the same accident, clearly isn't having the problems the player is having, (also  betraying a considerable lack of concern for her pilot/ex-huband)  I encountered a wolf feeding on a dead deer. The game advised that one should avoid wolves. Which is odd as this game was clearly  blocking any further progress with a bloody wolf, which you then have to try and fight/chase off. Duly after some savage beatings the poor old hero suffered wounds which you the player simply don't have the resources to treat.
As my character slipped into the long dark after suffering these fatal wounds compounded by severe dehydration, hunger and hypothermia, which occured within seconds of the wolf attack, I finally ran out of patience with the game.
In short this a extreme weather walking simulator with extreme weather conditions, so extreme I kept wondering when product placement for Discovery Extreme weather was going to show up.
When it isn't trying to taunt you with how extreme its gaming environment is,  it constantly hassles you with various meters which must be satisfied min by min. Sleeping, heating, eating and drinking. All of which require resources or shelter which are difficult to find.  Making the game part resource management in addition to the walking, which you must do to progress the story.
The sand box version appears to have no real end goal apart from how much of this you can endure before switching off. The story mode, I had hoped, would keep me more engaged. It didn't. I was to engaged with the constant nagging of the heat, sleep, drink and eat meters demanding my attention during the 4 days of game time that elapsed. Two hours real time.
In the end this game was making me work far too  hard for any nuggets of fun that could be found in the wastes. This game wasn't hard as much as it was simply annoying.
The main characters are voiced by the same persons who voiced Shepard from Mass Effect. 'nuff said

The game is stunning, it's not entirely my type, but it has become one of my favorite games visual wise. The music gives you the vibe of the game, and there's so much where you can go.
TLDR; Buy the game if you want a survival game that can be a rightful challenge with some wonderful music and visuals.

This is, quite possibly, the best Zachtronics game yet. It has every bit of the Zachtronics competitive puzzle-optimizing fun we've come to know and love, but the infinite play area means that merely solving a puzzle is always reasonably easy.
The lack of an explicit "branch" instruction does make for simpler puzzles than TIS-100 or Shenzhen I/O (for example), but I find the result to be a tighter focus on the aspects that matter to this game, rather than being
simple. In addition, Opus Magnum should be considerably less intimidating to many people than those games were, given its much more visual nature.

As Zachtronics games go, this one is downright forgiving and accessible, which may be a huge plus for folks who were turned off from the complexity of their recent offerings. The most notable difference is that the player is afforded very little in the way of restrictions when solving the puzzles; the game lets you cobble together the most insanely inefficient solution imaginable, if you so desire (or can't find a better solution), but then the familiar histograms comparing your solution to the rest of the playerbase serves as encouragement to dismantle your awful construction and build something perhaps slightly less embarrassing.
Honestly, though, while seeing your placement on the histograms and getting to the next bit of the story (Opus Magnum has a story! It's not the most complex or suspenseful thing ever, but it's a nice distraction) is a nice enough incentive to complete each puzzle, watching the solution in action is the real gem here. Some of the more complex solutions are mesmerizing to watch, and it tends to be the case that the "better" your solution (as far as the three main metrics - size, cost and time - are concerned), the better it looks in action. Getting a "perfect" solution where you've got no wasted time and everything is constantly in motion is truly a hypnotic sight to behold.

This is a great puzzle game.  Easy to understand mechanics with multiple (hundreds?) of possible solutions for each puzzle, and yet once you are past the beginning puzzles, you still have to think a lot about how to make a working solution.
The game involves creating machine that use 'alchemy' to combine base elements into needed products.  You place manipulation arms and reaction gylphs to bond, unbond or change the elements you are working with to produce the needed products from the provided inputs.  You can attempt to just get a working solution, or you can optimize for cost, space, or speed of production.
The game also has workshop support and a puzzle creator, so there is a whole bunch of user created puzzles to play through as well as the official puzzles.  If you like creating machines, then you can't go wrong with this game!

Creativity meets problem-solving; there are countless ways to solve each puzzle. With a set pallate of tools, products, and reagents, one must create their own 2D machine to perform the necessary processes.
This game encourages a side of my brain which I have been out-of-touch with for a while: creative problem-solving. To provide original correct answers to set questions will force one to think creatively in ways that daily life simply doesn't promote.
The game starts off easy, to get one familiar with it's concepts, but gets quite difficult later on. Each puzzle is similar, yet distinct in nature, and continues be challenging even after solving it by trying to improve the efficiency. Combine basic tools into complex machines to take reagents and make products.
I honestly forget that this game is in early access with how well it actually plays - it feels like a fully released game and is very well made. I'm looking forward to seeing what else will come next!
TL;DR
Play this game and become a better person.

I debated picking this game up because it looked a bit simplistic.  I was completely wrong with that assumption.  Sure, stylistically it is pretty basic, but the puzzles in this game are so well designed it's almost frustrating!  After just a few really simple ones to get your feet wet, the puzzles quickly get complex and require a great deal of planning.  You would think breaking apart molecules and using the atoms to create new ones would not be so challenging, but it really is given your limited resources.
There are a few interface issues I wish were a little smoother, but since you can completely control how fast the game moves, it's not a big deal.  You'll be too busy trying to figure out how to break off 4 atoms and combine 3 others to create two separate outputs with just 4 bond zones to care about it.
SpaceChem is pretty much the ultimate mind teaser  for spacial awareness.  It's a lot of fun for a low price.  Do yourself a favor and pick it up!

Kholat is a horror game based off of a real life incident in Russia decades ago.  While it falters in some areas, it does some things so well that it merits a recommendation.
The game features a large open area that the player must explore.  The player has a map and a compass, but navigation is initially disorienting, something that enriches the experience. The landscape feels confusing, and mastering it is part of the challenge. The element of navigation in a unique snowy landscape brings something new to the genre.  It's the first game since Miasmata that made me feel as though I really had to pay attention to find my way around. This approach works particularly well in a horror game.
The sound and atmosphere design is amazing; snow whips and howls around the player constantly, and the baying of wolves seems to follow the player.  Occasionally, the player will navigate through narrow caves or dark forests.  Sometimes, you are not alone, and I experienced frequent dread and occasional shocks throughout my time.  The game varies the dangers you face, and I never got comfortable. Finally, it should be mentioned that the entire game is gorgeous.
The plot, however, features a number of themes-supernatural, government conspiracy, to name the most prominent- and mashes them together. The story does not tie together all of these ideas in a cohesive manner.  The voice acting works well, but everything is so scattered that it didn't hold my interest.  The considerable talent of Sean Bean is not utilized well. It's one of those approaches to horror that's designed to 'leave it to the player's interpretation,' but there's nothing solid to hold on to.  Nothing comes together, and the ending is insubstantial.
Had the story elements been more focused, this would have been a stronger recommendation.  However, the gameplay of navigation in a blizzzard, the incredible atmosphere, and the consistent chills, make this a worthy choice for anyone looking for a quality horror title.

I Would love to recommend this game, as it has a lot of potential going; but really the AI pathing is terrible.  It has the dubious honour of being the first game I've had crash since upgrading to windows 10 (3 times) - wait for it to eventually (hopefully?) get out of early access.

Overall Stonehearth is a good game with HUGE potential. First and most importantly, as of January 2016 this is still an EARLY ACCESS GAME.  If you want a complete game with all the bells and whistles then this is NOT for you. If, however, you don't mind playing a game while it's in development then you will benefit from playing Stonehearth.
The game is playable but with it's not without issues. That's what the Alpha players are for; they find an issue, report it to the website and the developers get to working. (unless it's DayZ lol)
Secondly, there will be updates!!! The more people to get involved the more WE get to influence the final outcome! To actually have some say in the development of a game is most excellent.
So with that being said, here is a list of pros and cons, and these are PURELY my opinion.
PROS:
Stated before, the game has huge potential
Even in early access it is still very enjoyable, it has an adventure mode as well as a leisure mode.
It allows you to actively manage and maintain villagers and their actions WITHOUT having to micromanage.
The graphics and character types are reminiscent of Bomberman (Nostolgia effect if you like that kind of thing).
Overall a good way to enjoy some downtime.
Time control that allows you to pause, resume or speed up gameplay.
CONS:
Sometimes the villagers are OFP (Own F***king Program) and don't respond to what you tell them. Im not trying to raise a Tomogachi with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ attitude, you know.
The layout for menus seems to be counter-intuitive until you get the hang of them, once you go through the ringer you learn where the items/options are. Sometimes it feels like a "Where's Waldo" search when trying to close out a window.
The Goblins... THE F**KING GOBLINS!!!! Their fingers are stickier than my keyboard. They seem to have an invincible leader that will absolutely annihilate your villagers. (Perhaps this is a good thing though).
As the game progresses, depending on your equipment (IRL folks) the game could get some lag going on.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summarization
The game is still in alpha, so of course you will find an idiot who is quick to review and say "Meeehhhhhh, the game isn't complete, it has bugs and i want my allowance back". These people are either dense, ignorant or just didn't read the product before purchasing, OF COURSE AN ALPHA GAME IS INCOMPLETE. The more people who purchase, the more input and the more the CUSTOMERS get to influence the final product. I can think of several things that I want added and have read many other great suggestions as well. While the game has it's problems, these problems are not, by any means, fatal.
Get involved or not. I do not feel like I wasted my money, and this is maybe the second game I actually took the time to review, so thats gotta say something.
Overall I RECOOOOOMEND

Any quality issues you might have because of the age of this title, such as graphics, are easily overshadowed by the brilliant writing, open-ended gameplay, and the level of completeness and care that was originally put into this game.
The Enhanced Edition is a welcome improvement. It launched for me first try with no issues on Win7x64/AMD 8-Core. If all it did was run the game and provide modern display resolutions, it would be a great success.
Visual enhancements and more options to tweak gameplay are also included. These are icing on the above-descibed cake. Documentation on some of these features is lacking, but it looks like Beamdog is in it for the long haul.
Other enhancements make the game more like BG2, adding subclasses, dual wield, extra weapon types, mechanics tweaks, NPCs, etc. By any measure these things are an improvement, BUT I have mixed feelings about it since I love the original, with all its limitations. In a way, BG2 is less good now.
In summary a great rerelease of an epic game. Bugs (new ones) are barely worth mentioning & since this was clearly a project by someone who loves the game I have no doubt that they will be eradicated.

Been quite a long road.  I remember playing this game back when it was 2D... like, 100% Sprite-Based 2D.
Ever since the "Kate & Baldspot" Era, pretty much.  I've been on this road since Alpha 0.1.2a, and have learned a lot through countless deaths, rebirths, and all-around restarts.  The hours played on Steam does NOT accurately represent the hours I've spent altogether.
I was Bob Smith, beloved husband to Kate Smith, who spent his final days  protecting her with his  life.  Before durability was a thing, I remember walking down the streets with my trusty ol' Nail Bat.  In my mind, I saw this bloodied survivor with a bald spot on his head... a man whose main goal wasn't even to survive... but to protect his beloved wife.  And with nothing more to do, I logged out there, having survived well over a few months.  I left it there, at a cliffhanger.
Skip a few years, and it's clear that his end was met eventually, as the Title Art "secretly" reveals. (Look at them when the lightning strikes.)  In a way, I feel a sense of deja vu every time that lightning strikes, because while most of the modern-day players would see a simple man and woman, I see a former life of mine, having succombed to the virus that has taken over most of the world... and it gives me the urge to run up to their safehouse, and face myself, to finish that old story, so that I may grant the old me his long-awaited closure.
THEN find Earl and tell 'em "Howdy, neighbor!" with a shotgun already at hand.
Long story short, this game has infected me with how addictive it is.  It's damn-near IMPOSSIBLE to forget this game once  you get hooked onto it!  Yes, you will die, but through those deaths, you'll learn from your mistakes, you'll grow stronger as a player... you'll become a battle-hardened survivor.  And before long, you won't die from the zombies anymore... no, you'll find NEW ways to die in the long run.
You find an armed survivor who has "THAT look" in his (or her) eye?  BAM! Shotgun to the head.  You've survived for a month.
Run out of food, and forced to eat rotten stuff?  You've gotten sick, and don't have the proper medication!  You've survived for 6 months.
You're constructing that huge tower for defense, but accidentally trip, and fall down four or five stories?  SPLAT!   You've survived for 10 months.
You've been through Spring, Summer, and even Fall!  Now you're at the end of Winter, and frostbite has your limbs frozen beyond a simple "patching up".  Hypothermia finally claims you.  You've survived for 1 year.
You've got the hang of things, now.  People recognize you, and come to your base.  You think you can trust them, since they have a skilled chef.  The chef, however, sneaks bleach into your soup, and offers it to you.  You've been poisoned!  You've survived for 3 years.
In the end, this game's still in "BETA", but has come farther than DayZ (AND most of its other competitors), offers you more freedom than most of them do, treats survival a LOT more realistically (We have to eat 3,000 meals in one day... WHY again?)
If there's one thing that I must warn you about, Reader, it's this... don't listen to the people who claim that this game is "Dead", because it is FAR from it.  Go to
and see for yourself, then ask those "Dead" sayers to SHOW us where the developers said that they "Quit", or "Give up".  Unlike SOME famous developers out there, THESE guys still dedicate at least ONE day weekly to tell us how they're doing, as well as how the game's doing.  At LEAST one day a week!  Now, go to another developer's website that's been around since 2011, and tell me how long THEIR last announcement was, following the one before it.
Six years.  Almost seven, now!  And they STILL haven't given up!  If these guys aren't considered "Dedicated", then please, do clarify the meaning of that word, so that we may better understand your train of thought, and compare it to the rest of the people out there.

I decided to rewrite this review, since quite a few things happened in the past months - unfortunately not in favor for changing my opinion on this game.
For transparency i uploaded my previous review here:
I have yet to play a game that kept me on edge like PZ did in my first 100 hours. Almost everything can become lethal, starting from drinking bleach, to getting shot (in multiplayer) or by simply being scratched from a zombie. My first death came from a glas shard up my a'ss that i never noticed. Woke up the morning after just to die two minutes later from blood loss. Another time I ran around in the rain for too long and succumbed to illness a few days later. Then i accidently ate rotten food and died again, again and again. PZ really made me suffer cause here you will never get the power fantasies you get in games like Dead Rising and such. You are Joe Schmoe, trying to survive in a hostile and unforgiving enviroment. Scavenge for food, try to learn how to craft the most basic wooden structures and eventually start growing your own vegetables for the upcoming winter when food is needed the most. Try to lay low, barricade your safehouse and avoid risks whenever possible in order to make it to the next day. In PZ, zombies are a threat. Fire a gun or accidently trigger an alarm and you rang the dinner bell for hundreds of zombies. If you dont play smart you will lose your hideout and everything you worked for within minutes. So be careful.
I dont even know where to start because PZ is hands down the game with the most messed-up development that I have come to see on Steam - and I do say that being fully aware that there is the shambling corpse of DayZ out there in the wilds of Zombie Survival Games. Over the past few years the development of this game has turned me from being a hyped fanboy to a disgruntled lurker that tries his best to stay in the loop of the so-called development of this game.
Personally, I'm not sure where it all went wrong but i felt that things were going south the moment the devs decided to outsource some of their features for further development. Another factor that underlines the impression of missing QA is the
We can only imagine how this works but with
it is somewhat safe to assume that there is way more room for bugs to appear then under different circumstances. And they did appear - even worse than they ever did before.
The whole release of Version .38 has been a huge mess, leaving the steam forums with pages full of "Omfg, cant start the game " & "Game always crashes!" threads. Hotfixed where thrown out within days but whenever one thing was fixed, another broke. It went on for days. Then foraging was broken by one of the patches and community modders found a way to fix that and uploaded a  mod to adress this issue. In general, some of most meaningful additions to the game have been made by the community. One of the most prominent features is the Driving Cars Mod (You find the link further up in this review). The first drivable cars have been introduced by a modders and that to great success. Sure, they were somehwat rudimentary but they did work. The same modder actually managed to implement his own NPCs - something the devs are still working on to this day. Anyhow: A few months later, most likely after having picked up on the success of the driving cars mod, the devs decided to add their own cars to the game. In early may 2017 the first iteration of this feature has become testable in a specific test branch and remained there for testing purposes up until today. While the cars have been messy to use from day one with bugs such as losing your inventory and infinite sound loops, they have become worse ever since. Right now the car branch is literally unplayable for me because constant freezes and memory leak eat away every ounce of fun i might have had testing this. Furthermore it didnt help that all those issues have been reported over and over and nothing has happened yet. Instead we got another broken and bugged profession (mechanic) flashing car lights, wonky car physics and
At times I simply cant help but get frustrated with all the new gimmicks that are constantly being added to the game when the existing ones are still far from polished or balanced even. Loot distribution, aiming system, profession balancing, etc. etc. but instead they just add more and more (broken) and at times even meaningless content. Why is stuff like Suspensions, a Nutrition System and dirty clothing that can infect you being prioritized over the things that everyone and their mother keeps asking for? Nobody knows. The worst part is even that I have so much to rant about without even going into detail about the mess that is the development of NPCs and animations. But then again - I'm pretty confident that 90% of the other reviews will cover that for me.

This is an interesting game where you mine for resources and then there is three type of situations.  One is the asteroid fields where you use your mining laser to get resources from the asteroids.  The second one is various visiting star ships.  The first two in a game are always friendly.  The rest are basically neutral or can be hostile.  Usually if you are well armed enough they stay neutral unless you commit a hostile action.  The third type of event is the star events.   Each star gives you heat generation and starts internal fires inside your space ship.  Therefore you need to have at least one person inside to put out any potential fires.
Eventually the asteroids become just a source of resources and not a hazard to you.  The stars just become a semi-random event that you need to put fires out.  The only issue there is that as long as you have sufficient heat venting then thee stars are not going to be a major problem.
The visiting starships need to be handled rather cautiously.  If you get too far along without having any weapons then they will become a major hazard.  The size and power of the visiting starships are completely related to your own ship's size or mass.  If you hover your mouse over the evasion modifier you can find out your mass and the same can be seen from the visiting ships as well.  For you to be able to build something interesting and powerful you need to worry about keeping your ships efficient or they will quickly fall to more and more powerful visiting starships.  My current ship has finished researching everything available and masses 123 and commonly has visiting starships that mass 140 or so.  I also get visitors that mass 60 or so.  Basically 3-4 designs are visiting me and I can kill all of them fairly easily.
Explosive weapons are your friends for killing enemy ships as they cause fires which directly attack the ship's structure instead of their armor.  Other routes to take is to have 3+ weapons stations which improves accuracy and take out the power plants of the larger ships.  Killing them all will disable all a ship's systems including weapons and engines.  For defense your best bet is to focus on shields and increasing your basic structure points by armoring all your hallways.  Also as long as you boost your shield regen enough they make a great way to effectively harvest asteroids as the shields destroy the rock but not the harvestable resources.
For operations, you need to have 1 navigation console so that you can go and direct yourself to the next event such as find a ship or find and asteroid field.  I avoid heat and mining consoles as their effects are completely minimal and it is just easier to fill that need by using components.  Armor and shield consoles are very useful and give out an improved regeneration rate for their respective type.  Shields protect the basic components while armor does not which is the reason shields are better in the long run than armor.  They also improve regeneration rates based on a combination of your station operator's ability and how much your base regeneration is solely based on your components.
One thing that confused me when I first was attempting to play this game is how to grow your ship.  You do not create walls and fill in with flooring.  This method does not work at all as you are not building a building.  You need to completely fill in your space with hull and then you can build a floor on top of the center piece of any hull structure that is 3x3 or as long as there is no point touching space itself in all 8 directions.  I was trying to remove a wall and fill it in piece by piece which made it so I ended up causing my crew to suffocate.
Having enough food is a challenge early on I recommend buying food from one of the first two ships if possible.  Also getting enough people to do the work that you need can be a challenge.  I have found that before I have unlocked enough of the components that it can be a problem.  I had 5 mining lasers and 6 laser turrets with about 10 mass.  In addition I had my navigation station and enough engines to give me a positive evade.  At that point I started using the navigation station to search for ships.  As long as I did not have to jump out from a much more powerful enemy which at 10 mass is not really much of an issue I was able to freely trade with most of the ships and all the other ones were not as well armed as me.  Make certain that you do not go overboard on building your hull out without keeping your ship well enough armed and defended to fend off any ships that you may come across.
With my current ship of 123 mass I have 16 medium engines, 28 plasma turrets and 16 torpedo launchers.  I have 38 personnel and have to use 2 large plant beds to keep enough food 3600 shields with around 300 regen for them.  This is enough to easily kill most anything that I come across and if for some reason I am not careful and let them get through my shields I have 3240 structure using lots of hull braces in all my hallways. I also have lots of open floor space for more development.
All my ships look a little boxy as that is a great way to use space.  I also do not have more than one room as building internal walls is a waste of space currently as those internal walls still would increase your mass which means that you would need to face larger ships.
Overall for a recommendation this game has a bit of a learning curve and then it is fairly easy to build some great and powerful ships.  Unfortunately you need to focus on efficiency if you want to keep your ships in space which means that making cool looking enterprise type ships becomes difficult to say the least.  Making a borg ship just works better.  That might be why the federation needed dozens of their enterprise type ships to take out each of the borg type ships...

The game is somewhat straight forwards, start in a small pod, and struggle up until you have a decent ship built. The key to this game is to work on effiency, which is to say that, if you build big, big ships come, so things come down to being able to make small but mighty ships. It is exceptionally relaxing to play, though it can get a bit boring if you don't have the navigation console, as it is basically just waiting for events to happen at that point.
Pros:
On the upside the game is pretty cheap, and for me I will for sure get my fun out of it, hell I already have gotten more than it's worth in fun.
It runs pretty well and I haven't seen many slow downs (save for small half second stutters if there are far too many explosions happening)
the game is similar to rimworld in many ways, but also much simpler, it has no social system and resources fall under only a few categories making it a bit more relaxing to play.
Cons: the real intensity for the game is in the start, and it can sometimes come down to raw chance if you make it to even early-mid-game where you have more power to shape things.
There isn't much of a late game, it often comes down to needing to build bigger and stronger than the final enemy ship and then just blowing that same ship up, over, and over. So the late game for sure needs work.
All in all I definitely recomend the game as you will for sure get your moneys worth from it.

Harking back to sprite based city management/builder games of old such as Caesar and Pharaoh. It's an interesting approach to have the inner workings of your cities handle themselves while your challenge is one of building placement and resource management with respect to supply/demand. Increasing the desirability of your human workforce houses through beautification and service provision will allow for more compact and focused cities rather than sprawling suburbs of low-tier houses to effect the same workforce level, yet even tents and shacks require maintenance facilities.
Constantly reworking your city plan is the core of the game, do not be afraid to destroy houses to make room for services and make healthy use of roadblocks to prevent your service providers from wandering to the far edges of the map.
Playing at some of the tutorial missions is recommended if you are struggling to get the feel of the services and supply/demand on resources.

Guaranteed Zachtronics: if you liked SpaceChem, you should like this one too. The main difference, as of about halfway into the game, seems to be that there are no sensors involved. As such, it's less "programming" and more "ordering commands for the machines to blindly execute". The puzzles feel easier than in the previous games, but that's perhaps why I like the optimization part more now. Again, there are three different metrics for optimization and you always need multiple solutions to cover the different optimizations (should you choose to accept the mission). The game usually also reveals several different puzzles at once so you don't need to proceed entirely linearly, one by one.

My first real foray into the world of Zachtronics games, having admired their complexity from afar for a few years. The open-ended format of the puzzles gives players a lot of freedom to solve them their own way, but the histogram stats at the end incentivise optimisation. Continuing updates keep improving an already great game and I have no doubt that the 1.0 release will be even better than the current Early Access version.

Opus Magnum is another great example of his. There are LOADS of puzzles, with many many solutions. In comparison to previous games, the learning curve is very gentle.
Every one of the puzzles offers a graph-style leaderboard on the 3 disciplines: "cost" (how many expensive parts), "cycles" (speed of the solution), and "space" (how big it is). You can create as many solutions as you like to beat all three.
THE KEY POSITIVES:
- The game looks and sounds brilliant, feels really industrial
- Many many puzzles
- Good value
- Can have more than 3 solutions to puzzles!
THE KEY NEGATIVES:
- Game doesn't feel as polished as his other creations yet, for example, the game involves "playing" a solution of the assembly line-style creation, but you can't fast forward or rewind the play. On longer creations (especially space/cost saving ones), you can wait 15 seconds to get to the key point you've changed, every time you adjust something, just to find it doesn't work.
- There is no zoom option. This means when playing you might not see the whole creation easily, and have to drag the screen about. This can be a faff on a laptop.
I love this game so far. If you enjoy Zachtronics, go for it. If you haven't played Zachtronics, check out his other creations first.
