Dungeon of the Endless is a turn-based rogue-lite dungeon crawler with tower defence elements. I guess. But it is awesome! That’s for sure.
Your team crashes on a planet and between them and the surface is 12 floors of increasingly hostile dungeon. There are character bios and such to flesh out the world a little but this is not a game to be played for its story elements.

Dungeons are made of rooms separated from each other by a door and opening one acts as a turn. Moving around (you or the monsters) happens in real time, but monster and resource spawning happens between turns. Goal in each floor is to protect your crystal, find the exit and move your crystal to it. Simple enough but what Dungeon of the Endless does extreme well is making the player balance resources in order to survive. There never is enough of everything and you always have to compromise.
There are four resources in the game: Industry is used for building things which includes resource gatherers and support buildings. You can build turrets to help you defend rooms or structures which add defence or heal your characters etc. Science is for researching new and better building types. Food is for healing and levelling up characters. These three can be obtained from resource gatherers or in rooms by random luck.
Fourth is Dust and this is where things get interesting. Normally rooms are dark which means that monsters can spawn at random when turn changes. Using 10 Dust can light up a room which prevents spawning and allows building turrets or resource gatherers. Dust is also found randomly or dropped from monsters. Lighting up a room has obvious benefits but there rarely is enough dust available to light up everything. Rooms can also be powered down for the dust to be used elsewhere. With this mechanic you can create dead ends that are not in danger of monsters and then filled with resource buildings. Or you can leave rooms unpowered and build up enough defences so that possible enemies can be easily dealt with and harvested for more dust. Or get overwhelmed and die horribly in the claws of crawlies from the dark.
Random spawning can also be stopped by occupying a room with a hero character. Your team can have up to four heroes with different abilities. Some are tanks that can hold the line by themselves. Some are fast and can be used to open far away doors and then escaping back to safety. They can also carry the crystal most effectively. Some heroes make buildings work more effectively. New heroes can be found in dungeons and unlocked for subsequent play throughs by surviving with them. Leveling up makes them stronger but the skills or stats cannot be customised by the player. You can give items to heroes which allows for some variation. With all of the resource management going on I think the levelling system is just right. Any more complex would have made it difficult to handle.
Make no mistake, Dungeon of the Endless is really difficult as it is! I tried 20 times (or more than 10 hours) on “easy” before switching to “too easy” and only then being able to finish the game. Dungeons are randomly generated which makes every try feel fresh. I’m sure more difficulty levels can be opened with completion though I haven’t been able to (yet). You can also open new game modes that change the ruleset and really change your playstyle so the game has a lot of replayability.
Dungeon of the Endless is a pixel art game and I personally really like the look. Animations are good and lighting effects make the game quite atmospheric. It’s also light on the system and runs on my ultrabook without problems exept the character select screen which has the only 3d objects of the game and really kills the framerate. Doesn’t have any effect on playability though. Music and sounds in general are also great and I had no crashing issues or anything. So great job on the technical front!
I was really hooked by this game. It made me skip schoolwork, it made me almost burn dinners and my back was aching for hunching down on the computer for hours. Dungeon of the Endless is great, really really great and I thoroughly recommend it!

Whereas Portal and its sequel are fairly easy puzzle games that excel at making you feel smart.  SpaceChem is a quite challenging puzzle game that makes your head hurt. This game is what great games are all about.  It has simple mechanics that lead to complex problem solving.  The game uses a simple mechanic called a “Waldo”.  It moves atoms.  You to tell it when to grab, drop, rotate or bond an atom.  That's about it.  Yet once you are into the game you are turning sea water and air into complex compounds.  You are filtering dirty water to power nuclear weapons.  While you are doing it you are also learning the fundamentals of modern programming and Chemistry.  It is one of those rare gems that will engage parts of your brain that you have probably forgotten exist, and at the same time leave you feeling immensely proud of your own creativity.  It is not flash.  It is not action packed.  But damn it is satisfying.
Educational, entertaining, challenging, and almost real chemistry puzzle game. Makes me feel like a real engineer everytime I finish a puzzle.

‘Efficiency and inventiveness is king.’ SpaceChem is more than just a series of challenges; it’s a set of tools for creating your own solutions to increasingly complex puzzles requiring you to combine atoms to form molecules in the most efficacious manner possible. What’s fascinating is the premium placed on computational logic, design and ingenuity when solving puzzles in order to ‘produce chemicals with the greatest possible yield’. The complexity and elegance of solutions combined with the fact they will be your solutions rather than the game’s is a mark of the intelligence of the puzzles here. It’s a refreshing gameplay mechanic rarely seen elsewhere, rewarding lateral thought and promoting logical thought processes real-world engineers and scientists are known for.
And it might just be used as a teaching aid in STEM education.

I've spent a TON of time with Fire Pro Returns and loved it to bits, although it wasn't without its faults. The customization options in the game were practically ENDLESS and you could literally create anyone you could think of, whether it'd be a wrestler, an actor or a comic books character. It was a really great game.
Now I've bought Fire Pro World in Early Access and I do understand that it's still in development and it will receive options like logos editor and custom music for entrances  (something that couldn't be included in Returns), but it really lacks as a sequel especially since it is 2017 right now, so well over 8yrs since Returns was released, and it didn't fix some of the really annoying stuff that was in the series for a while now. It is also missing new features unfortunately, as well as any graphical options, but I will get to those in a moment.
1st:
The most annoying thing in the series ever since I can remember: STRIKING MECHANICS!
The hitboxes are absolutely AWFUL. I fully understand that the devs do want to keep the "soul" of the series and not get on the fans bad side by introducing seriously drastic changes to its formula, but this needs to be fixed. I don't want the strikes to be super easy to do, but currently they are nearly impossible to connect unless the opponent is groggy/dazed, whatever you call it ;P.
You need to be PERFECTLY lined up with your opponent or you'll miss all your standing, running or weapon strikes. This is even more annoying since the environments are made in 3D and character models are sprites. If you're a mere half a milimetre above or below your opponent, again, you'll miss. Running strikes/grapples are impossible to do unless the opponent is groggy or you Irish Whip 'em and run to the opposite ropes.
The hitboxes for the strike game during a match are really in a serious need of an improvement. I didn't think I'll ever say it, but we've got 2017, and the hitboxes in this are worse than in really old beat 'em ups like Double Dragon, Streets of Rage etc.
2nd:
So far, the game seems to be a straight-up PC port of Fire Pro Wrestling Returns. Is it a really, REALLY bad thing? Nope, since Returns was a great game, but it's defnitely not a good thing either.
The game lacks features. Sure, it has the match types, customization options and the completely original and unique vibe of the Fire Pro series but that's not really enough anymore I'm afraid.
Why there's no new match types in this installment? How about a Tables match with some added table mechanics? Breaking tables in a Fire Pro game? THAT WOULD BE AWESOME O_O! Something like Hell in a Cell where we could climb and fight on the top of the said cage? More weapon moves, like weapon grapples? Why even add the announcer tables this time around if we can't even climb up on them :/?
This really isn't satisfying enough given that I've waited over 8yrs for a new Fire Pro game, just to get what I consider a port of Fire Pro Returns with new moves added to it.
3rd:
The graphical options. Now again, I'm fully aware that the game is in Early Access, but it lacks ANY video options at all. It only has a switch between "Full Screen" and "WIndowed" modes. Whether you choose one or another, the game is stuck in a resolution of 1280x720 which is 720p, My native resolution is 1920x1080 and the only way to have the game to run in this resolution is to change the game registry entries :x.
Menus fonts are really blurry, washed out and seem to be low-res. I was able to somewhat fix it with a 3rd party app called SweetFX/ReShade, but it simply makes them sharper, which helps a little but since they're in low-res and blurry to start with, it's not an amazing sort of improvement unfortunately. Not even having an option to change the resolution is a joke nowadays. Bad one at that. Two patches for the game were already released, but none of them added this option...
There's also no any textures options or at least some sort of filters that would make the game and the character models look better, as opposed to the current mediocre pastel-like look. Models look like the developers would use some sort of a brush feature of a picture editing program like Photoshop on them to make them look higher quality than in Returns. The result is rather, well, ok-ish at best. Returms models also had this technique used on them, but models in World seem to have a good 3 times as much of this effect applied to them.
This is just my 2 cents about the current state of the game. I'll update it somewhere down the road after a few months when the game gets significantly more patches and maybe some new match types, features etc. although I'm rather sceptical when it comes to new match types.
I'll still play the game in its current state as I simply love this series :), but this won't make me feel less disappointed with it feeling like a simple PC port of Fire Pro Wrestling Returns, with the only changes being added announcer tables which you can't even interact with, new moves, custom music option coming "in the future" and Steam Workshop support which, in the end, isn't even an actual in-game feature.
I can recommend this only to somebody who liked and still likes Returns a lot and doesn't mind playing the same thing again but on PC this time around.

Nothing significant has changed in regard to controls & gameplay, but if it's not broke it doesn't need to be fixed. There are a few new gameplay mechanics such as the fighting spirit feature where two wrestlers slug it out for a few seconds, but most of the game's real improvements are built around the strong creation features and integrated steam workshop support.  There are a handful of new animations/moves that have been added since FPR; many are moves from the modern day WWE and Indy scene. While the additions are not as numerous as I had assumed they'd be given the 12 year gap since the last Fire Pro game, I am hopeful that we'll continue to see new moves added to the game as development continues.
Sure there are a few bugs/glitches but this IS early access so that's to be expected.  It would be nice to see a story/career/gm mode of some sort as development moves along--assuming there is still time to do that.

I decided to rewrite this review, since quite a few things happened in the past months - unfortunately not in favor for changing my opinion on this game.
For transparency i uploaded my previous review here:
I have yet to play a game that kept me on edge like PZ did in my first 100 hours. Almost everything can become lethal, starting from drinking bleach, to getting shot (in multiplayer) or by simply being scratched from a zombie. My first death came from a glas shard up my a'ss that i never noticed. Woke up the morning after just to die two minutes later from blood loss. Another time I ran around in the rain for too long and succumbed to illness a few days later. Then i accidently ate rotten food and died again, again and again. PZ really made me suffer cause here you will never get the power fantasies you get in games like Dead Rising and such. You are Joe Schmoe, trying to survive in a hostile and unforgiving enviroment. Scavenge for food, try to learn how to craft the most basic wooden structures and eventually start growing your own vegetables for the upcoming winter when food is needed the most. Try to lay low, barricade your safehouse and avoid risks whenever possible in order to make it to the next day. In PZ, zombies are a threat. Fire a gun or accidently trigger an alarm and you rang the dinner bell for hundreds of zombies. If you dont play smart you will lose your hideout and everything you worked for within minutes. So be careful.
I dont even know where to start because PZ is hands down the game with the most messed-up development that I have come to see on Steam - and I do say that being fully aware that there is the shambling corpse of DayZ out there in the wilds of Zombie Survival Games. Over the past few years the development of this game has turned me from being a hyped fanboy to a disgruntled lurker that tries his best to stay in the loop of the so-called development of this game.
Personally, I'm not sure where it all went wrong but i felt that things were going south the moment the devs decided to outsource some of their features for further development. Another factor that underlines the impression of missing QA is the
We can only imagine how this works but with
it is somewhat safe to assume that there is way more room for bugs to appear then under different circumstances. And they did appear - even worse than they ever did before.
The whole release of Version .38 has been a huge mess, leaving the steam forums with pages full of "Omfg, cant start the game " & "Game always crashes!" threads. Hotfixed where thrown out within days but whenever one thing was fixed, another broke. It went on for days. Then foraging was broken by one of the patches and community modders found a way to fix that and uploaded a  mod to adress this issue. In general, some of most meaningful additions to the game have been made by the community. One of the most prominent features is the Driving Cars Mod (You find the link further up in this review). The first drivable cars have been introduced by a modders and that to great success. Sure, they were somehwat rudimentary but they did work. The same modder actually managed to implement his own NPCs - something the devs are still working on to this day. Anyhow: A few months later, most likely after having picked up on the success of the driving cars mod, the devs decided to add their own cars to the game. In early may 2017 the first iteration of this feature has become testable in a specific test branch and remained there for testing purposes up until today. While the cars have been messy to use from day one with bugs such as losing your inventory and infinite sound loops, they have become worse ever since. Right now the car branch is literally unplayable for me because constant freezes and memory leak eat away every ounce of fun i might have had testing this. Furthermore it didnt help that all those issues have been reported over and over and nothing has happened yet. Instead we got another broken and bugged profession (mechanic) flashing car lights, wonky car physics and
At times I simply cant help but get frustrated with all the new gimmicks that are constantly being added to the game when the existing ones are still far from polished or balanced even. Loot distribution, aiming system, profession balancing, etc. etc. but instead they just add more and more (broken) and at times even meaningless content. Why is stuff like Suspensions, a Nutrition System and dirty clothing that can infect you being prioritized over the things that everyone and their mother keeps asking for? Nobody knows. The worst part is even that I have so much to rant about without even going into detail about the mess that is the development of NPCs and animations. I do like this game so lets  get that out of the way. It is definitely an Early Access but compared to some it's very easily at a fully playable stage. As an Early Access I'm quite loathe to criticise the flaws but rather I'd list what could be improved in my opinion:
Difficulty levels:
The game is very difficult. Whilst this is a good challenge it's a fine line between challenging and frustrating. My first several play throughs left me thinking it was impossible but then I had a breakthrough and i've stuck with it but a choice of difficulty would be great as a new player.
User Interface:
I quite like the UI in that you can move the boxes around to find your style but a few UI/Game Mechanics issues can cause problems. Overheating is a pain in the a**e and you get very little warning other than your crew mentioning it in a speech bubble and the small indicator that shows a high number. As such an important game mechanic (i've blown up unexpecedly because of it!) I'd prefer a proper alarm/notification system
The Alert Levels could be drastically improved to add flair. This type of game is crying out for a Bridge Commander style "Go to red alert". Other than a wimpering alarm you'd barely notice. Red flashing lights, a proper alarm, that's what's needed, I want the drama - I want to feel that pressing the Red Alert button is a big deal.
Research Speed:
Far too slow. One of the best ways to extinguish a fire is to vent an airlock but if you don't have life support you can't then re-oxygenate the air and this is a locked item. Either speed up research or make some things available from the start.
Crew replenishment:
Most of my play throughs see me losing some crew. My current one has 2 and they manage but I need more to speed up research/repairs etc and its only occassionally possible through passing trade. A mechanism for crew replenishment would be good.
Asteroid Mining:
So mundane, especially in the beginning when oyu only have 1 mining laser. Once you get laser weapons the process is much quicker - fire at the asteroid to break it up and then mine mine mine. But some way of auto-mining would be a godsend.
Combat:
It would be good to see the health of the systems you target on hostile ships - i.e. is it worth continuing or should i move elsewhere? Also not sure if it's just me but i find when the hostile ship rebuilds a componenet i've destroyed it becomes MUCH TOUGHER to destroy, sometimes impossible.
All in all this is a good game and worth buying at the £8 mark i did. So much potential though.
As the game itself is endless, part of the appeal is to create mighty ships - some way to speed this up woudl be good. For instance how about arriving at a space station occassionally where you can build hull for free/half price etc.

The game is a  random event sort of game, where you cant really control dieing; so save often if you do decide to buy this pile of garbage(as it stands).  The games balance is dreadful/ non-exsistant.

This is an excellent game. I thought based on screenshots and reviews I'd try it, but probably not like it enough to keep. Next thing I knew, I'd played for 20 hours and was on my tenth attempt.
A Youtuber I watch referred to this game as the lovechild of Rimworld and FTL, and that analogy isn't too far from the truth. It plays a lot like FTL, only with a ship you build yourself, block by block, and no gaseous cloud of death spurring you towards a linear ending point. You basically fly forever, continually expanding and surviving. At least until you... fail to do that second part.
The Rimworld comparison comes in when you look at your crew's needs (hunger, thirst, energy, morale, and of course health) and the fact that they're responsible for building your ship. You place down "plans" and your engineers construct them, going out of the ship in space suits if need be. Yes, by the way, you can absolutely jump while your crew is spacewalking and leave them behind, so do be careful about that.
The game is really addictive, and many of the other reviews' complaints that nearly kept me from buying... I didn't see. I've heard one say asteroids will pulverize you no matter what you do. Well... That's not really true. Even one mining laser is enough to clear the way in many cases. Add a few more and you're golden. Alternatively, a single weapon on your ship is adequate to break even large asteroids MUCH faster. Further, as long as you have a good thrust:mass ratio, your ship will dodge a lot of asteroids anyway.
Another said fires are constant and basically can't be put out. It's true that fires are frequent, IF you're flying over a star and don't have adequate venting. There are some late-game weapons that can start fires on your ship too. But I've heard people say firefighting is pointless and that' simply not true. A single crewman can put out even a large fire on a given square within a matter of seconds. Further, the game shares FTL's system of venting, wherein you can seal off a room to keep a fire from spreading, then open an airlock in that room to vent the fire out.
The game WILL punish you if you lower your guard, though. It's a bit like RImworld in that way too. No matter how well off you think you are, never assume you're invincible, because the game may very well have a surprise or three in store for you. I learned that the hard way.
All in all, the game is just great. It lacks just a little depth that could make it truly amazing - for instance, I'd like to see docking opportunities (kept very rare, of course), and perhaps generated factions we can build rapport with. But the game is still in early access, and given that it feels very stable, I can only assume this is because more features are in the works. In time, I think this game could become a classic of its genre. In its current state, easy 8/10 for fun factor alone.

The game itself is very good and I recommend you to give it a try. Too bad it has some very annoying bugs and design flaws that can ruin the gaming experience.
I like the perk system and the variety of weapons, which also include alternate functions. Enemies can be very challenging at times too and one has to think twice before shooting them. Welding doors is a good idea too. It has some basic voice commands with the ability to bind certain commands to keys / buttons. It is also possible to give others money and weapons if they need some. It has some DLC content, but nothing one would need to enjoy the game. There are also basic server filters for various options like difficulty, vac security, excluding full servers etc. Lastly, it has lots of achievments!
Excluding bugs now. The game has significant difficulty spikes. It might be considered a good thing sometimes to make it more challenging, but its annoying when your team does well 8 waves without problems and then get wiped out within few seconds. Another thing is the difficulty settings. Beginner is suited really just for beginners to learn the game mechanics. Its very quick to learn for people who played some other FPS games before (like me) and gets boring fast. Then normal gets incredibly difficult, so you will keep dying unless some more experienced players join. It will get fun again after you level up the perks and get more hang of it. Forget about playing solo champaigns on normal or harder, since it is ubnplayable due to the difficulty.
Another thing I find annoying is the enemy spawning mechanism. It's the same as in other zombie game I played. Enemies simply spawn where you can't see, but that also includes the corner you were 2 seconds ago. The spawning rate also depends havily on the map, so while in open areas you have to wait minutes for enemies to come to you, on indoor maps you get them all at once behind the cornes quickly, massacring you.
The game could also get more champaigns (there are only 3 short ones) and maybe some more game modes.
Sometimes, randomly, the game switches to windowed mode. I'm not sure how it chooses the window size then, sometimes its tiny, sometimes large. You can change it back ingame, but if it happens when you're having trouble, you have to play in window (to not get killed). Also, once when I tried to change it back the game froze. So now I'll probably play only in windowed mode (with some decent window size) to avoid the distraction.
Another annoying bug is with the perks. Sometimes, randomly again, the perks stop saving (and yes, I check if the server can save perks and has no gray-listed mods, it always stops workign even in the solo mode then). I think I leveled up 3 times demolitionist until it saved successfully the progress. When the bug happens, you need to quit the game, delete the cache folder (there are tutorials for it) and start it back up. It's very annoying when you play 2 long games and suddenly realize all the hard work you put to leveling up is gone.
And now for the last bug, it affects only nvidia users though. The opengl renderer is buggy, so sometimes you see wrong textures and the stalkers are visible. Also, the iron sights gets opaque, so you cant see anything trough it. Setting the render mode from "model" to "textured" seems to fix the issue. The "fix" to all the other graphics problems is to use direct 3d renderer instead, but it is not available for Linux.
Soooo, yes, the cons list is quite long :p but I still enjoy the game a lot.

Story about something that happened to me in the game that was pretty cool:
I found a little log cabin just before dark and started to make myself at home. I'd been collecting wood on the way and inside I found some food and a couple of pieces of clothing. I lit the fire place inside and loaded it up with wood. Darkness had fallen by then and I only had enough wood to load up for about 4 or 5 hours worth of burn time. I knew I'd freeze elsewise, so I headed out the door to quickly find some more wood before I called it a night.
I left the cabin and climbed up a hill right by the cabin. It was quite dark and a bit of a blizzard blowing. I turned around and looked down the hill and the only light source coming from anywhere was out of the window of the little wood cabin. That light fliockered and danced on the snow as it should: Coming from a wood fire.
I kept up the hill... now pitch black... and then I realised I was now disorientated and didn't know which direction home was.
I tried looking for the flickering light, but alas... I was utterly lost now. I knew I was ♥♥♥♥ed. It was blowing strong now, and I was starting to freeze.
It's all too easy to get utterly lost in the wilderness. I died and it was all my fault.

Something in-between a dungeon-crawler and a tower defense game. In Dungeon of the Endless, you get to lead a bunch of characters - from the questionable hero to the downright criminal- through 12 floors crowded with monsters.
Pros:
- Enjoyable.
- Nice setting. There isn't a real plot - you have to escape the dungeon, full-stop - but Amplitude, as usual, fills the game with a lot of background information. In this case it isn't as prominent as in Endless Legend, sure, but it's nice nonetheless.
- Challenging. I'm not a newbie in this kind of game and i'm writing this at 40+ hours of gameplay. Almost every step (from the fourth dungeon level onward) must be kind of planned carefully, or you'll end up throwing your progress into the trash bin. Anyway, it rarely gets "too easy".
- Ironic. Yeah, it's barely a pro, but the inside jokes in the game can make you chuckle. The first time you read them, at least.
- Doesn't get too boring, at least not fast. Each run is slightly different from the other, depending which heroes you choose, what's the starting spaceship and so on.
Cons:
- Runs tend to be slow - we're talking about more than one hour, minimum. Particulary if you want to explore all the current level and maximixe resources. Of course, this is mostly an issue when you screw it up and die, wasting your effort.
- Challenging. Yea, it can be a con too. There are two game modes: "Too Easy" and "Easy". At first I thought that I had to unlock the "normal" difficulty completing a run in Easy, and so on. Now, I understand it's some kind of a joke from the devs. If you happen to buy the game and play as "Easy", you'll get it.
If you read this far, I'll throw in some conclusions. Dungeon of the endless is definitely a good game if you're a fan of rogue-likes, or dungeon-defenders, and is worth a try if you aren't (t also happen to be on discount quite often, so ...). Sure, there are times when you open a door and an unseemigly high amount of bone-breaking monsters will charge toward the team an make you swear, but that's part of the game.

An imperfect game when it comes to balance but extremely user-friendly when it comes to interface aside from a few choices, like it doesn't seem to actually save hero groups like the keybinding screen suggests it can. At it's heart I would classify Dungeon of the Endless as a tower defense. If you aren' a fan of tower defense games it doesn't mean Dungeon of the Endless isn't for you, becasue there are alot of other things going on here.
It has some RPG elements in managing a party of heroes, equiping them, getting attached to them, and then having to replace them when they die.
There is a definitely a roguelike feel to the game in both it's difficulty and in the hidden layers of depth. How the systems work aren't clearly explained, and it will take a few play throughs before you truly understand how to optimize your team and level setup.
There is also a hint of exploration, as your team delves deeper into a level you may wind up in triggering the fight for your life or just another empty room. Opening each door when your party is on the brink of death brings some real dread.
TLDR;
There aren't many games you can compare this to. It's a pretty unique style of game that blends tower defense, resource management, rpg elements, and roguelike difficulty. I'm a big tower defense fan and that's where the game clicked for me, but thw tower defense elements are different than in traditional tower defense games. Overall I'd recommend it for anyone who enjoys rougelikes and tower defense games.
P.S. I haven't tried coop, but I imagine that would be a blast. They've also added a bunch of new content since I last played, so give it a try if you're looking for a new experience!

I love a good Rogue-like. I've poured countless hours into Torchlight, Diablo, Isaac... so on. Similar to The Binding of Isaac, this game has a very steep learning curve. All the upgrades you purchase - new towers, tower upgrades, so on - only apply to your current run. This game is essentially RNG taken to the extreme. Unless you're the luckiest space marine this side of the galaxy, you're gonna die repeatedly. I get that some games can't just be picked up and played, that you need to sink hours into them before you're going to win, but when winning is locked behind random rumbers and not skill, it becomes a tedious grind that loses all sense of fun very quickly.
The graphics are cute, the soundtrack isn't bad, all in all, it's a decently polished game. Where it suffers is the complete lack of balance, the tutorial being summed up as 'die until you get it right', and a misleading difficulty system.
The above points wouldn't be so bad for a game in Beta, but given that this is a completed game, I was expecting more.

Spacechem allows the player to create different solutions to reach the desired goal. The goal being to output a chemical compound or element using discrete units. The order by which you combine elements can be important. Once the basic mechanics are understood, the game tests sequential planning. A casual game with challenging depth.

While building state machines is fun, I feel like this game could have some valuable lessons to teach in the realm of multi-threaded programming for those trying to optimize for the minimum number of cycles per level.
Many of the puzzles are devilishly clever and the way the game presents itself it is very well done.  The UI is clear, it allows for player documentation of your state machines, and tries to give you the tools to come up with the best solution possible.
This is one of those games where the leaderboards matter and trying to eek out that little bit of optimization to get the fastest machine of your friends is something I spent a lot of time doing, even after "solving" the problem.

Baldur's Gate: EE is a great game. Easily one of the top 3 RPG's I've ever played.  If you are into RPGs D&D you probably have already played it.
However, for those that are unfamiliar, there is immense detail put into the story and world in this game--the Baldur's Gate series has one of the best stories. The enemies and fights can be challenging--mind racking sometimes--while you figure out what works and what doesn't. Who to deal with right away, and who is less threatening to your party. Save often.
Test things out, what do spells do. Sometimes, I'd come across a spell that would have been really beneficial had I known about it earlier--or potions for the matter. I hoard mostly in these games, but learning how to effectively use what you're finding or buying can really sway a battle in your favor. Some battles become very easy, once you have a good strategy, appropriate gear and spells to cast.
Also, pre-read some tips about the new features, because they make the game a lot easier to play--quick loot. I played the 2nd in the series first, and I still had much enjoyment coming to the first 10+ years after. If you play them in order, you can import your character across games.
Some may find it slow--your characters move slow. There can be a lot of reading, equipment management, exploring, adventuring, etc. This game is about planning and executing strategies through a well written world. Deciding who to help--quests--and what to skip. Warning a party mixed with evil and good aligned party members lead to disagreements. So it may be difficult to see the entire game, or every quest, first play through.
If you enjoy the game you've easily 50-100+ hours of gameplay to immerse yourself into, though there is a level cap--to keep you from power leveling and steam rolling the near end. The Black Pits expansion seems interesting, an arena challenge, 15 or so fights to test your skills in battle. Played it briefly, though honestly, I bought this for the main story and game.

While I was watching some of the video reviews/let's plays, I saw that the characters don't have any sort of customization. They have no outfits, you can't assign them to a bed and decide where each one lives. This is fine with me, but I figured it was a trade-off for a more in-depth crafting system and/or building system. However, I was disappointed to find out that this was NOT the case. The crafting is very surface-level(and extremely annoying to level). The buildings have very little functionality other than to make your villagers do what they already do, better.
Overall, the experience was a bit underwhelming. It was too much of a simulator(and not even a good simulator at that) and not enough of an interactive city-builder, like I thought it would be. I actually bought this game because I played Cities: Skylines and felt that too much based on the simulation and less based around fun, but in the end, this game left with a similar feeling.
TLDR: Fun game. Cool art. No depth. Very little content.
If I could reccomend a couple things to the developers:
-Add more character customization. Instead of trying to build more into the "job tree", give each person with that profession a separate talent tree that gives each character some identity and gives you a reason to have more than one of them other than just that their job isn't being taken care of.
-Add more functionality to buildings.
-Increase villager cap and allow for more space to build on and allow towns to be converted into cities.
-Add more tutorial information. Almost all of the stuff I had to learn how to do, was learned via videos. The tutorials taught me very little about how to play the game.

I had high hopes for Lethis - Path of Progress, which were dashed by broken graphics, poor English translations, and an inconsistent UI.
I'm a fan of "Build a Town" games - Sim City, Banished, and the Anno series. And after playing these out, I decided to pick up Lethis which promised to be a combination of this gameplay and a steampunk world. On loading of the first tutorial mission, I was met immediately with a terrible English translation (That used the term "Bucholic" and called me an idiot for not having built one of the buildings already). The game is not voice acted, and the characters' thoughts are incredible long-winded. This led to confusing sentence structure and eventually, I decided to skip past all of the text and try to figure out the game using context clues.
But the graphics were all broken. Instead of seeing buildings, I saw large black boxes, as if the ground and the buildings upon which it was built was incapable of loading. This went unfixed even after reinstalling the game and restarting my machine. Not to mention that every graphics setting in the game required restarting the game entirely, which in this day of gaming is unacceptable.
Lastly, the UI was horribly inconsistent and poorly thought out. For one, you're unable to use typical shortcuts to perform tasks like opening the main game menu. Not only that, you can't close the main menu using the Esc key or Right-Click. Yet other menus are closeable using the right-click and aren't closeable using the Esc key. It doesn't make any sense. Add to this the inconsistent placement of buildings - some buildings project their blueprint onto the skewed tile grid in the game, so it's possible to view where they'll be placed. Other buildings are placed using a diamond-shaped placement box, making it impossible to tell where your buildings will be placed.
These issues make the game literally unplayable. The UI decisions could be overlooked, but the graphical problems with the game, and the inability to understand the English translation meant I refunded the game after 25 minutes played. It's a hard pass for me, which is a real shame.

tl;dr: Beautiful, spooky game set in the mountians with the backdrop of a real mountain tradgey. Map reading and orientation skills a must. Little rough around the edges but for the asking price, wonderful experiance.
First game developed by IMGN, a polish publishing company, which shows a lot of promise. Seemingly stranded on the Ural Mountains, the player is tasked with exploring the mountain range to uncover what happened. A key part of the game is exploration and orientation where the player is given and a compass. The map shows a number of paths around the range and written on the map are a number of cords that the player needs to find in order to uncover what happened in the Ural mountains.
While the game is open exploration and there is no set order that the cords have to be visited in, some of the paths that are on the map are blocked off with knee high walls and are meant to be travelled down rather than up. While many are well designed into the world so not to be too obvious, there are a few moments where it feels like the player is being sent down corridors rather than open to explorer where ever the player wants. It does not have the openess of skyrim, but that would never be a far comparison to make.
While having the invistable walls adds obvious direction, it can take away from the otherwise amazing immersion. There have been at least two times now where I felt I should have been able to easily access an area that was blocked off. Also it's really easy to get stuck between trees (never to the point of needing the restart I should say) and run for a gap thinking you can make it through but hitting an invisable wall like a fly on glass.
Still given the price and high quality of the assets, it being a little rough on the edges is something that can I can easily forgive and work with.
Running the UE4 engine, the game is visually stunning. There is a large and varied area to explore. At time running through forest, others scaling along and up mountians or going into a maze of caves. It's easy to get lost which is part of the fun, I had my compass up pretty much all the time.
The monsters are a weird one and ill not talk too much about them save to say they are less a threat in there own right but seem instead to try and confuse you and make you loose your bearings to the point where your sprinting through the snow, praying that you wont hit a dead end. They do there job fantastically, always in the back of your mind when trying to make sure you stay heading East.
I have to mention the voice acting which is amazing. It really lends some weight to the story as you piece the parts together. It's narrated by Sean Bean for crying out loud. The score is also great, if a little jumpy at times. The 'Chase music' will jump start and stop quite abruptly.
While it can be a little rough around the edges

A solid first person adventure mystery exploration game. The music is terrific with amazing vocals by the brilliant Mary Elizabeth McGlynn who is well known for her vocals in the Silent Hill games. The graphics are very nice and it's an interesting game to explore with some top notch scenes of creepiness, I loved Dear Esther all those years ago but I've never delved into these types of games, but Kholat has rekindled my interest in first person story exploration games. I got a good 20 hours of play out of this game searching for every single journal, the atmosphere is one of the best that you'll be wanting to explore every nook and cranny before finishing the game.
The few negatives I have are performance, it needs improving, the story is vague and while most of the journals are interesting, you'll wish there was more going on and a few annoyances of a certain visitor which you'll meet often but you soon understand how to deal with it.

Kholat is an open world horror game in which you play as a protagonist who is trying to solve the mysterious case of the Dyatlov Pass incident.
In the beginning the player is given nothing more but a map, a compass and a flashlight (which in my opinion is unnecessary, but gives the game a nice 'alone-in-the-dark-mountains' feel to it from time to time). On the map, there are marked some coordinates, and by following these you'll find pages to read, and to onward the story.
The game has beautiful graphics, the movement is working and the athmosphere is superb with all of its crushing anxiety and cold, snowy mountain scenery. Also the voice over is very pleasant to hear.
Unfortunately Kholat is a very short game for its price. 16,19 euros for 4 hours of playtime for me is not a good deal, but as a friend of horror, it was also not too bad. I think Sean Bean is not the cheapest actor to narrate your game.
Another poor thing in the game is; if you're trying to get all the achievements, you should not complete the story first. After doing so, you'll be stuck in a section called "Act III", and can never return to the main world, expect by starting a new game.
All in all, Kholat is a very good page collecting horror game, set in a beautiful, yet dark athmospheric world, but is a little bit too pricey for its length.

After much consideration, I finally paid ~$18 for Kholat, and I wish I hadn't. So, I'm writing my first review to save others from making the same mistake I did.
In Kholat, you spend the majority of time using a map and compass to walk around and explore a snowy, stormy, mountainous landscape, collecting notes and reports and avoiding the Anomaly along the way. If you don't know how to use a compass, it can be tough to navigate, but I had no problem doing so.
I'll start by describing what I liked about the game.  The graphics are incredible. I had some framerate issues at the highest settings, but I turned it down a bit and they went away. The soundtrack is also very good, with some haunting and resonant sounding tunes. Combined with the graphics, the game creates a chilling environment to trek through. I am a huge fan of the Amnesia series. Kholat has ONE similarity to Amnesia: notes scattered about the game, some containing excellent voiceovers. Others have no voiceovers, and are rather long and boring.
Now, on to what I did not like about the game. First, when you start up the game after installing, the first thing you see is the "set brightness" screen, and there is a typo in it. Not a huge deal, but definitely leaving a bad first impression. I thought, "Uh oh, what did I get myself into?" and continued on. There are various other typos in the game, but again, not a huge deal, and obviously an effect of translating into English. Second, the story leaves much to be desired for me. The "open world" structure of the game makes it hard to piece together a tangible, straightforward story from scattered notes and reports. Third, the game was too short. I beat it in about four hours, which is definitely not enough gameplay for me for the price. Fourth, the save structure is baffling. There is no manual save option, so you have to rely on auto saves, which only happen when you pick up a note, discover a camp for the first time, fast travel between already discovered camps, or (sometimes) when you approach an already discovered camp. Fifth, the game design is not conducive to people (like me) who like to collect everything. After beating the game, Continue brings you back to the previous Act, so you can explore and reveal more locations on the map if you wish. However, without spoiling anything, there are loud sounds and ground shakes constantly coming from the center of the map that are annoying and really discourage me to continue playing. So if you DO get the game, I recommend doing all of your exploring BEFORE travelling to all of the major locations listed along the left side of the map. In other words, leave at least one major location undiscovered or you will have to deal with loud sounds and ground shakes for the remainder of your journey.
In conclusion, I enjoyed Kholat for what it was, but it is simply not worth the money. It definitely creates a chilling overall atmosphere that will unnerve some players, and it was fun getting scared out of my wits and yelling when the Anomaly popped out unexpectedly a few times. But overall, I am disappointed. If you are a fan of the Amnesia series like me, and are looking for a similar experience, I'm sorry to say that you won't find it here. If you want to check out Kholat, I would wait for it to (hopefully) go on sale for at least half off (~$10), or wait for the developers to patch the game and address the various issues I described above.

Morph Girl is an FMV game with a horror movie twist. It's got some genuinely creepy moments that are well supported by the game's music and sound effects.
Despite a few branching paths and a bunch of more minor decisions, it plays out in a rather linear fashion and you can get half of the game's six endings just by replaying the final decision tree. The script is decent, but not amazing. It's also got some grammatical errors. Completionists can look through the Steam community forums for a guide to get all 6 endings, or watch the rest of the endings on YouTube (there's no fast forwarding feature for the video clips, so you'll have to watch through some scenes multiple times if you want to see all the endings in game).
Will take less than an hour to beat, but it's low price and on sale frequently. Despite its flaws, I recommend checking it out if you're a fan of the FMV genre and horror. If not, then I can't recommend it.

I wish I could give neither a thumbs up or down, but rather a wobbly hand. I enjoy seeing new FMV games, and am always willing to see what they have in store. These days, FMV can be done for relatively cheap, so there's a lot more out there. This one certainly isn't awful, or the worst that I've played, but overall, I was left wanting. Firstly, it wasn't scary at all. There were no jump scares or excessive gore (or any gore really), but that's usually not what I want in horror. The writing/directiong/acting were all satisfactory, but not powerful enough for the creepiness or story to get under my skin either. You get to make some choices about how the main character and her past lover inteacted in the past, and the consequences of those choices are some of the best parts of the game. However, as the whole plot goes towards a horror direction, those good bits get left behind. I did like the idea of including some old Public Domain movies to watch for some achievements, but I would've enjoyed that much more if the movies could've been enjoyed with VCR controls, and without the scanline and ambient sounds of the game. One of the movies didn't have any sound at all either, so that was a problem. Also, the whole game takes place in a VCR like aesthetic, even though the main character's movie collection is in DVD format, and the game takes place in present day. Oddly anachronistic just to be more 'RING' like without any in-game reason for it to be presented that way. I'll be interested in seeing what these people make in the future, and I didn't hate this game, but... sadly I just can't recommend it.
If, however, you're particularly found of visual novels, the japanese horror aesthetic, and can enjoy dramatic stories of somewhat questionable quality... then DO give this game a shot.
As far as FMV games go, this is just okay. The story is poorly written but I can appreciate what they were trying to go for. I'd say you get what you pay for.

I am so disappointed with Morph Girl, that I installed and played Her Story, just so I could compare them. They’re both indie games belonging to the nearly extinct FMV (full motion video) genre but Her Story is a masterpiece by comparison to Morph Girl. I really wanted to enjoy the game since I’m never one to refuse a story based on Japanese horror themes, no matter how unconventional it might be rendered. And since I never experienced enough FMVs over the years (apart from watching Command & Conquer  series’ funny cinematics), I thought that Jaydeb’s Steam debut, Morph Girl, would be a perfect (re)start. I was wrong.
J-Horror influences are subtle for the most part, yet the supernatural entity which seeks the attention of a young and grieving widow is nearly as convincing at its counterparts from The Ring or The Grudge franchises. Before crashing to desktop and never saving my progress, Morph Girl was starting to look interesting and offer some entirely distinct choices which the players must take and thus steer the female protagonist either towards curiosity and embracing that entity or rejecting it altogether. If this game would have at least autosaved after a certain time limit, I wouldn’t have wasted 30 minutes absolutely for nothing.
Filmed or at least manipulated in post-production to resemble a low-quality VHS (video home system) recording, Morph Girl has opted for visuals which showcase a Sepia filter with reddish hue and the occasional tracking desync effects. I get it, this is supposed to look like very old found footage. I didn’t have a problem with the concept, if only it would have run decently on my fairly potent configuration. The game wouldn’t even fit the interface on the screen when I played in my native resolution of 4K and no, unlike Her Story, there’s no way to simply toggle a lower resolution in Morph Girl.
I couldn't imagine for a second that the game would crash or that the save/load options would never show up during my brief play time. It's becoming such a rare occurrence in my Steam games, that it took me by surprise. Couldn’t even take screencaps through the Steam Overlay and since I rely on those visual mementos for my own review writing methods, I consider it a sin by itself if any title hinders or entirely prevents me from taking screenshots. For a game about visuals before anything else, Morph Girl failed at the most basic level by not taking into consideration that a PC is more complex than a “one-size-fits-all” console system configuration. I’ve played plenty of shovelware on Steam, which still scaled perfectly on 4K resolution without a single CTD in sight. I expected far more from Morph Girl, or else I wouldn't have agreed to review it in the first place.
If only our heroine, Elana Pierce would give voice to her thoughts. She’s quite the taciturn apart from the occasional sigh and even if I won’t call the actress’ performance as “wooden”, there still wasn’t nearly enough emotion poured into what’s basically an existential tragedy about coping with loss and the subsequent depression. At least the sound effects and the soundtrack were of adequate quality. But they alone can’t carry on their shoulders the entire narrative. The only aspect separating Morph Girl from an old-timey silent movie, is the absence of more piano songs played in haste. Too many text boxes where there should have been at least a handful of spoken lines.
I could go on for at least another page or two about what makes Her Story far better than Morph Girl, but as you probably guessed it, I shall both spare you the boredom and remind that I’m only reviewing the latter. Normally, it would be hard as it to discuss about the gameplay differences between two FMV titles, but Morph Girl still manages to stand out since its structure is inflexible and instead of cleverly cutting the film clips in “digestible”sizes, it went for a single reel almost. The reason I wouldn’t want to waste another half an hour to reach back at my last point in the game, is because it’s quite dreary and you’ll spend that time just watching Elana’s daily routine requiring as much interaction from the players as simply asking them to watch paint dry.
How does this title have six different endings, is beyond my understanding. I know for certain that I shall avoid replaying it in the foreseeable future. Perhaps eventually, it will run in decent conditions even on my PC. Jaydeb, the keyword here is “AUTOSAVE”. Learn it by heart and apply it in the game, if you can’t iron out the crashes to desktop issue. No one deserves to waste 30 minutes of their limited spare time on an experience which never gives staring down the window, a run for its money. I couldn't even receive a lousy screenshot to partially explain my short Morph Girl play time.
Edit: After the latest update, I managed to manually save the game progress, despite not seeing that cogwheel symbol while in Fullscreen mode. A step in the right direction nonetheless. Morph Girl still refuses to take any screenshots through the Steam Overlay.

I've been watching and playing this game for some time now; I recently came back for the release version, and wanted to share my thoughts.
For a game that has spent so long in early access, it is still very unpolished. I understand there are plenty of reasons for this, usually because of lack of time/budget/experience. But it does irk me, when during cutscenes you have models clipping through objects and furniture. It just seemed like the devs tossed them together, and didn't bother to play the them back. I was also disappointed with the number of bugs I found, with regards to NPC trust-o-meter as well as a few other annoyances. The bugs felt pretty hard to miss; and I didn't start playing until a couple of post-release patches have gone through. Overall, I am disappointed with the state of the game. And I was sad that the voice acting was... cut, mid way through?
That being said, I fully recommend this excellent survival game! It's a challenge, to be sure. I love the artwork, the mechanics, the level of exploration... the main storyline teeters between A and C writing. Sometimes its great! Other times, it's really lacking. But all in all I enjoyed it. Its really one of the best, most unique survival games out there.

Safe buy for everyone who likes Zachtronics games and the best game to start with for newcomers. Easier than previous games, because there are no space limitations, no programming knowledge required and all components are straightforward. Characters, story and world is more interesting and engaging, than what most of the AAA games have these days. The whole presentation is excellent.

Before Zachtronics brought their unique brand of programming-puzzlers to Steam with SpaceChem, there were a couple of free flash games. The first of them was
. The visuals and UI design weren't much compared to modern offerings and there was no story at all (good music though), but already there was that addictive problem-solving and optimizing gameplay that people would love in later games.
And it had a sense of Art. There is a great satisfaction in the beauty you can create getting the timings just right, and I still remember exchanging elaborate solution designs in forum threads, using a text format you could paste into the game (it wasn't convenient to use animated gifs or youTube at the time).
Now Opus Magnum is of course the developer revisiting Codex and bringing it to modern standards, with the production values and amount of content we've come to expect from their other games (as well as a decent amount of mechanics changes). For fans that will be enough already. For newcomers, I'll add that this is one the developer's more accessible titles, and is substantially more forgiving in that almost all of the levels leave you unconstrained in how much space and budget you want to use. This also means it's easier to create beautiful solutions, which you can then share using the built-in animated gif generator. If you're in doubt, be sure to take a look at some of the wonderful things people are doing in the community hub. IMO, the art angle more than other things distinguishes this from other Zachtronics games.
Similar in feel to Zach's prior game, SpaceChem, the unlimited area and variety of manipulators allow for wider variety and creativity in solutions.

A great game for those familiar with Zachtronics games. Open-ended puzzles that are more like engineering problems than puzzles.
Similar to SpaceChem but less frustrating since you don't have the same space constraints. You can expand indefinitely to get your first solution. The game will track your performance and you can compare yourself to your friends and the world. You can optimize for speed, area, and cost but not all at the same time. Players who want to push themselves will need to replay the puzzles with different mindsets to get to the scores.
Like all Zachtronics games it's incredibly fun, even when it's too hard for me to beat.

This is one of the best games I have ever played and something I think anyone who enjoys an extensive story will love this game.  This is a story intensive games to the point where there is just as much talking as there is fighting but the game is written so well that it never gets to the point where talking is too much.  The story and dialogue is all so engaging and interesting.  The story is Game of Thrones meets Lord of the Rings/Skyrim.  It is everything you could want in a game.
The dialogue choices you make in this game will affect everything that comes after and the biggest selling point of the game.  The ending is epic and the majority of choices you make will matters with the effects that show up in huge and little ways.  The story telling is better than ANY Talltale game.  Most quests that are given by NPC are memorable and the inclusions of side characters make the world feel real.  I played the game with the same party of 4 and I cannot wait to replay everything with a different party to see what they say.
Combat is strategic and intelligent.  You have the ability to pause and think about how you want battles to go.
The game does have its flaws:
1.  The dialogue is speeches can sometimes cut out (it happened 5 times during my 200 hour game play)
2.  You cannot really be an evil character who intimidates you allies into following you so you
3.  AWAKENING is an empty shell a game compared to origins in terms of story and what it could have been. DURING AWAKENING I ran into 2 game breaking glitches that caused me to go back to pervious saves.  At the bottom I elaborate on how to avoid this.
4.  The combat game play is either too easy OR too hard with no perfect balance.  I played on Nightmare mode (the highest difficulty) without too much of a problem.  This could be because of how OP mages are but boss battles always felt fair.  The game never feels really unfair though.
5.  I heard all the sequels are not done as well.
TIPS FOR NEW PLAYERS
1.	Turn up the graphics right away for the full experience.
2.	If you see a backpack BUY IT.
3.	If there are no special effects on equipment sell it.
4.	If you play the game for too long sometimes the game will crash.  You can tell when this occurs because enemy bodies will have a red box around them appear.  Every 7 hours of game play it is a good idea to exit out of the game completely and continue where you left off.
5.	Ice power for Mages are amazing so try them.

I think this is probably a minor fix but until it is fixed, the game feels pretty unplayable without regular save-scumming.

At its current full price I can't really recommend this game.
Pros:
Very clean visual, runs smooth, very reminiscent of old Sierra building games.
Con:
They've taken their artistic license for thermodynamics and ran so far with it they crossed the event horizon. (Your buildings are powered by 'condensed steam' i.e. water) Granted this is more of a personal peeve than a legitimate critique on the game.
While the art is clean and pretty, I got very little 'steampunk' vibe from it, at most the visual just looks vaguely Victorian with small sprinkle of fantasy elements. There's also very little character to each building or civilian walking the streets.
Lastly this game is pretty much exactly what you expect an old Sierra city building game to be like, which is good and bad. Bad because it has pretty much zero innovation compared to games like Zeus and Pharoah, I would even go as far as to say it's less complicated than Caesar 3. Consider all of Sierra's old city building games are now on Steam with lower price tag than this, you may be better off getting those.
Verdict:
Not worth it at its full price in my own opinion, unless you have a burning, aching desire in your heart for a Sierra-esque city building game (like me) with modern graphics, you may be better off waiting for it to go on sale.

Maize started very promising: A bit obscure, mysterious and engaging. Very nice visuals too. All the environments are full of little details and paint a picture on their own, there's this urge to explore.
Then the fetch quests start, which is okay. Then.. the game starts to get "funny".
The writing is what killed the game for me: The "jokes" are told endlessly on repeat (I really can't count how often I heard or read the words "stupid" or "idiot", well over a hundred times for sure) and they are never even modified in the slightest. This is regardless of which comedic hook you choose: Vladdy will *always* say how stupid you and/or American technology is, the sentient corns don't get how obvious human thing x works and then take a nap, the one guy always angrily comments on the actions of his other brother in the same tone via post-it notes.
It's clear that the writer took hints from other "weird" games like The Stanley Parable, but I would say he does not understand what really makes them good as a narrative experience.
Secondly, the game tries *really* hard to convince you it's self-aware and oh-so-quirky. It already starts in the store description "And that last sentence is pretty much the least ridiculous thing about the game" and continues to by showing lazy on-screen text after almost every action you do in-game. Example: "Used Marker to draw The Worst Face in the World. It appears you took drawing lessons from a Leather Couch." while drawing a crude face on a ball. "Re-started the Worst Nuclear Reactor in The World" after restarting a nuclear reactor.
First of all: I literally just did what you, the writer, need to remind me of. I *just* did it. Second: Haha, so random and funny, a leather couch. Look, I know humor is very much subjective, but this game would be MUCH better without these comments. The author tries to inject more "quirkiness" into the situation which frankly does the opposite. Just let visuals and actions speak for themselves.
Ultimately I can't recommend this game unless you can bear (heh) the amateurish writing which rams shallow gags down your throat on repeat, the numerous fetch quests and below-average sound design - It's a bummer because the visuals and environment is where this game truly shines.

I've loved wrestling games since Title Match Pro Wrestling for the Atari. So many good ones, especially in the late 90's, have come and gone. Unfortunately, the last few years have been pretty unimpressive overall, excepting the fancy graphics and presentations (commentary will never be great - but it can at least be ok at times).
So here's Fire Pro Wrestling World on Steam for $20.
I won't go over what others have said. Great controls, limitless customization, etc. You've heard that. I want to sum Fire Pro up slightly differently.
1. You won't be buying another version next year for $59.99 (not including DLC!)
2. They won't be shutting the online servers off when the new one comes out, or the year after if you're lucky.
3. You won't be having to figure out new and/or tweaked controls in 2018, because a AAA wrestling game doesn't have the money or creativity to have it figured out after 17 years.
4. "Why can't I do that?" Is uttered FAR less frequently in Fire Pro.
5. "Holy &#%! I can do that?" Is uttered FAR more frequently in Fire Pro.
6. Bull Nakano (translation - best edit/CAW community in the world)
7. LOGIC
8. The "YES OH YES!" moments of wrestling games are back.
This list will grow. I don't review games for this very reason. My opinion can change "later" for most games, and the list of reasons always grows, either for good or bad. But I've spent 14 hours with this version of Fire Pro and I can say with absolute certainty that any minor issues (and they exist - but are just that - minor) are nothing more than a blink. The fun I have had with this game is true, old-school fun at it's best.
The last thing I will say is this - take your time, learn the controls, do the missions. Fire Pro demands you learn patience, timing, and observation. Also, you will get no health bars, because you don't need nor deserve one. You get to focus on the action, and you will be SO thankful for this. Wrestling games are always more fun when you're not constantly having to watch what basically amounts to a giant cheat meter at the top of the screen.
I could go on and on. I want to. But it's pointless to just go over what many others have more than sufficiently discussed here already. They will tell you what makes Fire Pro such an amazing game in great detail. I'm just here to tell you that they are absolutely right.
$20.

I recommend Kholat for its story, and only its story.
Kholat's premise is based around the events of the Dyatlov Pass incident, in which 9 hikers died in the Ural mountains from an unknown cause. Throughout the course of the game the player will explore the treacherous mountain landscape, hoping to uncover the answer as to what truely caused the hiker's deaths.
Like most mystery based horror games as you start to uncover answers you'll also find more questions arise from your investigation which keeps you going until you reach a rather ambiguous ending. Unlike my previous attempts to play these sort of games, this one actually managed to hold my interest to the very end, and the ending itself made me want to go back through it and potentially uncover more information.
There's also some terrific performances by the voice actors in this game. Sean Bean's narration along with the voices from logbook/diary entries really flow well with the tonal shift of the story as the player progresses. And the ambient audio/music help keep the tension going as you get lost in the endless sea of trees and rocks.
In terms of actual gameplay, my favorite thing is that the map is an actual map. Player's have to read coordinates and use a compass in order to know where they are located in the world instead of having a little dot on a mini-map showing their exact location. This really helps to put the player in an explorer mindset and really keep track of their surroundings. Its just a shame the surrounding environment is what almost kills this game for me.
The environment, apart from a few key locations, is visually bland, poorly optimized, and riddled with so many bugs that I could never get truely immersed in the experience. The environment just feels too big and empty. Bugs included huge amounts of clipping, stretched textures, environment pieces popping in/out of existence, and sometimes the entire floor disappearing resulting in my character falling out of the environment to my death. Of all the things in this game that needed more attention, it would be the design of the evironment and the rest of the gameplay.
As I said earlier, the map function was an interesting design choice and one that I liked, my problem is the rest of the gameplay is just a walking/running simulator. As a player, nothing makes me feel more constrained and limited than being blocked by a 2 foot tall rock that I should be able to just jump/climb over but the game won't allow me to. I'm just asking to be able to interact with the environment and not feel like I'm trapped on a linear path surrounded by invisible walls.
My other problem is the monsters. While there are story clues as to what/who they are, they didn't really add to the tension and in fact felt more like an obligation because "its a horror game, which means we must have monsters to chase the player." They're more an annoyance really than actually scary.
But despite the gameplay and environment nearly destroying the experience, the story itself should keep players interested. My recommendation is to definitely play the game, but I suggest waiting for a sale.

This is THE pinnacle of Fire Pro Wrestling games, if you're on the fence about getting this, don't be, buy it immediately. The 2D sprites are more defined and sharper than ever. The classic Fire Pro Wrestling soundtrack has had an overhaul and I expect more classics to be added in the development stage too.
It's quite hard to grasp that this is only an early access title because of how mind-blowing it is. It has the largest customization options of any wrestling game to date. The classic timing based gameplay is here and it's easier than ever for new audiences to pick up and master thanks to the Mission Mode in the game which clearly explains the controls and how to perform the basics.
What's more is, the two newest features in this game happen to be the best parts. The Steam workshop allows anyone to upload any wrestler and download them instantly, so if you're like me and lazy, you can have pretty much any wrestler you want on the in-game roster without having to go and create them yourself. The other new addition is the online play which can be challenging and incredibly fun too, coming from someone who never plays online anything.
In conclusion, this is everything the Fire Pro Wrestling games were built up to be, it's still amazing, the whole community loves it and for good reason. It's been 10 years since the American release of Fire Pro Wrestling Returns and I'm so happy to see that people are still passionate enough for these games to be made. If you are in anyway remotely a wrestling video game fan, you should absolutely buy this game because you will not regret it.

Amazing wrestling game that has a dedicated fan community creating just about every wrestler you can imagine including just about any fictional character as well. If it doesn't exist, you can be sure someone is working on making it exist. The editor is incredibly robust and allows for an accurate simulation to the actual real life wrestlers.
As it's early access, the game is a bit rough around the edges in terms of some content, such as no story mode being available and some menus might feel stiff to navigate. There are currently few rings to select and while planned there currently is no way to add in custom BGM for your wrestler intros.
That being said, this is absolutely worth the asking price for just the sheer amount of possible wrestling matchups you can simulate, from historical wrestling matches to fictional what if matches like Spider Man vs The Undertaker.
I'm new to the FPW series but have played some WWE and other wrestling games in the past, and the wrestling feels fast paced and dependent on reaction time than button mashing for the most part. The game heavily relies on successful grapples and wearing down your opponent before you can pull off the finishers and bigger moves. This can be seen as formulaic, as most matches run the same course where you start with low moves, move up to medium and end with finishers and big moves, but the game still manages to be fun while going through this loop. The AI can also be pretty tough with the reaction times needed to succeed in a grapple, but you can also cheese the game with the same moves over and over. Though obviously you're meant to play it out as if it were a wrestling match.
I haven't tried much online mode except for a few cpu vs cpu sim modes. People actually do watch cpus fight it out online, which might seem a bit odd at first as to why such a mode exists where you just watch the AI fight with other people online, but the amount of pride people have for their creations and their logic makes it so it's actually interesting to see how the AI fares in a battle of edits. It ends up making sense why this is a mode. I hear the online functionality outside of this could use more work, as in the delay and lag makes matches unfun. As this is early access, I'll remain hopeful in this regard. If nothing else, the sim modes definitely worked well. There's a prematch lobby where you can chat with other users before the match. At least at a basic level, the online component is decent.
Overall, I'd definitely say this is worth your time if you're into wrestling games, especially since the game can only improve if they continue to update it with more features. The game honestly is worth it just for the sheer amount of edits available for pretty much any character you can imagine. I can't get over how this game has barely been out and has something like 5000 edits and will probably have more as time goes on.

Despite all the negatives this game is getting here is an honest review:
I have been playing this since before it came to steam, when it was on the now defunct desura. At first it was frustrating, the tutorial mission was more of an emotional grinder than most sad movies, to choose to stay and protect your wife despite the raiders, and zombies, and her criplled condition made it the toughest mission in any game I ever played.
However, after playing through the game modes, I figured out how to survive for extended periods which became tedious. But the developers had cards hidden in their sleeves for us, and things like modding, other survivors and multiplayer came about, which took it from just a zombie permadeath game to something like a personal cult classic.
Now I can tell you if you rush through the game just to try and "beat" it, my best advice is: you can't. "Well why?" you ask, Simple. You were never meant to survive for any period of time. There is no reward, no secret happy ending, no one to save you, just a day after day fight for survival against a heavily stacked deck. Power goes out permanently, gotta be an engineer to use a generator and wire up lights. Water goes out and unless you dig a well, you're S.O.L. because after some time, loot becomes scarce, and you are left fending off hunger and thirst.
Now that sounded depressing. It is supposed to be. It tells you in the beginning not as a joke but a caveat. you will die, its just you have the choice on how you exit the stage. Does this make a bad game? not really. It just makes a game that isn't not meant to be burned through in one sitting. You.will.die.alot. and the learning curve is steep, but not unclimbable.  you can figure out things, and have an epic base, but in the end, you probably will be forced to travel and well, good luck.
I can praise this game mindlessly, but it is worth playing, but not to be taken too seriously, because you will have controller/keyboard throwing moments, but thats what makes this game worth playing.
However, there are drawbacks. Graphics are meh, but not bone ugly. Ludicrous spawn rate of zombies, and loot distribution will make you scratch your head. Houses are the same, and resources are slim. But overall none of this should stop you from playing it at least once.
