I don't understand why this has better ratings than ACU, except that the mechanics are a tad bit better and it was less glitchy on launch.  Both games are dull, boring and uninspired.  I keep trying to like them.  I keep trying to finish them.  And in the end, I just can't because the substance that makes a game fun just isn't there.
Then again, I loved all the games through Black Flag, including ACIII, so maybe I just have different tastes.  I'm also not a city person, so being stuck in the same city, where every rooftop looks pretty much like every other rooftop, is just plain boring to me.  In ACI through Black Flag, I always felt like I was discovering new places and meeting new people until the end of the game.  A few hours into this game, and it feels like I've seen all there is to see, even when I go to new areas.  The missions are repetitive, the side quests lackluster, and the characters wooden.  Altair had his arrogance, Ezio had his charm, Connor had his anger, and Edward had his ambiguous morals, and all these characters had their traits and their transformations linked to their stories.  Evie (is that even her name?  I can't even remember) and Jacob (which I only remember because it's written in the game description) are so generic they're interchangeable and forgettable.  There's no backstory, no compelling reason for them to fight the fight they're fighting, and it makes for a dull tale.  I'm actually more than a few hours into the game, and I'm probably just going to give up on it because I don't care.  I'm not interested.  It's almost a chore - I should finish this game just in case there's something interesting that springs up - rather than a compulsion.
So in short, is this a bad game?  No.  Is it an interesting game?  Also, unfortunately, no.  And that's why I just can't recommend it.

I've been playing this game for a while and waited for launch and story mode to write a review. As of now, the sandbox mode is the best part of the game, much unchanged since the announcement of the story mode launch date - except for the addition of map making - and still with some issues (too many wolves, for one). Now, with the game complete I can safely NOT recommend the game, maybe buy it on sale or something.
The story mode was, to me, a major disappointment. I like sandbox games, but TLD's sandbox is a little bare bones in terms of context - you simply start somewere, there's no context, no broken plane or crashed car or waking up in your house, the only motivation is survival - and I hoped story mode would simply be a contextualized sandbox mode, with added quests pointing you in the right direction. Some people like the "just survive" thing of sandbox, I don't.
What story mode ended up being was a linear, Alone-in-the-dark-esque bizarre story, with silly characters and trust grinds, which, to be honest, are utterly incompatible with this game, that is also plagued by subpar production values - only a part of the dialogue is voiced, the rest is not, utterly destroying immersion. They should simply made all of it not voiced if they lacked the money.
In any case, I was waiting for story mode to fill in the issue the game had for game, but instead it created more issues. Since I frankly don't think these issues are fixable by patches or anything, I cannot recommend this game. Many people will say that the sandbox alone is worth it, but to them I say that only a WHOLE game is worth it, not just part of it. If a hot dog has the best meat you ever tasted, but the bread tastes like♥♥♥♥♥♥ well, would you still buy it? I know I wouldn't and TLD will be added to another of the reasons why I don't buy early access anymore.

In my mind, there are 3 reasons someone would not recommend this game…
1. The current state of the game. It is still an early access game. It is not a finished, polished product yet. It’s a work in progress that is constantly growing. Many of the reviews with less than 10 hours playtime not recommending this game are seeming to forget this. Giving something a ‘not recommended’ for it’s current state while it’s still being worked on is like saying you wouldn’t eat a meal that’s still being cooked. No one is saying it needs to stay the way it is, let it be finished before you judge it.
2. Difficulty. This game can be difficult and punish you for your mistakes, but that just means you need to learn from them. Too many reviews say it’s too difficult when they haven’t even played long enough to learn the strategies. My first couple, or 5 to 6, games were wipes. However, every time I got a little further and became better. I’d say I’m now at a point where I can make due with any starting situation. This game does have a rouge-like flavor to it, and I love it! Being realistic, you only get one chance in space.
3. Disliking the playstyle/gamestyle. If this is the case, then why’d you buy it? You knew, or at least could have look up, what this game is. No excuse, get a refund.

There's a history lesson about this game out there, but I won't go into it. Google to see how long it's been going. If you're new to this game, here's FPWW in brief: create real or fictional wrestlers, feds, belts, and more. Have the CPU sim matches for you (this can be amazing if the Logic is well-done), or control them yourselves. Seem too difficult, can't get the timing down? Drop the skill level until you get the hang of it. Too easy? Raise it to 9, have yourself an epic, thirty minute match.
I reccomend Tornado Tag with a friend, couch co-op style. Have a CRITICAL, or steal your opponent's move.
There's a whole series of Bear wrestlers, if you're into that. I mean the animal, but yeah, Wuvable Oaf fans will be pleased as well.
If you're expecting No Mercy-style gameplay, I'm not sure if this is akin to that. It's a different animal. If you're a fan of match pacing and storytelling, then this game is for you. Start small, work your way up. Think Omega vs. Okada, or Cena vs. AJ. The matches will surprise you, and near the end you'll be mashing buttons like you did back in the day, before quick-time moments happened.
I have spent an enormous amount of time just downloading wrestlers and assigning them to their respective feds. This is classic fire pro. The best 20$ i have ever spent.

Kholat is a rare type of game – one that challenges you and harkens back to another era in many ways. Kholat is a first person survival horror exploration game based on the real life Dyatlov Pass Incident. Unlike many other “survival horror” games, Kholat isn’t actually an action game or a crafting game with touches of horror.
Instead, Kholat takes you to a beautiful, yet haunting world that heavily relies on atmosphere to create tension. Set in the Northern Ural Mountains, you are there a while after the Dyatlov Pass Incident trying to figure out what happened. With you, you have no weapons, no cell phone, basically nothing other than a flashlight, a compass, and a map that you find. On the map there is a list of 9 coordinates – major locations for you to visit and find out information about what has happened.
Kholat is a difficult game to score because it is one that if it resonates with you, it will be in your game of the year lists I think. However, it is a pretty niche title with the difficulty, the genre, the map navigating and other factors, as well as a relatively short average run time (unless you get lost all over the place like me). If a game that focuses on atmosphere, beautiful graphics and horror generated not through cheap tricks and jump scares interests you, I recommend Kholat wholeheartedly.
Final Score: Very Good 7/10 "Kholat is a welcome challenging and atmospheric take on the horror genre"

So first of all, "About the game" section on the store page is very misleading. The game promises 4 to 6 hours of gameplay. I completed it in 3, collecting everything and exploring every location (yes, there's something i missed as seen via achievements, but this is due to the confusing nature of the map than anything else).
Next up, the art displayed is not anything you'd see during the game, not that there's anything wrong with it, but the art direction could've gone crazier, seeing how good the enviroments are.
Now for the gameplay, it's mostly one of those walking simulators you might remember, and people compare it to Slender a lot, which is pretty true. You sometimes get chased by spooky shadows that you can easily outrun and after an hour or so they become not much of a threat. Sometimes they managed to spawn right in my way and gutted me withot remorse.
The game itself is really pretty, there's a lot of cool areas, the atmosphere is cold and harsh, powered by Unreal engine it looks incredible most of the time. There are some hiccups though, with the flashlight being perfomance hindering and thing like DoF Blur popping into your face which brings FPS down somehow.
Now for the sad part. As all these games go, the first hour makes you curious and sets up a good premise, with eerie stuff that's going on and overall juxtaposition of alien horrors and harsh, grinded in reality enviroment.
But then as you collect the notes and articles that hype you up, you're only going to be let down. Maybe it was the path that i chose to explore the map, that put me through some of the best parts of the game first, but the story started to fall apart pretty fast. With things built up and never getting any closure it's not clear if even the devs made up their mind as to what's actually going on and what role the protagonist or the Sean Bean (Who's not narrating a lot, i might add. Certainly not enough to placate this fact as a selling point) play in this. The premise was cool and uncovering that, or even seeing the glimpse of the horrors described in the notes would've been way better.
The gameplay is nothing special, you go around collecting notes and sprinting around from scripted dangers, you can crouch but can't jump, and it really unveils the level design being way more linear that it seems at first
There are no survival mechanics that could've made this more of a game, and your main enemy will be your map.
Was it art? Not really.
Was it an exciting videogame? Not really.
Is it a great story? Not really.
Is 3 hours of gameplay a good amount of content for 20 bucks? Not really.
Was it the most terrifying journey of my life? Definitely not.
If you're itching for some chilling Soviet horror, coupled with the possibility of actually freezing to death, get Cryostasis, a way better game in almost every way.

If you don't mind exploring without too much guidance and the limited interactions with the world (all you can do is walk or run - for a limited amount of time - and collect notes to unfold the story), you'll most certainly enjoy the game's atmosphere and graphics.
It's more in the line of Dear Esther than Ethan Carter, but contrary to what The Chinese Room did, you are free to explore the open environment. To do so, you only have a map, a compass, and a bunch of coordinates. The realistic approach to exploration means you don't get to see where you are on the map as in most games.
The Slender-type mechanic is more or less scripted it seems, so you won't be bothered that much except when reaching a newly discovered area, and the threats can be avoided by simply running away, which worked for us most of the time. There are a few instances when you'll die when taken by surprise, but not that much in the 5 to 6 hours you'll need to complete the game.
It's not a game for everyone, but it's a game that deserves your attention in our opinion.

Here is my review in 30Seconds:
Based on the Dyatlov incident, where 9 hikers were found inexplicably dead in the Russian mountains, this exploration game throws you into one of the most realistic immerse games we'’ve tried yet.
The game just hurls you in. You find yourself all alone to apparently roam aimlessly. But you just have to use common sense, like you would in real life, and follow the road. Then, it gets weirder and weirder as the paranormal horror theme builds up.
There are mysterous creatures that creep on you if you aren'’t careful. After all, this is survival of the fittest. Your ultimate goal is to find what happened in that snowy night. You find scattered notes that slowly let you know more and more of the story. You have a map, a compass and your own orientation skills. Just like real life, there’s no red dot in the map that tells you “you’re here”.
The graphics are beautiful - you wonder how they managed to pull it off so well. But the sound is even better. It makes you feel like you’re there all alone… or maybe not that alone.
You are accompanied by the voice of Sean Bean, who narrates key plot points and a good voice actor makes this an even more thralling experience.
7 chills out of 10

I lost count of how many times I've played through this game. I love it, and for so many reasons: plot, gameplay, and replayability, to name a few.
First off, the plot it actually very deep. If you're not looking for details you could easily miss it, but when you pay attention you find out all sorts of things. Arkane added a lot of depth to the story to make it more engaging, and even hid a few Easter eggs for players to find (for instance, you can find High Overseer Campbell as a weeper in the Flooded District if you elect to brand him instead of kill him earlier in the game). It's the small things that count: notes and journals that give you a glimpse into life in plague-ridden Dunwall; overhearing conversations between characters, even minor ones; hearing the experienced assassin Daud's lament over killing the Empress. Playing this game and taking the time to scour the maps for clues that reveal plot is one of the more fun and engaging things to do, even if you've finished your first playthrough.
Second, gameplay. Ohhhh my, the gameplay. Even without magical powers, the gameplay is fun and there's always someone to stalk and assassinate (or choke out and hide, if that's your style). Drop assassinations never get old, and neither does taking out a Tallboy or taunting guards through an electric field that you rewired (the poor sods). But adding Blink to the party, not to mention the rest of the supernatural abilities, was the cherry on top. Allowing you the ability to do so many things, from moving silently across an open space without notice to appearing in front of an enemy and killing them before they could so much as blink (heh heh), the Blink ability increased the gameplay experience by an order of magnitude.
Some gameplay factors also increased the replay value of the game, namely those factors allowing you to choose between options. You get to experiment with so many different ways to take out a target, and if you want to spare his life, there's a way to do that too. Maybe you liked sneaking around on the ground but would like to jump on rooftops more. Do more side quests that you overlooked on other playthroughs. I even knew a guy who did a playthrough that he called "Extreme Non-Lethal," where he went undetected and only choked out the targets he absolutely had to, focusing on finding ways to slip past without being noticed. Even though the game is linear, you are still allowed enough options to permit multiple creative plays of the game, as I have done.
It is worth mentioning the game that Dishonored took its notes from, which is Thief: The Dark Project. I am happy to say that Arkane was kind enough to put in an Easter egg in the game in acknowledgement of their inspiration. This can be found in Daud's base, when you stumble across two assassins training for stealth; the dialogue from that scene is taken from Thief: The Dark Project almost verbatim.
TL;DR - I found Dishonored to be a very enjoyable game, and I recommend it to anyone who has a love for games featuring stealth or stabbing (don't tell my psychiatrist). It has good graphics, great gameplay, commendable replayability (especially for a single-player game), and an in-depth plot to boot.
Just get it. Its good. Bethesda, Arkane, they are good, just get it.

This game is a work of genius. It has won awards. Tons.
I bought the Monster Race Edition for $100. It later went down to $80. To say I didn't regret waiting until it went on sale would be a lie. But I certainly didn't lose any sleep over it.
As soon as I saw this game, I knew it was going to be awesome. I was right.
Gameplay:
The gameplay for this game is inspired. Players can play either as the hunters or the monster. There are four hunters, each with their own respective roles (Medic, Support, Trapper, Assault). Their job is to find and kill the monster before it evolves.
As the hunter you spend the game tracking the creature, all while dealing with ravenous plants and vicious wildlife. You know the monster could anywhere, and every second you waste grants it more time. Megamouths lurk in the shadows, indistinguishable from gigantic boulders, and aquatic tyrants swim the rivers and lakes, ready to lunge at you and swallow you whole if you draw too near to the banks.
You lay traps, mines, all kinds of devices. When the hunters encounter the monster, the Trapper can deploy a temporary forcefield that imprisons the monster with the hunters, giving them the chance to kill it.
If the monster has reached stage three, it might already be too late. All the monster has to do at this stage is to destroy the generator in the centre of the map, and it's game over for the hunters.
As the monster, your only goal is to feed, Always you must be on the move, and every second spent in one place gives the hunters time to close in and deploy the mobile arena. You must never double back, lest you encounter the hunters coming after you. You must take care not to frighten alien birds, which fly into the air and pinpoint your location for the hunters to see.
You must kill and devour all the wildlife you can get your claws on. The more you consume, the closer you come to evolving. You can evolve twice, and each time you increase in size and power. Stage three is your final form. It is at this stage that the hunters become the hunted.
Of course, this is not Evolve's only mode of gameplay. An in-depth explanation the other modes would require a review that would take far too long to read through. Among these other modes include a mode where the monster must assault a base controlled by the hunters, aided by countless smaller minions, a mode where the hunters must evacuate citizens while the monster is simultaneously trying to eat said citizens, and a multiplayer campaign mode where map effects change depending on what happened in previous rounds. For instance, the hunters win a round, and the colonists put up perimeter fences. The monster wins, and the instead of fences the hunters are faced with flooded areas infested with man-eating eels.
Progression:
Players progress through Evolve by leveling up the abilites on the various different characters and monsters by gaining experience. It used to be that you would have to partially master one character before you could move onto the next, something that was criticized in Evolve's offical reviews. This is no longer the case.
As you level up, you also unlock various perks that can be used to give your character an edge. For instance, 100% extra jetpack boost, 100% extra smell range. You can only pick one per match, so choose wisely.
DLC:
A lot of people give Evolve bad reviews because it launched with so much downloadable content. Most of this is just for cosmetic additions. As for the DLC characters, Turtle Rock just lowered all their prices by around 30%. The company also presents routine community challanges that give players the chance to earn free skins.
None of this DLC is required.
All in all, I think it is safe to say that this game is less of a cash scam than most MMOGS or free-to-play games. Pay-to-win it is not.
Community:
The community for this game has been in a steady decline. It makes matchmaking difficult. The highest number of players playing together during February 2015 was 20,403. In July, it was was 808. Now in September, the numbers have risen to 9,084, near a third of the game's original player base.
What happened to Evolve is a tragedy. It does not deserve its current Steam rating. However, I have high hopes for the future of the game. I think Turtle Rock is willing to do what it takes to make their game a success.
The Verdict:
I can't recommend Evolve enough. It is one of the most original games I have seen in a long while. Although 50% a shooter, the game is free of the often sickening realism of many games of this genre. If you're into giant monsters, cool gadgets, exotic alien locales, and wierd wildlife, then this is the game for you.
In fact, if you are very sure, I would recommend buying the Monster Race Edition. Although it costs twice as much money, it gives you 8 free DLC hunters, 1 DLC monster (not all of these have been released), and some cool skins, all at a massive discount. Although Behemoth doesn't come with this package, he only costs around $10 now.
The choice is up to you. I beg you, please take the reviews of the haters with a grain of salt. Take all reviews with a grain of salt, even this one. But if think you might enjoy this game, I can guarantee you one thing: You won't be dissapointed.

Dragon Age: Origins is one of my all-time favorite Bioware games. Their creative team came up with an amazing fantasy world concept and you feel like you're taking part in an epic quest to save the world. For most of the main game you have carte blanche to pursue quests in the order that you'd like, lots of dungeon crawling interspersed with interactive dialogue sequences defining your character’s personality and honor or lack thereof. Along the way your selection of companions expands, each with their own, usually great personality and sense of humor. Don't like somebody, just tell them to leave.
This is not open world in the way of something like Skyrim, but Bioware still did an exceptional job creating a wide assortment of locations that feel vast, well detailed, and fun to explore. The graphics do show their age to a degree, but even today it's hard not to be impressed by the incredible level of craftsmanship and originality compared to many other similar RPGs. The voice acting is also top notch.
The only downside, at least in my opinion, is that for as much as this was a phenomenal launch of a new game series, the subsequent Dragon Age titles have each been progressively more disappointing. Largely EA’s fault, but that’s old news now and there’s little reason to vent. What’s done is done.
In any case, Dragon Age: Origins is a game worth owning and my recommendation would be to get the Ultimate Edition. On sale The Ultimate Edition is a great buy. I personally prefer the smaller quest DLCs more than the full expansion, Awakening, which felt very padded, but it’s still worth playing through. I’d also advise adding some mods to customize and perhaps remaster the experience. I found mine on Nexus.

As a fan of the old Pharaoh-style games, I have been lusting to buy Lethis for a while now. I did now, while it was on sale, and I am both dissapointed and pleasantly surprised.
It definitely has the feel down. The games looks and sounds wonderful and I have become very fond of it's aesthetics rather fast.
The mechanics are solid, albeit a big shallow. There's not too much to explore and to tweak - once you get the hang of it, it's rather easy. It continues to be entertaining, however, as I personally find the campaign to be much fun.
If you'd ever wanted to loose yourself in a fast-to-pick-up version of Pharaoh for 1-2 hours, this is it!
A few mechnics are a bit frustrating, but mostly so because it can be hard to keep an overview. The "views" that show you how your buildings are reaching your citizens, for example, are very well implemented, but I only found 1 or 2 to be really useful. Some views are just missing, for my personal taste.
Some of the interaction between Player and Game had me also grinding my teeth, but those are probably easy to ignore if you just accept them.
All in all I am having a ton of fun with this game, but I keep wishing it had those few features that would make it work just a bit better. It does a good job of emulation the feel of the old walker city sim games, but lacks the fine details and finesse.
Oh, and also, it comes with a ton of technical problems for some people. Me included, although my problem is tiny and rather insignificant. I would suggest getting this game on sale and going through the forum first to get an overview of potenial(!) problem you might encounter - and why.

A fun little walker-based city builder reminicent of the old Ceasar/Pharoh/Zeus series by Impressions, but not as complex. You'll set up production chains and working neighborhoods based on available local resources and mission requirements over a pretty long campaign. There's a few sandbox maps to build mega cities in if you finish that.
It's strictly an economic/citizen management thing, there are no AI opponents or military working against you, other than scripted events in the campaign.  Despite that, it's well balanced and engaging to manage your workers, farms and industry alone (if you're into that sort of thing).
I found the art style and music pleasant with a cool vibe and a good sense of having it's own personality instead of being a complete knock-off of Ceasar. Although, I found the "trade balloons" a little dopey in a setting that called for steamships or steam locomotives. How much stone could a balloon carry really? I mean, the Montgolfier brothers were cool and all, but come on.
It lacks some of layers from the gameplay of its forebears, and once you figure out your favorite block layout you'll pretty much rubber stamp that over and over map after map. Don't expand too fast and plan ahead a little and the game isn't too challenging. But it's relaxing to play and does force you to pay attention from time to time. If you already like these sorts of games at all, this one is an easy recommend.

I'm deeply conflicted about giving this game the thumbs down.  It does some things very well
Things it sets out to do, and does wonderfully:
* Recreate the experience of playing Pharoah back in the day
* Establish a fun and charming new setting for the classical city-builder series of yore.  I would have liked to see more of the Punk aspect of Steampunk, but still.
* Drops the always unsatisfying military aspects of those old games entirely, along with the cartoonish myth parts of the later games that I hated (other people liked them so YMMV on whther that is a good thing)
One main problem is how well it succeeds at the first.  It doesn't just recreate the fun parts, it recreates the annoying parts.  It also takes away some of the innovations introduced later in the series (like the selective road blocks) which to me is bizarre.  It reminds me of all those un-fun times when my carefully crafted city collapsed in a cascade of devolving housing because a walker took the worng turn.  Yes you can prevent it through better planning, but IMHO building a city is more fun than carefully herding lemmings.  That's one of the reasons the series became such a narrow and unprofitable niche in the first place.
But the real, thumbs-down-earning problem is performance.  They've essentially recreated a late 90s/early 2000s game.  The graphics are a bit better than back then I suppose, but it seems to me that it shouldn't be heard for a modern computer to run this.  Yet loading times are long and stability is terrible.  And I'm not using one of the video cards they flat out said they won't support.  Since they aren't working on this one anymore, this is as good as it's going to get.
If you really, really loved Pharoah and have a high level of patience for crashes, go ahead and scoop this one up on sale.  Otherwise I have to say give it a miss.  Which is a shame, since it had tons of potential.

This is a Zachtronics game, so you should know what you're getting into.  There are puzzles to work through.  There's a storyline loosely wrapped around the puzzles.  There's a cool solitaire game.
However, the difficulty curve doesn't spike the way most Zachtronics games do.  Unlike the others, the main storyline is not space-constrained.  This means that any solution works, not just one that fits into the constrained space given.  (A recent update adds some space-constrained puzzles, but they're an optional end chapter.)
Add in an easy-to-use way to add your own puzzles, and you've got hours of enjoyment.  Highly recommended.

Of all the Zachtronics puzzle games -- all of which I highly recommend -- this one is most similar to SpaceChem, though it's more newbie-friendly. If you've played SpaceChem and liked it but thought it was too hard, this might be up your alley. If you've played TIS-100 or Shenzhen I/O, this game still has a lot in common with them even though you're not typing a program in assembly language.
One thing this game has that other Zachtronics games don't is an infinite canvas. There seems to be no (or nearly no) limit to the size of the board or the number of instructions you can give the machine components. If you've ever gotten frustrated at the space limitations in other Zachtronics games, you'll find this a godsend.
Don't worry about it being Early Access. This game is already more polished than many "finished" games. So what are you waiting for? Go play it!

Been playing this game on and off since early access, I totally fell in love with it. As you dig deeper into the mechanics and harder difficulties of the game, you'll find survival a simple objective, but many obstacles that stand in your way that will challenge you to push your character to her or his limit.  Multiple modes including story mode, challenges, and sandbox; intuitive but not necessarily easy crafting; simple and easily understood UI, including your health; and simple controls all come together to create, in my opinion, one of the best survival games ever made.
I was purposefully vague to try and not give anything away.  Go experience this wonderful game... and good luck, you'll need it.

I played the game for about 11 hours before finally deciding it wasn't for me. BUT. I am one hundred percent confident that it is just the right game for someone else.
Here's my beefs:
*edit*
(TLDR for people with no reading comprehension. I didn't rate the game down because it was "too hard". I rated it down because I did not care for it. These are not actually the same thing.)
*/edit*
First: I didn't care for the story mode. I found it was much easier to learn the game by just jumping into sandbox. It might be interesting to go back to, but as an introduction to the game, it wasn't working for me.
Once I got into the sandbox, I was more intrigued. It is definitely interesting... atmosphere is excellent, and I really enjoy some of the basic systems, such as how fires are handled, hitting rabbits with rocks, fishing, sleep, time management, etc. And I love exploring the abandoned places. There are definitely plenty of things here to like.
The thing that ultimately killed it for me is the crafting and maintenance of the basic tools/weapons you need to survive.
When it comes to things like crafting, in your typical survival/crafting game, you normally can craft your tools from natural resources, and all the things needed to produce the tool/weapon are also natural resources... and I emphasize NATURAL resources... but not quite so in The Long Dark... -_-
In this game, it is first of all literally impossible to make your own tools/weapons when you are starting out. You can't make your own tools and weapons because you will need SCRAP METAL, but you can't get scrap metal unless you just happen to find some (randomly placed and semi-rare, so you may or may not). But most scrap metal is acquired by breaking down small man-made metal items you find, which you can't do unless you first find those man-made metal items and also happen to have a hacksaw with you. How do you get a hacksaw? You guessed it... you must find where one has been randomly placed, and they are rare.
But suppose that you get lucky and you find a hacksaw right away? And then you find some man-made metal things and break them down for some scrap metal? Surely NOW you can make yourself a makeshift blade, right?
Hahaha, don't be silly. No, no, no, you can't make a makeshift blade unless you find a hammer with which to pound the scrap metal into shape! Where is the hammer? Oh, it's ALSO hidden somewhere random that you must find like everything else.
Okay. Suppose I stumple upon a hacksaw, then stumble upon some small man-made metal object that I can cut down into scrap metal, and then I stumble onto a hammer. I got all three things. So NOW I can make myself a tool.... right?
Hahaha, don't be silly, because now you must find the FORGE. Where is it? HIDDEN! Go find it!
Okay, fine, suppose that I somehow find the hacksaw, find the metal objects, make the scrap metal, find the hammer, then find the forge, all before I starve or freeze or die some other way. Surely now I can make one friggin' knife. Just a knife. ONE KNIFE.
Hahaha, no, because you can't make the flame in the forge hot enough unless you have coal with you. It takes a lot of coal, though, and coal is... well... it's randomly hidden out there somewhere. Just a bit here and a bit there. It would take you a while to collect enough. Unless you found the coal mine, wherever that is...?
SIGH.
Can I just have a starter knife to hold me over until I figure all of this crap out?
Oh ho ho! Sure you can! There are free knives out there somewhere. All hidden. So just try to find them. They'll only work for a little while, though, and then they break, so make sure you figure out all that other stuff. ;-)
Do you kinda sorta see what I mean? It just doesn't feel like living off the environment to me at the end of the day. It feels more like "find all of the absolutely vital tools we have randomly hidden somewhere before time runs out".
In other words, compared to a survival game like Don't Starve where you can basically make the tools you need once you locate the resources, in The Long Dark you often instead must simply FIND the tool (there is no other option), which is more like searching for a treasure before you die than it is like using the elements to survive. It gives the survival a different formula that is interesting but not really to my taste.
There are all kinds of good ideas in it, of course. I played it for 11 straight hours just because it had me so intrigued. But at the end of the day, its survival formula finally just got to the point where I decided that it's bouncing off of me more than it's sticking.
But I reiterate that I think the right kind of player, who may not share my peeves, will think it's just great. (Unfortunately Steam only has a binary rating system. I can't help that.)
My verdict:
7) A classic, essential, and/or must-buy game that is absolutely worth full price.
6) A solid good game that is worth the full price.
5) A pretty good game that may or may not be quite worth full price.
3) A bit rough, but with some interesting or redeeming qualities. Purchase with care!
2) Quite rough. You may find something to like, but brace yourself. Purchase with care!
1) Broken, unplayable, or otherwise impossible to recommend.

Project Zomboid,
is a zombie survival simulation that tries to stay realistic and challenging.
The game is 2.5D and can be played up close to the character or be zoomed out to the birds eye view of the area around you. There are many sytems that this is built around, these sytems come together to keep you busy and/or on the run. You start off with nothing, or some items depending on the preset or settings you have chosen, and you must search the cupboards, fridge and drawers of your home for items, tools and food. You may want to leave your home then, and go and search through other houses and stores. Then, you gotta set up a base which you can live in, store your supplies in, and where you know you'll be safe. You build a custom house or just barricade a house or store in the country or on the street. Just make sure you cover all the entrances. You don't want a zombie sneaking up. The thing is, the game is thrid person but you can aonly see what your character is facing. Everything else then becoms a fog of war. So check your back every now and again. After a few days have passed the electricity and/or water may cut out. So you will need to find other means to cook food and gather water. Unless you have a generator near by that will come in handy. Your story will go on and on, but eventually, you WILL DIE... They always do...
Like the game even states after every start and load up, "this is how you died..." And yeah, the game is permadeath and you cannot save and load back. It saves everytime you exit the game. Which is a good thing, you can't cheat. And the game is hard, too.
I've come to love this game, if I'm honest, but it is by no means perfect.
There are still a lot of bugs, and many features are yet to be added to the game still, like NPC's and Vehicles (Vehicles are out now in a test branch of the game which you can access now if you own the game) and other things too. The game has been in early access for years, but it is certainly improving. The Devs are active, so don't worry. Maybe a few years ago this game wasn't worth purchasing. But let me tell you, it's worth every buck now. So go ahead and get it, you wont regret it...

Five Word Review: A fun game about corn.

Least Favorite Thing: I found the store's screenshots deceptive. No matter your settings it's not going to look as good.
Date Completed: 2017-05-06
Playtime: ~ 3h

-Very enjoyable and pretty funny. The humor was reminicent of somthing akin to a lego game and can be a little too much at times, but I caught myself grinning most of the game. The storytelling reminded me of older games, with how the cutscenes played out, which I liked. Made me feel like I was a kid again playing an N64 game.
-The characters were well done. The voice acting was top notch and made each character believable. Actually suprised me to be honest, and I'm sure I have heard some of those voices before too. The recordings of each voice was done well too. Clear and no background noises or voice actors inhaling between each line of dialog. If there were any critiques, I would have to say to cut down on the insults. I do understand that it's part of the humor, but the charm, if there was any, dropped rather quickly after so many sticky notes. Vlady was rather decent in this respect. Wasn't too much, but I would opt for other descriptors. The lines: "stupid" and "idiot" wore out their welcome after a bit, but still held a bit of charm because I liked Vlady as a character.
-Gameplay was pretty solid, with a few small glitches, most notebly in the room with the giant statue next to the small one and Vlady somehow fell through the grates and was walking on the cave below (luckily he teleports to you when you are a certain distance away so it fixed itself), but nothing game breaking, Gamepad controls done pretty well. Though I would opt for Y being my portfolio and X to be the item description. I would also let the player navigate the options menus via the game pade to let them have full gamepad support vice partial.
-One of the biggest pluses was the sound track. There weren't many songs, the ones there were flat out amazing, with the recordings done professionally. At least that's what it sounded like to me.
-Graphics were crisp and colorful with a lot of it looking pretty realistic. My eyes were pleased.
I recommend to try this one if you have the money. It was a fun experience, and I am really glad I gave it a chance.

Pros:
- It has a fun-loving comedy feel to it, considering the stupidity of the corn and the angry Russian teddy bear combination.
- Although this could be a con, I liked that the "puzzles" were sort of easy, and it focused more on the story and comedy, rather than "how hard can we make this for them?"
- The game ran pretty well, and I'm assuming it would be well optimized to run on almost any system.
- I'm trying to think of a good adjective to describe the story... The only thing I can come up with is "warm". It gave me a comfortable, cozy feeling when I was playing this game. I rarely finish story games (especially in the manner to write a review on it), but I felt this needed some positive light to it.
Cons:
- The game was fairly short (but even though it's a con, I found that the short time was filled with quality).
- Someone might not find the type of comedy to be as funny as the rest (different senses of humor).
- The puzzles were in no way difficult. There was only one time close to the end of the game where I needed to look up where I was stuck. But when I found it, I realized it was just me overlooking a few things.
- The game was quite linear, but they DID throw in some comedy elements into the fact that it was linear.
I realize that my cons have sort of a "biased" feeling to them with my "contrary" pieces, but I felt that it needed to be backhanded with some positivity from my own person likes and dislikes that I find in video games. Hope this helps you choose, and I look forward to writing more reviews on games in the future when I find them appealing/displeasing.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
There's a lot to love about this game for long-time fans and newcomers to the series. However, I cannot wholeheartedly recommend this game to a wide audience of wrestling game fans, as other games offer a better overall experience.
Most of the enjoyment one will get out of this game will be from watching CPU-controlled matches amongst your meticulously crafted custom characters. I can get behind this concept of watching -- rather than playing -- the game so long as the viewing experience is enjoyable. However, the viewing experience is hit-or-miss for me. I enjoy the art style, move animations, and crazy match types, but realistic character behavior is an absolute must if I am going to be primarily watching the game play itself. Sadly, the realism factor is lacking in fundamental ways.
First, the in-ring action feels too much like an arcade game mish-mash of Greco Roman wrestling and professional wrestling. Most moves start with two characters dancing around in a circle for 1-2 seconds before performing a cartoony-looking collar-and-elbow tie-up (grapple). From this point, various suplexes, powerbombs, and signature moves can be performed. Beyond the repetitiveness of watching this goofy sequence frequently play out, this mechanic is unnatural for any sort of -- what should realistically  be -- a striking-type move (superkicks, enziguris, jabbing combinations, etc.).
As an aside, front-facing grappling moves are about 90% of the gameplay, mixed with a small pinch of Irish Whip moves and a smaller dash of everything else. The  CPU will rarely go for moves not initated by any sort of grapple, such as: running moves, apron moves, turnbuckle moves, or aerial moves. This severely hurts the enjoyment of watching these matches play out.
The striking system (kicks, punches, and weapon swings) is atrocious all around due to tiny hitboxes that require pixel-perfect spacing and alignment of the characters prior to initiating a strike. It's infuriating -- and frankly inexcusable -- to see strikes completely miss because the characters are too close or not aligned in a perfect horizontal plane. Generally speaking, rhe characters are constantly moving if they are upright so pixel-perfect spacing and alignment is difficult and makes striking an utterly useless game mechanic. Standing strikes may land once in evey twelve attempts. Strikes are quite common in real professional wrestling matches, so the broken striking mechanic detracts from the viewing experience.
The CPU will rarely initiate a straight pinfall attempt. There are often points in a match when a pinfall attempt would be realistic/logical (after finishers, big moves, weapon strikes, etc.), but the CPU will consistently stand next to a downed opponent until the opponent eventually stands back up. If it wasn't for other win conditions such as knock-outs, submissions, and rollup manuevers (e.g., small package), matches may go on indefinitely. A significant amount of the enjoyment, drama, pacing, and storytelling of real professional wrestling matches stems from pinfall attempts.
Almost all of my viewing enjoyment has been from listening to an entertaining streamer/YouTuber commentate during matches rather than watching the arcade-like action unfold on-screen. The viewing experience should be able to shine on its own, which it could if the A.I. behaved realistically.
With all of that stated, I prefer PLAYING matches in wrestling games rather than watching one play out. There is some enjoyment to be had in playing this game, for sure, but having player-controlled matches feels like a secondary priority to the overall experience this game offers.

I immediately got the sense that this was going to be a somewhat unforgiving game when I noticed that I could venture in almost any direction without any major guidance or hand-holding. Mix in stunning graphics from the Unreal 4 Engine, exquisite narration from the infamous Sean Bean, some eerily haunting tracks and truly realistic environmental sound effects and I knew I ended up buying a major winner.
I really liked the fact that this game is based on a true story from the 1950's, the 'Dyatlov Pass incident', where some truly horrific events occurred that were never really solved. However, I am slightly disappointed that it was only a 4-6 hours long gaming experience.
This game gave me the sensation of being alone in a vast harsh environment with the only exception being that evil was lurking all around. The only items available to me were a flashlight, a map, a compass & a few notes found in key areas of the map which, in my opinion, really didn't help me much in my venture to solve the mystery behind these unexplainable events. It took me a while to figure out how to use the compass & map but I managed to get the hang of it pretty quick.
Overall, I really enjoyed playing this game because it gave me a true sense of fear and that I was almost always... completely alone. I think it's well worth the price for everyone to enjoy playing and a very memorable experience.

Kholat is a horror game developed by IMGN.PRO. The game is based on the true-event known as the Dyatlov Pass Incident. In Kholat players take on the role of some person walking through the mountains and collecting notes and avoiding some teleporting/slow-moving entity (very similar to Slender) all while being narrated by the ever-famous, man who always dies, Sean Bean. The notes you are collecting are supposed to reveal the story and events around the Dyatlov Pass Incident but there really doesn’t seem to be much of a story present in Kholat and it feels more like the developers didn’t exactly know what they were doing and decided to just adopt the tired, and stale Slender formula we’ve been seeing in indie-horror titles as of late, which is a huge bummer coming from Kholat.
Basing a game around the events of the Dyatlov Pass Incident should be a solid premise, and make an amazing horror game but that doesn’t exactly happen when you dip into Kholat. Instead you get a pretty boring, and frustrating game that feels like a chore to progress through, and doesn’t offer much in terms of excitement or enjoyment. You’re thrown into an ‘open-world’ environment that looks gorgeous, I won’t deny that. Kholat is one damn good looking game, thanks to Unreal Engine 4 and the amazing environmental work that was done on the game. The mountains look foreboding, and unnerving especially when I came across two giant skulls carved into the face of a cliff. Sadly, that’s about all that Kholat really offers in term of a horror experience. Through-out my time spent with the game I really only found myself feeling creeped out by certain parts of the environment. The enemies weren’t exactly terrifying, and were more so frustrating, or downright annoying to deal with. They work pretty similar to how Slenderman works. A slow-moving, possible teleporting (it seems like they can teleport in front of you which is downright annoying) entity that stalks you the entire time while you collect notes. Seem familiar? That’s the core concept of Kholat in a nut-shell. Explore a creepy environment, collect notes, and avoid the entity that is stalking you. Even the entity seems to be confused during the game as well. I often found myself watching the entity stop chasing me and just stand still, or change direction and start walking away from me. Where’s the fear in that? And you’re most likely to be killed by the environment, which offers no sort of warning when you could die. It’s more like a random, gotcha sort of incident which is horrible. Kholat doesn’t exactly bring anything fresh, or new to the table in terms of an experience, which again is a bummer considering how good Kholat could of been.
The game also allows you to fast-travel at campsites that you discover which is a glorious feature that I’m glad was implemented due to how agonizing, and boring it is to traverse the environment after a while. This mainly stems from doing a ton of backtracking, and walking in circles. Then again, this could be intentional due to the disorienting environment and this could possible be what the victims of the real-life incident felt before their untimely demise. Sadly, it doesn’t work and just makes the game boring and again, feel like more of a chore to play. That and the entire movement system in the game is pretty godawful. You can sprint for what is maybe a few seconds before tiring out and moving at an extremely sluggish pace and it takes a fair bit of time to be able to sprint again. It makes the moments where you need to run-away from the entities, and the “orange fog” that tends to chase you to be frustrating. It feels like this was intended to make players feel tense and scared but all I felt was severe annoyance, which isn’t a good thing. You want players to have fun, and feel terrified. Not annoyed, and angry at poorly designed mechanics.
I’ve only put around 3 hours into Kholat and I can tell I’m nearing the end-game area. The story seems to be expanding, but is still extremely convoluted with no real direction. What am I doing in the mountain? Why did I decide to come here? Who the hell are these entities walking around? The game offers really no explanation for anything, and even Sean Bean seems like he didn’t want to be there, and maybe even he too was confused by the entire ordeal.
In the end, would I recommend Kholat? That depends. At $21.99 (currently on sale for $19.79) I wouldn’t. Maybe if the game were to drop to around $10 I’d be happy telling people to pick it up, but I don’t feel comfortable recommending a bare and a non-enjoyable experience like this for that kind of a price-point. Kholat had a solid premise, and some unique concepts but it sort of failed to deliver. It has amazing visuals, and the setting is great but it really just falls flat on delivery.
Pros
Awesome setting, and based off of a spooky real-life event with the Dyatlov Pass Incident.
Gorgeous visuals, and at times can feel really uneasy while traversing through the snow-ridden, blizzard like environments.
Sandbox-ish?
Cons
Not much meat to the game. More of a Slender clone by walking around, gathering notes, and avoiding some slow-walking/teleporting entity.
Sean Bean’s narration feels a tad phoned in.
The story is extremely convoluted, and the game doesn’t really have any sense of direction.
The game is more frustrating then it is fun. The deaths you experience are more so random, and put on a more luck-based feel. Maybe you’ll randomly get killed by the environment with no warning.
Doesn’t exactly feel like a horror game, and more so feels like an adventure narrative sort of experience in the veins of Dear Esther.
Sadly, Kholat just isn’t all that great of a game and for that price-point I’d recommend you check it out if it gets a price drop. I was really excited for Kholat as I’m super into the Dyatlov Pass Incident, but the game didn’t fully utilize what it could of with these events and sort of just falls flat.

Kholat is an open world horror game that immerses players in a wasteland that truly feels alive. Wind blows past your ears; snow falls in varying degrees of intensity, sometimes robbing your sight; mysterious beings howl in the distance; an old bridge creaks dangerously when you walk over it...
And whenever you find certain notes you'll witness a paranormal phenomenon that is certainly worth witnessing ... which is something that I cannot say about the rest of the game.
The incident it's based on is already the most interesting aspect of the entire story, whereas most of the notes I found told me nothing of importance. Some are written by the people who died, some by a guy who tried to find out what happened, and then there are theories trying to explain the incident. Once in a while, you will also hear Sean Bean's character calling out to you, mentioning things that happened long ago. He seems to have some plans for the nameless protagonist … but when the game fades to black only a minute into the final act, you will be none the wiser, as the game doesn't really try to explain anything ... or have a resolution ... or anything that could be called an ending.
Is the gameplay worth it, at least? No, not when you spend most of the time walking around aimlessly, always hoping to find whatever it is that the coordinates on your map are meant to signify. Sure, you might say that feeling lost is kinda the point, but not when it's so annoying that you'd rather stop playing than trudge on endlessly.
It could have been less annoying if the map was actually useful, but unless you're standing in front of a camp (which serves as a fast-travel-point), you'll have no idea where the hell you are. And even then you might have trouble charting your course. And if you happen to run into a monster (none of which are scary) and haven't found a camp or note in a while, then you're going to be screwed, as there are no manual saves. The first time it happened (when I didn't even know that enemies existed), I had to start over from the other side of the map.
Therefore, I can only recommend Kholat to those who like to explore the beautiful environment. Everyone else will be sorely disappointed by the lack of interesting gameplay or a story worth following.

I love horror. At least when it comes in the form of movies or written stories. And this might surprise some people, but I genuinely lack any positive sentiment towards horror games. The reasons for this are manifold. For one, most horror games rely heavily on jump-scares. And that’s not horror. It’s startling to see a freakish monstrosity jump out at you while your ears get assaulted by a string orchestra going through a meat grinder, yes. But it’s not scary and it’s not horror.
Another reason why horror and games don’t gel for me is that games are interactive. I have agency and I dictate the pacing of a game. I can take my time and explore every nook and cranny, or I can just jog through the level. I simply still have too much control over the game even if I’m completely helpless. And the final reason why I don’t play many horror games is because I’m just staring at a black screen most of the time. Horror games use darkness as a weak setup to hide stuff from the player in order to then build in jump-scares. Again, not horror. Horror is a feeling of underlying dread you get from being exposed to something.
So why did I voluntarily pick
to write a review about? Well, first off it seemed to not engage in all of the tropes mentioned above. Your surroundings are mostly well-lit, it rarely uses jump-scares and when it does, it makes sense within the universe. And lastly, it manages to setup an eerie atmosphere from the very start. It accomplishes this with the fact that it’s an adaptation of a real event that took place in the Ural Mountains in 1959 when a group of alpinists were killed in an unexplained event called the Dyatlov Pass incident. If you want to look it up, it’s a great read and it has all the ingredients to make an absorbing adaptation out of it. Because of its unresolved nature you can spin any yarn you want out of it. And it’s an incident that hasn’t been widely covered a dozen times by other, bigger productions.
The plot of the game takes you to Kholat Syakhl, literally “Dead Mountain”, where you retrace the events in search of an explanation. Armed only with a map, a compass and a flashlight, you set out to traverse the mountains in search for newspaper articles, diary entries and other reports to uncover the mystery of the incident. And you obviously do it all by night.
If you read the above paragraph and thought to yourself “This sounds an awful lot like the Slenderman games”, you’d be in the correct ballpark. You’re running through the wilderness in search of a variety of documents. And there isn’t really much that’s chasing you throughout most of it. Where
manages to really become scary is with its atmosphere. And it does so without artificially putting you in a dark environment. The mountains are brightly lit by a full moon and your flashlight – should you ever need to use it in the bright environments – has no annoying degrading battery that for some reason runs out in five minutes real time.
No, what makes
scary is the fact that it manages to invoke a haunting claustrophobia. Even though ironically most of it takes place outside in the wide open mountain range. Maybe this is a particularly subjective observation on my part, but my favorite horror stories –
– all take place in remote, wintry environments, in which the location and the weather themselves are equally as eerie and threatening to the protagonists as the horror that stalks them. The feeling of isolation probably resonates with me a lot for some reason. All that makes me appreciate
far more than most other horror games and it meant I could be fully immersed in its world.
It would’ve been too good to believe however if the game were an atmospheric mood piece for the player to experience without encountering hostility. During our excursions we cross paths with a bunch of specters who aren’t particularly fond of us wandering around. Encounters with them usually only last a couple of seconds, since directly engaging them leads to death. Running away is only a semi-viable option, since running in deep snow is very tiring for our character and they usually manage to catch up.
Besides this, the game does have a few more drawbacks to it. First and foremost, the game contains very little actual gameplay. It’s largely a very literal example of a walking simulator. In addition to that, the game doesn’t give the player a lot of direction. This is especially a problem at the very start of the game. We begin the game at a deserted village without any indication of where we’re supposed to go. The player has to bring his own hunger for exploration in order to eventually find the correct path to the tent where the alpinists found their ends.
But even prior to that, the game puts another obstacle in our way. We find ourselves in a blinding snowstorm in which we’re supposed to find the actual camp of the victims. The whole screen is white, you can barely make out where the ground stops and the blizzard begins, though luckily after a bit of aimlessly wandering around and eventually finding the tent, the weather clears up.
However this lack of direction turns into a strength later on in the game. When we receive the map of the mountain range, a bunch of geographic coordinates have been written onto it. Though you’ll have to figure out where they are yourself, because specific locations only get added to the map once you’ve found them. What turns this relatively simple objective into a challenge is the fact that your own position doesn’t get marked on the map. You’ll have to use the compass and the map itself to keep track of where you are, so it’s vitally important that you don’t become lost.
What enhances the already dense atmosphere of the game is both the phenomenal soundtrack as well as the voice-acting. Sean Bean in particular manages to set the mood very effectively with his calm, soothing voice. But also the rest of the voice-acting that’s used to read the messages you find to you is very good.
People who like jump-scare fests like
or
probably won’t find much to enjoy here. But I can definitely recommend the title to players who like subtle, introspective horror that is more concerned with building atmosphere and a feeling of dread rather than constant tension. With the caveat that
is rather lacking in the gameplay department and unfortunately, the ending doesn’t provide much closure and at less than four hours – even though the developer claims it takes longer to beat – maybe it’s a bit short for what they’re asking.

An interesting game that mixes genres very well, its like a hybrid of dungeon crawler and tower defense and feels very different from many other games I have played.
The atmosphere is great as it feels mysterious, which is really helped by the lighting as you open up new doors and power on rooms. The pixel art is charismatic and the dialogue is quite funny. I really liked the interface of how the game switched between. It feels very fluid and natural to switch between the two fields of view on the fly. The co op mode is also a very fun addition as you discuss and elaborate upon decisions with friends, as you can spend as much time as you want between battles talking over what you want to spend resources on, which is very fun, and the single player game is equally as enjoyable. There are a large variety of escape pods, heroes and modules to unlock and discover that keeps the game fresh and enjoyable and the gameplay is also very innovative.
I definitely feel there should be some gameplay adjustments though, as I really enjoyed the gameplay at its core but some of the rougher edges bothered me. One of the things I felt was missing was the lack of any sort of final boss of any kind, either a single tough monster or a horde mode could have helped, you just beat the 12th floor and the game just ends. Its very anticlimatic and it negates a lot of the choices you've made in terms of building your characters and unlocks. Why does it matter which modules I research and unlock and what researches I grind if I never have to use them in some sort of final battle? So you can simply stumble into victory without really earning it. This is one thing I'd definitely like addressed if the developers make a sequel to this game. Later on, it definitely feels like your victory is determined by which direction you pick. On my first winning co-op game, we picked to go right from the You kind of have to just, so some of the deaths feel quite cheap. The game also has only two difficulty settings, one of which is too easy and the other is too hard and is in desperate need of an intermediate "normal" difficulty to balance out the game a bit. The easy mode is so easy that there's no challenge and you'll have maxed out heroes in no time and thus the game becomes boring and in the harder mode felt like the developers couldn't figure out how to balance the gameplay for higher challenge so they simply spawned a ton of monsters so it becomes frustrating and not in a good way, and it becomes too random, even for a game with RNG.
Overall, the game is quite enjoyable and there is a lot to explore and discover in the game, experimenting with different characters and modules is satisfying, exploring the dungeon is very fun as is weighing up, co op mode is also a lot of fun where you can discuss what you want to upgrade with your friends, however overall the gameplay should have some adjustments in order to make it great.

Well that was fun.  It wasn’t quite the genre I was expecting.  Apparently the game starts in orbit above some planet.  This is the last place I expected a game to start off in based upon the title.  Quickly things go badly for the space ship, as it’s being blasted to pieces by ‘something’.  As the ship breaks in two, your escape pod emerges from the blast.  You quickly choose your heroes from a small roster of potential survivors, and smash into the ground.  This isn’t the best way to start your day, but makes for a great game intro.
Once you land, or rather, crash with incredible force into the unsuspecting planet, you discover that you’re quite a ways under the ground.  Fortunately, your ship just happened to stop its descent right next to the entrance to a network of tunnels.
These tunnels apparently and quite fortunately connect with the surface of the planet.  Unfortunately, these tunnels are filled with alien creatures intent on preventing you from reaching the surface.
You soon discover that one of the rooms on your level connects to the level above it. Each level of the network of tunnels is randomly generated, so each playthrough will be unique.  This adds a bit of replayability to the game.  This also means that you must search out and find the room connecting the floors each time.
There’s a bit of resource management involved; structures can be built in certain rooms that improve your chances of survival.  Research can be performed to discover new weapons and equipment.  Merchants can be found with various items for sale.  I’m sure that there are more secrets to discover that I didn’t find during my few attempts at the game.
One interesting thing I noticed in the beginning of the game was that your escape pod can itself be upgraded. Your beginner pod can only hold two heroes; but if you complete the game under certain circumstances, you unlock a bigger pod that can hold three or four heroes at once.  This is a nice incentive to complete the game, as a group of four adventurers could make the game much easier.  With only two heroes, it’s pretty much game-over if one dies.
What I liked: The graphics were pixelated 8-bit style, which were charming.  The animations of the various characters were done very well.  Even with the constraint of the 8-bit style, I never had any confusion as to what I was looking at.  Bad guys were very clearly bad guys.  The in-game mapping system is quite handy.
What I didn’t like:  The game felt very punishing.  Things went from good to disastrous in a heartbeat.  Perhaps on an easier
difficulty level the game might be more forgiving, but I felt like clicking the so-called “Too Easy” level was an affront to my gaming heritage.  The only other difficulty level was called “Easy”, and that was bad enough.
If you’re into rogue-likes, this one is a solid title and well worth a look.
Thanks for reading.

The amount of effort developers put into making of this game is amazing. Unfortunately game has minor annoying shortcoming that prevent it from being truly great.
The interiors, for example. In the previous game, Unity, you could enter almost any building. In Syndicate the whole center of London is just copy/pasted boxes a la GTA III instead of houses with detailed interiors with the exception of mission related buildings. Which are few.
The graphics certainly are amazing, the architecture is significantly better looking and more interesting to climb and explore compared to GTA V, but if you compare it to Unity, it's definetely a step back. The controls are typical for AC series and that's annoying that developers fail to make an enjoyable combat mechanics for the 9th bloody time. For example, I was aiming my revolver at the charging enemy and just as I was ready to shoot game switched me to melee mode and I had to use a quickshot with a separate button. The story is abysmal. No character development, no twists, uninspired cameo appearances of Marx, Dickens and few other historic figures become a boring routine. You're just told from the start that Assassins are good, Templars are bad, and you stab them in their backs one by one til the end credits roll.
Overall game feels incredibly solid and leaves pleasant memories.

Been playing this game on and off since early access, I totally fell in love with it.  On the surface, a great art style and a subtle but fitting soundtrack sets the tone for the game, making it enjoyable for casual gamers interested in immersion and exploration.  As you dig deeper into the mechanics and harder difficulties of the game, you'll find survival a simple objective, but many obstacles that stand in your way that will challenge you to push your character to her or his limit.  Multiple modes including story mode, challenges, and sandbox; intuitive but not necessarily easy crafting; simple and easily understood UI, including your health; and simple controls all come together to create, in my opinion, one of the best survival games ever made.
