Dragon Age: Origins - Ultimate Edition
-Released Oct. 2010:  EA Games - Bioware
Dragon Age Origins has earned its place on the stage as one of the best role-playing games currently on the market. While the game was released more than five years ago, it continues to hold its own against other RPGs and boasts a respectable following of loyal players. Although the game’s title may suggest it is merely the precursor to Inquisition, nothing could be further from the truth, as Origins stands alone just as easily.
Story
Dragon Age provides an immensely story-heavy and dialog rich gaming experience. At some point, you may feel as if you’re playing through a visual novel. However, the story and characters are extremely well-written and as a result, the world constructed is complex and interesting. This begins right from the start of gameplay, as your personal origin story will change depending on your race, gender, and class. Something else to note is that with the game, your words matter. With any conversation you engage in, the dialog chosen will change the outcome of your relationships, so it’s best not to be too flippant.
Immersion
I kind of touched on this when talking about the story aspect of the game. But because the plot is very story-driven there is a rather immersive quality to the game. Although Origins is not open-world or free-reign, just the act of playing and uncovering the story can take a great deal of conversation, allowing you to forget you’re playing a game. In much the same way, you may become immersed in a good book.
Game Mechanics
Again, Dragon Age is not open-world or free reign, so you must follow the bread-crumb trail of quests to reach the end of the story. However, the mechanics of battle are well thought out. While the battle scenarios are hectic, and do not function on turn-based fighting, the party control system is reminiscent of the Final Fantasy series. Pausing the battle and directing what each individual party member should be doing is often the best course of action. At the same time, make sure to take full advantage of the tactics slots each party member has available, as it will lead to a more fluid battle.
Controls
Dragon Age has full controller support, as it was originally produced on the Play-Station 4. However, I have found that because of the sheer amount of actions and items used during battle scenarios, it is typically easier to manage with computer controls. On the other hand, I realize this is a matter of opinion, my sister insists the controller is the way to go. I suggest trying both and seeing what feels comfortable for you.
Graphics & Visual Quality
While the graphics in Dragon Age are not impressive (strictly speaking) by today’s standards, design wise the game is aesthetically pleasing. Another plus in the column is that Dragon Age is actually able to run cleanly on the highest graphics setting. I have personally never experienced tearing, lagging, or glitches when running the game at HD levels. Additionally, a great deal of detail work made its way into the landscapes and background of Dragon Age that adds to the overall ambiance of the world.
Overall Opinion
Dragon Age Origins is a truly complete game with no glaring flaws, design or otherwise. While it is not open world, it provides an immersive setting with intriguing characters and plenty of quests with battles, blood, and mayhem. So it is that I gleefully recommend this game to the prospective player.

Dragon Age: Origins is a roll playing game made by my personal favorites of RPG makers, Bioware. Hands-down the best Role-Playing Game I have ever played.
PROS:
+A unique and interesting setting, full of lore and explanations for nearly every little thing.
+A compelling story with more depth than it initially appears to have.
+Fascinating companions with their own takes on everything and enjoy talking amongst eachother, leading to some great banter.
+In-depth combat system, requiring you to pause multiple times to figure out how you're going to plan your way through some of the toughest battles in the game.
+Instead of a karmic good/bad system like Knights of the Old Republic or earlier Fallout games, this game just has various companions (each with their own sense of right and wrong) approve or disapprove of your actions, leading into some interesting dynamics with the party. For example: while the former monk will approve of you helping the poor, the hardcore Darwinist will find it deplorable.
+An amazing capacity to determine what sort of person your character is.
+Does an excellent job of showing the world in shades of grey as opposed to good and bad.
+An excellent and atmospheric soundtrack.
+Barkspawn!
+Golems!
+Enchantment?
+Mods!
+Some of the best DLC I've seen for a roleplaying game.
+DLC Awakening: An excellent continuation of the main story, picking right up from where you left off.
+DLC Awakening: The player can make a choice which has the potential to change an enemy as we know them.
+DLC Awakening: New, interesting companions who, while not as amazing as those from Origins, are nonetheless fun to hang out with.
+DLC Awakening: You actually stand as a lord over a realm, called to make decisions for your people and pass judgement on criminals.
+DLC Awakening: Adds depth for Oghren, an otherwise simple companion from Origins.
+DLC Awakening: New powers giving an additional dimension to an already deep combat system.
+DLC Awakening: See what happened to a few of your old companions from Origins. Small, but a nice touch.
+DLC: Play as the Darkspawn.
+DLC: Hang out with another big, awesome Golem! I cannot stress how fun the Golems are in this universe!
+DLC: Tie up loose threads with Morrigan.
+DLC: Play through Leliana's origin story.
CONS:
-The graphics really are dated. Like, bad for 2009 dated.
-The Deep Roads are one of the most infuriatingly long parts of the game, accounting for about 1/5 of the entire game. Many also dislike the Fade section, but I found it intriguing.
-I've experienced multiple glitches and issues playing Origins on Windows 10. Strangely, the DLC worked just fine.
An excellent experience overall, and definitely worth full-price.

[SPOILERS BELOW]
There really would have to be two reviews, one for the sandbox, which is amazing, and one for the story mode, which is not. As the game is currently marketed for the story mode, thus the negative review.
My review is negative because of the way the story is told. Having an open-world setting and then introducing a very linear narrative to it does not make sense. The developers attempted to weave the open world of TLD into a story, but it just doesn't work.
The game either allows you to explore and meddle with important quest items, so you effectively complete a quest even before knowing it (the bank keys), or you are very bluntly told not to touch something (the rosehips). It should have been either a completely linear game (no exploration), or a sandbox intertwined with quests. The story mode tries to be both and fails.
You gain NPCs' trust (an important mechanic in the story mode) simply by giving them basic items from the game, which you effectively farm. Give the granny 50 bandages. Boring.
Most quests are simple fetch quests. They further the story in a very mechanical and uniteresting way. The NPCs are supposed to help you learn more about the world, but this is done extremely mechanically. The collapse? Ah, what's there to be told, just read this book! (No actual book, you have to explore the UI to find 'notes' about the world in some dusty corner of it).
The writing is painfully cliched. The dialogue feels artificial like a school play. The character's emotions are hard to believe. If I were rushing to find a person important for me in the midst of a frozen hellhole, I wouldn't be nice with an old hag who refuses to tell me where she is. I would threaten to kill her. Multiple choice for interactions would have worked amazingly well here. Why not deceive the old lady, take the gun from her and force her to tell you what happened? Why not intimidate her? Why not leave her alltogether and try to peace the whole thing by yourself? The single line of narrative, coupled with mechanical quests to progress through it, really kills the pace of the game.
I think the story would have been much more successful if it was weaved into the open world in a fragmented way (like the notes left by the departed people), gradually and randomly uncovered by the player with some interesting exploration side quests and a final quest after key points of narrative were discovered. I was looking forward to NPCs, but for some reason they just make the whole game much less immersive.
Hinterland's determination to actually realease an Early Access game is laudable, but it seems that the vision of what the game should be was changed so many times that it jeopardized the result. This is especially sad because the sandbox had a lot of potential to be developed into an amazing open-world game with interesting quests.

Update 1: (Reviewed)
Completed 10 missions now. Will probably try that last tutorial now that I know its trick. Its really easy once you get the hang of it. You must not rush building everything at once but balance the workforce and unemployment.  I leave it on x2 after 10 minutes into the mission and see that I always have above 6% unemployment, if not just build a neighbourhood of work houses. And never forget the maintenance. I make three rows of work houses, each row with 9 or 10 houses. Leave little space for each row for decorations like trees. The first to build is the maintenance and the well and when I have some food I build the shop. This way has never failed me in the 10 missions that I have completed up to now.
What I love:
Graphics especially the details. (Seeing a cat on the roof of the cafe)
Seeing all the people doing their jobs.
Houses being upgraded.
No bugs.
Menus.
Smooth gameplay.
What I don't love:
The music. So not buying the soundtrack.
Annoying messages from the emperor.
Story is boring.
Missions can be a bit boring too.
Tutorials are terrible. They are harder than the actual missions and don't teach you anything important.
Update 2:
What I would like to see added or improved?
Hop farm, grape farm and Sugar cane farm.
Building to make wine using the grape farm. Building can even be the abbey. Wine is essential.
Sweet shop using the sugar cane farm.
More workforce house types.
More rich people house types.
All buildings can be upgraded by the player, for example to make them more efficient.
Different roads.
More decorations, tree and flower types.
The well should be upgraded. Also there should be another type of water source for the rich people. Like there is the emporium instead of the shop. Those beautiful mansions and palaces and then that ugly well? Even the maintenance shop should be different for the rich people.
Will continue to update this after completing more missions and hope some cool stuff is added very soon. Thank you for reading this.

Furthermore DLC is continously being released which you have to pay for. The downloadable characters are overpowered in order to temp you to buy them but in fact it just ruins the game as it is no longer balanced.
Lastly, and perhaps most imperative is the fact that minimal game support is provided to gamers outside their main target markets. Thus gamers such as myself are forced to play with terrible connections. This makes the game almost unplayable if you are paired with someone from a far location- which is likely the case since their player base has declined so dramatically. The game experience for all concerned is utterly frustrating when this happens.

Be warned, there are some big issues with UI/Scaling/Resolution on this game that Zachtronics have confirmed on a recent Gamasutra podcast/stream (broadcast Nov 1st, 3pm Eastern Time - go to 15:34 of the video on youtube, search 'gamasutra opus magnum') that they have NO intention of fixing at any point during this game. It is an issue they don't hope to tackle until their NEXT game!
This has never been an issue on any other Zachtronics game .... but it is a big issue now. It goes like this, it appears they designed this aesthetically simple 2d puzzle game with 1080 resolution in mind, and nothing else. I am running 1366x768 ... and at this resolution, the game elements are HUGE ... the UI panels are HUGE ... and the gaming area you can see at any one time is TINY, likewise for the instruction lane that you need to input instructions is SHORT. You can only see 24 instructions at any one time, and this issue is compounded by the fact your view of the instruction pane won't scroll when you are trying to select a larger sequence of instructions, or when you're trying to paste a sequence you just selected (fingers crossed super firmly that at the very least that can be solved, otherwise consider this game a total write off if you want to play anything but the simplest of levels).
this is a big problem for more than just one reason .... 1st of all, the later puzzles of the game you will be asked to produce products that take up the entire visible gaming area (if you're on less than 1080) .... just imagine all the scrolling around you're going to have to do to manufacture the product, you will never have an over-view of the entire solution you are working on, and furthermore you will never completely see your solution in action unless you render it to gif and view it in a gif viewer .... what the actual feck.
the 2nd reason this is a significant problem, as if that really wasn't bad enough, is that the game is the most 'accessible' (i.e easiest, and I include optimisations in that summation) zachtronics game yet .... so to get a decent challenge going, you're going to be relying on those levels with larger products ... and if you're using a monitor that is less than 1080 the biggest challenge won't be in solving the puzzles, it will be in enduring the tedium of mousing around the gaming area of a 2d puzzler that absolutely should not be having this scaling problem.
people with 4k monitors seem to be having an inverse issue to this. But between people on the lower end of the resolution spectrum and the higher end of the resolution spectrum, this has been a frequently made feature request - to FIX this issue.
So, while I have not seen the issue addressed directly on Opus Magnum's Steam discussion area (where it should be addressed, I would have thought), I instead learn that Zachtronics have absolutely NO intention of fixing it via a Gamasutra podcast ... wtf ? .... Not only that, there is a brazen streak of arrogance in their manner of addressing the problem on that podcast .... basically anyone suffering with this problem has a 'terrible, dank, old laptop that's 5 years old' .... This laptop isn't 5 years old, it is a midrange toshiba 2.5+ years ago. Their attitude to 4k users isn't so toxic, but it is no more considerate. Basically if you're monitor isn't 1080, either larger or smaller, you're the problem .... Well, I put it to you that if a developer working on an aesthetically simple 2d puzzler is having these issues, to such degree that he can't solve it without 'rewriting the game' ... it is the visual programmer, or the game designer, who is the problem ... I am honestly not sure where the buck stops on that one, but I am really shocked that this is an issue. and an issue that won't be resolved.
to add insult to injury, not only have they not addressed this on steam, but they haven't even made a note of it in the minimum tech requirements to play the game on the store page .... how can they in good conscious speak about this problem as brazenly and dismissively as they do on gaming podcasts, acknowledging that it won't be fixed, but still refuse to alert potential customers of this problem ? that seems to be bordering on willfull deceit, imo.
this game is good in other ways ... but just past the midway point and the UI/scaling problem is already causing serious interface issues where enjoyment is taking a hit, and more time is being spent trying to compensate for the programmer's failings. this will only get worse as the products you are asked to produce get bigger, and the instruction sequences get longer.
So if your monitor is not 1080 ... beware. I can not reccommend this game for anyone playing at monitor resolutions other than that .... even if it would be at a 50% discount, I would say be prepared for a very awkward gaming experience if you're running a 'terrible computer' with a 'dank' 1366 x768 resolution monitor ... like, get real man, don't expect the developer to do something crazy like make his 2d puzzler scalable or develop it in such a way that it wouldn't need to be scaled.

Been playing the Early Access for 2 years now and I've always said that even if they never released story mode, I would have been just as happy playing the sandbox game. In the harder sandbox modes I felt like the hunger and thirst depletion system was just way overpowered and was worried about how much of a problem it would be in story mode, but actually it isn't bad. Dunno if things will get more difficult in the later episodes, but for now I like how things are. I haven't felt like the difficulty level has inhibited my ability to further the plot. All in all a great way to kill an evening.
For all the new players out there jumping in to story mode, I will say that there is definitely a learning curve when starting out. I feel like I'm surviving as well as I am because I've been playing in sandbox mode for so long and pretty much know the ropes. So stick with it, browse the forums for helpful tips, check out the Long Dark Wiki. Once you get the hang of it, I promise it's less running around constantly in a panic while steps away from death and more...running around only slightly less panicked but at least knowing what you need to do to survive ;)

All jokes aside, I've owned the long dark since shortly after its release into early access. The game has gone through many changes, most very welcome. I find the addition of the story mode to be the factor that makes it feel like a complete game. Sure, sandbox mode is fun, but it only takes about a week in game for things to start feeling monotonous. The story mode shakes things up with actual objectives to keep you interested in playing.
The main issue I have with the game right now is its balance. For example, sometimes firewood is plentiful, so much so you can practically put a fire anywhere you want to without any real concern. Other times its virtually impossible to find, leaving you with 3 sticks to stave off the elements. (Granted, this is how it would be if you were trying to survive IRL, so I really have no basis to complain)
Another issue I have is with some of the core mechanics of the game, primarily the lack of anything close to a "jump." I'm not asking for a super mario kind of jump, just something to make traversing the varied terrain a bit easier. The other mechanic I have an issue with is the throwables. There is nothing to give you any idea of where what you are trying to throw is going to land. I find myself consistently underthrowing just about everything, making early hunting tedious. This issue ties into the beginning of my review, as one of the primary ways you defend yourself from wolves, is by throwing a lit torch at said wolf. On 3 seperate occasions, I've thrown a torch within 5 feet of a wolf, only to have it completely ignore it. As one can imagine, having your wolf defense within striking range of a wolf isn't advantageous.
Overall, I feel like the long dark is about 95% done. With a little more polish and a few tweaks, I think it would definitely be worth picking up.

This game is great, other than the random wolf spawns.
I played over 350 hours of this game in the few months after I purchased it. I was really excited about the official release and the story mode, and was really disapointed when a wolf spawned on me shortly after avoiding the first scripted encounter after the cave in story mode.
I walked well around the wolf and avoided its attention as it feasted on a nearby dear. I found a road, walked to a nearby car,  searched the trunk and glove box and left the car to be confronted instantly by a wolf. This reminded me why I stopped playing the game in the first place.

Constant crashes during cutscenes. I've tried all the fixes I can find online, but it's all down to the Unity engine. Really disappointing as I was a backer for Kickstarter when it started and had great fun playing in the sandbox. I still recommend the game, the devs put a hell of a lot of work into it, and I had fun while it lasted.

The Good: This is a beautiful, immersive game that really puts you into the wild and gives you a sense of dread that nightfall is coming. If you've camped in freezing weather, you will relive that here. Although I haven't completed the story mode, I feel the story is compelling enough and wasn't just an afterthought after the devs made sandbox mode.
The Bad: The character models are lacking and don't really match the overall art direction, especially the inventory screen. The UI for inventory is frustrating, certain effects aren't really explained so it makes comparing equipment a crapshoot. THE GAME IS HARD! The reward for finally killing a rabbit with a stone is a sliver of hunger points... which now you're likely low on temperature, tiredness and water. Food is sparse!
The Ugly: The autosave state is rough. In story mode, I got myself into a deadlock situation where I ventured too far into my inevitable death, but the last save was seconds before my death. I was forced to restart from beginning (luckily it was early). Resuming a game also put me into a situation where I had to force myself to die in order to go to the "last checkpoint" save which is different than the "last save"... overall just confusing. I feel story mode should take it a little easier on the player and checkpoints and getting you back to a safe spot to try again. Another scenario it seems I stashed every ounce of food into granny's fridge only to find she locked it down, now I'm faced with "stealing" from granny to get those items back? Sheesh.
This is not a survival to craft A+B to get C, it's more about exploration and being proactive to get through the night. Your reward is seeing the next morning, having plenty of food and water to hit the ground running to the next spot.I spent $10 on the game and look forward to the next chapters. I see people playing 100+ hours and giving negative reviews saying "not enough content" ... I don't feel this game is marketing itself as a 100+ hour game.
** EDIT 12/30/17  - The save state has been fixed and while the game isn't as risky venturing out now, balancing your temperature/tiredness/thirst/hunger meter feels a lot like patching holes only to spring another leak elsewhere. The wolves add insult to injury. I've finally completed Episode 2 and I've said some choice words at the screen while spending 1+ hours getting lost on my way back to the trapper's cabin after reverting many saves. The entire Survival Stories feels way too late in the game (almost like a tutorial) and is a bit too tedious. To give you an idea of how stressful this game can be, at times I've switched to playing Outlast to get some relaxation. This game is best played in small segments with lots of breaks.

On my last attempt I died starting a fire, three steps outside of a church, as I froze and bled to death after a wolf attack. 10/10, would join early access again.

Dragon Age: Origins is a roll playing game made by my personal favorites of RPG makers, Bioware. They are really good at making not just a RPG game with different classes and such but the choices you make in their games can really change the entire story. The story in this game is really rich and beuitifull and full och good characters, each with their own voice actors (well, most of them at least).
The game takes place in a medieval world with swords and castles and the main enemy (the darkspawn) is just as basic as the world is, they are bad and they want to kill anything and all, except their own, unless they feel it's really necessary.
The story is that as usual you'r the worlds last hope and you need to gather an army to opose the darkspawn and their leader and to do this you will need to do many things. On your journey to do this you will meet several interesting companions and ordinary persons who will give you quests and tasks to complete as a usual open world RPG game is.
The combat in the game can be a bit boring but it's not like you are going to kill yourself over it, it's not that bad, it does it's job and it's easy. The main thing in this game is the story and the feeling of the gameplay overall and that is something that will make the game worthwhile.
I have this game on Playstation 3 too but not Ultimate edition so I don't have the Awakening DLC which is a absolute masterpiece in my opinion. The DLC you get with this edition are all worthwhile but I recommend playing the main Dragon Age: Origins story first, before doing Awakening or any of the other.
So on the PS3 I think I have completed the game about 8 times at least. There are 3 different races (not much but enough), 3 classes (not much either but enough) and depending on race and class 5 or 6 different origin stories. The origin stories is something that will introduce you to the game and they are really well made in story also. Not something that is thrown together to get a start and understanding. They really put work into them.
The enviroment in the game is well done and doesn't repeat to often. Some places have the same kind of doors and rooms which can be a bit boring but it's nothing that you really notice. You will be to busy listening to what someone is saying or trying to kill something.
Speaking of listening, if you want to hear some humour in the game, try to listen to your companions as you walk. At some places in the game 2 companions starts talking to each other about something random and they can be quite funny to listen to. It wont be a cutscene when they do, a talkbubble above their heads will appear if you have subtitles for all conversations on in the options menu.
The quests and tasks in the game are a bit different from each other. Mostly it's gather that thing and come back or kill that and come back but to get to that point might be a bit longer that you think. It's not meaningless to all the quests, you will get rewards for everything you do, one way or another, but xp is allways a reward.
Don't know what else to say. The game is great, very worthwhile my time. Bu the way, completing the main Origin story takes a little over 30 hours if you do most quests or all depending on difficulty and how many times you played the game. Then there is plus the Awakening and all the other DLC so 50 hourr or more for one way through.

Hands-down the best Role-Playing Game I have ever played.
PROS:
+A unique and interesting setting, full of lore and explanations for nearly every little thing.
+A compelling story with more depth than it initially appears to have.
+Fascinating companions with their own takes on everything and enjoy talking amongst eachother, leading to some great banter.
+In-depth combat system, requiring you to pause multiple times to figure out how you're going to plan your way through some of the toughest battles in the game.
+Instead of a karmic good/bad system like Knights of the Old Republic or earlier Fallout games, this game just has various companions (each with their own sense of right and wrong) approve or disapprove of your actions, leading into some interesting dynamics with the party. For example: while the former monk will approve of you helping the poor, the hardcore Darwinist will find it deplorable.
+An amazing capacity to determine what sort of person your character is.
+Does an excellent job of showing the world in shades of grey as opposed to good and bad.
+An excellent and atmospheric soundtrack.
+Barkspawn!
+Golems!
+Enchantment?
+Mods!
+Some of the best DLC I've seen for a roleplaying game.
+DLC Awakening: An excellent continuation of the main story, picking right up from where you left off.
+DLC Awakening: The player can make a choice which has the potential to change an enemy as we know them.
+DLC Awakening: New, interesting companions who, while not as amazing as those from Origins, are nonetheless fun to hang out with.
+DLC Awakening: You actually stand as a lord over a realm, called to make decisions for your people and pass judgement on criminals.
+DLC Awakening: Adds depth for Oghren, an otherwise simple companion from Origins.
+DLC Awakening: New powers giving an additional dimension to an already deep combat system.
+DLC Awakening: See what happened to a few of your old companions from Origins. Small, but a nice touch.
+DLC: Play as the Darkspawn.
+DLC: Hang out with another big, awesome Golem! I cannot stress how fun the Golems are in this universe!
+DLC: Tie up loose threads with Morrigan.
+DLC: Play through Leliana's origin story.
CONS:
-The graphics really are dated. Like, bad for 2009 dated.
-The Deep Roads are one of the most infuriatingly long parts of the game, accounting for about 1/5 of the entire game. Many also dislike the Fade section, but I found it intriguing.
-I've experienced multiple glitches and issues playing Origins on Windows 10. Strangely, the DLC worked just fine.
An excellent experience overall, and definitely worth full-price.
could use controler suport but still fun

A decent little game, Gomo doesn't take too long to complete. It would probably be good for kids, but if you're an older gamer getting this game in a bundle or on sale is probably the way to go. So with that said, here are some pros and cons.
PROS
- Art style is quaint but unique and will probably age well because of that.
- The idle animations in the foreground and background are entertaining enough.
- Puzzles weren't too challenging but not necessarily hand-outs.
- Does have bonus levels.
- The mechanics are easy enough to get a handle on.
CONS
- The animations of the main character, though cute, may sometimes try your patience.
- The story, simple though it is, is short and thus so is the game.
- The differences between the bonus levels are cosmetic for the most part.
- Just a pet peeve for me, the inventory automatically threw stuff out instead of letting the player figure out when an object was obselete. Probably not a con for most.
- Not very replayable. You'll proabably do all you'll ever do on the first play-thru.
So, all in all, it'll only take an hour or so to complete. I almost didn't recommend this game, but, all things considered, for what was offered you get pretty much what you might expect. And it's not like the game wasn't entertaining in its own rights, just don't expect to be playing it hours on end.

Game is very Early Access. Buggy and unbalanced, but the dev is fixing it quick as a lil bunny with feedback from players. Don't buy it if you think you can't handle a game in its early stages. This game is, in it's current state, horrendously broken.
There are four areas where any multiplayer-only game needs perform in order to do well and be enjoyable:
1) It needs to be bug-free (or at least have the bugs be small enough to have a minimal effect on the experience). Players should not feel as if their losses are outside of their control.
2) The players should have as little downtime as possible between matches. In other words, the ratio of playing in a match vs waiting for a match should be high.
3) The playerbase should be large enough to support the game (for most games, this requires the number of concurrent players divided by the number of players per match to be relatively high). This is often, but not always, related to point #2.
4) The gameplay should be enjoyable and varied.
Evolve, unfortunately, has failed on three out of the above four criteria.
1) Even now, months after its release, the game is incredibly buggy. I lost a match last night because I, as monster, hit a tree in the middle of my jump. I glitched out and wasn't able to move. That was just one bug in the past 24 hours -- I've had this game glitch out in so many different ways that I don't think there is a single mechanic left that wasn't affected at one point or another (for example, last week in the middle of a match I was on track to win as monster, I lost the ability to feed. Carcasses that I tried to eat fell through the bottom of the map. Feeding is an integral part of the Evolve mechanic, without it the monster literally cannot make progress.).  Search youtube for "Evolve game glitches" and you will see dozens of examples.
2) I stopped playing a month ago because the uptime-to-downtime ratio was around 1, which in my opinion is too low. I started playing again last week, and that ratio is literally down to 1/3. That's right, if you buy this game you can expect to spend three times longer waiting for matches than you can expect to be actually playing in matches. Matches are typically ~10 minutes long, and wait times (for me) have been upwards of a half hour.
3) The Evolve playerbase has dwindled at an unprecedented rate since its release. Go ahead, go check steamcharts dot com, and look at the numbers. Evolve's playerbase has dropped from ~27,000 concurrent global players at release to a current level around 1,000 (and this review is being written shortly after a free weekend promotion, which has artificially inflated the playerbase, and which I'm sure had nothing to do with the game's publisher's third quarter reports for 2015). That's a drop of 96.3% -- fewer than four out of 100 people who played this game at release are playing it a few months later. The game is simply unsustainable at these levels. If I leave a game now and try to rejoin a new one, the playerbase is so starved that I will almost always get dumped back into the same game, because that is literally the only match that fits my playing level.
4) This is where Evolve shines, and the reason why I have 350 hours on record playing. It really is a fun game -- when it's working. During the Alpha and Beta, the game was phenomenal. There weren't as many glitches (surprisingly), and the playerbase was huge, so there was no trouble finding a match. Unforunately, given the current issues (which have been getting worse since release), this one positive attribute is simply overwhelmed in a sea of problems.
None of the above even touches on the DLC issues. If you have taken the time to read this review, you probably already know about the flak that the publisher got for how they marketed Evolve and the associated DLC. At this point I consider the DLC problems to be a red herring. Yes, the 2K DLC is obnoxious, confusing, and expensive (especially for a full-price, 60$ game) -- but these problems don't really matter when the fundamental essence of the game itself is so flawed.
To summarize:
If you buy this game, you will be consigning yourself to a buggy game, where the wait-times are several factors longer than the play-times, and where the global concurrent playerbase population is about equal to the number of kids attending a medium-sized high school in the Bronx, NY. Please, save yourself the trouble.

I kickstarted Stonehearth and have been playing it since it was very, very simple in nature.  The graphics have remained beautiful (if you like voxels) throughout, each iteration has led to massive improvements in gameplay, and a number of bugs have been fixed - and the game is still in alpha.
One of the "big deals" about this game is that it takes the dwarf fortress approach to items in the world and materials.  It then layers LUA scripting and html (no joke) for the interface.  Its modding system isn't a modding system so much a content-delivery system.  You want a new race? Describe some things in JSON and boom.
This leads to some very, very awesome potential for BETA once all the systems are fleshed out.  The latest update added the second Kingdom, and playing as it evolves into a completely different playstyle.. and as near as I can tell it wasn't much of a code update, just a "mod" from the dev's standpoint.
This is working out to be the ultimate kingdom builder / simulator.  Like Dwarf Fortress? You're gonna love this.  Like Minecraft but don't like doing all the digging yourself? You'll love it.  Do you like casual games? Yep.

This game, where to begin. In truth, I have not been looking for another city-builder for some time. I still have my old standbys such as Ceaser 3, Stronghold, Space Colony, etc. Mind you that doesn't mean that I havent longed for something in that venue. I have always had a love of them and when a buddy of mine mentioned this I was immediatly impressed. I watched the video and then I hesitated.
Was this game going to be good? Was this going to just be me looking at it with rose-tinted glasses? Am I Elton John? But seriously, was this going to be the game that would be a return to the classics? Yes and no. To be fair this game is a gem. I feel that this game is trying to revive that old-school feel that us older gamers had the pleasure to experiance in the late 90's early 2000's. However, it does something by itself that I feel is more than just a supposed "pallet-swap".
It has character, its own character in itself. Like all the Impression games of the past, you play a person that is in charge of settlement, you obtain quests and stuff, and then you win. Unlike the old titles, this game is not set in antiquity. No this game is allowed to follow in its own footsteps without being restricted to reality.
"Can't make beer here! Use the Fae! Get the hunter to use a netgun to capture them and then squish them to make some!"
That is just one of the things that I got a chuckle out of. There are many more things in this game that will make you chuckle for just how absurd it is, but at the end of the day I see it doing that kinda absurd right.
In final thought, this game stands on its own. It might not be side-by-side with its counterparts, but it is far from being caught in the shadows. The only thing that I find that I can complain about is like with all games of this type. This is not for the generation that as born with a copy of COD in its hand. This is that kinda "Dad Game", something thats fun, relaxing, and not having to deal with people screaming "Noob" or "Pwnd" or other dumb dribble on another game.
Hats of to the developers for making a fun game, I hope to see more in the future!

If you never played Impressions Games’ Pharao, Caesar or Emperor, grab this game at once!
If you did play them, don't expect anything new. At all.
PROS:
- It looks amazing. The style is really cute, the animations are well done and the details are charming. Most walkers come in both genders which is a nice touch.
- The interface is much better than the Impressions games, aesthetically and in terms of layout. Showing the range of all walkers is really, really helpful in planning the city.
- It plays just like Impressions City Building Series.
CONS:
- It plays almost EXACTLY like Impressions City Building Series. I guess you can't do much wrong when you copy a good game (series). But aside from one or two production chains, you have to admit, it's really just a clone with a different skin. It’s actually easier than some of its spiritual predecessors.
- Steam should have played a bigger part. This is the only thing that's different from the Impressions games and there should be many more buildings that need steam. It would be a big step to set Lethis apart from the games it copies. Same with automatons. So much potential wasted…
- The statistics are only accessible when you build a town-hall, much like Banished did it, which is mostly okay. But worker distribution priorities should not be accessible through a window that’s only available when a certain building has workers. If you set the administration priority too low, your town-hall will stop working and you suddenly lose access to that window and then you have to deactivate your entire economy manually just so your town-hall has enough workers and you can change things back.
- The game does not warn you when you are about to quit the session and it doesn’t remind you of saving. If you click quit and you haven’t saved you will lose all your progress. Which is really irritating when you accidently clicked quit instead of resume.
- What are those trees that I cannot remove? Not the unique looking ones, those are cool, but plain old trees that you simply cannot remove. What’s up with that, Triskell?
- There should be more information about a building BEFORE you build it as it isn’t obvious what some of these buildings do. It would be nice if the tooltips showed more than just the price.
- Tooltips are annoyingly slow.
As someone who played the Impressions City Building Series, this game had nothing new to me. The only things I had to figure out were steam and automatons, which are both nice ideas but not developed enough, in my opinion.
Still recommending this game because it’s fun and gorgeous. But sadly, nothing new.

It's really hard to explain why this game is fun, because really, it's a game about driving crappy Russian trucks in some of the worst conditions imaginable. But it's unbelievably fun, it has enough sim-lite elements to make you feel like you're operating machines, and the multiplayer is the next level of satisfying cooperation: I like to use the crane, and my buddy is a better driver than I am, so I take a smaller truck with a hydraulic crane and load his truck with long logs, then follow along with a load of short logs just in case he gets stuck and I need to help winch or crane him out of a ditch or something. A large part of the game's fun and satisfaction comes from rolling your truck (or seeing your buddy roll his), or getting stuck in mud, or getting high-centered on a stump or whatever, then spending five or ten minutes trying progressively more ridiculous solutions until you get free (I once was only able to right my rolled truck by deploying and extending my crane's push anchors to slightly tilt my truck, then deployed and unfolded my folding trailer to flip my truck right over). Yes, it's fun, stop laughing.
Visually it looks great, it sounds great, the maps are a bit small but trust me, when you're barely able to travel 3 miles per hour because of the three-foot-deep mud they'll seem bigger than you like, and there's lots to do and lots of workshop mods for new trucks and cars. I don't regret a cent of this purchase.

Here it is, the first game in the Dragon Age franchise. It's probably been said enough times by now that it doesn't require me to repeat this, but I strongly believe it bears repeating. Dragon Age Origins is one of the best role playing games of all time! If you have the faintest interest in playing this phenomenal medieval fantasy RPG you should do so without a moment's hesitation. There is so much content waiting for you here that it's actually impossible to cover all of it without turning this review into an essay. Quite frankly the most compelling aspect of DA:O and what makes it such a great game, where even after playing through the entire story for the 2nd or 5th time, you can still come back to it having just as much fun and be as engaged as the first time playing it.
From my own experience this game should be played with as little knowledge as possible. That way you have the opportunity of getting as much out of DA:O as you can, and believe me when I say there is a lot of cool stuff that awaits you. There is such a rich open world for you to discover and be apart of, like the fascinating story involving The Great Wardens and impending Blight, not to mention your own story depending on the race and class you choose. All the memorable characters you encounter, who are all so well-written and might be the best aspect of the game, I mean the banter between the party members always get a chuckle out of me. They all have different personalities, which means they all react differently to your decisions and they all come equipped with their own talents and specializations.
Combat is an important part of the gameplay, this is where people might have mixed feelings about DA:O since this is pretty much a tactical game and it requires the player to be very strategic with their enemy encounters. However, this is not something to worry about since I think this is one of better and more accessible challenging games you can ever play. It's easy to understand even if you aren't familiar with this style of gameplay, but it does require you to learn and adapt your party members tactics. It also helps that you assess the situation by pausing anytime during combat.
Overall, this is an amazing gaming experience and I suggest giving Dragon Age Origins a chance, because this is truly an epic adventure you don't want to miss out on. A game I will personally keep coming back to for years to come!

Baldur's Gate - A 16 year old game stands up to the test of time, and it's co-op!
So during the steam summer sale, a friend of mine bought me Baldur's Gate 1(Enhanced Edition) so we could play together(the 4 pack was 20 bucks). 6 months later, we had never played together once so I finally decided that I wanted to play, so I played it solo.
Now there's a few things you should know about Baldur's Gate. The game was originally released in 1998. I played it while I was in high school my senior year. It introduced a LOT of new people to Dungeons & Dragons. It's a 3rd person isometric RPG in which you control all members of your party. It's paused based(instead of turn based), which means that when combat starts, you pause, issue commands, unpause, wait for something to happen, pause again, issue commands, etc, etc. There are lots of games with that type of system now, but as far as I know, BG was the first.
So the way you're -supposed- to play it solo is to create one character and go along recruiting AI NPCs to join your party of up to six. Well you can get around all that by playing in multiplayer mode by yourself. Multiplayer mode lets you create all six party members and tweak them to your desire. You can also export/import different characters at any time. You can easily get away with this from an RP(roleplaying) perspective by saving your game in an inn and swapping party members in and out saying "Oh I met this guy at this inn". So to start with, I created my own party of 3: Human Fighter(me), Paladin, and Cleric, then I pick up NPCs along the way. Not completely satisfied with the NPCs in game, I finished the game with 5/6 party members self generated, and only one in-game NPC(Yeslick the Dwarven Fighter/Cleric). If you enjoy character creation and tweaking things and micromanaging party members, gear, stats, and other RPG elements, this game is definately for you.
Lets talk about the story. This is where the game really drew a lot of people in. For those of you that have already played, you know what I'm talking about. I'm not going to spoil it for anyone that may play the game in the future(even if it IS 16 years old), but it's a great, great story that lets you choose your own path. Of course my path is that of the good soldier fighting for... well... good. But if you enjoy the darker side of things, it's always allowed, which a lot of games give you trouble doing. You can lie, cheat, steal, and murder and still complete the game.
Oftentimes now that I'm in my 3rd decade of life, I've gone back and tried to play games from my childhood that I remember really enjoying, and graphically none of them have stood up to the test of time(X-Com, Doom, etc). Since all of the assets in BG are more or less hand drawn and the enhanced edition lets you play at your native resolution, the game still looks pretty damn good, especially amidst the recent indy dev 8 bit gaming boom. So graphically, it passes the test. The environments are pretty freakin cool too. A whole lot of unique, hand drawn areas that I had forgotten about since I first played a long time ago that made me say "huh, cool" when I came across them recently.
And now let's talk difficulty. Holy ♥♥♥♥ is this game hard. It's been so long since I've played a game that didn't just blatantly hold my hand and coddle me the whole way through I'd forgotten what it's like to play a game that punishes you. AD&D 2.0 core rules are a huge ♥♥♥♥♥ and completely unforgiving. There are 5 difficulty levels in the game:
-Easy - Everything does half damage, all hit point gains per level are maximized, and characters can't permanently die.
- Normal - Everything does 75% damage, all hit point gains per level are maximized, and characters can't permanently die.
- Core Rules - Everything does 100% damage, hit point gains are randomized(so you can get as little as 1 hp/level on your badass front-line fighter that needs ~10 hp/level), and characters can permanently die.
- Hard - Everything does 150% damage
- Insane - Everything does 200% damage and you are a satan worshipping masochist
I may have added that last little part on the insane bit.
So being the badass gaming veteran I am, I of course choose Core Rules. I understand what THAC0 is, I know what the different classes are, I know how to D&D. I'm good.
Or so I thought.
I'm actually not as good as I had thought. I had to do a LOT of fights multiple times because Jesus Christ, this game can be hard. Mostly with the crowd control abilities the enemies get(note - If you fight against a group that has a mage, KEEP YOUR PARTY SPREAD OUT just like in ArmA). A lot of times I'd get hit with an AoE fear or confuse or stun, etc, etc, etc. It could be infuriating, but I kept re-loading and going at the fights in different manners from different angles, and analyzing my party and their abilities and switching things around until finally, at the end of the game, I had SOME sort of idea of what I was doing... I thought... until the final battle.
Let's just say that the final battle in Baldur's Gate had me curled up in a fetal position in the corner of my room praying to Torm asking him what I had done so poorly to have been punished so badly.
So somewhere between 20 and 50 attempts later, I managed to defeat the final boss and win the game. I even had to google strategies for the final boss. I actually felt a sense of accomplishment like I haven't felt in a game in a long, long time. The funny part is, 17 year old me beat the game in 1998 without the internet for guidance. I have NO CLUE how I managed that feat.
So I immediately went to steam and bought Baldur's Gate 2 enhanced edition, even though it's not on sale, and started a new game. This time, however, I'm playing on normal mode. It seems to be a much better balance of playability vs difficulty. I've still lost some fights, but I've learned a whole damn lot and built my party around the strengths needed.
I have a Cavalier paladin because he: 1. Can't be feared, charmed, mind controller, or poisoned; and 2. He can make the entire party immune to fear pretty much all the time. He's also a badass tank alongside my main character which is a frontline fully maximized fighter with sword and shield. I also have a pure Dwarven Cleric, Fighter/Thief, Fighter/Mage, and Dragon Disciple Sorcerer. I dual classed the Thief and Mage with Fighter bases so they could use longbows for good DPS instead of being relegated to a shortbow and a sling. The nice side to that is that they get fighter HP for their first 7 levels so they're pretty beefy on top of it all.
I just pretend(roleplay) that my entire group is a squad of trained military soldiers that have been sent on a mission, so they almost all have that base fighter class from their military training.
So I have 2 tanks(FIghter/Cavalier Paladin), a pure healing Cleric, and 3 pure DPS(Thief/Mage/Sorcerer). But don't be fooled, that fighter and paladin can put out some melee hurt too. The cleric is really the only non-dps class. Oh... Make sure you -always- have a thief in your party with the script that makes him passively detect traps. Trust me on this. You don't necessarily need a thief/rogue that can stealth, but you damn sure need one that can detect/disarm traps and pick locks.
And on that note, there are pre-set scripts that you can use for each character. There are about 20 for all the different classes in the game to mess around with. I pretty much have my whole group on the standard "I see an enemy and attack with my equipped weapon", except for my rogue, who is set to always passively detect traps when not in combat, and my cleric who is set to dynamically run around and heal. I micromanage everything else(mage spells mostly).

Been playing the Early Access for 2 years now and I've always said that even if they never released story mode, I would have been just as happy playing the sandbox game. It's my favorite suvival game and, to me, watching the tweaks and patches the devs have put into the game over the years just shows the care and dedication they have for the project. Now that they've released story mode, I've been playing that as well and I'm liking it. It's still a challenging experience but not *punishing*. In the harder sandbox modes I felt like the hunger and thirst depletion system was just way overpowered and was worried about how much of a problem it would be in story mode, but actually it isn't bad. Dunno if things will get more difficult in the later episodes, but for now I like how things are. I haven't felt like the difficulty level has inhibited my ability to further the plot. And now there's actual NPC's and quests to break up the monotony of surviving. It's a beautiful and challenging game, and I'm really digging the voice acting in story mode. All in all a great way to kill an evening.
For all the new players out there jumping in to story mode, I will say that there is definitely a learning curve when starting out. I feel like I'm surviving as well as I am because I've been playing in sandbox mode for so long and pretty much know the ropes. So stick with it, browse the forums for helpful tips, check out the Long Dark Wiki. Once you get the hang of it, I promise it's less running around constantly in a panic while steps away from death and more...running around only slightly less panicked but at least knowing what you need to do to survive ;)

All jokes aside, I've owned the long dark since shortly after its release into early access. The game has gone through many changes, most very welcome. I find the addition of the story mode to be the factor that makes it feel like a complete game. Sure, sandbox mode is fun, but it only takes about a week in game for things to start feeling monotonous. The story mode shakes things up with actual objectives to keep you interested in playing.
The main issue I have with the game right now is its balance. For example, sometimes firewood is plentiful, so much so you can practically put a fire anywhere you want to without any real concern. Other times its virtually impossible to find, leaving you with 3 sticks to stave off the elements. (Granted, this is how it would be if you were trying to survive IRL, so I really have no basis to complain)
Another issue I have is with some of the core mechanics of the game, primarily the lack of anything close to a "jump." I'm not asking for a super mario kind of jump, just something to make traversing the varied terrain a bit easier. The other mechanic I have an issue with is the throwables. There is nothing to give you any idea of where what you are trying to throw is going to land. I find myself consistently underthrowing just about everything, making early hunting tedious. This issue ties into the beginning of my review, as one of the primary ways you defend yourself from wolves, is by throwing a lit torch at said wolf. On 3 seperate occasions, I've thrown a torch within 5 feet of a wolf, only to have it completely ignore it. As one can imagine, having your wolf defense within striking range of a wolf isn't advantageous.
Overall, I feel like the long dark is about 95% done. With a little more polish and a few tweaks, I think it would definitely be worth picking up.

The Good: This is a beautiful, immersive game that really puts you into the wild and gives you a sense of dread that nightfall is coming. If you've camped in freezing weather, you will relive that here. Although I haven't completed the story mode, I feel the story is compelling enough and wasn't just an afterthought after the devs made sandbox mode.
The Bad: The character models are lacking and don't really match the overall art direction, especially the inventory screen. The UI for inventory is frustrating, certain effects aren't really explained so it makes comparing equipment a crapshoot. THE GAME IS HARD! The reward for finally killing a rabbit with a stone is a sliver of hunger points... which now you're likely low on temperature, tiredness and water. Food is sparse!
The Ugly: The autosave state is rough. In story mode, I got myself into a deadlock situation where I ventured too far into my inevitable death, but the last save was seconds before my death. I was forced to restart from beginning (luckily it was early). Pros:
- A well designed/built urban gameworld that captures Industrial London extremely well
- Switchable player characters
- A nice sized cast of memorable fictional and historical characters
- Fluid, albeit easy, combat
- A balanced amount of side missions, collectables, and gear
Cons:
- Modern day storyline leaves a lot to be desired
- Abnormally large amount of technical issues with the Jack the Ripper DLC
The Bottom Line:
Simply put, Syndicate is an improvement on Unity in almost all aspects. The storyline is comprehensible, the characters are three dimensional and memorable, combat returns to a simpler but more fluid and visually entertaining design, and above all else Syndicate manages to properly balance its amount of side missions, collectibles, and weapons/gear. Additionally, Ubisoft learned from its mistakes in Unity by NOT trying to force us into co-op missions or obtaining a smartphone/tablet application in order to get the full experience.
However, Syndicate does show us that Ubi is still having some issues getting its modern day storyline/characters off the ground post-Desmond era. Things were much more straight forward and interesting when it was just Desmond and friends trying to prevent the end of the world in 2012. Now, the modern day plot has just become so bogged down with Sages, Abstergo entertainment fronts, the Initiates, and Juno having free reign of the digital world (and of coarse what they've now added in Syndicate involving the Shroud and the Precursor race). While players may have complained about poor ol' Desmond during his time I think it's safe to say we miss him and are in dire need of a new modern protagonist.
Finally, it does appear that a portion of the player base continues to have technical problems on the same scale as with Unity. Personally I have not experieced any of these issues outside of the Jack the Ripper DLC which crashed quite often and glitched out with things like throwing carriages across the map. If you're looking at purchasing this game I would go ahead and try and figure out what kind of setups those experiencing issues have to avoid any possible disappointments.
All in all, I would certainly say that if you lost faith in the series after Unity you'll want to give Syndicate a spin - it may very well restore your faith in Assassin's Creed.

This game isn't finished, It's that simple. The producers of this game did not have the care to make a quality product, and have given the gaming community a gimmicky arena type fighter that always ends in the same anti climactic way. I'll admit, this game was fun... for about 2 hours, then it became the same damn thing every match. If you still want to buy this game, be prepared for the following...
1. Limited Roster: I should point out that there are 16-20 hunters in the game right now, and 4 monsters. However, about half of the hunters are in DLC packs, and 1 of the monsters is as well. They have it all bundled together for around $30.00... that is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you bought the game while it was on the recent steam sale, you would've  spend $20.00 on the original game, then $30.00 more on the DLC? since when is add-on content more than the game itself? No thanks.
2. The same 20 minute game over and over and over:  If you play as the monster, you won't have too much fun... your match consists of running and hiding, eating, hiding, running, eating, getting caught, spamming your abilties, running, healing, eating, evolving, eating, attacking, running, hiding, eating, attacking for the final time, and probably still dying.
Now if you play as the hunters, you are looking at an even worse time to be honest. All 4 roles on the team are imperitive, and so 1 weak link will throw the game. The hunters' match consists of tracking, killing wildlife, tracking, finding the monster, doming him in your arena, fighting, getting a downed medic/support, watching the monster escape, healing, wait for the stronger evolved monster to show up, get picked off, and die. Again, I swear every match feels exactly the same, there are a few other game modes, but I seriously don't find them balanced, or even finished for that matter.
3. Glitches beyond belief! You will find there are issues with the collisions a lot of times. Many monster abilities can cause the humans to be forced through the floor and into the void. I recall a specific intance, I was learning the ropes of the game playing the assault class. I kept finding my health dangerously low, and hoping the medic would come heal me, it wasn't until after I had gone down, I had realized she was about 40 feet under the map, trapped in limbo. Is this really a AAA title?
4. Dumb leveling: When I first started playing, the game was up for a free demo. I had picked up the Wraith monster, he being the 3rd of them all. I really started to like him, and had many of his abilities skilled nearly to the second tier. Well once the demo was over, the game reverted me back to default unlockables. Which meant I would have to learn and play  Goliath, and skill him, then do the same with Kraken, just to be able to play the monster I like again. The same was true for the hunters too. Remember the $30.00 worth of DLC you could buy? Well in this game, that doesn't mean jack♥♥♥♥♥♥apperently, because of the 16-20 hunters I had available, after the demo, I was limited to playing and skilling the basic 4, before I could unlock the others. Let the players play who they want to play... seriously.
5. Matchmaking is garbage: Evolve uses skill based matchmaking, which is great! I'm all for having a fair game. The problem is that skill based matchmaking takes the number of players online, and limits your matchmaking potential. Combine that with the fact that evolve has hardly anyone online anymore (can't imagine why) and oh ya! all that DLC you can buy, limits the number of compatible matches too! I swear, I've waited 30 minutes before, for a 20 minute game. Waste of time.
6.Becoming insulted as a gamer: It is a game producer's job to ensure quality, and deliver an interesting gaming experience in every title they produce. That's not to say a company isn't able to flop occasionally, that will happen. However, when a AAA company takes a title they had miserably over-scoped and over-hyped, and decides to still release it, knowing they aren't done, just to add DLC within the first few weeks of launch, is downright insulting to the consumer. We deserve better than this.
In conclusion, I am unimpressed with Evolve. I believe it is an abomination of a game, that was glorified for no justified reason. The game is gimmicky as hell and feels like a beta. Not worth the $20.00 I paid, definitely not worth the $70.00 they charged at launch, and sure as hell not worth buying add on content for. If you still want to buy this game, please save your money, I wish someone had warned me. I would have taken my $50.00 and spent it on indie games or something, at least indie producers still care.

I've been playing this series since the Sega Saturn - back then, you had to import it from Japan and play it in Japanese.  I stuck with it through the Dreamcast, PSX, and PS2 incarnations, including the English and Japanese versions of the Gameboy Advance games.
I even bought the horrible XBOX 360 one - don't worry, these guys had nothing to do with that one.  It doesn't count.  Forget it existed.
I've been playing this series for almost 20 years, and am a loyal customer that buys everything as soon as it comes out - I had to get my hands on a new Firepro every time it dropped.
What sucks is, it's been 12 years since the last one came out (I'm going by the Japanese release date, because I imported that one too).  So I've been playing that one for 12 years, thinking we're never getting a new Firepro again.
NOW WE HAVE ONE.  Yeah, it's an early access title and there's still a little work to be done here or there, but this is everything I wanted from a new Firepro game, and more.  The overhaul of Wrestler Edit and the addition of layers has really let you make some revolutionary stuff.
Mission mode is pretty fun.  I'm at around mission 25 or so, and completing it unlocks moves and edit points.  These are useful moves you're going to want in your game, too.
Yeah, there's a learning curve for new people.  There was for me 20 years ago, but I was able to pick this up right away and start dropping mofos on their heads.  Once you learn to play, you're gonna have a great time.  Patience is key.  You'll get it, don't worry.
If you're new to the series, your biggest obstacle to enjoyment is learning to play the game.  Mine was figuring out how to get it from Japan, getting it to run on my US console, and navigating a game completely in Japanese.  You're being handed everything!  Put the work in and you're gonna love it.

I am a die hard Fire Pro fan and right now I am having a great time playing this. The hype is real.

Finally... The greatest wrestling series of all time, has come to Steam!
Fire Pro Wrestling World is a dream come true. I've been a fan of the series ever since I found out I could play SNES roms on my computer way back in the day... I accidentally discovered Fire Pro and I've been hooked ever since. I don't know if it was the charm of the old school 2d sprites, or the fact that the wrestling was pretty deep. Tons of moves, and the possibilities of creating tons of my favorite wrestlers. It was just addicting.
With Fire Pro World, all the features we've come to love have returned, and more. Currently the game is still in early access, but it's very playable in it's current stage, and the community is posting thousands of workshop creations making this one of the greatest Fire Pro games ever released... And the full version isn't even out yet!
So what are we working with in early access. We have standard offline modes with all the match modes from Fire Pro history minus one. So that means, normal matches, tag matches, cage matches, barbed-wire exploding death matches, landmine matches, an MMA style cage... It's pretty nuts. There is a mission mode that serves as an in game tutorial. Honestly my only complaint comes from the mission mode. I find the tutorials helpful, but they've locked away attribute points and some moves for your created wrestlers... I think this is a dumb move since the last game pretty much came with everything unlocked. I guess the devs want to try to encourage people to play the game instead of just simming matches. Yes, one thing that is very big in the Fire Pro community is just sitting back and watching the action. Part of process for creating a wrestler is that you can actually design the wrestler's AI behavior, or as it's refereed to in the game, "Logic". This makes the game even more deep, as you can create wrestlers and have them perform matches anyway you like. This is my first experience with a Zachtronics game and Wow! it is just amazing!
The genius behind this concept is remarkable, you are tasked with constructing "products" from "reagents" using various mechanics available. The mechanics function in a kinematic and transitional way such that well conceived arangements will achieve the result required... However, there is a twist, you are given data related to your resource usage which is shown on a histogram of statistics available from the community. This gives you the option of replaying your design to attempt to match or beat the best results available granting endless replayability... Genius! You can also create a GIF of your result and show it to your friends meaning aesthetics are a consideration as well.
Graphics and Sound are excellent and I love the overall theme of the game. Personally, I have been skipping the story part because I found it to be tedious, but that is just my personal opinion. I think it should be an option to turn off the story elements if you don't wish to see it (those who enjoy it can leave it on) this is my only small criticism. The game is (at the time of this review) in early access, however it feels like a complete game.

Opus Magnum is a game that's similar to one of Zachtronics' previous games, The Codex, (available online on their website) at first glance, but once you dive in there's just so much more to it all. As you try to create products throughout the several puzzles in the game to complete, you'll see that you have so much more freedom than in other Zachtronics games to get the task done. This in turn, may not necessarily mean that the game is easier, but it sure feels more welcoming/accessible. (Perhaps that might just be for me though, as of writing this review I'm currently on chapter 4/5 of the main campaign after roughly 11 hours of gameplay.)
I also appreciate the continuation of a story being behind all of the puzzles that you solve, just like how they did it in Shenzhen I/O. As a whole, it's very intriguing as well. This and the combination of the game's music changing from puzzle to puzzle acts as a nice motivation tool to keep going and see what happens next. (Everything's still enjoyable though, sorry if that sounded like they were just extremely minor to the game..which they kind of are, just not.. extremely.)
Oh, and the new solitaire, or rather, mahjong (the matching tile one, not
mahjong) mini game, Sigmar's Garden? Hell. Yeah. I kept coming back to it whenever I had some time to add a few wins to the counter or just relax from the main campaign before going back into it. Just like Shenzhen Solitaire it's easy to pick up and semi-hard to master.
If you're more into the non-coding Zachtronics games like Infinifactory, Spacechem, and The Codex, (especially The Codex,) I highly recommend giving Opus Magnum a try, it's beautiful. You could even say Opus Magnum is Zachtronics'...

I didn't even know anything new was in the works.  I was just craving a programming puzzler, I looked up Zachtronics to find a "similar to" link, and there it was.  I'm a simple man.  I see a new Zachtronics game, I buy.  I imagine if quasi-programming-logic-puzzle games appeal to you you already do the same.
This one is actually a fleshing out of an old Flash game he had done many years back.  So far it feels like a SpaceChem that you program in Turtle.
In addition to the clever puzzle mechanics and perfect difficulty scaling, Zach has come so far in world-building.  I loved the immersive "desktop" environment of Shenzhen; this one is a bit of personal correspondence mixed in with some 3rd-person comic panel dialog.  I would never ask for it in a puzzle game where I was already happy with the gameplay, but characters and environments just pull you in a little bit more.

If you played city builders by Impressions Games in the 90s and 00s (Caesar III, Pharaoh, and so forth) then you pretty much know all you need to know to play Lethis. So you can skip the tutorial, which is good because it's annoying.
The same game mechanics of buildings housing to attract immigrants, plunking down buildings that spawn "walkers" to provide services to the houses, which make the houses level up, building farms and buildings to move raw materials along a chain. The one improvement over the Impressions games is they just dropped combat altogether, which was always the worst part of those games anyhow.
Graphically it's prettier, of course. IT has a hand-drawn look. Steam page says it's Steampunk, but think cheerful Studio Ghibli-ish steampunk, not the grittier kind so in vogue these days. The music helps sustain the Ghibli vibe, and in some ways is more surprising than the game itself.
Its a French game, and the English translation is amateurish but at times hilarious. I still don't know what to make of the game promising to "reward you portly" for successfully completing the first mission.  (You will be rewarded so much you'll become portly? You'll be rewarded with a cask of port? Je ne sais pas.)
So it's very much a sort of tribute to that style of city builder, which has largely been replaced by more sophisticated games. You can't, for example, delve down into your population and see what individuals are up to, it's just a numbers game of balancing your population (you need enough to get your buildings to function, but too many and the unemployment will cause problems.) There are few small innovations--creating a network of steam extractors, for example--but for the most part the strategy is the same.
SO, though I like the game, and enjoy the aesthetics it brings, I can't recommend it for everyone, or even for all city builder enthusiasts. It's a very specific kind of city builder. If you liked Pharaoh or Zeus, then you will probably like Lethis, But I can't really say whether you'll like it more, or whether it brings enough new to the game to justify the purchase. Especially when you can still get ahold of those Impressions games from gog.

I kickstarted Stonehearth and have been playing it since it was very, very simple in nature.  The graphics have remained beautiful (if you like voxels) throughout, each iteration has led to massive improvements in gameplay, and a number of bugs have been fixed - and the game is still in alpha.
One of the "big deals" about this game is that it takes the dwarf fortress approach to items in the world and materials.  It then layers LUA scripting and html (no joke) for the interface.  Its modding system isn't a modding system so much a content-delivery system.  You want a new race? Describe some things in JSON and boom.
This leads to some very, very awesome potential for BETA once all the systems are fleshed out.  The latest update added the second Kingdom, and playing as it evolves into a completely different playstyle.. and as near as I can tell it wasn't much of a code update, just a "mod" from the dev's standpoint.

This game... is hard for me to put into words. There is a apocraphyal rumor out there that this game had been developed to completion by BioWare before its sale to EA. And that EA freaked after the sale when they discovered this. But when you play this game, you can see the detail and attention that BioWare put into it. Some would say it is the finest game BioWare ever made (I still say Knights of the Old Republic was better, but this is a darn close second).
The quests are epic. The gameplay is fantastic. The characters are well-developed and have rich backstories. There are six origin stories for your PC, and two of them have differences depending on factors (the Magi differs slightly if you are human or elf, and the City Elf Origin differs in a rather signifact way depending on gender). You have some of the greatest companions in BioWare games (Leliana, Morrigan, Sten, even Alistair). The romances make sense... depending on who you pursue.
And the background... The Fifth Blight, the Grey Wardens, Ferelden... all of it is wonderful. And then there is the soundtrack... some of it is heart-wrenching.
And of course... you have to save the world. And in this game, a lot of that saving is from itself.
And since the Ultimate Edition brings along with it all the expansions... it gets even more epic.
Cannot recommend this game enough.

Ah, X-COM. A game with a learning curve like running into a brick wall and a margin of error comparable to the pope's patience with me, which is to say almost nil. That said, this is an extremely engaging tactical/stratetic game that demands you exercise the 3P's of X-COM success: Planning, Patience, and Paranoia. You'll be put in charge of what amounts to the UN (but with more guns) and told to fight off incoming swarms of aliens, nick their stuff, and use it against them, then take the fight back to them. Sounds simple enough, but once you go into the game and really get your feet on the ground of your first battle, that changes. Think tactically, use your turns wisely, and never let your soldiers go Rambo, or else you'll end the mission with an even higher casualty count than usual. For those who are already familiar with turn based tactical games, try the Ironman challenge, and only save between missions. A great game series and set that's easy on the processor and the wallet.
