While it's flaws are glaring, Dishonored still manages to be one of my favorite games, and I wholeheartedly recommend it.
NOTE - This review contains the endings of the game so spoiler alert.
Gameplay: The gameplay is fantastic. It has probably the best first person melee system I have ever seen in a game. Combat is quick and sharp, and it manages to make seem like you are acutally fighting with swords. It's not like most games where; with a razor sharp weapon, you can be bashing at a guy for 5+ hits - Enemies go down in 1 to 4(MAX) slashes, but so do you, so you actually have to be careful when taking on enemies because you can't simply tank blows.
Dishonored also manages to do first person parkour pretty well. Movement is quick and free, and you usually dont have to worry about falling off of ledges simply because you moved a fraction of a centimeter to far in any given direction. The powers are very fun, and add tons to gameplay. There are also many gadgets that are fun as well, such as spring wire traps (I recommend attaching them to a rat, possessing it, and moving it close to guards; it never gets old), crossbows, and the coolest sword I have ever seen. However, the gameplay still has flaws. The hitboxes can be... challenging. Time and time again a man has swung a sword at me from the opposite side of a room and I have taken damage from it. The AI is pretty wonky as well. There will be times when you are moving along the top of a building and a guard will see you from the other side of a courtyard and other times you will be right next to a guard, nearly touching him, and he will not notice at all. However, these are mostly minor flaws and the gameplay is probably one of the best, if not the best thing in the game.
Story:  While the world the story takes place in is fascinating, the main plot is nothing special. It's a classic tale of revenge, and while this type of story is one of my favorites, I admit there is nothing special about it. The characters are underdeveloped and shallow, and simply act as reasons for there to be more gameplay, and while the gameplay is fantastic, it still doesn't excuse the robots that you have to deal with on a regular basis. My main problem with the story is that it feels rushed and unfinished. Like I said earlier, the game world is fantastic. It is a victorian era  with steampunk, magic and even a bit of lovecraftian elements mixed in. However, ALMOST NONE OF IT IS EXPANDED UPON. There is a character called the Outsider who gives you your powers, and seems to be some sort of dark trickster god. While he is interesting, and cool, he offers very little to the story and is mainly to the side. Why? It would be so much more interesting if he played a bigger roll in the story, or if he even had a bigger presence, but no. He simply gives you your powers and pops up every so often to chit chat and to narrate the ending. There is such  a huge disconnect between the magical elements of the story and the main plot that they seem to be taking place in different rooms. THe second to worst flaw are the endings. For instance, the plague, which is a HUGE, HUGE, HUGE part of the game world and story is tossed to the wayside at the end. Now let me reiterate - This plague has been ravaging your country - people are dead and dying in the streets. There is a part of a mission where the ground is LITERALLY MADE OF THE CORPSES OF PLAGUE VICTIMS. And how it this problem solved? It's never explained. IT IS NEVER EXPLAINED. In the good ending (which has to deal with the moral choice system, and trust me I'll get to that later) the plague simply goes away. You never learn where the plague comes from. You never learned why it happened. You never even get to see how it is cured, it simply goes away. This is particularily frustrating because you find documents in the game that allude to the plague being a part of something bigger, but then it just throws what could be buildup to an amazing ending away like it was nothing. The good ending is saccharin. Like I said the plague magically goes away and everything is good always and forever. The other two endings (The bad and really bad) just feel like non standard game overs. The normal bad ending ends with Emily going WAY out of character and becoming evil out of the blue, and the game basically just calls you a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and ends. The really bad ending is basically "Everyone died horribly and you ran away; The End." Not to mention the fact that the so called "twist" that happens is so forced and unnecesary that it is simply painful. This is a shame because it feels like Dishonored could do way better than this, but for some reason, whether it be a lack of time, money, or simply a lack of enthusiasm towars the end of development, the game simply throws up it's hands and says "Screw it."
This all leads to the biggest problem I have with th game is the moral choice system. OH GOD THE MORAL CHOICE SYSTEM. I hate it so much because it tries to ruin everything in the game. You may not believe me, but it really does. Almost all of the gadgets, upgrades, and magic you get are lethal or could be really fun when used lethally, but guess what: Killing guards gives you the bad endings. So not only does it give complete crappy endings, but the moral choice system makes it so that you cannont bring the gameplay to it's greatest potential without getting a non-standard game over as the ending.
There are so many good things about this game. The gamplay is so much fun and the game world and lore are both so interesting, and the art style is such a great and fitting match for the game. But between the moral choice system, short length, boring characters, and an unfinished story that is disconnected to the game world, there just seems to be so much wasted potential. I really and truly hope that Dishonored 2 can fix these issues, because if it can, it might just be one of the best games ever made.

Early Access Player, started playing 2 years ago, 120+ hours.
Early Access Impression: It has finally arrived and it is completely worth it. I have seen many changes occur throughout the development cycle and it has been a rewarding experience seeing it evolve. Most of the time Early Access games are a bit of a let down, but the developers have done a great job managing expectations, delivering on time, and fixing issues.
'After completing Episode One' Review: I would recommend this game to anyone who likes the survival genre, and wishes for a game that's closer to reality than others. It is pretty much like snow camping with a large amount of blizzards. If you watch survivor shows, all the rules apply here: you'll need to focus on how to conserve your calories, plan ahead for movement, manage emergencies, etc. Once you get over the learning curve, which can be assisted by basic survival knowledge, it'll be a rewarding game to play and invest time in as you see yourself get better and better at understanding the environment and gameplay.
Pros: Beautiful Graphical Style, Excellent Survival Mechanics, Genuinely Fun Game that has kept me playing for years, Wonderful Love Letter to the amazing outback of Canada. The length of the first episode seemed very good, and had a lot of activity and valuable lessons for new players cutting their teeth.
Cons: Many explainations on how to do things, or why you do certain things, are missing (see below for a few pointers). This makes it easier for old players, but harder for new players that do not know certain things. I have completely disagreed with two developers choices: matches should not degrade (thus limiting how long the sandbox games can go on), and ferro-rods should basically be limitless (as they practically are in real life). Finally, the dialog in Episode One is a little rough and halting, it doesn't really seem to flow very well and can be a bit tedious to listen to.
New Player Knowledge: 1) Crouch when hunting rabbits. 2) Whenever you find a place you're going to stay for awhile and your immediate survival needs are handled, you need to focus on curing pelts and guts before running errands. Look around the environment, find that deer carcass, start a fire nearby, and get the pelt and guts out of it ASAP and onto the indoors floor. Curing takes in game days after being dropped on the floor so it is important to get the process started. 3) Before sleeping, remove all your clothing if you are indoors (houses and large structures). This will decrease wear on your clothing and you will need to repair it less. 4) A huge amount of this game has to do with managing inventory and weight. You should think about things like, should I really be carrying 1kg of matches? Should I drink water or a soda? (I think the benefits of using soda before trying to work with plain water is preferred as it seems heavier for the same water value and has food calories). What kind of kindling should I carry?

First, you need to know that there are two game modes in The Long Dark: Campaign and Sandbox.
It is partly a brilliant game (sandbox), and partly a mess (campaign).
Sandbox is, in my eyes, where the core of the game can be found. In sandbox there is just you, nature, no tutorials. You explore the beautiful winterworld while trying to learn the mechanics and how you can thrive.
The beauty of The Long Dark is how slow it is. It's not a high-action game; it is slowly walking through snow on a foggy night knowing you'll freeze to death if you don't find shelter, or the happiness of a full belly and a fire to warm yourself by. Sandbox is permadeath so if/when you die; accept your fate, learn from your mistakes, and start over.
This game mode has been out for years in early access and has been tweaked and finely tuned. There are also challenges and milestones to reach if you want something more than "just" surviving.
This is now fixed with a "Custom" mode where you can edit separate survival settings!
Campaign/story mode combines the free-roaming permadeath sandbox mentioned above with a railroad story. The campaign, unfortunately, has some issues:
* Only 2 episodes still out - not a full story yet. More episodes will be released 2017-2018.
* There is no save system, so if you end up at a bad autosave then you are out of luck.
* The tutorial is clunky at best, with some core mechanics never being thoroughly explained.
* No full voice acting
* As of 2017-08-06 there are a lot of bugs in the campaign. The developers are active and are patching the game with an impresssive speed. Hopefully within two weeks or so the campaign will be stable enough without any frustrating gamebreaking issues. (Update: 2017-09-17 there are still issues. Wait until more episodes are out before starting play...)
* The majority of quests are fetch quests. Get 1000 of that, 20 kgs of this, 500 of those etc...
* You have to play the game one way - no dialogue choices. It would have been an interesting moral dilemma to be able to leave the NPC's behind to starve but as of now you have no choice but to play along with their whims.
* No difficulty slider if you find the campaign too easy or too difficult.
* Wolves not optional; In campaign mode, you will get attacked by wildlife from time to time. At the start I liked them; They brought an edge to the game and kept me on my toes, but after a few hours I realized they just kept me from exploring the world.
A big plus is the intriguing world lore and learning of the state of mankind when disaster hit.
I think my problem is that I expected a long, finely sculpted, story-rich survival adventure and I find myself on the forum sending wishlist requests and reporting bugs. If the issues in story mode are fixed, I will definitely change my review to a positive one.
I really want to like this game. It has so much potential, but the state of campaign paired with the fact that the story is the major selling points on the store page, I can't give The Long Dark a positive review.
If you like survival games, sandbox will give you hours and hours of fun. Just don't buy the game for the campaign.

Do you enjoy RPGs, the forgotten realms, and dying over and over again?  Do you oft fondly recall the days of yore, when video gaming didn't hold your hand, and gaming worlds were as brutal as real life?  Do you know what THAC0 means?
If you've been answering yes, by golly this game is for you!
Baldurs Gate was a game I fondly remembered from my younger years of gaming.  I had never beaten it, and my discs (all 5, yes 5 for an isometric top down RPG) got so scratched from removing them from the stupid cardboard sleeve that I thought I was never going to play again.  But lo and behold, the Enhanced Edition came along to remind me that games used to be hard.  The quicksave button will be your friend, as you should be using it roughly every 2-3 minutes.  Going to enter that house?  Quicksave.  Finish a fight?  Quicksave.  Going to talk to some guy?  Damn right you better quicksave.
If you ever played Dungeons and Dragons with the second edition ruleset, you already know what you're getting into, and I shouldn't have to convince you to play this.
Bottom line:  This is one of the best PC RPGs ever made, and if you enjoy a good RPG not created to the Japanese style, you owe it to yourself to play this game.  It is difficult, stat heavy, humerous, long, and rewarding.  Combat is a turn based system, with a "pause to issue commands" structure.  On screen combat looks real time, because everything happens in the background.  I highly suggest turning on combat rolls, and other combat messages in the options so you know what's actually happening.
Oh, and the quicksave button is "Q".  Now get out there and kill some Kobolds.  Enjoy.

If you're a fan of pro wrestling, and maybe even if you're not, you'll likely enjoy this game. This is as much a simulation game as it is a multiplayer fighting type game. You can create your own wrestling promotion with custom belts, wrestlers, etc. and the Workshop is full of faithful recreation of wrestlers past and present, plus tons of fantast creations, and it will only get bigger. Just about any match type or ruleset is represented, and The graphics aren't the most cutting edge, but even without hyper realistic 3D graphics the game is pretty, smooth, and you can make very strong likenesses of modern wrestlers. This is the kind of game where even if you don't play it, you can easily enjoy making dream matches of various wrestlers and other characters and seeing how they fare in various match types.
Some shortcomings personally are that while the controls are great and smooth once you get used to them, certain things aren't really intuitive or explained in any way, even with the tutorial. For instance, nowhere does the game tell you how to pick up weapons when inside the ring, or how to properly throw your opponent over the top rope in a Battle Royale. Once you learn these minor intricacies everything feels very smooth, but I wish they were more adequately explained. Another issue I've personally experienced is that weapons such as chairs, bats, and kendo sticks feel like they have very spotty hit detection. Swings that look like they would hit aren't hitting, which can be irritating when you just want to smack someone with a steel chair.
The game is in early access, but doesn't feel particularly unfinished. Though I hope there is a very long support cycle, the game as it is doesn't feel particularly barebones or overly buggy to the point of unplayability. All in all it's definitely worth keeping an eye on at the very least, either to purchase now or follow until it leaves Early Access.

The first thing to know about Maize is that it’s one of those games that’s gloriously ridiculous, from start to finish (i mean, a game about talking corn has to be, right?). Besides knowing that, i had very little idea about what the story was about, what the gameplay was like, and what, or who, i was even playing as. In today’s age of sometimes being overwhelmed by information about upcoming games (or even movies/tv shows), it was actually kind of nice to go into this mostly blind. And since I had no idea of what to expect, i learned almost everything about the world, story and characters as i went along. Right from the beginning then, this gave the game a nice sense of mystery. And although it’s a pretty linear experience, that sense of mystery helped make everything feel much more open and interesting as you wandered around, discovering something new around each corner. Add in some witty writing, unique and funny characters, and a wonderfully detailed and graphically enticing world, and you get a very enjoyable little adventure.
The game begins with you waking up in a corn field. You’ll explore a bit of the surrounding area before descending deeper into a complex below the farm. You quickly realize there were a few people conducting some weird experiments, and from there, you’re on a quest to find out exactly what happened and where everyone went. As you go through the game, you’ll find tons of sticky notes that reveal the history about the place and the people in it. You will also run into a few other characters who will help guide you on your way, fill in more of the story, and insult you constantly. The more lighthearted atmosphere of the game is broken up by a subtle eeriness, that reminded me a lot of the feeling i had in Portal 2, especially the older, subterranean office areas.
While gameplay is somewhat minimal, i wouldn’t call it a walking simulator. Most of what you’ll be doing is solving light puzzles, that usually entail finding objects and carrying them around until you can combine them with other objects. Nothing complicated or overly challenging, but enjoyable enough. One of my favorite parts of the game though, deals with the things you find while exploring. Once you get an item, you can bring up a brief description about it, which is always entertaining to read and usually quite funny. I was always excited to find something new for this reason, even if it was just a simple rock on the ground (your character loves rocks). By the end of the game, i was left wanting to know more about the main and supporting characters as well as the complex itself. That’s always a good sign imo, letting me know the developers succeeded in creating a world worth knowing about. As for the controls, you can run and crouch, but no jumping (boo!). And just a heads up for the controller users, you can can use it while actually playing, but not in the menus (at least for the time being).
Graphically, the game looks really good, especially in the above ground areas. Detailed textures mixed with fitting post process effects and colors help give the game a unique look. I also appreciated the subdued retro aesthetic, that helps add to the history of the farm. You can definitely tell the artists spent a good amount of time making this a visually interesting place to explore. Voice acting is top notch and while there isn’t a ton of music, the tracks that are in it compliment the atmosphere perfectly.
Like Ghost of a Tale, Albino Lullaby and The Cursed Forest, Maize is another gem of a game that tends to fly under a lot of people’s radars. Which is a shame since it’s such a fun and unique experience. If you’re looking for a quirky, laid-back game, with talking corn and condescending robot bears, this is the one for you! Highly recommended.
Thanks to Daniel at Finish Line Games and Victoria at Evolve for the review copy.

Fans of the original Fire Pro Wrestling games - don't be afraid. As you can see by the reviews pouring in on Early Access Day 1, this game is another hit from Spike! FPW Returns again, this time on Steam! That means that you can empty those CAW website bookmarks. No more following those old GameFAQs-styled guides; getting a solid AJ Styles, Kurt Angle, Andre the Giant, WHOEVER you want is as simple as clicking that little plus button on the Steam workshop! For curious new players - if you're a wrestling fan and you want a wholesome, realistic experience in the squared circle, then look no further. Nobody will deny that Fire Pro has a slight learning curve once you first get into your first couple matches, but the key factor is learning the timing and not mashing all the buttons. Once you get the hang of that, you'll be addicted. And if you're a superfan of the sport, you're going to find yourself going through your own simulations of shows and creating your own worlds. The animations are all spot on. The graphics are retro, but awesome in their own way. The movesets and CPU logic systems are some of the most detailed I've seen in any game. Of course this gets my recommendation!
Us veterans have seen previous FPW games and how they work, and not much has changed in regards to the gameplay other than the back and forth striking mechanic. Here are things I hope that they improve coming out of the Early Access:
- More default wrestlers and organizations like in the older games
- Custom music files for entrances, match background, menus, etc.
- Attire system fixed
- Online play fixed
- Logo maker
- More arenas
- More modes
I know some of these things have been addressed and are going to be done before the game has its full final release. At its core, I'm just glad we have this heavily customizable game finally on PC. I do miss some things that were stripped from Returns, as it makes the game feel a little hollow (match booking mode, anyone?)
But overall, this is the supreme version of FPW and I'm so happy we've got it on Steam.

Evolve has the potential to be something great, but lacks content.
No campaign or storyline, other than the hunters talking to each other for short periods of time before a match.
Only one multiplayer mode "Hunt" is being played by the community, a community that dwindles to only 200-400 active players at times, leading to long matchmaking waits that can last longer than the match itself. For example, at one point, matchmaking took me 12 minutes to connect only to have the match last for 5 minutes.
The other mode that my friends and I enjoy "Defend" has only 4 maps.  :(
This game desperately needed a single player  / co op campaign to tell the story of these amazingly designed and voiced characters. Something similar to Borderlands 2 would have been great, with objectives and multiple smaller monsters to hunt and receive rewards for on the way to the larger ones.
The maps are also beautiful in their design and stunning to observe in game.
Certain developers / publishers seem to be steering towards a trend of giving less and asking for more, in response to higher production costs brought on by economic issues.
What stops me from being sympathetic is that I, as well as most others,  am now paid much less in my own profession and am expected to work harder,  so I'm not sure why certain devs / publishers feel they should be exempt from floating on the same boat as the rest of us.
TL;DR
Pros: Great voice acting, wonderfully designed characters & worlds, cool weapons & abilites, great concept
Cons:  No single player story, match making sucks, balance issues, frequent crashes to desktop, feels empty
Overall  6/10
PS: My downvote was not given because I think this game is terrible, but because I cannot in good conscience recommend it, as empty as it is, to others for $60 or even $40.

This game is a spiritual sucessor of the Pharaoh/Cleopatra/Caesar/Zeus/Poseidon and Emperor from Impression Games.
That said, it has the same core mechanics.
Graphics: are AMAZING,  the game is h pretty, animation too.
Sound: beutiful soundtrack and when you click in buildings there is also sounds for each of them. There is no background sound yet, but Devs said that will be added soon, so I might update the review
Interface: Most of the interface is intuitive, there is tabs for each production chain and services. There is also graphics and most of the time you dont need many clicks to get what you want to see.
Tutorial: Its good enough for teaching the basics BUT it does not provide players in depth explanation to some core important aspects of the games and how to use it - Walkers and roadblocks.
Overal gameplay: The game is fun, no doubt of that. There is no combat (donno if there will be) but the management city building thingy is good and can be challenging in Hard mode. There is a happiness system that takes place and its important to the city. If taxes are too high and payment too low they will riot, no food they leave etc etc..
CORE Mechanics:
Production: If you need cooper, you need to build cooper mine right? If you need potato, build a potato farm. That is the basic production. The citzens have needs for food, drinks and services like theater, papernews kiosk etc. The production is intuitive and easy. To make bread you going to need to build a wheat farm, then a Wildmill and finally a bakery. There is plenty of resources to explore and a Steam system that is quite nice and fit the steampunk nature of the game
Delivery: After the production, your citzens are going to need buildings to deliver the goods to them. A shop will deliver food and drinks. The storehouse will deliver the goods needed to the production facilitys. The delivery system is a core mechanic because if you place buildings far from the material needed it will decrease the production because of the time the walker needs to get there.
Walkers: Its the old impression game style of city building mechanic. Each service or production building has a Walker (little person who walks arround the city) to delivery the services/goods to the houses. When they pass in front of the house, the service is provided and the walker need to constant pass that location from time to time to deliver the service again or the house will no longer get the service.
Roadblock: This is one of the most important little thing that you need to understand. This will block the passage of the walker, so you limit the area that the walker will deliver the service. When you do that, you start to see that you need to use this often so you can create neighbourhoods with all the services. The roadblock only block the walkers to go to another area to provide the service, it will not block the walker from taking any goods that he needs to provide the service to the houses. Example: Shop/food walker wont pass the roadblock to delvier food but will pass the roadblock to pick up food from the granary.
Updrading Houses: There is 10 lvls of houses. Each lvl demands a type of good to be delivered so the house can lvl up to the next lvl. That is why sometimes you going to need 2 types of food for example, or you going to need garments for elite houses, or alchool etc etc.Each lvl can acomodate more people and generate more taxes for you :)

Did you know X-COM was on Steam? Do you not already own it? If you don't, take a moment to feel ashamed, and then read on.
Set in an alternate 1998 in which the world is being slowly infiltrated by a sinister group of aliens, X-COM is a tactical turn-based strategy game with a very deep research/production metagame that involves capturing alien technology and adapting it for use in the field. There's a great deal of pressure to advance your bureau's capabilities in this manner before the alien threat overwhelms the world, making for an unforgettable first playthrough (and subsequent playthroughs years later!).

If you missed out the first time around, I heartily recommend addressing your initial error by picking X-COM up now. Besides, it's only five bucks (and probably even less if you're reading this while Steam's having a sale).

First Steam review here, so go easy on me please!
I had been following Stonehearth since its Kickstarter campaign back in 2013, and I finally bit the bullet back in August.  Since then I have enjoyed (almost) every minute of gameplay.  As many reviewers have noted, this is really a niche game, and if you are into a slow-paced city building sim with some RPG and RTS stuff mixed in, this is the game for you.  For me, I love setting up my little town so that it is self-sustaining, and then sitting back and watching.  Seeing the little Hearthlings running around, farming, shepherding, and cooking, all the while getting hungry and eating, and eventually relaxing by the fire and sleeping, it is really quite pretty to see.  Let me detail some pros and cons as I see it:
Pros:
+Voxel Based graphical style
+Custom Buidling Designer
+City Building and strategy combined
+Playable! (can't say this for all EA games)
+Crafting system
+Frequent Updates
+Easy to learn
+Game Community
To explain some of those, lets start with "playable."  You can install the game, launch it, and play away.  It works, and you can easily lose a couple of hours right off the bat.  Next, the custom building designer.  Is it perfect: no.  Can you make any building you can imagine: not yet.  But unless you are really trying to build an abstract, strange angled, multi-story building, chances are you can build it.  The crafting system is very nice, particularly the interaction between the crafters.  You start the game with a carpenter.  He/she can make basic furniture, building elements (like doors and windows), and a few other things.  He/she also makes some tools, like a farmers hoe to allow a farmer to be promoted, a mason's chisel for a stoneworker, a weaver's spindle, etc.  Once you promote another Hearthling to a new position, more crafting elements are unlocked.  For example, by him/herself, a carpenter can make a basic bed.  Promote a weaver, spin some thread, and a high leveled carpenter can make a fancy bed, with bonuses for the Hearthlings who sleep in it.
The final pro I listed which I want to detail is the game community.  Stonehearth has a fairly active community over on their forums, and everyone there is kind and helpful.  Members on the forum do their best to help each other out, and support is quick.  When I first joined the forum, I was greeted by a moderator after my first post, and recived quick help when I had an issue.  That made me want to spend time there, and as I became more familiar in the game, I started to help people out myself.  The developers are very active on the forums too!  They will help with game issues like crashes, keep you updated on bug fixes, and join in the many discussions about the game and where it should go.  They also stream development sessions 3 times a week, where you get to see work on the game live!
Cons:
-Bugs, you will encounter bugs!
-Crashing can happen
-Saves are not always compatible between versions
-Game is not feature complete
-Can't build everything
-Hardware intensive
To explain the cons: the game has bugs.  If you were not expecting that, I suggest you review what Early Access is.  That being said, the developers are amazingly responsive to fixing them, especially if they are game breaking.  Patches are frequent (sometimes too frequent), and they can break save compatibility.  Fortunately, they have 2 branches of updates on Steam, so if you do not like frequent updates, you can stick to a "stable" branch, and not deal with the frequent develop releases.  Crashing can (and likely will at one point) happen.  Many times it is due to driver issues, but also due to anti-virus programs.  As the games AI is based in an embedded chrome browser, programs that add extensions to chrome can cause havoc.
Final con, the game is not feature complete.  You cannot build every possible structure, there are many classes/professions that are not availible, and the game is not fully optimized.  I have played games where Stonehearth has used as much as 9 GB of RAM!  While the usage has dropped significantly in the latest patches, it is still not perfect, and honestly higher than I feel it should be.
So, should you buy this game?  I will answer with a qualified Maybe.  If citybuilding, simulation, strategy games are your thing, then this is an awesome game.  If you want a say in how the game is developed, than take the plunge.  If you like being a part of an active community that is passionate about the game, then hop aboard.  However, if you want a bug-free, fully optimized, feature complete game, then this is not for you (yet).  The game is in alpha, features are in active development, but it isn't quite there yet.

Very torn, between "recommend: yes" and "no".
I really wish I could like this game, but I can't. Graphics are beautful, UI is excellent and intuitive, game mechanics are worked out fine, it's balanced -- and on top of that, it's pretty damn cheap.
So why don't I like it? Because it's a super-traditional rogue-like, in terms of difficulty, and, well, player death.
Don't get me wrong, I understood before playing it that it's a rogue-like. But there's one kind, and another. The ones that punish any minor mistake of the player first by death of one character, and then, inevitably, of the entire party. Nethack is the prime example of that, I suppose.
So on a difficulty/death frequency scale from "Diablo" (rogue-like by name only) and "Nethack" (I don't know anyone personally who actually finished the game), DotE is leaning a lot more towards Nethack.
While I enjoyed Nethack when I was younger, I just don't have the taste anymore for playing games where the "rewards" are rather infrequent, and your party being wiped out because of one minor random event is so common.
So here's my /real/ recommendation:
If you enjoy a game like Nethack, and you don't mind a high difficulty (which I don't), in combination with very frequent deaths (which I do), then: Get this game!
If on the other hand you like your games to be just a bit more forgiving (not "Diablo" forgiving, but, say, "XCom" forgiving), then you might still want to give this game a try (it's great value for that price), but be prepared to get frustrated rather quickly.

I need to stop believing people when they tell me that there is such a thing as a good roguelike.  I bought this game on the strength of the combination of Roguelike / 4E / Tower Defense... except it's not.  It's just another terrible little roguelike, a sadistic RNG that takes the place of creative level design.  The concept is nice.  Open a door, explore your environment step by step, do some research, build defenses... die, lose everything.... Repeat?  Why?  I get the idea that the makers of DotE are confused by the concepts of TD and 4E games, both of which I love, and both of which are predicated on the idea of slow, steady, calculated improvement.  Every time you conquer a level in a TD, you unlock more and more of the game, your skills get better, you gain more towers, and you take on greater challenges.  In 4E, resource gathering and untilization, slowly expanding your sphere of influence... these take hours or days, and garner iterative improvement.  In DotE the floors just aren't big enough.  Your empire consists of a couple upgrades, maybe three or four production units total, and maybe a dozen turrets.  Upgrades you research on one floor and almost everything you built are lost when you move up a level and nothing is gained from game to game besides a slow, inevitable feeling of malaise at the realization you've wasted money on this.  I love hard games.  I love overcoming challenges, but I like to feel like I'm the master of my fate and the utter blithering randomness, the "haha, you lost, now start over from the begining with only your sense of shame!"... that's not what makes a good Adventure, 4E, or TD game.  Not even Nintendo Hard Platformers like Ghosts and Goblins did that.
Oh, and everyone who raves about how simple this game is? So what?  Minecraft is one of the least simple games out there and it's massive.  Ditto Fallout 4 and Skyrim.  Ditto Bridge and Chess.  Know what's simple? Hopscotch.  Simplicity means nothing if the core game itself isn't good.  DotE could be good, if each dungeon were dozens or hundreds of rooms spread out across a vast area, which would have to be protected from invaders as you research and level up, battling wave after wave of monsters crawling out of your barely protected lightzone... and then, once you lose, as you inevitably must, you unlock some potential upgrade that you can use to get farther the next time.  Oh... I would have loved to play that version of DotE if it had true 4E and true TD, instead of just stealing "elements".  That would have been amazing

I was very critical of Unity.  The story was unfocused, Arno had very little character development and just felt like an Ezio copy.  The gameplay was changed for the worse, I only remember 3 characters (including the main playable) and it was too crowded.
Syndicate feels like a true AC game, better than the Ezio trilogy.  The best part is having two characters makes for more to go off of for them.  Jacob is a fighter & takes the most action, but his weakness is that he causes the most chaos.  Evie is the stealth character that is much smarter & applies critical thinking to situations, but at times doesn't take enough action to help out.  Having the character flaws isn't bad, they both make up for it with a yin/yang mix as twins.
The villains this time are FAR more memorable.  Each character got so much more development and much better blue screen deaths than in the past.  Having each character's role outlined (ie: the banker, the scientist, the doctor, the transporter, etc) makes their missions, motives, character traits far more memorable.
The actual assassination missions were the best.  Not since AC1 have I looked forward to actual Templar assassinations, but that was because AC1 had ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gameplay elsewhere other than the assassinations.
The music is incredible, by far the best since AC2 & Brotherhood's soundtrack but actually I'd say even better.
-At the beginning, the Mentor named George lectures the twins about staying away from London.  They disobey him and he's never heard from again.  I was expecting him to show up in sequence 4 or 5 with his monacle broken & jowels flapping.  I was disappointed.
-The main villain, Crawford Starrick, is a really good presence & very well acted.  However, literally every scene but the final sequence has him in his office assigning other people to do dirty work.  He never does
actual fieldwork or has any interaction with them face to face.  Granted, you can say "Well, London was completely under his control so he didn't need to leave his office", but tha'ts weak.
-The sidequests have very little payoff.  I only did them for fun.  Hell, I cleared out a huge chunk of chests & collectibles for fun, but that was just me enjoying the game.  There really is no actual payoff to it unless if I was achievement hunting, which I'm not on Ubiplay garbage.
Anyway, great game, worth the $20 I spent it on.  Hope the one in 2017 is even better.

This game could be good.
Currently it's not.
The high reported difficulty in the game beginning is basically due to 2 factors:
- you don't know the game before you start it. There is no tutorial. There is no explanation about what does what. Yet there is 1 single build path and series of actions that will get you through the game. Only one.
- the game beginning is random. Start with a huge asteroid on your path, and it hits a component that you can't replace ? You're dead.
I can't understand how, in 2017, more than 30 years after video games become mainstream, people still don't include tutorials in video games.
I can't understand how, after the large quantity of rogue-likes that came out, devs still do the mistake of putting fake difficulty at the start of their game so it looks like it's "hardcore", spawning ridiculous reviews like "you need to use your brain". Nope. There is one build path at start. Either you know it or you die. Also, you need to reactivate all tooltips at each restart of the game, and your toons don't come pre-assigned. So, every game start, not only you have to rebuild all the same parts in the same place, but you also have to redo your interface again and redo the toon assignment.
There is also issues with game flow. Currently there is 4 "events" that can popo-up: asteroid field (only way to get ressources), sun (you will die if you didn't build have enough vents, have fun micro managing your toons because they are too dumb to move to fires), ship appearing, and nothingness. There are times where you spent litterally 2 minutes staring at the screen and nothing happens. This one's probably due to early access.
Last, the mining mini-game. Not only there is one build path at the start, there is also one and only one action to do. Mine asteroids. And that's a luck game. Either you get enough silicium or metal to replace whichever part of your ship gets blown up by asteroids... or you die. And mining has to be done manually. And... it's boring. You also don't have a lot of margin nor choices here. You have to blow up the small & medium asteroids, ignore the large ones (you don't have the power to kill them), and hope you get enough ressources to build water dispenser, more energy, more CPU, food thingy, then lazors for when enemy come. The start is a race on which you have no control - get a series of 10 asteroids with no silicium ? You're screwed. Oh, and... you need about a dozen metal & silicium to build stuff. Mining gets ressources one by one.
Maybe, maybe later when those get ironed out I'll buy this game again and regret the refund I just did, but I doubt it. Why ? Because, as it looks now, it's the game's vision that's wrong. The early game needs to be ironed out so that stuff happens, quests, events, whatever. The only "choice" there is for the first 10 minutes of the game basically is which asteroid to mine.
Again, I stress what I think is the game's main issue. Video games existed for 30 years now. Even if your game's end-game is better than sex (which ain't the case), no one cares if the beginning is boring, unintuitive, or repetitive enough to make people flee.

Recommended with caution.
EA description strongly applies: only buy the game if you're excited for it in its current state, and don't buy for what it will be when finished (which will probably be an awesome game). That being said the game is already interesting, the music is good, there's a good amount progression and challange in it.
The devs are really active: there were at least 3 patches since release (2-3 days ago). Including bug and balance fixes, mostly based on community feedback, which is really nice.
There is NO TUTORIAL, so you'll just have to figure it out. However you don't need to read pages to do it. Mostly because there isn't that much description, because it's not necessary. The game has quite a lot of elements, but they are kept simple, and intuitive, so you'll figure it out. Takes about 5-10 deaths to get the build order for necessities, and another 10-20 to optimize it. Yes, you will die a lot.
That's mostly the reason of negative reviews. The game was extremely unbalanced when it came out, but it was made easier with every patch. There's still a relatively strict build order at the beginning, hence the part below.
IF you decided to get the game I'll give you some help, in case you don't want to figure it out yourself, or you wanna enjoy the game without dying too much (for 1.0e):
0. Re-rolling your crew: Get 1 Engineer lvl3, 1 Science lvl 3, and preferrably another Engineer 2-3. Just click "Select new" until you get it.
This is necessary to get your ship ready for the 1st asteroid field, and to get new parts fast. Science also helps in lots of other things.
1. Assign all your crew to Engineering.
2. A good build before the 1st asteroid field:
- 2 Hull tiles
- 2 Mining Lasers (at the front of the ship)
- 3 Small Heat Vents
- 1 CPU panel
- 2 Small solar panels
To do all of these you'll need to deconstruct the Small engine in the back. It doesn't have much effect, and you want to mine as much as possible, so might as well get rid of it.
3. Your next priorities are: buying Food from a trader, building another 1-2 heats vents, a Small chest and a Water cooler before your crew starts dying of dehydration. This last one can be a temporary addition, if you really need materials.
4. After those you'll also want to feed your crew, so a Food dispenser would be nice. Depending on materials, you might be able to get a 3rd Mining Laser (but have at least 5 heat vents for it).
5. Now you've probably encountered 2 ships, which are guaranteed friendly, however the 3rd isn't, so start getting weapons. You don't need to have these on all the time, so you don't NEED to add extra solar and cpu panels, you can just turn off your Mining lasers. However you can encounter ships in asteroid fields, and you might want to keep firing on the enemy while breaking rocks in your paths.
You can survive the 1st hostile encounter with just 1 turret, but that won't restroy the enemy ship, I think you need 3 for that.
6. Build a Research Station and go for either Small plant bed, Medium solar panel or Mining console. If you have 30 food, then forget plant bed, and go for the other 2. If you have 2-3 turrets and 3 mining lasers AND you micromanage a lot, then you can get crazy amount of materials from asteroid fields.
7. At this point you've reached what I'd call mid-game. Your biggest problem is probably getting more crew. You can buy them from trading ships, and sometimes they join you from destroyed ships, I haven't had anything else.
Additional tips:
- keep an eye on HEAT: fires will start on your ship and you can lose your weapons and mining lasers easily if you're not careful.
- don't forget to BUILD: after getting 3 Mining lasers and 6 heat vents you might really be enjoying getting all those precious materials while mining, but even then you need to remember to build stuff constantly. You need Hull or Floor to add anything relevant to your ship, so plan and build ahead! You can just pause the game any time to do so.
- always keep in mind the CPU and Power costs.
- buy Food from the first 2-3 traders, it's unlikely that you'll get the research done and build the equipment needed to make your own food in time.
- always sell Water: very common, you don't need much of it and Credits are hard to get.
- don't run out of STORAGE SPACE: materials just get destroyed if you do. Especially at the beginning, where starting with the engine deconstruction means you can't get everything built before the 1st asteroid field. Also get that Small chest in time!
- use the CONTROL GROUPS: CTRL + [1-9] to assign them and [1-9] to use them. Very useful for weapons, mining lasers and possibly non-essential equipment, like Research station, Water cooler and Food dispenser, if you're stretched too thin on Power or CPU.
- build vertically: this means you need to break less rocks to be safe.
- mining laser in front, weapon placement doesn't matter. Mining lasers have a relatively short range, while weapons don't.
- that being said rocks can be broken with the Laser turret, howeve you might accidently destroy resources.
- SAVE A LOT: since there isn't much variance between games atm, you might as well savescum and just experience the whole game without restarting all the time. But ofc you can do ironman and just torture yourself like I do.
- build smart: at the beginning you won't have the luxury to build long/wide corridors, or to make your ship look good. It's an escape pod, you're barely even alive. Prioritize what you really need.
It's definitely not the only way to play the early-game, but it's an effective way.
Good luck!

Right now the game has enough content and is fun enough to justify its price at $12.  And it very much feels like it has the potential to be a really great game with more balancing and content.  I have enjoyed my first few hours of playing the game and have seen the game get better with the updates that have been pushed out.  At this point at least this definitely is a game that doesn't guarantee that every run will be successful.  Sometimes there are a group of adverse events that occur that are difficult if not impossible to recover from.  So be prepared to start over a lot.  But even as asteroids are hitting/destroying vital components and my crew is (clumsily at times unfortunately) struggling to put out all the fires and repair the damage, the way the game is designed it can be fun to try to figure out how to recover from being on the brink of disaster.  And I feel like I am learning from the failures and getting better at the game and that is one of the things I love about playing video games.
So I recommend the game for people who are willing to spend some time to learn how to play.  There might not be much of a tutorial until later in the development process since the frequent updates that this EA is likely to get would be very time consuming to keep the tutorial updated day to day.  And also for people who don't get too frustrated with having to start over while they are figuring things out.  This game doesn't guarantee a path for success in every run although it does give the player options to recover when things go wrong if they can stop and think about how to use the game's functionality to solve the problems.   If you are uncertain about buying it now in this early state of EA then I would definitely recommend putting it in your wishlist and watching to see how it develops over time.  I like what there is now and can't wait to see what this game becomes in the future.

First let me say that I loved this game.  It has a unique storyline, simple gameplay mechanics, and is full of humor (depending somewhat on your personal sense of humor).  The story is the main focus of the game, with gameplay being a means to progress that story.  At least in my opinion.  And that was perfectly fine with me.
If you're not sure what to expect based on the trailers, I would classify it as an item-based 1st-person adventure/puzzle game.  You can run around like any 1st-person shooter and collect items, which are needed to solve puzzles, open doors, fix objects, etc...  Along the way you can collect extra items that aren't necessary but can either flesh out the story or be purely for a laugh.
The game plays pretty smoothly, although I did find a few glitches.  Some being inconsequential, like graphics not looking right in rare cases, to more substantial, like when you try to walk around some areas with an uneven edge bordering it it seems to get sticky and you have trouble moving.  But those instances were few enough and spread out enough that it didn't negatively impact my game experience very much.  And at no point did I have to restart the game or do any reinstalls.
I'd rate the game difficulty as easy-moderate, as a few items might be hard to find for some.  If you're wondering about content I'd consider this an "E for Everyone" game, although younger children might not fully appreciate some of the finer details of the story that can be gleaned from extra collectibles.
Overall I'd highly recommend this game if you enjoy solving simple puzzles and a game full of quirky, silly humor.

I had been looking to this game for almost a year - listening to its promise of old school Sierra city building influence. It was steampunk and it sounded too good to be true.

1) The AI has no intelligence at all - which is okay and they've implemented road blocks to contain these 'walkers' that distrbute resources - but the townspeople's patience for these AI to make it to their home is almost nil. You will have masses of workers leaving your city at ALL times almost crippling your economy and upgraded homes. I realize this is part of the game - but you will need to make 2-3 of each building within a small radius to keep the people from leaving. EVEN THEN they will still leave from time to time because someone made 10 left turns and never made that 1 right turn down the road you needed.
2) Maintenance on your buildings is pathetic. You will need at least 3 maintenance buildings for every little 'village' otherwise the entire place will collapse.
3) The game plays much too fast. Everything happens quickly - your ecomony will destabalize within seconds from a mass exodus.
I could go on but I've depressed myself thinking of what this game could be. Apparently the dev's are releasing updates. At the writing of this review it's not worth the money since the game is just too damn unfair - and the scenarios are almost unwinable.

Gomo is a short but sweet little adventure game, offering adorable graphics coupled with a silly story and very low puzzle difficulty. Best suited to younger gamers.
Gomo is a sweet little point-and-click adventure in which you control Gomo, a cuddly lil' dude who gets his pet dog stolen by a mean old alien overlord! The only chance of return for our poached pooch is a mysterious red crystal (naturally imbued with mystical powers of course), which our alien overlord is actually very happy to swapsies with us. So off we embark, on a quest to find this crystal thingy by any bizarre means necessary.
Now while "by any bizarre means necessary" includes zipping down garbage chutes, out-smarting security robots and firing atomic warheads across alternate dimensions, Gomo's gameplay is actually highly linear, and the solution for how you're supposed to do all these crazy things is usually pretty straightforward. You also have just three inventory slots for objects (which are rarely used), and each "scene" will only offer one or two puzzles to solve - most of which you'll understand as soon as you see them. So I get the impression that Gomo is probably aimed at younger players, and reckon the last reviewer's description of it as an "interactive animation" has it spot on.
I am personally a big fan of point-and-clicks, so I was happy enough playing through to the end and really enjoyed Gomo's silly humour. However, after a while I started to get frustrated with the character's movement. You often have to click multiple times simply to get Gomo to cross the scene, as he needs to be in precisely the right place for you to perform certain interactions. Because of this you're often left confused as to where your character should be standing simply to progress to the next area, even though you know exactly what to do. However I doubt children would be put off by this.
If you see this game on sale and have a younger gamer or two to entertain, maybe pick it up for a rainy day. Otherwise I personally feel there are far better "low difficulty" point-and-click titles on Steam on the moment, such as Detective Grimoire, Broken Age, Samorost and so many others.

I just played this, and my verdict is basically "Yes, if it's on sale." It's only $5 at full price anyway, but it's really short (took me less than an hour and a half from start to finish) and there's not a lot to it. The main impression I got was that they wanted to make a cartoon but for some reason they were forced to make video game instead. It's fairly whimsical and things don't really happen for any particular reason, but the puzzles are easy enough that that's not frustrating. There are a couple of sliding tile puzzles that don't really fit the style of the other puzzles in the game, but they're not randomised or anything so you can just use a walkthrough (which I did).
It reminded me a lot of Journey of a Roach, only not as good. The protagonist does speak, but rarely, and the dialogue is not important. Mostly you just press buttons and see what happens and then move on to the next screen. I was briefly stuck in a couple of places just because I couldn't work out what I was supposed to achieve, but most of the time there's not even really a puzzle, you just find the thing to click on. Sometimes you'll have to use an item from your inventory, but they're almost all one-use and given to you right where you'll need them. It's not a challenging game, there's not much story and very little characterisation, but the animation is nice and it doesn't take long to get through.

The game's progress is rather slow because the movements of the character "Gomo" are also slow. Every time he picks up an item he just has to put it in his back (not backpack, IN his back) even though you might need the same item in a second. I played the game again just to unlock the bonus minigames but it was just a waste of time as all three are slight variations of a "whack-a-mole" game.
Overall the game is okay, but in my opinion it's the type of game you'd rather give to a 10 year old to keep them busy for a couple of hours.

A fun rougelike game which requires good micromanagement and some strategy as well as tactics (singleplayer) and teamwork (multiplayer). This is definitely a game which will make almost anyone keep playing due to the sheer diversity. There are two versions of the game, Pixel and Crystal edition. Pixel edition is the barebones version, it has enough to get a player going whilst Crystal edition contains one additional hero, one additional spaceship and some skins.
There are a large variety of characters, or heroes as they are called in game, to choose from. All of which excel in certain skills and are core to certain aspects of the game. Each hero generally differs in four types of stats, Health, Speed, Attack Power and Wit. On top of this, there are also additional stats such as Defense, Attack Speed, DPS, etc. Whether it be in singleplayer or multplayer, good team synergy is crucial to clear all thirteen floors of the dungeon.
To progress in the floor, one needs to open doors to find the exit. Opening doors takes up one turn. Each door leads into a different room. The room may be lit or unlit by default and to light up a room, one needs to spend dust which is found randomly in the floor. There are also resources which are required in order to make things easier. They are Industry, Science and Food. Industry is used to construct the buildings and defenses (modules) and is generated by an Industry module. Science is used to research new modules through a research shrine and is generated by a Science module. Food is used to either heal or level up your hero and is generated by a Food module.
In order to clear a floor, one must get the crystal from the starting point to the exit. Only one hero may pick up the crystal and during transportation, cannot interact with anything. Additionally, hostile mobs will continuously spawn during this time. Your team must protect the crystal carrier from harm till he/she reaches the exit. Repeat that for thirteen floors and you will have completed the game.
An interesting feature of Dungeon of the Endless is the permadeath feature. Once your hero dies, he will NEVER respawn until everyone else has died. You can share heroes as well as resources between your team in order to supplement holes in the defenses.

I won't talk about Baldur's Gate itself, because it's easily one of the best RPGs ever (if not THE best) and that's all that needs to be said, so I'll focus on the EE features only.
An enhanced edition of Baldur's Gate will always have to be compared to BG Tutu, which does similar job and has been around way longer. Like EE, Tutu offers better resolution and fixes bugs (in fact, more of them than EE does). While I still prefer Tutu over EE, I think EE is well done and likely better for players who are not willing to spend hours/days picking the right set of mods. Moreover, EE has extra content - The Black Pits arena and 4 new NPCs.
I was surprised myself that I mostly liked the new NPCs. Since all four of them are of different class than the original potential party members, EE offers new strategies, which is something both new and veteran players can enjoy. Baeloth (who is a bit hard to obtain, since he's an easter egg) was even a key member in my party and I can recommend EE just for the perk of having him around. Who wouldn't want to give orders to a brash drow sorcerer?
The Black Pits is, frankly, an add-on for powergamers and nothing else. If you are in the game mainly for the combat, you'll enjoy it; if not, don't bother trying the arena at all. It's not related to the main story in any way (unless you count Baeloth). Nonetheless, the fights can be fun and challenging, so there's that.
Overall, I'd say that EE is a good way of keeping Baldur's Gate alive and adjusted to 21st century. It adds new content that fits in nicely with the original game and spares players the need to poke around game files themselves. But if you're someone who's been playing Baldur's Gate for a few years, you probably know BG Tutu and have modded the game yourself by now. In that case, EE is redundant.

Rewrote this Review due to new updates, current Stable: Alpha 17, but Alpha 18 is playable and looking good too. Previous Review had 4 of 7 Helpful votes.
Short Version: It's still a Dwarf Fortress/Gnomoria style game, but less focused on deep digging and more on exploration, crafting, and building. Class System is simple but interesting and more unique than simply assigning jobs, and much more user friendly than most. Don't let the simplicity fool you though, you can pour some fair time into this if you like these kinds of games.
Since my previous review, it's still in Alpha, but has resolved or at least lessened alot of the Optimization issues, with more tweaks focused on that to come - judging by the dev blog and their videos, they genuinely care about fixing this, and they should since 2d Dwarf Fort lags up pretty bad once you have a big enough population going, imagine how bad it's going to be in a 3d game like this. Smart focus on their part, one of the rare devs that learns from others' issues, unlike every MMO dev out there.
The AI is much better now, though still a little prone to bad decision-making. You can somewhat "control" their pathfinding by building Roads, as it favors those almost exclusively unless no road exists to follow nearby. The Building issues I had before seem resolved for the most part, though I'll still find a ladder or scaffolding stuck floating and undestroyable without using the Console.
Combat has advanced by leaps and great bounds since my previous review - many more weapon/armor options, as well as 3 new classes: the Knight, with heavier armor and 1h/shield focus, bonus defense/stats and buff auras for his allies, as well as Taunt skills to protect the squishies - the Archer, your standard ranged attacker who can either slow or burn enemies based on their Arrow Quiver equipped(and double-shot at max lvl) - and most importanly, the Cleric, a Healer Monk who can do melee dmg and defend himself but puts their first priority as healing any nearby units with damage, both directly and through a passive aura. I make 2 groups of 1 of each class and it protects my bases pretty well + deals with the Story armies nicely.
The Mining system is a little more controllable now but still not as fine-tuned as I would like to see, and usually see in other games of this kind - there's no Ramps or Stairs to be dug, and manually digging them up doesn't usually work because the AI prefers to build and use Ladders instead of stepping up/down 1 block steps.
Overall they're making nice strides in the right direction, and I'm eager to see more.
Bonus: There's already a decent-sized Mod community, and they make some pretty good mods so far, from whole new classes and items to entire Biomes(The Archipelago one is awesome)

I have a strict "don't buy games in early access" policy. I caved and bought this one to give it a try.
That was late Wednesday (seems it had just come out too). Now it's early Friday, I'm standing at 18 hours played, and I'm very glad I waivered my policy.
Yeah, it's a difficult game. Yeah, it lacks a tutorial and that makes it even harder. Try a couple of games, fail hard, go read a beginner's guide, then try again. I promise it will click.
Most reviews mention this being "RimWorld meets FTL" and it's pretty bang on, if you like both you'll probably dig this one, though it is much more RW than FTL. It succeeds at what to me is the biggest flaw in RimWorld: pacing. While I spent hundreds of hours building unnecessarily complicated fortresses in Dwarf Fortress, in RW after a couple hours in a map I feel like I don't have anything else interesting to do. It's now a boring game of amassing resources so I can get to some arbitrary end game tech (never got to that point but I assume the objective of RW is building a ship and buggering off).
In that regard, ST feels like DF: I'm building a ship just for the sake of building a ship, and it's fun to do it and there is always something I'm aiming to do. Resources are hard to come by, research takes a long time (which is possibly what makes RW reach end point so fast), so your ship will be ragtag for a long time before it starts getting powerful enough to stand up to enemies. Stars are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ mostly because your pawns are kinda stupid regarding putting out fires sometimes, but once you learn to set up so you vent areas of your ship while crossing stars it becomes an interesting addition to the challenge of designing your ship.
It has a lot of things that are not as good as DF and RW (pawn psychology is very simplistic and they have little skills, save scumming is very easy), but it does other things better, which makes it worth the try for fans of the genre. As far as early access goes it's not the buggiest by a long mile - had one crash once while loading a save, paws sometimes get stuck trying to perform a job - but it's definitely not an impediment to making the game enjoyable.

When I was younger, I went to the local market one day and acquired myself a freshly-pressed copy of Fire Pro Wrestling D for my Dreamcast.  I'd never heard of the name before and the screenshots on the back looked a bit crap, but I put it down to the dodgy photocopied 'insert' that accompanied my disc.  It was only a fiver, so I figured it was worth the risk.  I got that game home and fired it up.  I briefly wrestled with the Japanese text, but after a short while, I managed to get an exhibition match going...
Boy oh boy!  What a surprise!  The graphics were drop-dead gorgeous.  The gameplay was sublime, bordering on absolute perfection.  I knew at that exact moment that I had discovered a true masterpiece of gaming history.  I fell in love with that game, on that day, way back at the beginning of the year 2000 and it thereby displaced Soul Calibur as the permanent fixture inside that amazing little grey box.
I played that game to death with the help of a translation guide I found on the Internet.  I still have my Dreamcast, lying in a box somewhere in my mother's attic - I imagine it's probably still got that old burned CD of FPWD inside it.
Now, in 2017, I can start to relive that thrill, that enjoyment, that beautiful, blissful gameplay that I discovered all those years ago.
Being Early Access, the game is rough around the edges, for sure.  But that magical feeling you get, only when you play a Fire Pro Wrestling game, is there in all its unmistakable glory!
In fact - having rekindled my affection for the series, I immediately felt obliged to buy FPWR for my PS3, having never known it was available on that format.  Doubt I'll ever play it, but... you know, now I'm a grown man, I figure I owe the developers! :o)

This review is going to be a work in progress as I spend time in the game, but I'm going to start with a few opinions here at the top for anyone curious if this game is for them.
I've seen a lot of comments directed at "Fire Pro Wrestling World" that go like this "I don't understand all the hype about this game, why are people excited for the release of a 16 bit wrestling game?". Well, if you've made that comment or one similar to it, you are correct. You don't understand, and you don't understand how much you don't understand.
So, let me take a few moments to help guide you in the right direction. You probably fall into one of 4 categories:
1: If you don't like pro wrestling or have any knowledge on the topic, go away, FPWW is not for you. Go check out the latest FPS or something, you'll be much happier.
2: If you do like pro wrestling but playing games like WWE 2Kxx leave you with a warm feeling of satisfaction, then go play that, FPWW is not for you.
3: If you've ever purchased a modern day 16-bit Retro sprite based game (Steam is boiling over with them, so I know you have) and yet it doesn't make sense to you that a developer could market a game with "dated" graphics to wrestling fans, FPWW is not for you.
4: If however, you fell in love with professional wrestling anywhere between the years 1909 and 2017, and wish you had a way to wittness impossible dream matches, relive the territories in their prime, See all the matches WCW failed to give us when the NWO was comprised of the entire roster, experience the history of the WWE from Samartino to Hulkamania to Attitude to (God forbid) the looming Roman Empire, well pick your Era. Fire Pro is a wrestling Delorean fitted with a flux capacitor and the plutonium tank is topped off, ready to take you anywhere in wrestling history you want to go. FPWW is as good as the hype, but you must fall into this category if you are going to appreciate it.
Note: $19.99 is a steal, all you have to do is hit the download button and click play. If you're new to FPW you'll never know how good you have it right now. Many people (including myself) expressing excitement about this game paid top dollar to purchase previous installments as imports not to mention having to monkey with their consoles to make them able to play the imported game, and then once they finally got it working...all the menus were in Japanese. I have several hundred dollars tied up in FPWD and FPWR alone, not to mention time and effort importing the many excellent Edits the community has created over the years. Now  instead of juggling memory cards and usb drives with Edit (CAW) limits, we have steam workshop and the entire free space on the HDD for storage. If there is hype or excitement associated with this game..this is why!

As far as I know, I've never really played any city builders before, or at least, didn't enjoy them enough to remember them. Figured this one might end up the same way, but thankfully it hasn't.
I'm really, really enjoying this game so far.
The art is wonderful; the designs are charming and eye-catching, very creative, especially the characters, and I'm really liking all the detail put into everything. And the music! It's very light-hearted and fun, but it's also very fitting and not at all distracting. I thought the little details - the use of the French Republican Calendar, the references, sound effects, etc.- were all pretty neat, too, and personally I think stuff like that makes the game even more fun, makes it more appealing when there's extra stuff to catch your attention.
I thought the tutorial, for the most part, was easy enough to follow and helped me understand the game much better -isn't that what a good tutorial is meant to do, though?-, especially as someone who has never played any city builders before. There was some stuff I struggled to understand at first, particularly in the last two chapters of the tutorial, and some parts seemed to progress a little slower than I'd have liked, but maybe that was just me being a novice, ha! I do wish I could have had a way to repeat some of the instructional dialogue, but maybe there is and I just missed it? If not, it'd be nice to have that just in case someone else is like me and clicks too fast.
There were a few minor problems I had, but nothing major at all. The game crashed a few times on my older laptop, but once I put it on the newer one it's worked just fine so far. It seems to freeze when you select certain options (loading a chapter or a saved file, etc.), but then it works just fine after. Not a problem, but it can get just a little annoying. So far, I haven't had any problems in-game, just a few minor annoyances mostly related to me just being impatient or not understanding something clearly enough.
It's been pointed out before, but there could also be a bit more proof-reading with the translation. Personally, I didn't find the errors that bothersome or noticeable, but it did sometimes make it a little difficult to properly understand the instructions they gave you, especially during the latter half of the tutorial. I also didn't mind the few stray bits of text that were left in French.
There are things that could be fixed or improved, sure -and the team is working on it, this game is frequently updated!-, and some parts are a little slow, at least, for me, but I'm not used to the pacing of city builders, yet. But, the art style is great, the game is very colorful and visually appealing, the text -even if it's not quite translated right-, is charming and to me it seems pretty fitting to the era the game is supposed to be in. Some of the tasks are fun and challenging, and I like that little rush I get when I've done something right, even more-so when I'm rewarded with a nifty little achievement!
I also really, really appreciate the fact that the game's creators are very involved in the discussions and forums, that they answer all your questions and critiques honestly and are willing to listen to complaints and find ways to solve them. From the looks of it, it seems like they're working really hard to get all the bugs and kinks worked out, translation errors included. :>
It's my first real adventure into a city builder game, and so far I'm really starting to like the genre. I'd definitely recommend Lethis, especially once it's gotten most of the bugs smoothed out.

This is an odd game, in that, completing the objectives on each map: load up your trucks with logs, deliver logs to destination, are in themselves not overly challenging - one can select a fairly basic truck, and carry small logs and make several trips.
The challenge, and fun, come in the problem-solving when you've cocked it all up because you decided you wanted to deliver the long logs, and you're going to go through the trees, rather than around them, and you've gone into the water and lost the load. So you have to get the crane-truck, or the log-loader and try and fish the logs out of the water, and get your truck back upright. Use the winch, but the only anchor points are fragile trees that break before you've got the truck upright. Now what ? Solving that problem is where the fun happens.
It's also quite a tranquil game in a way.

After logging over 40 hours on Assassins Creed Syndicate I feel that I can finally write a worthy review. ACS is the story of a brother and sister assassin couple who you get to switch between to play the story, which is an interesting way to play a storyline and, personally, I liked it a lot. This is the second AC series game that I've played(the first being Black Flag) and although I may not be the most die-hard fan like some others, I can definately see how the AC series has a certain feel and groove to it, and ACS most certainly fits that groove in new and interesting ways. You're able to hijack trains, carriages, free children from factories, and steal cargo from ships which are all great additions to the gameplay of AC. The map itself is absolutely beautiful, the details are all perfect and it really feels like being in victorian London. At times, I felt that the main story was not very interesting and fell into a dull pattern of assassinating characters and I felt that Ubisoft could've made the storyline much more fascinating, and conquering boroughs is incredibly repetitive and takes so much time. Eventhough the main story is a bit dull, I felt that the side missions made up for it - meeting historical characters like Alexander Grambell, Charles Dickens, and Charles Darwin and fulfilling missions for them was very fun. Even if the main story was dull, the assassination missions themselves were extremely fun, because you are able to pick your path to assassination of the caracter instead of having it already layed out for you. All in all, ACS is a worthy addition to the AC franchise and is definately worth the money for a fun game to play (especially if you get it for cheap on a steam sale). The AC franchise is on the right track with this game, and with only a few changes, I feel the next game will be greatly improved.

I haven't yet had the chance to really dig into it but regardless of what's next I feel it's a great addition to my collection.

Gomo is a very basic point-and-click game where players take control of a lone, sack-boy who abruptly wakes up from a frightful nightmare to discover the absence of his best friend/dog. He is then charged with the dutiful task of retrieving a sought after relic for the perpetrators of the dognapping as an equivalent exchange for his companion.
Visually, the game has intriguing, monochromatic, hand-drawn environments along with rooms and characters oversimplified in design. While venturing and trekking through each level, little events play out to entertain the player while having no necessary connection to the actual plot.
Controls are entirely devoted to the mouse, making the protagonist move, observe and gather up key items which is then stored in one of three inventory slots. The animation of the character tends to feel deliberate and, at many moments, appears to take too much time to execute; however, the quirky mannerism of the protagonist makes up for it as you can’t help but smile at his awkward demeanor.
Throughout the exploration of the game, players will encounter puzzles which aren’t created with much complexity. The challenges seem too simple and it was felt at times like they could solve themselves. There’s no means of direct dialogue but just the sound of the creepy, overly husky grunts from the main character and high, incoherent murmurs from the antagonist.
GOMO is definitely a relaxing game because of its slow pace which is a nice change after a long stressful day. Only downfall is that it’s far too easy but still an enjoyment. :)
