Having just finished the second of five episodes, I feel like just sharing my thoughts on the game thus far.
Overall, the story mode is quite enjoyable. Of the two episodes released so far, I personally feel that the second episode is much better than the first. Whilst I liked the new area that was introduced in the first episode, I feel it was a little too hand-holdy. I understand why this is done, as many newer players will have only begun playing now that the full release is out, I just wasn't personally a fan. In saying that, the new area introduced in the first episode is quite good. There is a good mix of travelling and the ability to hide in doors, which is perfect for a beginner.
The second episode was quite good overall, although some parts were quite annoying. Without going into detail, primarily to avoid spoilers, there is one part where the player must wait for a specific event to occur. In my playthrough, I had to wait roughly four to five days for this event to occur, which was kind of annoying. In saying this, it was quite enjoyable to have to survive in a single location for that amount of time, I wish it was just communicated to the player in some way.
Apart from that problem, the second episode was very enjoyable. Being able to explore three areas in the one episode, compared to a single area in episode one, was good fun. For example, one mission requires the player to travel through all three areas to complete an objective, which was both difficult and satisfying at the same time.
The biggest problem I have with the story mode is the dialogue and cutscenes throughout. Whilst the voice acting is pretty good overall, the dialogue within the cutscenes isn’t the best. Some lines just come along as weird, and the transition from voiced dialogue to text-based dialogue was quite jarring when I first saw it. This might turn some players of, which is understandable. However, I am much more a fan of the gameplay within this game, rather than the story.
Moving on from the story mode, almost all other aspects of the game are fantastic. The UI is amazing, with the player being able to hear pages flip and zippers open whilst they navigate through different menus. Moreover, I personally enjoy the lack of HUD in the game. Being able to limit what a player must see to a few bars at the bottom of a screen, and a clock at the top of the screen is amazing. Whilst it might be confusing for newer players, once he/she becomes familiar with the game, it assists in immersing the player into the game world. The sound design and visuals are superb, with a player being able to feel completely immersed in the game.
Moreover, small details like a player being able to follow their own footsteps back to their base during a snowstorm, to smoke coming out of a chimney when a player has a fire going inside of a building. Another fantastic game-feature is allowing the player to scare wolves away by utilising a torch or flare.
Another aspect I enjoyed was the inability to combat wildlife when the player begins his/her journey. Whilst it is possible to fight a wolf in the early game, the player is close to death if done so without proper first-aid-equipment and clothing. Thus, in the beginning, the player must navigate through situations with great care.
Apart from the newly introduced story mode, The Long Dark offers two other game modes. Those being either, a classic survival game-mode, where the player is dropped into the game-world, and told just to survive. No hand-holding, no direction. This is where I personally believe the games shines the brightest, allowing players to develop their own stories through different gameplay mechanics. Moreover, allowing players to travel between the different interconnected areas further assists in providing emergent storytelling.
As well as this, The Long Dark also offers a variety of different challenge runs for players to partake in. For example, the player may have a challenge where he/she begins the challenge by being mauled to death by a bear, and must travel between different regions to find a firearm, then in another challenge, use that firearm to track and kill the bear. These types of missions allow players who want a little more direction, compared to the classic survival mode, to enjoy the game, yet still have examples of emergent storytelling.
Many people hold the belief that someone should only buy an early access game if he/she is satisfied with the amount of content that is currently in the game, and not what is promised further down the line. I purchased this game whilst it was still in early access, roughly a year ago, and was satisfied with the amount of content in the game then. However, with many overhauls being added, as well as a story mode, I feel I can recommend this game. It tackles a niche that not many companies can complete successfully, and is one of the most immersive games I have ever played.
Regarding performance problems and bugs, I did not have any troubles. Whilst I have heard of some bugs related to missions, I did not personally experience any. Hinterland does seem to be on top of bug reporting, with four patches being released so far, which is quite impressive.
For me, The Long Dark is one of the better games I've played in a long time. I like to think that the story mode serves as a great tutorial for players to begin with. However, the survival game mode is where the game truly shines. Whilst I only have a small amount of hours on the game at the moment, I look forward to see what other stories I can experience in this quiet apocalypse. I understand that this genre isn't for everyone, but if you are interested in picking it up, I highly suggest you do.

Evolve has the potential to be something great, but lacks content.
No campaign or storyline, other than the hunters talking to each other for short periods of time before a match.
Only one multiplayer mode "Hunt" is being played by the community, a community that dwindles to only 200-400 active players at times, leading to long matchmaking waits that can last longer than the match itself. For example, at one point, matchmaking took me 12 minutes to connect only to have the match last for 5 minutes.
The other mode that my friends and I enjoy "Defend" has only 4 maps.  :(
This game desperately needed a single player  / co op campaign to tell the story of these amazingly designed and voiced characters. Something similar to Borderlands 2 would have been great, with objectives and multiple smaller monsters to hunt and receive rewards for on the way to the larger ones.
The maps are also beautiful in their design and stunning to observe in game.
Certain developers / publishers seem to be steering towards a trend of giving less and asking for more, in response to higher production costs brought on by economic issues.
What stops me from being sympathetic is that I, as well as most others,  am now paid much less in my own profession and am expected to work harder,  so I'm not sure why certain devs / publishers feel they should be exempt from floating on the same boat as the rest of us.
TL;DR
Pros: Great voice acting, wonderfully designed characters & worlds, cool weapons & abilites, great concept
Cons:  No single player story, match making sucks, balance issues, frequent crashes to desktop, feels empty
Overall  6/10
PS: My downvote was not given because I think this game is terrible, but because I cannot in good conscience recommend it, as empty as it is, to others for $60 or even $40.

I notice there are a lot of negative reviews for this game, so much so that it is rated "mixed," and that is a travesty. To help you decide whether this game is for you, I will say this; If you are a gamer who enjoys using your brain, you will probably like this game. If your idea of fun is to completely divorce yourself from critical thought and still succeed, you should look elsewhere.
All the negative reviews complain about the game being too difficult. I picked the game up for the first time a day ago (the hard start version) and succeeded on my first run. To make sure it wasn't a fluke, I restarted 3 more times. Every run was successful. I am not a genius. If you make an intelligent plan to build what you need, in the order you need it, and do so efficiently, you will almost certainly succeed. If you have no knowledge of the game and want advice, that order should be...
1) Get 2 mining lasers and 3-4 heat vents to mitigate asteroid damage and facilitate resource acquisition.
2) Get a water cooler and food dispenser.
3) Get a third mining laser or a laser weapon to be entirely safe from asteroids (the weapon will let you intimidate ships for credits as well and let you mine more efficiently).
4) Get a research station and research plant bed, then get a plant bed to secure your food supply.
5) Get a navigation console or engines so that, if a scary ship insists on attacking, you can turn them on to have positive evasion and jump away. First recourse should be bribery, though, to keep the jump in reserve as much as possible.
6) Make sure to have at least 2 cargo containers, life support, and airlocks so that you can't be crippled in a disaster.
7) Congratulations! You are now totally safe.
Only the first few steps are really hectic. You might lose a few components to asteroids but you should be able to replace them if you are mining efficiently.
That issue addressed, this game is currently limited in scope and has no story but it is a VERY promising foundation. Only the first half hour or so really presents much challenge because the difficulty doesn't seem to scale throughout the game but that is all still being hammered out. There is still a great deal of ship-building content in the game right now and I have encountered no bugs at all. If you enjoy games like FTL or Rimworld, you should enjoy this. For $12 it is definitely worth a buy, in my opinion.

The long awaited pc edition of Fire Pro Wrestling World has arrived.  But was it worth the wait?
Background:
This iconic series got it's start in 1989 and was a huge hit in japan, finding a home on the super famicom, ps2, gameboy advance, and other popular consoles.  While most wrestling games were heading in the direction of 3d gameplay with licensed characters, career modes, and true to life entrances, Fire Pro was something different.  Using 2d sprites and a robust character editor, Fire Pro was often thought of as more Simulator than game, with people often running entire EFEDS off the software.  The easy to use customizing features allowed virtually any wrestling superstar or character to be added to the games.  This was important, as the developer (HUMAN early on, then SPIKE) did not have the rights to use actual wrestlers.  Instead they put characters with similar looks and movesets in and let the fans do the rest.  Another popular customizable feature was the AI behavioral logic, which allowed you to make an ai controlled character behave the way their real life counterpart would.   The games gained cult status over the years in america by fans wanting something a bit different than the usual yukes/jakks wrestling games that would appear every couple of years.  On July 10th, 2017, Fire Pro wrestling world became the first release in the series released exclusively for pc, with a ps4 version planned for the near future.
Graphics:
Nobody has ever purchased a fire pro game because of the modern graphics and stunning visual effects, but the 2d sprites are well done with smooth animation.  Explosions and blood effects look better on the new version but very little has actually changed from the original style, they just look bigger and a bit more detailed.  Best looking fire pro game to date, which shouldn't surprise anyone, given the hardware it's running on.  That said, if you are primarily interested in graphics, wwe 2k17 is available for purchase fairly cheaply due to 2k18 being announced for release soon.
Sound:
This is fire pro's weak spot throughout the series and FPWW is no different. The japanese rock themes are well done and fit well, but the character vocalizations are just unpleasant at times.  When performing certain moves, the characters grunt in a very artificial way repeatedly, the referee will also repeatedly ask give up? give up? give up?  give up?  during submission matches.  I get it's audio on the same tech level of the video, but while they used the limited visual capabilities to fullest extent, you feel like very little effort was put in to improve the audio experience.  The 3 counts sound good if that helps lol.  No custom music or themes for characters yet, but there's always hope for that to be added in later.  Including a sound editor using wav or mp3 for the sound events in-game would have been an amazing add here.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is timing based with some button mashing thrown in.  The grapple moves involve waiting for the wrestlers to lock up and pressing a button/direction at the instant they make contact.  This doesn't appeal to some but it really does work well, providing a fair and equal way of battling.  The button mashing comes into play during kickouts and submission escapes, and isn't overdone.  Tests of strength are resolved by repeatedly pressing back and forth on your directional controls.  If I had a complaint here, it is that some striking moves require a very specific angle and distance to connect.  You will miss many dropkicks that you feel made perfect contact.  Sometimes moves delivered from the top rope connect right on the guy yet it registers a miss.  These occurances happen often enough to be irritating, but not so often as to ruin the experience.  Hitting those moves becomes much more satisfying when done perfectly.
Play options:
More coming after the early access period.  For now, standard match types for fire pro, including 8 man battle royals, 8 man tags, MMA type matches, cages, barbed wire with c4 explosives, exploding ring deathmatchs, there's some good stuff here.  Run leagues, run tournaments, the level of customization here is really nice and should keep simmers busy for a long time.
Online:
Matches at the moment are hit or miss.  Connecting is a problem, staying connected is a problem, lag is a problem.  This may be a drawback of early access to be improved on later.  This is the first online version of the game so some bugs are to be expected.

Presentation:
This is another thing that might just be a personal nag.  The game was originally japanese.  There's going to be some translation issues.  But It doesn't feel like it would have been very difficult for an english speaking employee to change some of the wording to a more north american friendly version.  Exploding rings are referred to as landmines.  MMA contests are called Gruesome Fighting.  The instructions in mission mode are often misleading because of eliminations in battle royals and such being labelled disqualifications.  And a further note on mission mode, often the controls for what you need to do to perform the required action are left unclear.  There is also no digital manual or instruction to find information on how to tag, perform cage jumps, and other items.  These are things that I'd like to see improved in future versions, but in game changes to the language is unlikely, although a manual will likely be created at some point to assist new players.
Fun Factor:
This is such a love it or hate it game.  If you are only playing verses the cpu, you will learn the game quickly and squash everyone you face.  This will get dull.   If online becomes more stable, it may be worth getting for that.  But the sort of people this game will appeal to are the people who will download or make wrestlers from the past, present, or their own imaginations.  Make their behavior as true to life as possible, and put them in cpu controlled matches to see what happens.  If that seems fun to you, there is no greater wrestling sim in the world and you need to drop that 20 bucks right now.  If you just want an arcade wrestling game, go get 2k.  It's much better for what you want.

(This review pertains to the early access version, and will likely be replaced once the full version is out)
So after 12 years, the sequel to Returns, Fire Pro Wrestling World hits Steam (and later PS4), much to the surprise of a lot of fans (my jaw dropped when i first saw the "lockup" trailer). How does it fare atm? Let's find out.
The Good:
* The sounds are a massive improvement over Returns by a country mile, and even without the comparisons, hold their own quite well. (The main menu and match results themes are really catchy, for one, and the critical sound is heart stopping, in a good way)
* Strike exchanges! These really are a great addition to the series, and even I can't help but say, "Yeah! Ooh!" during a really epic one.
* Full tutorial mode. This is great for those who could never get into Fire Pro, and also helps to sharpen up many a veteran.
* Blood on the mat. Kinda minor compared to the rest, but a worthwhile addition.
* New moves added, with more to likely come
* UNLIMITED EDIT SLOTS. (well at least as much as your hard drive can hold) Correct me if I'm wrong, but this is the first wrestling game to pull off such a feat.
* Match results are back! (Not as deep as the GBA games, but there's room for improvement)
* The new 9 layered system is great, and I think it's heavily slept on.
* The new visuals look great, and strike a balance between modern and retro. Games like these are long successors of the 16 bit era.
* Various issues seem to be fixed, like Returns's RNG bug, the breathing/spirit bug, and superior camera work being added to matches involving seconds to point out a few.
The Not So Good:
* The game has quite a few bugs, like keyboard users being unable to preview sounds, and extreme menu lag (which is thankfully being addressed by the devs). That being said it is Early Access, so these can be ironed out over time.
* Mission 30 will likely drive you nuts if you're inexperienced to begin with, because the cage match escape AI has not been improved since R, and shaking the cage (unless you're the CPU, bleh) is useless.
Thoughts:
Despite a few (admittedly annoying) bugs (remember, Early Access), this game is already looking like an improvement over Returns in almost every area, and can definitely be considered a great successor, as well as a great standalone game on its own two feet. I seriously believe that even for a....late stage beta, this could definitely be put in contention for the GOAT of wrestling games.

Needed to play: gasoline, vodka, cheeki breeki radio, camo pants and several pairs of clean boots.
In Spintires and Mudrunner you get your hands, better, your tires, dirty pretty fast since you get to operate in old Muddy Russia; purpose is clear: get a truck (out of many), select your activity gear, move to a specific point, load logs, come back in one piece. Or, pull another vehicle out of a pond, repair other vehicles and so on, it basically never gets old.
Graphics are gorgeous and physics are simply amazing and unforgiving. Mud is not at all to be trusted, even if you are driving a powerful 4x4 truck. Rather, it will be the main reason to get stuck into it with all four wheels.
Most of the time you will feel powerless against a terrain like this, but there are several solutions for each problem: winches, truck cranes and grabbers, fuel stations, support units and such will be your best friends in these cases. Just do not push your luck too much, it's often better to take a long rocky road instead of cutting through a muddy pathway to spare time. Also, fuel is not limited and pushing a heavy vehicle on a bad terrain sucks almost all of it in a few minutes.
Your best weapon against all this is, guess what, patience. Do not expect a fast-paced gameplay with jumping off ledges like some kind of movie, this job is difficult and less rewarding than you think.
As I said, physics and graphics are ineccepible, but camera angles tend to be difficult to manipulate and may give you hard times.
On the other hand, controls are both keyboard and mouse, making the experience a bit less immersive, but funny anyway.
To summarize...
PROS
- Gogerous looking and sounding
- Most realistic physics ever
- Technically perfect
- Challenging as hell
- Moddable
- Extremely optimized
CONS
- Hard to control camera angles
- For amateurs and patient people only
- Not very different from the original title
9/10 keep up the good work

Criticism can help to shift and mold a game into something amazing, as well as provide insight for folk looking in before committing. This is hands down the best zombie survival and crafting based simulation available, however, it’s taking far too long to develop and like others have mentioned, it’s not delivering on all its promises, and this is the main reason I can’t recommend it… yet.

I personally have no interest in multiplayer in most games as I prefer playing alone, so enjoy high quality AI and realism, as intricate as possible. This game is getting there.
While it shows 65 hours of playtime for me, I’ve likely put in a couple of hundred over the years.
-The way the menu functions — whether you are accessing your inventory, crafting an item, making modifications to a structure, or building your own place, it seems a bit clunky and slow in terms of responsiveness of choices made.
-Looting can become like farming. Because of the amount of structures in the game, and places you can search, it tends to get a bit boring after a while. How could this be improved? I suggest a larger variety of items, and a look at the randomness factor, such as restricting certain items to specific structures (which can be improved); if you have a chance of finding some quality items, some more superior than others, and more of a variety, this would really spruce up the game play a lot.
-The information supplied, or lack thereof, around what you need to cook. There are pots and pans and utensils and this and that which you need to make specific dishes, yet it’s not clear. So you could carry around some ingredients and yet find you need a pan or tray to make the actual meal. The same goes for other things you craft in the game. The wiki is great, but it should be easier to understand these things. This has improved through updates, but it’s not quite there yet.
-It would be nice to have some kind of story to the game, so you are not simply surviving, but have a goal in mind. Perhaps the only functional vehicle in town could be repaired from finding parts, and the goal is for you to travel to another town where your family is, so you can see if they are alive; something similar to the scenarios in Zafehouse Diaries. This really has the potential to be the perfect combination of Faster Than Light (Oregon Trail-like) and Rimworld (Dwarf Fortress-like). It's clearly early access with in-progress and TBD features. Sadly, forgiveness for this early stage and the game's genre seems lacking in current reviews. In my not so humble opinion, the vast majority of bad reviews boil down to "it's too hard". These further break down into "It's too hard by design" or "It's too hard by accident", neither of which deserve criticism at this stage.
The difficulty is constantly being tuned as new features are added. If the extremes aren't tested, then the optimum can't be found. Many of the problems that existed when the game was initially put on sale were fixed within 12 hours. I personally never experienced the extreme starting difficulty that a lot of people reported within the first few hours of launch. In its current state, I don't feel the difficulty is any worse than FTL. In terms of time played before dying  to RNG, it feels right about the same as Rimworld to me.
To address the game rather than the reviews:
Like all games in both genres, there are several thresholds to pass before you can survive long term. Each one of them has its own set of challenges, completely separate from the increasing difficulty of ship, star, and asteroid encounters. Make no mistake: you
be RNGed in this game. An early asteroid hitting your cargo hold such that you can't gather materials to build a new one is a hard restart. A hostile ship that takes out a key component right after you finished construction that used up all your silicon is GG.
And that's a Good Thing.
The risk vs reward tradeoffs, and the ways that different choices can play out in unexpected ways are what makes games like this truly enticing. While some things still need tuning, the overall feel of "Crap that thing I did two asteroid belts ago doomed me" is easily made up for by the breakthrough moments and the "HOLY CRAP that thing I did two asteroid belts ago just saved my♥♥♥♥♥"
You have to go into games like this expecting to start over a dozen times in an hour so you will be delighted by your own improvement. If you miscalibrate your expectations, you will not have fun. The more you play, the more you will find yourself handling situations that you would've screamed at the RNG a few hours earlier.
Once you pass into the midgame where you have a functioning ship and crew the, builder aspects of the game kick in. You have more time to focus on the layout and aesthetics of your ship. You will add new subsystems that begin bringing more FTL aspects in. Various consoles, engines, plant beds, etc. require crewmembers assigned to various roles to "tend" them. For example, when manned, the navigation console increases evasion and allows you to get to new asteroid belts or other ships on command.
The sandbox-like flexibility in ship layout alone will probably draw some people to this game. The choices you make for the shape and size of your ship have real consequences. Do you have spots of hull to reinforce with armor plates? Do you invest in big engines to avoid incoming damage in the first place? Building wider might help you mine more asteroids, but it might "help" you crash into them as well. Putting all your consoles in one room might look nice, but what if a large asteroid hits that room?
I haven't gotten past the midgame in my own gameplay, but from what I've watched on lets plays, the difficulty grows proportionally to your ship's complexity and to the time the game has been going. If you get the knack and the luck, your ships capabilities will grow faster than the environment's/enemies' and you'll reach a pretty much steady state of growth. But don't get complacent, because you will still have struggles that can amplify each other and escalate quickly to the point of destruction.
That said, it does seem like the encounters get stale after a while. If you aren't held by the design & artistic aspects of shipbuilding, you may find it a bit flat. For $12 the amount of content feels *almost* ready but there are a few things that I would like to see added before release:

Where to begin... It's beautiful! The art direction is fantastic, the style is really appealing and especially the animations are stunning - The little foxes hiding behind trees, the faes around the mushrooms, the steam condensor, even the dust whirling around once you build something.
It's full of life everywhere. Each time you look at something, it moves and you can't stop examining every little detail.
And I really love steampunk! The music is really good as well, it's uplifting and fitting the game perfectly! Even though there are some sounds missing still, many of them made me laught , especially the ranch's sound!
But let's talk about gameplay. I like it, it's cool and you have plenty to do – there's always something to build or to improve. You can spend hours building your perfect city, and optimizing your layout. You have many possibilities, there are 5 kinds of food, there even are wonders as for example in Pharaon at the time.
Also, each population has it's own needs, the rich people want jewellery, the poor want cutlery, everybody loving production chains will be satisfied (Raw materials, stockage, transformation, distribution and so on). You feel the game was inspired by Sierra's titles, and the building layouts are similar: maintenance is superimportant, and there even are ghosts! You need to carefully plan your cities, because one loose joint may make everything very difficult. So, there really is always something to do!
On a technical standpoint, the game is fine. You can always look at stastistics via that little eye button, or the full one, once you've built a townhall. They come in handy for people that want to build THE perfect city, but you do not absolutely have to look at it to win the game.
And  finally, I love the little annotations and the humour! There is a short text for every building or person, often with some pop-references that are genuinely funny.
Really, get it! Really! The content is amazing compared to for example Banished, where you only have 3 things to do in like 10 hours. Since they both cost the same, and the programmers will patch add new content to Lethis, this game has the potential to become gigantic!
P.S: For all people who experienced bugs, I haven't encountered a single one yet, perhaps they have been fixed already. And as I've seen so many people raging about the chipset stuff: Why didn't you just read the requirements section on the Steam store page? There's no point in complaining, if you simply did not read them!

Super charming.  Appealing aesthetics.  This is reminiscent (positively) of SimCity 2000 in its tile work and mechanics thus far.  When it's beyond Early Access I suspect it'll be very nice.  However at this very moment, there are a number of issues plaguing it.
1)  The crashing is incredible.  Click the wrong box and it'll crash.  Change options and it'll crash.  Complete the tutorial and it'll crash.  Breathe on it funny, and it'll crash.  Early access is one thing.  Non-functional is another.  I'd wait a little longer on this one as it's not done baking.
2)  Localization in English is awkward.  Probably need two or three more passes at the text and smoothing the tutorial a bit as while the mechanics aren't wholly foreign (especially to SimCity 2k folks) there are some nuances that aren't explained really well (which NPCs will go through roadblocks, which won't, which buildings will behave like this and which ones won't.
3)  Reaction time to disasters is pretty extreme.  Rubble might need some identifying marks or the game have some mechanism to display what building type was on the plot.  Buildings going into decay based on a building not working SHOULD happen, but not quite so FAST.  Again with a SC2K comparison, say a water source fails, the buildings don't go into immediate decline, it takes months, giving the player time to rebuild and redo the water/sewer system.  Either a reduced radius of effect, or more gradual decline in capability would be greatly appreciated.  And I'm sure that's not the only mechanic issue that needs some massage.
Anyhow, very charming, VERY Early Access (this should be highlighted more on the store page honestly -- I wasn't aware it was early access until I started hitting some issues.)  Hopefully all this resolved though and get a nice working city builder!  And the art and sound is extremely nice.

SO normally I don't leave reviews for games unless it gives me a very positive or negative impression and sadly this hit me the wrong way, don't get me wrong I see work was put into this game but it just seems to unoptimized and glitchy to be worth $20 and I'll explain why.
During my time in the game (which only took about 3 hours worth to get through) I encountered multiple times where the dialog wouldn't play, textures would either poorly load on high or they would slow you down as they all started to load at once, and there were parts of the map that I could actually see through "mostly" inside the beginning house when you looked out the windows. There was even a point where I went through the maze under ground during the nuclear meltdown situation where a part of the pipe maze was not blocked off and I fell right through the map and saw a game object in the lava where the bucket drops into or when I had to make a fake dummy for the coffee trolley to break down a security door and after finding all the items I accidentally put coffee in it and it took off without even needing the items I found and with the team it had the backing it had and the amount of testers it had I don't understand how things like that could of gotten past the testers.
So now lets get to the "enemy" and characters. First off lets talk about vladdy the bear now I know he was supposed to be the "comic relief" character but constantly listening to "stupid idiot" and "stupid american technology" and stupid this and that I really got to be an annoyance and just a downright nuance of a character that you had to lug around during your trip and honestly I couldn't tell if I should of been relieved or sad at the end when he perished but that's how I feel about him. Now onto the enemy and the corn, the only purpose the corn had was to delay the main character with small messages that I'm sure you already saw or would of figured out by yourself and besides that they served no real role in the game, the enemy was just that to me he was a typical old time cartoon enemy where we would blurt out his secret plans and made multiple mistakes and run off.
Besides that the puzzles were too linear, the ending wasn't any sort of surprise and the game just seemed bland to me and had no real redeeming factor that would make me want to come back and play it again. So those are my thoughts, I wish it would of been more then what it was but it isn't the worst thing I've ever seen.

Before I give my criticisms, I recommend the game; it will challenge you to learn and adapt and is challenging overall. That said, I do have strong thoughts about the game and feel as though the game is being held back a bit. My review is less for the consumer who wants to see if they should play the game, and more speaking to those who have already played.
Firstly, balance needs tweaking both with the characters and items; there are definitely characters who are not only better than others, but there will be instances where finding a certain character in the dungeon literally drops your chances to succeed dramatically, even if you didn't have a full team. By itself, this isn't game breaking or a true problem, but tied into the general item dynamic of the current game it becomes one. The problem with items is more a problem with the merchants; you will find many merchants, but rare is the merchant who has anything you really want. There will be tons of items that marginally improve a character maybe, but the vast majority of times it simply isn't worth the resource expenditure for a marginal improvement; almost always the resources are better kept to reinvest in the current floor. This makes merchants essentially and singularly resource generators (by selling to them). Then you have to deal with characters who are item dependent. The two problems go hand in hand. There are definitely strategies to make an initial food investment to pick up a character as nothing more than a dark room dweller (and be replaced later by another character), but that character is basically just a tiny step above dead weight while you have them in that case. All that said, the various modes (pods) do tons to make different characters more viable. (TF2 Medic is good in infirmary where you don't get restored after waves, etc.)
The second main criticism I have for the game is that the vast majority of wins are going to be based off a select few minor modules, and your ability (or more aptly, your luck?) to obtain them in time to farm. Like most things in Endless, Dust is random and there are strategies to farm dust; however, there will never be enough dust, and your characters can not hold different areas by themselves unless you use inordinate amounts of industry to set them up to do so (of course, you will have to have researched the right mix of minor modules in this circumstance as well). By that point, you get to asking yourself how many more doors, is it worth it, etc and thats all well and good. The problem really is that neurostun modules and neurostun modules alone make it possible to continue farming floors when in other runs you'd be forced to leave to the next. This reality makes a very narrow gameplan for the majority of runs, and while its definitely possible to force yourself to not use neurostun modules for whatever reason and still win, it is far, far from optimal.
When you put these two points together, you obtain a very narrow gameplan by which you judge your current run by floor 3-4 perhaps. If you didn't have a suitable hero show up on floor 2, you might as well reset, and then if you don't have neurostunners (or an otherwise extremely strong and prolific researching game up to that point), you might as well restart around floor 4-6 since you must farm well in the middle of the run to be set up for the end. Regarding floor 2, if you'll have 3 heroes (you start with 2, and find 1), you want at least 1 operator by then to help you set up your run and if you didn't start with an operator, naturally you're hoping for one etc etc. Once again, makes a narrow gameplan for the majority of runs.
I will say also, that most set ups and starts will work for the majority of runs, but its the end of runs that quickly reveal that your team is lacking. Of course it is more than possible and even viable to hope to finish the last 1-2 floors quickly, but as a player you don't want to rely on that as a strategy, and especially not when you've spent the last 3-4 hours getting to the end.
To be clear, my criticisms are not that the game is too hard, but simply that the optimal strategy to winning is extremely narrow, and clearly the best route to take, making it the only route to take for the majority of runs. I believe the game will get better and continue to be balanced a bit better, and in my opinion it has to start with improving character viability, which stems from the general item dynamic being too sparse and ineffectual and minor modules being singular in strategy (singular in strategy only because of effectiveness, the variety is definitely there.) I think the monster waves are as brutal as they are because the winning strategies are so effective... if those strategies get nerfed a bit, the monster waves can also be nerfed a bit and everything should be generally more equal and the game can still be challenging in such a case. A great game regardless and I am hard pressed to think of another game I logged 100+ hours on as fast.

The Long Dark a 2hr review
“A cryptic and chilling experience”
I had originally written off the long dark as another post-apocalyptic crafting game after seeing “the four horsemen of the steampocolypse” “Early access”, “Crafting”, “Open world” and “Survival”.
However I could not of been more wrong; I had bought the game in October of 2014 and at this point not much of the game other than the art style is the same in the current version, However what I saw was a unique little gem of a game that showed promise from its art style and tough yet fair gameplay; I have found myself being out of breath after being chased by a wolf in game.
On the 1st of August the long awaited story mode was added including a staggering 16-20 hours of gameplay in just the first two episodes, that’s longer than it took me to complete Battlefield 4’s campaign and that was a triple A tittle. Upon loading into the game you are depicted a landing strip during a heavy snow storm, the cut scene that would not feel out of place at an indie movie festival shows us this surreal place and introduces us to our character, the manly yet rose tipped cheeked character who I would over the next two hours become emotionally invested in to the extent of almost having a heart attack at the sign of a wolf. The first cut scene reveals parts of our cryptic backstory and reveals that the lady who has come to see us is in fact our possible Ex-wife, we are instantly immersed in intense mystery as she refuses our questions and insists we help her get to a remote area in our plane. At this point we are less than five minutes into the story of the game and we have already learned we have a troubled past with our possible ex-wife, whilst in the plane she notes that we still wear our wedding ring and that she does sometimes too, this suggests to me that its likely we both still have feelings for each other which only adds to the tension when we see sparks coming from the planes controls followed by a sharp descent into the unknown wilderness.
Upon waking up we are surrounded by a horrific crash and trapped in a deep ravine of which there appears to be no escape. This start to the game acts as a tutorial in the sense it shows us the basic crafting of fires and finding food such as the dear we cut with A LITTERAL PIECE OF METAL WE PULLED FROM OUR HAND, god our character is so manly. I must praise Hinterland Studios for this tutorial as they have created an experience that doesn’t just hold your hand and take you through the steps but gives you commands like “Find wood for a fire”, now this may seem like a simple task but it does not explain we can get wood from smashing crates and braking branches to sticks along with the ‘what burns best’ explanation that does not get explained but you actively learn through creating multiple fires and experiencing the annoyance of getting a fire almost lighted until it suddenly fails and your left in a cave freezing to death.
Once you have learned the basics the game throws you into the deep end. As you ascend from the deep dark cave you have called home for three nights since the “Mysterious Geomagnetic Storm”. Upon your escape you find the rest of your crashed plane and the metal case your companion had insisted on keeping the contents of which to herself, the case is the first piece of a binge worthy collection of clues that keep the games mystery and need to find your companion/ex-wife.
Moving away from spoiling too much of the story for a second I want to discuss the first character we meet after our crash, assuming you don’t count the wolf that almost gave me a heart attack after appearing in my peripheral vision. Anyway GreyMother the blind elderly rifle wielding psychopath lady is the first character you meet and the only one I met in my first two hours; this choice of few characters in the game I believe adds a surreal and abandoned feeling to the area which along with the decay and notes littered throughout the game make you as the character feel somewhat responsible for these peoples suffering. The notes throughout the first town of Milton show us the “Mainlanders” as a selfish narcissistic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who have abandoned these people long before the storm. GreyMother tells us of a previous event the “collapse” after an earthquake when the people of Milton were in desperate need for help the ‘Mainlanders’ did nothing leaving the town to despise all ‘out of towners’. The game at this point requires us to achieve her trust to learn more about our companion and the town’s history; we are tasked with gathering wood and food, to gather the food we are offered a moral choice of whether to just take some from the gas station or to hunt for it, I chose to take it from the gas station as at this point I was so desperate for any information due to my now acute addiction to this game. The trust system itself I do not like, my reasoning for this is the ability to cheat it, for example I made lots of bandages from cloth I found about the town and gave her them to quickly achieve the required trust level to progress the story; now please not the game has been patched several times over the last two days and I imagine will be patched continually and this feature could have been removed by the time you read this. Apart from the trust system I did not notice any bugs or glitches in the game during my gameplay.
The narrative changes in my mind at a moment’s notice with trying to guess what’s going to happen next. Towards the end of my two hours I was asked by GreyMother to head towards the tunnel at the edge of town to search for my friend and to find an exit from the mountainous town; upon reaching the tunnel we find a half buried prison transport bus along with a dead inmate and a manifest listing several prisoners that are nowhere to be seen. This sudden threat to the character was not what I was expecting, unlike the constant threat of animal attacks the threat from other humans is unexpected and adds a new series of thoughts rampaging through my mind; the thought that these may be the men travelling with my companion make the urgency of the situation more evident. Upon returning to grey mother we are faced with a saddening cut scene in which she states this is the end for her as although there is another way for us to pass the mountains there is not for her; this scene almost brought a tear to my eye as she asks for some time alone to rest we are a faced with the horrific notion that we will most likely have to abandon this vulnerable lady who has helped us with information on how to survive.
That’s all she wrote folks. Seriously try this game out, you have nothing to lose you can always refund it. In this review I only touched on the story and the sandbox and challenge mods add so much potential game time I cannot recommend this game enough.

I have sunk some time into this game, and I genuinely enjoyed it.  I don't remember what I paid, but it was early on in the EA, so probably less than the $30-35 they want now.
I logged all of my hours before the game was "released."  And only played through the first few hubs of Wintermute.
All in all I'd have to say I enjoyed my time playing the sandbox, and I REALLY enjoyed my first few plays.  But, as others have said, the game loses it's luster after you've survived for a decent time (~30 days+) during multiple plays.  As the map is not procedurally generated, and is static, you really lose out on that feeling of "I really should be wary of venturing out in this storm" because you know exactly where you are going and have no chance of getting lost.
I really don't leave reviews....feel free to check....but I felt compelled to let everyone know that I am dissatisfied with the developers of this game.  Now, I'm not one to cry wolf (see what I did there) but these devs really dropped the ball.  This game was in EA for HOW LONG!?  And then they release exactly the same game with a hacked-together low player-involvement "story mode."  Sorry Hinterland, this just doesn't cut it.  How do they wait years to release a buggy, somehow-less-involved-than-sandbox, singleplayer, when this was the carrot on the end of the stick?
I really think the problem lies with the static map.  Without randomization of locations, you lose out on the entire "survival" atmosphere.  Have only 132 hours on record, I can tell within seconds of spawning in (night or day) pretty much where I am and where I need to go.
Obligatory edit after the fanboys are attempting to crucify me:
You're all entitled to your own opinion, or just entitled, we may never know.  Many of these hours were surely logged by having it running in the background -- I can't recall exactly of course -- but I feel like I've played the game "seriously" 6-7 times, surviving for a decent amount of time.  I think I have a 30 days achievement, not sure.
As I said, I played most of my time very early on and I am not impressed by what the developers have done with all the time they have had.  Perhaps this is more of a problem with steam and "early access" a.k.a. "We need more money but our game isn't finished."  I do agree with others who have said that the story mode is really "on the rails" without the true sandbox feeling that I (wrongly) assumed would come with the story.  They have also done next-to-nothing to increase the wildlife AI and you can easily skate around the map without fear.
If you want to disagree with me, that is alright.  I don't base my self-esteem on the opining of random internet strangers.  I even stated that I thought the game was fun at first, which is probably why several people with low hours are disagreeing with me.

So far I can say that this is my favorite survival game. The atmosphere is perfect, the soundtrack is great, and the gameplay is strategic, and slow paced, but its still extremely tense and gets your adrenaline pumping. For those of you who have seen The Grey with Liam Neeson, It gives off that same tone. Fear, Tension and tough decisions.
Graphics: This game doesn't have extremely detailed, realistic graphics, but its art style works fine for this genre. Its kind of a mix between the walking dead and skyrim.
Gameplay: As I said before this is not an action packed game. It is slow paced, strategic and tense. It comes down to choices like going out at night for food and risk freezing to death or being mauled by wolves, or stay in a shelter for the night and try to sleep the hunger off till the morning. I think it boils down to your survival instincts and it is the among most accurate survival games out there. It is challenging, but fair.
Story?: This game does have a single player story, and its definitely worth playing through, but the most cinematic experiences ive had playing this game were in survival mode. Getting stalked through the woods by wolves, nearly freezing to death far outside any shelter and just barely starting a fire to camp for the night, reaching the top of a mountain peak as the music starts playing from the beautifully written soundtrack. All of it creates the perfect wilderness survival game.
Problems: I think it could be a bit easier for players to find things like hacksaws and coals to allow the player to forge items. Right now it seems the only way to play is to clean a region of resources, pack up and walk to another region. Being able to stay in one region instead of being forced to move should be a bit more viable of an option.I expected a bit less loading screens, but they arent that long so no big discount there. Also, the game starts for the first time in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ resolution that you have to fix in the settings. Lastly, campfires require you to get within inches to actually warm up, causing you to possibly burn yourself (which sucks). I also think this game should be a bit cheaper. $15?
Overall: 8.5/10 refreshing and well done

When you find yourself making notes and flowcharts on post-it notes during worktime, or waking up in the night to make notes in your bedside notebook, all for the next session of SpaceChem... then you know you've found a truly addictive game.
The visual block approach to programming makes this a really nice game for anyone who enjoys programming or similar tasks. The fact that you can compare your results to those of your friends makes you go back to levels you've already completed to try and optimise them further or for a different criteria.
My only issue was that the later levels were just too hard for me. That and the fact that I quickly ran out of post-its.
Not your average puzzle game. Very challenging and immensely satisfying when you solve a level.  If this game were on a console, people would break many controllers ... WITH THEIR MINDS!

Spacechem is less about chemistry and more a programming-puzzle game - You leave signposts on a grid, directing two grabby-thingies and several molecular bonding things to assemble and reassemble molecules.
The difficulty curve is a little steep after the first few chapters: it starts you off with making O2 from oxygen, or H2 and O2 from H2O. Eventually, the puzzles become a lot more complex - the one that sticks out in my mind is a boss battle where you are given an infinite supply of water and told to make rocket fuel and plutonium. A later one that has you manufacturing ruby crystals (or a molecule I'm told is supposed to be one) for a laser.
That said, it's really rewarding to manage something so complex.
-- tl;dr: Puzzles that are hard but not impossibly so. No chem-classes required, but being able to think like a programmer might help.

When it first came out, I was skeptical to graphical presentation, despite being fan of isometric platform. At the time of this review I have officially played only 14 hours, but mind you, 14 hours in one sitting. This game is as rewarding for your bravery and fast reaction as it is punishing for mistakes and miscalculations. I still have not grasped all concepts of the gameplay, but I can surely say, that despite this being an early release, it is off to a strong start, never mind the shortcomings, such as lack of vehicles (which as I understand are soon to be implemented), or limited crafting options and guidance through more obscure aspects of this experience. I would greatly recommend this to both players who enjoy arcade style zombie shooting and those keen on tactical survivalism. For past few hours, I have guided my limp legged, half burned, overweight character through endless hordes of undead, only to disappoint myself with outcome far worse that anticipated. During all this time I can't even say I have explored one percent of content available. Don't let shallow negative reviews influence you - those who do not perceive this masterpiece for what it is, have barely even skimmed the surface and left, after game refused to just throw guns and ammo at them for no effort whatsoever. Crawling on all fours away from zombies only to eat dog food for next three days while skimping on ammo and water is what zombie survival genre is really about. You can't say that nothing has changed, map few years ago was constricted to one city only, now it offers several points of interest and amazing adventures along the way. Those experiencing problems and crashes, well, you don't have anyone else to blame but yourself. This current version is by far the most rigid piece of work, and some complains lead me to believe cause of such problems is error in users own ways towards his system. At the end of the day, I realise that there can only be so many people who can truly appreciate realistic struggle in absurd scenario, but this is exactly what it is. If you do it right, and you do it slow, and shift into difficulty that is by far hardest to manage in and face it as challenge, not obstacle, you will have days after days of grind and hope rewarded in absolute harmony between RPG elements and action packed isometric shooter. If anything, title screen accurately displays how the game should be played.
P.S. - those who are discouraged by performance of pirated versions of the game (I can, however, only speak for myself), legitimate Steam release greatly exceeds all expectations (with comparability mode also available (?)) even on low spec computers. I'm running PZ on Intel Core 2 Duo 2GHz machine with 2GB of RAM and Cthulhu knows what♥♥♥♥♥is this video chipset made out of, but I can still boast a stable 60fps on minimal settings, be it with or without Steam overlay.

So far I can gauge this game being a "Minecraft/DF town sim blend done right". Things that are in the game work well and good (until you meet bugs), and the whole process of managing your town is quite smooth and nice, easily the best or near-best of that I've seen in similar games.
So, why it's "not recommended"?
At the moment, there isn't much to do there. The amount of content that you can try is extremely low, vertical progression is basically nonexistent - you can unlock all the things that are currently implemented in the game in 2 to 3 game days (that's 1-1.5 hours of playtime at most), and afterwards there's nothing left to do apart from "build more stuff because you can and it's the only thing you can".
Additonal grain of salt is the building editor - customizable buildings is one of the defining points of the game (that is, one of the defining points
), but the editor is rather clunky and hard to use in cases other than traditional 1-story building (multiple stories aren't implemented at the moment) with simple inner structure and minimal amount of walls. Try to do complex multi-room irregurarly-shaped buildings, however, and you will be fighting the UI much more than actually planning.
And finally, the pacing of development is nothing to write home about. The initial plans (from Kickstarter campaign) were to release the game towards the end of 2014, you know. Now it's the end of 2015, and we recently had an alpha version where devs were mostly fixing internals, such as pathfinding. Going by this, it is extremely unlikely that we'll see any reasonably-sized chunk of gameplay - that is, content and actual mechanics - available until the end of 2016, and beta/release stages may follow even later. And that's only if the development won't stop abruptly at some point.
To summarize, it's a game that promises really great things, but currently allows you to plant turnips, design and build simple small buildings, dig through mountains, and hit randomly-appearing enemies such as goblins with some swords (archery is not implemented yet). That's all.

Okay. Let's begin the review. This is a honest summary of my experience so far with Lethis.
1) Gameplay
The game plays like a city builder should. You construct your city in whatever manner you seem fitting, you rotate buildings, you position infrastructure and decoration as you wish to.  There are bugs, but i will let them slide as this is the teams first title and most importantly, a fairly decent experience that they are willing to improve upon.
It seems like it might get very advanced and have a greater sense of depth to it. I am only 4 hours or so in however, but i have witnessed the ability to grow my cities by levelling up the housing for families (which requires me to provide for their cares, be it alcohol, washing facilities, food supplies or jobs). There is also maintanence, which means buildings can collapse unless you have a maintanence man checking in on them regularly. This is just a small part of the picture, you can build a lot of cool things to play around with.
There is a lot of intricacy, certain buildings require certain resources to run properly which means developing a well thought out road structure so your stockpiles of resources get distributed to the proper places.
i am sure a lot more will be coming.
2) Graphics
Oh the graphics. They are awesome. At a glance it looks pixel, zoom out all the way and it looks like im playing sim city or OTTD with a steampunk theme (which is fine, by the way) but then I found out i can zoom in all the way and look at what everybody in my city is doing.
Thats right. EVERYTHING is animated. I was amazed to watch the fishery after catching a fish, a giant fish is inside the building and the fisherman cuts meat from the fish and places it on a table. Then, a worker from the storage facility arrives and takes the fish in his cart (which is animated) to the facility and wham, now I can see fish stored in the crates. Your workers move to and fro, when a building is fully staffed there are animations and effects that play but its not just buildings. Environment is also animated!
Build a flower garden, watch as butterflys take up home. Build trees, and see birds flying about. In the wilderness itself, there are a combination of birds, foxes and rabbits if you look carefully enough they will peek out and dart around the map.
3) Sound.
The game has a lovely musical track which is very fitting to the theme and pleasent to listen to. A lot of the buildings have little sound effects when near them and when you click on them, as does the scenery. This is a very nice touch and i hope they expand upon it.
Now, the downsides:
1) Bugs - There are a lot of bugs, i am told. So far I have only encountered a crashing problem, other than that none but the forums suggest there are many so we shall see.
2) Interface - Its a little clunky at times, especially when rotating buildings. It's not always clear what side a building needs a road connected to function properly.
3) No control over worker routes - Currently you have no control over your workers routes directly. Workers will go work where they wish to work, they will walk randomly about the city to their establishments and this does pose a problem with supply. If your shop is constantly picking up the wrong product and sending it out to the wrong place for instance, its very difficult to figure out how to get around that problem without moving the shop itself.
You can place roadblocks which stop workers from passing through, so perhaps creative use of roadblocks is going to be the way forwards past that.
4) No control over workers in buildings - You simply have an on or off switch. You cannot assign workers to the buildings you wish them to go to. This currently forces you to construct more housing to fill any gaps. Not sure if this was intented or not.
Overall?
A great game that needs some more work. I highly reccomend supporting the dev team as it is currently playable and lovely to experience.  I am a huge fan of city builders as a concept, but i have only really played ANNO for a lengthy period of time but Lethis has become a personal favorite.  So what are you wating for, like steampunk and city building? Buy it, buy it now!

Lethis - Path of Progress is an old-school city builder like Pharaoh or Caesar which takes us in the middle of a steampunk industrial revolution. If you ever played those games you shouldn't have any problems to know what to do in order to make you cities prosper.
While the game doesn't bring a lot of innovations gameplay-wise, the artistic direction of the game is just... fantastic.  Both the soundtrack and the visuals are top-notch and really fit the universe of Lethis, and as a conqequence give a really good feeling to the game.
However, be warned that the game is pretty much at a state of early-access at the moment, despite being officially relased. Indeed, there are still some bugs depending on your hardware and overall the game still requires tweaking. I'm thinking about the sandbox mode in particular which feels a bit empty and the lack of information when browsing the building list.
In brief, I recommend giving Lethis a shot when the major problems will have been fixed (which should not be long since the developpement team is actively working on it).

For some reason I had low expectations of this game, but it pleasantly surprised me.
At first glance this game gave me a “Samorost” meets “Machinarium” kind of feel.
Machinarium in sense of the art style and even character design, but Samorost in terms of length and quality (Free web game/demo kind of feeling).
Despite the first impression I got from it, I got a lot more time out of it then I was expecting and did actually enjoy it. I thought it was going to be a 20 minute kind of game, but I managed just over 80 minutes on this. Which I don’t think is too bad.
In terms of story, point and click games don’t usually lack. I’m not saying this game lacks story, it’s just a lot simpler than most point and click games I have played.
The general story to this game is that your dog has been kidnapped by aliens and you have to get him back by finding and trading a crystal with the aliens.
It’s nothing too special of a story but it was simple and it worked.
This is one of those games that leave out dialog all together and just use simple sound effects and noises. The sound quality itself isn’t that great and I’m not too much of a fan of that whole approach although some games can make it work. This game is somewhere down the middle for me.
In terms of using spoken sound effects and noises for people talking, I can usually stand that. But using the same kind of mouth noises and sound effects for more general things like walking or to emphasis gestures kind of annoys me. I’m not sure why, maybe just the sheer childlikeness of it?
Luckily for me, this game is charming in other ways. So much so that it didn’t really bother me.
The art style is nice. It’s cute, and it definitely adds to the charm of the game. Throughout the game there are background noises/animations that did make me smile to myself a few times.
In terms of puzzles this game is very basic. The puzzles are pretty easy but the game itself is still fun despite that.
All things mentioned so far, I think it’s important to mention now that maybe this game is better aimed at younger audiences. Although I did enjoy it, it’s very simple in many ways so if you are looking for a challenge and a time sinker, this isn’t likely it.
All in all I liked it. It was a fun way to kill a bit of time. If you are a fan of the point and click genre and are looking for something else, maybe give this a go.
TL;DR : Fun, light-hearted, little point and click game maybe aimed at younger audiences. It’s charming, cute and a fun way to kill an hour or two.

Simply one of the best role-playing games in history.
While the story is quite typical for high fantasy, it's the characters that really captivate you - so alive and believable they seem. Virtually any choice you make may affect the way the story goes, which makes you ponder more before making a decision.
And even after finishing the game you'll be surprised to see that you've seen less than a half of the game. Dragon Age: Origins is definitely not a game for a single playthrough. After finishing it for the first time you'll be tempted to begin anew to discover a new origin story and brand new possibilities that come with it.
The battle system is great and will be please both the lovers of fast-paced action-RPG-style combat and the tactical geniuses. In any case, the bosses are quite tough to beat without proper tactics even on normal difficulty.
I cannot ignore the hard work the voice actors put into filling their character with life. I was especially impressed with Claudia Black and her Morrigan. I couldn't imagine a more fitting voice for the daughter of the Witch of the Wilds.
Inon Zur's soundtrack for the game is one of the best I've ever heard. I would put it on the same level as brilliant works of Jeremy Soule for The Elder Scrolls series.
Finally, my verdict is such: if you love role-playing games, there is no single reason why you shouldn't play Dragon Age: Origins. In fact, if you don't, you will probably regret it.
P.S. You should definitely get the Ultimate Edition as it provides all the DLC that explore the stories of some of the key characters and one of them even lets you play as a darkspawn and also the Awakening expansion, which is quite long and gives you some insight into the origin of the Blight.

This is the definitive edition of the game. The DLC collected here adds an extra companion, two extra quests to the base game, a full expansion, two additional campaigns to cap off your warden's career, and two spin-off campaigns on top of that. If you're out to see and do everything, the game can be quite long and it can be very easy to become attached to a character once you've taken them from one of six unique, humble beginnings to a position of the highest honor.
This is a Bioware RPG, meaning the pull towards that final position is inescapable, but the actual nature of those 'honors' is for you to decide. There are plenty of dichotomous choices to make with far-reaching consequences, whether or not you actually get to see those consequences play out yourself. And of course there's a full complement of companions to react to those choices and to romance or banter with. The companions may not have been chatty enough for my liking, at least in the main game, but the expansion seems to have fixed this by forcing the same amount of dialogue into a much shorter adventure. The original crew - and there is a new set of companions for the expansion - was developed well enough, but it was too easy to run through everything they had to say before the end of your time with them. Companion dialogue isn't linked to plot progression, so even having access to all nine - or six in the expansion - companions in camp didn't prevent a quiet end-game as I was always inclined to spend time to visiting with those I'd left behind.
The expressions and gestures of characters also leave something to be desired as there are only a handful of them and even fewer that look at all life-like. It is often better to look away while characters are speaking as the wooden twitching and fidgeting does more to diminish the voice performances than it does to enhance them. Glitches are not uncommon either, though none of them were exactly game-ending, unless you count the handful of crashes I experienced over my 120 hours with the game.
Arms and armor selection is sparse, which would feel like very minor gripe if not for how important aesthetic choices are for role-playing. It's difficult to create a character whose double in both appearance and equipment can't already be found in the world. There's an air of incompleteness around the game as a whole, as if there were plans to add a greater diversity of everything and that just fell through. Perhaps it's the richness of the codex entries found throughout the game that encourages that feeling. Each entry is written in character, many from the same historian or scholar, and they provide a window into a world far deeper than what is presented in-game. Though I suppose if the worst thing you can say about an experience is that you wanted more of it, maybe that's not such a bad thing.

TWO THUMBS UP

Everything is incredibly resource intensive, but it's supposed to be a harder survival game where you're not supposed to coast after the first initial resource gathering, and that's cool; but it starts to fail when my character is drinking 2L of water in one go and eating 3kg of cooked vension for a single meal only needing another 3kgs before the day is done.

Many times have I randomly been walking over the frozen lake and take "fall damage" spraining most of my joints, ripping my clothes and dropping my carrying capacity so I can barely move. There's also no jump feature so don't ever try getting creative with your pathing, you will get stuck and you will have no way to escape.
The way mapping works is also an interesting concept that's just so poorly executed, it takes a ridiculous amount of charcoal to map a very small area and it's resource intensive just to gain.
It requires no light to clean your rifle, but you can't break down furniture with a hammer in the dark.
The game has a really cool concept, it just feels so locked in and restrictive while alluding to freedom.

Spacechem is less about chemistry and more a programming-puzzle game - You leave signposts on a grid, directing two grabby-thingies and several molecular bonding things to assemble and reassemble molecules.
The difficulty curve is a little steep after the first few chapters: it starts you off with making O2 from oxygen, or H2 and O2 from H2O. Eventually, the puzzles become a lot more complex - the one that sticks out in my mind is a boss battle where you are given an infinite supply of water and told to make rocket fuel and plutonium. A later one that has you manufacturing ruby crystals (or a molecule I'm told is supposed to be one) for a laser.
That said, it's really rewarding to manage something so complex.
-- tl;dr: Puzzles that are hard but not impossibly so. No chem-classes required, but being able to think like a programmer might help.
Cool idea for a game. Will have you playing for some time.

SpaceChem is one of the best puzzle games in years. Brain breakingly hard, but never unfair, and when you DO manage to solve a puzzle you feel like the smartest man on Earth. Paired with a simple but beautiful design and a story that while sparse is interesting, they really could't do any better. On top of that, every solution is unique and truly yours - never the developers
Its the Super Meat Boy of Puzzle games. You'll be frustrated often, but every victory feels truly earned!
Be prepared to see Waldos dancing in your sleep.

This game starts out fairly simple, but quickly becomes challenging as new concepts are introduced.  At its core, it's a computer-programming game wrapped up in a layer that's somewhere in between chemical engineering and alchemy.  The majority of the gameplay involves designing reactors, where various chemicals are deconstructed and reassembled at the atomic level.  For example, you might have a level where your inputs are water and chlorine gas, and you want to convert that to oxygen gas and hydrochloric acid.  So, you have to figure out how to give instructions to your automated "waldos" to disassemble the input molecules and reassemble them into the desired outputs. Along the way, you learn more about your employers and the secrets they're hiding.

This game is SERIOUSLY difficult, but rewarding. This puzzle game is mix of process engineering, faux chemistry, and programming. It's a little intimidating at first, but built-in tutorials are excellent. Give it a try, if you're into challenging puzzles.

A game based around taking the time to devise a plan, and then setting it into clockwork motion.  If you are looking for a game that you set your pace on, where using your mind is more important than a twitch reaction, this is the one.
A fascinating puzzle game loosely based on chemistry. Challenging but very rewarding to see the end result of each puzzle.

Spacechem is difficult and wonderful. The game is intelligent and requires quite a bit of thought but it makes it better puzzler. There are two puzzles in the game: molecule formation where you must take an input, route it around the playing field, and produce an input; and a smaller factory-routing puzzle that also provides a larger context, along with the brief backstory spinnets,  as to why you're making molecules in the first place.

Take any regular puzzle game, rearrange it into an algorithm designer, add several moles of chemistry, fuse it with graph theory, dope it with action, brilliant music and brain-twisting, cast it into a friendly learning curve and, finally, polish it to a mirror sheen.
SpaceChem will be the result.
Buy it. Or, at least, spread the word about it. It is seriously underappreciated.

I love a good Zombie Outbreak. Film, games, print, graphic novels. It doesn't really matter. Often Cheesy and far fetch. The best I have found don't explain why any of it is happening or even all the rules.
Zomboid is one of those Half Romero style zombies. They are slow moving, manageable as a single individual, deadly in a pack of more then a couple.
Worse yet, you are not just worried about the walking dead. You have to eat, sleep, fortify, stay healthy and sane all while the world falls deeper into hell as time progresses.
Running water stops. The lights will go out. Winter is coming and as things get worse, more and more Zombies will start to appear.
This is not a game where you will solve the zombie plague and win, this is a story of how you fought hard to stay alive as long as possible and died trying.
There is really no happy ending for this game that I have ever experienced.
The gameplay and visual is Alot like the Sims games, but instead of controlling a happy go lucky family of sim people. You control the day in and day out choices of one poor soul who has yet to die when the dead refuse to stay still.
The graphics are rough at times but very good for the style. There are houses everywhere to explore and loot. Town areas and wide open spaces to navigate.
When food is scares, soccer moms will negotiate the price of milk with machetes. And for that matter she might not be doing it for her babies.
This game can get down right depressing at times. There really is no rescue. No happy ending, and no decision that won't ultimately mess you over without a fix or warning. It's bleak and moody and if you don't have survival on your mind at all times, hard as hell to keep a game going for more than a week or two.
The controls, especially when combat is concerned, are somewhat clunky and slightly counter intuitive. But the mood and tone of the game is spot on for what a good Zombie Story should feel like.
It's still feels like it is very early access and has lots f room to mature and grow. It's taken some time to get to this point, and the update rate seems a bit on the slow side. But it getting better every time I get back into the game and try for a longer run then the last time.
A word of advice? Don't get too attached to the survivor. Their ultimate purpose is to eventually die. Just try and make the next run better than the one before.

It is honestly a game I recommend completely if you're willing to deal with early acces bugs, and a small developer crew. So many people buy these titles expecting big developer turn around on bug fixes or content implementation, knowing full well, and being excited about, the small developer vibe that comes with them. This one is no different. If you like games with heart, you have the spare cash, and want a very immersive experience in a genre like this, get after it! It offers a real chance to deal with the nitty gritty side of a zombie breakout. When will power cut out? Water? When will I honestly have to leave the confines of my neighborhood? What happens when I get scratched? How well will I handle a horde moving through? This game let's you play that out.
Let's enjoy the developers vision, and support them as much as we can.

Despite some really rough balancing initially, this game is now really cool.  Still in development, of course, but the Dev seems to be putting out pretty much daily updates, fixes, tweaks.. Very responsive and very active. I'm well and truly impressed.
Far as how the game works.. you start out in an escape pod with a crew of 4.. you set roles for your crewmembers, build a mining laser and heat vent, mine asteroids for metal, silicon, gold, and water.. use those materials to build out your ship, add more stuff, rinse, repeat.
Eventually you can research things like armor, shields, weapons, expanders and extenders for most stuff, better versions of equipment..
You'll find threats from asteroid fields, stars frying the hell out of you with radiation and setting fire to your ship and its components, hostile aliens..  but you'll also find aliens you can trade with too..  you can bribe hostiles to leave you alone if you have the credits, or gun them down in a blaze of glory if you're strong enough and then mine up the resources left when the ship breaks  apart..
It's quite good fun, really.. I've wasted quite a number of hours on this already, and that number will be increasing quite a bit here in the future :)
