Evolve, the 4v1 game we all waited for. The game was hyped through the proverbial roof, and for good reason: Evolve was going to revolutionize the way we looked at gaming, with other AAA games to follow in it's footsteps, such as Fable: Legends. When the game was finally released it was met with far less friendly reviews than the praise it gained prior. Filled with bugs and glitches, Evolve quickly lost the spotlight... That was then however, now Evolve has been updated and is an incredible hunter/monster experience, unfortunately the reviews for the game hold it back, with a mixed review status.
While most people no longer play evolve there is still a number of devoted players, and those players are loving the game. Evolve mixes all the elements of a great shooter with that of a Alien Cabela's game. You track, trap, and hunt to win, while also fearing for your life; as the tables could turn at any moment, and you could be the hunted. The game is fast-paced and filled with action, if you like FPS games than this is for you, if you like hunting than this is for you, and if you like mass-genocide... This is the game for you. I promise, this game has gotten a whole lot better since it first released. Give it a second chance!

Dungeon of the Endless is a rogue-like game that combines the genres of tower defense, dungeon crawlers, real-time strategy, and a hint of resource management. Together, these make the game very unique and quite possibly one of my most favorite rogue-likes out there.
To start off, I'd like to acknowledge the fact that this game's 16-bit pixelated aesthetic is very well done. The animations are smoothe, the lighting effects give off a toned atmosphere, and the soundtrack is great. Props to Amplitude studios for making this game one of the most aesthetically pleasing rogue-like games for me.
The base objective in DOTE is very simple. You carry your motherbrain-like object  ( referred to as the Crystal ) from point A to point B. The challenge all comes from the threats that lie in between. Your goal is to explore a mysterious dungeon through every level ( up to 12 levels ) with a small group of characters that you control. It's your responsibilty to keep your crystal alive long enough through multiple waves of enemies to find the exit, in which you will then carry the crystal to that exit. You can place down a multitude of gadgets that will defend your crystal along the way, including turrets, decoys, ally-buffing modules, and so forth. Each character that you control has unique abilities, stats, and personalities that keep the game fresh with replayability ( There are 16 different characters in total, not including the DLC ). Despite my basic run-down of the game, there is a lot of depth involved with the mechanics, which I will not go into detail with.
The combination of both the fun gameplay and the appealing aesthetic of DOTE instantly gets an appraisal from me. I would highly recommend this game to any rogue-like / strategy fans out there. And please, don't hesitate to pick this game up with a couple of friends. The co-op experience is top-notch.

A mix of dungeon exploring with tower defense all wrapped in a rogue like game. Many items, research, characters to hire and unlock, the objective is to take a crystal from one point to another to escape the dungeon. But when you pick the crystal endless hoards come for you.

I am a long time Fire Pro player. I have been playing games in the series since Fire Pro Wrestling: Six Man Scramble for the Sega Saturn, over 20 years ago.
Gameplay in this edition is very similar to Fire Pro Wrestling Returns on the Playstation 2. This is a timing based game, so may be tough for some if they are used to button mashing. Fortunately, there is a tutorial "Mission Mode" that helps teach you the timing so you can pull off the moves.
Yes, graphics are 2D, and Fire Pro is best that way. The sprites are charming without being overly cartoonish.
There is once again an extremely robust "Edit" mode, which is Fire Pro's version of Create-A-Wrestler. I have not had the chance to play with this mode much yet, but the Edits already available on the Steam Workshop are very varied and impressive. As of this morning, there are already over 1000 Edit Wrestlers submitted. You can make any wrestler who has ever existed with this game.
With an Early Access price of $20, this game is a steal. The developers are promising a more polished final product, possibly with more gameplay modes added. Do yourself a favor and pick up the newest edition of this classic series!

I had to buy this game as soon as it came up to purchase in early access. I've played a lot of Fire Pro Wrestling Returns, and some of the older games, including imports. It never seemed like there would be a new game, especially when after Returns, all we heard about was an Xbox Live Arcade game where it's just avatars in an arcade style wrestling game. Also, a few jerks on the internet starting rumors with no proof, giving our hopes up. But this is the real deal. It is early access, but what is out is very polished, like the wrestling and fighting is just as good as Returns. It's just early, so it'll be some time before they get stuff like logo and ring creation, which will be amazing, since Returns on PS2 was so in depth that people made the actual WWE logo and rings, I don't even know how that worked. What we have is great so far, on the first night, there were over 250 workshop creations ranging from legends of Japan, WWE superstars, a few MMA fighters, video game characters, The Simpsons oddly enough, and so much more. So far I have a lot of custom characters downloaded, and a lot are 100%, mostly because fans used AI logic settings and apperances from Returns to re-create them for the new game. There are a lot of work in progress creations on the workshop. It's the workshop that will be the main reason to get this game, the default roster are just generic people, and I haven't seen any based on real people yet. To get the game now, you'll want to check that workshop page and get everyone you're a fan of. I've had a lot of fun so far, like having exploding barbwire death matches and putting wrestlers into MMA rules cage fights. There is a little bit of a learning curve going from playing Returns years ago, similar interface and menus, but I've heard character creation is much more simple and user friendly. The game play, it's classic Fire Pro Wrestling with some new tweaks like a random chance for strikes to have a back and forth sequence. The main thing is that the best features are the same, and it seems like the early access is more about community feedback, things they can tweak, add to the game, see how global online play is through testing, and steadily get more player creation tools in the game. So far, it feels very polished, like it's never froze on me, and the only glitch I can think of was a wrestler got really Jacob's Ladder twitchy for a moment, but nothing that affected the match any.

I'd keep them neat and store them up on my dresser. I spent many Saturday afternoons arranging battles and building up storylines. If I had a ring playset I'd use that - or just the corner of the kitchen table; didn't matter because
Those that need to be spoon fed a story will be disapointed. But on the other hand, if you want ultimate creative control and
gameplay, you are in for a real treat. I've loved wrestling games since the N64, and I gotta say that this title has more customization than I've ever seen. Just outstanding.
+Even after little playtime -
I see the vision and understand what sets this apart from all the other wrestling games. Instead of feeding you fish, they give you the fishing rod. The sky is the limit.
+At first the artwork was just slighly off-putting. The trailer doesn't do it justice. Now I find it incredibly charming. You have to understand how modular the wrestlers are and the deep customization.
+Controls are great, and in fact I'd give it a second thought about buying if you are not using a controller.
+This is perhaps the best implementation of Steam Workshop that I've ever seen.
+Even though its Early Access, this baby is ready to go.
+The price is cheap considering what you get.
-Music is 'meh' and I look forward to add your own songs feature.
-Now I'm not talking about grappling here, but the actual punching system doesn't always connect due to the sprite system; I'm fine with it, but it is a weak point.
This is one digital sandbox game that I'm oh-so excited to revisit those Saturday afternoons with.

Unless you’re a real sim grognard like my father, mentions of racing games are inevitably going to lead back to Mario Kart. Just as Super Mario became ubiquitous for platformers, so too did his high-speed outings become for racing. It’s for good reason, of course, because that unique mix of technical driving and cartoonish chaos has made it perfect for gatherings of friends and family to shriek and shout over. Plenty of other games have aped the formula and that’s where you’ll find SkyDrift, an aerial racer very much inspired by Mario Kart and some less ubiquitous titles. And perhaps if it had been a more robust package, it could have found similar success online.
SkyDrift places you in the cockpit of sleek, colorful racing planes designed to swoop and streak through precarious canyons and structures. The courses are jam-packed with tight turns and narrow gaps to show off your ace flying skills, along with powerups that let you harass your competitors. Flying dangerously builds your boost which can give you a brief edge on the pack, and can also help you find shortcuts through the course. All this is packaged up in a campaign of seven circuits where you need to finish in the top three in most races to progress and unlock new planes.
It’s pretty standard fare for a racing game of any kind, so what sets SkyDrift apart is the aerial aspect. Racing planes adds an entire dimension to racing, where you can swoop over or slip under hazards, cut off racers on steep ascents, and maneuver out of the way of incoming attacks. It requires a bit more of the old attention and reflexes to keep from smashing into walls, but the daredevil stunts you can pull off are all the more satisfying. In addition to standard controls your plane even has a fine control stick that puts you up on knife edge, allowing you to slip through the narrowest cracks and perform barrel rolls with ease. Here the game very clearly takes a page from Crimson Skies, giving just the right balance of speed and danger to make you feel like a true ace.
That’s just half of the chaos you can gin up, too. The Mario Kart influence comes out most clearly in the powerups, and how much mayhem they cause with eight angry pilots firing them off all at once. Pickups include homing missiles, machine guns, shockwaves, and mines, all extremely deadly if applied with the most basic sensibilities. You can carry two at a time and picking up a second of the same type grants you an enhanced version, like quad missiles instead of double. Add to this how respawns are incredibly quick, and you have a formula for a great gaggle of planes gunning and exploding all the way through the race.
SkyDrift seems balanced towards giving everyone an equal chance to stay in the race, without resorting to potential irritations like blue shells. There’s no rubber-banding whatsoever in the game, so if you straight-up outfly your opponents (or they outfly you) then there’s little recourse. Instant respawns keep pilots from being blasted entirely out of the running, while still allowing aggressors to take advantage of their handiwork. The AI pilots will still give you a run for your money, though, and at least once I’ve been blasted back to second place right at the finish line.
All in all it’s a bright, frantic, and plain-old fun racing game for a few runs here or there. The issues that hold it back are twofold, and build rather unpleasantly on each other. For one thing, there’s no multiplayer community left. That’s understandable for a little-known 6-year-old title, and can be overcome by mobilizing some of your own friends. But the other problem is that there’s a distinct lack of content or depth to the game, so without the multiplayer you’re not left with much. You get plenty of planes and skins for them, granted, but only five maps and three game modes (two additional are multiplayer-only) to race them around in. This is all the campaign consists of, which will only last you two to three hours if you’re determined to snag gold in all those AI races.
I really wish there was more to recommend here, because the fundamentals are rock-solid. The planes handle great, have intuitive controls, and look like proper souped-up racing planes. The whole game looks great for that matter, with plenty of detail and bright color to the tracks. Even the sound design keeps up with the buzzing turboprops and cannon fire that permeates every race. There’s just not enough to do with any of it, either in content or competition. SkyDrift stands as a monument to a great idea, a great evolution of arcade racing, that’s simply been left behind and forgotten.

Harkening back to the golden age of the Impressions city builder titles (Pharaoh, Caesar 3, Zeus and Emperor) Lethis is able to proudly take its place among them. This game doesn’t aim to innovate on the genre- no- it does the opposite. It takes the old impressions formula and adapts it to a brand new theme... Now you may be thinking to yourself “that sounds terrible, why is this a positive review?” and if that is what you are thinking right now then likely you just don’t understand what exactly made these games magical. Fans of this series have been dreaming of the day when we would finally find another 2D title/developer capable of taking the torch and running with it... while Lethis is not perfect (I will come to my current issues with it soon) it certainly does do exactly what it says on the tin.
Lethis is comprised of a comprehensive (albeit buggy) campaign, a number of sandbox maps and a decently sized series of economic chains all with a focus on steampunk aesthetic. It has wonderful soundtrack and art to support the setting in a colourful way. You will see your small plebs squishing fae, cutting giant fish, washing massive silk worms and more. While the game does not have voice acted plebs like the impressions titles did, it does boast an impressive array of walker sprites which add variety to the game immensely. The only thing which is really cutting away at the immersion is the huge number of spelling and translation mistakes- but this can be easily forgiven when you realise that the developer is not a native speaker and they will likely be fixed over time.
The largest problems with Lethis in its current state are mostly found in the early game- but could likely be tweaked away. Food production seems too low for the amount consumed but industry production seems far far too HIGH. Covering a district in walkers often requires far too many buildings because the decay rate between building stages upon losing access to things seems far too fast. Someone doesn’t walk past for a few? Well- suddenly your entire district will go down three levels in a blink of an eye. The large maps are great and all, but with how quick houses can devolve that is counter-productive. One massive swarm of people leaving can often meet another swam of people coming to replace them... That seems screwy to me.
All and all though, the good far outweighs the bad and the game more than manages to scratch the itch left post Impressions. If you love these kinds of games chances are you will love this one too. If you didn’t love them though I doubt there would be much (if anything) here that would interest you.

I could tell you of how this game is a solid City Builder in vein of Impressions Games' Titles such as Casesar III, Pharaoh and Zeus. I could tell you of the variety of buildings in the game with an absolute 'motherlode' of content that would have any fan of City Builders to dig up a copy of SimCity IV. However, that's not what made me really like this game. It was the aesthetic, the freaking epic soundtrack that immerses you in the eventually complicated webs of services, residential zones and beautification monuments. Your bustling city full of working citizens from supernatural exorcists to copper miners and shopkeepers. An artstyle that screams originality and further draws you in to this Steam Punk world of industrialized Urban centers. Faes sparkle in the woods outside your city, water pours from pipes jutting out of the edges of the known world while steam bellows from the chasms of magma bellow the surface. Life, though artificial, is mostly certainly alive here. And undoubtedly, that's the best feature I've found in my time with Lethis.
Now that's not to say the game is perfect. You notice very quickly that the soundtrack is the most prevalent noise in the game as sound effects only cue when you click on buildings or citizens. It's eerie that so much activity is occuring in your city but you could hear a pin drop if the music was muted. Personally, I would've appreciated there to be voice actors in the game... not annoying voices that talk every five seconds but rather, Pharaoh's approach or Stronghold where citizens would recite lines of how well their lives are going in game. A minor request, for sure, but it sure would bring a human element to this otherwise lively, bustling world.
All in all, this game is well worth 20 bucks and I can see myself pouring dozens if not hundreds of hours into perfecting my little Victorianesque Steam Punk cities.

Starship Theory shows great promise. It has the potential to be a fantastic game, and I would argue it already has the core mechanics in place to be a great game. However, as of this moment, it suffers from a severe case of balancing issues.
After spending a few hours in this game, I can say the pacing for at least the very beginning of the game is fantastic. Nice, steady progress takes place, with you slowly getting the ability to expand your ship and gather resources more efficiently. Heat becomes almost a non-issue before long, and asteroids are much more easily managed shortly after. Once you can handle heat and asteroids well, you can delve into weaponry to defend yourself from hostile ships. I don't have much experience beyond that, but I assume the pacing is still fairly nice all the way to the current endgame.
Unfortunately, the game doesn't always play out this way. RNG is pretty much a core mechanic of this game, and it needs somes balancing tweaks. For one thing, it is very possible to lose within two minutes of starting a new game. If you happen to encounter a star mere moments after beginning, you're done for. Along with that, asteroids have a fairly high chance of hitting your ship if they pass over it, which will almost always destroy at least one piece of equipment. If this is your storage, or your mining laser, you can no longer continue. This can be helped somewhat by expanding your ship and creating duplicates of vital equipment spread out from each other, but this also makes you more susceptible to asteroid strikes. And if you happen to get unlucky enough to encounter a hostile ship before you are about 30 or more minutes in, you might as well restart, because they will make short work of you. You can't even attempt to quickly build a weapon, because if your crew's AI is smart enough to get it built, it will only be after you no longer have the power or CPU to support it.
All of this having been said, there is no way I can't recommend this game. It is Early Access, still in a VERY early alpha phase, and with continued support and attention, can only get better. It has already recieved one update that has made it much easier to survive the earliest points of the game. It is already worth investing a couple of hours into, and I feel like I've already enjoyed the game enough to justify its price. If Starship Theory in its current form doesn't sound like a worthy investment, I suggest adding it to your wishlist and keeping an eye on it. It will only get better with time, and is bound to reach a point that will be worth the investment for you.

2. Core combat is terribly executed

You have to be a specific range to hit medium and heavy punches but light punches seem to have generous range. That's a 2nd game breaker for me. You lose stamina so fast, the deceptively fast clock doesn't help. That's a 4th game breaker.
Basically, this game does everything horrible wrong that a competitor that's releasing soon does right.
3. Some game modes are simulation only

When I tried tournament mode afterwards, I could not set any contestant to 1P.
That's a 5th game breaker for me.
4. Game only visually works in windows mode

5. No signatures or finishers

After reading the reviews of this game, I waffled about picking it up, but I really wanted to give it a chance.  I love point and click adventures, I'm a fan of anything with aliens as a major plot device, and I really liked the art style.  Unfortunately, I can only halfheartedly recommend this game after experiencing it.
The major problem I have with the game is the pacing.  For such a short game, you spend a great deal of time waiting.  There are unskippable cutscenes that are too long for the information they convey, and your character's action animations are incredibly slow.  The animation itself is cute and well-drawn, but it shouldn’t take longer to pick up an object and put it in your inventory than it does to walk to where you need to use that object and solve the puzzle.
Additionally, the game initially gives you a sense of urgency with a countdown timer, making it appear like you have to rush, and then the game immediately and frustratingly takes away your control - the very next screen, your character starts playing around with random stuff in the scenery, wasting time.  Five minutes later, though, it doesn't even matter anymore because they seemingly throw the entire timer plot point out the window.
Speaking of plot, nothing really made sense in this game.  Sure, you are questing after your kidnapped dog, who you can only free by recovering some sort of glowing crystal that the aliens want, but everything beyond that falls into the "because we felt like it" category (especially that WC scene).  Randomness is not necessarily a bad thing - there are some cute sight gags, and some of the crazy content is downright fun - just don't expect a coherent narrative.
The item-based puzzles in this game are actually pretty straightforward, though.  Pick up a thing, walk a few inches, use thing.  Not too complicated.  The only aspect that might throw you off is the interface.  Each screen is programmed to act like an aggregate of smaller areas instead of a whole, so you will need to click on an excessive amount of movement arrows to access all of the individual sections.  Additionally, aside from light switches, the swirly "interactable item here" icon will usually only appear if you are within arm’s reach of the object.  Gameplay would have been greatly improved with the ability to smoothly walk across the screen, and with all of the interactables showing an indication on hover.
The game contains a handful of mini-game puzzles that range from mildly interesting to exceedingly frustrating.  I actually had to look one up because I could tell that the colours were significant, but the puzzle as a whole was not intuitive.
Another frustrating puzzle was the bonus content.  There are three unlockable bonus features to uncover over the course of the game.  Once you find the trigger in-game, the new content is permanently available from the main menu.  One of the keys is pretty obvious, but I found the other two to be easily overlooked.  I actually played through the game three separate times before I found them all; however, I didn't feel the payoff was worth it because they are basically three versions of the same thing.
I played through with "easy mode" turned off, since most people said the game was not challenging enough.  I found out the only actual difference between the difficulty settings is that puzzle solution targets are not highlighted in hard mode.  This factoid is never explained within the game.
Overall, I liked the game's art aesthetic and atmosphere.  Some of the humor was funny, there were a lot of amusing background details, and the main character was endearing.  I also liked many of the locations, and the puzzles were pretty decent for a short casual game.  I still can't give this game high marks, though, because of the annoying mini-games, the clunky interface, the repetitious bonus content, and the consistently inconsistent pacing.  I rate this game a 5.5/10.

An insultingly short and uninteresting point-and-click. There are only a handful of unoriginal puzzles, and the rest is just clicking through slowly.
The graphics and animation are cute, though a bit rough. As others have pointed out, the style is a very obvious ripoff of that of Machinarium and Botanicula, which are both infinitely better games.
I did enjoy some of the little jokes happening in the background, almost like easter eggs: at one point you see the Big Bad Wolf attacking Red Riding Hood and she responds by pulling out a lightsaber and then riding the wolf. The ending credits are also fun -- though it's a bit sad to see how many people worked on what appears to be a game made by a single art student for a final school project.

Gomo is a very short game with no replay value. With the exception of two headscratchingly-vague puzzles, the rest are tediously easy. Gameplay is either finding the thing to click on and pick up or find a use for the thing you just picked up. In only two instances are you going have to look beyond your immediate surroundings in either case. Items are nearly always used in the same room and only once in the following room.
The entirety of the "story" is getting your dog back, though none of the rooms give you the least indication of why you're there or how they interconnect. The trip is inscrutibly disjointed and I never felt any sense of connection to what's going on. All the events are random and without purpose.
Unless you have a fascination with "find the thing to click on" games, give this one a miss and go buy Machinarium.

I remember, 2 years ago, backseat gaming with my best friend who was playing a very early pirated copy of
, in the middle of a cold, Winter's night. I remember how the moment was tense and the atmosphere was icey. We came across a double-story house, seemingly abandoned, so we set up a base, yet there was something horribly wrong about it. There was this disturbing, monotonous thump, repeating every few seconds. We searched every room in the house, thinking we were safe. My friend and I were ranting about how the sound was glitched just before opening the storage closet and then
A zombie bursted out of the sotrage closet, latching onto my friend's shoulders, biting at his neck, just before getting its head smashed in with a baseball bat.
This is just one of my greatest memories I have had playing
, among hundreds.
is a true zombie survival game and is the closest game to replicate the true zombie apocalypse experience, in my opinion. The soundtrack is emotional and atmospheric, the gameplay is unforgiving, and every playthrough is different from the last. I've spent most of my hours playing multiplayer cooperatively rather than PVP, and it's a great way to bond with fellow players and really lets teamwork be the name of the game.
Clearly, since
is an early access game, it's not perfect. There are many bugs and glitches, but the beautiful thing about
is that the devs are constantly at work updating and perfecting the game piece-by-piece, bit-by-bit. The Discussion Officers are always ready to help if ever there's a bug that needs fixing, and a specific Discussion Officer persisted with me for a month and a half to sort out an issue that prevented me from playing. That's dedication!
To sum up,
is definitely my favourite game at this moment in time, and will probably be for many years to come, always keeping me coming back for more with things like the in-depth survival and crafting mechanics, and just having a really good time with my friends. If you think you'd get tired of it after a short period of time, the community and the active updates are always things to look forward to and keep you coming back, over and over.
Seriously, this game isn't pricey at all, but your best opportunity to buy this gem is during a sale. There are so many more features I have not mentioned in my review, but I'll leave it up to you to discover them all if you decide to buy the game.

So riding the wave of negative reviews, I'll drop my 5 cents on one of my favourite genres of all time.
Project Zomboid is a fantastic game at it's core. It's immersive, fun, tactical, well designed. It has pleasant graphics that don't compromise mechanics of the game. The AI is smart, the feeling of progress is present, as well as reaching late stages of the game (after all, this IS how you died). And god DAMN, if it isn't one of the best survival zombie simulators out there!
However, with a heavy heart, I can NOT reccomend this game. I absolutely love the zombie genre, and anything with it, naturally Project Zomboid came about in 2013 and I had to have this game. I loved it at first sight, but after seeing limited progression, I quickly dropped it, waiting for updates. Fast forward 3 years after the release, downloaded it with a friend and had a blast, playing Co-Op together, building up actual zombie forts, with renewable sources of food, water and wood, far away from any civilization (and zombies). But there was something else creeping in. That was... boredom. Don't get me wrong, game is fantastic in it's own right, has everything it needs, but it's still lacking in many areas. Developers are very spares with updates, hyping up things that come out year after or even later, if at all. Last time I played this in September 2016. Now we have June 2017, and there was maybe 1 or 2 updates since then. Promised animation overhaul? Promised blood effects, clothes, zombie decay? Cars? None of that has been implemented.
The game is saved by an active modding community, actually adding things, that the game is severly missing, and more. However, due to limited tools and a small fanbase, those mods are also quite rare, and sparsely updated.
Nevertheless, if you love zombies and sims, pick it up at a discount, have a blast for 20 hours and just let it sit in your inventory for the moment, when the devs realize that this game is a goldmine. If you are not, wait for official release.

A game about sequencing the movements of simple mechanisms .
The basegame is not too challenging, it can be a challenge when you attempt to optimize the solutions.
Pros:
-good challenge in the newly added journal puzzles
-simple game mechanics that combine to create complexity
-lots of ways to solve puzzles, adds replay value and encourages creativity
Cons:
-storyline text is very small and not easy to read on high resolutions
-progressing requires clicking through a cumbersome text scroll mechanism
-the instruction line feels half-baked (copying, cutting & pasting blocks of instructions is not as simple as it should be)
-difficult to locate the correct position of the single block you want to change
-no way to higlight instructions to track changes or repeated instructions
-the repeat instruction copys from the start always, so you cant use small chunks over again
-the repeat function hides all instructions in a single block that makes it difficult to see where
corrections or instructions for other parts belong
-no break points or easy way to jump to where you just were, so you have to wait through
the entire set of instructions before you get to the spot
-if you accidentally go too far playing through the instructions set, you start the process of
finding your spot again
- ...and then run every instruction again, to find the spot again, just to correct the edit or add
a single instruction
Ultimately the game is fun until the complexity of designs increases,
then it becomes an ugly chore.
For a game with a main selling point of creating complex machines and optimizing them,
the unpolished instructions make it annoying, instead of fun to edit instructions.

Oh, and one more grief is the online play. It's best to play with friends that you know already and to communicate using skype or something. I've never finished to the end on any online play, someone almost always drops out after the second floor, if not the host dropping everyone immediately after game start. I once made it to the eighth floor with someone online. But what started with 4 became 2 after the third floor. If there was a way for the resources to be divided up among the players or something different than the current system it would help a lot. I've had games that quit immediately because someone used up a resource right away or built a module that made the host upset. All and all, unless you have friends like I said before, just don't worry about the multiplayer.

So riding the wave of negative reviews, I'll drop my 5 cents on one of my favourite genres of all time.
Project Zomboid is a fantastic game at it's core. It's immersive, fun, tactical, well designed. It has pleasant graphics that don't compromise mechanics of the game. The AI is smart, the feeling of progress is present, as well as reaching late stages of the game (after all, this IS how you died). And god DAMN, if it isn't one of the best survival zombie simulators out there!
However, with a heavy heart, I can NOT reccomend this game. I absolutely love the zombie genre, and anything with it, naturally Project Zomboid came about in 2013 and I had to have this game. I loved it at first sight, but after seeing limited progression, I quickly dropped it, waiting for updates. Fast forward 3 years after the release, downloaded it with a friend and had a blast, playing Co-Op together, building up actual zombie forts, with renewable sources of food, water and wood, far away from any civilization (and zombies). But there was something else creeping in. That was... boredom. Don't get me wrong, game is fantastic in it's own right, has everything it needs, but it's still lacking in many areas. Developers are very spares with updates, hyping up things that come out year after or even later, if at all. Last time I played this in September 2016. Now we have June 2017, and there was maybe 1 or 2 updates since then. Promised animation overhaul? Promised blood effects, clothes, zombie decay? Cars? None of that has been implemented.
The game is saved by an active modding community, actually adding things, that the game is severly missing, and more. However, due to limited tools and a small fanbase, those mods are also quite rare, and sparsely updated.
Nevertheless, if you love zombies and sims, pick it up at a discount, have a blast for 20 hours and just let it sit in your inventory for the moment, when the devs realize that this game is a goldmine. If you are not, wait for official release.

Let me be clear here, this is not a 'Myst-like game' or even much of a puzzle game, there is one real puzzle near the end and the rest of the time is spent picking up and using various items (about half of the 'solutions' involve using either the hammer or the nail on something, with many of the other items being used all at once or alongside the hammer and nails).
This is also, however, not much of an exploration game either. You do not explore the island so much as you walk back and forth across the shoreline on a single side of the island  with little in the way of variety beyond two small caves. Despite largely being a straight line, many of the screens look nearly identical and it is easy to get turned around when searching for concealed hotspots.
In terms of plot, you get a small plot dump at the start, a single journal, and a larger plot dump at the very end and that's it. The game ends so abruptly that it feels as though I missed something or that there is meant to be an alternate ending. Unfortunately, if I did miss anything it seems like the only way to go back and check would be to outright reinstall the game as either through a bug or an odd design choice starting the game up puts me back into the ending scene.
I realize this review sounds harsh, and I wish I could say something positive beyond 'there is one ok puzzle near the very end', but there is so little to this game and what little is here is so unsatisfying, especially for a commercial release, that I honestly cannot think of any possible reason to even consider recommending it.

I've played every game by Zachtronics except for TIS-100 and this is definitely my favorite one. Shenzhen was great but I prefer a more fantasy settings of Opus Magnum; and especially when compared to SpaceChem I love how it offers you much more freedom - you choose the location of both input and output which may make it easier, but lets you get a lot more creative. Graphics are much improved and feel fresh compared to CAD-like Shenzhen. The story lets you feel like a powerful alchemist and while perhaps a bit cliched is really fun to explore and I would love to see expansion packs that explore the world a bit more.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough. If you like puzzles then this is definitely one of the best games on the market, if not THE best one. I really love it that what I do really means something - you're not just solving one puzzle after another to solve some mystery, but you get a lot of opportunities to produce something that will be of importance - like fuel for an airship, waterproof sealants for ships, or a device that will let the surplus lead be turned into gold. Solving every puzzle, however, lets you advance and explore the story so your price is twofold, at least for me.
The price is low for the amount of fun, and the game, though Early Access, is not buggy and seems very polished. It's truly a staple of quality.
1. The setting. I like it much more than the previous ones, and would really love to see it explored a bit more.
2. The graphics - they are definitely a huge improvement over previous ones and are, simply put, gorgeous. The world is colorful, elements symbols are clear, and the way machinery works made me simply keep staring at the working machines for a long time - they are very elegant, yet simple, something that a person that loves engineering can truly appreciate.
3. Steam Workshop - you can easily download and solve hundreds of different puzzles available online and easily make your own, which allows for an almost endless replayability.
4. Sigmar's Garden - a rather simply minigame, but really addictive.
5. And finally puzzles themselves - the difficulty progression curve is handled very smoothly, and you get a really well-planned tutorial that explains pretty much everything in a very simple way; the graphs that show how effective your design is compared to those of other players makes you feel really competitive, striving for the utmost perfection; and they're no longer too constrained due to the predefined inputs and outputs like in the previous games. Overall, solving them was much more fun than in any other puzzle game .
1. There are not that many metals available - just six, but that's a nitpick.
2. I would love it if there were some storage containers for what you make - like vials and flasks, but then again, there are no liquid ingredients.

This game is phenomenal! It provides a satisfying intellectual challenge while allowing you to say 'screw this' and throw together a huge, complicated, inefficient solution when you just can't seem to find an elegant one. In other words, no more getting stumped and flipping your table, which is what happened to me eventually with Infinifactory. It provides an interesting story as you go along, making you feel like you're doing more than satisfying some nigh-faceless alien taskmasters, and if the later, more complicated design requirements get frustrating, you can always go back and try to further refine an earlier solution, to compete against your friends, the community at large, or just yourself. It's also VERY polished, so much so that I'm not entirely sure why the developer is bothering to call it Early Access. The ability to generate animated gifs of your more visually pleasing solutions, to keep as trophies or with which to tantalize your friends, is a very neat perk (and a devilishly clever advertising mechanic; staring at a few of my friend's solutions is what led me to buy the game myself.) 10/10; if you like open-ended puzzles and programming-style control mechanics, this is the game you want.
I know it sounds corny but any time I see a new Zachtronics games, it's an instabuy for me.

Construct and program mechanisms to build curious compounds. That's it in a nutshell; it's also really fun. It's the most polished Zachtronics game yet (Infinifactory is close, but I think Opus Magnum edges it out). It's like SpaceChem, but with shiny elemental marbles and a semi-mystical alchemy setting instead of sci-fi; plus, instead of the path-based programming of SpaceChem, Opus Magnum has a very intuitive "this action happens at this point in time" programming method. Just creating little machines and watching them run is a joy, and the "Create a GIF" button makes it super easy to share your creations.
I think Opus Magnum may be a bit easier than previous Zachtronics games, but in my view that's a good thing; I played through and only once or twice did I feel like I had hit a wall where I didn't have any idea what to do. The world and setting are intriguing, the story is interesting enough, though I find myself hoping there will be more released so as to develop things more. Of course, in terms of puzzles, the Steam Workshop already has more than a hundred player-made puzzles to cut your teeth on!
If you like puzzles at all, it's highly recommended.

It's a mix of roguelike dungeon crawler, tower defense and RPG.  It's unique, refreshing and hard.  Yet, the interface (like many of Amplitudes offerings) is exquisitely well done which focuses the difficulty squarely on the task at hand.  Despite having no idea what you are doing initially, you'll come to grasp the various benefits and dangers of this Dungeon of the Endless over time.  So, unless the idea of dying and losing is completely unacceptable to your fragile little mind, that is to say that the idea of a game presenting any sort of challenge or obstacle that requires you to learn and adapt to overcome is foreign and frightening, the wanton difficulty does little to detract from the experience and serves to mark your progress as you become better suited to survive and succeed.

A charming party roguelike and tower defence mashup. The basic idea is exploring rooms, protecting your generator from incoming mobs and then carrying your generator through the maze to the next level before the mobs get you. Works well. There's also manufacturing the resources familiar from Endless Space, but very simple. It can be harshly random in the manner roguelikes tend to be, but the game provides easy starting difficulties to compensate. For the replayability there's unlockable characters and game modes (landing pods).
I can't resist making comparisons with SotS: The Pit even though these are fairly different games, The Pit being pure Roguelike. Both are still games with similar theme set in same respective universes as previous 4X space strategy games. Specifically, the different approach to the lore interests me. SotS has well constructed universe that is often explained with lots of text. Endless seems more haphazardly build, focusing more on overall feel rather than details. Filling in the blanks is left to the player if he wants them filled. I would say SotS is more like a novel while Endless is more like a painting of a landscape or and instrumental piece of music.

Finally, Fire Pro Wrestling HAS COME BACK!!!
It's early access, so be patient. (Executive Director) Mr. Matsumoto has been working tirelessly on this project, and he's kind enough to actively listen to the community's input. So long as we stick with it, we can help to make this indisputably the greatest Fire Pro of all time!
My friends and I would spend hours on end having match after match, randomized battle royals, as well as forming the "Critical!" list where we tried to hit at least one critical on every single wrestler in Fire Pro G (PS1). This series will always be one of my all-time favourites in gaming. To see it coming back again after surprising me with FPR on PS2 back in the day, as well as getting a chance to provide input in helping to provide the most polished product possible, is all icing on an already awesome cake.
If you've never played these games and you're a wrestling fan, or even just generally into Japanese culture and video games, then you don't know what you're missing out on!

Finally a followup to a great wrestling series that never really had proper exposure in the west. Right now this game is great, if the devs continue to support and expand it it could be the greatest wrestling game of all time. Most wrestling game of the last two decades have basically used AKI's grappling mechanics from all the great N64 games. Fire Pro Wrestling World follows a wholly separate lineage, and it really works well. The symmetric, timing based grappling is exciting throughout the match, though it does take some getting used to if you are used to any other wrestling games' controls (the AKI games, the 2K games, the Smackdown lines, etc). There is a single player "Mission Mode" that serves to introduce you to the basics gradually  and give you time to practice.
The translation is awkward in places, mostly it is fine but some Mission titles are misleading. However, this is early access, and these are easy problems to fix, so I bet they will be fixed eventually. Hopefully quickly.
The thing that makes this most worth buying is Steam Workshop support. Being able to browse and easily download such a large collection of edits (this game has been out for barely more than a day and there are nearly 1000 wrestlers already!). Unlimited custom wrestlers in a wrestling game is a dream that, up until now, hasn't really been fulfilled. Strangely enough, even the new 2K games have a pretty low limit on CAWs. This game has the potential to have practically every known pro wrestler of all time on one PC, given enough time for edit makers to work (They've done insane things in Fire Pro Wrestling Returns over the years). The potential is huge.

TL;DR - Hard, takes a while to get used to, fun, fluid combat, fighting game (not just wrestling game), 8 players, worth the money. 9.5/10
This game is amazing. It's incredibly hard, but amazing.
Overall, this is a FIGHTING game, even though it is advertized as a wrestling game.
There is boxing, mma, wrestling (match, cage, deathmatch).
The style is very different than the average wrestling game as well. WWE games consist of spamming buttons to get to a finisher. You don't feel like a badass, but you can win a lot more often. In this game, however, it's a timing based style. It's VERY fun, just that it takes about an hour to get used to. Play the tutorial (the beginning of mission mode), and you'll be set.
Combat is very fluid, going from one move to another without glitches or bugs, as WWE games are known for.
Now to the character creation, oh man. You can create just about ANYONE you want, from WWE to NJWP, to TNA, to UFC, your own ideas. Your creation can be made just about EXACTLY as you want to, and with match settings, and creating belts, characters (with every move customizeable), rings, and even REFFEREES (Red Shoes fans cheer), there's something for everyone. And with Steam Workshop support, it's amazing what you can find.
Pros:
- Fluid Combat
- More than just wrestling
- Fun mechanics, 8 player fights
- Creator
Cons:
-Online mode is currently being fixed, as sometimes it breaks.
-Repetative music, not really a problem for me.
-Not many options in the options menu.
-No real create-an entrance.
-No downloadable entrance music, just certain songs for entrances.
Overall - Fun game, if you like fighting games of any kind, I'd recomend this one to you. And with early access still in effect, we'll be getting more content soon!

I have played many of the Assassin's Creed games (not all of the additional content, mind you) and played this game immediately after replaying Black Flag.
As far as graphics go, the improvements are minor. Fluidity depends on your operating system and tweaking some of the graphics settings is not difficult and can vastly improve performance. I played on highest graphics settings with no hiccups but I was playing with 2 GTX 970 graphics cards. I did notice that in cut scenes often times sounds or voices did not sync up with graphics.
The gameplay itself is very similar to all other Assassin's Creeds, with the added bonus of having a character solely meant to beat people to a pulp. I did love Jacob's character because you could take a break from Evie's infiltration and silence to ruthlessly beat down baddies to your heart's content. While this may not be the most effective way to play the game, the option is there it makes the battling so much more enjoyable.
The game itself is significantly less cluttered than other AC games. It does have the collectibles that all the games have, but the sidequests don't become too much of a task to complete and scale well with the leveling system. The main story progresses rapidly in comparison to the other AC games but I didn't mind this as much as I do with games like Far Cry.
All in all it is a good game worth getting. It is nowhere near as long as the other games, so i wouldn't exactly suggest spending 60 bucks on it, but definitely pick it up at a sale.

I desperately want to give this a positive review. But I can't. Not compared to the original, anyway. I'll just list some pros, cons, and personal disappointments for now I guess.
Pros:
-It looks considerably prettier
-The physics are much more impressive
-The interior camera is excellent
-All of the cameras seem a bit better
-There are new engine sounds, with better variety
-More default trucks, and better ones
-The UI is much nicer
-Little things like visual indication of diff locker and engine starting is nice (though an option to shut them off would also be nice)
-The game, of course, is a ton of fun
-Gamepad controls are vastly better (though I don't use one, it's nice)
-There are a few nice features added, like the border checkpoints and a better winching system
-The game is much, much better optimized, and runs wonderfully (with one caveat, as explained next)
Cons:
-On my machine at least, the game is EXTREMELY unstable. I have a gaming laptop with an i7 and an 800 series Nvidia GPU, I'm well above the system requirements, and I've verified the cache and redownloaded the game several times. The game just isn't stable for me, mods or not.
-It does look prettier, but not THAT much prettier. The vehicles are better and of more consistent quality, and lighting effects are dramatically better, but ultimately terrain looks about the same
-Wheel/tire customization has been removed
-Many, many vehicle attachments and customizations have been removed
-Multiplayer is disabled when using non-vanilla maps
-Both single and multiplayer maps are locked behind completion of objectives, with no apparent way to unlock them without doing so (old one had all open, and frankly I don't enjoy actually logging)
Disappointments:
-Manual transmission mode is still almost entirely worthless. I was really hoping they'd implement something like ETS2/ATS or BeamNG, where you can use buttons to shift up and down, but they retained the same system from before, which is sad.
-Rocks are still bizarrely slippery, rock crawling still looks doable but pretty much isn't.
-I'll reiterate again how much it bugs me that wheel and tire changes have been removed. Maybe if I complain enough they'll add it back.
-The game in general appears to want to make you play it as a logging simulator. I enjoy it simply as an offroad simulator. For me, this is a limitation of the way I used to enjoy to play the game, and definitely a disappointment.
In general, I just don't feel like I *got* anything for my money honestly. I loved the original, and I want to love this, but between the crashing, the removed features, and the general lack of any compelling reason to play this over the original, I'm just left feeling almost like I've gotten scammed. It's the same game, with some features removed. Given that the original looks almost as good, is more stable, and has more options, I really have to recommend anyone looking at this game to go buy the original instead. At least at this point, the original has far more mods available as well (though I'm sure that will change over time). So that's my verdict. Maybe, just maybe, this time Pavel will stay with a publisher, and updates will be released making the game more stable and more fun, and some of my complaints will be addressed. It has been stated that wheel and tire customization may be brought back if there's demand for it, so hey, who knows. But right now, as of November of 2017, given Pavel's (and Focus's) prior history, I do not have high hopes for future updates, and in its current state the game is ultimately a disappointment.

The entire game is just a huge love letter to 30s style animation, hard as nail run and gun games like Gunstar Heroes and you can tell they put maxmimum effort into every detail they could. All the animation was painstakingly done frame by frame in the exact same process as 30s cartoons, the music was recorded with real jazz instruments and the games complete disregard for checkpoints and lack of HP pickups evoke the coin devouring arcade machines of old. The game can get tough, but not to a completely unfair extent and it is always ready to let you get back in the ring, maybe this time your run will be 'the one.'
I would recommend the game based on the sheer effort of the Moldenhauer brothers attempts to finish this alone, with all the animation, music and gameplay work not to mention they REMORTGAGED THEIR OWN HOUSE to get Cuphead finished. Cuphead is a beautifully well made game and its success is proof that pouring your heart into developing a game will always lead to a high quality product.

You awake near what seems to be an abandoned farm and begin exploring and picking up objects such as this English muffin for example, you're told pressing Q does nothing, you then also pick up random objects around the environment for your “folio” as the game calls it and you also construct a teddy bear named Vladdy who can assist you on your journey, oh and of course... Let's not forget the sentient corn.
But is the game....



The best aspect of Maize is it's writing and humor. The game really gives me a strong portal vibe in terms of it's sense of humor, for example from the moment you start up the game, the tutorial text is seemingly mocking you through out it.
It helps as well obviously that the voice acting for all of this is superb, as well as the items you'll collect and find, each item you pick up either in your inventory or your "folio" will have a description of some kind, some of the these I found were the funniest moments in the game for me.
To even the random sticky notes you'll find across the facility from it's two co-founders who are seemingly opposite personalities.
Next up are the varied environments you'll be exploring in this game, everything from starting out at at the abandoned farm house, to going down into the facility below the farm itself.
It helps as well that the over all game looks pretty solid, running on the Unreal engine 4, I played this game on max settings, my experience averaging roughly around 30 fps due to my entry level set up, but considering this is just an adventure game, I was fine with the frame rate.
As for what you'll be doing in these environments, well there's not really any kind of major puzzle solving, which is fine for me personally as this game is more aimed and advertised as being an adventure game.
Every puzzle in this game is honestly just finding the correct place for items you've found around the enviroment.
As for the soundtrack side of things, aside from some of the humorous segments in the game with music built around the game's setting itself, the over all background music is your typical synth tunes and it's nothing too memorable I found.

As I said earlier, Maize really doesn't have any kind of actual puzzle solving, everything revolves around simply finding items and placing them in their correct place.
But with that said, this game also doesn't have any kind of challenge what so ever. Maize starts off feeling vast in terms of what you can explore... But that feeling will quickly dissipate as you realize just how linear the world is, but worse yet how much the game will hold your hand through it.
For example, you'll notice orange boxes block off certain areas, at first I figured this was for a new area I've not unlocked yet... But in reality once you've found out where the items correctly go in the environment you're in, these boxes will adjust and re-align to guide you to the next area you need to go next to progress.
So basically the game guides you in the correct direction the entire time using this method, making the over all experience disappointingly linear.
On more technical side of things I noticed regardless of what graphical setting I was playing on, I didn't really get any boost in performance, now do take this with a grain of salt, as this could be vastly different on different computer set ups.
But for me personally regardless if I set the game to medium or low to the high or epic setting, I never noticed any boost in performance in terms of frame rate, so I was constantly stuck with 30 frames dipping down into the low 20s at times when I was exploring the general farm area of the game.
But once I was down inside the facility I was getting anywhere from 30 to 60 frames, so it was pretty sporadic. I'll include my computer specs down below.
You'll also notice while playing the game is extremely heavy in post processing effects such as huge amounts of motion blur, bloom, etc and I wish I had more control over actually editing specific effects aside from the entire category just being labeled from low to epic.
As for bugs, during my roughly 4 to 5 hours I spent with Maize I never had any crashes and I only noticed a small bug where the seat of a tractor was magically floating for whatever reason.
Over all despite my complaints with technical issues and how linear and easy Maize feels, I still had a great time exploring its world and witnessing its cast of characters, the over all writing and humor in my opinion still make this game worth playing and checking out, so if you're looking for this in a game then I can't recommend it enough.

Maize is a first person puzzle/comedy-adventure. I would say it's like an Escape the Room game but with a lot of walking, picking up items, placing items down, opening doors, move on to next area.
The story is a mystery. You awake on a farm and find talking corn. You make your way through the labyrinth of cornfield and science lab to uncover the secret of why you are there and the corn that is walking and talking.
It's hard to describe this game but one word comes to mind as I played through......."Stupid." But the word isn't necessarily a bad thing. Stupid is what the devs were going for and they made it work.
-The conversations between the corn were stupid but the jokes were pretty clever.
-A teddy bear with a robot-backpack-arm spends the whole game calling you and everything stupid.
-Walking into countless lobbies with the same stupid golden statue.
-Picking up collectible items with stupid info on it.
-Reading the stupid arguments of the so many posted notes between the two who ran the lab.
But with all that stupidity in there, it was pretty clever to see everything put together.
Some of the things I didn't like:
-It felt kind of dragged on. The puzzles weren't that hard to solve as long as you check every room thoroughly to get all the items. My issue is walking back and forth through the huge field or hallway of the labs. There wasn't too much distinction of halls that broke away from the main hall so tended to walk through the same rooms to look for the room I needed.
-The Notes between the two scientist. They were everywhere! It was all nonsense. Mildy entertaining to read but I felt I wasted so much time in my life reading some of them. It was all the same. One of the scientist was spending money on ridiculous things while the other called him an idiot.
-Walking Bear. The sound of his robotic walking grew very annoying. Think the old Robocop movies but faster. Never stopped. As I've said above about the amount of walking I did, the sound did the same amount.
My likes: (Not Much)
-Entertaining story. Enough to keep me wanting to know what all the secret is.
-Puzzles were Meh. Pretty linear and self explanatory but creative nonetheless.
-The teddy bear. Though the sound of him walking was annoying, his constant insults kept a smile on my face.
-The time. I've read people have completed it in 3-4 hours. I was really getting bored of the game and was happy it ended when it did. Just the right amount of time.
Overall:
It's not a bad game but it's not good either. I recommend this only because I believe the devs deserve recognition for creating a wreck/masterpiece. It really was an interesting game from start to finish. Would I play it again? No.
6/10 Rating from me.

This is hands down the most challengeing survival game I have ever play. The Long Dark sets itself apart from the competiton by placing the player in the middle of a SHTF scenario where a global geomagnetic event wipes out virtualy all modern technology. You find yourself in the middle of the harsh tundra of Northern Canada with few supplies and nothing in the way of preperation to survive such an unforgiving environ.
There are no monsters, you will not be stalked by mutants or hounded by zombies, it's you vs whatever mother nature can throw at you. Your task is not to build a fort or stronghold to defend against an fictional menace but rather to find shelter against the elements and supplies to keep yourself fed, hydrated and healthy. For me personally the biggest challenge has been finding enough fuel too keep a fire going to warm whatever shelter I have found myself in come nightfall. The only enemies you will encounter are natural predators such as packs of wolves and roaming bears and trust me they are not to be taken lightly. Being that The Long Dark is based on a largely realistic depiction of wilderness survival your best bet with dealing with predators would be to avoid them at all cost. You are not a trained soilder or gifted with any preternatural powers like so many other games. You are simply a regular person caught in  a bad situation so it's not a good idea to try to take on all threats head on.
The graphic style is very immersive beautifuly illustrating the frozen wilderness while also convincingly depicting the harsh and unforgiving character of the wilds of Northern Canada. The game utilizes the typical hunger, rest and hydration mechanic of the genre. I foung it well balanced overall but couldn't help but wonder why my character  would not be able to simply grab a handful from a clean patch of snow to hold in his mouth to stave of thirst rather than having to build a fire to melt snow to drink.
If you are a fan of survival games and are looking for a change from the (IMO) overdone zombie/nuclear holocaust trope then you should absolutley pick up The Long Dark. It's the closest you will get to the real thing wihtout having to be stranded out in the middle of nowhere.

(Full review follows below)
is a riveting, immersive, and downright pleasurable experience.  Decent graphics with superb artistic direction and a fitting soundtrack set the ambiance.  There is a captivating world to explore, rife with a subtle-but-present wealth of lore and history.  The gameplay can range from stealthy-pacifist style to murderous-warrior style, or somewhere in between; it is easy to find a playstyle that suits your preferences.  There is much to like.
The atmosphere of the game is really its heart and soul.  The gameworld is masterfully crafted to be immersive and intriguing as you explore your way through the campaign.  Wandering through side passages and windows, you not only find collectibles and items but also notes and books which provide lore and background information.  This supplements the primary storyline and few sidequests that compose the main narrative.  That narrative being enticing and well-told, although not without a few clichés.
The gameplay is structured to offer varying, branching options to choose from as you progress toward your goal.  In each level, there are various paths to take and various ways to take them. You could blow open the front door and slaughter everyone or you can slip through an attic window and never allow your presence to be known.  A lot of games try to offer this, but
is exceptional in how balanced the gameplay is to truly allow for both stealth and loud options.  It does lean slightly toward stealth, undoubtedly, but you really have a lot of freedom to get creative in how you want to go about each mission.
Another premiere aspect of the game, tying together the atmosphere and gameplay, is the evolving gameworld.  Depending on your methods of completing earlier missions, as you get deeper into the campaign the gameworld changes to reflect how your actions have impacted society.  The effects are ultimately rather subtle, but contribute to further highlight the outstanding atmosphere of the game.
The various styles of play and mission paths combined with achievements and collectibles make for some good replay value and decent playtime.  If you explore and immerse yourself in the lore, the game can be quite substantial; if you bulldoze through the main campaign, the game can be quite short.  Also the DLC can add a decent amount of content, so the GOTY edition is probably a good bet if you are looking to maximize gameplay hours.

This game is phenomenal! It provides a satisfying intellectual challenge while allowing you to say 'screw this' and throw together a huge, complicated, inefficient solution when you just can't seem to find an elegant one. In other words, no more getting stumped and flipping your table, which is what happened to me eventually with Infinifactory. It provides an interesting story as you go along, making you feel like you're doing more than satisfying some nigh-faceless alien taskmasters, and if the later, more complicated design requirements get frustrating, you can always go back and try to further refine an earlier solution, to compete against your friends, the community at large, or just yourself. It's also VERY polished, so much so that I'm not entirely sure why the developer is bothering to call it Early Access. The ability to generate animated gifs of your more visually pleasing solutions, to keep as trophies or with which to tantalize your friends, is a very neat perk (and a devilishly clever advertising mechanic; staring at a few of my friend's solutions is what led me to buy the game myself.) 10/10; if you like open-ended puzzles and programming-style control mechanics, this is the game you want.
I know it sounds corny but any time I see a new Zachtronics games, it's an instabuy for me.

Construct and program mechanisms to build curious compounds. That's it in a nutshell; it's also really fun. It's the most polished Zachtronics game yet (Infinifactory is close, but I think Opus Magnum edges it out). It's like SpaceChem, but with shiny elemental marbles and a semi-mystical alchemy setting instead of sci-fi; plus, instead of the path-based programming of SpaceChem, Opus Magnum has a very intuitive "this action happens at this point in time" programming method. Just creating little machines and watching them run is a joy, and the "Create a GIF" button makes it super easy to share your creations.
I think Opus Magnum may be a bit easier than previous Zachtronics games, but in my view that's a good thing; I played through and only once or twice did I feel like I had hit a wall where I didn't have any idea what to do. The world and setting are intriguing, the story is interesting enough, though I find myself hoping there will be more released so as to develop things more. Of course, in terms of puzzles, the Steam Workshop already has more than a hundred player-made puzzles to cut your teeth on!
If you like puzzles at all, it's highly recommended.
If you like any of Zachtronics other games then you'll like this one. That's all that needs to be said really.

Oh look! Another zombie survival game!

I've been playing this game since before it came to steam, and it is one of the best zombie survival games out there to focus on survival instead of FPS combat. The primary focus is on scavenging and survival, looting houses for supplies and making sure you eat, drink and sleep enough to sustain yourself. There's also a reasonably detailed medical system, where your quick getaway through an upper-floor window could leave you with a fractured bone, or thoughtlessly climbing through a broken window can result in deep gashes - requiring stitches, glass removal, and bandages that you better hope you have in your safehouse.
The game also has a good system for base building in the long term, with construction of entire buildings and farms to sustain you. Temporary bases with sheets and boarded windows are a must. It's a complex and fun ride as it is - and over time it only gets better. Many reviewers complain about the time in development, but PZ updates constantly and has a weekly 'Mondoid' blog where you can see what the developers are working on. It also has a prolific modding scene that adds a myriad of other features to the game!
Absolutely worth it.

There's so much to edit and customize that this game would get a recommendation even if all you could do is simulate AI matches.  Luckily that's not an issue, as the game is loads of fun to play.
A few things that warrant fixes as of Early Access Version 0.9001:
-Wrestlers escape the cage too quickly in cage matches.  Computers can and will win in under 2 minutes if you give them 8-10 seconds to escape.  Climbing should be slower, and more importantly, the transition from inside to outside the cage should be considerably slower.  Maybe there should be a transition state where wrestlers sit atop the cage before being able to climb down the other side.
-Wrestlers should stay down longer after losing via pinfall or submission.  As it stands, wrestlers generally get up right away after losing, which isn't realistic on 10+ minute matches.
-A.I. characters in free-for-all, last man standing style matches will frequently break up pins and submissions on their opponents.  This would make sense in "first pinfall wins" matches, but in Royal Rumble-style matches they have no reason not to let their opponents pin each other.  It can make for some goofy matches wherein 2+ wrestlers stop beating the crap out of one another to break up a pin on one of their opponents.
-While standing on the ring apron, it's seemingly impossible to hit or grapple someone who is in the ring.
-While playing as a manager/valet, the camera does not pan out enough to be able to see your player character.

This game is a passion project for its designer, Tomoyuki Matsumoto. It is a legit effort to make the best Fire Pro Wrestling game since 1989, and it draws on decades of development. The project is being headed by somebody who loves playing this game. That has really shown through during the early access. The team is passionate, and engaged with the community.
The gameplay is based on timing, and engine is deep. Every match gets a crowd rating, and you have to be entertaining as well as effective to get a 100% rated match. The fundamentals of the game haven't changed since the 90's, and I say that because it's solid like a classic 90s console game. They've just refined and expanded almost everything over the years. As somebody who has been actively playing the game since 2001 my opinion is that the early access has already made this the greatest version of the game I've seen.
It offers numerous modes, including MMA, pro wrestling, shoot fighting, and boxing. The CAW mode is limitless, with an encyclopedic move set, detailed stats/ai settings, and a really cool cosmetic editor. A community of fans who have been creating wrestlers/fighters for decades have made well over 10,000 workshop submissions.  There aren't many wrestlers, MMA guys, shoot fighters, boxers, kickboxers, cartoon characters, musicians, super heroes, action heroes, celebrities, and historical figures that aren't already made and ready to rumble.
This review is pretty enthusiastic, but that's how behind this project I am. This franchise is as classic, as Mario, Metriod, or Zelda. I mean, it's way less popular, but in terms of  generarions of development that both expand the franchise while respect the core tradition, this Fire Pro game is already a classic.

Albeit simplistic and easy to play, Gomo is a fun little point-and-click adventure game. The strongest point is definitely the sound design, but the artwork and animation require a worthy mention. The story is fairly basic, but cute nonetheless, while the setting and the atmosphere are nicely constructed. There are enough puzzles to keep you busy every  once in a while, but the difficulty is very low for all of them. The game's strongest point is definitely not working your intellect.

Running this game on my native 1440*900 with full screen enabled rendered the active window of the game surrounded by black borders meaning the game has a fixed resolution and will not scale at all. In conclusion, if you want a fast, easy and fun point-and-click with basic puzzles, great sound, good artwork and a nice atmosphere check Gomo out, but make sure to get it on sale, as the 7.99 EUR they charge for it over in Europe is pretty high compared to what it has to offer.

Tripwire Interactives Killing Floor is what you would expect of a polished mod, but doesn't exceed expectations as a retail game. It's good, but unfortunately far from perfect. A nice addition to the survival-horror genre though, and it has an attractively cheap price tag.

Killing Floor is my kind of online shooter. It is sinister, horror themed, features awesome metal soundtrack. It also has a very team oriented gameplay. A couple of bad players are usually enough for your team to fail the campaign so it is quite important that everyone knows somewhat how to play the game. For the same reason, it currently suffers from the recent free giveaway as the servers are full of newbies trying to learn the game.
What I loved the most about Killing Floor was the shooting mechanics. I have played shooters for more than 20 years now and rarely have I seen games where it feels so satisfying to shoot an enemy. This is not just about the weapons, but also how the enemies and sound & visual effects react to your bullets. It really feels great.
The game also has great gameplay value. You can’t just jump into it and expect to do anything more than licking the floor if you are playing on a difficulty higher than normal. Your approach should be to start with easy or normal, learn the game mechanics, get accustomed to your perk and gain some levels on your specific perk before you move to higher difficulties. Otherwise, you will simply not survive as Killing Floor is a quite unforgiving game.
Talking about perks, I have tried Sharpshooter, Firebug and Demolition in my 75+ hours of Killing Floor and each perk felt like playing a different game. If you don’t like your perk so much, definitely give a chance to some of the others (firebug being my favorite). And finally, the maps. There are dozens of maps with unique atmosphere. Beating one game in each map for the first time should take you around 30 hours. To conclude, Killing Floor is one of the best online shooters out there. If you liked any of the Left 4 Dead titles and you are ok with a similar but much darker game, look no further.
PS: Toy Master DLC is quite boring, imbalanced and in my opinion is not suitable for the Killing Floor mechanics. Feel free to ignore it.
