The idea behind the Long Dark could become a great game, but fell short.
--- FIrst, the sandbox. It can generate some nice situations (being lost in the storm, hiding under the rock during blizzard trying to not freeze to death etc.) but it grows old realy REALY fast. Simply because:
1) The whole world is a bunch of boxes surrounded by mountains and connected via tunnels, so it doesn't realy deliver the feeling of being stranded in a vast area.
2) The world is not randomly generated on the start so the moment you've explored quite the limited number of locations there is little room left for surprise.
3) The surviving mechanic seems challenging at first, but once you've struggled for a few hours through contr intuitive UI and learned how pretty much nonexistant the crafting system is, how deranged wolves replace your casual zombie  and how stupidly gluttonous the character is, the game has nothing else to offer.
The core gameplay consists of overexaggerated nutrition system which forces you to wander from one location to another to satisfy your glutton with occasional camp stop in between. The higher difficulty doesn't do much, except completly removing the potential joy of exploration since surviving on it requires you already knowing the never changing map well, the location of its crafting stations and loot sites.
All in all the sandbox looks like abandoned props for the story with 0 incentive for playing after exploring the limited number of locations since the progression and survival itself is pittifuly shallow as if serving as basic skeleton for the future plot. And speaking of which...
---The story. Oh boy, even the long standing fan boys are divided on this one, check the forums for yourself. I won't even mention how cliche the plot is with its forcefull omissions. It's just plain boring to follow. Interactions with NPC's end up with you doing menial tasks for them, fetching and gathering quests and so on. The progression through the story is extremely linear, almost void of free exploration, and is littered with wolves around every corner, probably as an attempt to add some tension. It succeeds only in adding wandering in circles annoyances.

The release of the story mode is unpolished, ridden with bugs, graphical glitches. Also some people reported their disapointment in larger parts of dialogue being unvoiced. The tutorial is of little help for  new players as well.
I had high expectations for the story  mode but it failed to deliver. Real pity, the engaging writing could potentially become the saving grace of the game.
The story mode is simply sad, and not in a good way.

***
To be fair, the Long Dark is not a terrible game. It's just not different from most of the Early Access survival games out there except from being pretentious -- having no zombies (replaced by overly agressive wolves) while being "thoughtful survival experience" (it isn't). It's just an another EA survival game. It has unique setting but is ultimately shallow.
P.S.
As one of the other negative reviewers said, the large part of the community suffers from the Stockholm sindrom. The majority doesn't mind slow development progress, constant delays, the infamous PR decisions, their posts being deleted by the developers, lack of mod support. I for myself just hope that EA survival games trend will die out soon enough, no more supporting such devs.

Easily one of my all time favorite games. I was able to get over 150 hours in the survival mode alone. I do recommend this game for anyone who enjoys survival orientated game play, but I do think a few things should be mentioned before you purchase the game. For starters, this is not a fast-paced game. You struggle through the snow, explore and loot an area, and then move on to a new location. That's about it. The dangers you face are purely from the environment and wildlife. The enjoyment of this game comes from exploring and surviving another day. It is very simplistic and atmospheric. The journal feature is a nice touch for planning your next move or role-playing. Depending on the difficulty of the survival mode, the game can be incredibly difficult to survive through the first 48 hours. You'll die. A lot. Even when you get the hang of things, you'll die a lot. This game doesn't hold your hand as much as some would like. So be warned of an ultimately frustrating but enjoyable learning curve.   Story-mode is also very simplistic. I found it engaging, but if you're looking for a telltale-like story... look elsewhere. It's hard to say exactly how the developers will continue the narrative of the story, but at the moment, you essentially survive in a particular area while aiding an NPC. The NPC will give you knowledge that will improve your chances of survival and allow you travel to a new area. The main story is not something new, as I'm sure most players will recognize the direction of the story quickly. Granted, more episodes will come out, and more twists or flare to the story may be added. Point is: if you want to play a story rich game, this probably isn't for you. The story is passable, but the real appeal of this game is the survival and exploration side of it.

The Long Dark is about you, some random hoser, freezing to death in north Canada whilst gathering firewood, being bullied by wolves, hiding from murderous bears, and scrounging enough foodstuffs to survive one more day in the endless winter.
Excellent atmospheric piece with solidly built mechanics that feed into each other. The visual style is limited graphically, focusing on environment and weather effects over character detail. The models are stylized and artistic, but not enough to take you out of your immersion.
My main complaint would be the AI and interaction of the animals, which can be inconsistant or wonky at times. Road flares are finicky, torches seem less effective then advertised, and stones all but useless. The game is about furtive survial and not animal combat though, so in my mind it's not enough to detract from the whole,
The Long Dark was a functional survial sandbox in early acess (where most of my hours played are), and now has additional challenge modes with a scripted campaign as well. Exellent replayability with a simple to grasp but hard to excecute core game.
9/10 would get mauled by wolves again.

For only 1.2 hours on this game (at the time of writing this review) It is the best survival game I have played so far. If you want a solid survival game without any zombies, this is the one. Even if you're not into the survival genre, you can still play the story mode of the game and have a wonderful time doing so. One of the best games I have played so far, 10/10 Hinterland Studio.

I have just under twelve hours on the game, all in Story Mode. I picked the game up on release and haven't touched the Survival Sandbox mode, so I have no judgements on that, but also no pre-concieved likes or dislikes because of playing the sandbox before the story.
I've really enjoyed the story, which is called Wintermute. I've completed the first "episode", which is composed of several chapters, and am now in the second episode. I'm being pretty vauge because I don't want to give up any spoilers. The story has been very interesting and engaging. The first couple of hours of gameplay was just pretty much me trying not to die too often (no Permadeath in Story Mode, you'd hate it if you had to repeat the story over and over anyway) and then do some exploring. Soon however it was all about finding new things and people and... well, again, I'm avoiding spoilers. I'm just going to say that it was pretty interesting. And challenging.
So for folks looking for something beyond the usual sandbox survival game, I can really recommend "The Long Dark".

Sigmar's Garden is a fun cross between solitaire and chinese checkers, with a couple dorks providing color commentary every so completions. The rules are puzzling at first, but the elements of strategy and forward thinking gradually develop through play. It's relaxing to map out your pathing strategy around the quicksilver and metal marbles, or to find ways to cut through bunched up lanes. Overall, a great complement with absentminded YouTube watching. The attached game, Opus Magnum, is a pretty neat programming puzzler too.
In all seriousness, the main thing to mention is that Opus Magnum is the most beginner-friendly Zachtronics game yet. For instance, you get a luxurious unlimited scrolling canvas for you to make incredibly inefficient contraptions.  This makes the game so much less frustrating to work through, as you won't be constrained by space was you were in SHENZHEN I/O, more so in TIS-100, and infuriatingly so in SpaceChem.
For all the discussion about the game being easier, the real difficulty lies in defeating your friends' histograms, as Zach has somehow realized that friends do a much better job at motivating better solutions than a difficulty wall.  And really, there's something a lot more intuitive about clockwork arms passing around marbles, as opposed to trying to grok how XBUS works or avoiding message collisions between TIS-100 nodes.  As such, this is probably the most friendly game to start with for a newbie Zach-like player.
That the solutions often move like beautiful clockwork and can be easily exported as animated gifs also helps with the feeling of recreational accomplishment.
Update 10-26-2017: (Finished the main story campaign, and ordered the iron-on patch)
Wow golly this game could use a way to speed up to later breakpoints, or to skip state to a program location. And divine architect help you if you need to insert more steps near the beginning of a long work-in-progress instruction chain, where you need to delay the rest of the concurrent multi-page instruction sequences in all the other components.
Still, it's very doable to beat this game, but the last few levels involve some very intricate bonding patterns, and can take a ton of instructions to complete. In the end, I was satisfied with how the plot wraps up, though the level design was a grind for me at the end.
I'm not sure if the depth of the systems and puzzle design lives up to those of SHENZHEN I/O, but the relative simplicity may be a strong reason to recommend this game as a first Zachtronics game. For more theoretical players, I'm not sure if the systems here are Turing Complete, and I can't imagine how you would implement NAND (perhaps the needed components can be introduced in a later update?).
That said, one could argue that it is elegance, not systems design, that shines in high skill play here. Along those lines, I'm looking forward to seeing some really elegant animated solutions from others. Just seeing Notch's solutions on Twitter just proves how messy my problem solving style was.
In the end, this setting and story is easily my favorite out of all the other Zachtronics games, being strongly evocative as a mashup of The Diamond Age and The Baroque Cycle. This is an incredible remake of The Codex Of Alchemical Engineering, and suggesting the latter flash game as a demo doesn't do justice to the massive improvements since the last decade.
If Opus Magnum was this much of an improvement, I'm kind of curious what a remake of Bureau of Steam Engineering could be like. Come on Zach, you know you've thought about rebooting the universe of Ironclad Tactics. ;)

Gomo is a short, highly atmospheric puzzle game, but it's more of a really nice looking flash game than anything. I bought it for less than a dollar, which was a fair price as it turns out. It's a fun little game--but there's not much to it.
The game's aesthetic is its biggest strength. I've seen someone say that Gomo gives off a "Winnie the Pooh" vibe, mostly on account of the gentle, determined, kinda derpy protagonist. But I think the game's world has more of the feel of a Tim Burton movie--the characters, events, and atmosphere all walk the thin line between cute and endearing and dark and creepy. The visuals all look really good, and I appreciate that the main character's animations are all custom-drawn for each screen. Just don't be surprised at how eerie the game can be, what with the color palette of mostly browns and grays, the minimalistic music and sound effects, the slow pacing, and the near-total absence of comprehensible dialogue.
In terms of gameplay, Gomo definitely functions as a more casual puzzle game than most point-and-click adventures. Your character only has three inventory slots, meaning that most of the game's puzzles are pretty straightforward and require only a few short steps to work out. The game doesn't allow much backtracking, which is nice in a sense since you won't get stuck wandering around wondering where to go next. But the game's linearity also means that you won't ever face any truly complex puzzles.
The puzzles themselves generally represent a healthy degree of challenge. Pay attention to every detail onscreen and you can usually find your way forward after a few minutes of hard thought. Unfortunately, the puzzles don't really get any harder as you play through the game, and they can be a little uneven. You'll find yourself saying "That was obvious" or "What the heck am I supposed to do?" a little too often in this game. And sometimes you'll say both things about the same puzzle.
Ultimately, though, the game feels kind of empty. There's barely any story to this game--aliens kidnap your character's dog and offer to exchange him for a crystal--and absolutely no coherent through-line explaining where you are or where you're going next or why you're there. Each new screen and new set of puzzles seems totally arbitrary. You jumped through the last hoops, so here are some new zany hoops to jump through. And while your character goes through some wacky and amusing steps in his journey--battling an ancient robot, launching a sheep in a hot air balloon, and breaking into a squirrel's house--there's no narrative thread or even logical connection to give them any larger meaning.
So there it is. Gomo is painfully short, which wouldn't be a problem if it had anything resembling replay value or content. But since there's really nothing at all behind the game's nice visuals and modest puzzles, I'd give this game a pass unless I could get it for pennies.

Gomo is...different than any puzzle game that I have played and some of them, I didn't even like.  When I played Gomo, it was a unique experience from beginning to end. Short but oh so sweet, Gomo is a wordless room-by-room point-and-click/puzzle adventure game that may end before the 90 minute mark, but those 90 minutes are guaranteed to be memorable and fun.
There is a very small sub-genre among point ‘n’ click games which relies solely on visuals: no narration, no dialogues, everything is told in pictures. It is a great artistic challenge for the designers, since everything has to be told by actions and facial expressions; plus it opens up possibilities to include a plethora of details that would probably go unnoticed otherwise. In Gomo’s case these are small (or sometimes large) visual gags that are littered all over in every scene.
The gameplay follows a room by room design, where you have to interact with scene elements and sometimes collect and use items to get to the other end of the screen. There are also a few more conventional puzzles here and there, but even with those Gomo is little more than an interactive cartoon. For adults at least. For small children it may act as a good educational software to teach common problem solving.
Like most similar games, Gomo is short, 60 to 90 minutes long. But even at full price it costs about as much as a movie ticket, providing at least as much fun as a film would.
So simple and short that it hurts. Don't spend on it more than a 1 euro. Level of difficulty is for small children.

Having loved the original Spintires, I instantly pre-ordered this game, when I saw the announcement, without much reasearch about the game's content. Shortly after, I became a bit sceptical about my decision reading that the game would not offer much new compared to Spintires.
More than 20h of gameplay later, I must say that I do not regret my purchase at all. This game gives me so much fun. Admittedly the maps (that I have played up to now) tend to be very similar, but some modifications - also in terms of available vehicles and their placing on the map - and the overall improvements ensure that I don't have the feeling of re-playing something old.
Playing with my wheel, clutch and H-shifter instead of keyboard, which I had used for Spintires, also gives a new dimension to this game.
+ New vehicles
+ New Interesting and challenging "Challenge" mode
+ New Cockpit view (although quite rudimentary dashboard graphics and without working mirrors)
+ Improved graphics
+ Improved water animations with credible current simulation when crossing rivers.
+ Good wheel and shifter support (at least for my Thrustmaster equipment)
+ Detailed vehicle animations and physics simulation
+ Dynamic terrain simulation
+ Possibility to make nice screenshots
o Camera mode in general still not really optimal
o I have the impression that Mudrunner is a tad easier than Spintires.
- Still only 6 maps available. After having finished these (in addition to the Challenges and some further achievement farming), there might be not much replay value.
- Still no official Steam Workshop support for map mods. (Update on 2017-11-30: This is apparently currently worked on by the developer(s).)
- The steering and camera handling for the K-700 picker arm is really annoying.
- Modifications of the truck wheels are no longer available.
- Short logs now give 3 points instead of 2, which makes the easier short log deliveries preferable over the more difficult medium log deliveries.
- Still no different weather conditions apart from day & night cycle.
- No crawl gear (gear "1+") available when playing with manual H-shifter.
- HUD of crane steering overlaps with multiplayer chat HUD

If the idea of driving a logging truck through difficult terrain appeals to you, then you will love this game. Best ground physics you will likely ever see in a game.
For those who already have the original Spintires; this one adds a rudimentary cockpit view, challenge missions, and multiplayer save games. The latter made it worth it for me. The saves work very well; all player trucks remain in the position that they were left in.

SkyDrift is a fast-paced aerial racing game that will feel very familiar to anyone who's been to an arcade in the last decade. The gameplay is basic, but the action is quick and twitchy as one might expect.
Flying in SkyDrift is quite simplistic, and again arcadey - with basic arrow keys for pitch and roll and 'W' and "S' for throttle control by default, the game is quick to learn which is good as the courses can feel challenging but still ultimately forgiving.
I played through over half of the game, and found at about the half-way point the game becomes repetitive as you will have played through all of the unique tracks by this point. The game proceeds to increase AI difficulty and increase the number of laps in each circuit to artifically extend gameplay. For an arcade game, keeping the player feel refreshed is usually a requirement, and the game fell a bit flat by that point.
The visuals are on par with what i'd expect in an arcade again, but I particularly like the level design and the planes a lot. The level design is really well created, with pinch points, branching paths, and a requirement for a lot of twitch flying to avoid obstacles. Each race truly does feel intense purely by navigational standards.
As a huge fan of Crimson Skies, I absolutely love the plane design as it entirely reminds me of that game.
Overall this is a pretty fun, and quick arcade game - It's about 2 hours or so of gameplay before things will start feeling like a grind, but to get all of the planes unlocked you'll have to muster on.
At the time of this review, Multiplayer no longer exists which isn't entirely surprising, but I bet it would have been pretty fun too.

SkyDrift is an aesthetically pleasing 3D aerial racer with enough details and diversity, to recommend it as one of the best games for this subgenre, in recent years. The main flaw of this title is the fact that it contains two DLC packs that feel like they were cut on purpose from the main game, only to be resold. It has a vast array of race/class choices to make, each class having their own specific sub classes, these characters can be taken across to Baldur's Gate 2 upon completion. You are also given your 9 alignment's to choose from, be it Lawful Good, Chaotic Neutral or True Evil. These will have an effect on any NPC's you wish to take along with you on your quest to save the lands, or destroy them?
The loot is great, there is a vast source of loot within the game especially towards the end game content when you get to say Durlag's Tower. You think you hit God Mode but perhaps the lack of petrification protection will make your Beserker get one shotted by a Bassilisk.
The voice acting, whilst small, is passable with a few exceptions being fantastic. Perhaps not enough customisation options. I personally love the isometric top down graphics, but they aren't for everyone.
THE ONLY downside to this game is the multiplayer, If you are buying this to play with friends, please research the problems you may encounter first. They have patched the issues now to some degree of success but I have had issue when playing with more than 2 people with it booting one of us out. I know a lot of people who have played the entire game with no problem at all as well though. Just be careful if you plan on Multiplayering.
All in all, one of my favourite games of all time. 10/10.

There's hope for this and I will repurchase a little later on (if that means I pay more then so be it) to re-review, but for now it's got a few issues that stop me recommending it (wish Steam would add a middle ground option instead of the Yes/No because I feel the No is too harsh).
* It runs smooth as butter.
* The game itself has excellent 'Pick up and Play' capability.
* The visual style is 'old/classic' but carries a great Arcade Charm.
* Controls seem intuitive on Controller.
* Wrestler Customisation (and Workshop compatibility by proxy) is incredible. The moveset customiser is light years ahead of anything anyone else has made.
* AI vs AI matches are genuinely fun to watch and setup.
* The total number of moves and the style of the wrestlers are outstanding.
* Strikes do not connect well. This is partly due to the angle of the camera mixed with the style of the sprites and ring design. Not sure how much this will improve, but even the AI in exhibition matches miss each other all the time.
* The lack of a 'Story Maker' or Feud system means that you're not able to add any meaningful weight to what you want to do. And the lack of a Card Builder for a series of shows that build to a PPV makes it feel a little hollow.
* The Belt Customisation is very lacking. Not sure if they plan to add Workshop support and allow full customisation here, but so far it's quite poor when compared to the ability to add to the belts. A lot of the front plates don't fit any of the straps at all.
* The Menu for adding Stables/Promotions is far too basic, and doesn't offer enough customisation for you to give it your own twist/design style.
* The method for adding Wrestlers to a promotion is a little fiddly/not clear.
* Online only supporting 4 players is a little disappointing. Having more in a lobby would be better so people can build match cards with larger groups and have people in and out. Would be nice if we could get 6 players in a match, but not a dealbreaker to stay at 4.

Sigmar's Garden is a fun cross between solitaire and chinese checkers, with a couple dorks providing color commentary every so completions. The rules are puzzling at first, but the elements of strategy and forward thinking gradually develop through play. It's relaxing to map out your pathing strategy around the quicksilver and metal marbles, or to find ways to cut through bunched up lanes. Overall, a great complement with absentminded YouTube watching. The attached game, Opus Magnum, is a pretty neat programming puzzler too.
In all seriousness, the main thing to mention is that Opus Magnum is the most beginner-friendly Zachtronics game yet. For instance, you get a luxurious unlimited scrolling canvas for you to make incredibly inefficient contraptions.  This makes the game so much less frustrating to work through, as you won't be constrained by space was you were in SHENZHEN I/O, more so in TIS-100, and infuriatingly so in SpaceChem.
For all the discussion about the game being easier, the real difficulty lies in defeating your friends' histograms, as Zach has somehow realized that friends do a much better job at motivating better solutions than a difficulty wall.  And really, there's something a lot more intuitive about clockwork arms passing around marbles, as opposed to trying to grok how XBUS works or avoiding message collisions between TIS-100 nodes.  As such, this is probably the most friendly game to start with for a newbie Zach-like player.
That the solutions often move like beautiful clockwork and can be easily exported as animated gifs also helps with the feeling of recreational accomplishment.
Update 10-26-2017: (Finished the main story campaign, and ordered the iron-on patch)
Wow golly this game could use a way to speed up to later breakpoints, or to skip state to a program location. And divine architect help you if you need to insert more steps near the beginning of a long work-in-progress instruction chain, where you need to delay the rest of the concurrent multi-page instruction sequences in all the other components.
Still, it's very doable to beat this game, but the last few levels involve some very intricate bonding patterns, and can take a ton of instructions to complete. In the end, I was satisfied with how the plot wraps up, though the level design was a grind for me at the end.
I'm not sure if the depth of the systems and puzzle design lives up to those of SHENZHEN I/O, but the relative simplicity may be a strong reason to recommend this game as a first Zachtronics game. For more theoretical players, I'm not sure if the systems here are Turing Complete, and I can't imagine how you would implement NAND (perhaps the needed components can be introduced in a later update?).
That said, one could argue that it is elegance, not systems design, that shines in high skill play here. Along those lines, I'm looking forward to seeing some really elegant animated solutions from others. Just seeing Notch's solutions on Twitter just proves how messy my problem solving style was.
In the end, this setting and story is easily my favorite out of all the other Zachtronics games, being strongly evocative as a mashup of The Diamond Age and The Baroque Cycle. This is an incredible remake of The Codex Of Alchemical Engineering, and suggesting the latter flash game as a demo doesn't do justice to the massive improvements since the last decade.
If Opus Magnum was this much of an improvement, I'm kind of curious what a remake of Bureau of Steam Engineering could be like. Come on Zach, you know you've thought about rebooting the universe of Ironclad Tactics. ;)

I'd highly recommend it to anyone who has enjoyed any of the other Zachtronics games. It's a game for the sort of person who likes the idea of coming up with their own unique solution to a puzzle.
Although optimizing for cycles is very satisfying, the other two metrics (cost and area) don't feel very worthwhile. I think some tweaks to pricing might improve the cost metric.
Some of the later levels feel quite chore-like. The size and complexity of the products (particularly those with circles in them) becomes so large that you have no real choice but to build very long solutions. I don't know whether this is due to the nature of the game itself or the design of the products, but it's not a feeling I ever had playing TIS-100.

If you've played a Zachtronics game before you will have either already bought it or have already closed the tab. This is a beautiful, feature rich Zachtronics game that shares many structural and presentational commonalities with the superb
, but with entirely different puzzle mechanics, superficially similar to
, but in reality quite different again.
The biggest thing that stands out to me at this early stage of playing is how advanced it is at getting out of your way. Layout-wise you are completely unconstrained. Where in other Zachtronics games the input and output formed part of the problem, here you can place them wherever you'd like, ultimately allowing you to optimise it fully. In earlier games, cycle optimisation and resetting again formed a lot of the problem, and usually not the most interesting part. That too has been remedied, with parallel cycles automatically interleaving and a simple return command that returns the gear to the starting point, taking the necessary steps to do so.
If that stuff doesn't make any sense to you, don't let that scare you off. This is a much more approachable version than most, probably a great jumping in point for people new to this type of problem solving game. Finding a solution that merely works seems simpler in Opus Magnum, but that and the beautiful graphics just make you want to spend hours more finding a faster, cheaper or smaller solution than anyone else.
As always Zachtronics is the master of "engineering" puzzle!

Of all the Zachtronics puzzle games, this one feels the least like a game. The gameplay is well designed for optimization, but I don't personally get much enjoyment out of optimizing the cost, size and time of a device with a completely abstract size, cost and run time.
To expand:
SpaceChem, Infinifactory and Shenzhen I/O deal with real engineering concepts. Reactors are expensive so as an employee we would try to build fewer of them. A factory exists to produce a product so we would want to reduce the time it takes for a run cycle to maximize factory output. Smaller circuit boards can fit into smaller devices. Etc. These all fit the role that you play as an engineer. The alchemy machine is not physically represented in the game world (or reality) and is therefore a departure from past titles. It has no equivalent in our world apart from magic. Measuring the cost of a machine that can turn lead into gold is irrelavent in an economic sense, whereas real world chemicals have a known value. We have no idea how long alchemy takes since it has no bearing on gameplay or story and has no real world equivalent; the process could be effectively instantaneous for all we know. SpaceChem reactors could arguably be the same way, but sending chemicals through a pipe to a tanker does give us some kind of time frame. The alchemy machine is not represented physically and has apparently infinite internal space, and there is no need to optimize an infinte resource from an engineering point of view.
I should specify that none of these issues I have relate to the puzzle component of the game. If your motivation is to puzzle for the sake of puzzling then yes, this game works very well. If, however, you are role-playing an engineer within the game world, which I derive enjoyment from, then the sudden lack of these underlying principles is a disappointing departure. Evidentally I am the only person who feels this way, but I stand by my assessment of engineering.
One last point: this game could have taken the opportunity to challenge you to optimize anything at all. Free from the restraints of reality, yet still judging your work based on real world economic biases. I think that's what disappointed me the most.

: this is an updated review. I removed previous review after trolly downvotes and feeling the need to update some points that were no longer in line with my current view of this game.
Killing Floor is a wave-based FPS focussed on the extermination of Horzine's test subjects referred to as Zeds, and their leader Kevin Clamely, better known as the Patriarch.
PROS:
+ many different maps, weapons, perks, characters, Zeds and themes (Halloween, Christmas, hillbilly and circus maps and Zeds)
+ killing stuff is very satisfying. Shoot, burn, slash, disintegrate, explode, gib, intoxicate, dismember, and decapitate the enemy as you please
+ multiple game settings like length, modes and (on custom servers) playstyles. You can also play maps in various spots and with various perk setups
+ there are many options with the console, like making custom text + voiceline binds, useful gameplay commands, commands that make certain tasks easier, commands for fun stuff, etc.
+ good replay value. I've crossed 600 hours and still haven't had enough of this game. Some even have 3000, 4000 or more hours logged and still play
+ the voicelines of Briar and Masterson are golden. As an avid spammer of the L4D2 vocalizer, I've never gotten tired of their voicelines, either. They really add up to the Britishness of this game
+ playing with pings up to and over 200 is still quite possible without being excessively annoying like in other shooters
+ a very not-demanding game. Some pretty old and/or crappy rigs can run this game just fine. A friend of mine who has a 10 year old laptop can still run it
+ configuring binds like voice, text and even tactical binds is rather easy

+/- a lot of the characters, weapon skins and actual weapons are DLC. The more content the merrier but as long as it's not on sale it's usually not worth the money. It's worth noting that you can unlock a few select characters and weapons for free

Chemistry. Space. Two-dimensional multi-threaded programming. If you have ever wanted to see those three things combined in a video game - and honestly, who hasn't? -, this is it. SpaceChem is a very well designed and very addictive puzzle game based around the concept of producing complex chemical substances from simple raw materials (and occasionally the other way around). You start off programming these reactions within the confines of a single reactor, but as you progress through the story you're required to construct more complex pipelines consisting of multiple reactors, some of which may have special capabilities like atom sensors, fission and fusion lasers, and quantum tunnels. You're also introduced to programming concepts like loops, branching, thread synchronisation and subroutines. Special challenge puzzles and the ability to go back and refine your previous designs using new techniques you've learned provide hours of additional playing time. Thoroughly recommended.

I really enjoyed SkyDrift. The best way to describe it is Mario Kart with fighter planes. The single player mode has six tracks (12 if you count reverse mode) and three race types: (1) power (like Mario Kart - race around the track and collect power-ups that allow you to shoot at your competitors); (2) survivor (same as power, but instead of a fixed number of laps the player in last place gets eliminated every 30 seconds or so); and (3) speed (power-ups are replaced by boost rings that increase the speed and difficulty of racing around the course). The game mixes and matches these three play types and the 6/12 tracks with varying levels of AI difficulty to create a single player campaign consisting of about 40 events, and for each event you can choose between about 10 planes with varying specs (some are faster, some are more maneuverable, etc). The tracks are spectacular and the controls and overall gameplay are also great.
With respect to single player mode, my only complaints are that there are only 6 tracks and the "campaign" is very loosely put together. There's no story, you don't even need to finish first in an event to progress to the next, and by the time you've completed the first 10 or so of the campaign races you've already seen all six tracks.

Some people would probably look at Fire Pro Wrestling and see it as a cheap crap alternative floundering in the Internet's virtual bargain bin. But this is the real deal, the crème de la crème. This series has been around since before dinosaurs walked the Earth and it's still one of the greatest game series ever. You think you've enjoyed creating your own characters? Think again. This game features one of the most in-depth creation features in any game, period. You not only get to create giant turquoise bears with anime girl faces, and make that bear the strongest (or weakest) character in the game, you also get to manipulate that character's CPU logic so that it constantly rubs its butt in its opponent's face.
One aspect that might turn people off to this game, though, is the fact that it's not necessarily action-oriented. The game has action, but you can't just mash buttons and constantly punch-kick your opponent to a bloody pulp. The game requires more finesse and psychology, much like an actual pro wrestling match, so in that sense it's a simulation. That doesn't mean the action isn't great, however, as the more you dig into each match you are able to pull off more moves, so if you get tired of rubbing your butt in someone's face you can smash them over the head with light tubes and hammers as the ring around you literally explodes from C-4 planted around the ring. Good fun for the whole family. In any case, the game gives these occurrences an extra sense of purpose than they would have had, becoming more than just a silly joke that's fun for about five seconds. It's actually engaging.
Even MMA fans can enjoy this game, actually, considering you can also fight in an octagon with custom MMA rules and even customize MMA fighters with some actually decent accuracy. The whole "match psychology" aspect in pro wrestling still applies, but I'll definitely take that over other MMA games I've played where I roundhouse kick my opponent in the head thirty times and they still don't bat an eye. At least it can lead to almost guaranteed excitement in an MMA match. There's a joke there somewhere.
Oh, last thing. I should revert back to the creating stuff features because you can create more than wrestlers. You can create virtually everything: stables, the ring, the belts, the refs, entire companies! You can build your own company and even book it. You can finally book everyone's favorite wrestler, Dirt Bike Kid, to be What Culture Pro Wrestling World Champion! "The boyhood dream has come true!" Can't create commentators, because there's no commentary, but would you rather have no commentary, or the commentators WWE has today? Hell, that's all I should've said in the first place, now that I think about it. "There are no WWE commentators, buy this game!" You also can't emulate backstage politics, so you can't run a Wrestlers' Court and can't make your wrestlers be bullied backstage by JBL. But that means you CAN make Triple H work Tuesdays whether he wants to or not, and he can't back-talk you from jobbing him out constantly.
But no, seriously, buy this game. It's (currently) twenty bucks. That sounds like a lot, but it's one of the best games on all of Steam and so it's actually a steal, such a steal you'll have to worry about Repo Man repossessing the game from you for ripping the developers off so hard. It's practically extortion. Instead, though, I will thank the developers for their sheer benevolence for keeping in mind that most people are not made of money. If people were made of money they wouldn't be sentient anyway, but whatever, what's important is the difference between, "Let's see, Fire Pro Wrestling or food?" and "Wow, I can afford both now, thanks developers!" And no, this game won't make you a huge nerd like me, making obscure wrestling references. But you can have a giant turquoise bear with an anime girl face rub its butt in Triple H's face in a barb-wire C-4 exploding death match with Repo Man as the special guest referee in a What Culture Pro Wrestling ring for the TNA Australian Heavyweight Championship without any WWE commentary. That's worth twenty bucks.

Each party member has special abilities that add to the overall survivability of your DotE run and more can be found while traversing DotE's dangerous depths and procedurally generated floors.
Finding new party members is a treat (and a life saver) as having a larger party means more meatshields to soak up the damage, and more unique abilities that can help you through the endless dungeons. While each party member is unique, at times it can feel like any random party would do and that each individual member is not very unique. This gives to a strange feeling somewhere in between luck and skill at times, as it's easy to wipe in the first level or two (and even easier as you progress.)
Managing resources can be a lesson in patience and trial and error. As you uncover rooms you discover that some can have modules installed in them that increase your resources each "turn." A "turn" basically counts as each newly discovered room. Other rooms provide nodes to research new or upgrade modules at a cost. Even others offer random treasures and trinkets, and the occasional gamble. There are a myriad of varied and different strategies in terms of investing in and managing your resources, which can help make each play through a little different.
5/5.

I have never played Baldur's gate or any of the dungeons and dragons games before playing this about a month or so before writing this review, meaning my opinions on this game come from no sense of nostalgia or fond memory. I went into this old game with the mindset of a current-gen game player. This is what I found.
They don't make games like this anymore. Baldur's gate, despite being over 15 years old as I write this, can genuinly be described as unique because you simply will not find other games quite like it in modern game design. Its a huge, sprawling RPG with fantastic writing, a brilliant sense of humour, an engaging plot and an openess to approaching each situation the way you see fit. The game rarely shackles rules onto you, and your free to use all the mechanics the game gives you in most situations, unlike most modern games which are designed to have a set way of each event playing out. The only criticism is its very wordy, and you will spend a lot of time just reading text, however, the script and writing of the game is actually one of its finest highlights, making this criticism a slim one. If you want an RPG that makes you feel like your really playing a role, and not being guided down a path like most modern games, give this a go. If you get lost in it you'll easily spend hours wrapped up in its enthralling world.

Trying to optimise for that last piece of area, or those final few operations (I've given up on cost at this point, though it's often proportional) is an addictive quest for constant self-improvement. The scoreboard pushes you that extra mile because you're

Chemistry. Space. Two-dimensional multi-threaded programming. If you have ever wanted to see those three things combined in a video game - and honestly, who hasn't? -, this is it. SpaceChem is a very well designed and very addictive puzzle game based around the concept of producing complex chemical substances from simple raw materials (and occasionally the other way around). You start off programming these reactions within the confines of a single reactor, but as you progress through the story you're required to construct more complex pipelines consisting of multiple reactors, some of which may have special capabilities like atom sensors, fission and fusion lasers, and quantum tunnels. You're also introduced to programming concepts like loops, branching, thread synchronisation and subroutines. Special challenge puzzles and the ability to go back and refine your previous designs using new techniques you've learned provide hours of additional playing time. Thoroughly recommended.

This game is EPIC. The challenge is to program reactors with a series of tracks and commands that will produce a specific molecular result. It's far more complicated then it sounds and you have to think on many levels and try to perform the tasks efficiently and in a multitasking manner with the waldos (grabber/activators) that reside in each reactor. One reactor is hard enough, but try stringing together several and producing 2 or more different results to send to different freighters. This is definetly a programmer's game as the system seems remeniscent of a programmable processor that manipulates data and seperates the results to specific outputs. An instant favorite of mine, I'll never tire of looking for the most efficient and effective way to produce the desired output.

Little Backstory of Assassins Creed Syndicate first, you play as the two main characters Jacob and Evie Frye who were trained by their father to be assassins. Through out the game you are working on taking out the templars that control the streets of London. Your main goal is to take out Crawford Starrick and take control of London for yourselves.
That's pretty much how I saw the game at least.
Assassins Creed Syndicate brings back parts of previous Assassins Creed games that haven't been seen for a while. The game is very entertaining for the most part, but can get to the point where it starts to drag on in the end. You gain experience through out playing the game that allow you to increase your combat skill, add additional perks to each character and unlock new items to use upon reaching new levels and completing sequences. You also have to look for items throughout London to upgrade you gang by giving them better weapons, horse carriages to drive around the city, and just making the stronger in general. The game includes a lot of the fighting style and combat mechanics as Unity and a few from Rogue.
Aesthetics, the game looks... well... decent. I'm not able to run it on the highest of settings but I can run it decently and it looks okay. I think they could have done a way better job on how this game looks even though it's during the "steampunk" era. Like Black Flag that game was absolutely gorgeous, this game is honestly kind of a let down to me personally when it comes to graphics but it still looks amazing and is fun to play.
All in all or TL;DR:
This game is fun and has a lot of exciting moments in and brings a whole new feel to the Assassins Creed Franchise in my opinion kind of like how Black Flag and Brotherhood change the series as a whole. I would recommend this game to anyone who is just looking for a really fun game to play that might take them around 40 - 50 hours to complete in total. I rate this game a solid 8.5/10 overall gaming aspects but for an Assassins Creed game it gets 9/10 from me. Nothing will ever be better than Black FLag and Brotherhood to me. If you haven't played those you need to do so.

The Sandbox mode is the bulk of the enjoyment for me from this game.  The story mode just feels a minimal added bonus.  The story itself is okay and at first it feels like it serves as a tutorial, it's just the quests in it feel tedious at best and if anything they distract from enjoying the game.   Also if you require extreme hand-holding in a game with quest markers and waypoints, etc, you're not going to have a very fun time in story mode, though the quest journal for the most part lays out what you need to do rather well and you have to be pretty thick to not know exactly where to go and what to do unless you get extremely sidetracked.
The game is worth it alone for the survival sandbox mode.   If you're strictly planning on playing it for the story mode, I'd suggest waiting for a sale, especially if you're the type that want to enjoy the story and not endure the hardships of an unforgiving survival simulator because that's just ultimately not an option, trying to survive will always take priority over progressing the story.   As for the survival aspect of the game, it's very unforgiving and as it should be.  Managing water, food and warmth can be an extreme chore, especially warmth.  If you find a good place to call home with a fireplace you're pretty set.  But once firewood, water and food become scarce, that's when you're going to have to brave the low freezing temperatures, low visibility blizzards and hostile wildlife.  On a survival level this game is definitely up there for having a good balance of challenge and feeling like you accomplish something when you actually hunt something successfully for animal hides and meat.

As a newcomer to the series, I've only played 2 actual matches so far outside of the tutorials. I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked in both. I still haven't completely gotten the timings down, and the game is pretty difficult. But that's okay, because the game is so enjoyable it makes you want to learn how to play it. The game makes you want to master it. That being said, however, even if I were to never touch the controls for an actual match again, I'd still get amazing satisfaction out of this game. Since I haven't fully gotten the gameplay mechanics down yet, I won't mention anything for that. What I will talk about is the amazing experience to be had in the other departments.
This is where Fire-Pro excels in. For Create-A-Wrestlers, you can literally customize everything. Full movesets, accurate attires and faces, even AI logic for the character in simulated matches. There's so many customization options and it's incredible. I can only imagine what the possibilities of a supported mod community could bring to this game as well. The only thing the customizationcould use is custom logos, which I'd imagine mods could bring to the table sometime in the future. Assuming of course, that it isn't an outright Developer supported feature added later.  You can also create your own referee, and change his logic for fast counts or slow counts, or make the most neutral referee ever. Plus, the refs have all the same attire and face options as the created wrestlers do. So, with that many face and customization options, you can make them look as whacky or professional as you want too.  There's also a create-a-ring mode which isn't super in-depth like the others, but it doesn't need to be. They have pretty much every ring style you can hope for in the ring-editor. You can customize the turnbuckle style, the pattern of the mat, and the ring post and ring rope colors. You can create full promotions, with factions for all your charcters. You can even create your own titles, however the options here are very, very limited at the moment.
Does all that customization sound too hard to you? Well that's perfectly okay too. With the Steam workshop support, you can download all the characters your heart desires. Whether it be famous TV show characters, or the most popular wrestlers of past and present, there are already hundreds and hundreds of options avaiable to download right now. You can also download created referee's from the workshop, and everybody's favorite referee Red Shoes is already made and ready to be downloaded. Fire Pro is a game series known for it's amazing creators. Fire Pro Wrestling Returns (A 10 year old game) STILL has community support to this day. I don't see that being different here with Fire Pro Wrestling World either. This is a game that will have plenty of longevity, and the workshop will only help with that.
This is the area most of my early play-time has been spent in. I was able to do a full 16-Man Tournament to determine my IWGP Heavyweight Champion on my New Japan promotion in-game. I didn't even play a single match in it. I simulated the entire thing. I have never had as enjoyable of an experience just watching something as I have here. The sim aspect of Fire-Pro is truly something special, especially with the creators getting the logic down so well so far. I watched Shibata deliver nine headbutts in a row to Marty Scurll to win the match, which left both of them bleeding. I watched Kenny Omega deliver a One-Winged Angel to Hiromu, which Hiromu kicked out of at 2.9 and set-up a Time Bomb for the win. The simulations the game can deliver are a fantastic experience. You can straight up never touch the controls in an actual match and enjoy playing the game from a managerial aspect if you wanted too. If you've ever played the WWE 2k games, you almost never want to sim a match in your Universe because its boring to sit there and watch. That is not the case in Fire Pro. I have and can continue to spend multiple hours just watching matches I set-up play out. The CPU AI and Logic system can truly make for some amazing matches, and I was truly surprised with how much I enjoyed it. I always heard the simulated matches in Fire Pro could be incredible, but I never expected them to be this damn good. Seriously, even if you never plan on actually "playing" the game, the 20 dollars for the sim experience alone is well spent.
This might be the best 20 dollars I have ever spent on a video game. As a massive wrestling fan like most people I assume buying this are, the game does everything right. I don't like using a "Perfect" label on things really, especially for a game with more features still to come, but this game is damn near perfect. The combat is actually fun and it doesn't feel like a massive guessing game against the AI, the match types are amazing, and the simulation experience is a joy to watch. Overall, I'd say this game is well worth your money, and I very much look forward to sinking countless hours into it.

There are only two game series that have held my interest for 20+ years: Fire Pro Wrestling and TNM.
TNM, being a 16 bit DOS based, text wrestling simulator is one of those things that even though I have nothing but love for it...I couldn't play it if I wanted to...it won't even start on modern computers.
That leaves Fire Pro as the sole survivor of a 2 decade long hobby. I love playing "fantasty booker". I've tried this in the recent WWE games and their universe mode, and it's fun...but it's not sandbox enough. You're still shoehorned into stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥that you might not want to do.
Fire Pro doesn't rely on half-cocked modes that leave you feeling disappointed because of the wasted potential. It focuses on wrestling and creation...it is the ultimate wrestling sandbox. This open ended gameplay is really what has kept me coming back for 20 years. There's nothing else quite like Fire Pro.

All the bosses are unique and require a strategy. They are challenging on times, but it is possible to collect and cook enough healing and buffing items to get those bosses down even when you are not a pro-gamer. ;)
There are a lot of nice puzzles and challenges. Some optional, some required.
There are also collectables to change your appearance and to decorate your home.
And pets. Cute and useful pets. And cute.
The music in Aquaria is wonderful. It is always fitting and supports the surrounding in the best way. It never gets annoying and even when you feel like smashing your head on the keyboard because of a jumping puzzle that is particular hard you still can take a deep breath and listen to the music. Hahhhhh....Better.
Said jumping puzzles are the only negative of this game as I found. There will be times when you burst the surface and jump around. Naija has legs. But she can' walk it seems. More than once I jumped way too far or too short and had to redo all of it. It requires a bit of practice to figure out how to jump, but luckily most of the time the hard jumps are only for optional things.
You cannot save everywhere, but the save crystals are placed conveniently, so no worries that you have to replay half a dungeon when you lose to a boss.
in short:
- beautiful game
- great music
- challenging bosses and puzzles
- pets and collectables
- controls sometimes difficult
AWESOME GAME

2- A BIG nuisance was that builders kept taking furniture from completed custom buildings in order to build other buildings. Effectively making my town with 11 buildings to have a grand total of 6 beds.
3- A functional nuisance I had is that there is no way to influence what workers will do. I kept trying to expand up a mountainside, jut to have all my workers occupied elsewhere and none dedicated to mining.
--As of late, I have noticed that most of the workers will pick an item, pick another, then drop the first one, then drop the second one on the spot. They do this over and over and then forget about the issue, setting off to do something else.
4- As of the latest couple of patches, farmers will tile about half the farmland area I set, then ignore it and do something completely different and not farming-related.
The game becomes generally unstable when the goblin invasions become "upgraded".
The game is simple and a bit cathartic, but I can't in good conscience recommend it at this point. A lot of bugs need to be solved, and with the current early access trend, I'm on the fence about this game being abandoned before it's finished.

Dishonored is an interesting take on the stealth genre, though I think it has some major flaws. The game takes place in a plague-ravaged, post-industrial world where the main source of power is derived from refined whale oil, which has somewhat mystical properties it seems. However, despite the engineering marvels of the day, there are also supernatural forces at play that bestow the player character with magic abilities.
For my very first time playing through the game, I chose the hardest difficulty available, turned off the 'cheaty' UI elements such as objective markers, and avoided using magic entirely (with the exception of the two or three places you absolutely must use Blink).
These are some of the things the game gets right:
- The atmosphere is quite unique
- There are a great number of ways to go about navigating through the missions
- You can choose non-lethal alternatives to completing objectives
- Graphics are very decent
- Smooth controls
- The game provides options for disabling UI elements, such as floating objective markers and NPC awareness markers.
These are some of my criticisms and observations:
- First of all, the Game of the Year edition comes with pre-order packs that give the player a bunch of free upgrades and money after the first mission. ♥♥♥♥ that! Why do game publishers do this? Thankfully, it is possible to get rid of the free♥♥♥♥♥♥by disabling the pre-order packs in Steam settings, then starting a new game.
- The plot of the story is extremely clichéd and predictable.
- The game introduces quite a bit of mystery surrounding the supernatural agent that your character comes in contact with, however there doesn't seem to be a story resolution that explains its motives. As a result, it feels like a shallow way to write in game-mechanics rather than being about good storytelling.
- While the missions themselves provide a lot of leeway as to how you go about completing them, the actual story progression is entirely linear. The choices the player makes ultimately have no impact the way the events of the story unfold.
- Enemies repeat the same lines over and over, which gets old very quickly.
- The characters you encounter throughout the game are fairly interesting, but your ways of interacting with them are extremely limited. They often feel like walking tape recorders set up to play their few lines of dialogue, rather than actual people.
- The game pushes you toward dealing with threats through lethal means by giving you a substantial arsenal of deadly weapons. Actually using them generally throws the concept of stealth out the window though.
- Very early on in the game, you get the Blink ability (teleport) as part of a tutorial and you can also choose to get Dark Vision (see through walls) immediately after. These abilities in particular make the gameplay utterly trivial. It is possible to use these an unlimited number of times and quickly speed through the game.
Overall Dishonored is a game worth playing, but I don't recommend it highly.

I have never played Baldur's gate or any of the dungeons and dragons games before playing this about a month or so before writing this review, meaning my opinions on this game come from no sense of nostalgia or fond memory. I went into this old game with the mindset of a current-gen game player. This is what I found.
They don't make games like this anymore. Baldur's gate, despite being over 15 years old as I write this, can genuinly be described as unique because you simply will not find other games quite like it in modern game design. Its a huge, sprawling RPG with fantastic writing, a brilliant sense of humour, an engaging plot and an openess to approaching each situation the way you see fit. The game rarely shackles rules onto you, and your free to use all the mechanics the game gives you in most situations, unlike most modern games which are designed to have a set way of each event playing out. The only criticism is its very wordy, and you will spend a lot of time just reading text, however, the script and writing of the game is actually one of its finest highlights, making this criticism a slim one. If you want an RPG that makes you feel like your really playing a role, and not being guided down a path like most modern games, give this a go. If you get lost in it you'll easily spend hours wrapped up in its enthralling world.

With a compelling story, great writing, neat monsters, legitimately interesting characters, and lots of dark corners to explore, Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition (BG:EE) is an alluring RPG. I could easily drop hours into this game just wandering around talking to NPC's, collecting quests, and going off the road in wilderness zones--all of those things are rewarding despite being completely optional. This is a great game. Once your eyes adjust to a 90s spectrum, it's also a great LOOKING game. The new content is also well-integrated, and the new characters provide a nice bonus for veterans of the 90s iteration.
Unfortunately, BG:EE is held back by the tabletop rules set it emulates. Slow level advancement and combat being resolved purely by random chance makes the game needlessly frustrating in its early stages. The Nashkell mines are especially painful. One minute you're murking every kobold (reptilian terriers who live underground and get off on ambushing adventurers in their sleep) at-will, and the next thing you know your party is completely wiped out by a lone survivor because no one could roll above a 10 to hit. Stupid THAC0. The slow advancement means you could play the game for several real hours, mowing down waves of enemies, and see no real improvement in your characters' ability to deal with enemies. It can be very tedious. Combine these flaws with an abundance of combat, and the whole thing plays out like a scripted roguelike.
Although combat grated on my nerves at times, I don't necessarily have a complaint about the tough difficulty. For example, when my main character was one-hit killed by an arrow trap in the mines, I cringed but remembered all the warnings I got about traps and used the party's thief to meticulously scout them out upon reloading. The game's difficulty improves the experience: figuring out ways to keep your walking targets safe in the face of lots of cheapshotting obstacles adds a dimension of gameplay missing in this post-Diablo RPG climate.
I do recommend BG:EE though. Anyone willing to endure the frustrating tedium of the early game combat will find a challenging and rewarding experience within.

OK, after playing this quite a while, and following several updates I can write a more complete (for an Early Access game) and fair review.
Pros:
-Always something to do
-Non-Restrictive world and environment
-Town and Citizen advancement
-Resource Management!
-Looks good for a voxel style game
-Random events
Cons:
-Can be draggy/grindy at times
-Town can get too big quickly and become laggy, or cause FPS loss.
-Item Storage is buggy, sometimes making it to where citizens cannot find a needed resource
-Can get repetitive
-Custom building designer is basic and restrictive
Discussion:
Stonehearth is a voxel style resource and town management game with some degree of progression, but no real endgame. There are monsters to fight, houses and defenses to build, resources to gather, and citizens to keep happy. There are many different professions, some of which require you level up in the preceeding profession to be able to promote to the new profession. The scale at which you can build is pretty impressive, making entire towns and cities with only a few clicks of the mouse. There is, as of yet, no means to share the custom buildings you create, but I'm sure the dev team will be adding that in the future. And speaking of the dev team, talk about communication and presence! Narry a week goes by without some sort of update from them, whether it is an unstable testing release or a stable build update. If nothing else they simply write to the players to let them know what the team is working on with a few teaser images added in. They are very friendly towards the player base, and have added elements suggested by the players on many occasions. All in all, this is a team that understands the true purpose behind pre-release and are one of the few that make it worth-while.
Gameplay:
When you start the game you have 7 citizens, a campfire, a few resources, and maybe a couple tools to get a couple of your citizens started on a job, and some very basic resources the you selected at the beginning of the game. This is of course after selecting your citizens, the starting resources and starting position of your new town. From there you can decide what kind of town to build, how big to build it, and the layout of it. Just remember that the layout is very important. Things that are too far away are not going to be accessed by your citizens unless there are roads and/or building nearby. Houses are not specifically necessary, as you can dig tunnels through rock in order to build underground cities. As your citizens perform their duties, if they have a job they gradually level up gaining access to better recipies.
A few key things you need to start on right away with a new town:
-Food. Seriously, food is a HUGE issue. If you selected the food starter pack, you have maybe 3 days before you start running out of food. You need to make a food source quickly. You have a choice though: Farming or trapping. You can of course pick both, but at the very beginning of the game, the more workers you have the better. These are the people who are going to mine your mines, chop your trees and build your houses. So pick one. Trapping generates barely sufficient amounts of food and hides (valuable, and can later be used to make armors), and farming generates a lot of food, though the food is pretty bland, and resources. Be careful though as it can take 3-4 days to actually generate enough food to keep your citizens fully fed. Farming can also generate other resources (For your hebalist and Weaver) as well as start generating new trees to plant, grow and harvest.
-Shelter. While not as important as food, shelter is needed in order to start increasing your citizens happiness. Shelter is where you place beds, tables and chairs to eat at, and eventually the craftsmen tools and tables. Morale is a big thing, and without shelter, morale quickly starts taking a downward turn. Personally I start off by digging a couple of 24x24 caves, putting two 20x20 stockpiles in the center of them, building a few rooms off the 24x24 areas and start adding beds. Putting in a dining area will also start increasing morale, as your citizens won't have to sit on the ground to eat anymore.
-Traders and Daily Updates. Caravans, traders, and the occasionaly odd event pop into your town from time to time via a window that pops up to let you know something is going on. Traders can be there to buy/sell goods or offer you a timed trade deal (Give me 3 Wheat bundles and I'll bring you some watermelon seeds, or other such offers). Daily Updates give you an idea of where you stand with your town, and when you hit certain threshold allows you to get more citizens.
Almost everything else is intuitive and can be learned in the game.
From when I bought this game, to where it is now has been a journey. While the game still resembles what I bought, the inner workings have been expanded to the point where this feels more like a full game than it does an Early Access game. Would I recommend it? Absolutely, and the price is always right.

That said, it does have one somewhat annoying problem.  There's no native controller support; instead it emulates a keyboard and mouse. You might want to pass on the controller and use keyboard and mouse for this game.

Put simply, if you liked SpaceChem, buy this immediately.
All Zachtronics games have similar logic behind their puzzles, but Opus Magnum is by far the closest to SpaceChem in theme and design, with plenty of its own style and mechanics to make it feel like more than another iteration. I, personally, was particularly excited to dive into it because (as much as I like all Zachtronics games) I prefer the visual puzzles and the satisfaction of moving gizmos in a complex machine to the code-based puzzles of more recent titles like Shenzhen I/O.
As for people who have never touched any Zachtronics games, I wouldn't necessarily say that this is a better entry point than any of the other games. It basically depends on what looks most interesting to you; SpaceChem for chemistry, Infinifactory for industry, Opus Magnum for Alchemy, and Shenzhen for electronic engineering. Beneath the theme, they all challenge your brain in a similar way, with freeform puzzles with infinite solutions, challenging you to find the fastest/smallest/cheapest design. If the idea of such "creativity puzzles" is appealing, you really can't go wrong with any of those games.
After my short time with Magnum Opus, I would personally place it in a close second to Infinifactory, with SpaceChem coming in third.
An important note on Early Access: Zachtronics tends to have an unusual approach to early access releases, and Opus Magnum is no exception. Rather than releasing a beta version, Zach tends to more or less finish the game before it can even be purchased. There's rarely missing content or features, and the only changes tend to be very minor bug fixes or tweaks (with the exception of Infinifactory which was a little more ambitious, and had an extra story chapter). My guess would be that the "full version" will only differ in having more player-made puzzles. So, if you're the sort of person who shies away from early access, I'd say there's little to worry about here. The Zachtronics reputation is too strong at this point.

My rating: 8/10

If you are looking for a challenging puzzle game, SpaceChem is the way to go.
The whole Chemistry thing only provides an outline for the story, you won't actually need any knowledge about chemistry (and you will neither learn much about it). Yes, the game has a story which is presented in text form. It's okay, you might want to give it a chance, but you can also entirely skip through it without missing much.
The core game requires you to transform some input molecules into different output molecules. You do this, by laying out two independent "conveyors" on a grid. In each step, you can assign some functions to the conveyor, for example grabbing onto or dropping an atom, fusing them together  or splitting them up.
The first few levels are relatively easy and gradually introduce you to more concepts once in a while. If you ever programmed something, you already have the right mindest for this game and will probably enjoy it (if you enjoy programming, that is :)). If not, don't worry, you should get the hang of it.
In later levels, the difficulty ramps up massively. Some levels even require you to combine several inputs to several outputs by setting up multiple reactors and figuring out for yourself, which intermediate steps to take in each of them. Furthermore, the last mission on each planet also features a boss fight where you first setup your reactors and then interact with them to defeat the boss.
If you got the hang of the mechanics, the problem will soon be not to come up with a solution in general, but to fit it in the limited space you have.
I only have some minor gripes with the game.
First, the music: It's not bad in general, but it is some strange epic soundtrack that does not really fit the game. The game is already taxing enough on the mind and I found the music to become exhausting after a while.
Second, the boss battles: The idea to have boss fights in a puzzle game is cool, and doing the puzzling is just as good as the rest of the game. However, the live interaction part is fiddly and rather annoying in some battles.
After all, I found the game to be very enjoyable. Bear in mind that you will have to use your brain a lot. If you are looking for some casual puzzling fun like, say Bejeweled, this is probably not what you are looking.

I was looking at games the other day. Figured I’d support the Indie scene and… what’s this? SpaceChem? Okay, that looks like something I’d enjoy. Turns out I was disastrously right. Here’s why:
SpaceChem is a training tool for many of the skills I value.  Process optimization, design problems, spatial layout, programming, continuous flow problems. It fits snugly in my mind.
There is no “right” solution (just like in real life!), only better, worse, and wrong.
I find SpaceChem really difficult. There’s a constant struggle to create a linked sequence of elegant solutions to unique process challenges.
I think I’m good at it. Judging from the “others solutions” charts (which is a brilliant idea by the way) I’m coming in below average (which is good, since they are all minimize optimal) on all three metrics at once. Consistently. Often on the first try. Of course, this only drives me to attempt ever more elegant solutions, making the game even more challenging.

This is the hardest and most rewarding puzzle game I've ever played. New mechanics are introduced gradually. Difficulty ramps up very quickly.
There is no "one way" to solve a task, the general idea is that you program the reactors to perform a goal. As long as the job gets done, it still counts. However efficiency and speed does result in higher ranks on the leaderboard.
In tasks, you are limited by the number of programmable reactors you can use, and indeed the notion of limited space is real catch. If you run out of reactors or diagram space, you'll need to find a way to optimize your layout.
I've been programming for many years and these puzzles itch the same portion of the brain. I suppose it's analgous to trying to write a program in 256 bytes of assembler.
Unlike many puzzle games, this one fits into a context that makes sense, the story line and the objectives you complete don't seem forced or fanciful. And watching a completed system in action is highly rewarding.

It's a well know fact that dogs are man's best friend. A lesser know one is they're also pals with strange sack doll people, who don't take so kindly to having their pet kidnapped by demanding aliens. But what are friends for besides rescuing each other from extra terrestrial life, while dooming the planet in the process, and thus Gomo sets off on a mission to steal a powerful crystal and save his canine buddy from the slimy captive. Unfortunately he isn't able to save his game as well.
Daedalic's Gomo is a much smaller game than the developer is used to, and this emphasis on accessible, simplified mechanics envelops the whole of the 1-2 hour experience. I'm fairly forgiving of short games, but in this case the lack of content and interactivity is rather shocking. Significant portions of the game amount to little more than cutscenes, with "gameplay" effectively revolving around clicking the right of the screen to keep things moving. When you do come across a puzzle, it's so basic and quick to solve that it almost feels insulting and a waste of time, forcing you to momentarily slow down and wait for animations to unfold before progressing to the next equally tedious moment.
Gomo isn't a hopelessly bad game, in fact numerous parts are rather charming and enjoyable to watch, but it's design is painfully shallow and ultimately, entirely forgettable. The significant lack of interactivity leaves it in an awkward position feeling more like an extended animated short than an actual game, but the few entertaining moments are not at all enough to carry the experience by itself, which ends before you even realize it's started or has any chance of becoming more than a dismissible novelty.

If you're a fan of RPGs, especially D&D, then Dragon Age: Origins is a must-play.
If you've played previous Bioware entries, namely Baldur's Gate and (to a lesser extent) Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, then you'll feel right at home. They've created their own homebrew world that clearly takes heavy inspiration from Lord of the Rings and D&D, but is still their own unique world. Just like they did with Mass Effect, they've made a world that I would actually want to live in.
Almost uniquely to the RPG genre, DA:O permits several valid ways of playing:
-If you prefer real-time combat or a more story-focused experience, you can set the difficulty to easy and pretend tactical pause doesn't even exist, in which case you'll pretty much only need to care about how your main character's class plays. Heck, you could probably convince yourself you were playing a single-player and much more story-focused version of World of Warcraft.
-If you want to be a bit more involved, try normal difficulty, and tweaking your party members' tactics lists.
-If you truly want some tactical challenge, and don't mind needing to learn how all three classes play, you can turn off auto-tactics entirely, crank it up to hard or nightmare, abuse tactical pause, and give everyone new orders every (unpaused) second. With a zoomed-out camera, this feels a lot like 3D Baldur's Gate.
