I still remember hearing birds chirping outside around sunrise the first time I beat this game back in 2009. Good times.
An ode to (and direct descendent of) the era of classic RPGs such as Baldur's Gate, Dragon Age: Origins is a classic in its own right. BioWare games (at least prior to 2011 or 2012) are known for their superb storylines, party-based gameplay, engaging plot sequences and dialogue choices, and memorable characters. Dragon Age excels in all of these categories, though this time around you're not a Jedi or a Spectre, but the last of the Grey Wardens, struggling to save Ferelden from the assault of an Archdemon and the ensuing civil war.
Per the game's title, your Warden's background and overall place in the story is determined by one of six 'Origins' (a seventh one is specific to the Awakening expansion campaign), selected at character creation. The standard fantasy class selection of warrior, mage, and rogue are found here as well, supplemented by a plethora of abilities, attributes, skills, and class specializations. The sheer variety of playstyles, coupled with in-game plot choices, gear, and the origin story of your character, make for a game that will have you thinking about your next playthrough well before you even reach endgame and the DLC—which is 100% worth it, especially since the Ultimate Edition comes with everything.
Combat heavily rewards a tactically-oriented mindset, as well as appropriate use of companions to complement your character's playstyle. Pausing combat and making use of the tactics system, tactical view (a classic isometric camera, as opposed to third-person), CC, and spell combinations makes a world of difference, though those who are unfamiliar with RPG mechanics/gameplay or are more accustomed to ARPGs may find combat slow or tedious at times. If you dislike the gameplay of KotOR, Baldur's Gate, and Pillars of Eternity, chances are Dragon Age won't be for you. However, adjusting to the aforementioned mindset may significantly increase your enjoyment of the game, and I highly recommend giving it a chance.
The music is incredible. The lore is rich in detail. The visuals are dated (even for 2009); however, the outstanding art style makes up for this, perfectly capturing the dark, mystical, and visceral atmosphere of the Blight-stricken continent of Thedas, as well as contributing to the classic feel of the game as a whole—map, menus, and all. The mod support only serves to push things over the top, and, while lacking Steam Workshop functionality, is simple enough with the DAUpdater and a trip to Nexus Mods. I always keep a .zip of my favorite mods saved to my Dropbox in the event that I'm reformatting, reinstalling, or downloading DA:O onto a different computer.
To me, Dragon Age: Origins, alongside Mass Effect 2, is the last of BioWare's true masterpieces. I found Dragon Age 2 to be a terrible mess of a game, and Inquisition, though a vast improvement over DA2 and, at times, enjoyable, still doesn't come close to matching the standard set by Origins. Perhaps I'm letting my expectations deny me the enjoyment afforded to many by DA:O's sequels, but I nevertheless found them disappointing. Maybe the next entry will win me over. At any rate, the silver lining is that Origins' relation to DA2 and DA:I is far looser than that of the Mass Effect Trilogy, and as a result functions wonderfully – moreover, satisfyingly – as a standalone experience.
I absolutely cannot praise this game enough. Dragon Age: Origins is a fantastic experience that has ruined my sleeping habits far too many times. Do yourself a favor and grab the Ultimate Edition during the next Steam Sale.

Maize is a first person adventure game about sentient corn, and the scientists who developed them.
The game starts off with you being dragged around by corn, and then waking up in the corn field without any idea of what just happened. I was very curious about this sentient corn, and how it came to be. As you venture into the research facility, the story focuses more on the scientist’s overly dramatic relationship with each, rather than the how or why of the whole situation, so expect to read a lot of dialog on post-it notes from these two. By the end, I find myself left wanting more details about the sentient corn, and I think they could have done more with the story.
The gameplay is mostly what you would expect from a first person adventure game, but with a lot more of a walking simulator feel to it. You’ll need to walk around, explore, and find objects to complete tasks to unlock other areas and progress. There’s not much difficulty in completing these objectives since you can see the shape of the objects that you need to find, and the objects also have hints on them about what their use might be.
After a little progression, you get a sidekick named Vladdy. He’s a sentient teddy bear that you’ll need to do some tasks for you. In contrast to Vladdy, the different corn characters were amusing, and entertaining at times, so I liked them, and would have liked to have seen more of them.
Performance wise, I was usually able to maintain 60 fps on epic settings with some occasional drops (GTX 1070).
Maize has a ridiculously fun and silly concept, and it’s definitely a game that doesn’t take itself seriously. The sheer goofiness of it all made me smile at times, but the constant overuse of the same insults gets very, very annoying. I also found the game to be lacking in content for the price, and I would have liked more depth to the story. Overall, it was an alright experience; it’s not great game, but it’s not a bad one either.

Dishonored is an interesting take on the stealth genre, though I think it has some major flaws. The game takes place in a plague-ravaged, post-industrial world where the main source of power is derived from refined whale oil, which has somewhat mystical properties it seems. However, despite the engineering marvels of the day, there are also supernatural forces at play that bestow the player character with magic abilities.
For my very first time playing through the game, I chose the hardest difficulty available, turned off the 'cheaty' UI elements such as objective markers, and avoided using magic entirely (with the exception of the two or three places you absolutely must use Blink).
These are some of the things the game gets right:
- The atmosphere is quite unique
- There are a great number of ways to go about navigating through the missions
- You can choose non-lethal alternatives to completing objectives
- Graphics are very decent
- Smooth controls
- The game provides options for disabling UI elements, such as floating objective markers and NPC awareness markers.
These are some of my criticisms and observations:
- First of all, the Game of the Year edition comes with pre-order packs that give the player a bunch of free upgrades and money after the first mission. ♥♥♥♥ that! Why do game publishers do this? Thankfully, it is possible to get rid of the free♥♥♥♥♥♥by disabling the pre-order packs in Steam settings, then starting a new game.
- The plot of the story is extremely clichéd and predictable.
- The game introduces quite a bit of mystery surrounding the supernatural agent that your character comes in contact with, however there doesn't seem to be a story resolution that explains its motives. As a result, it feels like a shallow way to write in game-mechanics rather than being about good storytelling.
- While the missions themselves provide a lot of leeway as to how you go about completing them, the actual story progression is entirely linear. The choices the player makes ultimately have no impact the way the events of the story unfold.
- Enemies repeat the same lines over and over, which gets old very quickly.
- The characters you encounter throughout the game are fairly interesting, but your ways of interacting with them are extremely limited. They often feel like walking tape recorders set up to play their few lines of dialogue, rather than actual people.
- The game pushes you toward dealing with threats through lethal means by giving you a substantial arsenal of deadly weapons. Actually using them generally throws the concept of stealth out the window though.
- Very early on in the game, you get the Blink ability (teleport) as part of a tutorial and you can also choose to get Dark Vision (see through walls) immediately after. These abilities in particular make the gameplay utterly trivial. It is possible to use these an unlimited number of times and quickly speed through the game.
Overall Dishonored is a game worth playing, but I don't recommend it highly.

Another intensely relaxing game that puts me in the exploration mood, Aquaria has been described by some as Ecco the Dolphin (a classic SEGA Genesis underwater title) meets Metroidvania, my overall favorite genre of 2D game. And I’m pretty sure it fits that description.
You play Naija, a cute fish-girl (with legs instead of a mermaid’s fin) who (according to her narration), as far as she can remember, is the only one of her kind. She’s always just lived as a feral creature, only wanting to do her own thing, until she receives a vision from a mysterious visitor; she is meant for more than her mundane existence, and she sets out to discover her destiny.
It may take a little getting used to, but eventually you’ll find your ideal method for controlling Naija as she swims through her massive undersea world; I prefer mouse and keyboard. Early on in your adventure you discover that the means to progress through the world is tied to the Verse; the life energy that flows through the ocean is manipulated by Naija’s songs. You’ll learn about a dozen in your travels, from those that protect to those that change your shape, and others that manipulate the world around you.
Said world, unfortunately, is not all songs and rainbows, no pun intended; even in her Home Waters, Naija must deal with threats in the form of giant, mutated sea creatures, from fish to nautili and more exotic ones the further out you go. Fortunately, you learn how to become a being of pure Energy early in the game, and thus able to shoot balls of fire (yes, fire in water; how that makes sense is a good question) at your enemies. Still, your battles will be quite challenging; you’ll have to solve puzzles on the fly (er, swim) during most of the ‘boss’ encounters, but it’s not normally too difficult.
To improve Naija and buff her abilities, you’re able to ‘cook’ or synthesize many of the items you come across. From increasing her speed or firepower, to healing her in a critical moment, your judicious use of the many recipes you find will definitely boost Naija’s chances of survival. Also, you may find certain cosmetic objects that will be placed throughout Naija’s home cave; another collection element, but it’s a pleasure to find things in this beautiful watery world.
As you probably know already, I thoroughly enjoy Metroidvania games, and this one is no exception! The atmosphere is downright soothing, the music is great and evokes both calm and danger in proper proportion, and the narration really draws you into the story. Five out of five!

The enhanced part is how much it doesn't work.

"Enhanced Edition" - no. They updated the resolution and probably removed the (now useless) performance-vs-quality options as well as a few visuals. Other than that it's just a few tweaks and features, but the whole engine (!) seems to have stayed the same - especially the netcode.
How is that a problem? Well, the game crashes frequently, multiplayer is unreliable and lags, and the game freezes on various occasions (saving/connecting/transferring items/etc) that should not let a modern game freeze. Well, I thought that at least, regarding the "Enhanced Edition" suffix.
I played BG2 in multiplayer before, and the UI is almost exactly like it - a good thing. But to my disappointment, all the bugs haven't been fixed, instead this game actually crashes more often than BG2 original.
If it is reduced, you like RPGs, and you plan on playing singleplayer only, get this. Otherwise, better not support this attempt on getting money with a slightly updated old game (their only work was to fix/enhance the game - and they failed the first part).
I feel like I should add that you get the "DLC" for the game (2 new chars, sound and icon packs) for free on the Steam edition.

Never played the original Spintires to this review is from a new player to the series.
First up the graphics....amazing, cant think of a better way to say it. the environment is stunning and the way the water and mud moves is fantastic.
Modes, i never played the multiplayer (not my thing) so for those like me you have two options in this game.
Challenges - basically the tutorial and are well worth doing, they offer you a good chance to see what the game is about and with optional bonus objectives that make them a little harder if you want to do them.
Campaign Mode - Main mode for single player, consists of 6 maps each with its own challenges and problems to overcome, you start off with a small selection of trucks and you can unlock others on each map to help you should you need them, each truck can be fitted with several different trailers or back which do all the various jobs to deliver the lumber, i opted to run with large logs in mind which was slower for transit but got each lumber mill done with one run each mill needing 8pts and the large logs offer that, the medium logs are worth 4pts and small are worth 3pts, so its up to you how you want to complete them.
Replayability - unless your into multiplayer then this game is very limted for the price i paid (£24.99), 6 maps and a small amount of challenges that were completed fairly swiftly without any real issues, i feel this game could have been so much better if you were given more things to do within the maps or perhaps more maps to play through. i have several ideas but its pointless to put them here and i do realise that everyone has their own opinion on this matter but this is just my personal view.
Controls - these are customizable and oh so simple, i used the keyboard and mouse to my play through but this game does support gamepad and wheels as well, while i own a wheel and would have loved to use it for this game one huge thing stopped me from doing that, the camera angles offered for this game is a major issue for me and overall seriously let this game down, i spent more time fighting to find a suitable viewing angle for navigating over terrain than doing almost anything else, if i could plead with the devs to do one thing for this game it would be to overhaul this awful issue.
Overall:
On the whole this game was very enjoyable but very short, with more content from the start or a better career mode this game would for me end up being one that i would enjoy playing for alot longer than i did but as it stands its limited and i cant honestly say i got value for my money, my personal advice would be to new players to wait for this one to drop in price unless your interested in the multiplayer side of things along with the single player modes.

Ok, I got this game expecting something like Machinarium, which I enjoyed immensely. Well, I was hugely disappointed. Here is why:
Absence of the story:
There is none. The supposed story is that you have to save your dog. However, after the first minute of the game until the last minute of the game, nothing makes sense. Even after finishing the game and reading some walkthroughs to see if I missed something, I still do not understand why things were happening. The entire game can be viewed basically as a collection of random puzzles stitched together by a loose thread.
Laughably simplistic puzzles:
Did I say puzzles? Sorry for misleading you, but there are no puzzles in this game. Everything is straightforward. Unless you are 5 year old or braindead, it should not take you more than an hour to finish the entire game. I finished this game in 118 minutes, and I am quite bad at puzzle games.
Point and click:
There is only one puzzle in this game. It is figuring out what is clickable and what is not. Earlier, I said it should take around 1 hour to finish the game. Well, half of that time you will spend trying to figure out what part of the scene you can interact with. This is the only puzzle in the game, and very annoying one.
As a conclusion, avoid this game even if someone offers it to you for free.
Instead, try Machinarium or Botanicula.

Pros:
- Excellent graphics and sounds.
- Immersive atmosphere.
- Fantastic presentation.
- Great concept.
Cons:
- Completely reliant on Steam's unreliable community servers. When the "friends" part of steam goes down like it does several times a day, every day, you will be thrown out of any multiplayer game you currently have running.
- Huge amount of DLC. I picked up the game with the Season 1 pass. The Season 2 pass doesn't give me the rest of the content and it is very pricey. Luckily it's mostly all crap too, the few things worth picking up aren't in season passes and are really expensive. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
- Unskippable cutscenes. Every. Single. Map. Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ you.
- TERRIBLE AI. Want to play as a monster against an AI team of hunters? You won't last long as they always know where you are no matter how much you sneak, every shot will hit you and every snare will hit. Want to play against an AI monster with AI team mates? All of a sudden, those lethal, psychic terminators you fought against as a monster turn into a team of pacifists with down syndrome who will not heal or resurrect and will often run off alone. Seriously, why is the AI given a labotomy when they are allies? To give you a challenge? Heh, didn't work.
- So you'd rather play vs players? Great idea! But the community is dead, so tough luck. It took me ages to find a match on the matchmaker, even with the free weekend event where I picked up the game.
I see where all the potential in this game is and I really want to love it. Because of all the problems that mar the experience, I'll have to just say that it's okay. I don't regret buying it and I do like the game a lot, despite the problems, I'm just hoping that the problems get fixed but that's unlikely. If you have 4 friends that you like to play the game with and get lucky with steam, it's incredibly fun... but seriously, who has 5 friends who all play the same games at the same time? And who can predict steam's down time?
This game could be more playable, in my opinion, if they had their own servers or at least the game didn't rely on steam. Also making sure the AI isn't buffed or labotomised. Proper difficulty levels maybe. Make no mistake, this is not a multiplayer game. It's community is dead.

So, after reading tons of bad reviews from earlier this year I went into the free weekend with lack-luster expectations. I was very happily rebuffed by a fantastically fun game. The issues regarding finding matches, or matches that had already started, were non-existent (with the latest update[s]?). The gameplay seemed to be wonderfully balanced between good teamwork on the side of the hunters and solid, intelligent play on the side of the monster.
There are absolutely certain maps which 'favor' specific monsters -- giving the monster an edge in certain ways -- but this in no way keeps the game from being fair or playable. Often hunter losses are caused by a team that's not communicating and, surprisingly, I ran into a lot of PUGs that were actively using their mics and communicating. Only a handful of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s soured that, and often they had a degree of poignance to their asshatiness (non-mic'd player totally ignoring everyone and legitimately helping the monster).
Unlike Titanfall which very, very loosely had a storyline stuck around its matches Evolve actually FEELS fleshed out and leaves you asking questions in good ways (e.g., who is CIG9? What happened on Shear? Is your preferred Hunter actually a good guy... or is he just doing it for fun?).
Of course, I can't support the tons and tons of DLC, but it's honestly cool. Each character in each class feels unique and fun and, I dare say, is worth the cash for them.
Overall, I'd totally recommend the game, especially at $19.99.

This review includes my opinion, and some of the fixes for certain issues to the game (Nvidia users).
If you are an AC fan like me, you would appreciate Ubisofts effort for making a better game after what happened with Unity. Jacob and Evie's different personality and play style offers so much more experience than previous games. The parkour was somewhat the same as unity, although this time they added the grappling hook (not to be confused with the hook blade of course) for easier navagation, since in the late 1800s, roads are wider. At first I thought that would just killed the entire parkour experience AC fans loved so much about, and even though i understand why the grappling gun was neccessary and that it's just a game, I still find it weird at times how this physics defying tool can exist in victorian london. But trust me, without it you will be miserable in this game. I just think the game developers can come up with a more realistic/ better navagating tool for that period, or at least limit the features like gliding upwards with your hand.
The covering system/ stealth mode is quite nice, although since they got rid of the "enter cover" button i sometimes am not sure if i am in cover or not, but trust me, it does not affect your stealth play one bit, in fact it's an improvement. And one of the things i like about this newly installed AC game is the enter stealth mode feature. Wearing a hood all the time makes you look more suspicious doesn't it? especially in an era where its not a fashion trend. So they added the feature where jacob and evie will only put on their hood when you're entering stealth mode, jolly good!
Issues with the game:
I'm playing this game on my MSI GS60 gaming laptop, i got a intel core i7 6700 HQ cpu and an Nvidia GTX970m with 16 gs of vram. I thought this is more than enough to play the game, but I encountered some problems when launching the game.
Issue 1: Full screen/ windowed problem.
My screen supports 4K, but as you gamers know playing on 4K requires much more than what I have, so when turn the resolution down to 1080p, the game wont let me enter full screen, to fix this simply click on the diplay option and select "borderless fullscreen"
Issue 2: Frame rate drop
Now i know this is a graphic demanding game, but come on I got a GTX970m.... sigh oh well i will admit gaming on a laptop, you win some you lose some. But to fix this issue just turn off ambient occlusion, you really cant tell much of the difference, and set your anti aliasing to FXAA. Overall, depending on your gaming rig, if you are like me, or close to mine, set your graphic preset to high instead of ultra, gaming on ultra for this game you probably need a better gaming rig than what i have.
Issue 3: ACS auto select GPU as integrated GPU
So like i said I got a GTX 970m, but my integrated GPU is of course ♥♥♥♥♥ier, a intel HD 5000 or something like that. After I install the new Driver from GeExperience for my GPU, ACS suddenly uses my integrated GPU. son of a ..... anyways, to fix this, just find nvidia control panel on your computer, select manage 3dD settings, program settings, and then select ACS as the program you want to customize, and then underneath it select your prefer graphic processor as "high performance nvidia processor". It worked for me. Also like to point out all my other games like Fallout 4, ACU, Far cry 4 have no issue with this, so maybe its something to do with the game. I have no idea.
Issue 4: Game crashes/ stopped working after a while....
All i can say for this, is to play the game as admin, locate your game in your steamapps file, right click on ACS icon, play as admin, ever since i did that, no crashes for 2 hours of gameplay. so..... yay....i guess....

The game is seriously challenging too, starting off with some easy levels so you get the hang of things, but quickly ramping up to missions that require complex solutions that actually take planning and ingenuity.

For puzzle fans the game is well worth its normal price tag.  For everone else, at least try out the demo; the demo in itself is a decent length and will definitely make you decide whether this game is for you or not.

The amount of complexity can be overwhelming and one mistimed reaction or misplaced pipe can lead to compounding failure and rage. I recommend this if you enjoy puzzle games, but prepared to visit youtube for solutions. A nice feature included is a built-in youtube recorder and uploader to show off your own solutions too so they are easy to find.

I received Maize for free today from a friend who helped with the marketing. I am normally not one to play single player games but the humor of Maize drew me in. I almost said no to the game just because I get bored playing adventure / puzzle games but Maize really isn't like that... it's quite odd frankly.  And that's why I liked it!
You start out not really knowing where you are and why you are there.  You fit the pieces together slowly as you are taken through a few different environments.  There is some exploration but the game is quite linear. It's the dialogue and quirky cutscenes that made the game for me.
You will need to be thorough in your exploration as many items have a function, even if it seems completely ridiculous.  Throw logic out the window and you will have a great time.  All the characters' voice overs are great, if not completely cliche but that is the charm for me.
I did find how the music cuts out right before a cutscene a bit jarring, had some performance issues at various points of the game, and the lack of inverted mouse support did make me cry a little.  There was a few bugs I noticed while playing but the worst thing that happened was I had to go back to the main menu and reload the save, nothing game breaking. I persevered and I'm glad I did.
Maize is a unique experience with a story that is cleverly written.  In total it took me about 4 hours to play through. Recommended for anyone like likes a good single player experience with a sense of humor!

Have I not reviewed this yet? I'm shocked. Origins is everything an RPG should be. It's spectacularly well-written from the larger world-building aspects to the companion characterizations to NPC dialogue. Everything is entirely fleshed out and wholly immersive, and the moral dilemmas characters face are truly multi-dimensional (something I find the later games tend to lack), leaving a serious degree of forethought necessary for each decision, and both positive and negative consequences either way. The dialogue options for the unvoiced protagonist are funny enough that I acutally laughed out loud a couple times. The graphics, while not superb, are easily forgotten through the story-telling and action (and the special kill animations are awesome regardless). Gameplay and combat may leave something to be desired for someone more interested in a hands-on experience, but the strategem required is just as engaging, even if it can be reduced to a series of clicks. Does get repetitive, especially if you don't switch out companions, but I got over it just to hear all the AI banter. Voice Acting is top notch across the board (except for one player-determinate instance but I got over it pretty quick). I'm not willing to admit whether or not the soundtrack made me cry. Decisions and choices matter and have effects on this game and subsequent games and just, the plot delivers, the action delivers, the stakes deliver. And with the amount of different decisions you make and how interconnected they are (not to mention all the optional side quests), it's infinitely replayable.
I only played Origins because it was on sale when Dragon Age:Inquisition wasn't; it wasn't as pretty and I was really only interested after hearing about some of the Inquisition companions and wanting to see it for myself. Figured while Origins was cheap that I could start from the beginning, and I am endlessly glad I did. A remastered version of this game would blow the other two out of the water, easily. The effort put in over 5+ years of production shows through and through.

Recommended, but only with reservations.
It doesn't run completely stable. I've had it crash several times when opening the party's inventory screen directly after a larger fight in the city of Denerim. Other players have had similar crashes years ago already.
The Wiki mentions various bugs in quests and other parts of the game.
The game's playtime is long enough, if it's your first playthrough without following any guides/walkthroughs. If you want to rush through the game a single time, note that some guides are controversial.
The game's is easy enough at "Normal" difficulty, and even more so, if you don't mind reloading an older save from time to time. Such as when you've found out something that's not explained in the manual.
The included manual only gives a very sketchy picture of how everything works. Don't expect to find any maths in there. Searching the Wiki and discussion forums will be needed, if you're interested in details, such as how exactly an attribute influences a skill's efficiency.
Combat is very repetitive, especially since the party's size is limited to your player character and only three NPC companions, which you control. Companions, which you remove from the party, remain available at the party's camp site till the end of the game.
I think the skill/talent tree has been dumbed down pretty much. The variety of enemies could be much greater.
It is not an open world. Quest locations on the overview map get added/removed as you progress through the game. The quest areas themselves often are very restricted, and even in the wilderness you can only move through an area on predefined paths and not move freely.
In some parts of the game you enter meta-gaming hell. Such as an ambiguous answer during conversation leading to an immediate and unexpected ambush of a potential companion, because that's how some of the conversation trees have been designed. Reload and avoid the WTF-moment. Or one of your long-time companions, who has been with you almost since the beginning and  calls you a friend, leaves permanently before the last few endgame fights just
because the game only offers two story-driven choices for taking either the evil or good path. Or merchants at various stages of the game, who offer unlimited supplies of some very important crafting materials or a recipe you need. Once you've gained such meta-gaming knowledge, the real planning can start. Or else the potential for multiple playthroughs would be low.
If you only want to do a single playthrough, the game is entertaining enough for sure. Its beginning varies in quality. Don't quit in rage early. The middle and end are better. The voice acting is fine, but sometimes a bit silly (they couldn't resist adding crap when you select a companion). And there are lots of cutscenes that add to the atmosphere.

If this isn't something that disuades you in the slightest, here are a couple more highlights:
-maps are massive and detailed, with lots of fun little surprises and bleak jokes to be found
-Spiffo is probably the greatest mascot of all time

It's a solid game with strong foundations but it's severely lacking in end-game content. No NPCS yet, no story, nothing to do once you get your base set up and become self-sufficient. There are some cool skills like electricity and carpentry that let you disassemble electronics for parts or build wooden cabins out in the forest, but good luck training them to the levels you need. And even if you do manage to train your skills to the levels you need, all it takes is one small mistake and your character (and all of your progress) is gone; getting bitten is a death sentence. You can minimize those risks by playing it safe and trying to find armor but it doesn't matter, eventually you're going to mess up. This game is very unforgiving. It gets annoying and if you're not up for a challenge, don't bother.
Mods like Hydrocraft are basically a necessity if you want to stay entertained past 20 or so hours. Even still, the mods can only add so much. You'll encounter the same problem of not having anything meaningful to accomplish in the game world. All of your time will go to either looting houses for supplies or building up your base. But again, once you've got a farm, a generator, and a few rain collectors built, you're basically done with the game. From that point on, you're waiting to die.
All of that being said, it does what it set out to do. Survival is challenging, zombies pose a significant threat, the workshop offers a nice selection of gameplay additions and maps, and it's fun to explore the world and loot stores and warehouses. It gets so many things right. If I were to judge it purely as a survival game, it'd pass with flying colors. But if your only goal is to just not die, one has to ask themself why they're even playing. Buy the game by all means, but understand that you'll ultimately feel unsatisfied. Cars alone aren't going to provide the content that this game desperately needs and I don't think the developers are committed enough to take this game to greater heights. Another indie game that'll never reach its full potential, I'm afraid.

A good concept and gem of a game that neverthless ends every session in rage due to game-design missteps, woefully underexplained shortcuts, unskippable death scenes. For example:
- Camera gets trapped in look mode during combat and pressing E cannot cancel.
- Song mechanics that are fun to use normally but woefully unsuited for tight situations, patched by using number keys to instantly transform (which are not mentioned in game), but at the same time revmoing the flavour completely.
- Sun form's annoying sound that you have to use everywhere in the Abyss.
- Unreliable jumping mechanics out-of-water, used to climb and explore some places.
- Non-removable visual effects that are bad for a subset of players: Whole Screen flashes on transformation, screen warps when crossing the water surface.
- Uneven game pacing, and in certain cases too much freedom with unwarned dangers. E.g., lower Open Water sections before Fish form heavily penalises early exploration. (1) Sudden jump in enemy numbers (easily doable if you're experienced), but moreso (2) leeches that attach to players and slow them down to a crawl after ~4. An optional fish form is required to detach them, or spend 10 minutes crawling back to a save point to load a new game.
Having said the above, I still think it's worth considering, but the dev breakup meant that many of these QoL problems would never be fixed.

I played this game when it first came out on the iPad many years ago, and I absolutely loved the game from start to finish. When I saw it on Steam, I immediately bought it again, just to experience what it was like to play this game after so long away from it. The music, the visuals, the mechanics; it all adds to give you an experience where sometimes you'll be amazed at your discovery, and sometimes you'll feel truly scared in the shadowy depths of Aquaria's world.

This game had an interesting feel and I'm sure a lot of people can agree that though underwater levels are some of the most hated in the history of gaming, Aquaria made it so that it was at least slightly more fun.
For me though, I was so bored of this game that I couldn't go back to it after playing it once. Some people would probably say that there's more to the game once you get deeper in, but if I can't even get hooked in the first level or two then there's really no point. I really wanted to like this game because of all the positive reviews, but I'm one of the few who just didn't enjoy this game. The enemies and gameplay were uninspiring and bland, and there were no unique qualities to this game that kept be coming back. Gomo is a short point-and-click adventure game where you play a lil alien who has to rescue his missing puppydog.
The first part of my review must put emphasis on "short", I completed this game in 1.2 hours, which, for a point and click adventure, is incredibly quick, since a portion of that time is spent pixel hunting and being confused over puzzles, which for Gomo wasn't a huge concern.
The game is very easy, and very short. It's an enjoyable experience if you get it at a nice price, but again, it's a rather short game. There are some sidegames which you can unlock as bonus extras, but with the lack of coherant story throughout the game (drawing more on the quirky side of storytelling rather than the world-building side) there's no real draw or attraction to spending more time in the Gomo world.
That aside, I'd still recommend the game! As someone who is very familiar with point-and-click adventure games, Gomo was a little easy for me. But, it's the perfect game for someone new to the genre who fancies getting their feet wet at the prospect!
The game is light and breezy, a nice way to spend a few hours of your evening, and the perfect gift for a friend or relative who might not have dabbled in this genre but you feel may get a kick out of it.

What’s this?
Gomo is a short and sweet point & click game, with a quirky, 2D Tim Burton feel. The debut game from Slovakian developers ‘Fishcow Studios’, Gomo is a great steading to start on, and shows the talent that could come from ‘Fishcow Studios’ in the future.
And what’s it like?
The fun and challenging game follows the sack-boy styled character Gomo on his search for his beloved dog, Dingo, who has been cruelly kidnapped by an alien. By completing puzzles and fixing all manner of machines, you must navigate Gomo to a crystal, the ransom for his sack-dog.
The game itself is interesting, and caters to all levels of puzzle-solvers, with an “easy” mode for those who could easily end up throwing their PC across the room otherwise. There is a good mixture of object-based puzzles, as well as simple point and click elements. Some of the puzzles take longer than would be hoped to even figure out what is needed to be done, and there are even some that you have to just fiddle with until they work – despite this, Gomo is largely a creative and exciting game.
Travelling through many different locations, the background is always amusing. From satirical army posters in the testing bunkers, to a stick man reaching the top of a mountain, then sliding back down. In-keeping with the quirky-traveller style of Gomo’s character, his body has a back zip to solve the omnipresent problem for all game characters: what happens when you pick up more things than you can hold? The whole style of the game has a very hand-drawn and honest indie feel to it, but the story and gameplay are as refined as you would find in any major puzzle game.
To some audiences, the non-verbal style of that game may be increasingly annoying, as being stuck on the same puzzle for five minutes makes the music a little grating. But, the satisfaction of finally understanding a puzzle makes it worth the struggle.
What’s the final verdict?
Despite being a quick play-through, Gomo challenges and amuses, with an endearing design, traditionally repetitive music, as well as some humorous “WTF” moments to be had in alternate dimensions. ‘Fishcow Studios’ have created a game for all levels of puzzle-solving gamers on the quest for a sack’s best friend.
Words by Louise Egan

Let's get this out of the way. Maize is one of if not the strangest video game that I have ever played. While some people might find that to be a negative, I think it is Maize's greatest strength.
If I had to classify Maize I would probably say that it is a walking simulator. You basically walk around exploring and picking up objects. The objects you pick up are used for some light puzzle solving. The puzzle solving in the game is really easy to the point where the game sometimes tells you exactly what you are supposed to be doing. If you want a challenge, Maize is not going to be the game for you. On a whole there is nothing wrong with the gameplay but you probably don't want to buy Maize for its' gameplay.
The reason to purchase Maize is for the story. It should not surprise anyone that a story about sentient corn is quite ridiculous. The game's ridiculousness is the game's greatest strength. Basically the game's story is about the sentient corn and the facility that created them. The story is ridiculous which leads to many funny moments in the game.  I would actually kind of compare Maize to The Stanley Parable without the ability to mess with the narrator. The game's stories are quite different but feel similar at the same time.
Lengthwise I would say Maize is around 4-5 hours long if you explore every area fully. If you want to rush through the game I think it will take closer to two hours to complete.
Maize is not going to be for everyone. If you enjoy gameplay over story or actually want a challenge, Maize will not be for you. If you want a funny completely ridiculous story though I think you can have a lot of fun with Maize.

Science has clearly gone too far in this surreal first person adventure game that has you chasing after walking, talking sentient corn and solving puzzles with the help of an irate, Russian Teddy Ruxpin. It's as if the X-Files and Day of the Tentacle got together to create a genetically altered baby in the 80's and then hired the Monty Python team to teach it to read & write.
So Maize starts off strong dropping you in the middle of a mysterious farm with just hints as to what lies beneath the surface (literally). A wonderfully realised world of weaving paths and object puzzles that are a staple of point 'n' click genre. All of which is brought to life with the power of the Unreal engine, that gives the game an undeniable visual flair.
And even though there is a fair amount of back-tracking the game never feels artificially long, like a lot of those older point and clicks. With the paths all clearly marked out and the puzzles though not blatantly obvious are easy enough to solve and never frustrating. Also the story unfolds nicely in the various cut scenes with polished animations and high quality voice acting.
But there are one or two things that stick in my teeth (like a stale corn husk).
Despite the developers saying the game will take 6-10 hours it will infact only take you about 3-3.5 hours to complete. And if you are not a big fan of linear games this may well be a little too "walking simulator" for you with none of the puzzles really providing much of a challenge.
Also after the first hour things start getting a little repetitive. Jokes and puzzles start getting recycled and you start to get the feeling the game may well have been scaled back and short cuts taken in development after those opening sections. Bugs and glitches become more noticeable, with texture pop in becoming more and more frequent as you open up more of the facility. I also noticed major performance issues about two thirds of the way through. On returning to the farm I suffered a lot of dropped frames and lag. Which is a little disappointing considering how well presented the game is.
All in all I would recommend Maize, especially for anyone who has enjoyed games like The Stanley Parable. Though I would say to maybe curb your expectations. It is a fairly short game with not a lot of challenge but a nice enough story to carry you through.

The concept of the game is interesting, but it's really, really difficult to play. I'll elaborate.
The game consists of two parts mainly.There's the story mode and a sandbox mode (which also offers an imbedded challenge mode). Now, most players will have jumped in quite early through Early Access. I did acquire the game in Early Access as well, but haven't played it much as I awaited the Story. This has been released recently.
The setting of the game is a wintery Canada. Lots of snow, lots of forest. You have to rely on your wits, luck and resources to survive. In the story, you lose track of your ex-wife and are set on a path to find her again. Stranded without resources, your first days are spent learning the basics of the game: gathering supplies, keeping warm, learning how to craft basics such as (potable) water and edible food.
When you've somewhat recovered from the crash you start your search. It is then that you will meet the wildlife. Some of it's rather unfriendly, such as wolves. The wolves don't roam in packs, usually in pairs. The wolves in the story are quite aggressive. Possibly due to lack of food, I'm not sure. In the sandbox mode you can play the game at an easier level.
Surviving an attack is not quite likely. You lack weapons whatsoever and the ability to climb anything. You're hard put to either run or keep away if you still can. Obviously, the wolves may be between you and a certain point, such as a safe place to keep warm and prepare some food or water.
I have yet to find a weapon to combat wolves. The only thing that somewhat works is a torch, but obviously these burn out quickly. You'll have to create a fire first, by means of the wood you've collected. So make sure to pickup supplies on the way.
I've spent well over 10 hours to finally get a grasp of the basics. Less regular tasks, such as opening safes or climbing ropes still lead me online resources to find out what it is I have to do.
So, how to evaluate this game? I'll stick to my first advice and won't recommend this game. The strong points of the game are it's unique setting, the atmosphere and the anxiety you experience when your life is in danger (due to sleep deprivation, hunger, thirst, wildlife, and so on). But the weak points outweigh the strong points, as this game is very hard to master and sometimes doesn't make sense. It takes perseverance in a player to really understand the mechanics, make the right choices and keep on doing so.
The story thus far is interesting enough to keep me at the game. But the sandbox is not for me. Surviving for the heck of it doesn't make any sense to me. I like games where I have to achieve a certain goal. Staying alive doesn't cut it. Just suppose you'd find yourself stranded in Canada with the certainty that you won't find anyone still alive. What would you do then? I think I'd try to go south to escape the snow and find a more hospitable environment. Or perhaps have a player survive for X days while help is coming to a certain spot? These are simple goals that would give the sandbox a raison d'etre, without the need for the studio to have to invest heavily to create additional content.
There's a large community supporting this game and you may find a large number of resources online with tips on how to play. I think that most of these people are veterans who played the sandbox a lot and probably learned to play the game by growing into it by playing all the releases that were published in Early Access.

The storymode (Wintermute) took every single crap part of the sandbox mode and slaps you in the face with it.  Way too scarce supplies? Wolf torpedoes that one-shot you unless you're at full health? Breaking my ankle on the slightest incline? Horrible instructions or intuitiveness of gameplay & control scheme? All combine with the lamest, most cliche characters and storyline imaginable to make the game simply frustrating and BORING.
Guess what saps all my interest when playing a game: Getting jammed up by a crap save point and playing how many 10s of seconds before the wolf torpedo executes me again on the way to the next car OR starting over AGAIN.  After reaching the 10 day mark a couple years ago, I'd essentially reached the end of my interest in simply surviving in a Lighthouse or shack with no other goal.  I checked back in last year to see nothing had changed to make me care.  Now, story mode is released - the one thing I was hoping would give me an objective like "reach the lighthouse and light it to signal someone" or "get to the bunker protecting other survivors" or "gather survivors and build an outpost to survive X days" or "clear the wolfpack that's hunting you".  Instead, I get "Follow this stale, boring railroad story with carefully portioned out supplies that are never enough to do anything with, die to wolves a hundred times, and maybe complete chapter 2 before you kill yourself in real life".
Really? The Telltale piecemeal Chapter crap?  And after all this time you've only got 2 lousy, poorly structured and written broken tutorial missions with hideous character design.  Played 2 hours of Wintermute and became angry and bored, switched to sandbox for half an hour, became just bored and quit.  I can't imagine EVER wanting to run the wolftorpedo gauntlet again in the same area with the same crap and the same stupid story.
TL;DR - The updated console inspired control scheme is awkward garbage.  Story mode is boring, frustrating garbage.  Sandbox survival mode is essentially the same, and one of the better examples of that increasingly tired genre, so if you're into that, you're best served just going there.

Recommended, but only with reservations.
It doesn't run completely stable. I've had it crash several times when opening the party's inventory screen directly after a larger fight in the city of Denerim. Other players have had similar crashes years ago already.
The Wiki mentions various bugs in quests and other parts of the game.
The game's playtime is long enough, if it's your first playthrough without following any guides/walkthroughs. If you want to rush through the game a single time, note that some guides are controversial.
The game's is easy enough at "Normal" difficulty, and even more so, if you don't mind reloading an older save from time to time. Such as when you've found out something that's not explained in the manual.
The included manual only gives a very sketchy picture of how everything works. Don't expect to find any maths in there. Searching the Wiki and discussion forums will be needed, if you're interested in details, such as how exactly an attribute influences a skill's efficiency.
Combat is very repetitive, especially since the party's size is limited to your player character and only three NPC companions, which you control. Companions, which you remove from the party, remain available at the party's camp site till the end of the game.
I think the skill/talent tree has been dumbed down pretty much. The variety of enemies could be much greater.
It is not an open world. Quest locations on the overview map get added/removed as you progress through the game. The quest areas themselves often are very restricted, and even in the wilderness you can only move through an area on predefined paths and not move freely.
In some parts of the game you enter meta-gaming hell. Such as an ambiguous answer during conversation leading to an immediate and unexpected ambush of a potential companion, because that's how some of the conversation trees have been designed. Reload and avoid the WTF-moment. Or one of your long-time companions, who has been with you almost since the beginning and  calls you a friend, leaves permanently before the last few endgame fights just
because the game only offers two story-driven choices for taking either the evil or good path. Or merchants at various stages of the game, who offer unlimited supplies of some very important crafting materials or a recipe you need. Once you've gained such meta-gaming knowledge, the real planning can start. Or else the potential for multiple playthroughs would be low.
If you only want to do a single playthrough, the game is entertaining enough for sure. Its beginning varies in quality. Don't quit in rage early. The middle and end are better. The voice acting is fine, but sometimes a bit silly (they couldn't resist adding crap when you select a companion). And there are lots of cutscenes that add to the atmosphere.

A lot of games rely on the storytelling crutch of amnesia, despite few using it well. It's an easy and useful way to write off having to explain everything to the player through their character but it can make wrapping up the story far more troublesome in the end. Aquaria starts you out in just this way, with an amnesiac protagonist coming to learn about herself and her world. What I didn't expect was how effectively the game could surprise me, moreso than it did its own character. If you want the full experience of discovering Aquaria's world yourself, stop reading right now and get it. I assure you it's worth it.
You take on the role of Naija, a pleasant little fish lady all alone in her corner of the ocean for reasons even she does not know. An auspicious event causes strange memories to come flooding back to her, starting her on an epic journey through the seas of Aquaria. I won't spoil what she finds but lost civilizations and mystical enigmas are definitely in the cards, along with a boatload of clever powers. There are monsters to battle, beings to befriend, and no end of secrets to uncover in your quest.
When I say "epic" I'm not just overusing the word. Aquaria is built like a metroidvania, with a wide-open map gated by the many powers you'll gain as you progress. But just like the actual oceans, this map is absolutely enormous, almost prohibitively so. Each region of the waters is a network of maps that stretch far and wide, featuring undersea caverns, canyons, islands, peaks, and clefts. Hidden in these vast locations are items to scrounge up, enemies to battle, and passages into the many places you need to explore to get anywhere in this game. And the powers you gain to access these places are dramatic and transformative, utilized through a clever musical mechanic where you sing songs Ocarina of Time-style.
With all this facing me as I took my first steps (strokes?), I was fairly lost in Aquaria for the first hour or two. The starting region is decent about leading you to your first few powers but once you move on from there the ocean appears just that, an endless ocean of secrets and possibilities. Aquaria feels pretty aimless most of the time because of this and also because the story is told in brief snippets of monologue from Naija, who doesn't know a damn thing more about what's going on than you do. Finding your next power to proceed is going to take a lot of wandering and exploring and experimenting and backtracking, and that means a fair bit of patience if traversing the world doesn't grab you.
I wager it will grab you, though, thanks to the wonderful attention to details here. Naija's world comes alive with all kinds of colorful sea creatures, from tiny anemones to massive sea stars, harmless guppies to deadly nautiluses. Despite the slow and peaceful start to the game there are a ton of enemies to battle, with some areas needing to be cleared of hostiles before you can effectively proceed. You do get some very cool powers to deal with them, of course, and those powers can be used to turn up ingredients for the game's cooking system (which makes helpful healing and buff items) or artifacts (for decorating your lovely sea home).
The graphics propping all this up are simple but charming and have plenty of detail where they need them most. The sound design, though, my God this game has a magnificent soundtrack. Once you get out into the world you're sure to come across a region you never want to leave because of how enthralling its theme is. And while there aren't as many effects as you might expect, the ones there are do a lot to maintain the atmosphere of the deep seas. There's so much to see and do in Aquaria, including a wealth of unexpected elements I haven't even touched on, that you're sure to find something to hook you.

TL;DR 9/10 Very unique, vivid underwater 2D exploration!
This is a large world to explore, collect items, craft boosts.  Rebind keys--TYVM.
Everywhere you go, you can kill most any fish, which will drop an item 40% of the time.
Instead of different weapons, you morph into different "Forms" which have their individual uses. For most the game, I stayed in Energy Form to blast any fish. I never used Beast Form to devour.  I explored and completed the entire game without using hardly any of the booster items except an occassional heal.  For endgame, I would suggest looking up the Jelly costume for its self-heal to 1/2 full when in your docile, non-attack, Song Form.  Of course, to acquire this costume, I had to kill the Jellyfish boss--tough to do without waiting to acquire all 8 Forms. For end boss, I used a few Defense boosters +2, Energy booster +1.
There are just so many little secrets that it is very tempting to start using a Walkthrough Guide halfway through the game to ensure that you do not miss anything.  In hindsight, I believe you could push forward without a Guide and simply return later for a second walkthrough to pick up a few missing pieces--but you know the backtrack/repeat frustration. "I already did this."
9/10 Lovely to play.  No flaws.  This game is a model of what indie gaming is about--a simpler game can be a wonderful experience.

+ Large beautifully detailed world with various different looking areas
+ Dozens of spieces to discover
+ Astonishing soundtrack
+ Lifetime (about 20h)
+ Sweet story and swell voice acting
+ Lightweight system requirements
- No RPG elements
- Stiff controls on the land (very rare)
- Pad is supported, but basically useless
Many might have not heard about Aquaria which was released in late 2007 by two men independent game company Bit Blot. Being an indie title is one of the oldest of the genre and it was realeased much before Braid which is considered a game that launched wide a boom of independently-developed video games since 2008 and onward. Whatsoever Aquaria is absolutely marvelous game all the way! Thanks for its excelent gameplay design and classic colorful graphical design - years have threated it very well.
Story tells about Naija, a female, humanoid sea creature who suffers from amnesia. She wakes up alone in the submarine cave unaware about her wherebouts, family or friends and thus she starts an adventure where she will meet many dangers, discover secrets and find her love. I really loved that the story is narrated from protogonist part of view by future Naija, which voice over Jenna Sharpe makes her job well. Every now and then there is well set cutscenes consisting animations and art, telling that what caused the disaster of the civilizations that inhabited the lands of Aquaria and what's Naija's pupose and destiny in this.
Having Metroidvaniaish gameplay the player is not be able to explore everything at the beggining of the game, until specific spells have been learned, in this case they are songs. The first hour can cause frustration for Naija is completly helpless and moving is very limited. Everything will change nevertheless when the first songs are collected. Casting.. I mean singing system is very easy to learn and use - different songs consist 3 or 4 different tones that must be picked in correct order and in real time from the circular menu. The different songs are swiftly sang, which makes it easy to change from normal form into fighting form when needed. In addition of normal and infernous flame throwing fighting form there is also a form that allows jumping higher and reaching areas much above the surface. There is also an fish form which is good in long travels for its speed and player can squeeze through narrowest tunnels which would be impossible in any other form.
Most of the areas are passed automatically during playthrough, but there is some corners in the ocean that hold treasures inside and it's up to player to find or leave them. These trophies are usually leisure items for Naija's home decoration, but they can also be skill boosting armors or artifacts, even new songs!
The world of Aquaria is a beautiful and diverse place. Enviroments change from coral reefs to underground ruins and from the deepest dark abysses to sandy shores beyond surface. When the enviroments change so do the creatures inhabiting them and while some places can be full of harmony and life there also lies some extreme dangers in the deepest caves of the abyss. There is also plenty boss battles that are challenging and well designed, having that classic puzzle element in them.
While it is a shame that there is not specific RPG elements, the cooking system provides some conpensation. During playtrough the different receipes can be collected for making various dishes from many ingredients found from enemies and enviroment. They have many effects like upgrading speed, making attacks stronger, enchancing light radius in dark places or just simply healing, which also happens by interacting with red crystals or collecting blue energy. Some ingredients are harder to find and it is recommended to use rare dishes only when you really need them - in boss fights for example. If one should run low in ingredients it is always possible to grind them by exploring resourceful areas again, but this never happened to me. The game is not one of the most challenging that I have played, but not nearly the easiest either.
In conclusion Aquaria is a real shining pearl in the game ocean of Steam. Excluding the clumsy land controls and lack of RPG features it is really hard to find anything bad about it and it bothers me that this never might get a seaquel which it would deserve. Aquaria really was ahed of its time in both good and bad and while it gathered good reception among critics it did not sell too well in their web store. I really think that if this was released now with better marketing it could be a hit who knows. If you like metrodvaniaish - try this one without hesitation!

While In Alpha, Stonehearth is an amazing game.  Build your  town up from nothing, with your very own sla- workers! Your hearthlings will do what ever you tell them to do. What are you waiting for? Get Stonehearth Now!

As a big fan of games like Minecraft and Civilization I decided to buy Stonehearth even though it is only an Alpha. I am very impressed from playing so far (Alpha v11), yes there are bugs which can be game breaking and there is so much more that needs to be added, but this really has the beginnings of a good game. I've done a couple of play throughs and am getting the hang of managing the little town and it is very addictive. At the moment there is a bit of a lack of things to do at the later stages of the game, mining for minerals has only recently been added and beyond upgrading gear doesn't seem to have much purpose, but I'm sure more will be added.
Of course, it is still in Alpha so there are many issues that can be annoying, the AI of your workers can be poor at times and they can just get stuck doing nothing. I think it would really benefit this game to allow some control over individual workers, or at least allow some prioritization of tasks because at the moment it is a bit frustrating when for example you want a worker to pick something up that he's stood next to but he just doesn't do it.
These bugs aside the game is very promising and I will certainly be following its development closely. If bugs annoy you then I would wait for the retail version. If, like me, you like the look of the game and can't wait, then I don't think you'll be disappointed.

Unlike many people that happen to rave about this game, I cannot in good conscious recommend it to others. Yes, the story is great, yes the idea is quite well made, and the environment is beautiful...but that's about where it ends.
Here's a big thing. You get demerits of sorts for killing people. Rats and the plague spread more if you kill more. Yet...there are only two ways to knock out an enemy. 1 being in VERY limited supply and expensive to procure, the other being inefficient if you're near any shape or form of a group of enemies.
So you get two choices really. Be a murderer with a hard game, or be a cheater. Kill everything in sight or keep on reloading those save files/ running away like a madman.
Add that with the fact that outside the detail of the outfits the actual models of the characters are rather poor unless they are extremely important, and even then it's lackluster in comparison to the beauty of the environment.
All in all, it was a great idea, but the execution wasn't the best. If there were more ways to take out enemy non-lethally...instead of "Here's you sword, gun, explosives, arrows, and everything you need to kill people horribly!" this could actually work its way really high up as a game, but as it is I cannot say I recommend this. In where it does things well there are things that it does horribly too in turn, and those horribly done things glare in contrast to the good. Hopefully they can further improve it for the sequel as it really does have great potential.

If you're looking for a fun game to play then this is the game for you (if you have friends its even better).
The game has tons of character customization but mostly the character customization is just looking like characters from other games or movies even tv shows, you can look like Bill from L4D, Leatherface, Jacket from Hotline Miami and even ricky n morty.
The game has a easy learning curve so if you think that you need to learn some special tricks or anything to survive well...not really, but this game is somewhat punishing on players if you just keep killing the last zamboo  for the rounds do not have a starting delay, they just start instantly.
There is a level system and character upgrade system even weapons and unlockable weapons, however some of the unlockable weapons are meh compared to the other ones but sometimes they can preform just as well as the higher unlockable weapons.
Be warned, this game has...cheese...and by cheese I mean the voice acting, there is only one voice and it's this guy that sounds like he is having a bad day (Houston from payday?) Though it would be nicer if there was a way to edit the voice to something else as I looked in the files and couldn't find a single thing, so you're stuck with a dull boring guy.
The game isn't that hard, it's mainly COD zombies to some extent but it is original in some ways, though the cod aspect is mainly upgrading your weapon from a upgrade machine, using the fridge (Mystery fridge!) Which gives you a random weapon for 300$ rather than the cod amount of 900$ and it does the same thing as the cod zombies box, it teleports if you get the bear, but this one has limited used in the game.
If you're looking to play as a female character mainly because you find it more fun or whatever, sadly this game does not have that but you can look like a female anime character that looks like a maid, I believe it's from the touhou series?
All in all, game is good should buy, but there are a few reasons you should not.
There aren't that many melee weapons, only a katana which you cannot trade out at all, if you pick up the chainsaw you mainly screwed yourself over as it takes up a weapon slot and not the katana slot, there should be more melee weapons like a scythe or even just start players off with bad melee weapons yet you can upgrade your melee weapon or maybe get a random one from the fridge.
The VA is another reason why you shouldn't buy, it's a dumb reason but if you get easily annoyed by some dull voice then you should either mute your sound and play your own music so you don't hear the voice or just well, get used to it.
Too little character customization, you can only customize your head, torso and legs but the head and torso cost credits,  there aren't anyways to add gloves or completely look like a specific character like the touhou character, I'm sure she is ment to be wearing leggings of some sort but since well your character is male and there is very little customization, you can't get the exact look.
Too little weapons, well that's what it feels like to me, once you unlock those powerful weapons by spending credits you're pretty much set if you also get the perk or skill to have a random weapon at the start and by RNG you can get the D.O.M which is mainly the BFG that 1 shots everything except bosses unless upgrades, there should be a ton more weapons to mainly increase chance of not getting the super powerful weapons from the fridge as it makes the game easy.
Too little barricade options, I mainly dislike the barricade style, you simply place a box down and that's about it, you cannot stack them and there isn't that much variety so it gets rather stale with putting up defense, if there were more options like maybe a couch which breaks in segments when it's attacked or maybe like a bookshelf.
Jumppads feel too common, you buy them once for 100$ which allows zombies to use them but you then have to buy them with 10$ each time to use them, it'd be nicer if there were 2 routes, quick and easy route allowing you to take a jumppad or a long route which uses stairs
Unable to play custom maps in MP (From what I've noticed) I have no option to select custom maps to play but I'm sure I can, I haven't tried yet but I will attempt.
Anywho, those are some of the cons of the game, it is still a good game it just needs to be updated and worked on some more to grab the attention of people, as I feel that people bought this game, played it and then forgot about it and just uninstalled having it sit in their library.

TL:DR - Buy for the multiplayer, otherwise buy it at a discount price for singleplayer. This game can get addicting once you are a few waves in and is better with other players.
+ Nice pixel work
+ Addictive
+ Multiplayer
+ Workshop
+ Character customisation
- No explanation of what power-up does what
- Lack of multiplayer rooms
- Music gets annoying after some time
I really like this game, it is addicting yet simple. Singplayer is ok, more fun when you find a bot or two to help you last longer. I figured out what some power-ups do, some are simple to understand but others may take some time to actually click with your mind on what they do.
You can make your character stronger with skill points and even upgrade the guns on their own making the one you prefer even better. Plenty of perks to go along side as well as your own workbench, which is a nice touch for a zombie game such as this.
I enjoy the cameos in the character outfits, such as Bill from L4D2, I just wish the workshop allowed us to make our own heads and torso's to make customisation a bit better but the outfits you can buy and unlock are great enough.
However multiplayer is where this game shines. If anything get the game for the multiplayer.
Multiplayer is where it can get hectic while also having its easy moments depending who is with you. You can use your skills or items you made into multiplayer and so far, I found no users who judge off level, the high levels don't mind level 1 players and so forth. There is a chat box so you can communicate though not sure if voice-chat would make it better, specially when you have more hordes and you will indeed get seperated.
My only issue with multplayer is
- If you join a game already in-play you are left at the start, if they are a few rounds in you may die very soon and they may be too far in the map to get around back to you, I can see this putting players off joining matches. It should really drop them off with the healthiest player IMO
- You get your own money to spend, this is an issue a bit later in maps when other players want someone else to open the doors because each player is saving up for upgrades or the mini-gun. If you have the most cash, they will expect you to fork-out even if you are close to what you was saving for. But I don't see this that often and a skill does help you get cash easier
- At the moment of this review, only 3 rooms were up and around 9 players for multiplayer. I hope more players actually play and get more rooms in multiplayer to make it more enjoyable for others
Otherwise, it is a total blast and is the best way to level up. Buy it and start slaying hordes along side friends, I already did 6 hours alone just today because how easy it was to get lost in multiplayer.

Well, what can I say about this game? First of all, it's a short point and click-adventure with minmal interface and almost no real story development. You're playing Gomo, a Domo-kun-like creature with a zipper bag in its backbone, whose dog gets taken by a mad alien. It demands a trade off, only giving your beloved pet back if you bring him some sort of crystal. That's it and there is not much else to it. You walk from screen to screen, almost always hindered by some problem in your environment that you have to solve. If you played Samorost or similar flash-based games, you know the drill. Click here, click there, see what happens. If nothing happens, try the same thing again, only add this time that one single item you picked up in this screen.
As long as you buy this game to a minimal price (5$ or even lower), you won't feel cheated, but if you want a complete game that keeps you busy for the weekend, then Gomo is a waste of your money here =/

Full review:
Gomo, a point-and-click adventure about a journey to get a best friend back. I have not played a proper point-and-click game in a while, but this was quite a treat.
Gomo is a small game, and I mean that story-wise and resolution-wise. The game does not run at widescreen, which was fairly annoying. I would have liked to see the game running at 1080p. Gomo is like a lot of other point-and-click games. It consists of a variety of primitive puzzles, some being stupidly easy, with some others taking a bit more time. These puzzle elements made the game a bit more enjoyable in a gameplay sense and I enjoyed them.
There's not much else to the game, it is a point-and-click adventure after all. There's a little exploration to it and the game contains no violence. You don't even need to be literate to play the game, it's very simplistic. That's not necessarily a bad thing, it'll just be more appealing to those looking for a nice, short game.
The game conveys a nice story without the use of language. It's quite neat actually. The story is incredibly generic, but the way it is conveyed makes it much more powerful. Gomo is searching for his best friend, who was taken from him. He'll end up going far beyond what players would expect in order to get his best friend back. The game's art style was lovely, as was the music. The music was very atmospheric and immersive, when combined with the backgrounds and art displayed throughout Gomo's adventure.
Overall, Gomo is a short, but nice adventure that appeals to point-and-click fans with little time on their hands. It combines a charming story with great music and art into one small, enjoyable package. I recommend Gomo for any point-and-click fans.

Gomo is a cute, quick adventure game for kids or the young at heart. Older players who want a challenge or a long game are going to be disappointed.
