The concept of the game is interesting, but it's really, really difficult to play. I'll elaborate.
The game consists of two parts mainly.There's the story mode and a sandbox mode (which also offers an imbedded challenge mode). Now, most players will have jumped in quite early through Early Access. I did acquire the game in Early Access as well, but haven't played it much as I awaited the Story. This has been released recently.
The setting of the game is a wintery Canada. Lots of snow, lots of forest. You have to rely on your wits, luck and resources to survive. In the story, you lose track of your ex-wife and are set on a path to find her again. Stranded without resources, your first days are spent learning the basics of the game: gathering supplies, keeping warm, learning how to craft basics such as (potable) water and edible food.
When you've somewhat recovered from the crash you start your search. It is then that you will meet the wildlife. Some of it's rather unfriendly, such as wolves. The wolves don't roam in packs, usually in pairs. The wolves in the story are quite aggressive. Possibly due to lack of food, I'm not sure. In the sandbox mode you can play the game at an easier level.
Surviving an attack is not quite likely. You lack weapons whatsoever and the ability to climb anything. You're hard put to either run or keep away if you still can. Obviously, the wolves may be between you and a certain point, such as a safe place to keep warm and prepare some food or water.
I have yet to find a weapon to combat wolves. The only thing that somewhat works is a torch, but obviously these burn out quickly. You'll have to create a fire first, by means of the wood you've collected. So make sure to pickup supplies on the way.
I've spent well over 10 hours to finally get a grasp of the basics. Less regular tasks, such as opening safes or climbing ropes still lead me online resources to find out what it is I have to do.
So, how to evaluate this game? I'll stick to my first advice and won't recommend this game. The strong points of the game are it's unique setting, the atmosphere and the anxiety you experience when your life is in danger (due to sleep deprivation, hunger, thirst, wildlife, and so on). But the weak points outweigh the strong points, as this game is very hard to master and sometimes doesn't make sense. It takes perseverance in a player to really understand the mechanics, make the right choices and keep on doing so.
The story thus far is interesting enough to keep me at the game. But the sandbox is not for me. Surviving for the heck of it doesn't make any sense to me. I like games where I have to achieve a certain goal. Staying alive doesn't cut it. Just suppose you'd find yourself stranded in Canada with the certainty that you won't find anyone still alive. What would you do then? I think I'd try to go south to escape the snow and find a more hospitable environment. Or perhaps have a player survive for X days while help is coming to a certain spot? These are simple goals that would give the sandbox a raison d'etre, without the need for the studio to have to invest heavily to create additional content.
There's a large community supporting this game and you may find a large number of resources online with tips on how to play. I think that most of these people are veterans who played the sandbox a lot and probably learned to play the game by growing into it by playing all the releases that were published in Early Access.

The storymode (Wintermute) took every single crap part of the sandbox mode and slaps you in the face with it.  Way too scarce supplies? Wolf torpedoes that one-shot you unless you're at full health? Breaking my ankle on the slightest incline? Horrible instructions or intuitiveness of gameplay & control scheme? All combine with the lamest, most cliche characters and storyline imaginable to make the game simply frustrating and BORING.
Guess what saps all my interest when playing a game: Getting jammed up by a crap save point and playing how many 10s of seconds before the wolf torpedo executes me again on the way to the next car OR starting over AGAIN.  After reaching the 10 day mark a couple years ago, I'd essentially reached the end of my interest in simply surviving in a Lighthouse or shack with no other goal.  I checked back in last year to see nothing had changed to make me care.  Now, story mode is released - the one thing I was hoping would give me an objective like "reach the lighthouse and light it to signal someone" or "get to the bunker protecting other survivors" or "gather survivors and build an outpost to survive X days" or "clear the wolfpack that's hunting you".  Instead, I get "Follow this stale, boring railroad story with carefully portioned out supplies that are never enough to do anything with, die to wolves a hundred times, and maybe complete chapter 2 before you kill yourself in real life".
Really? The Telltale piecemeal Chapter crap?  And after all this time you've only got 2 lousy, poorly structured and written broken tutorial missions with hideous character design.  Played 2 hours of Wintermute and became angry and bored, switched to sandbox for half an hour, became just bored and quit.  I can't imagine EVER wanting to run the wolftorpedo gauntlet again in the same area with the same crap and the same stupid story.
TL;DR - The updated console inspired control scheme is awkward garbage.  Story mode is boring, frustrating garbage.  Sandbox survival mode is essentially the same, and one of the better examples of that increasingly tired genre, so if you're into that, you're best served just going there.

This is an excellent "Metrodvania" style game.  Nearly everything is underwater, and you have a great deal of natural mobility, so the genre's gating and backtracking works by learning different form (to swim against currents, turn into a fish to swim through small passages, grow plants that open certain passages or block off enemy pathing).
There are a number of secrets, challenges, optional bosses, and like any good Metroidvania, ways to skip/bypass/sequence-break the required forms if you have the skill to do so.  The overall challenge of the game isn't too difficult, but there are enough optional bosses and secrets to keep interested.  Most of the bosses have a bit of a puzzle mechanic to figure out how to make them vulnerable, if you get stuck, there is a good guide on
.
The music is very well done, and I found it getting stuck in my head quite a bit.  The voice acting is also well done.
Your loot is either cooking ingredients to make consumables; or decorations for your home.  Cooking isn't too difficult, but it can be time consuming to make a number of items in the base game (cooking is streamlined in the open source engine).  While you have no limit on the types of consumable items you can hold, you can only hold a maximum of 8 of each individual item.  If you already have 8 pieces of fish meat, any additional you pick up is wasted.  Inventory management can sometimes get in the way of gameplay.
For controls, I tried a Steam controller, the recommended mouse-only movement, and the keyboard/mouse combo.  For me, the keyboard and mouse combo worked best.  I use WASD for general movement, mouse jumping only for the out of water segments, and the 1-9 and 0 shortcuts for the forms/songs.  I mainly used the mouse to fire and aim.
I had very few bugs or gameplay issues at all.  If you do run into any, on the developer's forum is an open source updated version of the engine.  It supports modding better, and does fix several bugs I did not encounter in my  playthrough.  The open source engine (OSE) does change how your character moves a bit, mainly giving movement a bit of momentum.  You won't stop immediately, but drift a bit after releasing the button.  In addition, the OSE does not interface with Steam, so it won't unlock achievements or report your time played.

The game currently has no resolution options and is locked to 720p and users are reporting that the game is unplayable unless fps locked via vsync, it is expected since the game is early access but still something to keep in mind. Now onto the gameplay.
If you are familar with Fire Pro wrestling games and adore them like I do get it.
However if you are coming from something else like the WWE 2K series then please read the rest of this review.
Fire Pro Wrestling games grew to popularity due to its in-depth wrestling system. Due to this depth, the game is much more difficult than WWE games. For Instance, grappling is done by timing your button press too late you fail, too early you fail, press a button more than once you fail. This game is not forgiving but once you get the hang of it becomes a rewarding experience. This cannot be stated more, this is a simulation wrestling game so basic wrestling concepts apply here. If you go out of the gates trying to hit heavy moves like a wrestlers finisher you will always be reversed. This game is in-depth. If all of the above has turned you off then I can't recommend this game for you. However if you decide that you want to put in the time to learn the system you should also understand that this game does not have any licsensing with any pro wrestling companies so there are no real wrestlers in the default roster. However Fire Pro Wrestling has an amazing robust creation suite for wrestlers, that even allows for you to edit the cpu behavior of your wrestler. To add on to this if you are not a creative person or dedicated enough to create a wrestler you want(like me) then you can hit up the workshop in which users upload their created wrestlers and created referees(Look at it right now to see if a wrestler you want has been created). Finally this game is in Early Access, so there are alot of features that are missing or that are barebones such as mission mode. However, the devs are super responsive to the community and are already taking notes on complants and wanted features. Currently the only modes are Mission(Tutorial with added objectives), Exhibtion, League, Tournament, Battle Royale, and Online. If you feel that are not enough things to do, then I would recommend you wait for the game to come out of early access and see if it appeals to you later with the final version released.

No major changes in gameplay has appeared over time, its been pretty much the same from start;
#1 Harvest resources
#2 Build a house
#3 Meet requirements for a new villager to join your town
#4 Kill occasional hostile mobs attacking your town.
#5 Repeat
After 200 hours of this i got a bit bored you could say. My gameplay mostly went with building a massive town and nitpicking it to look nice and neat untill i reached the 25-30 villager "limit" where performance takes a dive and game goes matrix mode. It became tiresome.
Dissapointing is the word to describe the game for anyone whos been with the game at start. Wishing for some new features besides a new type of chair or goblin to find in the game.

maybe some friendly human NPC's that you could engage with in quest/trade/war.

Also, tough it may not mean much for you but for me as a city builder gamer i would enjoy some bigger variety in terrain, map, etc. You are only given a tiny square with either yellow/gray blocks or green/gray blocks to settle and build on. The water has no feature besides being a obstacle in the game; no fishing, boats or anything.  I find map layout/design overall to be shallow at its current stage considering how much time and oppertunities they've had to add some new changes.

This is a fun little dorflike city builder. As with most of these, you start with 7 people (In this game, they're "hearthlings") and from there, you need to set up for food, shelter, resources, and defense. So far so same, right? The two largest twists on this one are how you can set up the housing (completely planning out a building, instead of either a hole in the wall or a prefab structure), and the animation style.
I'm trying to find a good descriptor for the animation style, and I keep coming back to "cute". It's not the word I'm looking for, but it does indeed match, in my opinion. I feel emotionally vested in these hearthlings in a way I don't really get from the likes of Gnomoria, Towns, or even Dwarf Fortress, and I honestly feel it's the way they're animated. When goblins are charging into your town and you see your farmers scatter from their fields and cower, it makes you want to protect them. Project Zomboid is a sandbox zombie survival game where you will be scavenging for food and resources (or making your own), exploring abandoned buildings, crafting all kinds of items and basically just doing all you can to survive. The beauty of this game is in how in-depth everything is, from placing sheets on windows to restrict the undead's vision inside to making bandages out of clothing. The game also gives you a lot of freedom in how you wish to play the game with extensive options for your sandbox world.
Although the game is pretty good, I just can't recommend it. After so many years of development it still hasn't fulfilled its major promises, such as vehicles and NPCs. Many bugs also haven't been squashed yet, and there hasn't been an update in a long time. When the game finally gets updated I'll likely recommend it, but as of right now the game doesn't seem to be moving forward.

Note: My character was a former female Nurse, my friend being a male former Park Ranger.
Me and my mate tidied up our little home into an easy-to-organize containment zone.
Everything had it's place, and to think only days ago we had whiskey in the bathroom and bedsheets in the living room. Now, they sit on windows, and the whiskey sits with the meds. No real action, just setting up shop and preparing for Hell to come knocking.
We wake up and decide to scavenge our neighborhood. We don't make it far before things go bad almost instantly. Some see us, but we don't see them, and I get scratched on the side of my head as I pulled back to swing with my golf club.
Friend tried creating diversions, just ended up with wounds and barely making it out alive and back home without attention. Exhausted, we feast and sit down to rest and read, passing the sudden rainstorm by.
We awaken suddenly to a burst-fire rifle firing outside, the amplitude causng stress to take over us both.
We covered our windows and locked our doors, cowering in the bathroom as a last resort. We stayed for a while, finding solace in talking and passing the time.
Later, we went out looking for more supplies in our neighborhood again, this time with more success. We come to an off-path with a store, but it is filled with them. We instantly turn around, dashing through houses and zig-zagging our way across the fields and into the woods as the sun set. We wandered around in the dark for a while before my sense of direction kicked in, and got us back home. Tired, we both fell asleep almost right away.
We awake yet again to gunfire and dogs barking. We set up again, but not as long this time, me pointing out that we needed construction equipment to repair our weapons for a big trip we were planning to make, to escape from all of this.
We roll out once more into our destroyed community, passing by a house we set up in a night before. Outside the house in question, we encountered a large group of those things. Rather ignorantly, we took them on.
We both sustained injuries and vaulted through many hastily broken windows. We come home, barely making it. My hurriedly applied bandages dirtied up quickly. He questions my situation as he only suffered some scratches from glass and some bruises. I choked on my words, heart pounding as I was barely able to even bring myself to communicate. Inquiring to me, he comes up and notices the bandage I had applied to my neck, and how bloody it's gotten. I didn't stop him as he revealed my injury.
A deep bite wound, pus already forming and excreting from the edges.
He could barely hold himself together, a faint 'oh' wisping away from his lips as he put the bandage back on softly. I almost began crying as I fell anxious to what would happen.
Is it over? I pondered my choices as I constantly changed bandages and sat around the kitchen, eating and feeling worse by the second, mentally and physically.
My energy has been seeping away for a while, until the sun cast it's orange goodbyes across the sky. I state that I'm going to bed, and leave for the upstairs, but not before thanking him for what he'd done to save both of our hides. Or... at least how he tried.
I wake up, barely able to move, my heart beating faintly in my chest, my head pounding away, blurring my vision. I struggled to stumble upward out of bed and open the door into the hallway. He comes out of the opposite bedroom and asks me how I felt.
As if by cue, I begin to fall faint, world fading to oblivion as I utter whispers of disdain and struggle, crashing to the floor, blood spewing from my eyes, ears, nose, and mouth from hemorrhage. What was once me, seeped away, blowing into spiritual wind, gone forever. Turned away, my friend heard the thud of my body, and turned to look at my departure. He just stared in disbelief.
I couldn't tell what out of. Sadness? Fear? Guilt? All? None? It didn't matter. Realizing what was going to happen, he began getting his golf club out of his bag, but that's when it got back up.
What was once me turned around, muttering incomprehensible gibberish, and yelling in triumph as they lunged towards him. He didn't utter a word as he stopped it's advances, looking into the thing's eyes and trying to search for me.
But I was gone.
He reared back and slammed the golf club into it, yelling obscenities and frustration with each and every swing until he hit the floor where it's head was. I would never know what became of him, but I do know that there were many means of a way out in our bathrooms. I shudder to think what was once him now walks those same halls we used to call home, even though my friend has been long gone.

I played this for a while in early access after I bought it, not much. I came back for the addition of the story mode and I am really enjoying it so far. Im finding the story interesting and I want to know more about the world and the characters. I like the difficulty of surviving the cold and the animals and the game has really improved since early access. Everything feels like it fits together well. It runs smoothly for me and looks great on max settings although I have encountered a few bugs (an invisible wolf that never attacks, a glitchy bit of scenery (last one just got patched out)).
I don't understand most the of the complaints about wolves, I only died to them once in story mode, and then learned to avoid them. I definitely recommend headphones so you can hear them early and know where they are, and also knowing the risks before you go outside.  If you're low on health don't go out. Heal yourself and rest for a day, then go out. Always have healing supplies. If you don't have any then they are what you should be looking for before you carry on with the story. Always have a bandage and disinfectant.
The Long Dark is about the challenge of getting from one place to the other and surviving while you do it. It is slow paced because things take a realistic amount of time to do. If you sharpen your axe it will take you ten minutes to do that. If you stitch your clothes it might take half an hour, so it's about prioritising what you need to survive, and it isn't easy. The first episode has an NPC that gives you missions that force you to get better at planning and surviving.
If you like a challenge and don't need explosions to keep you entertained then I would definitely recommend this game. It is slow, methodical, and can be really difficult, but the joy of finding a cave with wood for a fire when you're a few minutes developing hypothermia makes it all worthwhile.

You play Syndicate as Jacob and Evie Frye, a brother-sister assassin team who are both well-written and skillfully voiced. Jacob, while predictably cocky and sarcastic is still funny and likable, and Evie, the more serious of the two, is herself prone to moments of charm and levity. They're also superbly animated. It's not often a facial expression in a game will elicit an intended laugh, but it did here more than once. I liked both characters a lot, especially in the scenes they shared with one another.
The twins are often at odds with each other, too: Jacob wants to loosen the stranglehold of the Blighter gang and kill Templars, and Evie wants to hunt for a 'Piece of Eden,' a magical doohickey that grants eternal something-or-other. For most of the game, they're basically interchangeable to play: save for a few high-level abilities they have identical skill trees. Only near the end of the game do they really begin to feel distinct. Jacob is more of a brawler, Evie more focused on stealth, and crafting or unlocking gear like sneakier outfits or deadlier weapons can complement their respective toolkits. You can switch between them whenever you want in the open world, while story missions can only be performed by one or the other.
:: FINAL VERDICT :: 66%

Second, this is yet another japanese title that does not automatically add itself to the Nvidia control panel, so that has be done manually.
Third, no resolution options, like at all.  The game runs at 720p.  You have to run regedit and edit a couple things in order to change it.

If Ecco the Dolphin starred a frog-woman and had a more sane difficulty level: Aquaria.
This game has a lot of heart and soul. The demo, in which pretty much nothing happened, was misleading. Disregard my Steam hours. I 100%'d the game before I even had a Steam account.
The player controls "Naija", a female humanoid aquatic creature who can sing to use abilities and change forms. As she explores more of the world, she learns to question who she is and begins to see the darkness and light around her, and within her. The story is told rather subtly. Words are few, but environments and events connect together to weave something rather bittersweet. I felt like I might have been seeing through the game straight to the developer's emotional turmoil as I followed Naija's bumpy road of self-discovery.
Aquaria is a Metroidvania Shoot 'Em Up. The thought "this is a Shoot 'Em Up" never occurred to me, perhaps because enemies and objectives are not fed to you- you take the world at your own pace and kill what you want to kill, when you want to kill it. And this is how I like it. Many of the "enemies" behave more like "territorial co-inhabitants" than traditional enemies. I saw most of them, not as a wall of challenges to get through, but as part of the living world around me.
One of the strengths of the game is the sheer variety of mechanics, from the abilities you discover, to the different enemy attack styles, to the varied designs and challenges of each region. Along with exploration and combat, you'll collect ingredients from containers and enemies. Cooking these ingredients into the right foods for recovery and buffs can really turn the tide of battle in some boss fights.
The core mechanic of the game is Naija's ability to change forms or perform special actions by "singing" some sequence of the eight provided notes. Aside from its gameplay purpose, I found myself improvising harmonies along with the background music far too often.
Difficulty in some places is a bit high, but never impossible. Sometimes you may just need to explore a bit more to gain a new ability, some food buff, or a larger health pool. Difficulty in some areas arises purely from tricky mobility. Swimming in tight spaces, boosting off of walls properly, and the few platforming areas can be frustrating and seem to rely too heavily on lucky timing (and advance knowledge) at times, but successfully pulling these off feels very satisfying.
The open world can be tedious to backtrack across, but shortcuts do open up eventually.
Music, sound effects, and visuals are very well matched in this game, enhancing the bright underwater feeling, or, in other cases, very dark feeling.
The music was composed by Alec Holowka, one of the two developers. The game includes one vocal track at the end, and the separate OST has another vocal track that I would encourage you to check out if you become as enchanted by this game as I have been.
The graphics are lush and beautiful. A lot of the motion in the game is simplistic but not abrasively so.
There's also a bit of voice acting for the main character and it's very well done.
The game is peppered with optional unstated challenges and secrets to discover such as minibosses, interactable background objects, and a difficult-to-catch creature that might drop an exclusive cooking ingredient. Collectible items hidden around the world can be sent to your home area. There are even three outfits and four pets (that are not just cosmetic!) to unlock.
If you try to get everything in the game (and don't straight up follow a walkthrough the whole way) I think you'll be playing for over 20 hours, though I can't say for sure. (For the extra stuff, you may need a walkthrough eventually though- some of the secrets are quite well hidden, some of the recipes not very obvious.)
I feel like this is the "replay it a few years later to rediscover everything" sort of game, but I've known people to play the game several times in a row simply because they enjoy it that much.
There's a level editor and LUA scripting support. It's not terribly user friendly though. You might be able to find some decent levels made by other players.
Aquaria brought me to a dangerous underwater wonderland that I will not soon forget.
The game's greatest asset is the environment and sense of discovery that it creates. However, combat is not lacking either. The biggest con is that there is no sequel. The second biggest con is the finicky platforming in some areas.
I give it an 8.8/10, a must-play if you are into Metroidvanias or if you are intrigued.

It's Fire Pro Wrestling on PC.
Barely any non-wrestling fans will care about this game. Huge wrestling fans will probably love it. If you're already a Fire Pro fan you already know you want this so I won't have to sell you on it. This review is intended for everyone else.
A: Customization and gameplay.
FPW only comes with a couple dozen fictional characters but that's where the Steam workshop support comes in. You're going to be able to download any of the big-name wrestlers (and lots of lesser-known ones) from all kinds of different promotions. If you come from WWE 2k you're probably thinking that's not a huge selling point because you know that even the best created wrestlers in WWE 2k usually look they they don't fit in perfectly compared to the wrestlers already in the game. That's not the case with Fire Pro. The best created wrestlers look just as good and fit in just as well as the wrestlers already in the game. With a fanbase as dedicated as Fire Pro's, in theory you can end up with a roster of 1000 wrestlers that mostly look and play really well (there's no limit to the amount of wrestlers you can download). Then throw a bunch of them in some mega league and see what happens.
Then there's the actual wrestling which may feel like a gigantic breath of fresh air compared to the stale, joyless gameplay found in the WWE 2k series. The basic jist of it is that you have to start out small with minor strikes and whatnot and work your way up before you can start doing your big moves like powerbombs and piledrivers. If you try doing one of your biggest moves early on it probably won't be successful and your opponent will counter it. It's even fun to watch cpu vs cpu matches because every move feels
.
I didn't mean for this review to just bash 2k left and right but in many ways this game is the anti-WWE 2k. 2k has all kinds of bells and whistles, career modes, universe modes, etc. Fire Pro doesn't have that, it's very straightforward. You can play some mission modes but the bulk of your gameplay will be in exhibition, tournament, or league (think G1 climax) matches. So if you want to get a game for the actual gameplay, get this. If you want to get a game with career modes, this in all honesty might not be for you. It's a niche game for sure but it does what it does very well.

This is the game that truly opened my interest towards the rpg element to a lot of games such as D&D.  From someone who came from Skyrim with the hit and slash tactics, adapting to strategic combat and so on that Dragon Age has to offer was somewhat awkward at first but I quickly got used to it. I've been looking for games that really has consequences to every action that you make and I found it in dragon age. If you're new to dragon age and absolutely know nothing about it, from my experiences, I suggest playing it blind and learn as you go. It gives you the thrill of not knowing what will happen next or having to regret the decision you made.
On the topic combat and all the different classes and stuff, I'm still learning as I go but don't try to make your first playthrough as a perfect one. There's no perfect way to play the game! Lots of choices to make with a lot of different outcomes, it's amazing. The game makes you feel like you're truly in the game itself. NPC's and party members seem real enough that you grow attached to a lot of them, if not, at least understand why they do what they do. Really has a lot of replayability from what I've seen so far which is great.
Story!  Almost everyone has something to tell you. I'm always intrigued of what's going on in the lives of the people in the game because it's different from our modern world. It's pretty catchy if you're into fantasy and medieval type of things and I enjoy knowing more of the lore as I proceed. I also like the fact that your followers are not hollow 3D models because they have a backstory to telll and I lappreciate the fact that they react to a lot of things that I do whether I hate it or not. Their contradicting personalities between one another and my own views affects my choices a lot but that just adds in with the welcomed challenge.
Soundtrack is pretty good. It's making me feel the mood that it plays during a certain event or level that I'm in and the ambiance that I hear whenever I'm in cities are pretty immersive! Graphics fits in with the gameplay pretty well and I've yet to see a bug or a glitch and I hope I never do haha. (Maybe it doesn't even have any for all I know)
But the largest tip I could ever give to someone who is willing to play this during their first time, save often and maybe try playing on normal. You will literally die no matter how good you are so it's just a 'just to be sure' thing and I think that playing this game on easy would loose its spark. I like challenging myself and giving in, and changing the difficulty to easy is not an option to me. Thats how I found out that there's the 'Pause' button for a reason!
I still have a lot of time to waste on this game to fully experience it and I'm willing to do just that.

PLEASE READ THIS!!!!
Crashing and Mods:
Okay, so I looked through all of the reviews about this game and noticed something that they all had in common, complaints about crashing and the game play. When I initially got this game it was for the Xbox 360 (no modding possible that i know of) back when it first came out (2009) It was fun and intriguing. The mods have made this game much more interactive and fun in my opinion, plus playing this game on the computer is much easier seeing as i use the computer more than my xbox. I run about 25 mods together and yes the game crashes from time to time, because these mods change the core file of the game, completely alturing the game. These mods were not made by 'experts' nor the creaters of the game. So if you are planning on adding multiple mods do the research to make sure they are fully compatible. If they aren't fully compatible and requires you to change the core game even more, then expect crashes. If you are wanting to play this game with no mods no worries.
Game play:
This game came out in 2009. That may not seem like a long time, but with video games it is. This game is no PacMan, Sonic, or Mario Bros. However this game is one of this first of its kind. Its a role playing game, where you get to create your main character. The fighting isn't the best, however what do you expect from a slightly older game? If an enemy goes to swing and you get out of the way, it'll still effect you and still damage you. The difficulties are increasingly harder from easy to normal, but after that it steadly gets harder in the game play.
I would recamend this game, I have only played a 100 or so hours on the computer but with the xbox I have played 100s of hours. It is over all a fun game. You have a choice of being a dou*he or being really nice; you can side with elves or wolves. There are so many decisions to be made in this game that can't be made in other games. It is a role playing game that is one player so you don't have others to contend with.
One of my favorite RPGs.  It would be nice if steam had the rest of the series avalible...hint hint...

The vast array of diverse options in terms of classes to pick from is amazing. And even within those classes for the Hunters, each class has a up to 5 unique characters with abilities unique for that character and class combination, making the different team combinations a very fluid and unque experience. Mind you, there are some combinations that are rather obviously better than others for certain situations. Bucket's Support ability to lay down turrets for example is amazing for defense games, but no so great for hunting.
All that aside, I still won't be buying the game, because all those great aspects of the game I just described like the diverse roster and combinations of classes are not readily available in the full game. They've been sectioned off as separately paid content. Mind you, I'm still recommending this game because it is still an all around solid game. But I'm certainly not going to pay $80 full price to condone the marketing practice of splitting content that should have came with a game to begin with.

So I decided to play Evolve for the free weekend and was genuinely impressed. The game seems to be at least trying to extend its playability with different gamemodes (although monster vs. monster is still something I hope to see added).
Most players may just have to enjoy the single player component, mostly because the online player base is far and few in-between. But for the most part, I thought it was a fun game with a variety of characters and strategies to work out as you either hide and farm your way to a stage 3, or put all your points in an ability and try to duke it out as a stage 1.
But then I realized the horrifying truth.
DLC. And not a DLC that's free either.
What seemed like a fun game with a variety of monsters and hunters turned into a rather dumb game that not only forces players to play in one niche, but expects those players to pay for it too.
Considering how small the fan base is, I'm not impressed that you have to buy characters now. Honestly, it's usually games like these that I tend to stray away from, especially since this game isn't F2P.
So with that in mind, I do not recommend this game.
-Most of the Monsters you get in the free weekend will not be available when you buy the game.
-Hunters like Jack and Lennox will not be available till you buy their DLC
-I'm fairly sure most of the monsters you play as will not be available until you finish grinding with one monster you may not even like.
-A single season pass will not get you everything either.
For a game based on adaption, Evolve really sucks at well...evolving. The developers have no idea how to adapt to a player fan base and prefer to trick players into buying their base game and then spend an extra 20 dollars on DLC.
That is absurd in my opinion. The reviews that say this game isn't worth it ring true. The game itself might be fun, but the DLC and the future of this game's survivalibilty are at an all time low and teetering on the edge. It's sad to think a good game like this could be ruined by its creators, but its definetly there.
So for those of you thinking of buying, Evolve, do not let this free weekend deceive you. I hope people check the recent reviews because they should know what they're buying into.
I will wait for Evolve to lower its price or for the developers to get a better grip on what kind of community they're dealing with. I honestly think Evolve has potential for much longer playability, but until the developers start releasing free DLC or make the game F2P, don't buy it.

Wow...I think I'm in love, with the series, again. Ok, I admit that I was never "out of love" with the series at all, but there were definitely some games in the franchise that were way better than others. I tend to see the positives, much more than the negatives, unless those negatives far overshadow the others.
And with Syndicate, that's just not the case. Likeable player characters, likeable NPCs finally, as well as a decent story make this one of my favorites since the AC2, Brotherhood, and Revelations trio that I judge all AC games against. Yeah, I thought those were the best 3, but I still like the rest of the franchise as well. Even Unity, which I got well after all the dust had settled and was able to play pretty much trouble-free except for some minor inconsequential issues.
Syndicate makes me love the series again, though, like I did back when the best ones came out. Even though Syndicate has dumbed down a lot of the combat, it's still fun and exciting to undertake, rather than dread it, and even the finishing moves are kinda cool, although a tad repetitious after awhile.
It's a fun game, feels like Assassin's Creed again, and I just love the history and ambiance that I can just immerse myself into. I love reading all the history, and like AC2, Brotherhood, and Revelations, I'm intrigued enough to start researching into the history on my own to read more about it. I've always loved reading about other time periods, and AC: Syndicate is pretty amazing.
Music is great, graphics look amazing, the character detail is phenomenal, and the architecture is really cool to climb on and sightsee from. Unless I just haven't come across them in the game, I do miss the crimescene investigation mechanic from AC: Unity that was a lot of fun. What little investigation is to be done in Syndicate is just a follow-the-dots type (dumbed-down) process that leaves a lot to be desired.

Recommended. Everything in this game is much simpler than previous assassin's creed titles, for better or worse. Well, everything except combat, that is. This is an uncharacteristically awesome port, a rather nice game on its own, and a great addition to what is frankly becoming a stale and dying franchise. If you've got money to blow, go for it.
Assassin's Creed Unity is a refreshing title. For better or worse, it strays far from the "tried and true" Assassin's Creed formulae in basically every conceivable way. Everything from parkour to navigation, stealth to combat, assassinations to spreading influence across the city to just wasting time with side activities--hell, even the story is far away from what we're used to.
You actually have a sneak button in this game. While sneaking, you're harder to see, get detected much slower, and move slightly faster. Additionally however, you can't blend into crowds like you could if you were standing up. You also have a few new tricks in your aresenal... You can now sneak up on people to knock them out as opposed to killing them, and you can kidnap them, in order to use them as meatshields and to avoid detection, and you can now whistle at guards to lure them to your current location. The stealth system is otherwise more or less unchanged; the AI is still♥♥♥♥♥♥ and most of your stealth missions still boil down to infiltrating location X and killing Templar Y. Not sure what else you'd expect from a game called "ASSASSIN'S CREED" though, in all honesty.
The game also features a different combat system, as well. Like in Assassin's Creed Brotherhood, there are now a whole host of different weapon types--the difference is however, this time around you'll actually have a reason to use them! Your weapon choices include kukris, brass knuckles, and sword canes. Brass knuckles have a lot of stunning power, and keep enemies off of you for longer, kukris kill enemies much quicker than the other weapon types, and sword canes are more or less somewhere in the middle. Unlike previous games, you can no longer switch to just fighting with your bare hands or with your hidden blade in the middle of battle. Instead, your hidden blade only peeks out when the next killmove decides it should. You can also chain your other weapons into your combos more easily now. It feels like they tried to emulate the Arkham games' freeflow combat system... With "meh" results.
By far the most drastic change is the parkour system. Parkour boils down to three buttons now: The "Free Run" mode button, which you hold down to start free running, and then two buttons to either attempt to run up to HIGHER terrain or drop down to LOWER terrain. Just holding down the free run button will cause your character to try to run on an even plane. It feels much simpler than previous games... I'm not a fan of it, but it works MUCH more reliably than previous games, I have to give it that much. It's much more difficult to accidentally run off of a building, or go up a chimney you were trying to run around, or run face-first into a wall you want to climb...
Another big change to the parkour system is the addition of the rope launcher. Once again, it feels like they were trying to emulate the Arkham games, with "meh" results. The rope launcher allows you to grapple up onto ledges from the ground without having to climb up the wall, and it also allows you to create ziplines between ledges, which you can drop off of to assassinate guards and goons. It's a rather temperamental little contraption however, and it can be excessively difficult to get the damn thing to shoot at the ledge you actually want to go to. Thankfully however, it's something you can get through most of the game without even using. It'll save you time, but you can usually climb without it, not withstanding some rather tall vantage points and other cliffs.
The storymode is also very different. We actually have likeable protagonists! Not just one, but TWO! Yes! TWO characters! AND there are MUCH fewer missions with instant failure states. It's like getting a cupcake, AND getting a cherry on top. The game also focuses much more on the "memory exploration" side of things and less on the "real world" side of things. You now only get a couple 2 or 3 minute cutscenes between memory sequences every now and then, chronicling the activities of the Brotherhood in the outside world.
Back on the two character thing... You actually get to play as both Jacob AND Evie Frye, twin assassins. You can freely switch between the two of them, and each has their own preferences. Jacob prefers to charge into the situation and murder everything that twitches, while Evie prefers the "Classic" subtle approach. Each character also has a few missions exlusive to them. Despite their specializations, they're still both able to beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of people and sneak around effectively, so they're both worth playing, regardless of your preferences. They're also both really likeable characters, so that's a bonus.
In conclusion... The game is good. The PC port is great. UPlay integration won't make you want to rip your balls off this time around. If you need a new stealth game, or you need to renew your faith in the franchise, this is worth picking up.

I've never thought i'd have to give this game a negative review and it's mostly related to Wintermute.  Survival mode is amazing, after all these years of slow progression, experimentation and feedback it offers us fun and challenging gameplay. Yes, UI and several gameplay mechanics have some issues but it doesn't ruin your experience. It is a sandbox that both developers and community should really be proud of. And i am sure that so many new features and adventures for us are there in the future.
But the story mode  - it is a disappointment. It has such a huge disconnect with fun and understanding of how narrative works. I've expected the story about brutal survival in frozen wastelands that change the nature of our character due to the losses he suffers and hard decisions he has to make in order to survive. But this story treats you like a child shouting "You must do what other people tell you to do!" You are playing not as a survivor but as a stupid soulless courier for these npcs with their tedious tasks and boring stories we've heard for a million of times in previous games or films. For new players it would be ok, i guess - some sort of tutorial before the sandbox mode. But this story has nothing to offer to people who have already played this before. There is no emotion, no story, no even survival here. I do realize i don't have to play wintermute if i don't like it. I just want to hope that devs would manage to make the story more comprehended in next episodes, because they sill have time for this and this game deserves so much better.

Amazing game. Beautiful artwork, great world design and detail, wonderful music and sounds. Hinterland Studios have really shown that they know how to make a game.
Survival mode is one of the strongest experiences you'll get out of a survival game. Its simple in design, but quickly and effectively immerses you into the world. You really become attached to your investment and feel like you are your character.
Story mode is new and needs some polishing with glitches and quests, sure, but it follows the creators' approach of letting the world speak for itself and having your character and you become a part of the experience of exploration.
I feel that the best part about this game is that it gives impactful memories of your experiences playing it. I remember the first time I encountered a bear. I was out in a fishing hut at night and heard a strange sound. I left the small building looked around, only to find that to my right there was this huge shadow charging at me. Needless to say that fishing hut became my home for the evening. Every bear encounter past that is still remembered so vividly, from making a stealthy kill with a bow and arrow, to nearly being mauled to death going up a hill and finding one of those furry brutes on the other side. Along with being able to remember my excitement the first time I found a rifle, the adrenaline rush of climbing to the highest, coldest peak in the game, and the joy of figuring out which building should be my base and setting them all up for each area, to name a few.
This is the type of game that has shown that it only continues to get better and improved upon, making it a great investment if you're looking for a survival game to add to your collection.

I loved the hell out of the sandbox, but this story mode is not making me care to play it more. It's a terrible introduction to the game. The whole point of the game was to throw you in the water and you sink or swim. You survived or died. The sandbox feels intense because you KNOW you will die, but you don't know when it will happen. Eventually your supplies will run out, you'll get caught in a storm, you'll run across two wolves and be out of ammo or decoy meat, something will happen to end it. One day you'll be fine, have a great store of supplies and food built up, medicine in reserve, and then on a typical outing to collect your rabbit traps or to gather wood, you'll have to stare down a bear or a wolf, your gun will miss, your clothes will be ruined, you'll bleed out, and you're dead. That creates such a deep tension to the game. It doesn't hold your hand. The story mode is not that experience. And considering many of us have been already playing it for years, for the early alpha players who have basically mastered the game, to force us to play some half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tutorial disguised as a game is such a let down. We waited for this?
Edit: Played it some more. I can see how someone who never played the sandbox before could get a lot from it. It does still have intensity. But the problem for "veteran" players is its like playing the game on hard for 100 hours, then switching to easy mode. Hard to find it that stimulating. Though I will admit it does still have a lot to offer, especially if you haven't played for awhile. I like a lot of the new changes since I played last. Nice exploratory elements. Good tweaks to the inventory systems, etc. Fighting wolves is still as confusing and unfair as ever. And the caloric requirements are still laughable, i.e. breaking apart a branch into 3 sticks takes 10 minutes and 40 some calories. And to survive you need a steady diet of one deer a day if you do anything. I get that the game wants to push you to survive, but sometimes I'd like to focus on exploring more than keeping a constant supply of animal corpses to fuel my outings. It's hard enough surviving against the wolves.
The new storyline is pretty generic and boring. Two Canadians post divorce having melodramatic conversations. "This isn't ABOOT the weather, is it?"
All of that said, the game is ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. You can forgive it all its faults. It's something truly different, and definately worth a look. It's worth it for the sandbox alone.

Pros:
+ Good retro graphics and sound
+ Easy to learn and use controls
+ The combination of RPG/Arcade/Simulation, (good karate fighter lifestyle simulation, too)
+ Matches can be strategic
+ Body part damage and injuries
+ ENGRISH!
Cons:
- No explanations to training parts
- Training parts can be excruciating with the button pounding and analog moving
- Dull story
- All fighters fight similar
- Becomes repetitive and unchallenging near the end
My 30 minutes of intended playtime ended up being hours into the night. What hooks me is the strategic fighting in the beginning and the RPG elements. The quick KO's and injuries can really make you think before diving in and button mashing (you can mash buttons and win, but it's exciting to comeout with no injury or without being quickly KO'ed). You can really see your fighter improve with the training, too. You also learn new moves. You'll need to work to make money to enter tournaments which can also award you training sessions.It really makes you feel like you are a karate athlete. Building up your character and entering him into a match is the addicting part of the game.
I really enjoyed the game, but there were some aspects that I didn't like. The button and analog moving during the training sessions were a bit tiring and had no explanations on what to do; there not hard to understand, but some kind of explanation would have been nice. Most of the fighters fighter similar and don't feel really challenging. It would have been great to make each fighter unique and make me use different techniques to beat them like how you play Nintendo's Punchout! Because of this, once you learn how to beat one opponent, it'll be just as effective on future opponents. Therefore, the game gets repetitive and unchallenging down the line. Even with this major flaw, I still enjoyed playing it. The developers could really improve the game and make it a classic if it would improve on the figthing system. Overall, it it's a fun little indie game that will hook you in, but it doesn't have that right touch to make it a classic.

The combat has been frustratingly bad since the first build and has hardly improved, it is only 'in-depth' in the sense that it is soul-crushingly boring and the only remotely RPG-related feature is the skill system.
The multiplayer consists of running around an empty, isolated wasteland scattered with the empty remains of old player bases. Anyone playing is either too busy role-playing or squatting in their fortresses to do anything but sit in the chat. I haven't even mentioned the constant connectivity issues... Game cells can take up to five minutes to load while in multiplayer with single digit ping. So you'll usually find yourself constantly running into a black wall, being chased by hordes of zombies you can't even see, with nobody around and nothing to help you.
Maybe they'll fix these things and add more content in the future, but for now I do not reccomend this game.

Brilliant, amazing, fantastic, a real nice supplantation of the CoD Zombies formula into a side-scrolling shoot-em-up.
I figured one day I had enough money to pick up a super-cheap game on steam. That's just what I did - and fell in love near-immediately. ZKW Reborn is a pixel-graphic sidescroller shoot-em-up in the vein of such classics as Thing Thing Arena. Move on a 2D plane, your bullets fire towards your crosshair, you get nades and an assortment of buyable weapons. Maps are mazes of buyable doors and level setpieces, but they are only a small frame of the action - find a zombie spawn point and most of the time you can go to town, only returning to clear the round-end stragglers. One map is a bit crap, since going to a certain area before a certain round has a chance to lock you in and neccessitates a restart, but it's much less common than a now fixed glitch.
If slaughtering hordes of zombies on your own is too easy, you could always bring in a few bots to really put the smackdown on the fleshy tides - reaching the end of a series of buyable and round-locked doors in each map and claiming a phone pickup will grant you the ability to summon an AI-controlled companion to your cause, with each pickup giving you an additional virtual pugilist, up to a maximum of 3. While the AI for these companions is a bit lackluster and uncomplicated, if you need a gunhand and a medic at your side, these guys get the job done.
Other things that will help turn the tide in your favor include many more
import mainstays - as before - buyable weapons that instead of being one set weapon, are selected from a category, a weapon upgrade machine, a random weapon box (a fridge, much more
after TranZit and The Farm), bonus drops and buyable doors. As you progress into higher levels and the waves get tankier, you'll need all you can to beat back the living undead.
Persistent progression appears in the form of a leveling system - prove yourself to be an enduring, enterprising renderer of flesh and you'll get points to spend on increasing the abilities of your zombie slayer and greater and more prestigious access to the tools of the zombie-slaying trade - and trade you shall, because you may be able to wield these weapons, but weapons and their mods don't come for free - ZKW points are the currency of the day, and they are earned per game by hitting round milestones, and when you level up, complete achievments, and fulfil the Objective of the Day.
With ZKW points you can buy new weapons to appear in the Mystery Fridge, purchase perks to change your strengths, equipment to be deployed in the heat of battle, and weapon modifications that can turn a lowly spray and pray into an efficient zombie lawnmower.
The aesthetic of the game is simple yet satisfying. Think a fusion of pixel-art and Flash Low Quality settings and you'll be quite there. It will call to mind every memory you have of playing flash games on dodgy websites while dodging the web filters on the computers at school during your lunchbreak.
And the music is downright awesome - the 'Boss Loop' track is brilliantly cathartic - although you will want your volume control to hand, the game is ♥♥♥♥ing loud - which may or may not be a bad thing ;)
Perhaps the only downside is that higher waves seem to drag on - it becomes a loop of 'expend ammo, hit the boost cooler till you get max ammo, lather, rinse, repeat'. In that way it may be more fulfilling to set a max round for yourself, and submit yourself to your
when you're done. Additionally the voice acting is a bit stilted and unenthusiastic. It's slightly charming in a B-Movie (B-, not Bee!) kind of way but it still sounds like the two blonde lasses from Drama class who seem to have more social blocks than a cathedral. The netcode is pretty uncomplicated too - Still Running make no effort to cover up the fact that you'll want a pretty damn stable connection to who you're playing with.
Nevertheless - at its cheap price it's easily reccomended. Good in nice small bursts.

Simply put, if you like strategy games, this game is awesome! A perfect example of the elegance of simplicity.
You have a mere 5 things you can do, with a suprising amount of strategic depth in how you utilize those 5 things: Energy, which is your life's blood in more ways than one; not only is it your economy, but lose all of these and you lose the game. Turrents, which are your basic form of attack, good to spam lots of them. Black holes, which are your sole means of defence, as they deflect incoming shots, but enough focus fire can overcome them. Sentinels, which 'claim' territory on the map, which is good because the enemy cannot build things in your territory. Also work in a pinch to draw enemy fire, and will instantly destroy any enemy units caught in their influence. And lastly Missiles, which are costly, slow to charge, but if they go off, can wipe out enemy forces in a wide area.
The key is positioning; your forces and theirs will fire upon the closest target to them. So depending on where you build things, you can protect other things, and the same with them. You can fly anywhere on the map, which is a giant ball of strands, and each vies for optimal positioning to take out the other, by whatever means they deem necessary.
Truly, this is a unique and innovative title; the only con I have is sometimes it can be akward to precisly position yourself exactly where you want to be, as when you stop flying you will automatically gravitate towards the nearest strand. Also, there doesn't seem to be a way to destroy a unit once youve already built it, which can sometimes be problematic with black holes, as they can affect YOUR turrets shots as well; depending on what they are firing at they might choose to fire through the black hole, which of course doesn't work very well....
Also the multiplayer is dead, so it is a good thing to have some friends to play with, unless you just want to skirmish with the AI.
All in all I would highly recommend this title!

Played more DAO than any other game except Civ5. Modding DAO is definitely a bit of work, but once I had all I wanted tweaked, the game was so immersive for me that there's no set of game characters I remember more fondly and was one of the few games I've completed start to finish repeatedly plus the DLC.
I still resist the notion of DAO being the "spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate," but after being a huge BG fan, then a huge NWN fan, this fit right in afterward despite it dropping DnD as a basis for the game mechanics (and Forgotten Realms as a setting, alas). DAO borrows from a lot of genre for inspiration- can take you through horror scenes to adventure encounters to tavern brawls to war scenes out of "Braveheart" to completely tactical encounters where you're using every fraction of a second to pull through.
DA fans tend to guffaw at DAO's "origin story" experience as "just a tutorial," but that's DAO's most endearing, immersive element for me, the initial investment in your character and his/her motivations that makes the rest of the game so worth exploring to the fullest with them. And not just the initial part but how things have changed when you return to the same origin location after becoming a Gray Warden (esp. the dwarf origins.) You will have a very unique experience with whatever race/background you choose, and the writers were very creative about how they introduce you to the DA lore and gameworld. It's the synergy between the attention to detail paid to your own character's story AND to the unfolding of the overall lore that's the biggest draw for me. Despite them dropping the ball in DA2 and DAI in terms of creative investment in your own character's story, the DAverse is by far the most interesting, engaging, and at times thought-provoking game setting I've encountered in any game regardless of genre or type.
If I had to criticize DAO I'd say the combat mechanics haven't aged that well. Like DnD it uses RNG in your to-hit chances (no dodge rolls or FPS aiming) which is fine really (XCOM uses it well), but the way it was implemented there is a lot of running in and watching your attack animation do diddlysquat while you get clobbered... at least until later in the game. So if anything don't prepare for a very robust combat system, even though the ability to control your full party is far better in DAO than DAI... The clunky combat is the primary reason I can't get into DAO any more, but that's not to say the combat's not enjoyable, esp. if you're new to the game anyway.
It's an old-style RPG- no spoken lines by your protagonist (though plenty of snarky, poignant, etc. lines to choose from), paused combat, less sophisticated cutscenes- but with a decidedly more mature narrative- both due to "mature" content and to a more sophisticated social outlook. And it works. Well. It's a great example of a very intelligent, creative dev team that worked the frickin frack out of limited game resources to turn out something exceptional.

So I don't know what happened to this game. Over the years it's been in development, I've put a lot of time into the survival mode in expectation of a story mode. Now that the story mode has been released though, I feel like there was a disconnect somewhere in development of it. The beginning doesn't explain anything to new players that will most likely want to do the story mode first. The UI over time has become very complicated and hinders the players ability to complete some of the early tasks the game gives you (specifically making tea).
Now I've put over 100 hours into this game so I know my way around a bit, but man... the radial stuff is just annoying as all get out. I get they want to make this game console friendly, but there HAS to be a better solution. Making recipes has become a game of hide and seek when before some of the most recent updates, everything was right in front of you. If you had the materials, it would show up in a separate section that you could make it. For example, if I had the materials for the tea, they would appear in the section where you would boil water or where your first aid is. It's just weird with some of the design choices they've made.
I want to love this story mode as I've held on for so long in anticipation for it. As of now however, I don't really like it. It's really dull at the beginning and the voice actors sound bored to death. It might be the way the developers want to portray their characters, but man... give them some life. The wolves (as I've seen other people complain) are absolutely out of control, too. Like, WHAT HAPPENED? They're fine in the survival mode, but in story they're crazy and all over the place! I stepped out of the church and got attacked by 2 out of no where! I've never seen 2 so close to each other.
PLEASE HINTERLAND, FIX THE STORY! Do whatever you can to make it as magical as the survival mode. I don't know if you're too far into the development of it to make drastic changes, but something needs to be done before it's finished. I love this game, just please don't taint it with the state it's currently in.

Tales is a colorful, comedic tale full of wacky characters -- but doesn't lack dramatic moments, either. While it's a modern retro game, it does play very much like the point&click classics of the early 90's. If I were to compare it to any of my all-time favorites, I'd say The Fate of Atlantis (an academic visiting ancient, mythical sites) and Kyrandia (magic and fairytales!). The puzzles are mostly very straightforward -- but, much like in these classics, there are a bunch of logical puzzles, with moving objects around to get a password and such. Now these can be tricky -- but while I'm not a fan, I only got stuck badly once, and it was because I made an incorrect assumption. Otherwise, it was a smooth ride -- and an epic journey. That's another reason why it reminded me of FoA: you get to travel to a whole lot of exotic locations, each beautiful in its own way. I loved the vivid, cartoony graphics. Kinda wished it was hi-res but I didn't really mind. Same with the voices: the audio quality or the acting wasn't always top-notch, but I get sentimental thinking back of those first talkie adventure games, lo-fi as they were.
All in all, I had a blast. Definitely one of the most fun games I played this year.
Pros:
- an engaging story cleverly making use of some more obscure classic tales
- fun puzzles: some easy, some hard, mostly fair, and even if one was infuriatingly tricky, I had to admit it was clever
- colorful, cartoony graphics
- funny characters, some of which I'll actually really miss
Cons:
- the teleport interface (bell & bag): traveling back to the library to enter other books was a hassle, especially since you're only able to take one object with you at a time (though the double-click did speed things up)

Tales:
~~~~
Alfred Walsh has been looking for a job for a while and after thoroughly scanning the local newspaper, he came across a very interesting advertisement. An establishment is looking for a new librarian. “What a perfect opportunity - a fairytale of a job,” thought our dear friend, Alfred. However, his first day on the job turned out to be totally unexpected! After discovering that his predecessor was in fact the guardian of this library of tales prior to his death, he accidently released (cough . . . cough) a terrible Demon from a black book that was safely locked in a chest somewhere in the room. The demon, Oblivion, wants to destroy all human tales from this library; it is a slight predicament for our new librarian, wouldn’t you say? Cheer up Alfred, the tales of the world are in your hands!
Tales is a point and click adventure game where you play of Alfred Walsh, who takes a job in a most extraordinary library.
In the preface of this story, you will discover what happened to the previous guardian of the library and see for the first time the demon named Oblivion. After that, our accidental hero, Walsh. . . Alfred Walsh, will be introduced to the story as the new librarian. In a heartbeat, Alfred will realize that as soon as he begins reading a book, he will be teleported into it, visiting places and meeting incredible characters, such as the Goddess Ninsun, mother of the legendary Hero, Gilgamesh. By the way, Gilgamesh defeated Oblivion in the past and you need to ask his help to defeat Oblivion again in order to save all the tales before it is too late!
Alfred will be armed with a couple of exquisite items: a magic bell and a magic bag! Every time Alfred needs to come back to the library all he has to do is to ring the bell and he will be teleported straight back. The magic bag is handy in the sense that you can take an item from one book to another, but only one at a time.
The puzzles in this game are challenging, especially when you have to figure out which article to use from another book to resolve a specific puzzle. A few riddles are also included in this game, so make sure to read the text carefully, you might find some very good hints there, too.
If you get really stuck on a puzzle, then your only solution is to talk to Merlin, who will advise you about what you might need to do.
The pixel artwork could have been a little bit more polished, but it is ok. The story is fun and really well laid-out, with challenging puzzles. The voice-over is actually pretty good but the Mayans sound very British to me.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great Story based on legendary tales
-	Challenging Puzzles
-	Good voice over
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~

-	Artwork could have been better
Tales is a truly enjoyable point and click adventure.
7/10

Sometimes the first time you play a game stands out in  your memories. Whether it is for the quality of the game itself, the unique experience you had with the game, or something else the playing of that game represents in your life. For me, Aquaria was all three of those things.
I purchased Aquaria back in 2008 from its own website. Over 2 years before I started using Steam. I was mostly a console gamer back then. Aquaria was the first time I played a game that encapsulated what made many 2D adventure games great, while still being something original enough that it wasn't just a fan-game of an existing franchise. The most surprising was that it was not by one of those big companies. This was the first exposure I got to professional indie game development. (As in making and selling a product).
To many it may not look like anything that special when there are many 2D adventure/exploration games available. But I just want to say this game stands up. Moving around fluidly is a ton of fun. The voice acting is good. The world is beautiful and mysterious. Most of all, the music is AMAZING. Aquaria single-handedly made me pay attention to PC gaming and see that where there used to be bold lines dividing the styles of PC and console games in the past, these lines were dissappearing and now are pretty much gone.

Things I wish I knew before playing:
* Repair your clothes! Things wear out pretty fast now...I found myself without trousers in one tricky game.
* It's not the end. After episode one you get the thanks to backers and it looks like you've finished the story. This is just the end of chapter one. If you go back to the story mode and click resume
you'll start chapter 2.
*No bedroll. No sleep. This is probably obvious but on more than one occasion I forgot to pick up my bedroll after sleep and ended nearly dying due to lack of sleep after a day of walking.
*The Map. There's a map that allows you to see locations once the story mode starts properly. While it doesn't show you where you are, as you discover new locations these appear on the map helping you to work out where you are if you get stuck.

I've been with this game pretty much since the beginning, and I must say that it's been amazing to watch it develop and mature over the years. Like everyone else, I've been patiently waiting for story mode, but have put plenty of time into both sandbox and challenge mode.
There are several important things I have to say to someone on the fence about buying this game.
1) Don't let anyone tell you that you shouldn't buy this game on the grounds that story mode isn't good. First of all, story mode, while nothing special, is not particularly bad. This game suffered from the Fallout 4 overhype syndrome; people had to wait too long for it and they expected perfection, then got pissy when they didn't get it. Regardless, the value of this game is in the environment, mechanics, etc. It is worth picking up just for sandbox mode in my opinion.
2) If you're impatient or can't stand anything that isn't an action packed, fast paced game, The Long Dark is not for you. It requires a good attention span and a certain willingness to get invested in your game. It is slow, but immersive and rewarding. If you can't handle that, just go back to CS:GO or overwatch, you manchild. This game is for men of culture.
3) Take the all reviews with a grain of salt. This game is very much subject to individual taste- some will love it, some will find it boring. Not only that, but a lot of people were rubbed the wrong way by Hinterland during the development of this game (not totally hinterland's fault imo), so I suspect some might still be a little salty or biased against the devs. Just something to watch out for.
Well, thats about it. Overall, this game is a wonderful, unique experience that I hope everyone will try out, even if story mode doesn't totally knock everyone's socks off. I've had a lot of fun with this game and have a ton of respect for the developers and their mission. Happy surviving!

Oh man what a fun little ride this was.
I had no idea what I was geting when I picked this game up, but felt very intrigued by the bright colors and music of the trailer. Bears, cars and bulls? Boxers? Wrestlers? No way the game had all of this. But oh yes my friends, it certainly does.
First off a big nod has to go to the presentation of this game. The graphics are large, detailed, very nice looking and overall just make the game very fun to watch. You definately get an old school SNES Final Fight/Street Fighter vibe from them. As well, all of the music is good, whether its the main menu or the bloody end of a fight, it fits and its damn good.
Now the game was obviously translated from japanese and it isn't perfect, but this leads to some hilarious lines, one of my favorites being "I"ll break your idiot face, you sucker!" But it's like one of those badly dubbed japanese films, you can't help but smile at it.
There is a story to the game, sort of. You can tell there is supposed to be large overall narrative but the actual story scenes are so few and far between you kind of just get some randomness. Basically your character wants to become a great karate master and open his own school. You do this by training, learning new moves, and beating the crap out of the other dojo leaders in the city and competing in tournaments. Along the way you get cutscenes asking you to do the crazy stuff like fighting bears and bulls, and all of this gets you more and more fame. The more famous you are the more dojo leaders you can confront and more tournaments you can earn until you get to the end of the game.
But really, the gameplay is where it's at. Even after over ten hours there are still some nuances like proper counters, etc, that I didn't pick up on. For me it was mostly back away and then attack, but you might do better then I did. You essentially have two kick buttons, two punch buttons, and a jump. You also get what is called a Ki bar and if you let it fill before you attack you do more damage. Like some of the best wrestling games, you also have body damage, so you can do damage to legs, torso, or head, and by doing enough damage to one part you can knock your opponent out and win the match. Also at random you can end up losing your breath, taking damage to your liver or getting 'brain shock' which disables you a There is a fair bit of depth here and it's a shame the engine they came up with is single-player only as this would make an excellent competitive fighter.
In terms of the progression, it oddly enough, has a difficulty drop rather then a spike. At first it is tricky, as you are weak, have to earn all of your money working as a dock worker via a mini-game, and fight in tournaments and probably lose. But whenever you lose you get some experience towards your skills. Eventually you'll win a tournament and be able to train up a bit more. Once you get some training under your belt and raise your stats a bit, you'll end up breezing through most of the tournaments and can start to challenge the dojos, which are FAR easier. You can actually challenge the same dojo over and over again, getting experience, and fame each time, along with training points to use towards upgrading your skills and learning new moves.
As a tip, be sure to learn the new moves, or WAZA,  as soon as possible; they make the game easier and more interesting. I screwed up and I didn't learn them until near the end of the game. With these moves, and your upgraded stats, in some cases you might end up conquering the dojos in less then a minute. But some of the tournaments and special events hold enough of a challenge to keep you going. Plus, due to a feature called 'Ichegaki Hissatsu' there is always a chance for you to lose (or win) randomly, as one lucky strke can fracture a leg or even your skill and end the match immediately so you never feel totally invincible or unstoppable, and thus the game never quite hits the point of getting boring.
Overall the game is extremely fun to play, holds a great challenge, along with providing some very funny to read dialogue at some points. I encourage you to go master your karate as this game is a knock out blow of a recommendation.
And more thing, for those of you with Steam controllers, I've exported a controller configuration for you to use that works marveiously, so go get it once you have picked up this excellent game.

I cant really recommend this game since its so far from finished. But i've had so much fun with it i cant give it a "thumbs down" either.
Its a colony building game in the same vein as Dwarf Fortress or Gnomoria. You designate the little people to be farmers or blacksmiths or whatever, designate a building here and a building there and, whenever they get around to it, they'll build it & live in it. Some of the fun details are that while the game has prefab buildings, you dont have to use them, you can opt to design your own instead. And if you come up with a good design you can save it to use again later. Eventually you'll be able to share your designs & others can use them in their colonies, which will be cool, but its not in yet.
Theres a lot thats not in yet, if you read the design goals, the devs have a LOT in mind for this game. I'll be amazed if they can do half of it. But they keep working on it very steadily. Ive been following it for a long while now & updates & new features have always come in on a regular basis. The devs are very connected to the player community & it shows. Its certainly not another one of those "grab the money & run" fly-by-nights we've seen so many times on early access. These guys are serious about wanting to make a good game.
If you like to use early access games to observe the game development process, this is a great game for that right now.  If you want it to, the game is happy to show you the nuts & bolts of exactly whats going wrong inside the AI's little brain when it gets stuck on a lamp post or whatever. And if you post a bug report, the devs will almost certainly have a fix in the next patch.
However if youre the type who gets upset when you find yourself beta testing a game you paid for, perhaps skip this one for now... but keep an eye open for it, if/when it goes gold its gonna be really good!
