Even in the early stages, I'm finding Stonehearth to be incredibly addictive. Watching your Hearthlings build and thrive as you direct their actions is endearing. Though the characters are adorable, watching them slaughter adorable Goblins is great.
Still, there are a few things that could be improved in this game. Keeping in mind that, as an Early Access title at this stage, there are improvements and features yet to come anyway. Regardless, here are a few things that I feel could be worked on:
- The 'Build a Custom House' feature is in dire need of a more reliable 'Delete' tool. If the changes I wanted to make to an existing blueprint requires replacing something that has already been placed, I'm out of luck. I'd just have to tell my Hearthlings to undeploy an object and deploy the one I actually want there. (Like an improved bed.)
- I would like to be able to either see a queue of actions and be able to to change the priority or simply have a click-and-drag tool to call the Hearthlings to a certain area to work on it right at that moment. I have seen far too many crops wither and die because they become neglected by my farmers. Not to mention, the buildings that become abandoned in the middle of construction because my workers suddenly feel that everyone mining at once is more important than finishing another wooden dining hall.
- Please bring back the Name Randomizer for towns. I honestly liked seeing the sort of names built into the game and I'm horrendous with naming settlements in the first place.

There are some things about this game that bother people, but they are all because it is in early access, and will be fixed. Unlike many early access games, This game is still actually updating. it entered early access in 2013, and it is 2017 and it just got drivable cars in the test-builds just this month. the problems are in a lack of NPC's and multiplayer being a pain, both of which will be changed by full release. There are few early access games that I will recommend, and this is one of those. If you automatically thumbs-down early access, then why are you even reading this? Now for the actual review.
HOLY CRAP this game is good! I love my post-apocalyptic survival games. Specifically the, wandering an abandoned town or city, breaking into buildings, looting what you can cary, going back to a fortified base, and ALL OF THE CRAFTING, while occasionally having to deal with zombies and praying you never have to use any of your precious few pipe-bombs on crowds that might eventually wander towards your base. I FREAKING LOVE IT. it does everything right. This game is a proper post-apocalypse survival crafting game, which means at it's core, this game is all about scavenging, and resource-management, and it's NOT an FPS, So if you need it to be a shooter, or scavenging and resource management with zombies isn't your cup of tea, then I really don't know what you're doing here.
It has Proper inventory management. you can only get so much, but if you find a bag you can cary more stuff more easily, and if you can wear it on your back you can hold WAY more. and you can easily just drop things to lighten yourself up for fighting. it's GREAT.  like you can have a bag full of loot and just drop it if you have to fight and then pick up the bag, and you're golden.
It has proper freaking health management. Like, It even tracks your mental health in a way. your character can get BORED AND DEPRESSED and you have to stay entertained. And really, think about it. you're the sole survivor of the zombie apocalypse? in a way this is basically 'how long before you take a lead anti-depressant' simulator, and it's bloody terrifying. I haven't played long enough to exhaust all the towns loot, but I have no freaking clue what I'm going to do when I run out of books and magazines because I haven't figured out how the journals work yet.
Oh yeah, and did I mention the zombies? you can make things to make noise and attract zombies and get them to walk over traps and blow them up. it's freaking great. you can knock down walls, and apparently now they're adding cars. I wonder what you can disassemble them into.
Oh and it forces you to look around and pay attention because, guess what? VISION IS LITERAL. you don't get the birds-eye-view that sees behind you. it is 3rd person birds-eye view, but it doesn't actually reveal things unless you're looking at them. and zombies..... they're quiet. I have accidentally walked within about half a step of a zombie because I was looking the wrong way and legit didn't see it.
Next, yeah, it's not procedural, but that's a good thing. the map is HUGE, and it actually freakin' makes sense, and people can make custom maps.
IMO This is probably the BEST post apocalyptic survival & crafting game on steam, or even around. Every other one of these games is a first-person-shooter first, and an apocalyptic survival & crafting game second. This one puts the post-apocalyptic survival & crafting with zombies thing first, and EVERYTHING ELSE is secondary to that, which is FANTASTIC. it's a game that really knows what it is, which is something lacking the genre.

For my money this is the second best game ever made, the first being Baldur's Gate 2; it's a little unforgiving to newcomers sure, but if you stick with it and learn the systems then it turns out incredibly rewarding. The story is awesome, the sheer amount of content is mind blowing, and the game is just good old fashioned fun, that still holds up well today (why else would Kickstarter be flooded with isometric RPG's like Pillars of Eternity and Torment: Tides of Numenera if it wasn't such a timeless style of game)
The Enhanced Edition doesn't add a lot of content, but what it does add is extremely useful; a number of fan-made usability mods / patches / etc etc have been build into it to help it run on modern hardware, and there are four NPC's which fit seemlessly into the rest of the game. There's also a standalone arena-based combat mode, but I've not touched that, if for no other reason than I was so taken with the main game that I couldn't drag myself away.
Buy this game.
Buy it for yourself.
Buy it for everyone you know.
Buy about twelve extra copies to gift to people that are worthy of it's timeless glory.
You won't regret it. In fact, you'll be doing the work of The Lord

This game was a satisfying experience, emotional insofar as that the majority of the story was the protaginist's mental awareness of herself- her emotions, her thoughts, but most importantly her LACK of identity, which ignites the flame of desire for belonging in her heart. This game may be ten years old yet with puzzles that still boggle minds, with its own alphabet and secret, undebated lore, and a strong presence of spiritual parallels (though few are truly close to any truth concerning details for religious beliefs), on top of having a unique focus on aquatic movement in a 2D sidescrolling environment, this game's mechanics are sound for a game its age. Its music is unmatched in significance, and in fact you must join in the song yourself to reach harmony with the ending. The 2D visuals might be old, but its style enhances the sense of mystery in the game; older graphics reminiscent of paintings, a sense of value which emphasizes the sea's vastness, and creative morphing of real animals and fictional ones keeps the new player entanced by wonder.
If this game isn't listened to, you severly cheapen its value. The visuals and the mood are supposed to support the mood, and if one moves much during the voiceovers, or even speaks their thoughts to themselves, they lose part of the weight of her experiences. this game is emotional for the protagonist as she discovers the richness of life and love after a lifetime of complacency and loneliness, in a destroyed world where none else cares.

The first hour:  "Man this is a nice relaxed game, hey look there's singing and a beautiful ocean."
Pretty much every hour after that.  "Holy hell this is a hard game!"
Aquaria starts up deceptively simple.  There's a female protagonist and, a world that seems to not have a large amount of danger.  By the time the player gets to the first boss, the player will realize how wrong that is.  Aquaria is a HARD game, there's a lot of variety from the bosses and enemies, sometimes making the game feel almost like a bullet hell game, other times just an obstacle course that the player has to pass.
The game doesn't really assist the player with the game flow.  The player doesn't usually get told what to do next, as this is very similar to a metroidvania game.  The player will explore the ocean, and will gain powers that open up new areas.  In fact the game does this very well, as the player usually isn't beaten back by challenge, but rather beaten by a feature they aren't able to pass yet so they know they will have to keep exploring.
Examples of these features are the forms that the main character Naija gets, such as Beast Form, or Fish Form.  Beast form allows Naija to swim against very strong currents with ease, and Fish form allows her to swim into very small places.  I believe there's 9 total forms, and each form has it's own use.
The player also earns these forms from bosses , and this is where the real difficulty of the game comes in.  Most of the game isn't too hard outside of the boss battles (though the difficulty does ramp up later in the game).
However the boss battles are where they game really shines, there's a decent amount of difficulty with each boss.  The bosses are variety, but in addition there's only one or two bosses that require a direct beat down, most bosses are quite inventive, requiring taunting the opponent so they use a specific attack, and then the player either can capitalize on that or have to get the enemy to damage himself.    Most of these bosses are hard to beat, but with some work the player can beat them.
That's not to say Naija is always at a disadvantage, in addition to forms, she's also able to cook food (don't ask me how you cook food under water).  That food actually can heal Naija and enhance her power, however to gather the pieces of the food does take a decent amount of time.  The player can find almost everything but it's hard to really "farm" ingredients, and as she can only carry 8 of each items, there's limitations to how much she can carry.
The game does revolve around a merwoman or some kind of underwater adventurer (my wife calls her an elf for her ears, but she's more of a merwoman) and to be honest I am not a fan of the story as much.  I started the game thinking it might just be a simple low action adventure game, and instead found an excellent adventure game.  Though I will say I didn't finish the game, as the difficulty got pretty hard where I was in the game.
The game itself is decent.  There's a few flaws.  I feel like the UI could be cleaner and more direct.  Cooking can be annoying especially if you're cooking multiples.  There's a singing mechanic that works, but really you're going to use the short cut keys if you're smart (1-0 on the keyboard).  The game would benefit from an auto fire, as I had to turn on the turbo on my steam controller to avoid clicking the trigger over and over (And yet it also requires holding the trigger at times also at other times).  Is it a perfect game, nah, but it's a fun game, and different.
The biggest thing this game would benefit from was a better map system.  It's a decent map, but god, it really could use a few features to make it easier to find out what's holding back the player, or where there is still areas to explore.   Sadly while the game doesn't make it obvious where the player should go next, it also doesn't make it obvious WHERE the player can still explore, the former is a design decision, the second though is a usability decision, and it's wrong.
However as a whole, the game is good.  It has a lot of content, and even though I didn't finish the full game, I put in over 14 enjoyable hours into the game.   I'd recommend this game especially because it's going for 10 bucks, and you'll get your money's worth. It's not going to beat Castlevania Symphony of the Night, but at the same time, it's probably the best underwater game I've seen on steam, and a rather good metroidvania game at that.  If you like a game that doesn't hold your hand, Aquaria will give you a perfect world to explore.

This is a rather obscure little plane-racing game with a few maps, a few planes, and a few powerups.  I don't even recall exactly how it got into my Steam Library -- part of a Humble Bundle, I think.  So my expectations were not set particularly high when I finally tried it out.
And I was impressed.
The controls are really tight, the action is frantic, and the graphics are pretty.  It's not a flight sim (and not trying to be,) it's more like MarioKart with the addition of vertical steering.  What SkyDrift does, it does very successfully, with a great deal of polish and refinement.  A point can legitimately be made that SkyDrift pretty quickly runs out of variety, in terms of its maps, planes, and powerups, but it
a budget title, so it's a bit unfair to hold the small size of the game against it -- I'm more pleased by a limited but well-done game than a sprawling one that's buggy and barely-playable.

Fun, dumb, run and gun worth getting on sale, although full price isn't unreasonable either.
Runs well in local and multiplayer, and most of the features are intuitive and polished. Makes playing solo or with friends relatively painless and is perfect for a quick 10 minute game to relieve some stress. On the flip side, you'll occasionally get together a team that just clicks and goes on an endless zombie killing spree.
The mechanics, sounds and graphics are all solid and create an atmosphere of satisfying, gory destruction.
There are a good amount of weapons, though the balancing of availability, cash resources and enemy levels led me to focus more on mastering lower level gear. However a lot of people I played with stuck to heavy artillery, so maybe it's just a choice of play style.
The major downside is that the nature of the game is inherently repetitive. Campaign depth does not exist, but the variety of arenas and game modes is more than adequate for what it is.
EDIT: The developer (who I believe has an impressive track record of maintenance and updates) commented to remind me of the promised upcoming Campaign focused DLC. I forgot about it when originally reviewing, but if it matches the current quality level it should improve an already very good game.

My first Assassin's Creed game.  And so far, i'm very impress by the quality (graphics, sound) and the overall gameplay.  I very like it, even if i would want more Evie main mission.

Assassin's Creed Syndicate. Well, if you have played the previous ones and hate the controls, movement, story, yearly releases and whatnot, buy this. Once again Ubisoft proves to the world that AC is just another disaster under the publishers wings.
Quick summa summarum:
Game is set on victorian era London and you have to play as a dimwitted duo of Assassin Legacies (trust me, not assassins anymore. Gentle blend of brawling and the league of extraordinary gentlemen). The setting itself is fun and interesting, but it is not alive. The pedestrians walk aimlessly up and down the roads and after couple of hours you just start spotting the red guys who need to go. Walk close, press X, deal is done.
Cons
- The game is graphically satisfying, but falls short on delivering it.
- Remember the sticky slime-things you could buy from bubblegum machines in your youth? Meet our designer of controls.
- Story is not immersive, it falls short and it has nothing to do with anything, the last time Ubisoft delivered something new and fresh was 2004. The story is like watching the Kardashians after DMT.
- You can actually purchase in-game boosters for single player game.
- Did I mention the controls?
- The in-game crafting system and upgrading yourself as you go is like playing Farmville on Facebook. You shouldn't bother, and after a few accidents you realize there really is nothing more to be done, except waiting.
- Overall quality of the product is not that good.
- No multiplayer support but still they introduced micro-transactions to the game. (Not that it would be good to have one)
- Repetitive gameplay and mission mechanics, feels like doing the same thing for 15h.
Pros
+-0
+ Graphics are fairly good
+ Animations are fairly good, although sloppy and laggy
4.5/10, wouldn't recommend if it's not on -70% sale.

I went into this with quite high hopes due to the numerous reviews online, Unfortunatley I was diasapointed. The overall world is great, i live in London and I feel they really nailed the atmosphere and astetic however in terms of gameplay Syndicate really falls down.
The AI is terrible, it's truley awful. You can engage a guy in combat and less than 100 meters away thier friends wil not notice the fight. You can throw dynamite near a group and they will not flinch, explode it and others are not alerted unless it's in thier field of view. Guns work almost the same because the AI has almost no reaction to sound.
Added to this when guards are alerted the do very little to hunt you down and quickly revert back to passive state, you kill 3 guys they will be alerted for a short period of time and then quickly act as if nothing happened.
The AI is so broken that it destroys challenge and immersion for me, the things I have metioned have a huge impact on gameplay.
Also I feel that variety in stealth is very limited, you cant do as much as a game like black flag so it makes gameplay stale.
This wouldn't matter so much if the story was interesting but it really isn't, there is almost no decent story. Characters are generally flat and thier motivations limited to being very shallow. I liked AC4 because of Edward kenway as a character, he was genuine and funny. Evie and Jacob are dull and uniteresting, for example they go to London on a whim, no reason or explanation.
Honestly It's just not a fun game, maybe for the first few hours but then you realise how flawed and dull this game actually is, theres no gameplay, lack of focus and other than it's visual assets a generally dull game.
I spent £24 in a sale, but honestly I wouldn't even call that value for money.

I love the video story graphics a clever mix of 3D and paint style texturing. The story bits can be a bit long when you just want to play the game, maybe a skip button would have been nice.
Also with the story mode you have to keep up and try and accomplish the task before it gets dark or you face a slow death of trying to find fire wood in the dark while hoping to trigger the next day, but this does add to the tension...and what tension! Probably because I always seem to play this game at  night, but man it gets scary. The sounds and the way your vision and movement are affected when you're on your last legs had me in a panic....and righlty so cos I didn't make it.
So yes if you like survival style games..you'll like this.
Things I wish I knew before playing:
* Repair your clothes! Things wear out pretty fast now...I found myself without trousers in one tricky game.
* It's not the end. After episode one you get the thanks to backers and it looks like you've finished the story. This is just the end of chapter one. If you go back to the story mode and click resume
you'll start chapter 2.
*No bedroll. No sleep. This is probably obvious but on more than one occasion I forgot to pick up my bedroll after sleep and ended nearly dying due to lack of sleep after a day of walking.
*The Map. There's a map that allows you to see locations once the story mode starts properly. While it doesn't show you where you are, as you discover new locations these appear on the map helping you to work out where you are if you get stuck.

I've been with this game pretty much since the beginning, and I must say that it's been amazing to watch it develop and mature over the years. Like everyone else, I've been patiently waiting for story mode, but have put plenty of time into both sandbox and challenge mode.
There are several important things I have to say to someone on the fence about buying this game.
1) Don't let anyone tell you that you shouldn't buy this game on the grounds that story mode isn't good. First of all, story mode, while nothing special, is not particularly bad. This game suffered from the Fallout 4 overhype syndrome; people had to wait too long for it and they expected perfection, then got pissy when they didn't get it. Regardless, the value of this game is in the environment, mechanics, etc. It is worth picking up just for sandbox mode in my opinion.
2) If you're impatient or can't stand anything that isn't an action packed, fast paced game, The Long Dark is not for you. It requires a good attention span and a certain willingness to get invested in your game. It is slow, but immersive and rewarding. If you can't handle that, just go back to CS:GO or overwatch, you manchild. This game is for men of culture.
3) Take the all reviews with a grain of salt. This game is very much subject to individual taste- some will love it, some will find it boring. Not only that, but a lot of people were rubbed the wrong way by Hinterland during the development of this game (not totally hinterland's fault imo), so I suspect some might still be a little salty or biased against the devs. Just something to watch out for.
Well, thats about it. Overall, this game is a wonderful, unique experience that I hope everyone will try out, even if story mode doesn't totally knock everyone's socks off. I've had a lot of fun with this game and have a ton of respect for the developers and their mission. Happy surviving!

I really wanted to like this game.
I played in open beta and it was frustrating at first but after a few days it got pretty fun.  There were balance issues I figured they'd address, but overall it wasn't a bad experience.
When the game went live, the price was prohibitive for the state the game was in at the time so I held off purchasing.  This weekend though, it went on sale so I figured I'd give it a shot again and see if it had improved.
I was sorely disappointed.  Matchmaking takes absolutely forever with people constantly abandoning the queue for one reason or another (it never really tells you why).  I spent most of the time "in game" in the menu waiting for it to find players to start a game.
Graphically the game is pretty solid, and the sound is also pretty well done; I really like the concept of 4v1 PvP, the controls are pretty easy to get used to if you've played any other FPS games, and the characters have interesting personality and cross dialogue.  But these few bright points are far from enough to save what was ultimately a frustrating experience.
I haven't followed the game at all since beta but it doesn't feel like any of the balance issues that existed back then have been addressed in the slightest (though maybe I'm wrong, I couldn't actually get enough play time in to really tell...but Wraith is absolutely OP).
So in summary, even at half price this game is not worth the buy.  They should've done as everyone else has said before me and gone Free to Play with purchasable content like skins or player models.  As it is there are too few people even playing to make it worth joining a queue for a game.

SpaceChem is a really fun puzzle game! If you love making some fake science with a couple of puzzle solving, then this game is for you!

Puzzle game of the year?  Maybe!
No real chemistry involved here; it's basically visual scripting with a limited set of "instructions" (tools) and a geometric aspect. If you like coding/scripting, or if you like building contraptions and watching them crank along, then you'll probably dig it.
It does quickly get complex. This is not an easy game. Fortunately the solving process doesn't (always) involve just staring at the screen, but rather building different aspects of a possible solution to see how they work out. So it's engaging even when you're not immediately solving stuff.
The nifty thing is that each problem has lots of workable solutions. If you like, you can tune your solutions for efficiency or speed, and see how you compare to other players. I'm only halfway through the campaign myself, just taking my time and occasionally going back to earlier stages to tweak my solutions.

Good idea, but flawed implementation.
Story is interesting, but it's told in most unengaging way possible, and most interesting moment of it happens only if you find three certain things and complete the game. Said moment is cliffhanger, by the way. Also, message about killing is completely out-of-place and hypocritical. And point where you find supporting character is mishandled so much I think it was a mistake or something - heroine strives to find sentient life, finds it, and game shoves it away like "All right, here's other item for you, off to next area with you, fishgirl".
Art is excellent, but animation is horrible, flash-like and clunky.
Music is nice - probably only not flawed part of game.
Gameplay is good, but suffers greatly from weird design choises:
1) Transportation between explored zones is tedious, as turtles are uncontrollable and very rare. Nature Form's bulbs would solve problem, but, alas, they are used in fewer places and usually for secrets you must return to later. And spamming space for minutes at end is not really interesting.
2) Save points are rare too.
3) Fighting is abysmal, and quickly makes one evade it at all costs. Clicking right mouse one thousand times to kill anything is boring.
4) Cooking is nice addition, but out of 40+ recipies you need only healing/speed/damage. About 10 at most. All else is useless. Also, ingridients are too rare to use cooking effectively.
5) Padding/filler is out of control. Large areas are empty, serve no purpose other than eye-candy (which you can find elsewhere), but are required to be traversed since exit is on other side of this loooooooong cave.
6) About killing - message about it would be meaningful is Naija wasn't nemesis of every single creature around. Mad fishmen, I understand, they are ferocious and all that. But fish, animals and so on all have thirst for players blood too, despite living in lush world with plenty of food to eat. Not that they must be peaceful, but they are way too agressive.
7) Song mechanic is dreadfully underused, since quick shortcuts are just better.
All in all, it's nice game, but as far as Steam Reviews go, I can't 'recommend' it. There are better metroidvanias out there. But, if you can afford it, try it? It's not bad as in "I want my money back", it's "Welp, this was underwhelming".

Project Zomboid is my most satisfying early-access type investment. This game has come a long, long way; from the early days of 2d sprites where the zombies looked like little green aliens to where it is now, it's really fantastic.
If you love Romero zombie movies  -- Dawn of the Dead, Night of the Living Dead, etc -- then you will like this game. It's not an action game; it taps into that personal survival story, echoing Romero's movies. There is no storyline and your goal is to just survive and thrive. This involves scavenging the huge world map, managing your resources, and building a base to live, whilst engaging or avoiding any zombies that cross your path. Ultimately, the goal of the game is to see how long you can survive before your inevitable death, and as such the game has a brutal roguelike nature where combat is difficult and lethal, and just one mistake can lead to your demise. Very often I find my over-confidence is what leads to that one fatal bite that ends my character.
In an attempt to make the game feel realistic, PZ has a huge amount of micromanaging which I could totally see being a discouragement for some players. (eg, put the food in the oven, turn on the oven,set temp,  let it cook, remove from oven, chop the food into a bowl, etc) Personally I love it and it's one of my favourite things about the game because I can't get enough of that type of realism. I want my game to feel like I'm just some insignificant dude in a zombie apocalypse, and not some hero. Controls feel good for the camera view and the graphics style is perfect for this type of game.
The devs are quite responsive on the forums, engaging with the community and I feel they really do take fan feedback into consideration. PZ has experienced a huge amount of scope creep, which has been awesome in terms of the game, but also frustrating because the 'final' game release date edges ever further into the horizon. Updates can't come fast enough, and I say that only from a position of love and excitement for the game. However, if you are the type of person who does not have the patience to endure Early Access development, this game is going to drive you mad! I simply can't wait until the new animations and npcs make the game.
The modding community is outstanding and mods range from massive maps, to new items, to quality of life improvements. Workshop is also available, which is awesome.
My final thought is, if you love zombie movies, especially DotD and NotLD, this game is for you.

Knock Down Blow is largely a martial arts sports game, sharing more in common with Budoken (1989) and the like than most other fighting games. It does not feature magic attacks, energy blasts, or even flips; but rather fists, feet, blood, sweat, tears, karate, forklifts and a bear. This provides for a more realistic, restrained, visceral and violent experience that defies the game’s appearance and feels quite unique to the genre.
With liver injuries, skull fractures, brain damage and more all lovingly recreated, this game delivers a real sensation of beating the crap out of someone else, which will appeal to many Steam users. However, Karate Master also delivers a sensation of having the crap beat out of you, which many Steam users will relate to.
Some of the training exercises depicted are tedious, some are momentarily fun. And while there is a cheese strategy or two for the actual fighting, timing and technique are rewarded and the results are most satisfying.

The Great Gatsby: Secret Treasure is an easy casual H. O. Game.
The art syle, the graphics and the atmosphere are nice. It's a bit dark and that totally fits the storyline.
The story is fine enough and it's realistic. At least there's nothing fantastic or supernatural like zombies, monsters, ghosts or vampires.
It takes place at night, it's raining. All this contributes to the mysterious atmosphere in which  the inquiry takes place.
The music is not intrusive, it's not disturbing. It perfectly goes along with the overall ambiance.
Voice acting is fine.
The game isn't difficult at all.. that is, not very stimulating too. You go there, do that, take this, use it over there to solve a tiny puzzle and so on. None of the puzzles are original.
Puzzles and H.O.Scenes are easy : no head scratching, no screeening or pixel hunting during hours.. that means not challenging too. And it adds nothing to the H.O. genre, it's very classic.
Sadly that contributes to make the game lifetime quite short.
It took me
and with that I got stuck during a long time on my 1st playthrough because I didn't understand something with the game UI.
So, about that UI, be aware that sometimes you can click on a pocket watch or on car keys (bottom right hand of the screen). The watch can be use to relive scenes back in time and car keys are needed to travel to some far away places. If you don't get that, you'll soon be stuck like I was.. for days !! I eventually had to use the hint button once to understand that.. (probably because I didn't play the tutorial on my 1st run!).
About "Expert Mode" achievement (no hint/no skip button, on expert mode) :
Like I said, I had to go through the game 4 times to unlock it.
First I thought the "no skip/no hint" to achieve "Expert Mode"  was only applying to mini-games/puzzles and H.O.S. But when my 2nd playthrough wasn't enough, my guess was I still didn't unlock it because I skipped the 1st cutscene on my 2nd playthrough (even though I am still not sure of this).
Since my 3rd playthrough wasn't enough to unlock that achievement, I don't know what I did wrong and what's the catch !  I am sure I have not clicked on the hint buttton by accident and I didn't skip anything (no mini-game and not a single cutscene!).. I wonder if that may be a bug. Unfortunately there are not many players and too little discussions topics for this one to be tackled.
I gave The Great Gatsby: Secret Treasure a last try and it worked (on the 4th playthrough that is!).
Like every H.O.G. The Great Gatsby: Secret Treasure has little replayability value. That being said, as far as H.O.S are concerned I want to acknowledge (since I ran 4 times through the game), that even though you'll often visit the same H.O.S. in a same playthrough, from one playthrough to another the objects you're supposed to find in a H.O.S are not always the same (that's the only thing that changes from one playthrough to another).
Apart from that achievement glitch, there are a few other things I don't like about The Great Gatsby _ Secret Treasure:
-The game being a bit short. The 1st time I reached the end of the game I was surprised that the inquiry was already finished.
-The difficulty. Too easy, even on Expert Mode.
-The map. It shows where available actions are, but it doesn't allow to travel faster from a location to another. That just makes the game seem to be longer but actually it's only forcing you to go through useless places many times.
In conclusion, for those who are H.O.G. or adventure games beginners, getting The Great Gatsby: Secret Treasure on an interesting sale can be a nice way to entertain a few hours.
But achievement hunters and confirmed H.O./adventure gamers should stay away from this one, though I hate to say that, mainly because I really liked the atmosphere of the game and the way it was rendered.

I really wanted to like this game.
I played in open beta and it was frustrating at first but after a few days it got pretty fun.  There were balance issues I figured they'd address, but overall it wasn't a bad experience.
When the game went live, the price was prohibitive for the state the game was in at the time so I held off purchasing.  This weekend though, it went on sale so I figured I'd give it a shot again and see if it had improved.
I was sorely disappointed.  Matchmaking takes absolutely forever with people constantly abandoning the queue for one reason or another (it never really tells you why).  I spent most of the time "in game" in the menu waiting for it to find players to start a game.
Graphically the game is pretty solid, and the sound is also pretty well done; I really like the concept of 4v1 PvP, the controls are pretty easy to get used to if you've played any other FPS games, and the characters have interesting personality and cross dialogue.  But these few bright points are far from enough to save what was ultimately a frustrating experience.
I haven't followed the game at all since beta but it doesn't feel like any of the balance issues that existed back then have been addressed in the slightest (though maybe I'm wrong, I couldn't actually get enough play time in to really tell...but Wraith is absolutely OP).
So in summary, even at half price this game is not worth the buy.  They should've done as everyone else has said before me and gone Free to Play with purchasable content like skins or player models.  As it is there are too few people even playing to make it worth joining a queue for a game.

Let me explain you the concept of the game. You start with a few items (in unlimited quantity) which you can combine with each other in order to produce new things, which can themselves enter into all sorts of combinations. The goal is to create everything. For instance, combining `Life' with `Cave' gives you `Trolls'. Combining `Magic' with `Parchment' gives you `Scroll'. And so on. So, yep, all you have to do is to try all your items to find out which ones can be combined together.
You have hints at your disposal. One hint is free and it reveals one of the element that you can obtain with what you already have. You can spam this hint as much as you want, though sometimes it won't be of much help. The other hint shows you two categories of items and tells you that there exists a combination between two items drawn from each of those categories -you still have to figure which. it reduces considerably the array of choices and is quite useful. Once you have used this hint, it reloads with time (I'd say one minute or so).
Once you have completed the main game, which takes one hour approximately, you can do quests. Quests lie on the same principle of the main game : combination of items to get what you need or what you want. You have little stories to go along with the process, which most of the time has no interest (the Necromancer's campaign being the must funny). Those quests are shorter than the main game.
Finally you have this stupid mini game of a running hero who slashes monsters. You have nothing to do except clicking on heal when he is hurt, on reload when he is out of stamina, and on the occasional chests on your path. You can then buy upgrades with the goal, but frankly, it does not change anything. This is completely devoid of real interest but it can be captivating somehow (mindless clicking at a slow and dizzy pace ; perfect when you are utterly tired).
Also, this is a mobile port, so it says `tap' instead of click, but it is of no consequence. As for me, it works perfectly.

Doodle Kingdom is divided into three modes. First, there is the main game, the Genesis, in which you have to combine two elements to create one of the 116 existing ones : for example, mix "Elves" and "Lumber" to create a bow. Imagine the possibilities ; it gets a bit annoying trying to figure out what elements the devs established, so I made this
to save some players time. Then there are three quests to unlock by discovering the related element in the Genesis. The goal of those quests is regrettably to combine even more elements, although the themes vary : return your Kingdom's glory in "the Return of the King", show off your evil powers in "the Necromancer's Uprising" and breed four elemental Dragons in "how to Train your Dragon".
And then there is "My Hero" : the part of the game I was more interested in, since you're supposed to fight monsters with your character. Basically you have to clic on the chests you find on your way to collect some gold, in order to buy new equipment for your warrior. Your hero runs, flirts with redheads (I know, I know, heroes need some distraction too) and fights the creatures you previously discovered in the Genesis. There are some RPG basics, as experience, gold, quests (kill x monsters, collect x gold, run x meters, etc), equipment and stats (everytime you level up you can spend 2 points on Health, Stamina, Attack and Defense).
My first review was negative mostly because of the frustrating fact that the amount of gold and XP you gained remained the same, no matter your level, so it was really hard to progress and unlock new stuff. Developers don't always listen to the complains, but in that particular case, they actually did ; that's why I'm going to recommend their game this time. Since their major update, the gold and XP in "my Hero" now scales with your level, so you even get extra gold to skip quests (recieving the reward without completing it) to level up faster. There are also some improvements that make the game more enjoyable : for example, you can now sort the elements alphabetically.
Doodle Kingdom remains a simple game but has some entertainment potential nonetheless ; a game I would recommend to casual gamers or people looking for a simple and different experience, specially with a discount.

A very, very atmospheric survival game. If you enjoy scavenging or exploring, this is absolutely worth it for the sandbox mode alone, and the story mode is mostly shaping up great. Below are some good and bad aspects, as per my opinions:
Good:
It's incredibly atmospheric. Never before have you died this peacefully in a videogame, frozen solid under the beautiful northern lights. Speaking of dying...
The game's hard. It's like the Dark Souls of survival games. Play this on Interloper and you'll have to consider your every move like a chessmaster, or you'll die, and die, and die, and die...
The scavenging is top notch. Finding things feels immensenly satisfying. Every sound and every graphic makes you want to scour every nook and cranny.
The story, or at least what we have of it so far, is very interesting.
Bad:
Too many wolves, especially on stalker difficult and in the story mode. I can't step outside without one of those mangy curs howling for my sweet blood. It turns the game from a thoughtful survival odyssey into a hectic wolf-dodger at times.
Tutorials. There aren't enough of them. No, wait, I get why there aren't any in the sandbox mode, but in the story mode I'd appreciate pointers like "be sure to learn recipes from these people you meet, because otherwise you might miss them forever". Or how to turn the darn rose hips into tea...
All in all it's not perfect but for me it's absolutely worth the asking price.

I ♥♥♥♥ing love it.
You can be the best equipped survivor, best armed, stocked for days, and still be torn apart by wildlife, die from an infected wound or food poisoning, or whatever that crazy ♥♥♥♥♥ mother nature has in store for you. You have to balance your warmth, thirst, hunger, and overall condition with your need to continue to scavenge, or to hunt, for more resources.  "Do I have enough time to harvest this corpse before the storm gets worse?" "Do I stay by my fire outside or hope to find shelter before the sun sets?" Things like that you have to consider and weigh the pros and cons for your continued survival. If you fail, or make the wrong call, you go down, and have to restart completely. The game doesn't offer reloading from an earlier save, making every move you make that much more weighted (because, yes, it saves right after you get attacked or finish harvesting something, or dedicate time to an activity).
They streamlined the UI so it's easy to use and survivor-friendly, as well as adding new features such as quartering corpses and stunning rabbits (so you can look into their adorable, friendly eyes before heartlessly snapping their necks because you're starving to death) just to name a couple. All of this in a stylized design that's both beautiful and still ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying sometimes.
Play it. Die. Play it again. Survive. Die. Get better, smarter. Try again.
Go forth and survive you crazy s.o.b.'s.

1. You need to find and pick up a stone (okay)
2. You need to select said stone in your inventory
3. Aim for the rabbit and stun it (okay, cool)
4. Quickly run up to the rabbit and click again to actually kill it
5. Now, the bad design begins: you need to go to the inventory, select the rabbit
6. You need to click on 'harvest'
7. You need to select how much meat your want to harvest
8. Click again on Harvest
9. The raw meat is now on a different menu. It pretty muchs disappear.
10. You need to light a fire (okay, fine)
11. You need to click on the fire after its lit.
12. You need to select the food option
13. You need to select the rabbit meat
14. You need to keep selecting the rabbit meat to cook all of it (theres like 3 pieces)
15. You now need to exit the fire menu screen
16. You need to press space for the radial menu to show up
17. You need to select the food option
18. You need to select the rabbit meat, and eat it.
Calories drain so fast in this game, that by the time you are done (of course the game does not pause during this menu navigation extravaganza) you are actually hungry again. I'm not kidding. You pretty much cross a bridge and all your entire 2000 calorie food supply gets drained. Just like that.

Karate Master 2 Knock Down Blow is a martial arts sim/fighter with an emphasis on precision and coordinated attacks. The mechanics rely heavily on effective blocking, footwork, and precisely timed strikes that reflect the reality of competitive martial arts in that for every attack made, an opening for counter-attack is similarly created. The button-masher in me had his♥♥♥♥♥handed to him early in the game before realizing this was not your mama's typical fighter.
Real life knowledge of your opponent's school of attack will also factor in i.e. Tae Kwon Do's emphasis on footwork and kicks differs greatly from American boxing's heavy punches and speedy footwork.
Visually, KM2 resembles early Art of Fighting Neo-Geo hits with a close up view of the combatants that provides an isolated view of combat while eschewing any emphasis on overly detailed backgrounds. It's you and one other warrior face to face; that's it.
The sound effects, in juxtaposition to the realism placed on combat, are meaty and sonic-boomy in their slapping power while most attacks are chalked full of
that will make you exhale deeply as a roundhouse kick misses your grill by mere inches.
There is a distinct emphasis on training as well as a surface-level understanding of the various elements of real life Karate and those with a background in the actual martial arts will find themselves rather pleased by the integration of the rules & etiquette expected from combatants. These rules will vary and the degree of padding (or lack thereof) required adds an element of risk as bone-breaking attacks during more informal bouts can lead to a significant amount of time out of the dojo spent on the mend as you channel the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your spirit animal.

All in all, KM2's the kind of game you'll probably do a bender through in a day or two but, for the price, it's well worth the nostalgic beat 'em up feel along with solid mechanics and sweet training sequences in the rain while you look determined as a mother.

These meta games are what makes this worth buying at

A fun little twin-stick shooter with classical aesthetics, self-described as Smash TV meets Ghost 'n' Goblins, but merciful modernized additions, notably an easy mode for those of us not of an NES background. I purchased Iron Fisticle some years ago in the hopes of expanding my local co-op library, but It's agnonizing trying to find couch coop buddies these days. I confess to not finishing it.I noticed that this enhanced version of the game had been added to my library at no extra cost, and decided I should play it. I am glad I did. One major difference is apparent: Where Fisticle has only two-player coop, Crypticle upgrades it to four. I was quickly able to complete a basic run solo on easy, but the additional two stages posed by the new game plus mode are quite a bit more difficult. I can only imagine that Iron Crypticle's normal and hard modes would be hair-pulling.
The premise is simple enough: The treasures of the kingdom of Cryptonia have been stolen and its' Princess kidnapped by nasty beasties from the catacombs beneath the castle. Four color-coded royal guards spring into the depths to retrieve them. To this end, they must negotiate a series of square chambers filled to the brim with baddies by flinging various projectiles at them with eight-directional aim. Normally you throw slow-firing axes, but you can pick up temporary powerups including darts, richocheting hammers, shuriken, scythes, two-way bolas, three-way daggers, a blunderbuss and even rockets and flamethrowers, though intully only the darts and hammers are unlocked. New weapons and other powerups are unlocked by completing floors and can then appear in subsequent runs, much like the perk cards of Ziggurat.
Iron Crypticle is sort-of a roguelike, though the variety in the level layout is mostly just walls you can't shoot over, lava pits you can't cross and sandtraps that slow you down.  However, you often have a choice of two or three rooms to enter next after finishing each chamber, and if you find a map item you can plan your route ahead of time. You begin each run at level one, and can reach a maximum of 15 by picking up various food and treasures, with your total score also being your experience points. Leveling up increases your health and your maximum possible stats- but to actually upgrade said stats: movement speed, damage, fire rate and powerup duration, you'll need to actually pick them up. These can be purchased from shops using dropped coins you find, or found when you keep a score multiplier going by picking up lots of food in succession. Getting hit resets this multiplier however.
Aside from the shops, there are a few special stages types that feature enemies not found in normal ones, as well as a room containing an arcade cabinet, where you can pay 10 coins to play a side-scrolling minigame called "Castle Crushers" and earn extra money and score.
It's not my favorite twin-stick shooter, but it's a pretty good one and has a lot of style. Fans of such or action roguelikes may wish to give it a look.

Aquaria is a 2007 indie game made by BitBlot and a winner of Independent Game Festival this same year. The plot follows the female protagonist - a mermaid named Naija - on a quest to uncover her erased past.
The surroundings and ambient are well-crafted and fitting. They make the usual exploration and character upgrade process relaxing and calm most of the time. At times the vibrant sea ecosystem is a reason enough to just give the plot progression a break in favor of simply becoming an observer of wild and two-dimensional nature.
That is not to say the game is an arcade of casual difficulty, however. New areas bring refreshing challenges and require mastery of just-acquired skills.The core combat mechanics revolve around Nadija singing. The songs include shape-shifting and conjuration. Each spell requires certain notes to be sung, visualized as icons spread around the character in a circle whenever singing is initiated. The further the game progresses, the more songs come in handy to allow backtracking to certain blocked-before passages or upgrades. Also, consecutive boss fights are faster and some require juggling through many songs in a short time in order to succeed.
Enemies fought in the water commonly leave ingredients Nadija can use for cooking recipes. These mostly serve as health regeneration and temporary boosts. As enemies do respawn, this is an easy way for the player to balance the game difficulty; cooking may be used extensively to make a boss fight or a tight place easier.
The game controls and UI are consistent with the colorful visuals. Swimming is not frequently visited in games, especially Metroidvanias, however the game does not get in the way. With the size of the game world, map comes in handy almost every minute. The menu of songs, their notes and description is also helpful. On the other hand, cooking interface is crude and could use some user-friendly improvements (cooking many recipes at once, selecting known recipes, seeing which can be cooked with currently held ingredients, etc.)
The bottom line: Aquaria is an enjoyable and well-executed Metroidvania-type game. For current price tag (10 USD) it is definitely worth considering for any fan of this type of games or a connoisseur of 2D indies; If in doubt and no friend has it to share, a demo version is available on the company's site.

If you truly want a review on Doodle Kingdom in a nutshell then I can summarize it for you in three words. Bad. Mobile. Port.
This is a bit of a shame to be honest. I can genuinely see myself really enjoying this and JoyBits' other Doodle games quite a lot on a mobile device. That was what the game was designed for and that is where it is best experienced. However, unlike some other developers who port their games onto Steam as a bit of a money grab I genuinely believe that the developers here thought that their game would play well on Steam. Certainly they would have thought that it deserved to be received better than Doodle God which was the first game that they ported across to Steam.
The game has three modes. Arguably the best of these is the elemental match game where you have to pair elements, people, building, lands, etc. together to create something new. This is fun enough for a short play but can become rather irritating when you feel yourself missing out on combinations. It also doesn't control very well with a controller - or certainly as well as it could or should. Mouse makes the game easier to play and takes away much of the frustration.
The quests are a little short for my liking and are a classic sign that the game has been made with mobile devices firmly in mind. The horde runner style mode is nothing innovative and becomes exceedingly boring far too quickly Again, it would be better on mobile where you can pick it up and put it down and you would view it as an acceptable investment of a few minutes of your time but as a PC game on Steam it falls short.
I'd love to get my hands on this on mobile and spend some time with it there. Unfortunately, it's not a great PC game.

Original review:

The basic idea of the game is kind of neat; you have 3 different game modes to play. The most fun ones for me were the element matchings but that's over quite fast. I think I was done with the game after 1-2 hours, then only the hero mode and 3 more achievements were left for me.
Hero mode feels like an endless mode but without enough interaction. Your hero runs a path if you have enough energy/stamina, and you need to push a button on your controller or click the button with you mouse so he keeps running instead of walking. You basically do that every ~30'ish seconds. The other button is hero healing, you don't need it that often, if at all. Whenever there's a treasure chest above your hero, you press another button on your controller, or you click it with the mouse whever you spot it. That's 99% of it.
The last achievement for me is to get to level 21. After 13 hours of playing, I just hit level 16 (the second to last achievement for me). Getting to level 21 would require another 24 hours, I assume...so I'd rather spend that time on something else.

After seeing a bunch of gameplay videos of Evole i couldn't wait to play it. I expected it to be really fun and interesing,
and after playing for about 10 hours during the Free Weekend i can say that the game met my expectations almost perfectly!
Every match was exciting and fun. Despite the seemingly repetetive nature of the gameplay, every match felt different. Different characters really felt unique, and every monster had it's own feel as well. One match would feel like an exciting chase. Another would become a tence hunt where the hunters have no idea where the monster is, and the monster had an awesome stealth experience lurking around and confusing the hunters. Another match might burst into action in the first 2 minutes and become a long, continuous epic battle.
It's true that it's hard to actually find a match with people to play, but the reason for that is the overwhelming and often unjustified negative feedback on the game...
Everything you read about the dlc pricing, for example, is as relevant to the base game's review as saying that the steak wasn't tasty because the icecream was too expensive...
But even if you don't find a multiplayer game, you can just as well play solo with bots, which have surprisingly good AI, that will 95% of the time act like an actual person, employing different tactics with different characters, and being more effective with those characters then the avarage person, creating a more interesting gameplay experience.
Is it worth the full price? I think it does though you could always wait for it to be on sale.
Is the dlc overpriced? Maybe, but you don't have to buy it. The base game has 15 unique characters (including the

Confused Pelican's Iron Crypticle is a brand new, better realized version of their original, Iron Fisticle. New enemies, bigger maps, more game modes, and 4 player local co-op are added perks to this fantastic top-down, twin-stick, dungeon-crawling action retro game!
It's all about getting hi-scores here; you go room-by-room destroying every monster and picking up as many fruits, coins, and abilities as you can. The dodging and shooting feel intuitive in this twin-stick shooter and the power-ups actually feel powerful like the piercing arrows or scattering ninja stars. Destroying monsters is a joy and boss battles are rewarded with the likes of giant gold carrots, which boost your score! In good rogue-like fashion, each run is a new start, map layout changes, and unlocked abilities carry over, which aids in shooting for a high-score while keeping the game feeling fresh.
Once you have survived, a New Game+ mode opens up with more challenges and rewards like harder enemies and revamped bosses. An endless mode is also available which has you going round-by-round for top score. Take a shot and see if you can emerge victorious in the Iron Crypticle!

GAMEPLAY
Iron Crypticle is a unique roguelike game. Here you have to collect the lost treasures and keep alive when defeating a bunch of enemies.You use the WASD keys to move and arrows keys to shoot enemies. You have a bunch of paths to choose from and each one is a new adventure.Also,it haves some arcade mini-games inside rooms,you can play it again till you have no more coins to play.
GRAPHICS
Iron Crypticle features beautiful retro rogue-like graphics,it's simple,gorgeous and beautiful to see.
SOUNDTRACK
A amazing soundtrack composed by retro musics.
SUMMARY
Iron Crypticle is a game for who wants to play a fun game with a balanced difficulty,since it needs that the player be focused on the missions:Kill the enemies to open the room in time,collect treasure and keep alive.If you think that is a little hard playing alone,you can invite some friends to play with you,since the game has multiplayer support for 4 players.

A great twin-stick shooter with a nice variety of rooms and sense of progression in a run.  The gameplay is something like Smash TV crossed with Binding of Isaac.  Graphics are lovingly detailed and animated pixel art, and soundtrack is satisfying synthwave.  It's a retro style, but it feels less like a SNES-era game, and more like what a SNES game would aspire to grow up to be someday.
The food chaining is useful for score but key for survival: Pick up 8+ foods in a row to get an upgrade.  Getting hit, or going too long without a pickup, resets the chain and you have to start it again.  A couple of helpers: missing a food pickup doesn't break the chian, and picking up coins extends the time limit.  The rooms get more frantic on later floors, so getting powerups lets you keep up with the enemy power curve.
I'm glad I bought this and gave it a try - it has a lot of nice little touches, as well as satisfying moment-to-moment, in-the-zone play.

Do you like Mech? Do you like 3rd person shooters? Are you happy to play a game with a mediocre plot? If your answer is yes to all of these than Front Mission Evolved might be the game for you. Not that you many choices for Mech games on steam.
Front Mission is a series known for tactical turns and hard choices (depending on which console generation you played it on), with a discouraging plot which usually conveys that when the good guys win, they still lose.
Front Mission Evolved tries to convey this, but doesn’t do a very well job of it. It’s interesting that in parts of the game you are on foot as the pilot -usually to open hanger doors to let the Wanzer- (your Mech) through. In these parts you should feel vulnerable, but don’t, even on the hardest difficulty. Even though you are just an engineer, it feels like you are almost invulnerable (and it’s hard to not think that you are when your only options are to basically fire, move and interact with the requested object). It’s not much different when you are piloting your Wanzer. The single player missions are rail shooter like- there is very little deviation on where you mech can walk, but that’s not an issue as you have so many health pickups your Wanzer is again near Invulnerable. I found myself wading through enemies, until you get to the Boss Wanzer(s). These could put up a challenge, but the EDGE mode helps remove almost any difficulty – it gets to a point that it was more fun to not use it as so I could have a running gun battle.  Customizing the Wanzer is fun, but it’s easy to see what your expected to take into the next mission, rather than having real customization choices. If I want to run a Melee only Wanzer, I should be able to in any mission (it should make it harder, not impossible, and I should be rewarded for not overloading it with every gun known to man). All this said, blowing stuff up is enjoyable, even if it becomes repetitive.
Multiplayer was dead for this game in 2011- which is a shame because I think last stand would be fun playing with friends (Arena based survive each wave of enemies). You must earn your upgrades in multiplayer (so it means getting kills and being helpful by completing objectives), but again with no-one playing that’s going to be impossible so I can’t comment if this worked well or not.
You could try for 100% achievements, but with a few being multiplayer only, and some requiring you playing against someone who already has it (like an infection achievement) it’s likely going to be impossible.
This just scrapped by with a recommend, because I’m a big Mech fan. If Mech’s aren’t your thing, it would be best to stay away

I really want to like this game and recommend it, but there are just too many frustrations.
The biggest issue for me is the control scheme.  At first, the keyboard + mouse setup seems both interesting and novel.  You can control the direction of your swim independently from aiming your weapon.  In addition, you can context switch to 'singing' to generate a shield or switch forms.  When it gets to crunch time, though, the control scheme feels like it is working against you.  Boss battles require precise, quick movements, which prove incredibly difficult.
The artwork in the game is very well done.  The range of colors and the use of light and dark give each zone a different feel.  This is one area with no reservations: Aquaria is a beautiful game.  It will remind players who cut their teeth on the SEGA Genesis of Ecco the Dolphin.
The game world itself is enormous.  This would be a good thing if it weren't also so barren.  Much of the game world consists of loops and twisting off shoots that lead to nothing.  There's no reason to explore some of the areas except to learn that nothing exists there.  Worse, the player is given virtually no direction, so you'll spend much of the game simply mindlessly wandering around, hoping to find the next area that will allow you to progress.  Zones typically have at least one and sometimes multiple save points, but finding them can be a chore.
There are a broad variety of enemies, but their attacks boil down to two forms: homing missiles and rush.  Each area is populated with enemies that make sense for the zone, but you'll quickly find that if you just stay in energy form and creep forward you will kill the enemies without too much trouble.  This lulls you into a sense that the game lacks challenge of any kind.  Then you get to a boss fight.
Boss fights are extreme tests of your ability to rapidly change forms and accurately move, target, and react.  This is a monstrous departure from the rest of the game where you can spend most of your time in one of two forms (energy or beast).  Boss fights are typically preceded by a save point, so you don't have to retrace your steps, but you'll get very tired of seeing the (laughable) death scene.
The game includes a crafting system for creating food from recipes.  This is a great way to power up against bosses, but also feels out of place with the theme of the game.  You are playing this mer-person attempting to discover their past, and as you fight for justice you pull the eggs from your enemies, gut fish, and other myriad atrocities against your fellow water folk.  There's even a recipe for making sharkfin soup!  The disconnect is even more jarring when you are in a boss fight, get low on health, and then pause the game to 'cook' a variety of foods to restore health and power up.  I can just imagine the boss accepting you plea for a time out so you can roll some sushi and boil hot soup.  Finding materials for these recipes is a chore.  You'll occassionally run across a plant that you can sing to that will then burst into materials like green leaves or spicy fish meat(!?).  Sometimes a new item will appear and you will instantly know the recipe for it.  Outside of these locations, you'll need to kill enemies and hope they drop what you need.  There's a limit of holding 8 of any particular crafting item, but you'll likely never see that limit hit, as drop rates are terribly low.
I originally purchased this game in 2011.  At that time, I played it for a few hours, but quickly became both confused as to what I should be doing next and bored with the mindless exploration.  I didn't feel as though I was making any progress and moved on to other, more exciting options.  Flash forward to 2016 and with new Steam Controller in hand I thought I would return to the game.  The Steam Controller is ideal here!  The ability to easily dash out a song on the touch pad feels very intuitive.  I explored a bit more, then read the in game manual and found that you can double click the mini-map to get a world map.  This made a huge difference in focusing my wandering around towards specific goals.  I picked up a few new songs, recipes, and defeated a few bosses.  There are some spoilers ahead, so you can skip the rest of this paragraph if you like.  Then I came to the mother/father fight.  This fight requires that you quickly switch between beast and energy form, with no indication that you should be doing this.  In addition, switching forms leaves you open to attack as, at least as far as I'm aware, there's no fast form switching from the controller.  After watching a few videos on how the fight is done I finally managed to complete it.  In fact, I made my way to the final boss fight, and here is where I finally threw in the towel.   I don't have the full complement of health increases, nor do I have the full list of recipes nor mats.  I lacking a few forms, and while I am able to finish off the first form of the Creator, I don't see myself moving beyond that point.  I watched a video of the Creator fight to completion, and that sealed it.  That fight is ridiculous, and I have no desire to go farm all of the materials I think might be necessary to succeed at it.
Given all of these issues, I can't recommend the game.

I wanted to love this game, but to hell with it. It was rich in ideas, but the execution is so poor that it can't be recommended.
It fails to live up to its potential from the moment you get to the first temple. The singing mechanic could be cool if going back into the form you need to do that wasn't a guaranteed opening for the millions of enemies with homing attacks to beat the hell out of you. It's fun swimming around at first, but then the game starts asking for very precise movements out of player inputs that have always amounted to launching the character in a direction and hoping for the best. Giving the character different forms to tackle the hazards in the environment is basically pointless since anything other than energy form (which gives you a ranged attack) leaves you essentially helpless. The huge open world is exciting until you realize that the fast-travel system had a mind of its own and you can't directly select your destination. And enemies constantly respawn. And you have very limited access to healing. Basically the open world is just a way for you to lose health before the absolutely ridiculous boss fights.
The boss fights in this game are not "dificult." They are frustrating. You can't learn their patterns because there aren't any. Their projectiles are almost always homing, so good luck not taking stupid damage during one of your mandatory form switches during the battle. Oh, and keep a walkthrough handy to tell you how to actually beat these things. Does it look like they're taking damage from your blasts? Changing color like how boss monsters to in video games? Sometimes they aren't actually taking damage! Be sure to have at least two strategy guides nearby.
Think I'm being melodramatic? How do you feel about being close to killing a boss - a boss that has the power to launch you around the stage and take any control of your movement and placement in the environment WHICH ALSO HAS SPIKES EVERYWHERE - only for it to throw you out of the stage. You can take the long walk back to the room and finish him off, right? NOPE. Boss fight starts all over again except now you're completely out of healing items since you used them the first time! You had no input in whether or not you get launched out of the stage. This is just a thing that happens sometimes. There are no health items to pick up along the way back. And the tunnel to the boss is covered in spikes. Spikes which you can get bounced between and die from without being able to change into the form whose ONLY PURPOSE is to protect you from spikes.
I'm done with this game. It could have been so good, and that's what hurts. Even if there is a way to get good at the clunky movement, the imprecise aiming of your only weapon, and grind out enough healing items to simply brute force your way through a boss's health bar, it still might launch you out a window and make you start over. I only have one life to live, and I'm not wasting any more precious hours on Acquaria.

Great little metroidvania (but underwater!), full of surprisingly fresh design and great worldbuilding and attention to detail, but marred by unexplainably bad design choices. In this review I'm focusing on the negatives(which I feel haven't been emphasized enough), because the positives have already been described in good details by damn near everyone else.
- Gamepad support is abysmal. Truly, unexplainably abysmal. Menu controls are awkward (and plain don't work in the map screen) and there are no 'look' keys and no form-changing shortcuts (which makes several fights a LOT harder than they should be). The worst part is that the movement on the keyboard is equally bad, so your best bet is to play it on a gamepad and have the keyboard real close to tap the form keys as needed.
- Gimmicky boss designs, especially for some of the optional bosses. The octopus is a particularly annoying offender.
- Save points are sparse, especially in the early game, and always feel like they're slightly too far from the minibosses, which are almost universally harder than the story bosses and likely to take you more than one go.
- Most of the puzzles can be cracked with a little thought and feel quite intuitive, but one in particular on the second-to-last dungeon is a complete♥♥♥♥♥
- Achievement completion pretty much requires guide usage, as two achievements are linked to a hidden, unmarked room in a corner that no one in their right mind would try to poke.
- True ending ends in an obvious sequel hook that will never be covered, as the studio's dissolved.
Aside from all of these picked nits (some of which not so nitty), it's still a gorgeous game, with a great soundtrack, rewarding exploration and cute little touches here and there. Very much recommended, just be ready to deal with some eventual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

The Player and Lily set out to find the stolen invention and hopefully clear themselves of the false charges.

Great idea, and kinda fun, but really not ready for the real world. The game concept itself is great, a bit like other light-hearted racer/shooters such as Mashed or even Mario Kart. The single player offers a few hours of fun races against AIs. But there are two game-breaking shortcomings.
First, it could do with some kind of balance mechanism, like Mario Kart's "catch up" bullet bill. If players get separated from each, they'll just never meet again, leading to a really boring race. This is true for the AIs and human players alike.
Second, a fun racing game like this really needs to be played against humans, but it's so hard to. There's no single-machine (splitscreen or Micro Machines style) mode, so you can only play against someone else with the same game. There's nobody online at all, because it's such a small game. Even if you can find a friend to invite to play, the inviting-through-steam mechanism is really fiddly to get working. And then there's no humans-plus-AIs mode, so you end up with only two people in a race, and because of the first problem you might only see the other player for the first half a lap.
The single-player is reasonable for a quid or two, but the lost promise of what multiplayer might have been spoilt the enjoyment for me. I bought it having read earlier reviews complaining about empty servers, but hoping to play it with friends at LAN parties &c., but even that's no use: no splitscreen, no LAN play, and lack of player interaction in-race.

I like a game with a lot of depth.  I like a game where you an pick it up for a while, and then set it back down again without wondering why it's suddenly gone light outside.  I like a game that has a real sense of itself.  I like a game with a huge replay ability factor.  I like a game that's hard.  I like game where you can unlock future crew, weapons, ship designs, and such.  I like a game that's fun.
And those are some of the reasons why I like Dungeon of the Endless.  While it has perfectly fine sound and throwback graphics and such, the place where this game truly shines is in the mechanics. In the game structure.  In the  play of he game.   You open the door to another room, and then fight something, find resources, build things, and more.  And you explore and face danger constantly.  Different creatures have different fighting algorithms.
And it's an odd mixture of genres.  It has RPG elements, and base design elements and tower defense and exploration and such.  Ultimately, I would place it in the Rogue Like genre of games.  Numerous classes, RPG feeling, perma death, and other additions make me really confident about that too.
Your space ship breaks up, and pieces of it fall to the ground and crash.  You begin with a certainly piece of the ship and a certain character, and can unlock more .  You have different areas of a crashed space ship that you can apart in and gives you different aspects of game play:
Deep, compelling, rewarding and fun.  And sometimes a bit frustrating (in a good way).  That's Dungeon of the Endless

Karate Master 2 Knock Down Blow is in a game in which starts you off on the path of every 80's american martial arts movie ever. Where you start from the very bottom, get your♥♥♥♥♥whooped multiple times before becoming an unstoppable♥♥♥♥♥kicking machine through hard work and dedicated training and eventually running your own dojo. The game is a good for picking up and playing but my biggest problem with it is that after a while the challenge wears off. Even the face off with the big bad guy in the Kumite was very anti-climatic as I cracked his jaw with two blows and the fight was over. The Karate Masters of each dojo don't feel like masters just punching bags with arms and legs. Granted they did give the wrestling school master grappling however I don't think the AI prioritizes the grappling as the wrestler. This is a game that looks like it has a lot of promise behind it but feels horribly limited. Plus I'm not sure who thought the word BEATED was actually a word but apparently it is. The game tries to have some kind of plot as you climb your way to the top but fizzles out eventually and wasn't even that interesting to begin with. Sure each fight has a risk of you getting your skull cracked or leg broken but after toughness level 7 it hardly happens. I can't really complain at getting the game 40% off but there's an SNES Taekwon-do game  you can download the ROM for that's a lot more replayable than this is. There are some challenging side missions like fighting a bull or a bear or jumping over a car but those are too few inbetween the copy paste dojos. Even the Muay Thai dojo just felt like you were fighting one of the earlier Karate dojos. That's really my main gripe is that the masters of each dojo could've been so much more. The Kumite which is the last unlockable tournament could've been much harder than what it was. The move system is relatively easy to follow even to someone like me who gets easily turned away from most fighting games since I can't remember the super autistic combos. Overall if you ignore the thin story line the game is at least solid enough to play. It's easy to get lost on some of the training sessions due to lack of instruction on them but after a bit of trial and error it'll come to you. Really challenging as you start but fights stop going the distance once you start to level off everything at 8-9. Hell you can end most fights in 3-5 blows at that point. If you're curious about it pick it up on sale I wouldn't reccommend it at full price. Not a bad game at all there's just a lot of missed opportunities that are really blatant.

Aquaria was one of the first open-world games I ever played. I entered the gaming world later than most, & wasn't expecting such freedom. The music, artwork, & sheer amount of room I had to explore & challenge foes entranced me. I put over 50 hours into the demo without a second thought, despite the fact that it only allowed me access to two forms & a few areas. Everything from the battle system to cooking items to regain health & create effects was new to me, & I adored every moment of it.
The work that has gone into this game's artwork (much of which is done in watercolour) & music creates an environment that can shift from carefree to ominous in moments. Nadja's form, the environments she explores, & the creatures she battles are unique & beautiful-- & sometimes terrifying.
I own both the computer version & the iPad versions of this game, & the switch from keyboard controls to touch is seemless & inspired. I highly recommend the iPad version for individuals who want to connect with the game kinetically.
What stands head & shoulders above all other elements of this game, though (in my opinion), is the soundtrack. Each song is crafted to evoke a sense of wonder, fear, or joy with exceptional results, to the point that encountering silence creates the sense that something integral to the game is absent. To this day, I haven't encountered music that fit so well with a game's surroundings & personality. Above all, Aquaria's music is what creates the atmosphere I keep returning to, even years later.
While the developers have moved onto different projects, & don't plan to make a sequel, mods exist that expand the game's areas, making it worthwhile to download them. I'll always want to see a sequel, but part of me acknowledges that any follow-up to this game would likely fall flat in comparison.
My final recommendation is that you should buy this game, especially if you have a soft spot for atmosphere & exploration, And of course, incredible music. Aquaria's kept me entertained & inspired for years now, & never disappoints.
