Aquaria by Alec Holowka and Derek Yu is a gorgeous adventure game in the vein of Castlevania and Metroid.  Instead of gothic castles or spaceships, however, the world you’ll be exploring is a beautifully drawn underwater maze, teeming with plant and animal life.  Most of which will try to kill you.
Your avatar in this world is Naija, a blue-skinned, enflippered humanoid with no memories of her past.  When Naija is visited by a mysterious cloaked person who bestows upon Naija a deadly vision, she decides to set out and explore the ocean.  There are forests of towering kelp full of seahorses, ancient civilizations whose ruins hide powerful secret spells, and dark depths where monstrous creatures await to devour unsuspecting travelers.  Naija, in her initial state, has no offensive capabilities, which makes your first couple hours in the game a timid affair of running from fights and dodging enemies.  But she is not helpless for long!  She has the power of The Verse, a magical music power that allows her to take different forms, allowing her to attack enemies or overcome obstacles.  You sing songs by right-clicking and running the cursor over different symbols, to play short phrases, similarly to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.  This is the main way the game gates content.
Most of the world is closed off to you in one way or another at the start, and finding different songs will allow you to overcome these obstacles.  For instance, you might pass a powerful current that you cannot swim into, at least until you find the Beast-form song, which gives your dash so much power you can easily force your way into that tunnel, opening a new section of the waters to explore.  This can be a little frustrating at times, as it can seem that you have nowhere to go, when you actually have to backtrack quite far to find the one entrance that your new power allows you to open.  The game has an adequate map-marking tool, but more than once I gave up and had to consult a walkthrough to progress.
There is also a recipe system that allows you to combine ingredients you find in the world into different foods, which will heal Naija, strengthen certain abilities, or even make her invincible.  Some ingredients can be quite difficult to find, and completionists will be hard-pressed to find all of them without help.  The recipe system can also be a source of frustration, as some of the later boss fights are quite unforgiving, and almost require some of the rarer consumables to survive.
Holowka’s music is quite beautiful throughout the game.  Boss fight songs have high-paced intensity, while the open waters have a grand exploratory solitude to them.  Naija’s home has a quaint little ditty.  Overall the soundtrack is alternatively relaxing and driving.  I listen to it at work when I need to just escape and get stuff done.  The sound effects can get a little grating, as your energy attack will be used approximately 8 million times through the course of the game.  That *schwoosh* sound gets quite old after a while, especially during some boss fights where you’re spamming it constantly.
The visuals are where this game really stands out, though.  That this game was the product of two men is astounding.  The entire world is cohesive and beautiful, full of varied sea life and environments.  Yet everything fits together so well, and nothing seems out of place.  The 2D graphics really shine on any system, even an older laptop.
The mouse-and-keyboard controls are fairly intuitive, allowing you to swim effortlessly and propel yourself with your powerful legs from wall to wall.  The singing mechanic is fun, but sometimes can get a little difficult to control, especially in high stress situations where you want to change quickly between forms.  Nowhere in game does it tell you this, but your songs are actually mapped to the 1-9 number keys, and you can switch effortlessly between them without actually singing the songs.  This makes the game a lot easier, but also takes away some of your immersion.
The ending to the game leaves open the possibility of a sequel, but unfortunately it doesn’t look like that will happen.
This is a great adventure game, but it is not without its flaws.  Every Metroidvania adventure game struggles with backtracking and the potential for the player to miss an important passageway, but don’t let that drive you away from this game.  The game is just gorgeous, and you’ll want to explore each of the tremendously varied zones for their own sake, not just to collect some loot and leave.  You’ll want to go swimming after playing this game.  Just be sure to avoid any sea dragons.

Castle of no Escape 2 is a perfect game for the one who seeks the challenge. A game where you don't have a second chance. Where die means having to repeat everything. You have 3 playable characters, each with his stats and his technique of attack, to adapt to the style of the player, also there are other unlockable characters playing. Castle of No Escape 2 is a roguelike game which puts you in the metal boots of a hero who is tasked with going into an evil castle and defeating its owner. You start by selecting one of the three heroes, a Guardian, a Huntress and a Cardinal all of whom come with their unique stats and attacks. You can also unlock three more characters in the game later on. These characters are unique and feel different from each other than mere stats appearance.
For Example, The Guardian can enhance the length of the sword and has good attack and defence at the cost of his speed. The Huntress Lizard has speed and a mix of melee attack and ranged attacks but her attack is very low. The Cardinal is a whole different beast. He uses fireballs to attack but with an accuracy that is all over the place. The said fireballs can sometimes act as heat seeking missiles while at other times they will twist and turn to hit the farthest wall when your opponent is two steps ahead of you.
Castle of No Escape 2 feels like a nostalgic throwback to the games of 90s with the inventory management system, simple in game items and such. Enemies you kill drop some special items or coins. These special items can range from potions to sword artifacts which you need to collect to defeat the owner of the evil castle. The gold coins can be used at different vendors which you will find in various rooms to buy potions etc.
What really impressed me about Castle of No Escape 2 was its enemy variety. Ranging from a general minion to medusa like creatures who turn you into stone temporarily if you come in their sight to teleporting ghosts. The game has a few rooms which give out a very creepy vibe and keeps you immersed.
The story is basically nothing where a few seconds of lines explain the mysterious castle and tells you to go in just because you are a hero. The game has subtle humour inserted in it quite masterfully and you will often meet characters who seem like vendors but they will go on to say “I have nothing for you”. The randomization is good but repetition of the reused rooms set in quite quickly. There are a few rooms with puzzles but they are not head scratchers.
The problems with Castle of No Escape 2 lies in its UI. The inventory is not really user friendly and the game has the worst habit of taking you back all the way to the cutscene to the start of the game when you die. This can easily create frustration and the game also quits with a tap of the escape key which can lead to loss of your progress. The game did give me cheap deaths some times and the movement of the characters is somewhat clunky but those are minor nitpicks in what is otherwise a fun and enjoyable game.
Castle of No Escape 2 reminds me of the NES games of the old when pixelated art was still a thing. The game perfectly recaptures some of those magic moments and while the colour palette is not really that enticing, it is good enough to keep you hooked on.
Complimenting the visuals is the nostalgic soundtrack which recreates the environments of the previous games perfectly. This is a part where Castle of No Escape 2 excels in and it should keep you happy for the time you play.
Castle of No Escape 2 is a fun game. It is cheap, enjoyable, nostalgic and has replayability if you’re willing to put enough time into it. At the price it stands on, it is completely worth buying if you like roguelikes and/or are looking for a nostalgic experience.

I still feel as I'm only scratching the game's surface, but a basic review is quite due, as so far everything I experienced in the game was really nice, save the little weird menu system, but that comes from the very simple control scheme.
About the game in a nutshell: you're playing in a randomly generated, 6*6*6 cube, trying to find the *true* shards of the legendary weapon that's required to kill the boss. The graphics are exactly as shown in the story, the controls are working very nicely as they should, as the game only allows you to attack in the direction you're facing, so controlled movement is an essential gameplay element. If I noticed correctly using the normal attacks use some kind of stamina-like system, making the character tired after attacking, and using it at low stamina makes the attack, or it's reach to be less than at it's full potential. So, combat-wise caution and attention is recommended.
The rooms have a quite unique things compared to BoI and similar room-based games: they stay open, so if you can go around enemies, you can just leave the rooms without fighing, adding actual risk-reward system for stopping and fighting , as the game has quite some tricks up in it's sleeve.
There are traps (they damage enemies as well). Enemies that will change forms and required to kill multiple times. Teleporting enemies, enemies that ambush you in a seemingly empty/cleared room, enemies disguising themselves as neutral NPCs or hiding in chests (!).  There are rooms with spiders that shoot slowing webbings at you, while other rooms have ice patches that makes movement slippery and combat much more risky.  And considering all of this the game is still fair - after facing these problems one can prepare for them and avoid losing health or dying to them.
The game's difficulty comes from the unknown and new threats, but they can be overcome with practice, care and experience. The good controls are also encouraging one to return to the game, so it's safe to say that the game is a really pleasant experience.

Presumably none of the developers had ever flown a plane, played a flight sim or even tried a flight-based arcade game before.
You can put the plane in knife-edge flight not by using the aileron (roll left/right) controls, but a completely different set of inputs. I can sort of live with that. But when you ARE in knife-edge flight, the elevator/aileron controls behave in the same sense as they do in level flight. i.e. moving left will turn your plane horizontally left, not roll it. And pulling back on the stick doesn't put you in a tight turn; it moves the plane vertically upwards.
This is so counter-intuitive and WRONG I'm almost reluctant to play it any more, lest I get used to flying like this and find myself incapable of controlling any of the other plane sims/games/RC aircraft I own.
I understand this isn't trying to be a sim, but even the most arcady of flight games get these simple inputs right.

You build major modules to gather resources in different rooms, you control where the power goes (limited amount) and  you have to strategically play to create bottlenecks not to get swarmed. Fun and challenging, definitely hard, and gives a very rewarding feeling when you pull off some great plays. There are some minor annoyances that promote singleplayer ahead of multiplayer, but hopefully they will be fixed soon.
If you think the game looks cool, i'd urge you to give it a go. It's not for everyone though, so if you don't like it, steam has a great return policy.

A sincere challenge in terms of learning the best strategies to complete a dungeon.
Character's are very different and you have to learn to play with each one in terms of who can solo a room, who does well in a team setting and what combination of four characters can carry you through a dungeon. The possibilities here are immense in terms of outcome and with a bit of luck you can always end up with a solid team.
The dungeons themselvese can be brutal. What may have been a seemingly easy 4th or 5th level ends up being a game ending 6th. You really have to utilize your characters to block off choke points, garrison unpowered rooms to keep spawns at bay and know when you hold your ground or retreat. And since the dungeons get larger and larger, it only gets more difficult as you go along. Hopefully, you've learned not to swing open too many doors in too many directions...
In all, this game is great. The visuals are classic and stunning with a great aesthetic. There's a wry humor to the game, as  can be found in the elevator exposition, and the soundtrack is to die for. You should buy this game literally just for that alone.

Very impressive logistical/mechanical/logic-based puzzle game; each challenge is a mix of building a route, building a machine, and building a program all in one. The production challenges linking several boards (reactors) together to work toward an end result give it a level of freedom and satisfaction I've never seen in a puzzle game before.
It has more in common with building a road network in simcity or warehouse network in a trading sim than navigating a maze, pulling levers in the correct order, or rearranging blocks. You're given an input and are challenged to reach an output, but you're given a lot of tools and freedom to get there how you like. Check out the demo if It sounds interesting. Highly recommended.

Zombie Kill of the Week - Reborn is 2D survival shooter!
The game has a rather simplistic thematic, the objective is to survive as long as you can while wave after wave of  zombies attack you. Every wave increases its strenght and resistant so the difficulty to kill them all increases too.
You can earn gold during the game that you can use to upgrade your weapons (there are may kind of them: guns, bombs, shotguns,uzis and a katana) unlock doors or open some fridges.
Zombies drop money too, bullets or some power-ups that are going to help you.
The game has a "level-up" sytem with some perks and some more weapons to unlock.
Behind this simplicity is hidden an addictive way to play, there are some different game modes: single player survival mode, the challenge where you limit your basic weapons and can't buy or upgrade weapons, or the cooperative multiplayer for up-to four players. You can also play with bots if you find some cell phones in the game.
You don't expect to find the same graphics of L4D2 or the same kind of music and sounds but in general they are correct and nice, animations are smooth and there are a lot of pixels of the screen covered by blood.
In my opinion, four maps are too few, but you have an editor to make your own and share to the rest of the players.

After SIX YEARS this game is still not completed, and still lacking major features that were promised (in particular, AI characters). After not having played the game for quite some time, I booted it up only to find that the game stuttered constantly (on my PC, with an i7 6700k, 64GB of DDR4, and a GTX 1080) and had other issues related to screen resolution on my 4k monitor, which required me to manually edit configuration files. These relatively minor issues have much more significance when you've been waiting for six years for a game to release, with no end in sight.
I chose to hold off on leaving a negative review for quite a long time, solely because the developers have consistently made updates every Monday, complete with bug fixes, descriptions, and screen shots. Individual updates seem to indicate real progress is being made -- that major features are always just around the corner! -- but if you look at the progress that's been made in the last six years, and compare the state of the game today to what it was over half a decade ago, it becomes obvious relatively little has been done.
I get being patient waiting for games. I understand the point of Early Access. None of that excuses this. Don't buy this game, even if it goes on sale, and even if it releases with the features that were promised. This game is a great example of why you should be extremely wary of buying any games in Early Access. Buyer be warned.

In StoneHearth, you begin the game on a randomly generated map similar to a Minecraft map. The gameplay is similar to a strategy game, as you do not control directly any character. You just give orders and expect them to be followed. You start with 7 Settlers, each having their own sets of strenghts & weaknesses. One may be thriving in handcrafting while another is suited for military missions. With these settlers, you'll build and develop a camp thanks to all the resources available. These resources are various, and it can be compared here with Terraria for instance.
To grow, you'll focus on developing the skills of your settlers, assigning them jobs, and gathering as much resources as possible. But these objectives can be endangered by the presence of enemies at night: zombies, skeletons, goblins. You'll have to manage a small military force to protect yourself.
The final objective of the game in its current state is more or less to build your 'perfect base', and survive long enough to do so.
Similar games:
- Stronghold
- The Settlers
Cool features:
- Daily events and Trade, to earn gold and buy resources you lack of
- The Building design system, which is quite good and allow you to design your dream city/base
- Progression system for settlers
In its current state, the game is good, and the potential is interesting. I recommand it if you enjoy this kind of game (Check the Settlers especially).

The very first level is a tutorial that teaches you all you need to know, although the button prompts could be a bit more specific other than 'press the jump button to jump', as I use a 360 wired controller, I found myself referring to the controller scheme more often than not.
After that, it's mostly repetitive mecha shootouts until you reach the boss fights, each level you complete unlocks more parts to use (more limbs for your mech, better energy limit, more abilities etc).
These boss fights mind you are very sudden, there's no preparation phase before the fight so you fight them with what you brought in form the last level. There is however an option to customise in the start menu, but that restarts over from level/checkpoint start. They aren't a problem until you reach the really late game (which for me was about 4 hours in), where you'll need to pack a lot of fire power and a pile driver to even have a chance at defeating them, that is unless you spend more than 6 hours getting good at playing the game.
The only problem with this game is that it expects you to heavily rely on what the game calls the 'E.D.G.E' system, mostly an overclocked mode, similar to Trans Am or Destroy/Unchained Mode of gundam. It allows you to basically missile spam without wasting cooldown or ammo.
It's very low end rig-friendly, although you might encounter a few frame skips here and there form loading zones, which is to be expected from such an old game.
Apparently there is a new game plus mode, but no achievement for completing the game on any difficulty but hard after your first playthrough, which really limits the replayability.
I would reccomend this to armoured core/lost planet enthusiasts.

It's a fun 2d roguelike dungeon crawler with addictive playability that can remind you of the good ol NES days with it's music and art style. The exploration is fun and challenging as every room is randomized with different enemies. You're able to pick up a certain number of power ups to help you on your conquest to create the epic sword to vanquish the final boss but be wary of the debuffs!
You have three characters to choose from and there are 3 other unlockable characters which I assume you obtain by beating the game. Each character plays differently and shows the stats of what their strengths and weaknesses are. For example the Cardinal that I chose to play is a range character with high damage output and low defenses. His basic attack is ranged and the projectiles are random but they do go in a pattern, so let’s say his basic attack goes diagonal it will go diagonal for a set number of times then switch to going straight for a set number of times if that makes sense. His heavy attack is a three triangular projectile attack, you can only use it a certain amount of times but you can find items to replenish it.
I found facing random enemies in different rooms kept me on my toes as every enemy has a simple learning curve, for example if you're in a room with statue enemies they revive all the enemies in that room so it's best to get out of there! If you're in a room and it seems to calm it's an ambush!
The one problem I found in the game was the explanation of the power ups and debuffs, for example for the "Book of Stuck" debuff,,,,it took me a bit to figure out it disables your attack. That's the only thing I would fix is the explanation in game, the manual does well for explaining what does what but it would be nice to have a simple text or image of what the power up for debuff did.
I would definitely recommend this game for someone who enjoys simple dungeon crawlers and loves the old NES charm. I'd highly recommend playing this game with a keyboard and reading the manual!

A great rogue-like dungeon crawler. It's one of those games that requires you a few tries to finally get it. You'll likely die on the very first floor on your first attempt, but as you play again and again, you start to witness how much strategy and team micro-management is actually required to succeed.
The premise of the game is as follows: There are 12 floors in the dungeon. After every 2 floors you're in a new type of zone with new types of enemies, each time getting harder and harder. There's a wide choice of heroes to pick, though most are locked at the start. You can pick any 2 to begin with, and over the course of dungeon crawling you'll be randomly coming across others and able to recruit them to make up a team of 4.
Now here's where you have to get tactical. You have a crystal that is your power source, which you must protect at all costs, and as you make progress through the dungeons, you find Dust, which is used to power up the rooms. Rooms where you've restored power allow you to build researched modules that generate resources for you or act as buffs, whereas rooms without power are dangerous and can randomly spawn mobs every time you open a door anywhere on that floor. The goal is to find an elevator on your current floor and to bring your crystal power source there.
So the game involves a lot of planning, strategy, tactics, and team management, as well as a bit of luck. As with most rogue-like games, if you lose at any time (team gets wiped out or crystal gets destroyed), you have to start over from the very beginning again. Losing in this game can feel rather demoralising if you've gotten far, since a single dungeon run could take a few hours rather than half an hour that many other rogue-likes have.
A bit of trial and error is required to grasp the mechanics of the game and learning from one's mistakes, particularly where hero combinations are concerned, as some can result in unexpected cutscenes in between levels where one of the party members gets killed off by another.
The gameplay is really addicting if you like tactics and turn-based mechanics, but as I mentioned, it is hard, so be warned. There are two difficulty levels - 'Too Easy' and 'Easy', but they're more like 'Normal' and 'Hard', so don't be fooled by the wording. If you don't mind the challenge, then this game is definitely worth getting. You can play it both solo or multiplayer co-op.

I was freezing. My God, was it cold. I couldn't feel my feet. I couldn't see but four feet in front of me in the dark. The snow was falling in thick blankets, blocking out the moon and stars which I know had to be shining above. I continued through the snow one step at a time, until I found an abandoned tractor. I pulled myself into it and shut the door. I needed to take an inventory of my supplies.
I was severely dehydrated, so I drank the last of my water. I was starving, so I ate my last granola bar. I had to find some place to warm up. I was dead tired and needed sleep. I had light winter clothes. Nothing suitable for the conditions I was in. I had only one flare in my backpack. I couldn't stay in this tractor over night, or I would freeze to death. I needed to go find some place to weather this storm.
I lit my only flare and opened the tractor door. The wind hit my like a brick wall, throwing snow in my face. I took a few steps forward before I saw it. Only 6 feet away, lit by an eerie red glow from my flare. A huge bear. I stopped immediately and started backing toward the tractor, when it spotted me.
It lunged at me, knocking the flare from my hand. It ripped and clawed at my face. All I could do was fight as best I could. Finally it was off me. The bear took off in a random direction.
I was bleeding badly from my neck and arm. I desperately tried to patch myself up. I needed to stop the bleeding before I bled out. My hands, numb and clumsy, finally wrapped my only bandage around my neck wound. I was still bleeding from my arm, but not bad. My flare was a few feet away from me. I stumbled toward it. I was in bad shape. I needed help immediately.
I finally reached the flare and picked it up. As I picked up the flare I saw it in the distance. A cabin!! Finally!! If I could only manage to make it there. I could start a fire and warm up, find some supplies to heal, scrounge a sip of water and find some food. I could survive!
I started moving toward it. I was hurt badly and stumbling. I was close now, just a few more feet. My vision was blurry and everything hurt. I just needed to get to the door. Only two more steps and I'd be there. Then I heard it. The bear had returned to claim his meal. One step left. Just one more. I can hear the bear running at me. The last step. I'm at the door. I grab the handle just as the bear lunges at me.
All I see is snow tumbling all around me. The bear, face glowing red from my flare, is on me. His teeth bared, eyes crimson. He reaches at my face. Suddenly, all I see is blackness. "You have faded into the long dark."
That was my very first experience with the Long Dark. That was the moment I knew this game had potential. I sat on my sofa shivering at the thought of what had just happen. This game is like no other I've ever played.
It has its flaws. Certainly, I wish my stats didn't drop so drastically. I wish there was just a little more supplies around. If only it was a little easier, and I could survive for more than just one day. I suppose that's what makes this game so good to some people. It is hard. To me that makes it a little boring. I get tired of only surviving for a day or two. It gets old knowing how quickly I will need water or food. I can't even scrounge for enough supplies before one of my stats are empty.
The controls and menus are a little clunky. It feels like you go out and collect a lot of supplies, but you don't live long enough to ever use them. People talk about fishing and hunting. I'm never able to make it that far before dying of something else first.
There is so much going on in the menus, I don't have time to learn it all before I succumb to starvation or thirst. It feels complicated and I wish it could be simplified some and a little more user friendly.
The game is beautiful, however. The scenery looks amazing. The atmosphere really draws you into this world. You actually feel like you are there. There is so much to explore and see. Again though, I don't feel like I get to explore enough and enjoy the scenery and atmosphere because I'm too busy worrying about starving or freezing. It seems a little too fast paced for a survival and exploratory game. That is part of the appeal to a lot of people though. The constant threat of death looming over you. I just wish it had some quiet moments and down time instead of constant struggle.
Overall it's a great game. Not for everyone, but certainly has a lot of potential to be amazing. While I like it a lot when playing it, I find myself becoming a little bored after just a couple times playing.
TL;DR: Great game with a lot of potential. Awesome visuals. Hard to survive for more than a day or two. A constant struggle for survival with no downtime to relax and enjoy the beautiful scenery. I recommend trying this game. Maybe wait for a good sale to purchase it, though.

Inferno Puzzle is an ugly match 3 game. I'd like it far more if I enjoyed what I was looking at. The icons look like they're different art styles taken from different sources, the buttons have no images on them so they're just the default button. The meters on the side look out of place.
For those unaware, match 3 games involve sliding tiles to match 3 or more colors in a row. Once those are matched, they disappear and the higher tiles fall down because that's how gravity works. Getting four in a row results in the entire line being cleared, which I do enjoy. Its an enjoyable genre that I can get lost in. There are plenty of games out there that do it better and look like a cohesive product rather than a mishmash of backgrounds, tiles and buttons blended together.
The thing that keeps my interest with Inferno Puzzle is there's a goal, you have 10 moves to get some sort of score. Its never explained so I just assume that's what it is. Its good to have an objective and to diversify these puzzles. When one ends, a new one begins.
When you start the game, you select from an array of 21 buttons strewn about on the title screen. These are the 21 different puzzles. The higher the puzzle, the more hollow tiles there are. These hollow tiles cannot be used and tiles will fall through them as if they were ghosts. When you score high enough, you move onto the next puzzle.
Other issues I have with the game is there's no full screen, but there's barely a title screen. The game should use the inferno / Hades theme more. Work fire into the game, tiles should burn up as they dissipate. The Unreal engine logo is still on the menu bar.
Everything about Inferno Puzzle says its low effort. With that said, its a tough price to beat and the game is competent. You can always get a refund. A big shout out to Lawman who bestowed this game upon me. Now that's the magic of friendship when you can send your friend a game like this and still remain friends.

While technically playable, 'Inferno Puzzle' doesn't put in the effort to make their match-3 experience stand out from the deep pool of similar games.  While the lack of polish in every area makes this game sink to the bottom.

A grotesque dark-themed match-three game...with jazz music. A Review by
After selecting a level from a very unordered menu, you'll get thrown into a match-three game without any instructions. Obviously, you got to drag tiles into rows of at least three. There are no special tiles, but based on the positions of matched tiles and their number, you can eliminate one or two rows at once. Once a level is finished, a big button with laudatory words (depending on how many points you got) appears in the middle of the screen. You have to click it in order to proceed to the next level. At least that is what hopefully happens, but there is no way to verify this. The level also could just have restarted.
Nothing besides the mouse is needed, you'll use it to drag tiles from one row to another and to navigate through the menu.
Since the game image shown when downloading Inferno Puzzle has a white stripe right in the game logo, there is no exit button in fullscreen mode, some tiles lost their aspect ratio by improper scaling and the game's icon is the default unreal engine icon, it appears to be made by a single person without much effort.
Inferno Puzzle tries visually to create a very dark atmosphere, while the music tells something different.
Even though Inferno Puzzle does only cost $0.99, it is too minimalistic and unpolished in order to be worth the money.

Do not be fazed by my thumbs down. Come back to this game soon and it will probably have earned a thumbs up.
Pros:
-The noise you get when you have 3 or more in a row is ridiculously satisfying.
-The "dark" theme of the game is an interesting concept.
-I also like the idea of having holes in the board. I have never seen it before - but then again, I don't play too many of these types of games.
-The music is nice. Very nice. It makes me want to work as a receptionist.
Cons:
-Uncompressed, the game and its assets are a ridiculous 805 MB. This should not be the case; all the images are low resolution and the music shouldn't be too large. Common Redist is only about 120 MB.
-The game looks too amateur. It feels as if it was made for a school project or something - and in that respect, it's good.
-The level select menu looks messy.
-When playing a level, the text looks messy and out of place.
-The buttons beneath the score are not aligned.
-The icon when running the game is the Unreal logo.
-It runs slowly for a matching game.
-The game doesn't tell you when you're boned. That is, if you can't make a move, the game doesn't let you know.
-All of the buttons look different.
Possible Improvements:
-The game would look much better if the level buttons were placed neatly and looked the same.
-I like the idea of having a "dark" themed background image, but please consider having a background that won't make the left side of the screen look messy.
-Instead of using a generic font for the title screen and desktop icon, consider making some custom artwork.
-My biggest recommendation would be to code the game yourself, engine and all. UE4 is great, but you don't want to be giving them 5% of your profits and wasting several MB of space with their engine. It shouldn't be too difficult to code this game if you learn C++ or Java (or something).
tl;dr:
In my opinion, the game needs some work. The concept is nice, but the implementation needs to be touched up. There are places where the layout appears messy, and the game runs slowly.

This game brought out the kid in me! It reminded me of my childhood exploring a game with wonder, amazement and curiosity. This game brought out those familiar feelings. It's the best metroidvania's out there!

Good game, I quite enjoyed it! I suggest it to people that want a metroidvania type of game as long as they can tolerate some repetitiveness (especially on terms of the music).
Game length is aprox. 9-11 hours if you are aiming for 100% completion (getting all collectibles, extra bosses, achievements, etc). Far more if you go in blind without using a guide.
Pros:
+ World size and design. The map is massive and while yes most of it is underwater locations (ex: underwater caves, sunken ruins, the deep sea abyss, etc.) they all present a beautiful and proper design, each zone even has several unique sorts of flora and fauna that don't even attack you or serve any big gameplay purpose, they are just there to make the world feel alive and it works.
+ The story. It is not the best ever, but it works for the game and is good enough to motivate you on keep playing it.
+ The song system. At first it feels kind of useless since its mostly used for very easy puzzle solving but about halfway through you find yourself using it more often and becoming more adepts at performing the proper songs in order to quickly switch abilities/forms/attacks in the heat of battles.
+ Naija. The character you play as does start as the usual cliché of "amnesia case" deal but luckily that's not really the main focus or the big motivator for the adventure to start, rather more the fact she just wants to see the world and understand it. It also helps a lot that the voice actress really nails it on expressing the way Naija feels, thinks and evolves as the game goes on.
+ Boss fights. The first ones are simple and easy, which is fine, but as you go on you will find each boss requires more specific strategies and plays with all of your forms and abilities in order to beat them. Some of them can even have you sit there wondering how to beat them for a long time if you go in blind and don't use a guide.
+ Price. Considering the amount, quality and length of content this game has, I think it is entirely worth its full price, I'd even dare say a bit more than that.
Cons:
- The general combat. While on boss fights you will see each one requires very different and fun strategies to beat them, the rest of the enemies, the common mobs you will run into while exploring the map most of them are either pointless to fight and easily skip-able or just punching bags you spam the energy form bullets on. This also leads to another letdown because while Naija can get several forms and most come with an attack of some form, most of the time you will find yourself just using the "energy" form since it is the most effective (homing bullets) and easiest to fight with.
- The food/cooking system. Not really a very bad thing but it felt pretty dull. You are meant to go around farming for ingredients to make food, which is the only way you can heal on battles or to give you temporal buffs, while collecting lots of recipes as you explore the world... but not only there are a lot of pointless recipes and ingredients on the game, some of which you will probably never even use, but I never found myself in need to farm for ingredients or to cook food much, heck I only cooked food at the start, near the mid and right before the final boss.
Other:
The soundtrack is... a hit or miss. Half of it is different versions/mixes of the main theme song which even has a story importance, and if you like it cool, but If you don't like that one theme... well, yeah. (Hint: watch the trailer video here on the Steam store page of the game. That music on the first minute or so? expect to hear it and similar versions of it for about 50% of the game) Mind you, the music fits the theme of the game and the zones and I liked it, but it repeats so much it can be a bad thing for a lot of people.

Who is this Game For?
==================
For people that like 2D action adventure puzzel games. Something like an underwater Castlevania, with shades of a 2D space shoot-'em-up.
Is it good?
=================
If you ever find yourself staring at your computer monitor longing for a well made, easily accessible and thoroughly enjoyable action game then Aquaria is for you.
Does it have any problems?
========================
There seem to be no major problems with running the game on PC.
Final Thoughts!
====================
Aquaria's certainly prone to leaving you disorientated, some of its puzzles are quite oblique and it's in no hurry to tell you what to do, and its mechanics lack the inventiveness of a game like Zelda, but then the fact it's two friends coding together over the Internet shouldn't be overlooked when taking note of the fact that they come surprisingly close.

Fantastic game. I love rougelikes, but of the dozens I've played only a small handful have really captured my imagination (FTL, Isaac, Desktop Dungeons). This one is looking to be my favorite, mainly for two reasons.
The first is how much depth it gets out of very simple mechanics. The rules of the game are so simple that the tutorial only takes a minute or so, but their ramifications can give you all sorts of situations to figure out once you know what's going on. You're constantly deciding which door to open and who to send where, and it's meaningful because in such a tight game every move has immediate consequences. Combine this with a fairly low RNG impact (everything is random but no single roll is gamechanging and they roll rapidly enough to even out immediately) and you get a game that feels very fair (which is why it gets away with being as punishing as it is).
The second is how clear the game is, due to it's small scope. DotE is part of a trilogy: the one is basically CivV, the next is CivV in spaaaaace, this is a dungeon crawler with Civ-esque mechanics and a maximum of 4 units. In the large-scale 2 thirds of the trilogy, you'd pretty quickly have only a vague idea of what's going on because you've got so many distinct cities/planets with their own buildings/stats/etc. It was difficult to get too in-depth with those games, but in this one you can easily zoom out and eyeball the map and immediately see everything important. At first I found myself wishing that I could mouse over the enemies/structures/everything and see their stats, but then I realized that isn't what this game is about. Elements are set up in such a way that make immediate visual sense, and while there are some moments where it would be useful to pause and math out a solution to something, you can usually just eyeball it. Some may disagree but I really enjoy this aspect, since you spend less time comparing numbers and more time experiencing the gameplay.
So in short, if you have any interest in a fusion of rougelike and 4x mechanics, give this a try. It's hard and will punish you pretty hard for a serious mistake, but in a very fair way, and even if you're losing a lot it's still quite fun.

There is so much to fathom or take into account involving Undertale; is it taking a little too much from its predecessors, or has it hit the perfect spot of being its own unique experience?
Well i definitely think the latter is what won me over, being a person who has played and experienced the other games that Undertale has cloned slightly (Earthbound, Mother etc.). The game distinguishes itself overall by its own unique quirky humour and moments, something that is kind of missing in today's gaming industry. Something that gives the game its own distinguishable style. Games like Portal are examples of this as they use an engine of visual style of other games (Half-Life, Source) yet somehow easily distinguish themselves from the others due to their incredible small stories and little slice of atmosphere put into it through the labour of love from the developers.
I am kind of rambling on, but my point still stands; Undertale is a game which from a couple of glances could fool anyone into thinking its just some kind of clone Japanese-esque RPG, but what it brings to the table that really makes a far better game than the others is the sheer atmosphere and level of emotion the game invokes on the player. The characters designed and the unique idea of the "game state" style of interaction, where the game acts completely self aware really make the game for me. The style of the fighting involved is something that really hasn't been done before quite as well as this game. The polish and unreal attention to detail in everything in the game makes it pretty damn hard to find any plothole that sticks in your mind (looking at you Bioshock Infinite).
This game genuinely gave me hope for something great to come out of the Indie market. While a lot of developers these days are quick to throw "early access" and half finished products with little to no effort or labour involved in them, this game really shows that the indie market can outweight triple budget games by putting in some real passion to the works.
Overall I would give this game a 9/10 easily just from how well Toby Fox has made it, simply put. Well done, man, and I hope this isnt just the final game you make. This world needs more people like you, who make gaming be more than just playing a video game to pass the time.

First Impressions Video:
Castle of No Escape 2 is a surprisingly good little rouge like.
It is clearly made to resemble an old gameboy game. The controls are reminiscent of a D-pad and two button system. In the end, they definitely succeeded at making it feel like an old gameboy game.

SpaceChem is, without a doubt, the best puzzle game of 2011, and will likely remain the best puzzle game available for years to come.  It reminds you, again and again, that the reason you're failing is because you aren't thinking correctly.
You will open a puzzle, stare at it for five minutes just trying to comprehend how to begin - then spend half an hour designing your circuits only to find out that they fail before even nearing completion - then quit in frustration and spend the next two hours playing a different game; but it's there, eating away at you from the back of your brain.
Calling in a mortar strike - what if I moved the input to-
Slaying a goblin tribe - How about bonding first-
The tentacle glistens menacingly - I KNOW!
You'll rush back to your flawed design, it'll stare up at you mocking how dumb you were the first time you tried - how could you have EVER thought that would work?  Tinker a little here, move some things there - aha!  Success!
Time for another...

"Well it's just another dime a dozen roguelites. I guess I'll just give it a quick go"
I was never so glad to be wrong. Castle of no Escape 2 is a great roguelite with aesthetics resembling NES era games which actually extend beyond just visuals, with (optional) sprite flickering and NTSC and PAL differences that can be tweaked to your heart's content in the options menu. The game uses four main buttons: ATTACK / SPECIAL ATTACK / INTERACT / PAUSE and the arrow keys, which means you don't have four extra directional keys to aim your attacks; positioning is everything. This simple key scheme and ability to move at blindingly fast speeds with some characters makes for some great momments of fast thinking and quick maneuvering as you zigzag your way through enemies, rewarding fast thinking in unison with careful planning of your movements.
All characters have their unique playstyle which make revisits to the castle all the more unique, but with the current somewhat limited room layouts you will have seen almost every room pattern by the end of a full exploration run, something that may take away the game's lasting appeal. There is also not much space for character customizations, which is limited to a single slot among the various gems and mcguffins you'll be collecting in order to face the game's final boss. You'll be mostly doing your own challenge runs by limiting your pickups
Overall this game is a solid 8/10, only being held back by its current limitations but still being a damn fun experience! Got 7 dolars to spare? Then what the hell are you waiting for? The game's right there!
PROS
-NES fidelity
-Character playstyle variety
-Simple and satisfying combat and movement
-Smooth difficulty curve going up to the sixth floor
-Enjoyable boss battles
-Great cost x enjoyment
-LIZARD GIRLS
-L I Z A R D   G I R L S
CONS
-Somewhat limited replayability
-A few bugs here and there
-Slowdowns (intended and part of the NES charm, but some might find this troublesome)
-Can get visually overwhelming in rooms with lava
-Enemies might get cheap shots at the entrance of rooms
NEUTRAL
-Item functionality requires some guesswork or a quick look at the game's manual
-No challenge mode. Make your own
Probably worth noting: I was told by one of the devs this game will be receiving updates in the future, which may or may not include a room customization option! Stay tuned!

Excellent little arcade style rogue-lite game. The game's incredibly fast paced and pretty relentless, there's enough elements here to keep the pressure on, during an entire run there's very few moments where the player can get truly comfortable with their resources and the constant threat of enemies and traps. The music's servicable but nothing that will get stuck in your head.
I won't compare this game to Zelda or Binding of Isaac, because the gameplay reminds me of the Ys games more than anything else, between the fast paced and simple combat and how frantic things can get, as well as how quickly the tides can turn on you and you wind up dead.
The translation's a little odd but kinda like EYE Divine Cybermancy, I feel like it adds a lot to the game's atmosphere, which is very surreal, most of the gameplay mechanics are pretty straightforward though: Kill dudes, get gold, red potion gives you life, green potion gives you stamina, sometimes they drop little jagged things used to repair and upgrade your armor at anvils, which serve as a second lifebar as well as enhance your speed and stamina meter.
There's several different playable characters to choose from and each have their own quirks and different attacks, making it stand out from most other action roguelite games where different characters usually only offer minor stat tweaks and a different usable item.
Don't expect your runs to last very long, but there's definite replay value to be had here between how brisk the game moves and the variety of characters. I'd highly recommend this to anyone who's looking for an arcadey game they can pick up and play for an hour or two, set down, and then come back later for more.

It's a GREAT game with flaws and troubled history. I bought this game 3 years ago, and then played it for a couple hours. It didn’t' grab my attention then. I felt like playing a zombie game, and gave this another try. To my shock, this game is great. It's a huge world with tons of loot. The world ages and the zombie grow in number and change. Vanilla unmodded it plays like a survival isometric lite minecraft with zombies. There are little things that this game gets right like stealth, combat, and the zombie apocalypse setting done right.
The setting has urban, suburban, rural, and innawoods locations. These locales have their relevant advantages and disadvantages. More zombies downtown than out in the woods, this can be altered if you like in sandbox mode, this makes sense. It's not easy surviving innawoods without the right skills, but to get the right skills will require tradeoffs. These tradeoffs make the vanilla game necessary to specialize your character. It would take enormous amount of time, effort, and luck to be the master of everything. Do you want to hole up in a fortified house or go into the forest and live the survivalist lifestyle? A huge world where a variety of flavor of locals, solo or multiplayer, are available.
There is a low varied, food is highly varied, loot system in the vanilla game, and if modded it can be massive (Hydrocraft). This loot and crafting is where the game gets Minecraft lite. You can build your own furniture, walls, garden, and harvesting. This is the part of the game where the hydrocraft mod can add much more to this, but he vanilla game should expand on this.
The combat and stealth mix together to provide a thrilling experience. Unless changed in the setting, once infected your character will die to zombification guaranteed. Getting bitten is 95% zombification and scratches are 25% on vanilla. The stakes are high and once I survived for several hours I didn’t want my character to die, and the zombies aren’t threating individually or in small groups. But not paying attention or a sneaky zombie can get you and poof you’re done. No saved games (unless you do backups on your own) so you have to restart.
The negatives are there are no NPCs, lack of middle/late game variety, houses are too similar in loot, no in game option for a less rouge like experience, and the game has been in early access for 6 years!! Being in development hell for such a long time is worrisome. There are plenty of negative reviews about it, but I worry that the money will run out and the devs will just walk away. The core mechanics just needed to be finished and then let the modders make content.  NPCs with some questing, following, and scripting events would help make this a truly RPG. It’s a unique experience unlike any other game.

I was freezing. My God, was it cold. I couldn't feel my feet. I couldn't see but four feet in front of me in the dark. The snow was falling in thick blankets, blocking out the moon and stars which I know had to be shining above. I continued through the snow one step at a time, until I found an abandoned tractor. I pulled myself into it and shut the door. I needed to take an inventory of my supplies.
I was severely dehydrated, so I drank the last of my water. I was starving, so I ate my last granola bar. I had to find some place to warm up. I was dead tired and needed sleep. I had light winter clothes. Nothing suitable for the conditions I was in. I had only one flare in my backpack. I couldn't stay in this tractor over night, or I would freeze to death. I needed to go find some place to weather this storm.
I lit my only flare and opened the tractor door. The wind hit my like a brick wall, throwing snow in my face. I took a few steps forward before I saw it. Only 6 feet away, lit by an eerie red glow from my flare. A huge bear. I stopped immediately and started backing toward the tractor, when it spotted me.
It lunged at me, knocking the flare from my hand. It ripped and clawed at my face. All I could do was fight as best I could. Finally it was off me. The bear took off in a random direction.
I was bleeding badly from my neck and arm. I desperately tried to patch myself up. I needed to stop the bleeding before I bled out. My hands, numb and clumsy, finally wrapped my only bandage around my neck wound. I was still bleeding from my arm, but not bad. My flare was a few feet away from me. I stumbled toward it. I was in bad shape. I needed help immediately.
I finally reached the flare and picked it up. As I picked up the flare I saw it in the distance. A cabin!! Finally!! If I could only manage to make it there. I could start a fire and warm up, find some supplies to heal, scrounge a sip of water and find some food. I could survive!
I started moving toward it. I was hurt badly and stumbling. I was close now, just a few more feet. My vision was blurry and everything hurt. I just needed to get to the door. Only two more steps and I'd be there. Then I heard it. The bear had returned to claim his meal. One step left. Just one more. I can hear the bear running at me. The last step. I'm at the door. I grab the handle just as the bear lunges at me.
All I see is snow tumbling all around me. The bear, face glowing red from my flare, is on me. His teeth bared, eyes crimson. He reaches at my face. Suddenly, all I see is blackness. "You have faded into the long dark."
That was my very first experience with the Long Dark. That was the moment I knew this game had potential. I sat on my sofa shivering at the thought of what had just happen. This game is like no other I've ever played.
It has its flaws. Certainly, I wish my stats didn't drop so drastically. I wish there was just a little more supplies around. If only it was a little easier, and I could survive for more than just one day. I suppose that's what makes this game so good to some people. It is hard. To me that makes it a little boring. I get tired of only surviving for a day or two. It gets old knowing how quickly I will need water or food. I can't even scrounge for enough supplies before one of my stats are empty.
The controls and menus are a little clunky. It feels like you go out and collect a lot of supplies, but you don't live long enough to ever use them. People talk about fishing and hunting. I'm never able to make it that far before dying of something else first.
There is so much going on in the menus, I don't have time to learn it all before I succumb to starvation or thirst. It feels complicated and I wish it could be simplified some and a little more user friendly.
The game is beautiful, however. The scenery looks amazing. The atmosphere really draws you into this world. You actually feel like you are there. There is so much to explore and see. Again though, I don't feel like I get to explore enough and enjoy the scenery and atmosphere because I'm too busy worrying about starving or freezing. It seems a little too fast paced for a survival and exploratory game. That is part of the appeal to a lot of people though. The constant threat of death looming over you. I just wish it had some quiet moments and down time instead of constant struggle.
Overall it's a great game. Not for everyone, but certainly has a lot of potential to be amazing. While I like it a lot when playing it, I find myself becoming a little bored after just a couple times playing.
TL;DR: Great game with a lot of potential. Awesome visuals. Hard to survive for more than a day or two. A constant struggle for survival with no downtime to relax and enjoy the beautiful scenery. I recommend trying this game. Maybe wait for a good sale to purchase it, though.

Hotel Giant 2 was released in 2010, but received in 2015 an HD update which has met a lukewarm reception. And with good reasons too. If you can overlook these flaws, you’ll find a thoroughly efficient hotel simulator which lets you control everything from planning, building and managing the financial side of business as well. The gameplay mechanics are far from broken and you can find an educational purpose to this title. So don’t avoid it, thinking it’s a bad or generic game. It’s far from it.

TL;DR: Beautiful medroidvania-style exploration action-adventure in a mysterious aquatic setting with moderate combat system and fresh-feeling story.
is a hidden yet rough gem: it's got a beautiful shell that sweeps your legs off, overwhelms you with its enormous world and then drowns you in to its wonderful setting. Frankly, I was unaware it even existed before I started seriously playing through my Library to discover just hidden gems like this. I wonder how it could have flown under my radar for so long. On with the review:
In
you play as Naija, a barely feral humanoid sea creature with magic singing powers and vague memory of her earlier life. Curiosity gets hold of her and she heads to the outside world to see its wonders. The world proves to be both a beautiful and a grim place.
plays like a medroidvania but (almost) entirely in an aquatic environment, thus requiring none of the usual platforming skills.
For starters, the game is astonishingly beautiful, in both cut scenes and in-game. Aquatic environment is a tranquil place, full of weeds, plants and critters, many of them malicious. Soundtrack is nice and fits the theme marvellously. Voice acting is surprisingly good for a game with (almost) only the lonesome main character articulating by herself. It is used excellently to set the mood of mystery and wonder. The game encourages you to just hang around in its calm, alien world. Sometimes, an eerie, malicious laughter in the distance breaks the illusion of tranquility - who is that and why is he laughing?
Just about everything about the storyline and setting is tightly knitted into the lore and many things only become clear close to the end. The intro cut scene itself is confusing as its significance only becomes apparent late into the game.
In the beginning a while is spent simply exploring the limited area and trying to figure out what to do. The ever-present exploration aspect is both cool and dull: while the environment is pretty and contains a lot of interesting features and stuff to find, the whole scope of it is initially overwhelming. It takes a while to get through the slow start. Fortunately there's a map and you can easily mark interesting/unreachable areas.
Like expected in a good medroidvania, it takes a while to find out how to use the environmental features to your advantage and find a means to proceed into the areas previously unreachable. This makes returning to the known areas rewarding.
To reach those areas Naija may learn to take different forms that grant her special abilities like shooting homing fire bolts or fitting into tight spaces. The forms (and a couple of spells) are accessed through singing magic, though there are keyboard shortcuts for the numerous forms. The special abilities are used also in combat.
Fighting is simple, almost to a point of dull: shoot until enemy dies, sometimes removing/destroying the shield first, and avoid getting hit by projectiles or touched by enemies. It works but it sure could use some twists. The enemies are invariably sea creatures of various kinds but bosses are sea monsters or downright fallen gods of enormous size.
Boss monsters (which are a dozen) usually require one to make them expose their weak spot in some way and then shooting it as fast as you can. In effect fighting some bosses is more like a puzzle into itself as you look for their weak spot and study their attack patterns, which are just 2-3 per boss. Many bosses have also a fascinating background in the lore, though some are just nasty creatures who want to kill you.
The later bosses are better and more challenging (even difficult), while the earlier ones might be killed simply by dodging or blocking their bullet storm-like attacks and shooting like a madman. The later bosses may take several tries to survive, especially the final boss who has several forms and no saves between.
The scarcity of save points is a major fault: with the long distances between areas and the menacing world one would hope for frequent saves but there's usually just one per area. While death does not happen too often, when you do die you lose all progress since the last save, which can be infuriating if it was a while back. It also forces for rather long game sessions since you don't always know when you can save the next time. Food crafting, i.e. cooking, can be used to create healing and buff items that can sometimes help through the most dangerous situations to avoid losing progress.
The world of
is an enormous place with several biomes from amazing reed forests to fallen aquatic cities to pitch-dark caves. Several times I would just stop momentarily and enjoy the marvellous vista.
While mostly placed underwater, there are a couple of less-than traditional platforming sections later into the game. Wall-jumping is unfortunately way unreliable, especially since the same mechanic is used to travel on land. There's no way (that I could see) to control the strength of the pounces, making it hard to judge where Naija would land. Good news is that these sections are mostly optional and sparse.
Another qualm but a stupid one at that: it took me over an hour to get the first achievement, granted for reaching open waters.
could well have been more generous with achievements, especially in the beginning but also at the end, where you e.g. don't get one for beating the game or seeing the secret ending.
Nevertheless, after 20 hours I had completed the game and found all the secrets, though a few treasures remain hidden (why no cheevo for collecting them all?). Game had three instances where I unfortunately needed to use a walkthrough because I had totally missed the sheer existence of the puzzle despite them hiding in plain sight.
To be fair in two of the cases I felt like a fool afterwards for missing them. Perhaps in a less hectic age I would have had the patience to loiter around and eventually figure them out myself. The third one, however, was well put by the guide I read as "one of the least obvious puzzles ever" and I doubt I would have ever come across its solution except by sheer accident.
The atmosphere was tranquil throughout and I found myself being relaxed in all but the tensest of situations. The storyline (with the secret ending) was surprisingly grim and contains a cliffhanger. Unfortunately, a true sequel is unlikely since the devs have gone their separate ways, but the mod community is producing

I've been intrigued by the remake since I finished playing The Cat Lady last year. I didn't go into TCL blind, as I watched someone else play it years back. Even though I knew how it was going to play out, I was invested enough to buy it for myself and play it through. Playing it for myself gave the experience a much deeper ambiance and meaning. However, for Downfall, I purposefully went in blind. I didn't even research the original, all I knew was that it showcased the most fascinating and mysterious character from TCL- Joe Davis. So naturally, my expectations were that it would be good, although I didn't expect it to be better than TCL.
And I was wrong. It wasn't good: it was perfect. The introduction alone invokes so much fear, despair and intrigue that it hooked me in instantly. The style is not only an improvement over TCL, but it also gives the audience a way to perceive the world around Joe through his eyes without saying a word. Not only do the visuals do an outstanding job of conjuring a spiral of emotions, but the soundtrack also gives way into the player's psyche. These elements alone are enough to entice the player into playing more, and what awaits them is a masterpiece of interactive contemporary lore. The point and click gameplay combined with the story gives the player a feeling of human limitation in an inhumane world. Choices matter, people are desperate for action, and the only one who can make those difficult decisions is you.
For aspiring story-driven game creators, this serves as an excellent example of how to make the audience invested and determined to see the adventure to completion. I could not reccomend this game enough, nor do it justice, but I did do my best for those who are interested and have yet to experience it for themselves. Playing it gives so much more meaning than watching someone else play it, it's truly worth it. I'm looking forward to future works from Screen 7. :)

After playing The Cat Lady and finding it to be one of the best narrative driven games I've played in quite a while, it made sense to find more games like it. Looking into Harvester games, I was both disappointed that there was only one other game, but excited at the promise of more of to sink my teeth into. Downfall did not disappoint.
If someone asked me to describe what Downfall is about, I might say that it feels like if the shining was adapted to film by David Lynch instead of Stanley Kubrick. The plot follows Joe Davis, who goes to the 'Quiet Haven Hotel' with his wife, Ivy, to fix his struggling marriage. It doesn't take long before it becomes obvious that something strange is going on and that this will not be a typical holiday for the unlucky couple. I don't want to go any further into the story because it is something that you should really experience yourself. Like The Cat Lady, it goes into mature themes throughout the plot, concerning issues such as mental health. With that being said, while Downfall is similarly dark to The Cat Lady, and neither game is conventionally realistic, Downfall is more consistently surreal. This is not necessarily a good or bad thing, but is rather a notable difference between the two.
The art style is very similar to The Cat Lady (okay, I'll try to stop comparing the two so much) and the puzzles are typical of adventure games. It is challenging enough working out the solutions, but not so hard that it becomes irritating. Even if the answer is too obscure, the solution can usually be found by wandering around and trying to interact every object with every interactable piece of scenery until the situation sorts itself out.
Overall I enjoyed my time with Downfall and highly recommend it to anyone who likes adveture games, particularly ones of a dark nature. Even now I am anticipating the next title from this studio.

A hard one to review.  I got it because me and friends really enjoyed Blur, this game is very similar to that.  The gameplay is great - I actually usually play hardcore flight sims - and it's cute the way this game uses some analogues to actual flight (rolling your plane to allow sharper manouvers than simply yawing).  Vertical movement also gives it another dimension (literally) than Blur has and they make the most of it too with some great maps.  It's a blast to play and the sensation of speed is excellent.  I thought being locked to 30fps would really offend me but it doesn't actually bother me.  The motion blur is very well done and covers the missing frames.  Graphically it's really nice all together - and the sensation of movement is very visceral.
Okay now the problem.  There's no skirmish type mode where you can fly against the AI with human players "co-op"ing along with you.  Blur or Gas Guzzlers totally wipes the floor with this game here.  Basically I want to play this with my gf and gang up on the AI.  And there is no such game mode :(
So you have a fun single player campaign that will give you a few hours fun.  And an empty Online multiplayer.  BUT no ability to play with your pals or on a LAN against the AI - this really is a shame as otherwise I'd heartily recommend this.  What a shame.

I had high hopes for Dungeon of the Endless as I really enjoyed the demo released a while back. It had great premise just like many other difficult procedurally generated dungeon crawlers.
Starting with the graphics and overall audio-visual quality of the game. Retro pixel art looks good, sound effects are ok with pleasant sci-fi tunes in the background. The overall feel is ok. The user interface however has some problems. It is sometimes hard to use and overall not the most user-friendly nor the best looking one I have seen lately. There are no options to resize the hud and there are only two states of map zooming, normal and tactical overview. There are problems selecting and grouping the heroes at times. Moving heroes room by room can also be a chore sometimes due to the restrictions of their movement. In the end, it has it flaws but playable.
There is enough amount of content to worth the many tries while eventually reaching the exit. Hero factions, classes, stats, leveling up, active and passive skills, and equipment adds a lot to customization options. The four resources which can be gathered via various factories are each useful for different situations and requires tactical awareness right from the beginning of the levels because the placing order of the responding module. Some of the heroes also has operate ability which further enhances a selected modules producing capability. There are randomly spawning heroes who can be recruited, and various type of merchants who sell and buy goods. The random factor is really strong however, in fact too much. The fourth resource, dust, is only used for powering rooms, which prevents enemies spawning into them and of course powers installed modules. The main problem is that dust is gained randomly by entering rooms. After a few rooms opened there are usually a shortage of dust which means that many rooms remain unpowered. When waves are spawning every unpowered room is a potential spawn point for waves which basically multiplies the number of enemies. This can cause fatal amount of foes to spawn at one given door opening. This is where a good team is essential. There are classes which are good for either tank, speedster or operator duties. They can also be strengthened via various equipments. In my latest game I had two operators, one tank and one speedster. Escapes at the end of the levels were quite easy with a 61 speed unit running with the crystal. During the levels my tank could easily gather all the mobs around him with the aggro passive skill. Eeverything was ideal, my heroes were pretty high level. There are one more thing that I would mention, and that is the personal story part. Every hero has at least one story which activates if one other member has the same one. One that I had was between a prisoner and a crew member which ended up badly. After each floor there is a small dialog sequence which cannot be skipped. I just finished the 10th floor when my speedster just killed my tank in the elevator ending their personal storyline. Now, I left with a crippled team basically at the end of the dungeon. This is that kind of (kinda) randomness which is really frustrating. I cannot finish the game as my beefed up hero got killed because some personal affair. Also, all his expensive items are lost in the process.
Overall, I will not say that this game is bad, it is just one of those titles which are going too far with their random events. It encourages multiple playthroughs, has many heroes and ships which also adds variability, but ultimately too unforgiving to offer enjoyment without constant frustration. I would recommend it but only for those who are really into this kind of game.

A fun and challenging puzzle game.  The later puzzles take some serious thought processes to complete, but are very satisfying when you do figure them out.

This is the puzzle game for methodical and logical minds.  No stupid tricks or anything that breaks logic.  I'm not a huge fan of puzzle games, however SpaceChem is a lot like Incredible Machine, without the plethora of wacky components and mechanics.  Solutions in SpaceChem are typically discovered (rather than planned for immediately), much like a budding mechanical engineer would test things through trial-and-error.  If you are looking for a game that will challenge your problem solving, this is the game for you.
Possibly the most brain-breaking fun it's possible to have this side of a lambda calculus textbook.

Highly recommended for puzzle game fans.  Very complex puzzler but lots of room for creativity, seems like there must be innumberable ways to solve these puzzles but when you get a good solution that works elegantly it's extremely satisfying.

Spacechem is a construction game, where you attempt to create a contraption (with very limited space) that converts one set of input atoms/molecules into a set of output atoms/molecules.
It's a very good variation on the "assembly line" game.  I think this is the best game so far from Zachtronic Industries.  It's a pretty large, challenging, logic/process bending, thoughtful game.  And it's got cool music, too.  And an interesting plot.  And cool charts so you can see how well you did compared with the rest of the world.
Get it, play it, agonize over it's puzzles.
Addictive puzzle game. Simple concept that quickly has your scratching your head. Requires a very logical mind to advance to the later levels.
This game makes you feel stupid for an hour trying to figure out the puzzle, and incredibly smart for two days after you solved it. Highly recommended!

I've supported this game since Desura. It IS developing. But if you can't be patient, then maybe this isn't the game for you. You are buying early access on a game with no set release date, after all. And development cycles can be longer than many people seem to understand  (As an example, at the time of writing, Fortnite was just released. I remember when it was supposed to be released, alongside Fable on the original Xbox.)
Worth your time, worth your money. But honestly, don't expect a finished product until 2020.

First of all, I want to say that I have loved every minute that I have been able to play this game. Like games such as Rimworld, developers have placed the majority of their focus on creating in-depth simulation through realistic items, crafting, vision, sound, etc. This means that graphically, PZ is not on the standard of many mainstream games. If you're looking for an in-depth, true to life simulation, though, this game gets pretty dang close.
One of the best "features" to this game is that the developers are consistent in communicating and pushing out updates. In the time that I've owned PZ, the game has changed and grown so much, but hasn't lost the core pieces that made it what it was in the early days.
So why can't I recommend this game? In truth, it has to do with the fact that I cannot currently play the game due to bugs in the design. Starting in 2014, a build was released that made the game so that on my system, there were no menu options at startup. (Yes, there are some google search fixes for this, but none have worked so far.) In the next build, they game back and I enjoyed PZ again, until a patch dropped and I lost menu buttons again. Since that time, the chances of me being able to actually play has been a toss-up as to what version is currently running. Every build and every patch is a maybe that I can actually continue playing the game I paid for, or wait to see if they fix it in a later build.
Unfortunately, because of this, I cannot recommend that someone buy this game until it is consistently available to play. If that happens, I will gladly keep playing and might even buy copies for my friends to enjoy on multiplayer. But if you're thinking of buying this game, my advice is to wait until the bugs and issues have been ironed out, and it is functional as intended.
(I mean really, Indie Stone... Just the ability to Alt-Tab out of the game and shut it down in this case would be nice. As it is, every time I test out whether it's been fixed, I'm forced to manually shut down my computer and restart. Quality of Life here, lol...)
