I'm under the impression that this is a terrible port of a console game because trying to navigate your way through the menus is just sheer torture.
Give us the turn-based variety of Front Mission, please.  Spare of this derivative crap.

Downfall is a game similar to The Cat Lady with gore, symbolism and the the supernatural.
However while The Cat Lady was about finding light in the dark, Downfall is about going deeper and deeper  in the darkness to find what you lost. The game comes with two versions  the original(2009) and the remake(2016) and while they basically tell the same story they both do it in their own unique way.
The original (about 4h)
-Joe is going through a downward spiral to madness.
-At the end he has to decide how it ends (1 of 3 ways).
-It is presented in the old point-and-click style, with rather difficult puzzles.
-It has a more complete story, as it presents a lot more about the characters.

To be completely honest, I believe this may be the Strongest Ground Base Mecha Game on Steam today.
Despite the fact that this game has came out on 2010, it's core mechanics are
.
In combat, you will have four places to target in enemy Wanzers (otherwise to us, Mechas). The torso, each respective arms, and the legs. While the torso represents the main health, each other part will contribute to your Combat Abilities. You break them, your ability to fight will become that much more crippled.
Now this will mean you need to play smart. Seriously smart.



Your Wanzer's ability to
around is your most powerful tool the Controller can utilise.
That being said, if your Legs (aka, your Skating Mobility) gets destroyed, you'll be crippled like a horse missing a leg.
So better get looking for a health pack!
The main reason why I emphasize the importance of Mobility is because you can
dodge
'Oh, are those a trail of Machine Gun Bullets aimed at me? Let me keep dashing to the side!'
'Huh, is there a shower of Mortal coming down from the sky? Better Skate out of the way!'
'Grrr, is that a suicide brawler after my♥♥♥♥♥ Better Kite backwards while shooting!'
'Ah, is that a series of Homing Missiles Locked onto me? I think I should Stutter-Step left and right!'
On top of that, anytime during the game, when you realize that a certain Arsenal of Weapon Choice isn't working out and frustrating you,
Yes, I said that right; you can goddamn change your Loadout during the middle of the mission without restarting it.
As a gamer that enjoys trying each type of weapon available, I can't emphasize how grateful this
the developers have implemented into the game. It shows a great understanding for perspective on our behalf.
Gone are the days where you need to restart the game to change your playstyle!
☆ ★ ☆ ★ ☆
But there are some few problems…
Generic Characters. Linear Story. Cut Paste Voice Acting. Companion Battle Ai Non-existent. Lack of NG+.
Bosses can get sometimes infuriating at some OP things (but the game does its part in stepping stones to teach you how to overcome it.)
The Core Item Drops of Energy refills are missing for 95% of the game. I believe the flexibility of the Game could’ve improved so much more if that was available.
Multiplayer is dead. Q.Q I want my achievements pl0x!!! No other Single Player Options besides the Campaign too (least give me Survival Mode or something).
☆ ★ ☆ ★ ☆
Now back to the good points!
Did I mention you can Customize the look of your Wanzer?! :D
A nice touch if I do say so myself.
Did I mention that you feel like you’re in an actually 60-Feet Suit of Metal and Armor? You can actively Crush things beneath your feet! (Sure there’s isn’t much to even step on…) But still! The fact that you have
destructible debris is so trilling!
The Intro and Final Cutscenes were just really Cool in the perspective of a Mecha Anime Watcher. The Orbital Tower Defense Laser was really awesome to watch. The Big weapon that took it down was also really cool to see (despite we never being able to see it again later). While the ending thing really reminded me of the one scene from Gundam Seed (Destiny?). Quite Touching, really. Cue
So although you don’t quite feel like Jesus Yamato from the Gundam Seed Series.
I did quite feel like Suzaku Kururugi from Code Geass (Season One) with the excellent Mobility of the Knightmare Frames.

SpaceChem may be, as Robin Walker wrote, “pretty much the greatest game ever made”, but it undoubtedly is the most difficult game ever made. Fake science and a very interesting gameplay make SpaceChem a great experience.
Everyone who likes to think deeply and doesn't get too frustrated over a game will LOVE it.

Spacechem is fun, and taxing. Ideal for people who like cold hard computer logic.
Basically you program circuits to recombine various atoms and compounds into various other atoms and compounds. Early on, it's really simple stuff, and the tutorial levels are pretty good at cluing you into what's going on, but after a while you're on your own, and you really have to put your thinking caps on.
SpaceChem is really challenging, but rewarding.
Very, *very* good, specially if you have a programing background, or like to design logic circuits. A puzzle game where luck is not a factor.

A puzzle game about chemistry but that aspect really only serves as a stylistic vehicle because the problem solving is essentially mechanical engineering. Grabbing, moving, dropping, rotating, bonding, fusing, but instead of applying those actions to tenable objects, it uses atoms and molecules, perfectly fitting the abstract environment.
Conceptually it's a brilliant game and same goes for its execution and the challenges it provides.
A puzzle game succeeds when it's able to make the player feel smart and Spacechem excels here.

Do you like science? How about mechanics? Spacechem bonds these two together to create a puzzler that it a class of its own! The tutorials ease you into constructing (and deconstructing/reassembling) all manner of molecules, and the story drives you the rest of the way.
Be warned though - although there is many solutions to each puzzle, each of them is a real challange.

Swim, explore, sing, transform, fight, craft.
I had reservations to see a Metroidvania that you control with the mouse, but I'm happy to say they were misplaced. The controls work responsively and they fit the swimming mechanic. You feel acrobatic, dodging and weaving about. It made combat fun. Great job here.
The world is much larger and varied than I expected at first. Every new area was a pleasant surprise. Many optional secrets, so it looks like there's good replay value. The map system has two wonderful features: highlighting of areas you've explored, and the ability to place named markers to revisit things.
: The eerie musical mechanic definitely contributes to the atmosphere of the game. I got chills many times using it to unlock new secrets.
: I would have liked a little more balance between the different forms you can take. You wind up spending the majority of the game in one or two forms. A few of them, including my favorite (nature), are pretty useless outside of briefly getting past obstacles.
Most bosses have puzzle aspect more challenging to figure out than "shoot the glowing eye". This can be very satsifying if you like puzzle bosses, but if it frustrates you, don't hesitate to look up tips. There are enough other mysteries to solve without having to do it while you're getting shot at.
I'm not crazy about the item crafting system. The menu is a bit awkward, involving way more clicks than it should require to make recipes. To be fair, though, I don't usually like crafting systems anyway.

I enjoyed the system of crafting food and gathering ingredients.

I appreciated the ability to set custom map markers.

You can rain fire (energy) down on the local wildlife and slaughter schools of fish to gather ingredients.
Cons:
The control scheme, in conjunction with the song mechanics, can make it awkward to navigate, fight, and sing at the same time but overall I think it works.
The world is very large and backtracking can be tedious, but the ability to set map markers helps considerably.
The learning curve starts off nice but there is a period of time where many people will struggle with navigating around projectiles while fighting and using songs. Enemies hit hard and for a while you will easily come close to death.
The game is very good at what it does, but some might find the content to be lacking. Don't expect a huge and immersive crafting system, interactive npcs, or a very interactive world (you can, however, decimate the wildlife which I think is a nice detail). This is very much a side-scrolling shooter with puzzle and exploration elements, an interesting gimmick (the song mechanics) and a small crafting element.

I had a great time playing Skydrift, and while I'm not the best pilot for flight games, I have no problem playing arcade titles such as this and Starfox.
It's a "Mario Kart" style racing game, that is reminescent of Blur, but with planes, and many have compared this to Crimson Skies which I have not had the opportunity to play. Besides your expected steering, acceleration, and power user controls, you use have the ability to twist into the knife edge postion, basically rolling your plane left or right laterally (DO A BARREL ROLL!) which helps you fit into tight openings and turn corners. The game says you need this for some turns, but I think you can brake and readjust if you real careful if you really wanted to (though, that is much slower and a terrible idea for later stages unless you have no other option). You also can "burn" power ups to add to your boost, which is a great mechanic requiring the player to use strategy - do you attack a racer, defend yourself, or speed up? You'll generally find it better to speed up more often than not, but you will definitely have to defend yourself in mid-stage races and attack in all races.
There's only a few power ups compared to Mario Kart, but each can be stacked to a second level, creating another layer strategy, such as more mines, stronger bullets, or a bigger area of effect for the shockwave. Of course, you can just burn those power ups for a larger than normal boost as well. You can also perform "stunts" such as hugging the ground, drafting opponents, going through tight spaces, or damaging enemies to gain boost.
The modes available, though limited are rather fun. The standard race are Power Races, as you race a level using power ups to boost and dogfight to slow enemies down, since you can't permanently stop any racer since everybody has unlimited respanws (excluding Elimination). Speed Race involve removing those powerups, and instead, racing through rings that can speed you up like the ones found in a later mission of Retrovirus. As I earlier mentioned, Elimination is much like Power Race, but after a set time frame, the last place racer is eliminated from the race until the last man standing. I had some really fun clutch moments of getting out of last place just in time, which is a shining moment of the game.
The game has a pretty good art style and quality - planes look pretty good (especially in the intro sequence) and while level textures are a tad blurry on close angles (crashing, pausing, after race video), but you're often going too fast to notice, and the overall art design is similar to Sine Mora (another game developed by Digital Reality), but a bit brighter and sharper. I've read one person had a problem seeing power ups at times, but I've never had this problem unless I was being destroyed or driving near a mine - the power ups are well distinguished by different colors and clear vector icons. I like the guitar driven soundtrack, though I can't call it metal or hard rock, and honestly, it isn't something you'd feel you have to have in your OST collection - but I like what is there.
I feel the AI is fair through the majority of the game, and I don't feel alot of Mario Kart rubberbanding (not to say there isn't, I just can't tell) though I find the later stages feel damn near impossible to get in 1st place. Another problem is a strong repetitiion of the levels - and while I think SkyDrift actually did a good job of spreading the repeated levels out (you often race on tracks that are the same as others, but in reverse or a slightly alternate route), You are only racing on the same 6 or so tracks, compared to other games that might have 16 or more. I think this is excusable due to the price point. Multiplayer community is non-existant, but if you buy this game, that will add another potential player who can be on (and you can also join my Abandoned multiplayer games group).
Besides what I listed, There's really no major flaws with the game in my opinion and I'm glad I finally decided to play the game after having it installed for months and having purchased for a year or so, and having it wishlisted since it came out....I just wish I played it when there were more players - the DLC has a deathmatch mode that looks fun, but the Gladiator Multiplayer Pack is nearly impossible to recommend when practically nobody is playing, unless you play with friends (SO GET THE GAME AND PLAY WITH ME!). Regardless if you buy this on sale, or its $10 cheap price tag, it's a solid, fun arcadey racer.

I just paid $10 for 5 hours of gameplay.  It was worth every penny.  Well, it was worth most of the pennies.
This is a game that is very approachable despite its lack of tutorial or even an opportunity to get your bearings.  It throws you right into the action with no explaination.  However, it's easy enough to figure out.
The first challenge is the bad translation.  I'm not sure how this game happened, but I'm pretty sure it's a japanese indie.  Level up your strenght and perform the ching chong toyota weeaboo dahg suup.
After the translation comes the glitches.  I've only had to close it and reopen it twice, but it froze several times.  Have patience, and this won't be a problem.  There's also some funny glitches.  Tournament brackets will sometimes claim you've been eliminated when you haven't, and then the two contestants next to you have both beat each other.  It works itself out on its own.  There's also the boxing ring, where you can knock each other out at the same time but have to wait ten seconds before you crumple over and fall.
The final flaw is the grinding.  You have to go to work as a forklift operator to get money to enter tournaments, at least until you unlock the matches that give you money when you win.  There's also training minigames, which are actually really fun at first.  As soon as you get tired of doing them, you can just stop and let your stats level up on their own.  The button mashing will hurt your thumbs, but it doesn't go without reward.
The fighting itself consists of high kicks, mid kicks, low kicks, high punches, mid punches, and specials,  You can't throw fireballs, but you can do roundhouse kicks and high flying nose kicks.  You unlock those by pressing the "waza" button in the training menu.  Don't bother with the frontflip kick, spinning backfist, axe kick (leg goes straight up), or anything but the roundhouse and the spinning jump kick.
The fighting is really visceral, and you know when you land a good hit.  The game rewards you for having the skill to properly land a blow.  Don't be afraid to hit the body or the leg.  The head isn't the only way to win.  Working your opponent's leg is actually very effective.  Out of the three targets, head is the best - but not by much.
Don't worry about the story, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥and it doesn't get in the way.  Just kick someone's face in.  Story can wait.
When doing a tournament in the early game, I had a very intense second round that involved a lot of leg sweeping and face kicking.  It ended in me and my opponent punching each other in the stomach as fast as we possibly could, and then he fell over.  The third round consisted of the match starting, me closing in, one boot to the head, and it fractured his cranium.
The game will seem easy after a while, until you unlock the secret tournament.  I won't tell you what that is.  Just be prepared and have fun.
You'll end this game feeling proud of yourself.  You might even want to go again.  Personally, I would absolutely love to see the potential this game holds fleshed out a bit more.  Not many games need sequels, but this one does.  I want to see what else this developement team can do.  I see a lot of creativity in these people.

I had played this game as a kid and went into it with a huge nostalgia bonus, but I can't in good conscience recommend it anymore. Don't be fooled by the "Enhanced Edition"moniker, the game is still filled from top to bottom with bugs and frustrations. The storyline is decent (though those of the sidequests and companions aren't) and in the higher levels the tactical, semi-turn-based D&D combat still is a big draw, but it's not nearly enough to make up for all the problems.
Balancing for example simply doesn't exist. The early levels are especially horrible since dying or not constantly hinges on a single dice roll (you have less total hp than most enemies can dish out in damage with one hit). The later levels are mostly okay, except for the new content from the expansion, that is simply frustrating and no fun at all. Still, throughout the entire game it all boils down to quicksaving after every fight and then reloading whenever something goes wrong, over and over until the dice fall into the place you need them to.
I'm sorry, but don't buy this.

This game is like if you took an coding algorithms course and made it into a game. Merely completing the levels is not super difficult, but you will be compelled to optimize your solution until it's elegant. Not for any achievements or gameplay purposes, but because if you're the kind of person who will like this game, tweaking and optimizing your algorithms is just what you'll do.
There are no flashy graphics here; you will be staring at the equivalant of your IDE of choice and hacking out solutions to algorithmic puzzles. If you enjoy that, this game is great and offers a lot of depth and challenge. If not, skip it because that's all it is.

Easily the best puzzle game ever, this charming piece of a thinking man's entertainment has also managed to take a spot among my favourite games of all time.
SpaceChem doesn't actually have much to do with chemistry, but it has everything to do with programming. The puzzles effectively boil down to designing programs in a language reminiscent of Befunge, and unlike with many puzzle games, there's no feeling at all that you're trying to reproduce the game designer's contrived train of thought. Solutions always feel like a work of your own, and more often than not different people come up with vastly different solutions to the same problem. This alone makes the game extremely rewarding - but there's also a ton of potential for optimizing your solutions; or simply coming up with ones that seem particularly elegant.
Add to that a charming soundtrack, extremely competent writing and well over 40 hours of content even without DLC, and this becomes an undisputable must-buy.

SpaceChem  is a great pseudo-chemistry based programming puzzle game.  The puzzles are challenging thought exercises with limitless was to solve.  I find myself often going back for a more elegant solution to puzzles I've already completed.

Very fun game. Like the 2D Side Scrolling version of Call of Duty's Zombie mode. You can play online with people, though I haven't tried it yet. If you want to have someone or something shooting along side you, you can find the Cell Phones Hidden throughout the levels. When you get a Cell Phone, that Permanently increases the number of AI Human Helpers/Survivors with you by 1. So If I have 3 Cell Phones, whenever I start a level, I can choose to bring up to 3 AI's with me. The AI's are dumb as rocks, and have some serious problems path-finding in certain levels, but they're way better than nothing, and actually do help you quite a bit. The first Cell Phone is easy to get, but the ones in other levels are harder.
As for the rest of the game, There are around 5 Official Levels/Maps in the game, with the option of either building your own with the games Level Editor, or downloading more from the Workshop. I don't know how many guns there are. bit O know there's at least 13 different guns, and they're different enough not to seem like just a reskin.
Weapons are spread throughout the level in fixed spots, so the harder it is to get to it, the better, usually. There's also Items you can buy with ZKW-R Tokens, which are dropped by enemies occasionally or awarded to you when getting an achievement or finishing the Daily Challenge. The Items include stuff like meat, which attracts zombies to it, a Dual Wield Pistol, Molotov's, 3 different Turrets, and a bunch more.
There's persistence throughout the game too, when it comes to your character and the weapons. There's a 'Weapon Customization' menu, where you can use your earned ZKW-R Tokens to permanently upgrade the various weapons damage, accuracy, reload speed, and firing rate. Honestly, I don't see much a difference with accuracy, since you're usually close enough for it to not matter.
Along with the weapon upgrades, your character earns experience when he kills a zombie. Once you level up, you get a point to invest into various skills. There's like, 8 different skills, but I found only 2 of them useful. Gun Expert and Money Finder. Gun Expert increase gun damage and reload speed, which is very useful. And Money Finder increases the value of money pickups.
There's also a crafting system, however to craft the good stuff, you have to invest quite a few skill points in the Handy Man Skill, which means less for Gun Expert and Money Finder, and to make things worse the crafting materials rarely drop to begin with. By the time the materials drop to craft even the simplest things have finally dropped, you could have just spent ZKW-R Tokens to buy 4 more, since the ZKW-R Tokens drop far more often than both the craft mats and the pickups.
Oh yeah, there are pickups too that zombies occasionally drop. They're stuff like temporary fire/plasma/piercing bullets, temporary armor, ammo refill, healing, etc. Power ups drop less than the ZKW-R Tokens, but far more than the crafting mats, so they're fairly reliable. And unlike crafting, you can level up your 'Lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' skill to increase the drop chance of power ups.
There's an option, also, that tells you when a multiplayer games is available to join, which is nice since while the game isn't dead, there isn't a endless list of join-able games either. More often than not, you wouldn't have to wait more than 10 Minutes to find a game, and whether you're in the menu or in game, a message will pop up alerting you. You can turn this off of course.
Well, there's some other features, but they're small, though still convenient, and you'll find them out soon enough. The gameplay is fun and what you'd expect: kill the zombie waves for money to buy guns. Unlock doors with cash to get further in. Find cell phones, etc.
The music is decent. Fits the game, but I wouldn't call it good, but I wouldn't call it bad either. The voice acting of your character is so laughably bad though, but I found it more amusing than anything else.
So, fun gameplay, plenty of persistence in weapon upgrading and character leveling, good amount of levels and weapons, AI companions, and funny voice acting. The Dev plans on updating the game too. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes Call of Duty's Zombie mode, or zombie arena type games.

TLDR; A excruciatingly mediocre game.
The gameplay starts off bad, piloting/designing a mech is extremely basic, the combat is dull and the AI presents no challenge what so ever. After playing the first two levels you will have seen all of what the game has to offer. It only gets worse from there though with a poor attempt at "variety". Only square enix could think it would be a good idea to put all its marbles on expanding the franchise by turning the series known for its turn based strategy elements/depth into a shallow outsourced one off failure of a action game that desperately tries to appeal to a western audience.
This is one of the worst handled franchises by square enix, even though most of the games never came to the west they ended up being fan translated. FM: Gun Hazard (snes) spinoff from 20 years ago offers far more compelling story/gameplay/mech building then this game does.

I am a big fan of the Front Mission series, however this game takes the Front Mission setting and makes a game that is... basically worse than the Front Mission strategy gameplay in all aspects. It should really be called "Front Mission Devolved".
Youd think that they would put in some effort to justify switching Front Mission to a third person shooter, but it just feels like a cheaply made game.
The plot is laughable - the voice acting is very uneven (a lot of the characters are emotionless when they should show emotion, and ALL the emotional scenes fall completely flat) and it is just poorly written and generic. A major theme of the game is the incredible power of the "EDGE System" which supposedly makes you into a superhuman mech piloting machine, but gameplay wise EDGE is pretty terrible. It only slows down enemies slightly for a few seconds and I hardly used it at all. The one badass female character turns into an emotional wreck halfway through the game just from seeing someone who scares her. The main character is as boring as you can get, with no real motivation besides "revenge!" And the villains have massive plot armor, even after you fight them in a half hour boss battle their wanzers don't get a scratch.
The game's very hard to control with a controller so I would suggest using mouse and keyboard - ESPECIALLY in the (boring) on foot segments which will always crash if you use a controller. Even then however, the animations feel pretty stiff during combat. The on foot sections feel tacked on and even more like an attempt to make the game appeal to "westerners".
The graphics are also pretty poor. Even for the time they came out they were dated. The graphics look like a launch Xbox 360 game from 2006.
The music is of course generic without any of the incredible tracks such as the ones Yoko Shimomura made for the original Front Mission. While it's not horrible, it's also pretty forgettable.
All in all it would have been better if they just ported Front Mission 4 or 5 to Steam (and probably made more money too). The Front Mission series was merely the victim of executive meddling thinking a shooter would appeal more to Westerners. That may be the case but it certainly didn't result in a better game, even as far as third person shooters go.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is a refreshing change of pace for the FPS genre. It brings the genre back to it's 2000-2005 roots to the WW2 era, and merges it with today's technology to provide an authentic, immersive, beautiful experience. This game plays differently than your popular shooters like Call of Duty and Halo, so it's not for everyone. It's definitely catered to a more hardcore audience than most mainstream titles, but still offers game modes for gamers with all tastes. The combat in this game is fast paced, but realistic. There are minimal hud elements, like no crosshairs for instance. Weapon aiming is quite unique, too. Weapons don't shoot in the center of the screen, but rather the weapon moves with the mouse until you get closer to the edge of the screen, when your camera will shift. For anyone who's played the Arma series, the aiming is similar to that. Weapon and bullet physics are also very realistic. Firing SMGs in more than 4-5 round bursts will make it impossible to hit a target further than 40-50 meters away. The game also features a full ballistics simulation. Bullet drop and travel time must be taken into account when shooting.
The game features HUGE maps with up to 64 players. The vehicles in the game feature full 3d-modeled interiors, where players must realistically navigate the inside of the vehicle to move to each position. No more instantly teleporting from the driver seat to the machine gunner seat, for instance. Vehicles also feature realistic damage models. You can take out a tank's engine by hitting it with an armor piercing round, or even kill the gunner with a well placed shot to the gunner's seat, rendering the tank useless until another player takes over the position.
The graphics and sound design are all top notch in this game. The performance was a little shaky in the beta, but in just two weeks time they have greatly improved framerates and reduced lag. Red Orchestra 2 is a must have for anyone who is a fan of first person shooters who want a more authentic experience than mainstream shooters will give you. It is a game that game developers should take notes on when designing games in the future. Tripwire Interactive put a lot of hard work with limited resources into this game, and the result is something extraordinary.
Despite how old it is, it is still one of the best in it's genre.

This game is beautiful and I can't believe how small the development team is.
Pros:
The story moves a little slowly but it does a great job drawing you in with mystery and exploration.
I enjoyed the system of crafting food and gathering ingredients.
The song system was interesting to work with.
I appreciated the ability to set custom map markers.
The learning curve isn't too steep at first and the tutorial does a good job introducing you to the gameplay mechanics.
The music and visuals are phenominal.
You can rain fire (energy) down on the local wildlife and slaughter schools of fish to gather ingredients.
Cons:
The control scheme, in conjunction with the song mechanics, can make it awkward to navigate, fight, and sing at the same time but overall I think it works.
The world is very large and backtracking can be tedious, but the ability to set map markers helps considerably.
The learning curve starts off nice but there is a period of time where many people will struggle with navigating around projectiles while fighting and using songs. Enemies hit hard and for a while you will easily come close to death.
The game is very good at what it does, but some might find the content to be lacking. Don't expect a huge and immersive crafting system, interactive npcs, or a very interactive world (you can, however, decimate the wildlife which I think is a nice detail). This is very much a side-scrolling shooter with puzzle and exploration elements, an interesting gimmick (the song mechanics) and a small crafting element.

Aquaria is a beautful underwater game that feels very much like a mixture of Ecco the Dolphin and Super Metroid. If you're not familiar with the Metroidvania styele of game,s it involves  avast, open world where the player is given, generally, very little direction of where to go, with the only obstacles being environments or passages thta the player cannot explore due to needing to unlock abilities, find items, leanr amgic, or what have you.
Aquaria does this through songs, which lets you transform into other forms giving you new abilities, like energy blasts, faster swimming, or the ability to project light into darkness. The world is larger than I expected, and comprised of several distinct areas that run the gamut from the Kelp Forest, to a Sunken City, to the Veil, which should be seen in game to be properly experienced. Luckily, the game lets you put down as many checkpoints as you want, to let you mark down places you can't quite get to yet, or areas you might want to come back to later. If you want to collect veeyrthing, you'll be backtracking quite a bit.
Music is a focal point in the game, and so it's not surprising that Aquaria has fantastic music. The graphics are pretty for what they are, and the bit of voice acting in the game is good as well. Most of the songs seem to ebe a variation of the game's main theme, which becomes a point touched on in the game's plot later.
The game has tons of optional content, areas, and bosses, which lets you find either new optional forms, new costumes for Naija, the adventurer, or simply little trinkets that sit in your home that make the place look nicer and sometimes add little creatures to the area. The little touches like thsis bring the game from being good to much better.
Combat gets very 'shmupy/bullet helly' at times, and sometimes boils down to chugging healing items (which are made through a very robust recipe and cooking system - actually pretty neat!) and blasting away as fast as your right mouse button will let you click.
If I had any qualms with the game, it's that it feels like the fast travel is just few and far enough between to where you do a lot of swimming around, but if you get good at wall-boost chaining (and you will) a lot of this is mitigated. There's also a few moments where how to proceed is not immediately apparent, and it's only after i tried everything that i realized what the hint telling me what to do was actually supposed to be. The game also runs off of a save-point system, with no checkpoints in between, so a feath can force you to replay a bit more of your previous progress than you might like. This isn't a huge issue typically, though there is one optional boss that's quite a trek from a save point to get to, and isn't very easy to top it off.
Finally, the last problem: The game ends on a huge cliffhanger, and we will never see a sequel, more than likely. Oh well.

Ubisoft's Tetris Ultimate is the worst version of the classic puzzle game I've ever played. That said, it's still Tetris, and if you can overlook its faults: weird interface, boring music, Uplay-requirement, poor controller support, lack of online players, zero updates, etc. etc, what you're left with is a functional version of Tetris on Steam.
You can still do your T-spins, perfect clears and Tetrises. You can still play traditional modes like Marathon, Endless and Sprint. You can remap your keys, set player handicaps, and customize gameplay details such as speed of lateral movement, soft drops and key sensitivity. You can play with Hold, ghost blocks and Tetromino queues. And if you have no friends on Uplay, you can battle multiple bots in multiple game modes.
Tetris Ultimate scratches the itch, but I only recommend it if you don't have a system to play the far superior Puyopuyo Tetris on.

Pointlessly detailed simulation that prioritises emulating the boring minutiae of life over having fun.
Got a new bag? Great! In most games you'd equip it with one click and your inventory would be expanded. In Project Zomboid you need to unequip the old bag, equip the new bag, put the old bag on the ground, loot the old bag, and have all the contents be transferred across one by one.
The goal is realism, but much of the game is just frustrating rather than realistic. What exactly do game developers think tools and weapons are made of? Play-Doh? I think in real life you could poke more than five zombies with a kitchen knife before it broke. There has never been a game that weapon degradation has made better.

Project Zomboid is more of a simulation than a game. Perhaps it's supposed to be? For me, there are far too many components and you spend half your time sorting your inventory so as not to be overburdened. The other half of your time is spent reading books, and picking items off the floor which you accidentally dropped. Picking up 50 seeds one by one from the ground is not my idea of good gameplay. And what is this obsession in new games with degrading weapons? It's never been a fun idea to have your favourite weapon stop working. I don't think the "line of sight" rule works when you have a 3rd person game, especially in multiplayer where your mate will disappear if behind you. Yes, you can't see what's behind you in real life, but you can be aware.
This game/simulation feels like a chore, which is disappointing, given how good the premise is.

In short; this game is a mixture of a classic arcade title like Karate Champs, IK+, or the obscure Chatan Yarakuu Shanku - The Karate Tournament, with Art of Fighting's visuals and the recent UFC titles' attention to detail, with a touch of RPG and simulation.
If you look at the screenshots and expect Karate Master 2: Knock Down Blow to be a typical Street Fighter II clone straight from the 90s you'll be in for a surprise.  In this game you play as forklift truck driver and karate novice Ken during his young adult years in 1980s Japan as he hones his skills, tempers his body and soul, breaks his bones, and fights every rival in order to achieve his goal of becoming a karate master and open his own school.
To accomplish this you will be tasked with taking on the various dojos of this harbour town, most of which are variations of karate, but you will also fight boxing, wrestling, Muay Thai, and Taikwondo practitioners, as well as the odd bull or car, and defeating their students to make a name for yourself.
However, these dojos don't except a new face.  You need to earn fame by winning two types of tournaments, one with protective gear and one without.  The difference supposedly is face hitting is against the rules of the latter tournament, however there isn't any in game punishment for this so just go wild.  I did find it the tougher tournament of the two, but otherwise they're very similar.
However, you will also need to earn money in order to enter these, and other tournaments, which is earned with a rather simple yet satisfying forklift minigame that brings back memories of the similarly themed Shenmue.
Winning the tournaments and defeating dojos will earn you training days, which are used to increase your Stength, Speed, Toughness, Ki (stamina), and Tai Kitae (described as increasing the roughness of your skin, effectively it increases your chance of critical blows) which are handled via various mini games that are unlocked as you progress in each stat.  Unfortunately a lot of these are rather hit and miss, but they're short enough that they likely won't be too off putting, but you will be playing them a lot.
As for the combat itself you have the d-pad and four face buttons, which for reference I will be using the X-Box pad layout for further descriptions.  Much like Tekken or UFC titles the face buttons represent Kens left and right punches and kicks, and the d-pad is used to aim for high, mid, or low strikes, combinations of the buttons are used for various techniques, and pressing the two punches together, plus a direction, will perform one of your defensive katas.
Instead of a health metre, your body, as well as your opponent's, is represented by a small green silhouette which indicates damage to your head, legs, arms, or torso by changing to light green, yellow, orange, and finally red.  This increases the chance of being knocked out, but fortunately does recover slightly.  I'm not certain what governs recovery as such, but you'll sometimes be very grateful for a Yame, where the fight pauses due to either one of the combatants falling to te mat or going out of bounds, after which the combatants return to their starting positions.  This gives you a moment for recovery of both your health and Ki, though be warns, if you've taken too much of a beating you won't heal at all.
Fights are tense at first, as a single strike can end a match due to the opponent being too strong, or them breaking your bones with a critical.  When this happens you end up in hospital and must engage in a mini game to heal.  Fortunately this action goes both ways, meaning you can score a luck strike as well.
The game feels both technical and arcadey, I don't want to say I had to use a lot of skill beyond targeting a certain area, and some fights can feel like they're just a war of attrition, but at the same time are very enjoyable.  Hitting a heavy blow or dazing an opponent by getting in a Brainshock or similar feels great, and having to back off and rethink your game due to getting pulverised in the first few seconds and make a very tense moment or two, leading to a more brutal feel than the more famous fighters out there.
The visuals and sound really help there, seeing a realistic amount of blood splattering the fighters and the floor, heay blows sounding like an explosion as the game momentarily shudders as the screen is framed with a red haze, and the aforementioned Brain/Livershock, being left breathless, or a receiving muscle injury causes a dizzying, wobbly effect as the fighter starts staggering as they try to fight, all of it leads to a real sense of risk and struggle.
The graphics aren't superb sadly, the sprite work, while effective, does look very rough, especially on some of the fighters, and some of the backgrounds are poorly rendered polygon work, though it has some of the better audiences I've seen in a game.  The music is pretty good, if not very memorable.  It has the feel of an old Tokusatsu show, as well as a classic beat 'em up, and fits the game very well.
Unfortunately the game does have some issues, occasionally the controls would become unresponsive, and the game can be rather repetitive, as grinding is necessary to max out your stats, and get enough money to get through the game.  It also hurts that there's a distinct lack of multiplayer, which would be great in a game this dedicated to an authentic feeling fighting game RPG.
I spent around 6 hours in order to get to the credits, which considering the price is very good.  I can honestly say I had a huge amount of fun in that time, and would love to play more.  Hopefully there will be a sequel some day, with multiplayer included.

My overall recommendation is a definite "yes" for horror fans, as it is a solid game, and is superior to most horror games released in the past few years.  It has a compelling story, comparatively strong character development, and an overall well-crafted (for an Indie game) presentation with some gruesome and effective moments.  Its greatest crime is being released after The Cat Lady, which is one of my favorite horror-adventure games of all time, and as such feels like a step backward.
The story, compelling as it may be, definitely comes across as a predecessor to The Cat Lady - which makes sense, since the original version was the first game released by the developer.  It lacks the subtlety and quiet character-building moments, and the themes are not nearly as deep or well-explored.  It does have an emotional impact, but because the supernatural/psychological horror elements are so relentless, the humanity of the characters and their interactions is diminished and therefore is less affecting than it could have been.  Of course, this is all relative to The Cat Lady; it is still an order of magnitude above the vast majority of Indie horror games.
The primary flaw, however, is the voice acting.  It ranges from decent to horrendous.  Ivy's VA was the only one that seemed like she consistently knew what she was doing; most other characters seemed like they were reading the script for the first time.  And the person who played Joe in the prologue was just godawful.  Also, things get a little silly toward the end, which undermines the otherwise deeply emotional climax.
I mainly focus on the cons because I loved The Cat Lady so much, but as I said, this is still a good horror game.  I do not know if it is possible to mute the voices, but if it is, I would recommend doing so.  The music is too good to completely turn off the sound, but the voice acting can be cringey at times.

Downfall:
~~~~~~~~

Joe and Ivy Davis have been married for several years but their marriage has not been smooth sailing for a while. Ivy has not been herself lately as bad memories from the past keep haunting her. Joe organized a small vacation at the “Quiet Haven Hotel” in an attempt to work out their marriage. As they arrive at the “Quiet Haven Hotel”, they are welcomed by an incredible storm and heavy rain. Could this be an omen for what is to come?

Downfall is a point and click/rich story/adventure game where you play the character of Joe Davis.
First you will play a prologue (tutorial) where you will learn how to interact with other characters and as well as how use items from your inventory. In the prologue, you will be told how Joe and Ivy met for the first time when they were but spring chickens. It will also outlay Ivy’s prime concern at this particular time of her life, and what happened to Robbie, Joe’s little brother.
Then you will get a short, effective intro which will give you the feel of how the atmosphere will be portrayed in the game. As you enter the lobby of the hotel, Ivy will act in very strange ways, speaking in an incoherent manner and then back to normal several times. After speaking with manager, Joe will move up to their room and head off to bed. After a while dreaming, he wakes up in the room alone. From here, Joe will need to find out where his troubled wife is.
Throughout this dark adventure, Joe will meet interesting characters to talk to in hope of saving Ivy. There is Doctor Z, who conducts brain transplants; Agnes, who does not know Joe but will party with him; as well as other intriguing personalities.  Most of the story will be in the hotel, but Joe will also visit places on the outside, keeping you alert and entertained.
Downfall look goods graphically with its peculiar atmosphere. All the mechanisms are easy to control with your keyboard. The highest resolution you can play this game is 800X600. The voiceover could have been better.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~~~
-	Good & Interesting Story
-	Easy interface to use
-	Good graphics and atmosphere
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~~~

-	Puzzles could have been harder
-	Highest resolution is 800X600
-	Voiceover could have better
If you enjoy a rich story with a freaky atmosphere and strange characters, then downfall should be in your game library.

Front Mission: Evolved rides on a coattails of a beloved franchise which sold pretty well in Japan and had a decent following in the West; but where previous titles were tactical RPG's this one has been hit with a "borad appeal" mallet and is now a third-person shooter.
Putting you into a cockpit of a bipedal mech toting machine guns and shoulder-mounted rocket launchers sounds amazing and has a great cathartic potential, but some annoying bugs and strange design decisions make this whole experience a chore. First of all, I have a problem with the amining-recticule. Now that may seem like a strange nitpick, but aiming recticule is surrounded by an unecessary transparent rectangle taking about 10% of the screen which
gets in the way of you shooting things and spotting various collectibles (all of which do nothing except provide you with a small monetary bonus after you collect a set number of them). While on the subject of "getting in the way of fun" - AI partners. For most of the missions game partners you with a AI controlled Wanzer (basically another name for a mech) which I think were supposed to help you in larger battles by drawing aggro and damaging opponents, but they actually end up blocking your movement and line or sight while contributing nothing except stating the obvious (Yes, I realize my armor is low because my Wanzer is on fire thank you very much).
Combat is mediocre at best, lacking any depth and ticking off every third-person shooter trope in the book. Your objective in every mission is to shoot stuff until it explodes or stops shooting back, which is unfortunate because with a bit of tweaking it could've been really interesting. You see, consecutive shots in your arms and especially legs can easily cripple you; and in the case of legs, severely hamper your mobility. This will cause you to move at a snails pace until your next health pickup esentially making you a sitting duck for all enemies in the area. While really frustrating it wouldn't be a problem if you could do that same thing to your enemies, but (and it could just be due to the higher difficulty level), I've never managed to do that making that whole mechanic feel kinda cheap. It also serves to highlight how much
limiting "skating"; a fast sliding maneuvre, can really interrupt the flow of combat by making you wait for a couple of seconds in cover while the appropriate meter or even your armor recharges. You can argue that this forces you to take a more tactical approach by using it sparingly; only to dash from cover to cover, but I'd argue that if you're gonna base all your missions on blowing stuff up, you might as well make the player feel like a complete badass by allowing him to blaze through it at high speed. Besides, by using slide, you're always sacrificing accuracy for higher mobility and compensating for that requires a certain dose of skill.
To devs credit, they tried mixing things up by throwing different kinds of enemies at you along with the occasional turret section, and, god help them, on-foot segment. These only serve to highlight the rest of the game because nothing makes you lament for that mediocre mech combat like playing utterly awful third-person shooter for a few minutes. Boss fights are dull, unimaginative and sometimes downright frustrating with bullet-spongey bosses making the whole affair an endurance run, as you circle strafe around them holding every shoot button available and offering prayers to any god that'll hear you that they go down before you do. Oh, and if you thought that facing a single bullet-spongey boss was an exercise in attrition, good luck facing four of them which game will generously throw at you at one point.
Ability to customize your Wanzer to your linking is the only decent part of the experience and even that is offset by game forcing you to use specific parts for some missions, and the aforementioned on-foot sections. It would be interesting to see how this gameplay holds up against other players, but unfortunately as of time of writing, multiplayer has been pretty much dead.

This is not an easy game. You'll be confused, lost, sad, and alone at the beginning. However, as you progress through the game, you learn that life isn't so terrible, and that there may be a chance. Then you die and have to start over. Everything is different now; the randomized maps make predicting what your up against impossible. One thing is still the same though: you learned a little bit about how this game works now. You go through and get a bit farther, then die. Repeat. Repeat. Repeat. Eventually, you find out that there is a backstory if you are so inclined, otherwise you can continue to treat it like an evil arcade machine. This game has a lot of surprises in it that really make me happy: quite a bit of work was put into it and the fact that the creators cared is evident throughout.
I would definitely recommend this game to anybody that likes being challenged and having to figure things out the hard way on their own. There is nothing quite so satisfying as making it past a level that maybe you shouldn't have, or trumping the unstoppable forces with sheer cunning. Very entertaining, fun and easy to pick up and burn a few minutes or a few hours of your free time! Would recommend out of 17.

WARNING: So here we are, Dungeon of the Endless. A very different game from Amplitude studios; who specialized in 4X games (Endless Space, Endless Legend). And while this game has multiple elements of those previous games and 4X games in general, if you are looking for a 4X Game, this is not your pickup. If you are looking for a good rogue-like, a good tower defense game, or a mix of both and some 4X elements, this is the best pickup for you on the market.
Settings: The settings are useful and helpful, as everyone has their own preferences. Overall positive. This goes for the UI of the game as well.
Story: There is little direct story in this game, such as in The Binding of Isaac, but much is hidden in the lore and different unlocks you find in the game. These will not be further discussed, because spoilers.
Gameplay: Time for the meat of this review. The gameplay is relatively simple. Your characters progress through rooms on twelve different floors, each floor progressing in difficulty. There is always a chance for monsters to spawn, and you will fight them. But the big part of the game is the four major resources that come into play. Here they are:
Industry (Gear Icon): Industy is used to build things (notably modules): They can generate other resources, or defend rooms.
Science: Spend science to research new modules.
Food: Levels up/heals your heroes.
Dust: Does not generate per floor, but is picked up. Used to light rooms.
If a room is not lit, monsters might spawn in that room. So yeah. You're going to need some defenses. There is a crystal in the starting room, once you find the exit, you must take that crystal to the exit. You can't leave until the character CARRYING the crystal enters it. Once the crystal is picked up, in every dark room monsters will spawn.
Elements: The rogue-like element is pretty obvious. The 4X elements of resource management and production, and how to spend them is super important. But tower defense is pretty simple. Build things that help heroes, or hurt monsters, so that they can't get to your crystal. When the crystal is hit, you lose dust. When the crystal dies, you lose. When all the heroes die, you lose.
Difficulty: It is an odd game in difficulty. At the start, there are two difficulties: Too easy and Easy. Too easy after a few games to get the hang of things becomes too easy. Easy is brutal, and requires you to scrap for resources, mangage them incredibly well, and then most likely die to some fatass punching your crystal.
Replayability: Yes. It has proceduraly generated floors. And it's a rogue-like. Never heard of a good rouge-like without replayability.
Conclusion: This game isn't often what people are looking for, especially fans of previous games by Amplitude. But this is a fantastic blend of multiple genres, including the dying tower defense games, and the somewhat bland 4X games. This revitalizes these elements in a unique blend that requires the player to be smart, quick to adapt to situations, good with spending resources and leveling the hero, which brings some RPG into the game, and not getting too frustrated when that fatass kills your crystal three games in a row because you didn't upgrade those claymoar mines on floor seven to get a HUD module that no matter what you do keeps getting destroyed halfway through the floor because you haven't saved up enough industry or science to buy or research better protection, and now one of your heroes is dead because there wasn't enough food to heal her, and oh my god it's Midnight. I need to sleep. Well maybe let's have one more go.

TLDR: definitely buy it if you're a fan of game of survival genre because of its potential, regular update, it's also bug-free.
1) To date, most of the basic features of the game, eg skills, items, health systemm, zombie ai etc., have already been developed and they so far work out quite well. Some of the features may be lacked, eg more guns, car, npc, but luckily with the support of the community via workshop, the holes have been filled (having said that, you know, I would expect the developers to ship much better update in these aspects than workshop in the near future). The workshop also adds unlimited potential to the game.
2) The developers do care about the community and the game itself. I've played other early access games, the developers of those do not give a damn about hackers, opinions from the community; some even gave up updating the games. I've played this game for ~300 hours and the regular updates have never been disrupted.
3) Never seen a bug that would force close my games. (you know, unlike other early access games)
Just buy it and you won't be disappointed.

While not without its merits, this game has lots of problems that make it an overall unpleasant experience. I ended up quitting my playthrough at the clay golem boss (the one that the ghost child creates).
ART
First of all, the art is probably one of the most impressive features of the game. All of the different areas are very beautiful. Unfortunately, the effect of this is lessened by the less-than-stellar pivot based animation style. A lot of the scripted movements of the characters (for example during cutscenes) look very awkward and unnatural, which hurts the beautiful aesthetic that the art tries to convey. Even some of the movements during normal gameplay just don't look believable. It just looks like characters are sliding around on the screen instead of propelling themselves through the water (which is one of the things that makes aquatic life so interesting to look at in real life).
But what really matters most in a game is whether the gameplay is fun, so I'll focus on that now.
EXPLORATION
The game is called a "metroidvania" in the sense that, while it is a platformer, it is designed so that you spend your time exploring the environment and not being "on rails" playing through "levels". I can understand how someone who spent time playing games like Metroid would enjoy the nostalgiac appeal of that design, but I just think that, overall, it's not a very enjoyable way to spend your gaming time. The root of my complaint with the exploration is this: there's so many games out there that provide a constantly enjoyable experience, so why would you spend valuable hours of your life wandering around with no clue what to do when you could instead be playing something where you're constantly feeling engagement and enjoyment. Can you honestly say that you had fun swimming through an area that you've already seen, having to fight the same enemies, and hearing the same short music loop over and over again? If I spend an hour trying to figure out what weird action I need to do to advance the story, that's an hour I could've spent playing something more consistently fun (like Tetris, in my case), especially if the emotional payoff for advancing the story isn't very high.
I'll go into more detail on the issues with exploration in this game. A lot of the things you need to do to progress seem very cryptic, and not in a clear-cut "puzzle game" sort of way (like trying to slide blocks around to get to an exit, for example), but in an ambiguous "guess what the devs want you to do" sort of way. At the beginning of the game, it's pretty straight forward and I don't really have anything to complain about. You essentially get new abilities which act as keys to get you to areas that were previously locked (the Bind ability lets you move stones, the Energy Form lets you open Pearl gates, and the Beast ability lets you swim against currents). The way that the map works makes it obvious to you which areas you haven't explored yet, which means you don't waste much time wandering around. However, after you get all the various forms, it starts to go dowhill. Throughout the game, though, there's times where you'll waste time having unknowingly taken a turn towards an area you're not supposed to get through and having to waste time backtracking.
I only was able to tolerate the exploration by occasionally referring to a guide to make sure I was going in the right direction. I didn't want to waste my precious hours of game time taking a wrong turn to an area I'm not supposed to be at yet and having to backtrack and take a different turn towards some other area. I envy people who feel they have so much free time that they can enjoy an experience like that.
MUSIC
This game was praised for its music, but I'm not quite sure that the praise is that deserved. If you listened to the soundtrack by itself, I'm sure it would be enjoyable. But, in the context of the game, there's several key issues. The root problem is that the design of the music causes listening fatigue (which basically means that the music gets annoying and hurts the enjoyability of the game).
First, most of the song tracks are quite short, meaning you're going to hear the same song over and over again as you explore an area (which will happen a lot, because it is an exploration game). Second, music is played pretty much all the time. There's few moments where you are only hearing the peaceful ambiance of the water, and they are quite pronounced because they're such a relief in the face of constant, repetitive songs. Finally, the songs themselves are "loud". I mean this in the sense that there's not many moments where there's quiet parts or sparse, ambient parts in the songs.
COMBAT
Combat is generally frustrating. Many of the boss battles are nothing more than "swim around and shoot them and hope the many projectiles on the screen don't hit you, and eat healing items and hope you win". There's nothing really fun in that except a sense of relief when you manage to get a victory. A few bosses require you to use your various forms and abilities, and that's okay, but they still tend to be frustrating in a way that has you complaining about the design of the game and not analyzing your own tactics to prepare for the next attempt. I ended up quitting where I did because there was a bug where a projectile you needed to fire to defeat the boss wouldn't move in any direction and would just sit there where you initially fired it (instead of traveling where I was aiming), combined with a weird issue where my camera would start going crazy, and a poor design that made it so you had little window to avoid the bosses attacks. Also, you had to go through a pointlessly lengthy sequence where you build the boss every time you want to re-attempt it, which isn't fun at all. Why not just let me save before the boss is completed? Why would anyone want to waste their time doing that?
Throughout the game, the combat with the enemies isn't very fun either. A particularly glaring issue is that the screen doesn't show enemies that you need to see in order to avoid them. Some enemies will be firing fast projectiles at you or jumping at you from the edges of the screen, leaving you no time to dodge them. Simply zooming out or not having enemies attack you when they are a certain distance from you might've helped this, but there really isn't much to be done for a combat system that just involves swimming around and right clicking a bunch. A lot of the enemies take a lot of hits to defeat, so you'll be right clicking constantly during combat. Due to how movement works, dodging enemy attacks isn't very easy, even if you know what you want to do. You have the ability to do a quick dash, but I feel like the cooldown on the dash isn't enough to make it possible to avoid damage when there's a group of enemies attacking you. Precise control is also difficult using the mouse and keyboard - you either use the mouse and sacrifice precise stopping and starting, or use the keyboard and sacrifice fine directional control. Movement feels generally sluggish due to the considerable acceleration, which further hurts combat.
Overall, this game just has bad fun/minute when compared to the variety of options we have in 2014.

Evolved does not live up to its successors, lacking the scope of story and variation in presentation that made them interesting. Poor voice acting deadens what little emotional impact is written into the well animated cutscenes. There was so much potential here, and the port itself runs quite well.
This doesn't 'feel' like a Front Mission game. Is it the UI? the mechs? customization? story? Probably all of the above. Yes the wanzers you know from games past are lovingly modeled from other games in the franchise, and interesting mechanics like dashing are integrated well into real time dynamic first person combat.
It's just so ... dull, and that's not enough to warrant a sale when there are so many surperior titles available. A shameful, boring PC port that does not lend any credence to the franchise. Square-Enix, once again, letting down its fans.

The first negative impressions of this game, and which remained throughout it, were firstly the inelegant interface. It’s a point and click adventure in which you can neither point nor click - no mouse support at all! One can save progress, but never delete, and even saving with the same name just makes multiple saves with that name. The “Prologue” is started every time the game is loaded, as is my native language queried, which hasn’t changed since the last time I played. These may seem minor, but it gives a very cheap feel to the game. The second most pertinent issue is the unnatural animations for characters walking. It really looks very artificial. The “Black and white and red” style has been done too often before for it to be innovative. It is a game not about graphics however, it is about the story, but here it didn’t particularly shine either: it lacked coherence and was ultimately disappointing. Perhaps if I had bought and completed “Cat Lady” it might have been more meaningful but I am far from encouraged to do so. The voice acting has been criticised but I didn’t find any fault with it: not everyone can have a pleasingly euphonic voice and so if anything it is more convincing to have voice actors with less harmonious voices.
Do you like cats?  Do you like Ladies?  Then you will love this prequel!  A gripping and real look at some of the darker aspects of the human psyche.

As a fan of Cat Lady, I had high expectations for this game and they were mostly met.
Pros:
-the cast of characters. Joe has the charisma of a rock, but the supporting cast does a great job of keeping dialogue interesting.
-background music. There are more ambient tracks and song used than in the cat lady, and some additional plot progress actually depends on listening closely.
-over-all visuals. The game is not very colorful, but when it does vary from the grayscale, the effect looks great. I'm a big fan of merging 2D and 3D imagery for the backgrounds too.
-replay value. There are multiple endings, and getting something other than the default one requires a lot of exploration.
-your choices really do matter!
-quick saves and loads. Because of the requirements for multiple endings, these are a lifesaver. You won't ruin your perfect ending by accidentally clicking the wrong choice!
-voice acting acting is mostly very well done but...
Cons:
-the audio quality ranges from good to terrible. Some of the scenes were ruined because a supposedly emotional line had a bathroom-like echo to it.
-3D animation looked out of place to me, especially the bit of walking down stairs to the cellar. I had to backtrack several times because I forgot things, and had to watch it everytime. It just doesn't match the overall style in my opinion.
Nitpicks!
-the prologue/tutorial chapter. The twist at the end felt like nothing because I didn't care for the characters and I felt like the characters didnt like each other.
-some character art/animation felt out of place: your companion sure smiled a lot even while clearly in distress

If you're looking for the greatest karate simulator ever to grace this plane of existence then look no further! Karate Master 2 Knock Down Blow is a simple, yet immensly fun fighting game that comes with a set of mini-games. Despite having a bunch of bugs at the moment of writing this review it still delivers as a game and I would recommend all fans of karate and beat 'em ups to go give it a shot!

Oh man, that nostalgia. The electronic music, the city map, the cheesy 80's kung fu movie plot, and sprites that look like they come straight out of an SNK game. And that was the entire purpose: to relive the glory days of 16-bit fighting games.
Karate Master 2 does a great job of running you through the karate journey as you'd expect from pop culture. There's not much backstory - your character is a maverick karateka who works at the docks for money, fights in tournaments to gain fame, goes through harsh training, beats up other dojos, gets invite to the secret kumite tournament and dreams of opening a school. And surprisingly, through all the generic archetypes of martial arts films and games, it's still satisfying to play this one through.
The fighting system is actually quite good. No flash combos or special moves; just the straighforward punches and kicks that you can expect from a real karate tournament. Fighting rewards getting into the right range and using the right attack for maximum effect. Hits don't necessarily cancel each other out - one can still connect a punch or a kick after being struck. Rapid button mashing reduces the power of attacks. Training strength and hardness allows you to randomly perform critical hits that can stun the opponent or bring an instantaneous end through broken bones. And the same can happen to you.
The pacing feels right for a 80's fighting game and is executed well. The campaign does become grindy after a while as you have to earn fame and money to complete the story. After training up your stats, fights become too easy, only requiring several punches to end, and the story doesn't introduce more challenging tasks or complex events, making the replay value effectively zero. You'll be done with the game in a day or two.
But it was worth it.

A heart wrenching dish to be savored. Probably once.
+++PROS+++
R. Michalski serves us again a point and click adventure with sweet bloody themes and photographic visual that propels our characters through emotions to dwell upon.
Also in keeping with his take on player choices, you will not always know what to do to get the ending you want; the choices matter, and it's not like Mass Effect's GOOD GUY BAD GUY choices. You will sweat to make your choices.
There is a new quick save stat that players can use to make choices easier. In The Cat Lady, you cycled through menus after long dialogue sequences. Here, you press a button whenever you can.
His Tarantino like juxtaposition of upbeat music in insane situations continues. The soundtrack is delicious. At different moments when appropriate, it is sensitive, dark, scary, calming, and otherworldly, and sometimes rockin'.
This game is shorter than The Cat Lady, and much more concise; the story never drags, and the puzzles won't bamboozle you; Cat Lady had a few of those.
It seems as if the game was made with large expectancy of its players being fans of The Cat Lady. As such, fans will enjoy the awesome connections to that game, for epic moments big and small. It seems as if Michalski's preparing to build a universe here. On the other hand, it may bother some players that there was too much fanservice, putting in the much loved Cat Lady.
---CONS---
The endings were a little punishing, with the only likable one being the hard to get Golden Ending. Thankfully, I can choose for myself what I'd like to believe as canon.
The story is a lot weirder and has even more unanswered questions than The Cat Lady.
There are some parts where the dialogue and voice action isn't fully realistic, but that doesn't bother me. The reason it doesn't is because the game is stylized, and the level of realism in voice acting is not inconsistent with the level of realism in everything else. These are characters, interesting characters, not real people, who have their own ways of talking that make them stand out. Joe Davis might just be a really weird guy who speaks in that overly nonchalant way.
The story is a bit predictable, especially with what trailers have shown. Still, it can be interesting to see how it happens, even if you can vaguely guess what will happen.
I found it hard to care about Ivy. Then again, I think this was part of the point, that people around depressed people get hurt too. This game has taught me that unhappy people are unpleasant. I suppose this isn't really a flaw, except that it kinda messes with the motivation.
Fun game to play with friends, suprisingly much content for being an early access game. Totally worth it on sale.

Downfall is the prequel to The Cat Lady, expanding on the universe by going into the story of Joe and Ivy Davis, Susan Ashworth's next door neighbors. This is the remade and redone version of the original point and click adventure game, giving it the same format as The Cat Lady's keyboard mechanics. Given The Cat Lady's quiet success, it'd be easy for fans to compare the two to see how it has improved. So has it?
Let's look at the story, first, as most people will tend to compare to The Cat Lady here. Is it as good as the first? Yes. Is it as dreary and drepressing? No, because this falls under a different theme. While TCL was about the challenges of depression and melancholly, this story is more rough, touching on the subjects of anorexia, vice, the burden of the past and psychopathy. This game is much more "in your face" because of this, as evidenced by the last scene of the prologue. That being said, the story is still fantastic to go through and the characters are all well made in my opinion.
Mechanically, the game is a HUGE step up fro TCL. The functions are much more fluid and the graphics are a bit clearer. The game introduces a quicksave and autosave function, which is very helpful in the event that you have to leave. Also, dialouge isn't too long winded as some in TCL, where you may be sitting there for longer than anticipated because of a longer story and forget to save. It is more spread out and easier to take a break from.
As for the visual design, the characters are no longer animated like puppets with moving pieces, instead being done but animated 2D art, which are much more clearer and crisp than in TCL. The color pallete is what you expect from the game as well, but it doesn't veer too much from the black and white as often as TCL. One issue with TCL was some of it's color choices being too sporadic and lacking identity, but I'm actually going to say that Downfall might have taken a bit too much back. Still, the backgrounds look as if they were photographed and edited, which was a must for this game. And, of course, there are some good greusome bits of blood and gore and disturbing stuff.
As for sound, they did a much better job this time around. They used a much wider array of sound effects. As for the voice acting, it is on the whole better, but there are still some actors that either weren't that good or the audio quality was lacking. Still, it is an improvement in general, as some of the voice acting is very good, easily outweighing the bad. The music is very good too.
As for the puzzles, they are well thought out. I didn't find myself too stumped, nor did I find any of them to be ridiculously easy. One of the puzzles that I found engaging was the dialogue throughout the game. What you say and do in the game will affect the game's ending, and some of the choices leading to the Golden Ending are easily missed because you thought you were doing something right. It doesn't change the actually gameplay, per se, but it is a puzzle in itself to achieve an ending that you want/
So, Downfall, is it good? Indeed it is, and it is worth it. It doesn't follow The Cat Lady's theme to the letter, but it makes the choice of using its own theme to decide how it should play, therefore making itself its own game.

Ok, before you, fanboys and vanilla girls, start taping with your fat fingers smth like YOU WRONG GTFO ITS MESTERPIECE, let me explain why my opinion here is in a red box instead of a blue one.
Downfall'09 was a great game. Despite poor visuals and unpolished plot, it was a uniqe experience I've never encountered in videogames before. It was scary, humorous, even enjoyably stupid B-movie style sometimes. Most important - this game knew what it wanted to be and never changed its' tone until the very end. Even now, after seven years, it stands as a perfect "study in scarlet" for Harvester Games.
Unfortunately, Rem doesn't feel the same way. As a matter of fact, he called it "kinda ♥♥♥♥" in 2015, couple of months before this remake was released.
To begin with, nobody asked for anoher Downfall. And those who did lied to themselves. Because we all waited for another  Cat Lady. Everybody wanted to burst into tears once again and follow tragic characters who overcome not only disgusting villians but their own demons as well. Which brings us to the 1st major problem of the Downfall'16.
This game doesn't know what it wants to be. It manages to catch the spirit of the original, but strikes hard to push it in chains of a different narrative. The result is not only plotholes ( like
). Somehow it also affects visuals. I mean, art style is great for the most part, but it often doesn't work as it supposed to.
The most obvious example of this is the kitchen. Remember how gory it felt when you first encountered this room in 2009? With all this meat and dirt all around the place? The same kitchen in remake feels like a pale copy - less detailed and monochrome with slightly red. Cooking scene also lost its charm. The most stupid and terrifying sequence of '09 somehow became less entertaining and even boring in '16.
Black and white imagery, btw, is overused to death here. Original game was more competent about it - there were only few monochrome scenes, and it worked much more effectively. But here almost everything is monochrome, and it kills the mood completely. Main thing about Downfall'09 that I enjoyed a lot was black humour involving cannibalism and murder. And this kind of fun only works in full colour grindhouse-style. But no, only black and white. Mb red sometimes, but not much. We've got some serious story here.
And this brings us to the main problem of this remake. It tries so hard to make deep narrative using methods of "The Cat Lady" that it forgets about characters. During the whole game I didn't give a ♥♥♥♥ about Joe Davis, his wife or any other character in this game. Nobody talks like real human. Nobody feels here like real human, except Agnes,
. Achieving all 3 endings, I don't feel like I know these people. Who the ♥♥♥♥ is Joe Davis? Where does he work? What's his favourite dish? What he's afraid of the most? Poor voiceacting doesn't help at all. Sorry, Jessie, sorry, Chisaleya - you need a lot of practice.
Of course, you can tell that original Downfall also had poorly written characters. But this game wasn't about characters, you know. It was all about massacre, death, cannibalism, demons and subconsiousness that plays tricks with your mind. And you're just some guy with the gun and chainsaw called Joe Davis, who wants to make these things right. It was brutal, simple and rather satisfying game that didn't need any kind of remake.
Anyway, this game is also here in this bundle. So if you want to experience both of them and compare - spend your money. I do feel disappointed, but I don't feel decieved. Nobody does it to you like Harvester games after all.
