I tried our Evolve a while back, while they were still in Alpha/Beta testing. I thought it looked visually amazing, but felt a little unbalanced at the time. Evolve is a 4v1 shooter, Where one person gets to play the monster and hulk out, while 4 poor little soldiers, A medic, support soldier, trapper and an assault specialist all try to bring them down. There are multiple game modes to play, Rescue, Defend, Hunt, Arena etc.
Evolve still looks amazing. Actually, I think it looks better now than it did pre-release. Personally, I prefer playing as the monster, because I find it to be a lot more versatile, than playing as one of the soldier classes, but that's my personal opinion. You can choose from a variety of different monsters, though more are expected to be released eventually. Right now they have the Goliath, Kraken, Behemoth, and a Wraith. The playable tutorial has you playing as a Behemoth, I believe, and it takes you through the in's and outs of how to control your character, using the characters abilities and so on. Once you finish this tutorial, a tutorial is also available to learn how to play through the different soldier classes, so this helps lower the learning curve and enables you to get right into the game.
I think the game has come a long way. I remember being on the fence about it before release, even though the graphics looked fantastic, but I like the end product a lot. I think if you have an older graphics card you are going to run into some issues with latency, frame rates, and so forth, so keep that in mind, otherwise this is a pretty fun game, for a PVP title.

Personally, I love puzzle/adventure games that present this dilemma: bail and leave with what you have, or inch just a little further and get a bit richer. Each step you take, you have to reevaulate if you can open one more room and still make it out alive. There are no save points, there are no do-overs, and sometimes pushing a little too far comes with a bleak ending. The game is extremely unforgiving when you first start, and can be wildly frustrating, but each time you play, you improve steadily. The game rewards you for quick thinking and picture big reasoning, without relying too heavily on cheap deaths. Don't get me wrong, it happens, but had you bailed from that floor earlier, it wouldn't have.
I highly recommend this as a single player game, and you'll have a good time, surely.

A solid, competent enough exploration/metroidvania game set underwater. There's a variety of different, pretty environments and a nice soundtrack, and a pretty darn big world map as well. The movement is solid enough and the length of the campaign is just right. A few things I will say though; the game's stunningly linear for a metroidvania, very rarely can you stray from the set path laid out in front of you, leading you to spending a lot of time looking for the next place you're supposed to go. Also, the bosses have too much health and deal too much damage for how clunky the combat is. Fortunately you can get plenty of health items to counteract this, but it's still a pain. The final boss especially is just... way too long for a game that has nothing but manual saves. Really, the manual save system really discourages exploration in general and I could really have done without it. The powers all also don't tend to affect much except for the "puzzles" you need to solve with them. There's also some obscure, kind of dumb puzzles that I looked up because I couldn't be bothered. I don't think the game is great but it's okay, worth checking out if you need your metroidvania fix but not a game I'd recommend heavily over other indie metroidvanias or exploration-focused games. Just alright.

is a hidden-gem of an combat-racer game involving what feel like go-kart versions of airplanes.  It reminds me of
from back in the day, (which was like
but with planes). The game is a lot of fun, especially in multiplayer. If you’re looking for some simple-pleasure arcade action, you probably want to check this out.
At the core it is a racing game, so your objective is always to come in first. As you buzz around, you collect power-ups (like protective shields for your plane or missiles to launch at your enemies) which will help you win the race.  It’s simple and arcade like, and as such don't expect it to feel anything like you’re flying a plane for real.  But it is easy to get the hang of, and is a nice casual experience. That said, I highly recommend using a controller, because it is much more natural than a keyboard & mouse.
It is also noticeable that the graphics are pretty nice. They aren’t anything amazing, but for a game that is clearly focused on gameplay as a selling point, I thought the graphics were an excellent bonus. I mean: if you’re going to blow your opponents out of the sky while doing a barrel-roll through a hollow stone circle, it doesn’t hurt if it looks pretty cool too.
It’s pretty easy to beat the "campaign," leading to the game feeling somewhat short. You unlock new maps and new planes as you play through, but there is very little noticeable variance to be honest; regardless, the game is short enough that it doesn't really matter much.  By the time you start to become bored, you will have beaten it.
The multiplayer is a whole different ballgame. The game is much more exciting to play against other people. When I played I was able to find some games, but it wasn't very populated. If you can find some people who want to meet up, that is probably your best bet. I did it a few times on the weekends and a few random people jumped in too and we wound up with full games. That was fun, but I wouldn’t count on that being the standard.
Anyway,
is definitely a fun game. If you think you would like what it offers, it is worth your consideration. Doubly so if you have a couple of friends to play with.

I just finished the single player campaign and came away pretty dissappointed.
1. The story is the most cliche'd nonsense conceived.  Things happen, no real believable development and it sounds like an 80s cartoon with so much focus on the gameplay gimmick, all wrapped up in your standard pretentious references.  The acting is bad, but ....given what's there.. can't be expected to be better.
2.  Given it's essentially Armored Core lite, you would think they would stick with the gameplay in the former series, but nope.. not a chance.  The part selection is rather shallow, the AI is somehow dumber than in the former series, your partners aren't good for anything and the most serious fault is the on foot sections.  Why include the onfoot sections?  They are an interesting idea, but the execution is like an afterthought.  The control/feel for the on foot section is really bad.  You could call the overall mech game weak, but the onfoot sections are terrible.  At least the aiming in the mech sections is forgiveable.
3.  The sound effects in this game is straight out of Transformers the movie.  It is terrible, nonsensicle and has such a presence that I was annoyed from start to finish.  The music is generic "epic" and forgettable.
4.  I played through the campaign and resolved to uninstall it right away, so I have not tried the multiplayer.  The mech sections were not that compelling, so I don't think whatever community happens to be there would be worth my time.

I'm reccomeding this because the original game is bundled with the remake. The remake made no sense and tried to hard to be the original instead of standing on it's own feet. Buy it on sale, not for full price like I did.
I played the original right before the remake and actually prefer everything about the original. The original actually had me gagging at some points and not wanting to continue because I knew what was about to happen. This remake had me wanting to finish so I could get to the cameos at the end and then left me wanting.
My main issue is the plot. The remake skewed the story so much it didn't even fit in with what we were shown in the Cat Lady. It kept the same events and motivations from the first game but updated them to try to make them fit into the new game and they didn't. Characters were not fleshed out enough for their actions to make sense. Like the fact they kept the axe man from the original but didn't offer an explanation for him and he wasn't used to his full advantage in my opinion. And then he suddenly poofs and isn't seen for the rest of the game.
Spoilers: In the original game, Sophie is trying to become fat for the man she loves and becomes morbidly obese. In this game, she's trying to become skinny but still has a recipe for a fattening smoothie?? And still ends up obese. Also her final incarnation has become demonic despite the remake never explaining why.  Ivy, in the original, doesn't eat so Joe feeds her to death and is revealed to be large at the end. When we see Joe and Ivy in the Cat Lady, Ivy is seen to be obese. In the remake Ivy is battling anorexia but when we are told about her true form at the end she is skin and bones, that Joe wasn't trying to save her, even though that's the whole point of the game. Also Ivy went from having mental problems in the first game to just being an unlikeable character with an attitude and a negative attitude about everyting.
The voice acting was not done well. There was not enough energy put into most of the characters. This made listening to them difficult and I wish there was an option to turn them off. I liked the cameos they included and when Agnes was around she was great to listen to. Everything was voiced, they never just had text on screen, which is something that I really appreciated.

This was a well made game but for me there wasn't enough love put into it as there was in the original and I really wish they had either changed more or kept things more the same. This experience was horrifying. Of all the gore and overt attempts at disgust that games and movies deal with these days, only few are truly effective. In games you are either stopped entirely and put into a cutscene of some kind or you face these horrors with obliviousness, whereby the characters does not even to what we know he or she must be aware of, and that conventionally horrify you. Downfall has an interesting movement in this regard, it falls somewhere between the loss of control of a cutscene, but within the world of the played character. A loss of control in this sense is what we in real life would call a reflexive reaction. We cringe, brace ourselves, shield our face, eyes, cower back, etc, and the same happens in this game. This is one part of the realism that underlies the entirety of this experience. And it is that same realism that manages to hit so hard, and actually horrify as every absurdly surrealistic scene has roots to the physical world; yet becomes otherworldly in the compound of these worldly parts.
When I wrote about The Cat Lady, I mistakenly called it fittingly ugly. This was largely due to an inability to thoughtfully articulate what actually went on aesthetically in games of this ilk (only Downfall and The Cat Lady, as far as I know). Ugliness in regards to this game should entirely be replaced with the term unsettling, or uncanny. It is ugly in the sense that dissonance is ugly. It is jarring, but that does not necessarily mean that it is not suitable for the purposes at hand. In horror, the discordant, unsettling and dissonant are vital to engender a creepy atmosphere.
But Downfall falls far beyond the merely creepy, and actually lands in the sphere of horror, actual horror. And rarely with much pretense or by having disgust be the goal in and of itself, Downfall's disgust, conjured by the various scenes, serve a narrative purpose; they more often than not carry a symbolic value. This is in large due to the psychological aspect. Instead of straight up depression, as in The Cat Lady, Downfall instead deals with eating disorders or general self-hatred, basically dysmorphobia, where one has either a delusional or actual flaw that is exaggerated to the point of pathology. And it is this dysmorphic view that leads Joe Davis down this horrific path in his attempt to save his beloved wife, and the base which gives meaning to what you'd otherwise interpret as meaninglessly disgusting and surreal. Everything hearkens back to mental illness, allusions to schizophrenia and depression are as common as the dysmorphobia, and all add to the theme of the game, which I'd sum up as

Along those lines the game struts. It flaunts its horror without being hemmed by shame, comfort nor laziness. But what does it have to say about beating these thoughts? Anything beyond the clichés? The dark room of the hateful thoughts about oneself are said to be counteracted by company, by appealing to the other. At the same time, as the other, we are told it is hopeless (depending on your actions in game, really, but this was the case for me). The multiple endings all add to the aforementioned realism, but vary in what they propound about the hopelessness of the ill mind, making the experience fragmented, divergent, depending on who you are and how you approach this topic, or these suffering people.
The choices of this game are somewhat subtle. And your actions are free in a sense, and it is hard to predict the consequences of these actions without playing the game multiple times. In a way that gives you replay value, but also a limited first-time experience. I prefer a one-time holistic experience. I do not necessarily think more time played means more value. But real choice, in games, are considered to be those that in some way affect the story or change the final outcome, and on that note, the choices in this game are real choices. But for those who do not necessarily want to play a game 4-5 times to exhaust all the options available to them, it becomes a source of frustration. However, I imagine the latter kind of people are a minority.
While there are puzzle elements, they are rarely problematic. It's a matter of simple world association and paying attention to the dialog and at times the dialog options. Explore thoroughly and pay attention and nothing should be too difficult to overcome in this game. This can be construed as both a positive and a negative, there is no challenge, really, but there is also no frustration. The horror gets to play its part without having to be compromised by overly complicated puzzles. And despite there being no real challenge, there is satisfaction in figuring out the solutions of the quandaries of Joe and company.
It's a concise experience. It is genuine and simple in many ways, but it serves the purpose of making the symbolic relations shine so much brighter. It's clear, most of all. The equivocalness that may arise is not due to any fault in the game's ability to tell a story, but in the story itself and what it tries to portray, which tend towards equivocalness. Attempting to do this is very much admirable. To touch darkness as a sort of exuberant catharsis. To with your full body delve into absolute horror and see your way through it. Mainly because you are an observer, thereby excluded from it, but also by playing a character going through it, sometimes managing, sometimes not. Instead of alluding to psychological pathology as a pretext for silliness or surrealism, it is used with a great understanding of its reality. The imagery is forceful to signify the intensity of the feeling not everyone experiences, but can through this game. This game can intensify our understanding of these mental issues, or at least give us the blueprint of what such a game could look like. Because it can be done more smoothly, I imagine, with greater focus on inner experience in lieu of the focus on a flashy narrative. We can stay in the moment, in the atmosphere of an awful inner life, Silent Hill 2, along with games like Downfall and The Cat Lady, proved that. But what they have yet to figure out is how to truly create a game where everything leads to the same place, like in Spec Ops: The Line, for example. These games on emotional pain have yet to figure out a way to fully encapsulate themselves in their thematics; yet they remain on a very interesting path towards excellent game-creation, that eventually will have the added bonus of being truly emotionally fulfilling, profound and beautiful.

Polish developer Remigiusz Michalski in 2009 introduced an interesting adventure Downfall, which was praised for its horror atmosphere with intriguing story. It is now published in its revised version, which every obscure adventure games fan should not miss.
Downfall was inherently point and click adventure, but in a revised version this is more of an interactive story in the style of Telltale Games. The author left the classic point and click interface, completely redesigned graphics and music, let the dub characters (one character is dubbed by a fan of the previous games) and even rewrote the story to partially follow a different game The Cat Lady to please its fans. Remake is thus not only a newly released version of the game.
The first major change and the hallmark of the game is that the environment of the camera is viewed from the side, and the main protagonist is controlled directly via the keyboard. In essence, therefore using only the keyboard. The game does not use the mouse at all, and after a while you will find that playing with just one hand is so easy. Backgrounds are a mix of photographs, rendered 3D models and cartoon characters. Today's players might argue that the game is graphically outdated, but according to me it is a raw and original visual concept that somehow belongs to Downfall.
The graphical representation is related to a story that certainly does not mince words and warnings at the beginning of the game, that this is a game for adults. After the opening sequence, where we introduce the main characters Joe and Ivy reveals, that among them there is something wrong. Couple arrives at Quiet Haven to spend the night. Ivy starts to behave strangely and soon lost. If you expect it will be a classic horror plot about kidnapped mistress and some monster holding her, you are far from the core. In fact, it is a very thoughtful psychological horror that you’ll be thinking about even after finishing. Downfall is not afraid to dish out some very gory scenes and two rather gross tasks. Additionally, it is often possible to choose dialogue options available in a journey, which then leads to a different end. There’s no need to spoil anything, but Downfall offers more than just one conclusion.
The puzzles are well designed and items needed to solve them are in sequential order as the narrative goes. You could say that their difficulties are among the simple, basically it is impossible to be stuck on something. Here it's all about the story. Fans will be pleased that the story includes some characters from other author’s games and it looks like it is going to be a sequel.
The only drawback is the use of already aged Adventure Game Studio engine, where you can’t simply change the game resolution from the standard 800 × 600 pixels, for example, on a notebook. It’s a pity author didn’t use some advanced engine.
Overall this game caught me with its story and stylisation that I basically finished it in one sitting during the evening. It has achievements on Steam that reveal a few surprises, so playing time is extended. If you are into dark and unusual adventure games, I definitely have to recommend a new version of Downfall.

WARNING! Mild spoilers.
As a recovering anorexic, I really enjoyed this game. Anorexia is a highly misunderstood subject. The fact that it's actuall a mental illness, and a serious one at that, is hardly ever even brought up. Most portrayals of anorexia depict it as skinny girls not eating, no more than than. This game delves into the true horrors of the illness. The obsessions, the paranoia, and just how difficult it is to pull away. The way it was explained by the memory of Sophie in the room of mirrors was incredibly accurate. This game was clearly made by someone who understands eating disorders, and I really appreciated that.
Overall, gameplay was nice. It wasn't too long-- it only took me about an hour and a half to complete a single runthrough. The puzzles were fairly straightforward, but still provided a challenge. As in The Cat Lady, there's no real efficient way to move from place to place on the map (no quick transport, dashing, etc.), but the map isn't altogether too big. The plot was a bit nebulous at times. It was unclear what was meant to be real and what wasn't-- but maybe that was intentional, as a representation of Joe's mental illness. Confusing as is, the story was still very good, but all three endings were rather sad and dissatisfying, especially to fans of The Cat Lady. But horror games don't have to have happy endings, I suppose.
Taking everything into account, I'd strongly recommend this game. Worth the money for sure.

Also, the beginning of the game at times was a bit hard to follow.
Aside from that though, this game was very good and was a good 5-6 hours of entertainment just from one playthrough.  I have a feeling I'll play through this game again in the future to check out what happens if I try out some of the different options, because playing through it once only got me a very small chunk of the achievements. Zombie Kill of the Week - Reborn is a 2D zombie action game where you have to defend yourself against the horde. In ZKWR you have to fight off wave after wave of undead in hostile environments. Killing zombies will earn you money which can then be spent on weapons and unlocking doors. Killing undead also rewards you with EXP and when you get enough to level up you earn tokens which can be spent on customising/upgrading your character.
+Decent pixel graphics, they aren't the best but I've certainly seen worse
+Tons of customisation options for your character such as perks, weapon upgrades and clothing
+Quite a lot of different weapons with a few more to be unlocked
+Good variety of zombies to kill
+EXP is permanent as are upgrades and appearance customisations
+A few different pickups/powerups which help you, they're basically rip-offs of the ones you'll find in CoD so they're pretty self-explanatory
+If you have no friends to play with you can play with bots but
+The 5 currently available maps are very different to one another
+Nice soundtrack
-As soon as zombies start attacking you from both sides you're pretty much screwed, especially if the fast moving zombies are in play
-Zombies still function and are able to kill you for a few seconds after you destroy their head which is pretty irritating
-Playing this game Singleplayer gets boring very quickly
-Bots have to be unlocked by finding items on the maps which I found annoying
-Painfully bad voice acting
Verdict:
Solo only: Worth purchasing on sale (6.5/10)
Multiplayer as well as Solo: Worth purchasing (7.5/10)

The particularity of this game is the 3rd person view so you are not stuck in your ship (like World of Warships) but you can see all the map (there is fog of war where you and your allies don’t see). I was searching for a game like that for quite a long time, NF2 is the only one I found.

Now, the game:
There is no tutorial or sandbox, so get ready to lose your first battles trying to understand how to use your ship. The community may help, using chat or websites giving advices and tips. Otherwise, learn by yourself!
Controlling ship is however quite simple, it’s an arcade game. Submarine and Carrier Vessel are harder to control, but have a more interesting value.
Graphics are basic too, good point is you can play with a really cheap PC. No damage control (except when low life: you’re slower) so be sure to sink your enemy or he keeps his firepower ;)
With one account you may have 6 captains from 4 different countries (US, UK, Germany and Japan, quite balanced) but you won’t be able to up them all unless you spent a huge time on this game.
Tech tree isn’t really friendly: some ships are less powerful than the previous rank, and high tier ships require a lot of experience. However, there are nice ships easier to get and enjoyable.
Matchmaking is… strange: you may have 10 vs 10 battles (max I saw is 16 vs 16) but you also may get 1 vs 1 or even 1 vs 2… You can play with 2 friends, but you may face other teams, with bigger ships… or far less powerful ones.
It’s a free-to-play but I think 2-3 players spent a quite huge amount of money to have such powerful ships… Just avoid those guys and you’ll get interesting battles.
The User Interface is a joke: nothing is explained so ask the community or find what you search on internet, chat often goes down, etc.
To conclude, how to rate a game both that good and that bad?
If you search a naval arcade F2P with intense and quick battles, welcome at NF2!
It has a great potential and devs are still working on the game so they will eventually fix major problems (UI, matchmaking) before everyone leaves to find a better game…

I recommend this game to fans of Front Mission and giant mechs, but only if you can get the game plus all of the DLC on a decent sale - it's not worth the full price IMO.  Also, if you are on the fence about this game then you are probably better off not buying it.
To be blunt, this game is not remarkable, but it does provide a taste of 3rd-person wanzer piloting that I've often dreamed of.
Wanzer customization has always been central to Front Mission games and fortunately this one doesn't fail to deliver.  You have a reasonable selection from which to customize your wanzer parts, weapons, abilities, etc.  You can set yourself up to be a slow tank, a thin-skinned but swift machine or anything in between.  Then you can choose between a variety of weapons including assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, grenade launchers, missile launchers and more.  There are also backpacks that add certain perks.
The color scheme editor allows a great level of customization as well.
The story isn't amazing but it gets the job done.  You'll work your way through the missions, experiencing a variety of challenges as you go.  Certain missions demand specific loadouts and there is no single loadout that works under ALL circumstances.
Although there are some challenging moments the game is relatively easily, except when it comes to some boss fights in which the bosses can seem massively overpowered.  At this point you'll probably need to read a guide to learn what the best loadout is and what tactics to use for the battle.
There are segments occasionally in which you are in your wanzer while loaded into the drop-heli with dual chainguns and missiles that you get to use to unleash hellfire on enemies.  That's always fun.
The combat is entertaining.  Skating around enemies while blasting them with a variety of weapons and locking on with your homing missiles while using your own jetpack to dodge enemy fire can be rather fun.  However, the controls will take a little time to master before you can get to this point.
The environments leave a little to be desired.  They kind of remind me of Armored Core levels on Playstation 2 which always felt somewhat empty and lifeless.  At the same time, they aren't entirely uninspired.
Multiplayer is dead, sadly.  I bought the Last Stand DLC because I love that type of game mode, but unfortunately I've never been able to play it with another player.  You can play it alone, but you get no XP for upgrades and it is rather monotonous making it completely pointless.

Ive read many reviews for this game. After the first few hours I can cleanse those fears potential buyers had. I dont know if they updated the game after it got so many negative reviews, but Im enjoying it a WHOLE lot right now.
Ive read reviews saying the matchmaking breaks the game, that got fixed in an recent Patch, adding a Ranking System and fitting Matchmaking, ive never got the feeling in any of my games that my enemies ( while playing Monster ) were far better expirenced than me.
Ive read reviews saying the balancing sucks, as I already said I dont know if they patched the game some time ago but for me balancing seemed perfectly fine, giving the Hunters many tools and weapons to track, trap and kill the monster. Every  role in the game (Medic, Asssault, Trapper, Support) has its own choosable characters, each of them coming with a uniqe and differnt loadout allowing you to play the way you want. While playing, none of the Hunters seemed over or underpowerd.
Now to the gameplay which makes this game so unique, the Monster gameplay. And this is probalby also the reason why so many people think this game is unbalanced. Because that is kind of how the mechanic works, but its now improper balancing of the game its just improper understanding from the players side.
The monsters process iss divided into 3 evolution stages. Everytime you evolve you get to skill 3 points on your abilities and you grow in size, gain hitpoints and deal more damage. This system gives this game the thrilling, nerve-wiggling expirence from changing to the hunted to the hunter or the other way around.
On stage 1 you are fairly weak and your only objective should be to run, eat wildlife and eventually evlolve. At this stage of the game to Hunter obviously seem OP since they simply are too strong for you. You can kill one ore maybe two if you catch them alone but wont stand a chance against all 4. If you eventually arrive at stage 2 and skilled out your abilities you can give the Hunters a hard fight, but still if you have good hunters (this game putss great emphasis on teamwork!) you might loose. If the hunters still dont manage to kill you or stay alive until the gametime runs out (which makes them win) you will evolve to stage 3, if you keep eating wildife of course. At this point of the game only a very good group of Hunters will be able to bring down the Monster, which might make it look Op from the hunters eyes.
This is the main cause for people complaining about balacning isssues.
You can choos from differnt Monsters aswell, each coming with a differnt skillset and playstyle.
If you ask me Id recommend this game, especially for 15 Euros!

Don't let the outdated positive feedbacks in the past fool you, it's a facade of what used to be. Read some of the later reviews.
Pretty depressing. There's only a few games out there these days that really utilize early access to strive. Starbound was a prime example, the game hits early access, the developers keep on a rampant grind, and then the game is released. Top of the line, A++ quality game.
Zomboid was going to be my second on the list. The early access was amazing, I was playing with friends, having a great time, coming back every now and then when big updates would come up, but always waiting for specific promised features. I know it's early access, that's why I gave them years on years to add them, and it didn't bother me. However after a while, it became clear to me that the development team had changed.
I'd say from 2 years back now, the development hit a halt. Vehicles have only been remotely announced recently, but for years were in the silent. The promised NPCs / Bandits were rarely mentioned again, and the building system was still as buggy as day one. But through all of the bugs,
And then the weekly/monthly news releases and dev blogs would come out. ANIMATIONS. That's it. No feature updates, no vehicles, no multiplayer tweaks, rarely any potent bug fixes, and no AI. What was their latest update? Animations.
"We redid the animation system"
"New animations coming out"
"We've been working on animations for months"
"These new animation tweaks are golden"
2 years. They had 2 years of money and development, and the only progress we were seeing - was on animations. The game, admiteddly, didn't have the smoothest animations - so I get why they would want to overhaul them in preperation for a full release. 2 Years though? Really?
And then every other dev blog had an excuse for these animations.
"We have a new team helping us out"
"Here's our new animator"
"We encountered some bugs"
It was all nonsensical excuses to deliberately extend the moneygrab before they'd abandon the project. And it's clear that was the direction they were going in.
The biggest factor to take in right here, is that out of all of the updates in the past 2 years - you won't notice a majority of them. The bugs never affected anyone, half of the QoL fixes weren't needed, and the interface updates were honestly worse. If you update a game over 2 years and people can't notice the changes, it is a clear sign that priority needs to change.
If you are wondering why a game with "very positive reviews" has extremely negative reviews suddenly, it is because this is a practically ABANDONED GAME. If you like it for the stage it's in now, then by all means buy it. However if you expect vehicles, AI, or reliable multiplayer changes - DON'T BUY THIS. Downfall is a psychological horror game, and the gameplay mechanics are pretty simple. Everything you do, you do with the arrow keys. You find items, put them in your inventory, and use them to solve puzzles (which are pretty simple) However, the most important factor in this game is the story. And boy, what a story it is.
The game is very short, it will take you approximately 4-5 hours to finish - and that's if you're being thorough. Now, usually I would recommend picking up games of this length on a sale, this one however I think it's worth the full price. The replayability value in this game is insane. So many dialogue options and scenarios, and there are 3 possible endings. The good, the bad and the neutral. Though, the good isn't really all that happy either. Which I liked!
* Dialogue - the script for this game is amazing. It's worth playing just for Joe's mean lines alone.
* Artstyle - very unique and surreal. Hell, even the paintings in this game are great! Gloomy and dark with hints of color (red) throughout the game.
* Soundtrack - the maker of this game is very good at choosing the right music for each scenario. I love all the soundtracks, and I find myself listening to them outside of the game as well. Really helps creating the atmosphere.
* Replayability - I highly recommend taking your time to explore all the dialogue and all the outcomes. Will take you approximately 12-15 hours.
* Puzzles - not too easy, not too obvious either. Clever.
* Story - the story will mess with your head. It's weird, and I love it.
* Price - good price for an amazing game.
* Joe Davis - yep.
* Audio - sometimes the audio just sounds... off. Some of the voice actors have a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mic, which sorta ruins the mood and dialogue sometimes. This was a problem The Cat Lady had as well.
* Sometimes the controls feels slow and not responsive. Also a problem The Cat Lady had.
I highly recommend playing this, especially if you're already a Cat Lady fan. Those of you with a BBW fetish might enjoy this as well.

A fascinating game for all fans of horror. Using the already familiar art themes specific to The Cat Lady, the game bolsters the great idea of the original game into a true refined masterpiece. Unlike the original, the gameplay and puzzles are actually pretty intuitive here, with one or two small exceptions. Expect some gruesome and disturbing scenes and puzzles.
Using round, interesting or even mysterious characters, the game builds an emotional and often quite shocking story which will keep you gripped most of the time.
Apart from the obvious choices, some aren't that intuitive, so don't be surprised if you're left wandering what you did wrong when you get an ending different than expected.
The game is definitely recommended for everyone fascinated by horror or who simply enjoys this sort of art. I wouldn't, however, recommend it for someone simply looking for an emotional or engaging story.

Artistically and technically beautiful, Downfall provides an engaging story and wonderfully disturbing atmosphere that might possibly surpass that of The Cat Lady. The puzzles are intuitive enough to not require the 'try everything in my inventory on everything' tactic of progression, while still being challenging. Decisions you make feel like (and seem to) influence the storyline, and the attention to detail is fantastic. Highly recommended for fans of adventure games, and/or horror.

"Questionable" is a term that comes to mind.
(For the sake of clarity, I bought this item on XBOX One also, and had fewer issues than listed below - the PC port has suffered badly)
Unfortunately this WIDELY missed the mark, feeling as badly managed as the lesser titles Tetris Worlds (yuck), and the EA releases with MicroTransactions on PSP and various other platforms, missing several modes, etc.
Firstly patched over to fix a few issues, the game does include "partial" controller support (not the greatest feeling of accuracy or responsiveness I'm afraid), but requires the keyboard & mouse to navigate some screens and initiate a game, so there's little point in the seemingly 50% implementation.
The game must start in offline mode to prevent it from crashing, and often if you DO manage to keep the game running, exiting the app can be even more difficult.
Now there could be a million reasons here, but basically I think it's down to not understanding the engine used to build it (Unity), and a very poor, rushed Q&A / optimisation process. Ubisoft now own the Tetris license for PC and console, taking all but the mobile license from EA - and if this implementation (PC) is anything to go by, I don't want to contemplate any further titles. I love Tetris, always have, and I've bought every iteration I can for each platform, I've found the build quality at least acceptable on all releases (even the terrible releases mentioned above).
Feels like a cheap cash-in, made by people who either didn't have time, resources or inclination (possibility being powers from above leaving no time, money or peope) to do this in a way that does the brand justice. Don't get this one. It upsets me to say that, too.

One of the best puzzle games I have ever played. SpaceChem looks like it's about chemistry but it really is about parallel programming. The learning curve is steep but a great interface and informative tutorials make it easy to learn how to accomplish tasks. Of course, there's a difference between completing an assignment and completing it well, and trying to come up with more ingenious and efficient ways to finish a task will keep you coming back time and time again.

If you enjoyed "The Codex of Alchemical Engineering," SpaceChem is that -- turned up to 11. (If you somehow missed the Codex, just Google it.)
I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes "plan out a sequence of moves to accomplish a complex task and then enjoy the satisfaction of seeing your plan come together" type games (RoboRally and Rush are two examples -- if you like those games, you will almost certainly like SpaceChem).

A genuinely brilliant puzzle game, with a darkly funny plot, the occasional completely insane "boss" puzzle, and a slick interface. The underlying gameplay involves building automated systems to construct/deconstruct/reconstruct molecules from the constituent atoms, though no real understanding of chemistry is required. The game does an excellent job of teaching you the basics, then throwing an escalating series of complicating additional factors and new capabilities at you.
It has a large number of "meta puzzles" in which you must link together individual reactors (each of which you design) to perform some larger and more complex task. It's very challenging, but in a rewarding way. There are no cheap tricks here, it's just a matter of thinking through what has to be done and how best to do it.
The developers have supported this title to an extraordinary degree. It contains quite a bit of bonus content with more turning up all the time, and also supports user created puzzles.

Easily the best puzzle game of the last year. It's really fun and it makes you feel very smart when you come up with a solution. The gameplay mechanics and interface keep you from getting frustrated. Don't be misled -- no chemistry knowledge is needed.
This is not sarcastic: I never thought I could have this much fun in a game about constructing algorithms.

WARNING!: actual chemistry is involved.

I'm an avid Front Mission fan and I knew before playing that this game was bad, but I had hope that it wasn't as bad as it was made out to be, but wow, just wow.
Believe every negative review about this game, it's bad. Regardless if you liked old FMs or not, don't waste your money.
The wanzers for all they're worth are really nicely rendered.
The game crashes a lot. It's 2015 (at the time of the review) the game was created in 2010 and it still crashes because they didn't bother to fix its bugs forcing you to replay missions especially the on foot sections.
The story is bottom barrel garbage. It's like an extremely incoherent version of the worst Gundam story mixed with a poor interpretation of Front Mission: Gunhazard's story mixed with a heavily Americanised story akin to modern FPS at the time. Instead of crafting a compelling side story in the universe of Front Mission we've come to know, we get the "it's a reboot" trope with everything starting in New York like in the movies with a dumb plot with an even dumber love interest inclusion. I'll let that sink in. It has no saving grace.
The sound and audio are mediocre at best, as nothing stands out. The game's score has that Hollywood like feel which you'll recognise from the start screen and is extremely generic and lacklustre. It doesn't have the inventive score capacity displayed in the prior entries.
The weapons you equip feel so underpowered, either that or the enemies are enormous bullet sponges.
Customisation is garbage whether you're an old Front Mission fan or a newcomer. It’s nothing too complex, but just poorly done. You earn money in levels to buy parts to customise your wanzer, nothing out of the ordinary right. In prior games, before buying parts you'd normally select the parts, see how it looks on your wanzer then look at its stats against what's currently equipped. However in this game you can see the stats but you don't get a preview of the part, all you get is a picture with poor resolution under the stats. So if you want to view it on you wanzer you'll have to waste money purchasing it and once bought, there's no way to re-equip your previously equipped part unless you repurchase it...I'll let that sink in as well.
You can now paint each part (limb) separately, it sounds nice until you realise how much of a hassle it is. Each part can be coloured differently via a colour wheel however it's rather fiddly and doesn't remember colours when you want to recolour other parts. So if you want to use the same shade of a colour throughout your wanzer good luck remembering and finding the colour.
Why do you even have AI companions if they're going to be utterly useless? Your partners basically do nothing throughout the game. Sure they can shoot the enemies but what's the point if they do no damage and I mean no damage at all. Here's an example, missiles do a decent amount of damage where 4 missiles can reduce basic enemy health by a 1/4. However, when one of your partners fire their missiles in full barrage of 4, the enemies take no damage...I kid you not. I stood behind a building (so that the enemy wouldn't agro on me) in amazement as my partner fired barrage after barrage and watched the enemy’s health and it stayed at full health regardless. When the prior games used AI partners in certain missions, they came to work often outputting just as much or more damage than your squad.
The enemy AI is even worse than your partner's and I'm not taking in a dumb kind of way, I mean in an unfair kind of way. If there's a fire fight between your partners and enemies, the enemy AI's aim is potato but once you get into the picture their aim goes to pin-point laser assisted accuracy. Also, they become affixed on you no matter what, disregarding your partners altogether.
The on foot sections are so generic, under developed and buggy. I wonder as to why they were even included. When you dismount, you're equipped with an assault rifle and a rocket launcher which can take down an enemy wanzer with 4 shots. Now you might exclaim "4 shots?! That seems overpowered" and it is considering it takes 16 missiles while in wanzer to destroy basic enemy wanzers. Before anyone says "But, you could've dismount in FM3 and Gun Hazard" and while true once you'd dismounted, you either had to run for your life or find an unpiloted wanzer as you're squishy and only equipped with a pistol which did 1 point of damage. If it takes 4 rockets to take down a wanzer then what's the point of being in wanzers to begin with.
The wanzers designed specifically for this game do not match the current long standing design the series has or is known for and comes off as being out of place when compared. What you get is something more akin to concept sketches or anime with unnecessary sharp edges, curves and skulls as opposed to the rectangular or circular geometry.
You know you're in for a rough ride as a fan when the mispronounce wanzer as wanzer instead of vanzer in the opening cutscene. I tried to like it but it's a terrible game with or without the FM series applied biases. It brings nothing new to the table while poorly accomplishing everything which existed prior. Everything about this game is a let-down, from the incoherent story, poorly implemented customisation, forced and buggy on foot sections, generic audio offerings and unlikeable characters. Square-Enix should've had more confidence in itself and released a turn-based tactics game with the improvements that FM5 made as that was the most perfect version to date.
Can I recommend this game to long-time FM fans who may think "that it's not that bad, right?" No. Can I recommend this game to mech fans hoping for a new game to play? No. This game has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. If you're looking for a FM game to play do yourself a favour and play FM:Gun Harzard, FM3, FM4 or FM5 instead.

I didn't beat this game but I got close enough to the end to feel like I completed the game.  This game is incredibly challenging but for all the wrong reasons.  I spent about half the game wandering around trying to find the next location and hoping I didn't wander into areas I wasn't ready for (despite the fact having to pass through some hard locations to get to the correct destination at times) all the while wrestling with the controls to get the character to do what I wanted it to do.  For example, I'd press the buttons to swim up and right and the character would either not move or move up and to the left.  The controls are already wonky in the water but exasperated out of the water.  I spent an inordinate amount of time repeating the same action over and over again just to get to my objective because the controls are pretty much non-responsive.  In addition, the world map is a giant mess, poorly labeled, and nearly impossible to navigate.  On the plus side, the world is absolutely huge, varied, open, and beautifully drawn.  The minimap was utterly useless compared to the world map with big circles that didn't actually help locate anything useful.  The minimap was probably a "radar" map at one time but never shows enemy locations so there is actually no need for it.  These things made for a really frustrating experience.
This brings me to the boss fights.  This game is loaded with unique boss fights.  Every boss is carefully crafted and requires ingenuity to beat - something that the PC platform rarely sees and, as such, is really awesome.  However, the infuratingly frustrating controls drove me nuts.  Several of the bosses have huge mobility gains over the main character and so the ability tell the character to move to specific positions on the screen quickly is important.  After putting 15-ish hours into this game and getting to the last boss before the end-game boss, I had enough.  I just wanted the game to be over.  Looking up a game guide (I just wanted to know how much further I had to go) I found out that the final boss had twice as many phases as the Chrono Trigger final boss.  I'd already had my fill of this game at that point so I stopped playing rather than spend another 10 to 15 hours wrestling with the controls in more boss fights.
This brings me to in-game cooking.  I was mildly entertained by the fact that, in the middle of a boss fight, I could pause the game to cook up some healing poultices.  "Hey, I know you've almost eliminated all of my health and you still have 50% of your health left, but do you mind waiting for a few moments while I cook a meal to heal myself?"  "Go ahead.  I'll, uh, read a book or something."  What's more annoying is that the player has to remember to cook regularly because the character can only carry 8 of each type of item but will make items disappear upon touching them rather than leaving them lie around when the limit is reached.  There really shouldn't be a limit at all.  If I want to carry 100 healing poultices into a battle, so be it.  Let the player play the game the way that they want to play it.  Cooking is a little gimmicky as well.  I frequently wished the recipe book would just let me click the item I wanted to make and then let the game figure out how to make it and automatically cook it for me.  Dragging and dropping individual items is a massive waste of time.
Finally, the forms that the character can take defeats the likely purpose of the original form.  The game starts out with the main character learning to "sing" to do things.  However, I spent the bulk of the game in the second form (Energy Form) so I could shoot enemies and collect items for cooking.  This turns the first form into a gimmick when it should have been an adventure/puzzle game, which it still tries to be at times.  Such a wasted opportunity to make a truly unique game!  The only thing the first form ends up being good for is getting past certain points and moving a few rocks here or there.  The game could have done without all of the peons (annoying little enemies), stuck to puzzle solving with the various forms, and also kept the boss fights and it would have been a pretty sweet little game.
Overall, this game has a number of interesting concepts but it isn't worth your time.  If the control issues were fixed, the limit on the storage of items eliminated, the world map overhauled to be usable, and the radar/minimap improved or removed entirely, it would be a huge improvement (all fairly easy things to fix).  As it stands though, I can't recommend this game.

A lot of people can’t stand racing games anymore, although they enjoyed them a whole lot back in the day. And it’s not always their fault. For the most part, racing games have grown stale nowadays, and worst of all, they seem to look all the same! They’re nice looking, no discussion, the graphics are great. But great graphics are not a competent substitute for great gameplay, and most current racing games are proof of that. Now, if you have been looking for some racing game capable of bringing your childhood racing love back, Sky Drift could be a decent solution. Let me describe it as follows, so maybe I can manage to convince. It’s a combat racing game a lot like Mario Kart. You grab power-ups along the way. Some are momentary boosts for your engine, others are devices used to hinder your opponents way. The soundtrack resembles Rock n’ Roll Racing’s style, if that means anything. But, there are no cars in Sky Drift – as the title suggests. It’s an airplane racing game. No cars, just airplanes, which is a refreshing novelty by the way. Well, not exactly a novelty, but you get it. Anyway, this game has been severely overlooked. It’s an outrage, a real shame how the multiplayer is nearly dead for a game that’s so much fun. As always, the game is not perfect. Sky Drift could use a greater number of maps and deeper customization. But nothing a good DLC couldn't solve, had the game received more attention. Nonetheless, the game plays great and feels great. It’s lightning fast and the soundtrack adds a lot to the frenzy. The controls feel quite alright. And, well, the game is quite nice looking too, with wide and beautiful landscapes. When the plane hovers over the water, you can see drops splashing against the screen. Yes, you can fly over the foaming sea. You can fly past canyons and through ice caves. You can touch the tops of pine trees growing on ice cold riverbanks or crash on the tips of stalagmites coming out of hellish lava rivers. Watch out, things are as dangerous as they are beautiful, and you’ll be all the time on a hurry trying to tear your enemies apart with missiles, machineguns and mines, while boosting your shields up and repairing damage you suffered. Indeed, the game is a good challenge. It’s not going to be a walk in the park to master this game. Some races are going to be a real pain on hard difficulty, and you might see yourself retrying dozens of times just to come in 3rd place. Because of that, Sky Drift seems to possess the elements for a great competitive multiplayer. It’s a pity only a few care about it now. So much potential… It would be great if its multiplayer came back to life. The gaming world has been for so long in lack of a fun racing game like this. Now, for whatever reason (maybe bad promotion by the publishers), such a game is not fully appreciated as it deserves.
Buy this game! It needs more people for multiplayer! Think of Super Mario Kart and Jet Moto in the sky! 7/10

A more refined approach of the aerial races found in Diddy Kong Racing, coupled with risk-reward boost meter building similar to Burnout's as well as a power-up system akin to that of Blur's. In other words: offering leeway for counter-measures when under attack as there is no randomness, allowing pick-ups to be 'tiered' and being able to 'bank' a power-up for extra boost charge.
Overall one of the better current-gen arcadey racing games (with nice graphics) made from the devs who went on to develop Sine Mora and it's a decent enough PC port too. Only real drawback is that it's a little light on content, but it's a good impulse purchase regardless during a sale.
(I also hope Sumo Digital looks at this game for a sequel to Sonic Racing: Transformed, to further fine-tune their airplane sections and the way they handle their item drops.)

I really like the concept of this game.
Have owned it for a few years and occasionally play for a while to see how it's progressed - larger updates appear to be every few months and sometimes bring in a load more features, such as the note system and improved health system.
A lot of hoohaa being made about vehicles atm which is all nice and well but this game is still crying out for NPCs - being the lone survivor amidst the hordes of Z gets pretty lonely, and being able to drive to the off-camera gunshots and dog barks that give the illusion of a living world will not alleviate that. I don't want to play online - it's not my style as I don't have enough time - so I want to be able to form a group of NPC survivors; not much lone wolf zombie lore out there (I am Legend maybe, but even he had a dog). Also, it doesn't make sense that zombie population increases over time when there are no other living characters.
Over than the waiting game, I am hopeful for the direction the game is taking as the core mechanics are fun. Swatting Zs is satisfying and the crafting system is mostly deep enough for me. As it stands, the game is very playable (I have 75+ hours so far), though without NPCs etc the longevity isn't there. All in all, £10 is a bargain; I have paid more for games I have played for a few hours.
I think this will make it through Early Acces, eventually. Just hope it's not too long.

As far as psychological horrors go there may not be many better games released in 2016 than Harvester Games’ Downfall. This shouldn’t be a surprise to those of you who are aware with the studio’s work given the outstanding The Cat Lady that the studio released in 2012. Despite releasing only last month the original version of the game was released even before The Cat Lady in 2009. The original 2009 release of the game is now freeware which you can get from the title’s official website.
For those of you who are questioning whether or not you should just grab the free game or to pony up the $13.99 for the newly released version do know that the recently released version has been significantly remade and has been reimagined in a fashion similar to that of The Cat Lady – which to fans of the game should automatically raise a huge smile. For those unaware of the original title then I’d like to kindle your imagination with the thoughts of some of the best psychological horrors on the big screen coming to mind in 1408  and Identity.
I was a huge fan of the controls that are established within the game. The simplicity of the system makes the game a joy to play and allows the player to concentrate on the story being narrated. I’m not going to spoiler the game too much as it is another game that deserves to be played and experienced first hand. I know some of you have advised me that you consider it lazy writing but I firmly believe that there are just some games that demand to be experienced first hand rather than being narrated to you to the point where when you come to play the game it becomes impossible for the narrative to have the same effect upon you as it possibly could have.
The graphics while simple really help establish the atmosphere and aide immersion. The camera work is extraordinary and while I know Total Biscuit hates people referring to games as cinematic experiences this is certainly a game that deserves that phrase being applied to it. Animations are used sparingly but when they are used in each scene there is an undeniable purpose which is consistently well executed. The decisions made towards the utilization of monochrome with very minimal utilization of color is outstanding and extend through to the lighting used throughout the game. This makes the horror and the gore stand out at a level that is arguably greater than the sum of its parts. This in turn leads to the voice acting. Although there are some scenes that I feel lack the oomph that would have made it a truly great experience throughout there is enough strength in the delivery that makes the whole above average. The decisions behind the choice of songs that constitute soundtrack are also of a sound decision. The sounds again raise the level of the horror and demand praise. It is a game that I would recommend that you wear headphones for.
A word of warning for some of you to take heed of is that there is quite a significant amount of gore throughout the game.
Downfall is one of the best psychological horror experiences I have enjoyed across all media in a long time. It is highly recommended.

Downfall can be enjoyed as a remake/retelling of the original 2009 version, as a sequel to The Cat Lady or as a stand-alone game.  There are nods and allusions to both the original and TCL, but you honestly don’t have to be familiar with either one to play this game.  All the background information you need is given in the prologue; heck, you don’t even get this much in the original Downfall—it simply begins with a husband and wife seeking shelter from the storm in a hotel in the country.
If you’ve played The Cat Lady, you know what to expect in terms of graphics, sounds and gameplay.  The game’s color palette is almost exclusively black, white and red.  There’s voice acting! (More on that later.)  The interface is simple and easy-to-use with the names of objects you can interact with appearing on the screen whenever you walk passed them.  I’m not in the best position to judge the difficulty of the puzzles, having played the original Downfall in which many of the puzzles are the same, but I think they are easy, with clues that more-or-less tell you what to do whenever the solution isn’t obvious.  I’d say the difficulty level is lower than TCL.  Probably the designer wants players to enjoy the story that unfolds rather than getting stuck and spending a lot of time wandering around the hotel in search of what to do next.  I would have enjoyed some more challenging puzzles though; it’s a bit like one of those games where puzzles seem designed to keep you from getting ahead of yourself (e.g. you can’t get through this door until you find object X which is in the room where you meet Mary and that is because we want you to talk to Mary first).  In addition to the inventory based puzzles, you lead your character, Joe, through some conversations and places where he has to make choices.  These can affect the ending of the game.
I’d give the voice acting an 8.5/10.  For the most part I really liked it (I especially liked the voice of Joe, the protagonist), but there are some places where the voice actors make an odd choice on which word to emphasize (this is a pet peeve of mine); also Joe often speaks lines softly where it seems natural that he would raise his voice.
OK, I am a big fan of Downfall 2009 so I’m really aching to discuss my feelings about the differences between the remake and the original (And, hey, it’s included in the bundle so you can play both of them).  Some minor spoilers ahead…
* Some background regarding Joe’s childhood that we don’t get until the very end of DF2009 is expanded and moved to the prologue here—I thought this announced right away that this was going to be a new take on the story.
* I like how the Queen of Maggots is changed so her nature is more consistent with what we learn in TCL.
* I prefer the twist ending in the remake to the one in the original.  It fits better tonally with the rest of the game and it is set up more, so it doesn’t seem to come out of nowhere.
* Joe and Ivy’s relationship is developed more here and its changed some from DF2009.  I suppose it’s handled more maturely, it’s a more cohesive story and Ivy’s problems are more relatable.  That said, I miss the flashback with Lucifer in the bathroom.  I also miss the psychotic episode Ivy seems to be having when they first arrive at the hotel in DF2009 (screaming, seeing things).  In DF2009 it’s implied, at least at first, that this is a source of their relationship issues, but the problems they face in the remake are, I guess, more in keeping with the game’s theme.
* I really miss Joe’s descent into madness and (at least potentially) evil in DF2009.  I remember loving the dark choices he needs to make throughout the game.  Here his interactions with Sophie are less intense.  In the original he says at one point that she deserves a more painful death(!), and I really miss the extra ingredient you have to add to the smoothie recipe.  Maybe this is just me, second time through DF2009 I decided to play Joe as a total a-hole.
* In addition to thinking the developer might have a swung a bit too far in the opposite direction when it comes to the puzzles (eliminating some, giving the player big hints for others), I actually miss the chase scenes in DF2009.  They added a level of fear and exhilaration.
So that’s my 2 cents.  I would definitely recommend this game for its story, graphics and atmosphere and the multiple endings lend it replay value.  My one criticism is that, partly because of the lack of difficult puzzles, the game is on the short side.  It took me about 4 hours to complete it.

Karate Master 2 is a 2D single-player only fighting game well worth its price-tag, offering a roughly 6-8 hour SINGLE-PLAYER ONLY experience. For those wondering, it also offers controller and arcade stick support (for PC-compatible sticks).
The in-game graphics and music are well-made and truly represent the developer's vision in giving the game a late 80's/early 90's feel. Characters all either reference 70's/80's/90's era martial arts movies and famous figures (Most of which being 'Mas' Oyama) and cutscene artwork is well-made, however the art style for character portraits can at times look slightly off.
That being said, the dialogue (in English, at least) is hilariously inconsistent - Whether or not the developers intended to give the game that "B-grade action movie" dialogue - and is entertaining at many times, to say the least.
The gameplay offers only a single-player story mode that plays as a 2D-fighter with RPG levelling mechanics, all of which are delivered through various minigames.
These minigames range from timing to mashing, and while some may appear tedious at first they are easy to pick-up and never too jarring as the game allows you to reap the rewards from excelling at a certain mini-game over another, offering 4 options for each in-game stat.
The core gameplay is entertaining though at times inconsistent. Using a standard LP, RP, LK, RK setup without any set combos or movelists, the player already has all the tools they need to win. Therefore apart from the statistics [mechanic], the player has to rely on movement, spacing, counter-attacks and timing to win their fights. FGC enthusiasts could say that the game is heavily-'footsie' based, if that means anything.
The defensive system is where the game is most interesting: The player will always be guarding at the middle of three heights, and must hold up or down to shift this guard.
In addition to this are parries, which may also be performed at three heights using both punch buttons. Unfortunately and having played KM1, I can say that it is much more difficult than its predecessor to predict/anticipate/read enemy movements, making parries heavily luck-based.
Also available to the player are standard dashing mechanics and a ducking mechanic (which I find much better than attempting to parry or guard high attacks).
The enemy AI also seems to be completely random in terms of attack patterns and damage, where an enemy fought at the beginning of the game, at later stages, can randomly and instantly throw a match-ending attack. This is another aspect of the core gameplay - "Ikken Hissatsu" or instant-kill moves: Rather than being as they would be in other 2D fighters such as Guilty Gear/Blazblue, the instant-kills can be any move in KM2, so long as your 'timing' is perfect.
Instant kills are difficult to describe as the only explanation offered behind gaining one is that an average of the character's strength and damage stats must exceed the opponent's toughness. As none of these stats are given for opponents it genuinely does happen almost randomly, although timing a counter-attack at where the opponent isn't guarding tends to yield them more often.
In closing, KM2 is neither a fighting-game player's dream nor will it keep you coming back for more for too long over its short length, however it will scratch an itch for martial arts [and obviously, Karate] enthusiasts that other fighting games might not.
The game will not convert players who don't like fighters, however if you're looking for a solid, serious-yet-tongue-in-cheek action game that throws back to the days before Street Fighter 2, KM2KDB is a good place to be.

Nineteen eighty five called, it would like to have a word with you about cheesy Karate games. Specifically, I would like you to cast your mind back to the spectrum era. Long loading times, terribad graphics, but a blank canvas where game creativity was about pushing boundaries and exploring what games could be. One of those many explorations was a title called IK+ (International Karate +), a glorious bit of code involving some pixellated men in pyjamas whacking each other in the goal of changing their belt colours. The controls were tight, the fighting was good, and the feeling was very much that of a cheesy b-movie. Hell, the Amiga version had
on the cover along with what looks to be Chuck Norris delivering a trademark kick to some poor sod. Fighting games have wavered in and out of vogue, travelling between the more realistic and the more fantastical over the generations, but the pure, basic Karate game sortof vanished into the ether...
It's gloriously throwback, the graphics are retro Amiga era, the script has more chinglish than a motherboard manual, you get to Karate Fight a bull and a bear (yes, you get the opportunity to punch a bear), and you get to do a jump kick over a car to promote your dojo. It's that kind of finely matured cheese. Jackie Chan would be -proud- to feature in such a script. It has so much terribleness (like the fact you can exit without saving very easily and the game does a TERRIBLE job of warning you) that it has no right to be as good as it is. Yet, it is. It's good, it's good in the way finely matured cheese is good.
The game features a mix of tournaments, one shot fights against various opponents (who if you beat, will then appear in the said same tournaments), special encounters such as the aforementioned "DO A FLYING KICK OVER A CAR!", and occasional expositions of horribly written story, with english so badly written even google translate looks at me and throws it's arms up in despair. You can read it, and you'll laugh, it's that wonderfully bad.
In between the fighting and the b-reel script you get to train your fighter in a fantastically diverse set of mini-games (some are genius, others... not so much), and there's a limited RPG style progression system where you'll tinker with the stats of your fighter, and can even suffer injuries and get to participate in a mini game where you have to recover from those (and the first time that happens, you get some cringeworthy story for that too).
The fighting however is -good-, really good, it uses the tekken style approach of mapping left and right legs and arms to seperate buttons, and then you can apply "low" or "high" using down or up on the controller to give you a wide variety of punches and kicks. There's a good set of combos and a fairly fluid system tucked away in here, as well as a solid blocking and countering system, and button mashing is punished frequently with the AI giving you a damn good spanking in the later stages, so it pays to learn the intricacies. In effect, this is IK+ put on steroids, and then given a serious training regimen, the Karate is pretty full featured (at least that an outside layperson can figure) and has a much more realistic, crunchy feel to it, as opposed to the more fantasy based fighters that you tend to run into.
Training focusses on the various stats, or training you in new moves, the stat training can range from simple button mashing (for body conditioning, which will give you hand cramp, well, they did say it was toughness training - BEAR THE PAIN), to attempting to hit a tennis ball suspended by a piece of string, which feels a bit like the human version of a cat playing with a feather. Generally speaking some minigames work really well (the concrete bag, the strength tests, some of the toughness tests) and there's only a few real duds (the water droplet test can die in a fire). There's even a minigame where you work to build up funds to enter the starter tournaments, which... can go horribly wrong if you decide to fiddle about with your forklift (there's safety videos for that you know!).
With all this said, would one recommend it? At the price point it's pitched at? Absolutely. It's a -steal-. There are so many things to love about this game. The art is beautifuly stylized and the sound design is incredible. The sandbox/survival mode offers tremendous replay-ability and can easily provide hundreds of hours of enjoyable gameplay. Additionally, there are very few games I've played that have shared TLD's ability to elicit real emotional responses to the events my character/avatar has experienced.
All that being said, however, I cannot in good faith recommend this game in it's current state. The UI and the in-game interactions (that is, the process through which your character interacts with things in the world) have both gotten progressively worse over the past year of updates due to, in my opinion, really poor design choices. The UI went from being a set of simple menus to a radial menu system that is far less intuitive; and the interaction system was changed from click-to-interact to hold-to-interact. While this latter change may not seem large, it really makes looting far more tedious and far less enjoyable.
Additionally, the release of story mode has proven to be pretty buggy and lacking polish. Invisible wolves that strike out of nowhere, janky character animations during cutscenes (at one point one of the characters had a pearl necklace protruding from her chest), and voice acting that seems to end mid-conversation (some conversations abruptly shift to text-based interactions with no voice lines). All of these could be forgiven for an early-access game with a story that begs to be completed, but for a game that was just fully released with a story that is largely linear, over-dramatic, and borders on uninteresting, these are a bit too much.
I will certainly continue to play this game. I bought it cheaply during early-access and I've invested nearly 200 hours in the sandbox thus far. I wouldn't be surprised if I invested 200 more if the developers continue to support that mode (which, based on their past behavior, I'm not actually expecting). However, like I said at the beginning of my review, I would have a hard time recommending this to a friend as a great. or event good, game. Instead, I would say that this is a unique and beautiful survival game that is dripping with wasted potential.

In short, this game is fun for anyone who like surviving against the elements. I am sure that it can eventually be learned to a point where survival becomes easy. But the plethora of high-hour-count reviews on this page show that anyone can get his or her money's worth from this experience.

Name: Zombie Kill of The Week - REBORN
Developer: Still Running
Genre: Survival, Horde Mode, Resouce Management, Lite- RPG
Multiplayer: Yes. Not tested. Lack friends with copies.
Bots: Yes. Lobotomized but can carry a gun.
A resource managing zombie survival game with lite-rpg element. Now you can safely skip the longer version if you want straight into the graphic section. I wouldn't think less of you.
Game development for this game was rather 'convulated' so as to speak. I tried the version that was a standalone EXE all those years ago so imagine my surprise when i saw this game on steam. Both of horror and joy. A memory tainted by nostalgia and stained by terrible remembering ability. Anyways.....
It's basically a 2D pixel art zombie horde survival game set in a single location of your choosing 24/7. What 24/7 implies is that there is no cooldown at all between waves. You killed all the zombie? Well have fun because here is another wave, and another and another and another till you drop on your knees praying to a god which i do not know then die. Rinse and repeat! Also apparently you have all the cliche zombie weapons such as shotguns, katana and even the fabled chainsaw.
On with the review.

You start the round with a pistol and a katana that is supremely weak in all aspect other than the fact that the pistol can do headshots but that is pretty much it. Through slaying/shooting zombies you gain money to unlock door ala call of duty zombies style and to buy weapons. Also dropped by the zombies are powerups such as a medkit that heals you, bullet restoration and even a hit everything that will save your life a lot of time.
Guns come in all shapes and sizes but the best weapons are locked behind the refrigerator system which i will explain later and also you have to unlock some of the weapon via premium currency which i will also explain later. Most of the guns are the typical fare such as shotgun, machinegun and smg. Interestingly enough once you unlock enough room you gain access to the upgrade mission which for a steep price will make your guns better.
Zombies also fit most of the trope we find in films and other setting but you see i am unable to confirm zombies above wave 28 since i died at that point. You have the runner, the shambler, the fat guy and a few different bosses. Now it goes without saying that since this is a 2D game you don't have as much wriggle room as oppose to 3D game therefor brushing up against zombies is enough to incur damage on your side. BTW health are not represented by health bar but instead the more closer you are to death the bloodier you get but don't worry since your mate/bots can very easily revive you provided you did not die at a location where they swarm like mad.
Every level has a refrigerator where you can pay money to get a random weapon. Buy too often and it will disappear into another part of the map. The refrigerator is also the only place where you can get the very powerful guns in the game minus the rather useless minigun.
There are 1 mobile phone scattered in each level which allows you to call a bot in to help you with the rampage, They are dumb are brick but thankfully they can carry a gun which proves useful enough for them. Otherwised they are just dumb bricks.
You gain exp as you play and gain levels that you can spend on skillpoints that aids in a lot of aspect of your character such as money collecting, gun reload speed and oh well you know the rest don't you? The only one not in the list is increased resilient against damage. There are also Z-Token that are dropped randomly as you play. Used to upgrade your weapons, buy accessories, and unlock new maps you will soon find these to be in short supply forcing you to run through a map multiple time to grind through them.
Accessories are a unique thing. They have a set limit amount you can carry [at 10] and they have limited uses plus the fact that they are bought with Z-Token makes them a grind tool to help with the tougher wave and not to be squandered at the earlier waves. The inventory is mapped to the I button just in case you didn't know how to use them.
Z-Token are also used to purchase useful perks that helps your character in the game although the cheap 25 token Rampage perk is more than enough for any needs.
You can also customize your character look and err... apparently there is a certain maid in the game. Spoilers. You use Z-Token to buy those looks. Naturally.
2D pixel arts. At times the art look rather ugly but i suppose fighting off 20 undead at the same time makes you rather forgiving of this shortcoming. But hey, at least you will be able to tell the important thing such as guns, powerups and items at a glance. It's ugly in a functional way.

Sounds blend in good enough without getting in the way. Guns are boomy and everything works as expected although the in game character i suggest you mute him since his voice is rather jarring to the overall game. Seriously.
All these years the game hasn't change much but i argue that the core component that makes it fun is still there intact and not lost in the years. Therefor go look for 3 mates and buy all 3 of them a copy and go play this 2D survival game like no tomorrow. Because tomorrow is a farce anyways since it is merely the rotation of the earth that cause the shifting of light and darkness.
