This game, like The Cat Lady, deals with a lot of incredibly heavy and sensitive material. This game included the expected blood and gore, as well as murdering animals and children, and a lot of talk of eating disorders and the accompanying thoughs someone would have when going through that. Because of that, this isn't really game for everyone (if you have an eating disorder, think long and hard about whether or not you can handle this game right now), but it is a good game.
I think this is a game that you'll need to play after finishing The Cat Lady, as there are several references (and sections of the game) where you'll have no idea what's happening unless you know who Susan Ashworth is etc. It's not necessary to play the 2009 version of Downfall, though, unless you'd like to compare. The new version differs in story a bit, is much less colourful, and there's voice acting! Unfortunately, some of the voice acting was really off, and the inclusion of a "mandatory" prologue bit will put a lot of people off of finishing this, I'm sure. But please, if you're reading this, go through the prologue and you'll be happier once you start the actual game.
I wasn't fond of the redesign of Susan and Mitzi (Susan looked awful, not going to lie), and I thought Ivy looked very different than her 2009 character, as did Agnes. I didn't care for Ivy at all, mostly because everything felt a bit forced and the mic would crack sometimes, but I think that overall, she was a good character and she did well being a new voice actor. I loved Joe, and I wish the game were longer so we could play as him a bit longer-- that's another thing, the game is shorter than I would have liked. Agnes was a pain at first, and again, very very different, but halfway through the game she became my favourite character. Really, I think the only characters who needed more work or didn't have their characters explored enough were Dr Z (there was a LOT cut out in this version of the game), Joe's family, and Ivy as I previously mentioned. Also, nobody really says much about the evil presence that wrecks everyone's holiday beyond the cryptic things you'd expect, and this was also the case in the older game, so I wish they'd done something with that.
I think that the Axe Man was poorly used in the game compared to the 2009 version, but he was a threat and he did do what he was supposed to do at least for a little while. The game didn't have me as on edge as The Cat Lady, though, and that's a shame. I think the addition of "tendency hints" kind of ruins the game a bit, but I appreciate that they allowed you the option to turn them on and off.
One major criticism I have with the game isn't about the game itself, but about the Extras-- I felt like some of the dev bios etc. were really, really awkward to read. Some read like they were trying too hard to be edgy, and I took the game a bit less seriously after that.
Overall, I do think it's worth playing this game. It was moving, uncomfortable, and disturbing, and I think that anyone looking to play this expects that going in. The game itself is gorgeous except for the new Susan Ashworth, and the dialogue is great (Joe has some of the BEST lines!). I do recommend playing this AFTER playing The Cat Lady and the 2009 version of Downfall, and I also promise that things get better after the prologue if you just get through it.

This is a pretty great follow up to the Cat Lady. Whereas the Cat Lady was a deep exploration of depression and insanity, Downfall is a deep exploration of, well... insanity times ten.
The Cat Lady had some pretty surreal elements and sequences, but one of its strengths is that everything made sense, narratively speaking. Downfall is a bit less clear and much more surreal, although no less fascinating.
Joe Davis and his wife Ivy have been dealing with some marital problems. Ivy starves herself and will often have episodes where she says strange things. Joe. doesn't know what to do and depending on what dialogue options you choose, he is either someone trying to understand and help, or someone who is pretty self centered. He takes Ivy to a small countryside place called the Quiet Haven Hotel. Shortly after arriving, strange things start to happen, and Ivy disappears. Joe sets out to find her, but it isn't long before reality starts to warp into something ugly and unrecognizable.
This game is, as I said, incredibly surreal in a Silent Hill 2 sense. Very little of it is meant to be taken literally and instead is open to interpretation. The writing is consistently strong, and it's constantly engaging. The only problem is that, unlike Cat Lady, depending on the ending you get, there are many questions left. Whereas Cat Lady had slight variations on the same ending, this game has full blown different endings- as in the outcome is entirely different. So the confusion can be pretty frustrating.
Still, this is a must play for fans of the Cat Lady. It's visually stunning, has a terrific soundtrack, and returns the player to the well established, macabre world of the previous game. Just expect to get a little bit more lost this time around, but also expect to get wrapped up in another twisted, creepy story that is impossible to stop thinking about.

I picked up this game in a bundle with the first two titles in the series, and it was well worth it. If you've played the earlier two games, you'll appreciate the improvements made in this version.
The traditional obstacles and pickups are there, but now there's a queue for when you have multiple objects to collect at once. The result is that you're no longer frantically clicking to make sure your worker runs out as soon as they're available. Instead, a little "check mark" appears next to items in your queue (which you can remove with a right-click) and keep your workers moving, leaving more of the game to your strategy as opposed to the speed of your clicking finger. They've introduced oil/petrol as a collected resource, so now helicopters and boats have their own required resource and allow for the inclusion of fuel stations and oil wells.
Other enhancements and improvements in level design await you. Workers, doctors, helicopters, firefighters, and police all need to be deployed to solve the varied puzzles. Obstacles include piles of wood and rock, forest fires (which, on later levels, can spread and cause you to fail the stage if you're not quick enough to respond!), burglars, and even poison gases.
A snarky story ties things all together (impressive enough to include dialogue between characters!), and even hints at a sequel. The art has received an overhaul as well, so as you progress through the game you'll be greeted by varied stages, character renderings, and decent 2D special effects.
To sum up, this is a fitting entry to the series, and much improved from the previous titles. If you're already a fan of this series or time-management games in general, you'll be pleased.

Rescue Team 3’s revitalised formula—including faster, tighter gameplay and especially its sarcastic storyline—elevates it far above many similar time management games.
Rescue Team 3 is a sequel that changes things around, and changes them a fair bit.
On the surface, it may not be apparent, as gameplay-wise it is the same time manager game as the rest of the series. We use a bunch of rescue workers to collect resources, clear obstacles, patch up ruined buildings, and save civilians. Thanks to one nice trick though, it is also a lot faster than its predecessors were: workers stay on the field a bit after completing a task, which cuts downtime significantly, resulting in a tighter, more fun gameplay. (Also, we can finally use the civilians for one-time production bursts.)
The real strength of Rescue Team 3 lies in its storyline. Many may not like its approach, but it is a refreshing change compared to the sanitised cuteness of most casual games.
In this game, we have to rescue the citizens of one of the most corrupt government in existence, who wilfully neglected all safety precautions to embezzle even more money. Now, they use some of that money to pay off a bunch of amoral, lazy rescue workers who spend almost as much effort looking for ways to fill their own pockets as doing their job. Yes, this game is full of cynicism and sarcasm, but in an incredibly humorous, nonsensical way, and this change alone makes it probably the best in the entire series.

Что касается языковой поддержки в игре. Игра переведена на три языка: английский, немецкий и русский. Возможно, есть поддержка и других языков (где-то), но то, что устанавливается из Стима содержит только 3 языка. По умолчанию, игра запускается на английском языке. Возможности изменить язык в настройках нет. Что само по себе странно ибо реализовать не сложно. Если хочется по играть читая текст на русском (или немецком), то нужно сделать следующее:
ПКМ на игре в библиотеке -> "Свойства" -> "Локальные файлы" -> "Просмотр локальных файлов" (откроется расположение игры на компе) -> пройти в папку "\data\conf" -> открыть в блокноте файл "autoexec.lua" -> заменить в строке "en" на "ru" для русского (или "de" для немецкого) -> закрыть файл с сохранением -> играть...
Все изменения на ваш страх и риск.
В свойствах игры можно изменять язык, но русский там не поставить. При этом, если выбрать любой, отличный от Английского, то удалится и локализация на русский язык.

Don't let my "low" hours fool you, I have a copy of the original game that I've played for at least a hundred hours, and I quite often play my games in "offline" mode.
A huge amount of story depth, wonderfully rich characters with growth, a true-to-the-source gameplay and character creation...all these things are in Baldur's Gate. And the Enhanced Edition just makes it even better.
If you like Role-Playing Games then you'll probably like this game, unless you are a complete graphics-♥♥♥♥♥ that can't stand playing anything less than Crysis games or Skyrim. If you can "stomach" games like Diablo 2, Sacrifice, or any other "old games" with "bad graphics" then you'll discover a rich, wonderful story just waiting to be heard and explored. In addition, you'll find extravagently beautiful (especially for 1998) backgrounds, voice acting, sounds, paintings, and buildings in this game. If you played Neverwinter Nights (1 and/or 2), Planescape: Tormet, Divine Divinity, Icewind Dale, or any other "iconic" RPG then you'll definitely want to play this game.
However, you also might want to realize that in a game like this you'll want to micromanage the crap out of your party. After every round you'll probably want to pause, make sure your spellcasters (or damage dealers) are going to actually do something that round of attacks, and then unpause. I can't tell you how many times I've had to pause to make sure my Archer is attacking something, since he kills damn near everything in two to three hits and there's no way I'm letting him switch to his AI, which wants him to attack enemies with his DAMN FISTS. STUPID AI!
*Ahem* Anyway, yeah, you'll want to make sure your spellcasters do something after each spell, that your high-accuracy high-damaging characters switch targets, and that you probably won't want to use most of the AI (as is always the case in RPGs in my experience).

Baldur's Gate is one of the best RPG experiences created to this day. Originally released in 1998, BioWare struck gold with this great D&D-licensed RPG. Now, over a decade later, Overhaul Games/Beamdog have appropriately overhauled the game in this Enhanced Edition, but is it worth getting?
Definitely! The massive scale of the game, the sheer amount of quests with excellent dialogue and the huge sense of freedom makes this a fantastic RPG experience to this very day. The Enhanced Edition comes with the original, the Tales of the Sword Coast expansion and offers even more content with the addition of three new companions, each of which offer an excellent experience, in addition to the new "The Black Pits" campaign which focused on arena-style combat. The Enhanced Edition additionally contains all the improvements that Baldur's Gate 2 had, meaning you can now play every single race/kit that BG2 contained plus the Enhanced Edition adds a bunch of new options and possibilities.
But the game is old and the Enhanced Edition does little to change this fact. Although there have been visual improvements, most notably a better user interface, it still looks like an incredibly old game and as the Enhanced Edition comes with a shocking lack of options this becomes a problem. Furthermore, the game does no effort or attempt to guide you. Especially fans of modern RPGs will run into this quickly, as the game is not even remotely user friendly. You will find no quest waypoints and very little in the way of statistic or spell explanations, meaning you will have to have patience learning and understanding the obviously outdated mechanics.
If however you can deal with these issues, then Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition is definitely worth getting. If you've played these games to death in the past, and have dabbled in the numerous mods at the time, then this may not be for you though the new content might just offer you enough. It is a much more convenient game with some great additions that makes playing this fantastic classic an amazing experience any RPG fan should play.

Recommended for mecha fans ONLY!
If you've played Armored Core, then you'll feel right at home playing Front Mission Evolved. This is a 3rd person game in which you pilot mechs called "Wanzers". Like Armored Core, you can upgrade your Wanzer with different chassis components and weapons. You unlock better upgrades as you progress. There's also a 3rd person shooter component of the game that has you run around on foot, using a very small selection of infantry firearms (shotgun, rifle, or rocket launcher). It's reminiscent of another, older Mech game, Shogo Mobile Armor.
The mech combat portion of the game is alright. It's fun to charge around, throwing ridiculous amounts of missiles and gunfire at the enemy Wanzers. The hit detection is usually pretty clean and the enemy AI can get smart, dodging long range fire and running away from melee attacks. It is annoying that none of the enemies ever run out of ammo and can dash/sprint indefinitely. I also didn't always enjoy having every boss be incredibly overpowered. But overall, they seem to have gotten it right.
The 3rd person infantry part of the game is awful however. The character movement is terribly clunky and clumsy, with very little precision. The vast majority of enemies in this mode will consist of 2 types; those with shotguns who run at you, and those with rifles who stay at a distance. Occasionally they'll throw in a "ballistic" soldier with a rocket launcher, or give you a helicopter or wanzer enemy to shoot 4 times with a rocket. I didn't enjoy it at any point, and it could have been done much better. You will be struggling through these portions to get to more Wanzer action.
A problem with both combat modes is two-fold; poor friendly AI and enemy AI that focuses solely on you. Your allies are pretty useless and will very seldom kill an enemy (unless it's a cutscene of course). That, combined with the fact that the enemies usually prioritize YOUR destruction over anything else creates a less fun and more difficult environment to play in. There are also little in-game collectables, though they seem to have no purpose other than to be collected.
Graphically, the game looks pretty good, though it might be a bit dated by now. There were a few voice sync problems with the cutscenes, but no other problems. The soundtrack is generic and forgettable. The voice acting is a bit cheesy but it's okay, although one character couldn't decide if he was British or Australian. Front Mission's story is a bit predictable and has few surprises. There are a couple unanswered questions, some things that don't make sense, and a romance subplot you'll see coming a mile away. But then this isn't really a plot-driven game anyway.
Play this game for the mecha combat. Everything else is either pretty forgettable or barely tolerable.

Zombie Kill of the Week - Reborn is a challenging, fast paced, 2D survival shooter!
And when we say fast, we mean breakneck, flat-out, adrenaline fuelled fast! What’s different from the other shooters is your goal isn’t to run through levels and finish the game, but to survive for as long as possible under increasingly frantic conditions (we say as long as possible because ultimately you will die!).
Seems simple enough, but where Zombie Kill of the Week - Reborn really takes off is in the added layers of depth and huge variety of features and customisation available. Players earn money for slaughtering the zombies (money might not bring you happiness, but it does buy you guns!). We live in a consumer society after all, which is useful, as you can spend big on over 25 different weapons (including chainsaw, katana, mini-gun, RPG, D.O.M. and many others!). You also need cash to open doors, activate jumps, buy new weapons, or hunt for the magic fridge and see what loot drops are inside! In short… the longer you survive, the more weapons and prizes you get.
Surviving longer also gains you ZKW-Points which you can cash in to totally customize your character, customize your weapons, buy new weapons, buy different perks, open new maps, and a lot lot more! Players also earn XP as they play, allowing them to level-up their character and develop them to fit their chosen gameplay skills. Survival is all about the margins, and every little extra helps!
The Steam release also features an exclusive level editor for the Zombie Kill of the Week - Reborn community, which allows the community to create their own custom and bespoke maps, then share them with friends (and enemies) for everyone to enjoy. Endless permutations and maps means endless challenges.
With a compelling single player survival mode, as well as cooperative multiplayer for up-to four players, this is one zombie firefight you are not going to want to miss! If that wasn't enough you can even play cross-platform play with Android owners too!  - Highly Recommended!

Let me preface this review by saying that I have only written a few reviews, for games, that I believe are worth my taking the time to write about. I appreciate all of the Steam users out there that take so much time writing near professional quality reveiws of games, for all of us who are undecided when we want to make a purchase. However, I am not that person, and I only write reviews when I am so very passionate about a game, and I feel the need to tell the world! The only problem is when I sit down to type it I cannot ever seem to articulate my feelings for the game and I end up not doing the game justice. I say "this game was amazing, I loved it, buy it." I run out of ways to truly explain it after a few sentences. That being said, please bear with me!
I first played Downfall around the time The Cat Lady (TCL) was released. I loved TCL so very much and I was excited to not only find another game by the same devs but also a game that had a storyline that was intertwined with TCL. It was free to boot! The original version of Downfall, was lacking in the graphics department, (not complaining just an observation) but that did not matter whatsoever. The devs very wisely chose to use these "painted vignette" themed rooms, and the main character himself (Joe Davis) seemed like a vignette. Because of this specific artistic style, heavy atmosphere, amazingly haunting music, and story, story, STORY (OMG that story), the lack of graphical quality did not matter. Within minutes I was captivated by the story of Joe and Ivy Davis and had to understand what exactly was going on at The Quiet Haven Hotel. An hour into the game I couldn't stop playing and around 4am the following morning when I finished it, I wanted to play it again! Unfortunately I had to go to work, and I sat (exhausted) all day at my desk thinking about Joe, Ivy, "Sophie," all of it. I played through Downfall again over the next couple days. As far as I could tell then it did not have a branching storyline, as I got the same ending twice and don't remember any choices that were made where the screen dims or a sound is made letting you know you have made a game altering decision. Either way-I was still left with many questions, and I wanted MORE -sort of like when I was all done playing Silent Hill.
I forgot about Downfall for awhile, and just recently I was browsing through my games and thought I'd give TCL another go as it had been years since I played. Then I thought, wait-let me play Downfall again first then I will play TCL again. I had just really "cracked" Downfall open and was a couple hours in, when I saw there was a remake just released-with better graphics, but more importantly voice acting and additional content. I was SO excited I purchased it without even reading a review or watching the trailer. I didn't need to-I knew it would be amazing, and I would have paid AAA+ pricing for the game without a second thought.
The remake was everything I'd hoped it would be and more! The game is fine polished now and graphics have improved tenfold while still maintaining that "vignette" feel to it. The voice acting is absolutely superb, which is tough because, just like when you read a book and then watch the movie remake if it, the actors have to look and sound the part that you imagined while reading it. Well-when a game is all subtitled, you envision the characters sounding a certain way, and if the sound is too far from that, it is a tough sell. Joe, Ivy, the "manageress" (think the devs coined that term-but I like it), Sophie, Harrison (he cracked me up-what a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-and everyone else sounds just as they should.
Ivy's accent was so very unique, and hard to put my finger on, almost like a Northern European that speaks English as their second language, and learned English from someone with an Irish accent. Whatever it may be, it couldn't be more perfect that someone like Ivy would have such a hard to "put your finger on" kind of accent-it's beautiful, mysterious and magnificant! Joe's accent which is best described as "I'm just a American dude, who is sarcastic, indifferent to the world and usually stoned"  is also very well fitting, and had me laughing at times. Harrison's voice hit the nail right on the head as a perfect d-bag, he reminded me of "Steff" in 'Pretty in Pink.' The "manageress" was phenomenal, the best in the game and whoever she is should seriously consider acting IRL. She nailed the affect in her voice giving it the feel of "I am an incredibly intelligent, insastiably horny snob, who always has an ulterior motive."
This game falls into the horror genre, no doubt about that. I feel that is it very important to point out that, unlike so many predictable, slasher/gore/jumpscare fest games (many of which I truly enjoy playing BTW) this gem really does have a unique storyline, which does not follow any genre norms, or cliches. This game may mean very different things to different people, and thus it is difficult for me to try and "nutshell" the story, especially without spoilers. So, I will say that for me, this is a story of the human psyche and how the subconscious mind can take on a life of its own, and crush all hope of the conscious mind ever returning to "normalcy".  It is truly intriguing to me that the developers of this game are men, given the choice and more importantly the delivery of the story content. Not that I like to stereotype, but let's face it, we all have our biases and we do frame things with them everyday-ya just can't help it. I don't want to spoil the story here, but let's just say it touches on some very heavy subject matter, in a way that makes people truly see just how crushing, and sometimes even fatal, certain "mental illnesses/disorders" can be. I am not speaking from personal experience but I am a woman, and have a degree in the mental health field, which helps "set the stage."

Oh My Dog- what a game. "Downfall" is a dark descent into the twisted mind of a troubled individual; Joe and Ivy's marriage sets the scene for a compelling story arc throughout the title.
Downfall's world-weary art style and character perspective helps to create a world in which pessimism is not merely an option- but an unquestioned way of life. Depression has never been so enjoyable. Not as good as "The Cat Lady", but Harvester Games have once again brought the goods to the table- and did not disappoint.
Some of the few downsides of this game include the game's short length and the narrow-minded, conservative approach to murder scenes.
Rather than a completely scripted and uncompromising approach to murder, I'd have prefered a gameplay mechanism in which I decide how I kill the characters. The game in many aspects holds the players hand too firmly- sometimes leaving the gameplay feeling a bit little stiff and tiresome.
Regardless, this is a must play for any fan of "choice and consequence" games or dark storylines in general. I can honestly say "Downfall" is one of the most unique games I've ever played, and its numerous thought-provoking characteristics will ensure you never forget your stay at Quiet Haven.

To be honest from the start, "The Cat Lady" by R. Michalski brought me up to this game as a fan already even before I played "Downfall" and I left as an even bigger fan of the whole story. Although "The Cat Lady" is a storywise prequel to what happens in this game, "Downfall" still stands there as an independent game which can be played without playing the other game first.
Just a short summary of the story without spoiling anything: The marriage of Joe and Ivy Davis is not going too well, so Joe organized a trip to a nice country hotel as a chance to repair their broken relationship. After a fight between the two of them, Ivy disappears under mysterious circumstances and in order to save her Joe  goes on a quest through a creepy, disturbing and surreal environment embedded into the hotel they stayed in. Determined to save his wife Ivy, Joe is ready to go far into the abyss of human nature...
So much for the story. The player is playing as Joe Davis, exploring the scenery in "The Quiet Haven Hotel" using simple arrow commands to walk around and interact with the environment. To solve puzzles you are picking up items to use them on certain other objects. The difficulty of these was perfect for this type of game because they were not too easy but not hard enough to break the flow of the game in case the player gets stuck; but at the same time the puzzles weren't generic especially in terms of creativity due to them being incredibly disturbing sometimes. Another key gameplay feature is the ability to choose between dialogue options, making significant decisions occasionally (there are 3 possible endings depending on things you say/do on your journey). Furthermore the game supports full voice acting and the voice actors did a great job overall in giving the characters more personality and depth.
Now, the pros and the cons for this game.
First of all, the pros: Surrealism and horror are two terms which are made for each other and you will find a spectacular mix of the two of them in this game, crafted into a beautifully eerie environment; if you like things like that combined with a stunning soundtrack that always fits the situtation perfectly you will fall in love with this game (47 titles which can be bought separately as an addition to the game). Although it still is a game, much play time will be invested in plot development, this should be kept in mind when considering to buy this game, but luckily the story does not let the buyer down. I was totally content with the way the plot unfolded and unraveled (and especially with the appearing characters too!); all endings made sense and the game remained true to what it is, a horror game. Beside the plot which I liked anyway, the game also deals with real life problems (especially anorexia) in a hauntingly shocking way which I will remember probably long after playing it.
Now the cons: The one thing I need to criticize the most is that for the full experience you should have played "The Cat Lady" already, because the endings just make so much more sense with the knowledge you gain from this game (although I certainly recommend everyone to play it anyway). Another negative thing is the tutorial sequence. It just seemed forced and it was mainly unnecessary for the plot itself
. For the cost of this game a duration of 4-5 hours is not really much neither.
Summary: I can completely recommend this game to fans of horror who like a nicely narrated story with well-made characters. The different dialogue options and endings invite the buyer to replay it, justifying the short duration of this game.

There is certainly enough content to warrant to price tag, my first playthrough was about six hours, and there are a good number of endings to keep you coming back...
...but its hard to come back to a game that starts this slow, with unskippable dialouge that will test your patience to see more than one ending.
TL:DR Downfall was worth playing, but will certainly test what you're willing to put up with in a video game. I'm ready to start The Cat Lady next.

I didn't know what to expect when I picked this game up a year ago, other than a boilerplate survival game set against the backdrop of a bleak Canadian north setting. I couldn't have been more blown away. This game is a testament to everything survival RPGs, and gaming in general can be.
To experience this hopeless struggle against cold, hunger, thirst and sleep deprivation is to lose yourself in a seemingly endless world with no way out but inevitable death. Yes, this game will kill you. Over and over and over again. Yet you will keep coming back for more punishment, loving every minute of it. The world, music and deep sense of isolation will lull you into a false sense of wonder at the majesty and preciousness of life. All before pulling the rug and reducing you to an animalistic series of impulses driven only by desperation.
While the frigid lonliness of Survival Mode will always be this game's highlight (and why I purchased it in the first place) the now launched Story Mode is an beautiful extra layer full of rich story, captivating drama and voicework that grabs your brain through your ears.
This clearly committed Canadian dev presents a stunning game that will tug at your heartstrings and put the fear of the wild back into you.
9/10

I still really like the concept of the story mode, but after playing it for over 5 hours, I'm fairly bored.  The story mode has basically become a quest game.  You find a person, they give you a task, you complete it and then onto another person. I will continue to play the Long Dark as I know the delopers are dedicated to the game, however, I will probably spend more time in the sandbox mode again (where I know I can create an adventure that is more suited to my tastes).

For Early Access, this game is fantastic! I have played most games without any crashes. Indeed, there will be some bugs (it is Early Access afterall), however, most of the bugs aren't game breaking and can simply be solved by saving and re-loading the game.

So...this game is listed as still in Alpha, although you wouldn't know it from the tons already available in the game as opposed to some of those other "fishied" games (I'm looking at you, Banished). And for an "Alpha" game, this has been a great little game I go back to again and again - I recommended it to my friends as well as worth it for any price it is listed. The developers update this thing on a constant basis, keep people well-informed on their website about developments and timelines, and are very good with communication with people who want to offer suggestions and even the few complaints they might get here and there. Having said that...
...I have nothing but positive praise for this game. The world is not a simple build-and-go, nor is it a "starve and die of the cold in a single night" type of game. I know a lot of people compare this to Minecraft or similar games, and that is not entirely a bad comparison on the surface. But take your love of the old SNES-type games, add in the elements that we all enjoy from Minecraft - mainly, the crafting and building, toss in a dash of resource management for good measure, and you have the beginnings of this game. I can't honestly offer any cons about the game at this point because I feel like I have been playing a game in beta for a while now. I kickstarted the game like a lot of people, and have been there since the beginning development where things kinda worked. And the game is not even remotely like most of these "games in development." And yes, I'm confident that the developers will reach their goal of having the game fully ready by the time they predicted...and if not, it will be so close that it will hardly matter. This is a game that will be completed, not just slathered with fanboy press and tossed into the public domain half-finished. They are already well passed that point anyway, and it shows.
So, in all good faith, buy this game. Plan on playing a little or a lot depending on your mood. But plan on coming back often because it is that enjoyable.

I had to withdrawal my review of Tetris Ultimate to write an updated review on my current thoughts of Tetris Ultimate. As of now, I don't recommend Tetris Ultimate, at all. Not because of other negative reviews say, like the game freezes, you need UPlay, its DRM, will not launch, etc. My reasons for not recommending this game are completely different from what others have been saying about this game.
The simple fact that there are better alternatives in Tetris, like Tetris Friends which is free with cheap microtransactions for example. You can spend the $15 that this game costs and buy yourself a lot of neat stuff through Tetris friends. Like Tetrimino styles, ghost styles, backrounds, win backrounds, sound effects, etc. Also has many game modes, an active community of people who play Tetris Friends, leader boards, etc. More worth it if you are a Tetris Fan.
Another free great alternative that is 100% free is Tetris Online Poland, or TOJ for short. Which you can grab for free by just googling it. It has an online community just like Tetris Friends. Except everything is basically free and the microtransactions have been yanked out. Its an online Tetris viewer that was once Japanese and now translated into English. Which blows away Tetris Ultimate by an Ultimate Landslide.
Issues with this game? Allow me to break this all down for you. My dear consumer.
1) No one plays this online. At all.
2) You absolutely need UPlay to play this game. Because Ubisoft.
3) The game plays incredibly stiff. Moving your Tetrimino's left to right feels bleh, making it a huge problem in higher speed levels.
4) There is absolutely nothing new nor spectacular to warrant this the Ultimate Tetris.
5) Backrounds plays with your eyes. It has all this blue haze in the backround that trips your eyes out. Do not play if you are drunk or high. If your eyes are sensitive to constant motion, you may get sick.
6) The music is an uninspired remix of the original Tetris theme. Really shallow and doesn't put you in that, "Tetris" mood.
7) You need a high speed cable connection to be able to even touch this game. (Not a problem for me, however.)
8) Does indeed crash often with no updates from Ubisoft. Figures.
In conclusion my dear friends. Where should your hard earned $15 go? Go to Tetris Friends website, make an account, buy some diamonds, spend it on some cool stuff, and you have yourself a versatile active community of Tetris friends with a staff that actually cares for its fans. It is also completely free. Or download Tetris Online Poland (TOJ) which is completely free for everything.
Thank you for reading. Avoid purchasing this game as its the Tetris you are sure you haven't been waiting for. Or want.

The game has difficulty playing while Uplay is in Online mode, the game breaks most of the time and the only stable mode is Marathon.  Once in offline mode, Tetris Ultimate performs better and smoother, therefore shifting the blame onto Uplay for causing the instability of the game.  This however means that you are unable to complete Uplay actions and achievements for the game, as well as being unable to play against opponents online.
This game also likes to be played in Windowed mode, for some odd reason.
The only exceptions to this is the pre-included DLC modes, which provide an extra layer of depth to the game.  The ranges of the Tetribot are appreciated and welcome however.
using Z and X keys to modify key mappings is rather unintuitive and difficult as some players prefer the Z(cw)/X(ccw)/L-Shift(hold) and direction keys for movement/hard drop/soft drop.  A preferred enter press (and wait for next key input) would have helped here.
As is, the game starts off with a slow Delay Auto Shift (DAS) and Auto Repeat Rate (ARR), so it is recommended to modify them at start.  It would also be recommended to have a mini-matrix to test the DAS/ARR so that it can be tested on the fly instead of having to go into a mode to test whether or not it feels right.
While the game looks aesthetically pleasing, the use of shaders to glow the active tetrimino causes some difficulty in seeing where it actually is, added to that I had occasional headaches because of such. The glow coming from line clears was also unnecessary as it causes further delays and additional resources to be used.  It would be helpful to be able to disable them or use them conservatively for that.
This could be because of the shaders used in the version, as well as Uplay, but it's a shame that Tetris Ultimate has no multiplatform support.  It would be helpful to those who use either Linux or Mac as well.
Had this game had mod support for extra modes and custom tetriminoes, or a much more customizable outlook, the game would have had a better experience, but since it doesn't, it's more of a mediocre experience which is difficult to keep up on.

Don't let my "low" hours fool you, I have a copy of the original game that I've played for at least a hundred hours, and I quite often play my games in "offline" mode.
A huge amount of story depth, wonderfully rich characters with growth, a true-to-the-source gameplay and character creation...all these things are in Baldur's Gate. And the Enhanced Edition just makes it even better.
If you like Role-Playing Games then you'll probably like this game, unless you are a complete graphics-♥♥♥♥♥ that can't stand playing anything less than Crysis games or Skyrim. If you can "stomach" games like Diablo 2, Sacrifice, or any other "old games" with "bad graphics" then you'll discover a rich, wonderful story just waiting to be heard and explored. In addition, you'll find extravagently beautiful (especially for 1998) backgrounds, voice acting, sounds, paintings, and buildings in this game. If you played Neverwinter Nights (1 and/or 2), Planescape: Tormet, Divine Divinity, Icewind Dale, or any other "iconic" RPG then you'll definitely want to play this game.
However, you also might want to realize that in a game like this you'll want to micromanage the crap out of your party. After every round you'll probably want to pause, make sure your spellcasters (or damage dealers) are going to actually do something that round of attacks, and then unpause. I can't tell you how many times I've had to pause to make sure my Archer is attacking something, since he kills damn near everything in two to three hits and there's no way I'm letting him switch to his AI, which wants him to attack enemies with his DAMN FISTS. Baldur's Gate is one of the best RPG experiences created to this day. Originally released in 1998, BioWare struck gold with this great D&D-licensed RPG. Now, over a decade later, Overhaul Games/Beamdog have appropriately overhauled the game in this Enhanced Edition, but is it worth getting?
Definitely! The massive scale of the game, the sheer amount of quests with excellent dialogue and the huge sense of freedom makes this a fantastic RPG experience to this very day. The Enhanced Edition comes with the original, the Tales of the Sword Coast expansion and offers even more content with the addition of three new companions, each of which offer an excellent experience, in addition to the new "The Black Pits" campaign which focused on arena-style combat. The Enhanced Edition additionally contains all the improvements that Baldur's Gate 2 had, meaning you can now play every single race/kit that BG2 contained plus the Enhanced Edition adds a bunch of new options and possibilities.
But the game is old and the Enhanced Edition does little to change this fact. Although there have been visual improvements, most notably a better user interface, it still looks like an incredibly old game and as the Enhanced Edition comes with a shocking lack of options this becomes a problem. Furthermore, the game does no effort or attempt to guide you. Especially fans of modern RPGs will run into this quickly, as the game is not even remotely user friendly. You will find no quest waypoints and very little in the way of statistic or spell explanations, meaning you will have to have patience learning and understanding the obviously outdated mechanics.
If however you can deal with these issues, then Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition is definitely worth getting. If you've played these games to death in the past, and have dabbled in the numerous mods at the time, then this may not be for you though the new content might just offer you enough. It is a much more convenient game with some great additions that makes playing this fantastic classic an amazing experience any RPG fan should play.
Full review (Includes BG2: Enhanced Edition):

With regard's to Baldur's Gate itself: This is perhaps the greatest RPG that has ever been made. To be a fan of this genre and to have not played this game is pure blasphemy and should be reconciled immediately. All kidding aside, this game is truly incredible and it is a true testament to its quality that it can stand up to current generation games. Baldur's Gate is based upon the Dungeons and Dragons' D20 system and borrows from the Forgotten Realms universe. The game has an incredible cast of characters, varied environments, well-balanced gameplay and so much depth that you'll want to play every class again and again.
If there were any black mark's against this game, it is only that people who do not know D&D and Advanced D&D rules will struggle and the difficulty curve is more of a scatter plot on your first play through since the game gives very little direction and it is very easy to get into high difficulty encounters at low levels if you go into the wrong areas.
With regards to the Enhanced Edition: The game came out in 1998 and this edition manages to fix many bugs and update the graphics to make them less pixelly and more tolerable to play on high resolution systems. Additionally, several new characters, companions and quests have been added to give veterans something new.
There is no game I'd reccomend more than this... except Baldur's Gate II...

I was surprised, as highly rated and recommended as this game is; that I really did not enjoy it.  As metroidvanias go this one was one of the most open, never steering you in one fixed direction.  The game has only a light story in the beginning and leaves it to you to explore in any direction you choose until you come across the various temples and bosses of the game.  Bosses and upgrades don't have a strict order to be obtained, though some areas will require certain upgrades to access like any good metroidvania.  The story does flesh out a bit later on but never does anything engrossing or epic.  The game is fully voice acted, and the voice acting and music feels very high quality.  Graphically the game is 2D with nice crisp textures even at high resolutions.
One of the big reasons I didn't enjoy this game much was that the upgrades weren't terribly exciting.  The major upgrades in the game come in the form of new forms you can transform into.  Each form usually has one big trick, like shooting, or casting light in dark places, or being able to remove obstructions.  As focused as the game is on combat I would have preferred the upgrades to be more combat in nature.  The first one I received I used for almost the entirety of the game for combat, with only the last form added something I felt was "more powerful" to the mix.  There's only a few health upgrades, and the rest are just decorations for your home and different costumes.  Some of these are useful such as one that restores your health to 50% over time when worn, but most are just decorative.  Instead the key to success against the bosses comes from cooking, which is a simple crafting system that combines enemy drops to make various dishes.  Unfortunately the reliability of drops and later areas of the game being very barren for materials made this annoying.  Couple that with the fact that dying takes you back to your last save as opposed to the beginning of an area or boss, and many frustrations moments were had.
My other issue with the game was the controls.  You can move around with either the mouse, keyboard, or a combation of the game.  As far as actually moving these controls are great.  Transforming is done by playing songs with a mouse radial wheel, but there's also keyboard shortcuts (1-8) for transforming that are absolutely crucial to being able to finish the game, but the game never tells you these are there in the tutorials.  Beyond that as a game set in the water precision movement was difficult.  WSAD felt better than the mouse for dodging in boss fights, but it still felt very sluggish and sloppy, and things like wall jumping were more challenging than they needed to be.
If you're looking for a metroidvania this one will fit the bill, and there's lots to explore and many things to fight, but I would recommend Waking Mars if you want to explore something beautiful, and something like Cave Story+ if you want a good mix of exploring and combat.

SkyDrift takes the familiar kart racing style gameplay from games like Mario Kart, Crash Team Racing, and Modnation Racers, and puts a very cool spin on it.
Instead of controlling karts on a racetrack, you're flying airplanes through canyons, caves, mountain tops and other locales.
The great thing about SkyDrift is the focus on controls. Sure there are various weapon powerups, but unlike most kart games, they are almost secondary to the controls themselves.
There are virtually no "blue shell" woes to ruin the experience. Choose from a variety of different planes, all of which handle differently, and fly your way through varied and beautiful landscapes and obstacles. You'll have to actively navigate through a variety of different areas in order to survive each race and come out on top.
The powerups are interesting and varied, but none of them feel overly cheap and ridiculously broken. It's refreshing to see a game in this genre that is mostly based on skill first, luck second.

Did you like The Cat Lady? Then you will love Downfall!

Fans of "The Cat Lady" will appreciate this game, which adds another chapter onto that story while also providing a full new game in the same art and game style.
This 2016 game is a remake of its 2009 self, maintaining much of the original story, but morphing it into the new "Cat Lady" style and interface.  This is generally an extreme improvement, though also manages to be odd in amusing ways.  "The Cat Lady" managed to engulf all of the original "Downfall" into its own plot arc, and did so in a subtle way that worked very well.  Here, the Downfall remake attempts to reengulf "The Cat Lady," for an odd game-ception effect.  Fans of "The Cat Lady" are likely to be pleased, but any newcomers to this universe are more likely to just be clueless and baffled by the jarring and out of place late-game characters.
Also, while this version polishes some of the rougher patches of the 2009 story, I can't honestly say that this story is as good as "The Cat Lady."  Not that that's necessarily a bad thing.  "The Cat Lady (TCL)" was AMAZING.  As such, it makes sense that this game would pull so much of its elements into itself to get that boost.  It's a fair move, and it works, but not completely.  The game suffers most just in comparison to the game it's copying: the sequel (this game) just isn't as good as the original (TCL, 2012).  Even though, technically, this is both the sequal (2016) AND the original (2009).

Absolutely phenomenal.  This remake has, in many ways, surpassed the original, opting for an artistic and mechanical style more in keeping with The Cat Lady.  The surreal environments, unnerving music, and compelling characters make this a solid piece in its own right.
If you played The Cat Lady at all, there's a lot here for you.  Little nods to the game, both in dialogue and flavor text, are plentiful, and if you play your cards right, you may just see a few familiar someones at the end.

So...this game is listed as still in Alpha, although you wouldn't know it from the tons already available in the game as opposed to some of those other "fishied" games (I'm looking at you, Banished). And for an "Alpha" game, this has been a great little game I go back to again and again - I recommended it to my friends as well as worth it for any price it is listed. The developers update this thing on a constant basis, keep people well-informed on their website about developments and timelines, and are very good with communication with people who want to offer suggestions and even the few complaints they might get here and there. Having said that...
...I have nothing but positive praise for this game. The world is not a simple build-and-go, nor is it a "starve and die of the cold in a single night" type of game. I know a lot of people compare this to Minecraft or similar games, and that is not entirely a bad comparison on the surface. But take your love of the old SNES-type games, add in the elements that we all enjoy from Minecraft - mainly, the crafting and building, toss in a dash of resource management for good measure, and you have the beginnings of this game. I can't honestly offer any cons about the game at this point because I feel like I have been playing a game in beta for a while now. I kickstarted the game like a lot of people, and have been there since the beginning development where things kinda worked. And the game is not even remotely like most of these "games in development." And yes, I'm confident that the developers will reach their goal of having the game fully ready by the time they predicted...and if not, it will be so close that it will hardly matter. This is a game that will be completed, not just slathered with fanboy press and tossed into the public domain half-finished. They are already well passed that point anyway, and it shows.
So, in all good faith, buy this game. Plan on playing a little or a lot depending on your mood. But plan on coming back often because it is that enjoyable.

Single player is okay on a higher end PC: i5 processor, Geforce GTX 745, 8 GB ram gets me high 50s for frame rates.
On a low range Core 2 Duo, with 2 GB ram, and a Radeon HD 2400 XT I can get 25-30 frames per second with everything turned down in single player.
But why so hardware intensive for a puzzle game that's been around for 30 years? Obviously it was poorly optimized for PC.
Still, I could have overlooked this if local multiplayer worked right, but it doesn't. You can get an Xbox360 controller to work in single player by turning on controllers in the Options/Extra menu. However, when you try to add in a second player for multiplayer is where the real shortcomings of this poorly done port occur. You can add the second controller on the main screen to initiate multiplayer by pressing the A button but after that you can't actually start the match because the second controller then becomes completely unresponsive. So this completely ruined the main reason I wanted this game for 4 player Tetris.
Add to this wonky menus, uPlay (not that bad but just 1 more annoyance to a game that doesn't work) and no ability to rebind keys and I'm just waiting 2 weeks and keeping my play time under 2 hours so I can get a refund if nothing gets fixed. Actually, any kind of patch to any of these issues might at least convince me that Ubisoft cares enough about it's product that I might decide to keep the game. Sadly, this seems unlikely as most of these issues have been reported since the launch of Tetris Ultimate on December 10 and nothing has come out (ie: we know and we're working on it) or any updates whatsoever. The only thing Ubisoft has is a guy saying, "Submit a support ticket”.
Save yourself the trouble, don't buy it until you see that it's actually been updated to work.
Edit: I gave Ubisoft the two weeks to make any change or to at least acknowledge the many issues that are occurring, and unfortunately, nothing positive has happened, so I am requesting a refund.
On a side note, if anyone has a Wii, Tetris Party Deluxe is an awesome game that has multiple game modes, plays smooth and supports 4 player local multiplayer! It’s all the things Tetris Ultimate should have been. I picked it up used on Amazon for about $20.

A fundamentally flawed game: losing advances you more than twice as fast as winning.
You read that right.
Option 1: Play to win, support your team, stick around for 10+ minutes until the conclusion of the battle.  About half the time, you'll win and earn about 1500 Quatloos (abstract example).  The other half, you'll lose and earn about 1000.
Option 2: Rush forwards straight into the middle of the enemy, get off one salvo, then die as quickly as possible.  Eat torpedoes, hug a battleship so that it can't miss.  Get sunk within 2 minutes.  Earn... can you guess?  1000 Quatloos.
Add a generous 2 minutes for what passes for matchmaking between 'games' and it comes out to 105 Quatloos a minute for playing to win, and 250 a minute for losing.  Even factoring in the reduced repair costs from surviving (at best about half the time) and winning still comes out significantly ahead.
Give that the game is all about grinding, there's literally no incentive to try and win.  You proceed much faster by losing.  So you'll quickly get into a larger ship, which lets you earn even faster - you'll just never actually learn to use it.  Continue until you get to the endgame or bored.
There's not a jot of exaggeration here: in the world of Navy Field, winning is for losers.

Question #1: is Navy Field 2 a fun game? Absolutely.
Question #2: is Navy Field 2 as good as World of Warships? Not in a million years.
That really is the truth of the matter. World of Warships beats NF2 in pretty much every category. It has superior historical accuracy, it's more immersive, it has a larger player base, it has better support, more map and game mode variety, and overall is a better game. NF2 is a top down shooter with arcade models; WoWs is a graphically beautiful simulator with serious ships. There really is no contest. If you have a good enough machine and graphics card to play WoWs, stop reading this and go download it.
...aw hell, that would be too easy. Okay then: here are four things that NF2 does better.
1) NF2 has more ships. A LOT more ships. The US Navy, Royal Navy, IJN and Kreigsmarine are all featured, whereas WoWs is still in open beta and only has the US Navy and IJN. With the occasional exception (no King George V-class battleships), all of the notable ships are there-and yes, that includes the Yamato. And yes, those 18 inch guns hurt like hell.
2) NF2 has subs. WoWs does not. While some destroyers in WoWs can be savage little ninjas, you only get true stealth in NF2. It is actually fairly well balanced to boot. It's not easy to use a sub well, but when you do, the rewards are spectacular. Equally, it takes time for destroyer drivers to learn how to hunt a sub. When an experienced sub and an experienced destroyer meet, it leads to a tense game of cat-and-mouse.
3) Unlike WoWs, which puts similar tiers against each other, there is no such limitation in NF2. It is entirely possible to play your first game in a massive 15v15 match, with a Yamato and an Iowa blazing away at each other which you whizz about in your pokey little beginner destroyer. You really do have no idea what you'll run into when you hit the Battle button, and the possibilities for emergent game experiences are substantial. While that can lead to some difficult games as you fight against higher-tier ships and more experienced players, it can also be quite fun.
4) NF2 has decent community, overall. It is absolutely advisable to join a Fleet; like all multiplayer games, it's best played with friends. Doing damage to a Yamato in your tier 1 destroyer is great; distracting a Yamato while your two friends in their battleships sink the monster is even better.
I hope that helps. NF2 is fun-just don't expect it to be as good as WoWs.

Well, this game turned out to be a disappointment.
I bought it remembering the amazing experience I had with Front Mission III on the original PlayStation. Sadly, this can hardly be compared, let alone even be called a FM game. While FM III was a turn strategy RPG, FM Evolved is a third-person shooter - a rather huge step away from the franchhise's original concept. However, this alone would not bother me that much, provided that the game was enjoyable. Sadly, this was not the case. Here's a list of 10 things that in my opinion make this game a failure:
1. Generic plot - insert "save the world" template here and supplement it with a handful of overused cliches.
2. Boring characters - a yet another bunch of two-dimensional cliches you couldn't care less about.
3. Unconvincing voice acting - there is more emotion in the sound of a flushing toilet than in the voices you hear in this game.
4. Failed customization - even though there is a variety of wanzer models and parts to choose from, the default model is so OP in comparison that you will always go for it.
5. Annoying enemy AI - this game should be called "Dylan must die" because every single enemy is hellbound on targeting you. It doesn't matter how many allies you have in the mission or how much closer they are to the enemy than you - every single hostile unit will aim and shoot at you regardless of the distance or circumstances.
6. Failed role system - because of the enemy AI, you basically cannot play as anything other than mid-to-short range brawler. Wanted to play as a sniper? Forget it - the enemy will never leave you alone, regardless of the difficulty level.
7. Annoying bosses - fighting bosses is almost entirely luck-dependent as most of them have one or two ridiculous attacks that you can either hardly avoid and/or survive.
8. Failed ally AI - your allies are useless. Completely and always.
9. Human mode glitches - when running around as a human, prepare for some uncooperative controls and random kicks to Windows.
10. Lack of a save option - the biggest failure this game has to offer. You simply cannot save by yourself and are subject to the mercy of the autosave and elusive check points. You will have to replay a lot when the game kicks you out to Win, and trust you me that it freakin' will.
Not worth your time.

As with any game, you really shouldn't pay attention to most of these community reviews. People have opinions, and let's face it: No one but yourself can tell you whether or not you like a game. Me, personally, I find the game quite enjoyable, and easily worth ten bucks.
But let's ignore the subjective and get into the objective nitty-gritty...summarized.
Is this a traditional Front Mission game? No, obviously. Though Front Mission has roots in Turn-Based Strategy, Evolved is an Action game, more akin to Armored Core or Mech Assault.
Is this an objectively BAD game? No. At the VERY worst, it's average. At best, it's pretty good. The story seems to be written well enough, customization is above-average, and the graphics are certainly not poor.
Overall, if you want a cheap mech game with decent customization and fun combat, this is worth checking out.

Cuphead is Fantastic.  There's no beating around the bush.  Even when whiny game journalists cried about it, the developers didn't back down from the game they wanted to make.  Something where an actual challenge is presented, and the only way to get past it, was to get better at the game.  This giant middle finger to the SJWs who think they are owed things they didn't earn is fantastic, and gives me hope for more developers who won't cave into the SJW narritave.
Now that that's out of the way, lets talk about the actual game.  The name of the game is trial and error.  I know some people aren't a fan of this style of game, but I think it works very well here.  You will die, and change your aproach next time.  "One more try" is a phrase you will say a lot, and repeat it until you realize that it's 5:30am and you work at 6.  It's a game that forces you to adapt and try different strategies.  The game is both increadibly challenging, and also increadibly fair.  There were very few times when I had a death that was because of poor game disign, rather than my own shortcomings.  This makes it a game where the real enemy isn't the boss in front of you, but yourself.
The other thing, of course, is the art disign and music.  If you've seen anyone else talk about it, you know what I'm getting at.  The game sounds and looks like a 30s cartoon.  The one thing that often gets overshadowed by the artstyle is the music.  While the visuals are amazing, the music is the real star of the show for me.  Even when I was stuck on that MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING DRAGON for an hour and a ♥♥♥♥ING half, I couldn't help but tap my foot to his theme music.
This game is awesome.  I will be revisiting it at some point in the future, and it is well worth the $20 entry fee.  Unless your name is Dean.

This game employs a Metroid-like style of gameplay. That means you are free to roam around, but full exploration is only possible by finding upgrades that will allow you to get through certain obstacles that you couldn't before. This time around, however, your character is underwater and can swim freely, allowing for exploration in all directions.
The world is immense and there's a lot of backtracking to be done but I've found there to be little tediousness in the process due to what I consider to be gorgeous 2D graphics and masterfully crafted soundtrack, which made the whole experience that much more enjoyable to me.
The controls are very responsive and all of the character's moves can be done with just the mouse if the player so desires, but the game can otherwise be played with a controller or a combination of keyboard and mouse. The combat is very energetic and being underwater allows for a lot of dodging, which you will have to become proficient at to get through the game since the screen can get quite busy with projectiles and enemies at times and your character can't take a lot of beating.
A very important aspect of the game is the ability for the player to cook many kinds of food. Different recipes (which must be found or guessed, and require ingredients available throughout the world) can provide your character with buffs or healing, which can dramatically decrease the difficulty of certain areas and bosses. For this reason, I don't consider this to be a particularly difficult game if one chooses to take advantage of the cooking ability.
The game offers a plethora of secrets to be found (some useful, like cooking recipes and pets that will fight for you, and some that are simply aesthetic, like costumes), the rarest of them often protected by bosses. Pursuing all of those secrets at a normal pace may very well push the playtime past 15 hours.
Overall it's an excellent game in my opinion; To me it hits the right notes in all technical aspects, has an interesting story and a very satisfying amount of exploration and content. Greatly recommended for fans of the genre!

I have been a Long Dark Alpha user for as far back as I can remember.  The game has made many changes and additions throughout the years, and it's only gotten better with age.  Tonight, I fired up the story mode for the first time, and I have to say that I'm truly amazed.  The developers have done an excellent job of bringing life and vitality to the game.  In the past I created my own personal goals and challenges in the sandbox mode to make the game more interesting.  Now with the addition of the story mode, the game seems complete.  It's rare to find a game of such high caliber these days.  The Long Dark is now goes on record as one of my all time favorites.
Update:  Okay, now that my initial excitement has faded, I'm chaning my review from positive to mixed.  I still really like the concept of the story mode, but after playing it for over 5 hours, I'm fairly bored.  The story mode has basically become a quest game.  You find a person, they give you a task, you complete it and then onto another person.  Mind you, these tasks are also fairly crazy in themselves (things a person who is trying to survive wouldn't do for a stranger).  Also, as others have stated, the magic wolf's appear everywhere.
I will continue to play the Long Dark as I know the delopers are dedicated to the game, however, I will probably spend more time in the sandbox mode again (where I know I can create an adventure that is more suited to my tastes).

Let me first begin by saying I NEVER review a game. For this game I felt obliged. Before I begin to play the final release of this game let me say that beta has been an extreme pleasure.
I purchased this game in sandbox mode because I wanted a mood game. Something that transported me to another time and place every time I logged in. This did that with astounding success.
I hate "surivival games" and somehow this comparable attempt at realism allured me in, and now I find myself claiming to enjoy the "survival" genre.
True, there are no action elements to this game. Little ammo. Virtually no weapons. There are no zombies, no enemies of a sinister nature, no paranormal elements. Just you and elements. The sweet bitter cold. Sure there is the occasional bear or wolf, but the truth is this is a game about isolation. But if you're like me, well, thats just fine. It's a much needed break from the drone of similiar game titles. For this, I give my most sincere gratitude to the devlopers for sticking to their guns. It would have been tempting to make this the game it is not. Thank you.
As of now I cannot speak for the story mode and the worht of it at 35 USD, but I can say that without a doubt the industry needs more games from these developers. Let's do whatever we can to make that happen. It's up to us to fund the games that truly speak to a niche like this one. It's up to us to make sure our voice is heard in communities like this one to insure the future of games don't blindly follow popular trends in the hopes of trendy profits.
I will update after story mode has been played out.

My Story:
Waking up in my house, I look around. Im in a small neighbourhood, and in a bungalow too. I search and find a frying pan as a weapon. I drink some water and honey, and I eat a pinneapple. I'm well fed. It's time to scavange, I go outside and raid the nearby house. This nearby house is quite well stocked, but I hear a banging. The bathroom is fortified with a wooden plank, and something is banging the door. I unbarricade the door by ripping the plank out, and I open the door to be greeted by the dead resident, I smash his head in with a hammer I found in his house. The body is a bit unnerving, I'm panicked now.
It's evening time. I want to find a different house to stay in, but I seem to be surrounded here. There is a congregation of zeds outside, four of them. I lure one away, and I kill it. However, I attract the rest of them with the sound of the zed's face being smashed in by my foot. I am fighting them now, pushing them back. Though, I get stuck once.. A zed hits his head against me, and all of a sudden I've been injured. I quickly kill the zeds and rush back inside my house. I put sheets up everywhere. I then tended to my injury.. I was scratched on the groin. I am worried, though not too worried. Scratches only provide a small chance of catching the disease. I go to sleep.
It's the next day, and I've deteriorated. I am a nervous wreck, I read books and newspapers to pass the time until its more light outside. I'm a little nauseous, but I put this down to the uncooked chicken I ate. After reading the newspaper, I decide to head out. I go over to a nearby house, theres some zeds near it but I won't be doing that again! I'm looking for any good stuff. I have a hammer, food and some other items in my hiking bag.
On the top right corner, I turn very nauseous. My health has deteriorated rapidly since I've been scratched. My doctor, before the outbreak told me that I was a  chronic hypochondriac and never felt the symptoms of infection, I put it down to this, I'm now frantically looking for painkillers or disinfectants. I'm in need of antibiotics or any medical supply. I head out of the nearby house and run over to a two story home. At this point, I've got a heavy fever and desperate for medical items. The front door is locked, so I open the window.
The alarm goes off, it's so painfully loud for me.. I wonder how loud it is for the zeds. I ran, frantically to the coastline. There's a little shed, but the door is locked. I forgot that I had a pistol that I picked up from my sleeping home, so I took it out. I was ready to go out with a bang, knowing that I will likely die anyway, I start shooting at the horde of zombies walking towards me. I don't kill a single one, infact, I die before they reach me.
R.I.P

I mentioned earlier that the keybaord control scheme didn't make sense compared to the Xbox controller scheme. If you don't have the game, you're probably wondering what they did. I'll list it for you!
:
:
The keyboard control scheme did it's best to make all of the keys accessible within a certain area, but it doesn't feel right to me at all. I'm pressing space with my pinky, not my thumb, and that is awful. A better scheme for keyboards would give your left hand access to most Tetrimino control while allocating your right hand to rotation. Of course, that would be best for right-handed players- flip it for left-handed.
Seperately, the Xbox controller scheme is highly subject to human input error- accidentally inputting "Up" while trying to input "Left" or "Right" is very, very common.
Regardless, to enable a control scheme for usage in gameplay or in menus, it must first be selected in Options -> Extra.
Why on EARTH is this an "Extra" option?! This should be a Gameplay option, if anything.
As mentioned earlier, when you switch the control scheme, the UI doesn't change to match, so you have to guess inputs based on what I assume is "common sense"... except, as someone who doesn't play Xbox (360 / One) games, and purchased an Xbox 360 controller purely for native controller support, it's actually guess work.
The game also assigns buttons to actions that otherwise have no gameplay equivalent- the [O] key is used to confirm some settings, or replay the current game mode, with it's controller equivalent being "X" on the controller. These aren't used anywhere but when navigating menus, and they aren't listed in the game's (rather helpful) tutorial, also found in the Extra options.
If you're a member of Tetris Friends, several of these modes are familiar, though some of them are different from their Friends counterparts. (Check the game description for details on each.)  These include Marathon, which is a simple "clear 150 lines" challenge, Endless, which is Marathon but it goes forever, Sprint AKA "40 Lines" mode, Ultra, which is a three-minute score attack, Battle and Battle Ultimate, head-to-head without or with items, respectively, and three other gimmick-centered game modes. Most of these modes play exactly as they sound, and they are fun to play, generally.
Most if not all of the available game modes can be played side-by-side in a Versus mode, up to four players at a time. Additionally, they can be played co-operatively as well, featuring a larger, "shared well" that everyone drops their pieces into. Furthermore, a "Team Versus" mode is available, setting teams of two against each other with two shared wells, one for each team.  I have only been able to test Versus against AI opponents for this review, as there is a huge lack of players.
It's plays like a Tetris game, once it's actually running decently (which requires a super-high end computer of some sort for highest quality graphics, otherwise the lowest quality still needs a medium-end computer). I spent two hours of my life so far playing this game and actually enjoying it, despite having some input lag due to the graphics being inefficient. As far as I can tell, it's fully playable despite it's flaws!
Multiplayer is dead though.
A similar, better experience can be found in Tetris Ultimate for 3DS, which has even LESS music, but actually has people playing it and, better yet, plays well from the get-go; Tetris Friends, which is highly popular and more "family-friendly" looking; and Tetris DS, which uses an older Tetris Standard but is faster pased and more varied.
Players who are used to the speed, technical prowess, and feel of the Grandmaster series of Tetris games will not like Tetris Ultimate in any form.
(I purchased my copy as a DL code from Amazon while it was on sale, running me $7.50.)

I am really digging this game.
It kinda has an SNK fighting game feel to it, but there is a skill progression that really adds depth and playthrough time to the game.  As you progress further in your stats, you unlock new training minigames that really help keep them from feeling stale.
As for the controls, they're pretty tight for being an indie title.  However, the game assumes you have an Xbox 360 controller, as the on-screen button prompts are of the A+B+X+Y variety, makes it confusing if you're using a keyboard.  Personally, I'm using a USB-connected SNES controller and it works beautifully with this game.
The graphics really capture the feel of the transitional period between the 16-bit and 32-bit console eras (think NEO-GEO), and they are of much higher quality than your average indie fare.
The sound effects and music really make this game shine, once again perfectly capturing that bygone era that a lot of us spent middle school listening to as we played our games.
If I were to criticize anything, it would probably be the rough translation job, but it's a minor slight that doesn't take away from the game much at all.
The devs have some real talent, and this game is well worth the $10.  I'd like to see where they go from here.

An actually unique idea which I have not seen anywhere yet.
In Hobo: Tough Life you are all alone, trying to survive the cold nights. This can be done by either searching for food in bins, talk to people on the street or knock at the chirch's door to get helpful tips on how to get new clothes.
By talking to others, stealing, begging etc. you are getting skill points and level ups. There is also a crafting part and base building already, sadly you can't use a rope to hang yourself.
There are verious mini games, my favourite one so far are the scratch cards which you have one in your inventory each time you die. The dialouges between the characters are pretty diversified sometimes, but also quite difficult to master at some point. The police, for example, can be complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s when you ask them the wrong questions.
The game is using the Unity Engine but the current version of the game suffers from game lags. They are not game breaking but might be annoying, even on low I can't achieve fluent 60+ FPS (PC config on my profile).
For what the game is I would recommend it, the price might be a bit too high but if you are into survival games and are ready to try something new, it might be worth the investment.

Playing the free weekend trial, and I would suggest anyone who has the money for it should buy it while it's on sale.  But I stress, "on sale".  For now, the game is packed with players so even playing a monster yields very low wait times.  However I'm afraid this will change as soon as the free weekend is over.
Gameplay is fun, extremely fun.  Whether you're playing as the monster or the hunters there is plenty to enjoy and each side offers unique gameplay.  There were times where I didn't even care that I lossed as a Monster, because the match was enjoyable.
I do believe that there are some balancing issues, for example; as the monster you feel slow even with the ability to leap about.  The hunters are equipped with jet-packs and can easily keep up with you once they find you.  The only opportunity you have to run and consume more wildlife is if you can incapacitate one or more of the party.  Even then you're only buying yourself time to consume two or three animals before they catch up.  There's no incentive for the Hunters to set ambushes or make a defense point because they can just chase you down and kill you before you have the chance to evolve.
Another issue is general match-making.  I suppose when under normal circumstances it'd be impossible to even find players to play with, but even with the trial weekend I've noticed there's a slight disparity in levels and even skill.  I primarily have been playing as the Monster, so I'll speak from my perspective.  I will notice that one or more of the players I can slap around and punish pretty easily, but there will usually be one player who can practically 1v1 me.  Now, bravo to that one player but also it kind of says something about balance again, either in matchmaking or general mechanics.
Greed-game.  Like I said, if you have any means to purchase this game WHILE it's on sale, do so.  $40 for the complete package, it gets you everything you see during the free trial weekend.  If you wait, you'll most likely be screwed and have to pay $40 for the base game and end up not liking it. Yes, we know 2K/Turtleturd/Whatever screwed up bad when they first released this, but having played this it genuinely seems they're TRYING.  However once the sale ends and everything goes back up to full price, I'm not sure all the effort would be worth $70++.
TL;DR
If you have $40, buy it, no regrets.
If you wait until after the sale, don't buy it, no regrets.
