I assume at some point in this game's past, some major aspect of the game changed; the number of negative reviews seems unwarrented from my two days (so far) of playing. Sure, the MM is a little strange at times and every so often you get battles that one team is seemingly heavily stacked - but even then it is possible to win. But onto the actual game.
It has an arcady feel that, despite the drastically different camera angles and graphics, distinctly reminded me of Battlestations: Midway. Perhaps it's just because of it being an arcade, ship based game, but it doesn't really matter; as I played more I began to enjoy myself more and more. I initially intended to simply play a while whilst another game was in a prolonged maintainence, however this quickly changed into playing it heavily.
Initially you start off in an early (often pre-WWI) ship, for the first few tiers you can expect to unlock new ships pretty regularly, I think I'm up to Tier VI as of this review in approximately 10 hours of playing (half way to seven, but I'm probably going to change tree which will slow me). You can chose from 4 nations, with each nation having a relatively balanced tree, whilst still maintaining some national traits (Japanese Torpedos are really, really good for example). Whilst from what I gather the grind starts to become more noticeable from tier V onwards, I've already claimed a couple of tier IX, X and XI ships in my little destroyer and my CA just claimed a high end BB.
Which brings me to the MM - yes you get put in battles against high tier ships when you are playing low tier ships. And honestly? If you don't like the concept of merely being a cog in the machine for your team, this might not be the game for you. That said, I loved the challenge of having to take an early destroyer up against teams with Yamatos and Vanguards, and thus I see no issue with the MM. The biggest problem at the moment is slow queue times - but they aren't unbearably bad and at some times of the day you can get matches with decent frequency.
The graphics are a little poor - but really, they don't need to be any better, and the visuals are more than adequate for the game. The audio however is good - especially the music which fits the gameplay very well. The UI is a little complicated, and the extremely minimal tutorial you get means you are rather required to ask other players for explanations on certain things; but unlike most of these types of games, the community is helpful.
Speaking of the community - not only are they helpful as mentioned above, but also there is far, far less rage than in most online games, all of my matches thus far have been with light hearted people who often laugh at silly mistakes rather than screaming at you. Additionally, in several battles where I've been chasing the last surviving enemy in my DD, high tier BBs have allowed me to score the kill rather than taking it for themselves (which they could easily do) which speaks to a far greater level of decency than I've come to expect from online games.
On a final note, the F2P model in this game is instantly recognisable as a fair model - so far as I can tell, there is virtually nothing that is exclusively bought with gold, meaning you are never outclassed by premium vehicles, and never need to buy premium vehicles to sustain yourself, in addition to this the economy seems relatively generous - there are no repair bills, meaning no real drain on your credits other than things you chose to buy.
Overall - if you enjoy the challenge and the thought of tactical naval battles, and don't mind the queue times and occasionally unfair matchmaking, this game is definitely worth trying. I had hesitated over downloading it because of reading the negative reviews - my experience of being seal clubbed in other WWII combat games by higher tiers put me off greatly when I read about people fighting tier XI ships with tier II ships, but now that I've tried it, I'm glad that I did as it was certainly worth trying. Seeing as it's free even if you are uncertain - it could be worth downloading and trying it for yourself rather than listening to any review (including my own.)

In the first two hours, Aquaria is extremely uneventful and uninteresting. You will feel as though the music is bland and repetitive, the art is adequate but not unique in any way, and the game play is tedious. There is really not much going on in the game world or around you in the beginning. All you are doing is maneuvering the main character around the screen with very simple controls. Because the game play is so dull in the initial couple hours, this may deter many gamers from continuing. After you earn a couple special powers, Aquaria becomes something almost entirely different than the initial experience. It is a mixture of Ecco the Dolphin, Metroid, and Castlevania. The singing mechanic is elaborate and well thought out even if it takes a little getting used to. The cooking system is also fresh and unique, giving the player access to various combinations for producing food items and power-ups with special temporary effects. Combat is interesting and the controls are decent. At times it is a bit confusing since there are often sections of the map that you do not have access to as you go past them at first, which gives the player a feeling of having missed something. In addition to this, you will reach areas of the game world that attempt to give you direction, but end up being ambiguous and cryptic, making your progression unclear. This problem means that several aspects of the game will force the player to seek help through FAQs and guide maps. The save system requires the player to go to certain specific areas that are not widely available in order to save your progress. This means that if you die and haven't saved in a while, everything accomplished and explored since your last save must be done again, as if it never happened before. These save areas are often very far from each other, which adds severely to the problem. Once you adapt to this save system shortcoming, you will be prepared to backtrack just to save your game. The world map gets extremely convoluted and disorganized because some sections often overlap others. This can cause confusion and disorientation as you travel around the world. The enemies design is often interesting, albeit predictable, as you can imagine many of the creatures you encounter are from the sea. The different forms and abilities you will learn during the game are creative and fun to use, making them the highlight of Aquaria. Some instances during the game seem too cryptic and if you accidentally pass these areas by without noticing, it is possible that you may go through the rest of the game without certain items and abilities because of this design flaw. Some things happen in the game without any explanation whatsoever, which leaves the player, once again, disoriented. In addition to the forms and abilities you will learn, the other interesting and fun aspect of Aquaria is in the exploration of this large game world. The bosses are challenging, well designed, and fun to fight against. The mechanics required to defeat them make sense and puts all your skills and abilities to the test. Accomplishing some of the needed tasks in this game is so unintuitive, obscure, unclear, and unobvious that there is simply no way to figure them out on your own without seeking help with a FAQ. There are some parts of Aquaria that requires you to be out of the water. This brings some of the worst platform jumping controls I have played in any game, but all is forgiven as these instances are rare. Forgiving the save system and the occasionally extremely unclear and ambiguous progression, Aquaria can be enjoyed thoroughly.

So yeah, one of your dudes can kill another one of your dudes.
There's no precedence for it whatsoever. It's just a pretty highly specific scripted event between very specific characters, as if the developer were trying to troll the player. You won't even know it's a possibility until it actually happens, and except for the few pairings that it's possible for, you won't even have to worry about it.
This smells of very good quality gameplay, and I am sure all of this highly difficult game's difficulty is well-balanced instead of artificial, RNG crap.
For some reason, though, the game ended up uninstalled immediately, and I felt the strangest regret that I had ever bought the game, as well as this strange conviction to never buy any future Endless games.
Other strategy games should learn from this. For example, Civilization could base the outcome of wars on historical events, instead of actual gameplay.

My experience with Dungeon of the Endless has been mainly "struggle and frustration" so far, but because the game is just so ridiculously hard as in it requires a lot of managing, planning, and some luck, every attempt makes you delve more into the depth of the game. Simply opening doors without much thoughts will ONLY lead you to bad endings.
Lists below are what I believe to be the game's good parts and (rather than saying bad directly) parts that left me unsatisfied.
Good parts
+ Simple - collect and manage resources, survive the enemy waves, construct towers to help your heroes, RESEARCH: these are all you need to know to "endure" the challenges until you get the grasp of more details
+ The simplicity is what makes the game really Fun as well! Its easy to get into and rogue like element makes every round different from each other
+ Interesting characters to choose. Later into game, you would prioritize operator (for extra resource production) over other characters, but IT IS WORTH exploring other types too! They have their own unique taste of skills and playstyle.
+ To be able to level up and equip heroes you love and enjoy playing so that they can be even more stronger and sometimes.. a little bit OP under certain circumstances
+ Different dungeons to choose, finally managed to finished the first? Here comes the second with even harder (subjective) which may require different strategies
+ THE JOY OF BEING ALIVE at the end of each round. Seriously, after dying so much times and failing to clear due to stupid mistakes, this relief makes you go on in the game
+ Ridiculously hard sometimes - greatly recommended to those who enjoy challenges out there
Bad/Unsatisfactory parts
- Lack of multiple saves system, basically you are stuck in one game to either beat or be crushed
- Hard to play in a co-op game, as in barely any room to join (playing with 3 other friends instead is generally recommended rather than waiting)
- After awhile, you can notice some heroes are plainly just more "useful", balancing is left to be desired
STILL the game is just amazing, I really did not expect for me to have this sort of intense fun when I bought the game
Therefore, I would like to rate the game 9.5/10! :)

Downfall
Psychological Horror Adventure
Harvester Games
Screen 7
is a psychological horror adventure game developed by Harvester Games and published by Screen 7, the same people behind 2012's
. This is a remake of the 2009 game by the same developers, and it is included in this version.
You play as Joe Davis, a man who goes on vacation with his wife Ivy to the Quiet Haven hotel to try and fix their marriage problems. However, after the first night, Ivy disappears and weird, disturbing, violent and space-bending things start to happen.
If you played the developer's previous game or read some of Stephen King's horror novels, you know what you are gonna get: a creepy and weird story with depressed characters and dark humor. Saying more about the story would spoil it, but just know this: I was hooked from the get-go and I played the entire game in one sitting, which rarely happens to me. I laughed, I cringed, and I even cried while playing this. One of the best stories in a game since Telltale's first season of The Walking Dead.
The game is made with
, and you will either love or hate how it looks. It's mostly in black and white with 2D stripes and burst of colors (mostly a lot of red blood). There are some disturbing and gory images that might scar those who aren't used to them, and a couple of sequences will leave you with your eyes wide open in sheer terror.
The game is played entirely with the keyboard. You can pick up, examine and use items, as well as talk to the people that you will find. It is a very standard adventure game and there isn't any sequence that changes things up a bit, but the game focuses more on the story rather than gameplay, and the latter works more than well to move the story forward.
The puzzle are usually really intuitive and even non-fans of the genre won't have trouble figuring out what to do. Still, I would've liked a couple more thought-provoking puzzles than the ones that we got.
The voice acting is either going to ruin or make your experience. I personally really enjoyed it: the voice actors deliver their lines in a weird way that, surprisingly, works with the overall tone of the movie. I also really enjoyed the soundtrack that mixes quiet and eerie tracks with hard-rock songs.
There are many choices that you make in the game that will change the outcome, leading to one of three different endings. There are also 30 Steam achievements to unlock that will keep you completionists busy enough to play the game at least three times.
Overall,
is an incredible adventure game that delivers a compelling, eerie and romantic story with simple but effective gameplay, delightfully weird voice acting and good replayability. A must-buy for fans of great stories in video games!

The Long Dark is a fantastic game, wonderful landscapes, great enviroments, good gameplay, a very satisfying standalone single player sandbox survival game.

Tetris is one of my all time favorite games.  I keep calling myself a "Pro" even though i'm likely as fast as any average player of the game.  Tetris Ultimate is pretty much like every Tetris game you've played.  The game has a lot of modes in which can be unlocked by playing other modes.  I won't go to much into each and every mode cause most of them weren't that fun.  I'll say the ones I liked which included Marathon (beating 15 lvl's), Endless (...endless until you read the top), Sprint (get 40 lines).  Marathon can be a tad difficult but likely most people will beat it and Sprint is pretty simple cause there is no level increase.
The other modes for me were pretty difficult however if I give the game more time I will probably be able to play them a lot better.  Anyways the game is fun but extremely flawed and as big fan of the Tetris series this is the biggest downfall.  I would love to give this game a good review however as broken as it is there is just no way I can do that.
At this current time the biggest issue is the game crashes.  To solve this issue when the game starts up run Marathon mode and close it and start a new mode.  That pretty much solves the issue even though the game still tends to crash at random times.  Luckily for me the game has never crashed during game play its usually right before a match or when you choose to close the game.
The next big flaw is the multiplayer which is a big flaw and of course will make people quite upset.  For me I have family that will likely enjoy playing with me and that would be great if we could all sit down with controllers in our hands and play together... But of course that won't work unless one person is using a keyboard cause if you set the games main control method for player 1 to controller none of the other controllers will respond for input methods for more players.
That is a big flaw and I would really love to give more of good review for this game but at the moment I can't.  There is online multiplayer but cause of the issues this game has people are likely not wanting to play this game.  Maybe its the price which at this time I see balancing from $14 to $19 on Steam.  So if your a big online multiplayer fan you'll probably end up playing Tetris Friends which is free.  I haven't been able to connect to anybody on Tetris Ultimate yet.
People have been trying to contact Ubisoft about the issues I have explained.  I seen in the discussion for the game from Ubisoft in the community tells you ways to fix the game.  That is great that they do this however its not exactly methods that would fix the game and almost feels like they don't plan on updating the game so its a "we'll just leave this here and maybe this will help".
Anyways Ubisoft were waiting for you at this moment in time yes you'll see me playing this game off and on for its single player modes but I just can't recommend this to anyone who isn't advanced enough to solve the issues this game has.  I also can't recommend it if multiplayer mode is broken considering its something I would enjoy to do with family.

I've never written a review on steam before but felt that I had to after seeing the recent negative reviews here. This game is not dead or abandoned and although development is slow, the devs communicate their progress extremely well via a weekly newsletter or directly on their website.
Given the scope and depth of this excellent game, and the small size of the team working on it, it is of no surprise that the development takes time. However there is always something new and interesting to read about in their weekly updates, and regular content added to the beta build (unstable).
Some examples of current work in progress include:
Maps for players ingame
Vehicles
New animation system
Blood splatter
Identifiable clothing
Dials for cooking/radio/microwave
New town/areas
Lots more multiplayer server tools
And this is all mentioned in just one of their weekly updates.
Obviously this will take time to streamline and test and get into the stable build, but given that this is the most in-depth zombie game out there, I for one am prepared to wait however long it takes. Even if it takes another five years I will happily still be playing this superb zombie apocalypse simulation, watching it grow ever more realistic (if that can be said about a zombie game) and scaring myself to death!

I've found myself so immersed in the setting many times that I have to mentally step back and remember I'm playing a game.
- Immersive, well-designed world with developing storyline and random finds
- Early access, so a lot can still happen (which takes time)
- Complex building/crafting/cooking systems -- Build your survival base, or fortify existing structures. New metalworking has been added for increased defensive structures. Count your calories to maintain a healty diet in a dying world. (:
- Character specialization -- Be a chef, lumberjack, thief, or more! Varying attribute points are given to really tweak your character's performance.
- Clunky combat -- Anything other than melee is questionable to me with low skills, and even that sometimes gets odd. (*see footnote for expansion on this)
- I personally don't find the UI to be a nuisance, but I can understand players disliking it.
- Early access, so a lot can still happen (which takes time)
- Early access, so a lot can still happen (which takes time, and has). This is what holds up a lot of people from enjoying what you have, and instead focusing on what you don't have. Early development is going to be a rollercoaster, and things will get halted for reasons that won't always get explained clearly if at all. You have to understand this if you wish to assist in early development. I believe in this title, and I believe it could grow to be a massively entertaining experience for a lot of people.
- There is a slight lack-of-life to the world (no pun intended). No abandoned vehicles littering the roads, not much in the way of saying "there was an outbreak and panic ensued" other than TV or radio broadcasts during initial infection. Devs are working on introducing more world-clutter like this, but more important features take the front seat.
I could write an even longer post and say so much more but you should really just experience it for yourself.

Oh, and he then kidnaps your daughter, and in order to rescue her, you go along for the ride to his old fortress... where you discover the true history of his past... and the tragic last day he remembers.
The plot is engaging, the music atmospheric, the minigames fun, and the HO scenes challenging.

Still, it is worth the price.

The best way I can describe this game is "decent, but somewhat shallow." The mechs are cool enough, and the basic combat works nicely, but the whole thing comes off as just a little too linear and a little too scripted.
In a certain sense, I think the title suffers because it can manage to evoke shades of the "Armored Core" series. In doing so, it whets your appetite for things that just aren't going to be delivered. "Armored Core" had extensive customization, lots of opportunities for free-form movement in the environments, and pretty deep combat. "Front Mission Evolved," on the other hand, has much more limited customization, environments that are often rather constrained, and relatively simplistic battle.
This game works well enough as a "my first Armored Core" sort of experience, but it could have been more than it is.

Front Mission Devolved. A series best known for excellent turn-based tactical combat becomes a cheap third persion shooter. FME is of prime interest to those familiar with the series, its main target audience however are likely annoyed and disappointed that their favourite turn-based strategy game with mechs in it has become a linear smash, shoot and collect exercise, now featuring cringe-inducing villains and OTT dialogue. Gameplay is reminiscent of the early Armored Core games - in a stripped-out kind of way and there's a lot of mech customization on offer, but the combination of linear maps, bad squad AI, annoying bossfights and poorly designed on-foot sections ensure that Front Mission Evolved provided more annoyance than enjoyment.
AWESOME GAME FOR MECH WARFARE!

A lot of people seemed to give a negative recommendation simply because this wasn't exactly like all the other FM games, which are traditionally RPG/Strategy wherein you move your wanzer on a grid system, and spend points in order to attack the enemy every turn.  This is nothing like that, it's a third person shooter all the way, but as long as you realize that going in then there is really nothing to complain about.
As a shooter it's your standard fare.  Nothing special, nothing terrible.  As a FM game it has all the wanzers and customization you are used to (Grapple, Whisk, Husky, all the chassis make an appearance) with full ability to change colour, matte, decals, weapons, backpacks, battle skills etc.
The story is what you would expect from a FM game, a political intrigue about war, double crosses,  red herrings and military fiascos all with a plot about a young man trying to avenge the death of his father.  Is his father really dead, did the OCU and Da Han Zhong really start the war?  What is going on?  It's all your classic FM storyline which is paired with some well done cut scenes.
If you loved the previous FM games, and I'm sure many of you are fanatics about FM 3 and FM 4, and you don't mind taking direct control of the wanzer instead of having the strategy element, then you won't be let down.  If not, then fire up FM 3 and have Kazuki take on Lukav one more time, or guide Darril and Renges through South America and lead a revolution in FM 4.
All in all, for a FM fan, it's well worth the $10 as long as you know what you are getting going in.

Pick it up on sale and enjoy a decent enough Mech Shooter.

The Devil has wronged us and darn skippy we're gonna kick his keister back into hades.
Anyways Cuphead's a wonderful game, especially if you're into the run and gun genre as a whole. Every boss encounter is unique and beautiful, every level is a joy to experience and run through, there is never a dull or low moment in this game. Combine that high energy with a rocking jazzy soundtrack and you've got something great.
Cuphead's biggest strength comes from the fact that since 90% of the game is boss fights, the bosses are not only unique, but actually not that long to defeat. There's no moment in the game where you meet a boss and then think "for the next ten minutes I'm going to be picking away at this guy", every boss in the game can be beaten under three minutes. Most of them about a minute and a half. However that's not going to matter because until you learn the patterns for every boss you'll be spending at least fifteen minutes just learning what they can do at each phase, dying in between. But death is fine because after all the brawling you do, you'll be back to that point in a minute anyways. Every fight is constantly engaging with its own unique strategy. Though typically it's Charge Shot until dead (until they nerf it at which point we should see other interesting strategies pop out).
Even cooler is the fact that you don't need to beat every boss in regular (normal) mode, 95% of the game can be played and beaten in simple (easy) mode. Simple mode reduces the boss fight by one stage while reducing the impact of some attacks and removing some others. This is a mode for those who just want to play Cuphead to get a basic experience of it. Beating a boss in simple mode will give you a great feeling of what to expect in regular when all the holds are unbarred. And in order to finish Cuphead fully you'll have to beat EVERYTHING in regular mode. After that you unlock Expert mode which gives each boss stage more life and mixes up the fights ever so slightly. The difference is enough to be instantly noticible while pretty dang fair. At least most of the time.
Cuphead is wonderful, but it ain't perfect. A lot of the time your failures will be pointed out to you as "well buddy, you tried, but you need to get gud" and you'll notice something you can try next time. However, along the way the game will just decide that fudge you, time to die. Without spoiling anything, one boss has objects constantly and randomly falling from the ceiling. No matter the difficulty, they fall pretty quickly and can be hard to dodge depending on where you are with no indicator other than the fact that there's something about to fall on you. So if you're jumping into the air, and you're close to the ceiling, you could just jump into one of these presents and take one of your limited health points. Another boss randomly freezes you, which isn't a problem except that a massive amount of projectiles are spit out at random and there's about a quarter of a second before you're frozen and you'll be frozen for at least two seconds. And another boss has a hitbox large enough to accidentally protect weak killable annoying enemies just above it, meaning that you could jump into their swoop patterns despite your best attempts to ward them away. What I'm getting at is that most of the time you can predict and improve but there's 20% luck in there too and certain bosses are going to give you trouble no matter what.
Despite these things, Cuphead is a fun balanced experience for all skill levels. But you will need to become skillful as this is not an easy game. It's also not really "hard" either, it's difficult for sure, but on a scale of 1 to hard, this is a do-able and not really that frustrating. The frustrating unfairness will shine most in Expert mode but only on a few bosses, otherwise you'll be slowly improving and kicking lots of debetor butt in no time. Given Cuphead is a wonderful game and cheap to boot, it's a high recommendation. Just note that you will be struggling, but not too much.

Dungeon of the Endless is a mix of exploration, ressource management and tower defense with RPG elements. You chose two characters which have crashed into this underground complex, and have to get to the surface by finding an exit on each floor.
Each floor needs to be explored, essential rooms powered and defended against creatures. Once the floor exit is found, one of your team has to carry the crystal to the exit (slowing him/her down), while the rest tries to defend. Powered rooms spawn no enemies, so chose wisely before attempting the escape.
You have essentially four ressources: Industry (let's you build stuff), Food (let's you level up or heal characters), Science (lets you research stuff) and Dust (it lets you power rooms). Modules you build can generate more of a ressource every turn, but have to be defended if in vulnerable spots.
On the way up you can add two more characters you come across to your group. They can then be equipped with gear, which you either find or buy at the merchant, and which also randomly spawns on each floor. There are a total of 12 levels, all procedurally generated.
It's sort of a fresh feeling gameplay experience: a mix between round based (preparation phase) and real time (combat). You can however pause the game at any time and still issue commands (or heal) during it.

After I finished playing
(TCL) last year, I was eagerly looking for more games that carried on the same style. I came across
, a game released in 2009 and created by the same guys. I played it a little bit - never finished it though - and was definitely intrigued by it. When I found out that the developers were working on a remake, I felt like the happiest person alive. A 'new' game that would show why
got the attention it deserved. The biggest question is now ofcourse: was the remake of R. Michalski's first game what we hoped for, or was it perhaps a downfall too?
Meet Joe and Ivy Davis, a couple that has been struggling with their marriage for a long time due to Ivy's eating disorder. In order to try and save it, they decide to go on a trip to "Quiet Haven Hotel". Things don't really go as Joe had hoped, but as stubborn as he is, tries to keep fighting for Ivy. After all, he is supposed to love her .... Right?
Just like in TCL, the gameplay exists out of two major elements: progressing the story via dialogue and exploring the area to do various puzzles and actions. Being a character driven game, there is quite a lot of dialogue to be found, but luckily, the conversations never felt uninteresting. I was also quite surprised with the amount of different replies that you can give. You can behave like the sweet and understanding husband, or like one that is totally fed up with the whole situation. Furthermore, if the game's madness wasn't already enough for you, there's also that spoon of humour that they threw into the mix - it's rather amusing.
Being not a big puzzle solver myself, I was pleased to see that this game focused a little bit more on story progression. The puzzles that were present, never felt too difficult or frustrating. In fact, most of them are pretty straight forward. All in all, they are really fun to solve/do. Lastly, both of those elements (dialogue + puzzles) alternated often enough to keep the game fun and fluent: I never felt like either of them went on for too long or became tedious.
Personally, I am someone who plays through heavily story-based games (mostly) only once, but for those who so desire: there are multiple endings! So try to forget all about this game and maybe replay it within a couple of months. Or, if you just want to try out all the different dialogue options/hunt down the achievements, you can do that. Just make sure to save often enough or make use of the quick-save option.
The controls are very minimalistic: wandering around is done by the arrow keys. Inventory usage? Yep, you guessed it: arrow keys! All confirmation is done by pressing enter. Lastly, want to skip some dialogue during your second playthrough? The space key is your friend. The controls worked like they should, however ... 1 tiny little thing bugged me throughout my playthrough: at certain parts of the game, you have many items at the same time. Instead of having to press the right arrow key multiple times to get to the furthest item, it would've been useful if I could've just pressed the left arrow key to get to it.
As the original
was a little bit more colourful, this game presents itself in a 2d black-white style, with some sporadic colouring to be found. I like to think that the usage of black-white or colours reflect the characters' state of mind/certain events, but that is merely my personal interpretation. Whatever the developers tried to express, there is no doubt that it adds to the (creepy) atmosphere of the game. I also have to say that they did an exceptional job on the looks of the game. TCL already looked pretty good, but this game looks just gorgeous. Just about every area has been created with a lot of detail and care.
Along with the beautiful art comes the amazing soundtrack. I found the OST to be equally as good as the one in TCL. There was a lot of variety to be heard - from slow and creepy piano sounds to loud and heavy guitar riffs - that nailed setting the tone/atmosphere for the whole game. As it should be clear now, this is a game that makes you feel uncomfortable with almost everything that happens. Despite this feeling of unease, you just want to keep playing and discover how the story will unfold. These guys may not make bestselling games, but they are masters at setting an atmosphere so creepy, even at times when nothing's really happening: it's all in our head.
My biggest point of critique (regarding the sound section) concerns the voice acting (VA), especially during the prologue: as a prologue is meant to peek the player's first interest, I was rather disappointed. The VA during the rest of the game was ok though. A last point of critique goes to the different volume levels: there were certain scenes were one character was almost shouting in my ear, whilst the other was pretty much mumbling. Also, it seems like not every VA had a good quality mic, which is a shame. All in all, ok voice acting, but there is a lot of room for improvement.
I am glad to conclude that this game was not a 'downfall' at all. People who enjoyed TCL will not only play through a new story that they'll get to love, but are also in for quite a surprise later in the game! Fans of (psychological) horror are also in for quite a ride, but may miss some references: I definitely recommend playing TCL aswell. Even if you don't like horror, you still may want to give this game a try. I'm not a real fan of horror myself - on the contrary - I try to stay away from it as much as possible. Yet, I found a special joy and satisfaction in playing such a stylistic game that dares to embrace such confrontational subjects.

The Cat Lady was my game of the year back in 2014 (even though it came out in 2012) and It's still one of the best games I've ever played story wise. So the expectations I had for this game were huge. This review will be filled with comparisons between these two games so if you haven't played The Cat Lady and are reading this review, just stop here and buy both of these games. And note that I did not play the 2009 original of Downfall because I didn't know it existed until I already heard they were working on a remake, so I wanted to save myself for this one.
Did this game live up to my expectations? Both yes and no. Don't get me wrong, this is an awesome game and I highly recommend it to players that are into these kind of games. However, one reason that this game somewhat didn't live up to my expectations might be because it's a remake of an older game. I wanted this game to surpass The Cat lady which it didn't even come close to. The Cat Lady left me with a great satisfaction and a feeling for closure when I finally beat it (on all endings). This game did not give me that feeling, it gave more of a Telltale games ending, leaving you with a cliffhanger (at least with the first ending I got). Some might love these kind of endings and that's great for them. And some might argue that The Cat Lady is the sequel so it's not really a cliffhanger. This doesn't explain Joe's "cameos" in The Cat Lady though, as far as I know. There are some loose ends in this game that I hung up on and I'm not really a fan of games and movies where you have to interpret your own story or ending.
The second thing that made me a little disappointed was how short this game is compared to The Cat Lady. And yet again, I know that this is a remake and I won't argue against that. The Cat Lady took me around 15-20 hours to fully complete with all endings and 100% achievements (2 of the runs were with the help of a walk-through on YouTube). I completed this game in under 5 hours with 50% of the achievements. I don't see myself sitting for another 10+ hours getting the rest of the achievements and endings since this game was much more simpler than The Cat Lady (didn't get stuck more than a few minutes in this one while it could take me hours to figure out some parts in The Cat Lady).
Last but not least I have to touch on the subject regarding the voice acting. This is something I pointed out as the biggest flaw in my review of The Cat Lady and sadly it wasn't improving in this game. I know, I know, this is a small budget indie game, and so was The Cat Lady but I just can't take some parts in these games seriously due to the lack of emotions from the actors (not all of them though). I always get the image in my head of a person sitting in front of their computer reading of a script with zero emotion and effort when that said character in on screen, and that kills a lot of the mysterious atmosphere in these two games.
Enough of my bashing and rambling. I do still recommend this game and it's still one of the best horror/adventure games I've played in the past years and I would like to thank the developer who has given us these two great games. As a Cat Lady fanatic, I still hold that game highly over this one. I might edit this review in the near future after I'm done with my second play through. That's what I love about these games, they have a really high replay value.
TL; DR: Do you like The Cat Lady? If not, don't bother with this one, otherwise buy this game ASAP. Haven't played either of them? Look up short clips of either game on YouTube (the trailers don't seem to convince people since a lot of negative comments on these games are people not understanding the actual gameplay) and buy both of them. It's not a game for everyone though due to its very dark and twisted story.

I sit here in my desk chair, 3am on a cold Scottish morn. Listening to the gentle hum of my PC as I watch my little hillside hamlet of Edoras expand, 4 houses, a public feasting building, a guard barracks, a blacksmith and a completly filled food storehouse. Every little hearther is happy, at peace and happy in life as we press further into the hillside, ever expanding, handing out food to passing merchants - we have plenty- in exchange for fancy chairs and rustic fire pits for the long houses. We gather to eat and jest, then sleep in simple beds with roaring fires to keep us warm.
This is simple. Peaceful. This is Edoras.
Ok, I'll be truthful, i was expecting a quick hour or so to get into it, set up farms, housing... basic stuff then just steam roll it for a half hour then refund it cause i wasn't enjoying it.
But no, Stonehearth has this... charm to it that i just can't pinpoint. Maybe it's the building system - you have a few preset designs and the rest you can build using a fairly simple but effective system of drag selections and semi voxel based building -, maybe it's the constant strive to better your town and lure more hearthers (little voxelly pixelly villagers) into your town for workers.
Maybe you just enjoy the sense of wonder of seeing your town flourish by your hand.
Stonehearth is probably already worthy of a release, i don't even begrudge them £18.99 because the game is truly extremely fun.
BUT
One problem is... The AI... the hearthers are a little... single minded, monkey see, monkey do sort of thing. Like place desings for a house... they start building. Good. Place designs for another hosue and a... idk, a storehouse, and sometimes theyll  all flock to build the storehouse and begin construction. So that house you placed first unless you reinstate the build order, will become last priority. Not bad as such, just a little... irritating seeing half built buildings (storehouse and blacksmith in my village) being used and slept in with no roof, half a wall missing, and no door.. :p
Personal peeve and i'm sure others will feel the same way...

The Devil has wronged us and darn skippy we're gonna kick his keister back into hades.
Anyways Cuphead's a wonderful game, especially if you're into the run and gun genre as a whole. Every boss encounter is unique and beautiful, every level is a joy to experience and run through, there is never a dull or low moment in this game. Combine that high energy with a rocking jazzy soundtrack and you've got something great.
Cuphead's biggest strength comes from the fact that since 90% of the game is boss fights, the bosses are not only unique, but actually not that long to defeat. There's no moment in the game where you meet a boss and then think "for the next ten minutes I'm going to be picking away at this guy", every boss in the game can be beaten under three minutes. Most of them about a minute and a half. However that's not going to matter because until you learn the patterns for every boss you'll be spending at least fifteen minutes just learning what they can do at each phase, dying in between. But death is fine because after all the brawling you do, you'll be back to that point in a minute anyways. Every fight is constantly engaging with its own unique strategy. Though typically it's Charge Shot until dead (until they nerf it at which point we should see other interesting strategies pop out).
Even cooler is the fact that you don't need to beat every boss in regular (normal) mode, 95% of the game can be played and beaten in simple (easy) mode. Simple mode reduces the boss fight by one stage while reducing the impact of some attacks and removing some others. This is a mode for those who just want to play Cuphead to get a basic experience of it. Beating a boss in simple mode will give you a great feeling of what to expect in regular when all the holds are unbarred. And in order to finish Cuphead fully you'll have to beat EVERYTHING in regular mode. After that you unlock Expert mode which gives each boss stage more life and mixes up the fights ever so slightly. The difference is enough to be instantly noticible while pretty dang fair. At least most of the time.
Cuphead is wonderful, but it ain't perfect. A lot of the time your failures will be pointed out to you as "well buddy, you tried, but you need to get gud" and you'll notice something you can try next time. However, along the way the game will just decide that fudge you, time to die. Without spoiling anything, one boss has objects constantly and randomly falling from the ceiling. No matter the difficulty, they fall pretty quickly and can be hard to dodge depending on where you are with no indicator other than the fact that there's something about to fall on you. So if you're jumping into the air, and you're close to the ceiling, you could just jump into one of these presents and take one of your limited health points. Another boss randomly freezes you, which isn't a problem except that a massive amount of projectiles are spit out at random and there's about a quarter of a second before you're frozen and you'll be frozen for at least two seconds. And another boss has a hitbox large enough to accidentally protect weak killable annoying enemies just above it, meaning that you could jump into their swoop patterns despite your best attempts to ward them away. What I'm getting at is that most of the time you can predict and improve but there's 20% luck in there too and certain bosses are going to give you trouble no matter what.
Despite these things, Cuphead is a fun balanced experience for all skill levels. But you will need to become skillful as this is not an easy game. It's also not really "hard" either, it's difficult for sure, but on a scale of 1 to hard, this is a do-able and not really that frustrating. The frustrating unfairness will shine most in Expert mode but only on a few bosses, otherwise you'll be slowly improving and kicking lots of debetor butt in no time. Given Cuphead is a wonderful game and cheap to boot, it's a high recommendation. Just note that you will be struggling, but not too much.

First and foremost - I would like to really thank steam for FREE WEEKENDs!
And, for that - it made me realized that this game is actually....boring!  After 2 hours clocked into the game - finishing the tutorial as the monster and the assault and played some quick games, I've basically given up.
The concept was interesting - yet poorly executed.  Gameplay - this looks like a concept ripped out from other famous games out there - Left 4 Dead (Special Infected like the Tank against the other 4 survivors), Team Fortress 2 (where the 4 human players are of different classes), Diablo  (if you're playing as the monster it's like hack and slash and pick up the loot but in this case - EAT).  But for me, this feels like an overblown - PAC-MAN!!!  Being a monster at level 1 and 2 your are almost utterly worthless from the 4 human hunters so you must....RUN AWAY....chomp and at some point eat a power pellet (level up by evolving).  Then at level 3 you can now chase the other 4.  Where you deal each other damage until your armor goes down (Power-pellet ran out) and then you run-away again.  Chomping on those power pellets...errr...wildlife until you grow your armor back.  Then go after them again.  Rinse and repeat.  Being one of the 4 human hunters I felt a bit more fun, but it's more like Team Fortress 2 with a bit more jazz.
I can understand some reviewers' point of no one choosing to be the monster in this game.  It's utterly boring.  The human players are more than 20 times smaller than you.  You can't see their faces, it's like hacking some rag doll around but with overblown cheesy weapons.  Not like being the "Tank" in Left 4 Dead where you can still see the brutality of plummetting your adversary to the ground and smashing their faces and enjoying every bit of it.
To be honest - this game would rather make me play Team Fortress 2 and Left 4 Dead 2 again - I've played both throughout these years and enjoyed them.  And I won't mind playing them again with my friends.  Will I play this game again even if my friends bought this? - Yes, as a human player.  But we'll all just be standing there staring at the wall - since no one would want to play as the monster.

I was a huge fan of both The Cat Lady and the original Downfall, especially in how they fit together and the world that was created. When I heard Downfall was being remade I was super psyched, and now it's finally out! Just finished my first runthrough, and I'm so pleased with this new version.
Good
-Voice acting! A little awkward in some places, but generally good. Shoutout to Chiseleya especially! Also a few familiar voices show up, and it was lovely to hear them.
-Clearer, more streamlined plot, including integration with TCL.
-The least intuitive puzzles/least fun segments of the original Downfall were removed or altered.
-Even though I knew the plot of the game and generally what was coming, there were surprises and some moments were still genuinely scary.
-TCL lovers will be extra, unexpectly pleased in the latter portion of the game.
Bad
-Short! I finished in about five hours I think, but I also generally knew how to solve the puzzles/where to progress the plot from the original Downfall so it may be longer for others.
-Answers a lot of previous questions about integration with TCL, but raises some new confusing ones. Maybe it'll make more sense the next play, though.
-A few classic awesome elements of the original Downfall ended up scrapped or altered.
-The plot might be a little TOO in your face and easy to understand now.
In general, I absolutely loved it and I'm looking forward to some more playthroughs. I'm definitely not disappointed with this remake, and even better it's different enough from the original that there's still replayability for both versions. Absolutely awesome.

This game is a gem, and it should be looked at as such.
The gameplay is phenomenal, but remember this is just my opinion. The experience is heightened with headphones to really pull you in to the world, but without it still remains a tense and exciting environment. The subtle fade of the smooth atmospheric music which dynamically changes with your setting really helps, be it surrounded by deadly zeds and hearing frantic violins or on a roof cooking over a campfire to a soft piano. I've found myself so immersed in the setting many times that I have to mentally step back and remember I'm playing a game.
- Immersive, well-designed world with developing storyline and random finds
- Early access, so a lot can still happen (which takes time)
- Complex building/crafting/cooking systems -- Build your survival base, or fortify existing structures. New metalworking has been added for increased defensive structures. Count your calories to maintain a healty diet in a dying world. (:
- Character specialization -- Be a chef, lumberjack, thief, or more! Varying attribute points are given to really tweak your character's performance.
- Clunky combat -- Anything other than melee is questionable to me with low skills, and even that sometimes gets odd. (*see footnote for expansion on this)
- I personally don't find the UI to be a nuisance, but I can understand players disliking it.
- Early access, so a lot can still happen (which takes time)
- Early access, so a lot can still happen (which takes time, and has). This is what holds up a lot of people from enjoying what you have, and instead focusing on what you don't have. Early development is going to be a rollercoaster, and things will get halted for reasons that won't always get explained clearly if at all. You have to understand this if you wish to assist in early development. I believe in this title, and I believe it could grow to be a massively entertaining experience for a lot of people.
- There is a slight lack-of-life to the world (no pun intended). No abandoned vehicles littering the roads, not much in the way of saying "there was an outbreak and panic ensued" other than TV or radio broadcasts during initial infection. Devs are working on introducing more world-clutter like this, but more important features take the front seat.

Perfecting a formula is a noble goal, but the most important aspect of a great game is the fun factor. Not every system and challenge has to be tweaked just right, they have to be fun to work through. Dungeonmans gets that, and perhaps gets it better than almost any other roguelike out there. I started my adventures skeptical of the traditional mechanics and limited skills and sudden difficulty spikes, and soon found myself not wanting to stop. It doesn’t all fit together perfectly, but it fits together in a ridiculously fun way that I can’t seem to quit.
Guess what a dungeonmans is? It’s a mans that raids dungeons, of course! You’re responsible for an entire academy of aspiring dungeonmans, in fact, playing as their newest graduate on a quest to defeat some vague evil vaguely off to the southeast. Your journeys across the procedural world and into the procedural dungeons will yield loot for your mans and artifacts for your academy, increasing the former’s odds of survival and the latter’s capacity to aid future dungeonmans when your current one inevitably expires. And perhaps by building up the academy to legendary stature, you will one day cultivate a mans great enough to raid that final dungeon.
At the core of Dungeonmans is a wholly traditional turn-based roguelike, inspired by the ASCII deathtraps of yore. You scoot your mans across a grid of dungeon tiles, bumping into foes to defeat them and hoovering up the loot that drops. In place of letters and numbers are lovingly-rendered sprites of burly men, gooey slimes, and piles of coin. You’ll never misunderstand what you’re facing thanks to the detailed art and striking particle effects that highlight bosses and add real weight to the skills being thrown around. Screen shakes and massive explosions give Dungeonmans far more life than any game of NetHack you’ve played.
Lively too are the dialogues and item descriptions you’ll find no shortage of in your travels. As the name suggests, Dungeonmans takes a tongue-in-cheek approach to traditional dungeon diving on every level. Your foes include gelatinous geometry, bees that literally practice carpentry, giant pangolins, and cockney hooligans. Equipment is crafted from the finest Burlylium and Crushonium, yielding enchanted beatsticks and gladiator skirts. And every line spoken by you or anyone in the game is dripping with sarcasm and wit. It’s the kin of humor that could grate over time, but is smartly relegated to item descriptions and dialogues between dungeon runs, never overpowering the core gameplay.
What does impinge on the gameplay are some of the unpleasant holdovers of the genre. Roguelikes are tricky things to balance, especially coming from its dark and brutal originators. The top killer of your dungeonmans will no doubt be difficulty spikes, usually champion monsters far beefier and deadlier than the chaff you’ll cut through to reach them. Those with elemental attacks are the worst, because you probably won’t be paying much attention to resistances (or really know how to raise them starting out). The game certainly tries to warn you with general difficulty levels posted for areas of the world, combat log observations about powerful enemies, and glowing auras singling out bosses. But you’re still not going to know how you stack up until you go toe-to-toe, and by then it can easily be too late for your poor mans.
There are other annoyances to single out, like the item ID system that really just wastes your time (complete with an enemy that can UN-ID your items!) or the occasionally lengthy animations that break up the flow of turn-based combat. But despite these issues, I can barely stop myself from playing long enough to get angry about them. Even when I die after hours on a particular mans, I find myself immediately considering my next character. And that’s because what Dungeonmans does right is boil down roguelike combat to only the best parts, and layer loads of rewards over them. The skill system is limited in a smart way, leaving you just the core skills and passives you want for your style of mans. Combat can pass in a flash, enemies drop loads of loot, and the visual effects are lush and satisfying.
Then when the last foe falls and the blood pool on the cold dungeon floor, you haul your loot back to the academy and set about building the next generation of dungeonmans. Books, artifacts, and equipment can be donated to supply later characters. Gear can be melted down to make upgrades for current or future mans. Combat stats are tracked for the many enemy types in the game. And Proofs of Stremf persist between characters, allowing new mans to start with greatly improved stats. You can also upgrade towns you come across to access better shop items, or track down the final resting places of your previous mans for significant bonuses.
Above all, Dungeonmans is a game that wants to be played at your pace. The design of the random overworld gives you general difficulties for areas, and if a dungeon feels to hard you can always escape and shake down easier ones for better loot and more XP. Different dungeon and encounter types also offer different rewards so you can focus on developing however you want. And the overworld persists between characters so you don’t have to keep re-exploring, although you can always re-generate the world while keeping your academy if you’re so inclined. Any complaints about the game pale in light of how solid the core design is and how robust the progression can be. I expect to be dungeon diving with my mans for quite some time, with ever more to see and crush as the hours pass in a happy daze.

You pretty much try to get out of a dungeon your escape pod crashed deep into, floor by floor, trying to protect core/powergenerator of your escape pod. Very unique mix of tower defence, resource management, turn/realtime-based-strategy and RPG elements with character/hero progression.
Resources are your typical Industry, Research, Food and Dust like in other "Endless" games. Dust powers up rooms to prevent monsters from spawning(and powers up your modules), which can become very tricky and very tactical couple of floors forwards. Food is used to heal or level up your heroes, only latter once you figure out how to do things right. With industry you build modules to powered up rooms (minor defensive turrets/buff modules or specific-role main modules which do specific things). With research, you unlock new modules.
When you open door to new room, it counts as end turn kind of deal where you have chance of monsters spawning to (opened) rooms without power. Later down the line there are chance of it becoming even trickier with monsters everywhere. You'll see if you play ;)
Game also offers good deal of replayability with different kinds of pods that offer different kinds of starting situations/setups, one of them being drill pod which is endless mode - survive as many floors as possible.
Hero gear there are somewhat, but after succesfull replay or two, you've probably seen it all.

Nope. I missed one. Or two. Couldn't tell. It's RNG, and RNG gods did now fully favour me that day in that case.
I do not like content locking. Especially when it forces you to go through same content which is heavily on mercy of RNG to begin with, only to experience that same content a bit different way.
But hey, I got to drill pod, which was easy enough.

Let me repeat this point - the game is BRUTAL in SP, and equally BRUTAL in MP, but at least there, you get to lose together with your friends.
I recommend this title, because it fantastic, and Amplitude Studios has just released a 3rd, that's right, count it.  1.. 2... 3... free dlc adding content.

This is a hidden object adventure game from Artifex Mundi, and honestly I could leave the review at that and walk away, because there is really only one game by Artifex Mundi. Sure, they tell different stories and the specifics are a bit different from game to game. But these count as new and different takes on the genre the same way you wearing a fake mustache and talking with a bad accent is actually a totally new person, because the games are so similar from one to the next that you are already likely to know how you’ll feel about every game in their catalogue after you’ve played the first. It’s like comparing different slices of bread from the same loaf, and however much you think you’re going to like this, you are probably right. This one happens to be pirate themed, but beyond that there really isn't a substantial amount of difference between this and their other titles.

The game is built around these hidden object scenes, which themselves are perfectly “fine” but that’s about as high praise as you can have for them. If you’ve ever done a hidden object puzzle before, you sort of already know what to expect. The game vomits a pile of cluttered garbage at your feet and then asks you to find it red ball of twine, three buttons, and a flask full of ketchup because it got drunk and can’t do it on its own. The objects themselves are decently hidden, so if all you need is a hidden object fix, the game certainly has that at least. The scenes are all kind of boring though, all the same sort of jumbled mess that works well for hiding objects but isn’t particularly interesting to look at. It just feels sort of charmless, like you’re digging around in some hoarder’s trash bin for a variety of ordinary objects that aren’t too interesting to look for.

There are a couple of other issues here, like the fact the game reuses almost every scene at least twice in what appears to be a cost saving effort. The scene is exactly the same except for the objects you found the first time removed. This feels tremendously lazy, particularly when there aren’t that many scenes to start with, and digging around the same scene a second time makes things significantly less interesting. They also don’t always do a great job telling you what to find and there are several instances where the description of what you're looking for is kind of vague. Then there are objects that require you to interact with the scene in some way, like using a rag to clean a dirty mirror so you can find the “clean mirror” object. It sounds interesting, but isn’t used too well because the mouse icon changes only over these sort of objects that have these interactions, basically giving their location away.
Additionally, you can actually abstain from doing any hidden object finding all together, because every single scene in the game can also be finished by playing a game of mahjong instead. Because if there is any reason to play a hidden object game, it’s for all the mahjong. I am not quite sure why this is even an option. Is there someone out there that was like “yeah, I really like hidden object games, but they would be better without all the hidden objects”? It would be like creating an FPS where all the enemies could also be killed by finishing a game of solitaire, and allowing the player to remove every single hidden object puzzle from the game seems like a pointless inclusion. No one is playing these for the riveting stories they put together using a pirate themed Madlibs book and a bottle of expired cough syrup. Now, you don’t have to do these so it isn’t really a problem, but it is a sort of baffling decision to even allow this in the game in the first place.

Outside of the hidden objects, the other primary aspect of the gameplay is a handful of puzzles to solve. Apparently our nefarious pirate friend here has never heard of a lock, because it seems like every single door on his ship and on this island is blocked by some sort of puzzle you need to solve in order to open it. Apparently he was terrified of five-year-olds with remedial puzzle solving skills breaking into his rooms and stealing his stuff, because there really isn’t another reason for these sorts of locks. The puzzles here range in quality from mind numbingly boring to kinda sorta okay, but there really aren’t any standouts. Almost all of these can be solved in less than a minute and there were only a couple in total that made me stop and think for even a moment. Not every puzzle needs to tickle your cortex, but it would be nice if there were at least a few that posed some sort of challenge.

The production values here are also notably bad, even considering the fact this is a budget hidden object title. The voice acting is laughably terrible, but at this point “laughably terrible voice acting” and “hidden object adventure game” just come together as a package deal. The visuals are just on the bottom edge of “meh”, at least until you get to a cutscene. For some reason, the visual quality drops from fairly standard to “oh no I’m going blind” almost immediately, and the cutscenes in this game look like you’re viewing them through that giant eyeglass mask at the optometrist with the setting put on the worst possible choice. Things are so blurry it is hard to even tell what is going on, and the production values in this game are just unacceptably awful.

Nightmares from the Deep: The Cursed Heart is yet another dull hidden object adventure game from Artifex Mundi, and at this point I’m beginning to suspect that is the only kind of hidden object game they make. I’m not even asking for that much here. A decent number of hidden object scenes that don’t reuse the same background, puzzles that take more than a couple seconds to solve, a story that doesn’t feel like it took eighth place in the middle school writing contest, and visuals that don’t make me feel like I’m losing my eyesight. This is a remarkably low bar, but Nightmares from the Deep sprints into it, trips over it, and crashes face first into a haunted pirate ship. This is perhaps marginally better than the other hidden object games I’ve played, but really only marginally so. Maybe if you’re obsessed with the genre you can overlook all these flaws, but there has to be better hidden object titles out there than this one. Right? RIGHT? Because if this is the epitome of hidden object games, the nightmare is even worse than I thought.

A truly faithful adaptation of the old classic...
BG:EE is exactly what I played over a decade ago, but shined-up a bit for modern hardware.
In addition to the classic Baldur's Gate, BG:EE includes Tales of the Sword Coast as well as some additional NPCs, character portraits, and voices.  Nothing Earth-shattering, but it adds a hint of novelty to an old classic.
BG:EE is also running on an updated engine with a couple nice new features, like the ability to highlight interact-able items.
Of course, it is still the same old game...  Which may turn off some modern gamers.  The graphics aren't terribly impressive.  Combat is a little on the slow and stilted side.  The AD&D 2nd Edition rules are feeling a little old and stiff.  And there's precious little in the way of quest guidance.
Still - if you enjoyed Baldur's Gate the first time around, you're sure to enjoy BG:EE.
